Nonetheless, practical applications of biodegradable supercapacitors are still hindered by the lack of suitable electrolytes and electrode materials.13-15 In terms of electrolytes, natural polymers such as gelatin are widely used in preparing gel electrolytes due to their excellent biocompatibility and degradability;16-20 however, their weak mechanical strength often limits the integral stability of the fabricated devices. Introducing carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) into the gelatin matrix could significantly enhance the mechanical properties of gelatin through a crosslinked double network structure. Additionally, the polar functional groups on CMC could facilitate ion transport by interacting with electrolyte ions, thus improving ionic conductivity.21-25 This synergistic strategy provides a promising approach for developing high-performance and fully degradable electrolytes. For electrode materials, conventional electrode materials, such as carbon-based materials, metals and their compounds, and conductive polymers, fail to offer excellent electrochemical performance, biocompatibility, and controllable biodegradability simultaneously.26-28 Recent studies have shown that molybdenum (Mo) based materials can undergo complete degradation in vivo, and its biocompatible degradation products could be excreted through renal pathways, which minimize long-term toxicity.29-31 For instance, a molybdenum disulphide (MoS2) nanosheet based flexible cathode for zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors delivers a high areal capacitance of 93.5 mF cm−2 and an open-circuit voltage of 1.3 V and also undergoes complete degradation within 60 days in simulated body fluid, demonstrating its potential for application in short-term implantable bioelectronic systems.10 As presented above, a biodegradable and flexible all-solid-state supercapacitor is therefore fabricated as follows. For electrolyte preparation, a biomimetic crosslinking strategy is employed to construct a composite hydrogel system composed of gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) and CMC. In this design, the methacrylate groups on GelMA undergo photo-crosslinking under UV irradiation to form a covalently bonded polymer network, while CMC is assembled into a physically crosslinked network through coordination with multivalent metal ions. The integration of two networks results in the formation of a dual-network GelMA/CMC hydrogel electrolyte with enhanced mechanical integrity and ionic conductivity. The photo-crosslinking of GelMA enhances mechanical robustness, while the flexible chains of CMC improve fracture toughness. Together, they endow the hydrogel with excellent mechanical strength, moisture stability and biodegradability. For the preparation of electrodes, binder-free, monolithic MoS2@rGO/Mo is developed using biocompatible Mo foil as the substrate. Nanocracks are introduced into Mo foil by electrochemical oxidation as defect-rich sites. Subsequently, MoS2 and reduced graphene oxide (rGO) nanosheets are vertically grown on the Mo surface through hydrothermal treatment. The incorporation of rGO improves the electronic conductivity of MoS2, while the vertical nanosheet architecture shortens ion diffusion paths. The resulting MoS2@rGO/Mo electrode avoids the use of polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) or other bio-incompatible binders during the assembly process and leaves no solid residue after degradation. It retains over 90% of its original capacitance after 100 bending cycles at 180°. Furthermore, the supercapacitor achieves a high energy density of 9.63 μW h cm−2 at a power density of 72.98 μW cm−2. Two identical devices connected in series and parallel could modulate voltage and current output, confirming the good expansibility of the supercapacitor. The degradation period of the device could be tailored from several days to weeks by adjusting the thickness of the biodegradable encapsulation layer. Both the gel electrolyte and the electrode materials undergo hydrolysis-based degradation to demonstrate the feasibility of this system as a biodegradable power source, which holds great potential in the applications of implantable devices.

Consequently, the specific surface area and porous structure are the main factors affecting the electrochemical performance of carbon-based electrodes [101], [103], [104]. Yang et al. [103] used starch as the raw material and employed Na2CO3 templating and KOH activation methods to prepare hierarchical porous carbon as supercapacitor electrodes. Electrochemical measurements demonstrated high capacitance (234F/g at 2A/g), excellent rate capability (212.6F/g at 20A/g), and good cycling stability (98 % of initial capacity after 1000 cycles). Wang et al. [104] successfully prepared high-porosity carbon nanofibers as supercapacitor electrodes by using a blend of polyacrylonitrile (PAN) and hydroxyalkylated starch (HAS) as precursors. The CNF-20 electrode (with 20 % HAS content) exhibited a high specific capacitance of 344F/g at 1.0A/g, and the resulting supercapacitor maintained a capacitance retention of around 99 % after thousands of cycles, indicating its high cycling durability. This demonstrates that the green and low-cost HAS can be used as a pore-forming agent to prepare porous carbon nanofibers and applied in supercapacitors. Cellulose possesses numerous unique advantages, such as renewability, good biocompatibility, and eco-friendliness. In supercapacitors, cellulose can be used as: (a) a lightweight mechanical substrate, providing flexibility and strength; (b) a coating material or a template for other carbon species; (c) a diaphragm between the electrodes; and (d) an electrolyte or medium [105]. Through pre-oxidation and carbonization treatment, they obtained biomass-based carbon fibers (CFs) with intact fibrous morphology, high surface area, excellent flexibility, and outstanding energy storage capability. CFs were successfully utilized to fabricate supercapacitors with high energy density and specific capacitance. This indicates that the introduction of H3PO4 can effectively reduce the energy consumption of the pre-oxidation process while improving the energy storage performance of supercapacitors. Lei et al. [107] synthesized porous, nitrogen-doped cellulose-based carbon aerogels with an interconnected honeycomb-like structure using a simple and environmentally friendly method. These cellulose-based carbon aerogels exhibited several desirable characteristics, and the supercapacitors prepared from them demonstrated high specific capacitance (160F/g), good charge/discharge rates, and excellent cycling stability. Zhai et al. [108] prepared internally structured aerogels from chitosan and zinc chloride using a microwave hydrothermal method, followed by high-temperature carbonization to obtain nitrogen self-doped carbon aerogels (Fig. 6d). Additionally, it served as an activator in the carbonization process, ensuring that the resulting carbon aerogel possesses a high specific surface area and an effective pore structure. NSCA-1000 (nitrogen self-doped carbon aerogel carbonized at 1000 °C) exhibited simple preparation, low production cost, environmental sustainability, and excellent electrochemical performance, making it an ideal electrode material for supercapacitors. At current densities of 1.0A/g and 10A/g, NSCA-1000 demonstrated specific capacitances of 249.4F/g and 164.9F/g, respectively. In symmetric dual-electrode supercapacitors, NSCA-1000 achieved energy density and power density values of 26.15Wh/kg and 0.95 kW/kg, respectively, at 1.0A/g.

1.  **Transient batteries** are defined as power sources that degrade after completing their intended function, leaving no harmful residues. They are designed to power implantable devices, wearables, and environmental sensors, fulfilling their role before safely disappearing through physical, chemical, enzymatic, or microbial processes [2][5][10][12].

2.  **Biodegradable polymers are utilized in their construction** in several key ways:
    *   **Solid/Gel Polymer Electrolytes:** Biopolymers (e.g., carrageenan, pectin, cellulose, starch, chitosan, guar gum-cellulose aerogel, GelMA/CMC hydrogels) are complexed with salts to form solid or gel electrolytes. This replaces liquid electrolytes (like PBS), enabling thinner, more compact, biocompatible devices while maintaining sufficient ionic conductivity. These electrolytes facilitate ion transport between electrodes and eventually biodegrade [1][5][8][13][15].
    *   **Electrode Materials (Active/Scaffold):** Polymers serve as the backbone for redox-active materials (e.g., PCL functionalized with TEMPO as a cathode) or as scaffolds/binders for inorganic electrode materials (e.g., MoS2@rGO on Mo foil, PDA/PPy composites on fibers). They provide structural integrity, conductivity pathways, and biodegradability to the electrodes [3][7][11][13][15].
    *   **Separators:** Biodegradable polymers like chitosan are used as separators to prevent short circuits between electrodes while allowing ion flow and eventually degrading [7][11].
    *   **Substrates/Encapsulation:** Polymers (including cellulose, silk, PLA, PCL) form flexible substrates, encapsulation layers, and structural components of the battery, contributing to its overall biodegradability and mechanical properties [4][10][12][13][15].
    *   **Packaging:** Biodegradable polymers (e.g., cellulose/polyester/silicon blends) are used for packaging the entire battery system [3].

Since the last century, plastic industry has developed so fast that plastic products have gained universal application in many fields. However, most of the plastic products are not biodegradable, and this causes serious environmental pollution. Therefore, developing biodegradable polymers is necessary and it is important to solve this problem. It is well known that aliphatic polyesters are the most promising polymers among the biodegradable plastics. Among aliphatic polyesters, poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) has relatively higher melting temperature and other excellent properties. However, the insufficient mechanical properties of PBS have prevented it from being used in diverse applications. Thus, various techniques, such as physical blending1-5 and copolymerization,6-11 have been explored to improve these weaknesses. Crosslinking is another effective method to improve the properties of PBS.12-20 Up to now, there are mainly two different ways to attain a three-dimensional network. One is irradiation by electron-beam or γ-ray,12-18 and the other is by thermal process.19, 20 Irradiation is an effective technique to induce crosslinking. Kamarudin et al.12 studied the crosslinking of PBS by electron-beam irradiation. They found that the crosslinking introduced by irradiation improved the melt strength of PBS effectively. As a result, the foams could be produced. Moreover, a series of studies have been done by the research group of Fumio Yoshii.15, 16, 18 They investigated the effects of polyfunctional monomer (PFM) and inorganic material on the gel formation during irradiation. The results demonstrated that the presence of PFM and inorganic material in PBS had positive influence on the gel formation. Besides, they studied irradiation of the composite synthesized by PBS and glass fiber. All the articles suggested that the heat stability or mechanical property of PBS was improved, and the materials were still biodegradable in enzymatic degradation or soil burial test. Nevertheless, the equipment investment for irradiation is large. Furthermore, to prevent pollution caused by γ-ray or electron beam, rigorous safeguarding is needed. As a result, it is difficult to apply irradiation on a large scale. In addition, degradation of polymer may also occur during irradiation.
Hympánova et al.42 implanted (1) electrospun ureidopyrimidinone polycarbonate (UPy-PC), (2) textile lightweight polypropylene (Restorelle) and (3) non-degradable polyurethane in ewes for 60 and 180 days. The UPy-PC implant completely disappeared after 180 days, which raised concern regarding its premature degradation. Restorelle and non-degradable PU showed good compatibility throughout the 6 months of implantation, but the long-term effect of the non-degradable polymers is unknown. Poly lactic acid (PLA) has poor mechanical properties and degrades too rapidly. Mangir et al. incorporated ascorbic acid (AA)43 and oestradiol44 which increased the ultimate tensile stress (UTS), strain, and yield modulus to about twice that of non-treated PLA. Despite the potential of both drugs, and the ability of PLA to serve as a scaffold throughout the tissue, the regeneration time is still unclear. Polymers have widely adjustable properties which are attractive to resolve the pelvic mesh-related problems. However, pelvic mesh materials with optimum advantages and minimum risk have yet to be found. Mangir et al.45 also stated that the mechanical properties of polymers are time-dependent and non-linear. Therefore, the prediction of long-term polymer behaviour in such a mechanically complex bio-environment is indeed difficult. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. In particular, polycaprolactone (PCL) has received considerable attention due to its excellent mechanical and structural properties, and tuneable degradation kinetics. Moreover, the non-immunogenicity of PCL, combined with the possibility of using it as an interporous scaffold material, has resulted in better tissue ingrowth [2-4]. The above-mentioned benefits, in addition to the inexpensive production routes of PCL, have encouraged many research groups to investigate its potential applications in numerous fields of tissue engineering [2, 5]. However, the bioactivity of the tissue-engineered constructs is threatened by the hydrophobic nature of PCL [4, 6-8]. In general, it is known that a moderate surface hydrophilicity allows for an increased adsorption of proteins without modifying their natural conformation. In turn, this increases the cell affinity towards the surface, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and cell proliferation [9, 10]. As a consequence, PCL hydrophobicity negatively impacts cell-material interactions [1]. In order to overcome this issue, surface modification is required. Several approaches have previously been investigated, including wet-chemical treatments, and ion beam, x-ray and gamma radiation. However, the wet-chemical treatment route generates large amounts of hazardous chemical waste and often impacts on bulk properties such as structural strength and elasticity, while most radiation methods can cause severe degradation of the polymer [11]. As an alternative, non-thermal plasma treatment has shown to be a promising method because it is highly versatile, only modifying the top few nanometer layers of the polymer without altering the bulk properties [4, 6, 12, 13]. By choosing an appropriate working gas, this treatment incorporates oxygen-containing functional groups, either directly or via post-oxidation [14]. These polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability and thus improve protein adsorption and cytocompatibility [7, 12]. Many studies have shown that plasma treatment of PCL performed at low pressure enhances the adhesion and proliferation of a wide variety of cell types [4, 8, 12, 15, 16]. As an alternative to low-pressure plasma treatments using expensive vacuum equipment, a few authors have reported that atmospheric pressure plasma treatment is also effective, giving rise to high cellular adhesion and proliferation [7, 17, 18]. Medium pressure plasma is rarely used to treat PCL, despite its potential to easily acquire a larger volume of plasma compared to atmospheric pressure plasma treatments, with relatively cost-effective pumping systems [19]. Therefore, our research group has previously used a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD), operating in different gases at medium pressure, in order to modify PCL surface properties. Both air and argon plasmas introduce oxygen-containing functionalities onto the PCL surface and thus increase its wettability, positively influencing the adhesion and the proliferation of human foreskin fibroblasts and mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts [3, 20]. Consequently, after sterilization, PCL should maintain the introduced surface properties that determine to a large extent the success of the implant. Despite the importance of the material properties, the impact of sterilization on the PCL structure and surface is largely overlooked in the literature, as the majority of studies solely focus on the microbial activity to check for the sterilization efficacy [23].
Biodegradable polymers are degraded into natural metabolites by simple hydrolysis or enzyme action under physiological conditions.1, 2 Compared with metal materials and nondegradable polymer materials, biodegradable polymers have the advantage of not requiring secondary surgery.3 In recent decades, polylactic acid,4 polycaprolactone,5 polyglycolic acid,6 and other absorbable polymer materials are increasingly favored by researchers.7, 8 Poly (1,3-trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC) is an absorbable, flexible, and amorphous elastomer.9 Unlike other aliphatic polyesters, PTMC is degraded by enzymatic surface erosion.10 It can achieve zero-order release of drugs.11 PTMC hydrolyzes relatively stable in water or buffers solution (pH = 1-13) in vitro.12 There are no acidic products in the degradation process and should not cause serious inflammation.13 PTMC has great potential in biomedical applications, such as drug delivery systems,14-16 soft tissue engineering,17, 18 vascular prostheses,19, 20 or nerve regenerative systems.21-23 However, linear PTMC has very low modulus and low tensile strength.24 The amorphous structure and lower glass transition temperature result in poor dimensional stability of PTMC, and it is prone to creep at room temperature.25 This limits any practical application of PTMC. Therefore, it is necessary to obtain a rubber-like biodegradable elastomer network through crosslinking. The crosslinking of PTMC can be performed through nonionizing radiation such as ultraviolet radiation,25 and ionizing irradiation such as gamma rays26 and electron beams.27 Irradiation technology has gradually become an important method in the study of polymer material modification due to its advantages such as environment friendly, simple operation, less damage to substrate and high accuracy. UV irradiation needs a double bond moiety in the polymer structure, PTMC containing photoinitiators and crosslinking aids can be exposed to ultraviolet light for photocrosslinking.28 However, the low energy of ultraviolet light can only excite particles, forming PTMC networks with low network density. In the absence of initiators, strong ionizing irradiation can cause chemical changes in the polymer structure by forming ions, free radicals, and excited states.9 Meanwhile, high-energy radiation can effectively destroy micro-organisms and viruses. Compared with other sterilization methods, ionizing radiation has a high sterilization efficiency for materials (such as porous scaffolds) whose sterilizers are difficult to penetrate. However, ion and electron beam radiation rapidly attenuate and deposit more energy on the sample surface, potentially causing damage.29 Irradiation with an electron beam causes an essential change in the hole of the scaffold, resulting in partial melting of the scaffold's surface.27 Thus, we chose gamma rays to prepare cross-linked PTMC networks. The crosslinking reaction is also dependent on conditions including irradiation atmosphere, irradiation dose, and temperature. The free radicals generated during the irradiation can react with nearby oxygen, leading to autocatalytic oxidative degradation.30 The compressed molded films were vacuum-sealed and irradiated at room temperature.
In the biomedical fields, replacing materials implanted into a human body with biodegradable polymers has the potential to reduce the burden on the human body. As the candidates for such biomedical materials, aliphatic polyesters such as poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) have been actively investigated [[29], [30], [31], [32], [33], [34], [35], [36]]. Due to their hydrolytically-degradable polymer backbones, such polyesters can degrade and be absorbed in the human body, preventing adverse effects on the human body and unwanted second surgery for the removal of the materials. For example, in the previous study, Lendlein et al. developed a helical stent with the original outer diameter of 3.45 mm composed of biodegradable PCL-based shape-memory polymers with self-expandable properties. Xue et al. also reported a degradable suture for wound closure, exhibiting good shrinkage behavior on animal skin at relatively high temperature [16,37]. Among the biodegradable polymers, PLA has attracted much attention, because PLA can be synthesized from renewable feed stocks, possessing biocompatibility, superior mechanical properties (Young's modulus: ∼1.5-2.0 GPa), and thermal properties (melting point: ∼170 °C) [38,39]. PLA have isomers, such as semi-crystalline poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), and amorphous poly(d,l-lactide) (PDLLA). It is also known that unique crystal morphology called stereocomplex crystals could form in the PLLA/PDLA blend [40,41]. In the stereocomplex polylactide (sc-PLA) crystals, the molecular chains of PLLA and PDLA were packed side by side, where the L-chains and the D-chains could generate strong interaction as compared with the interaction produced by identical PLA due to the van der Waals interaction between C-H⋯OC and CH3⋯OC. The resulting high-density crystalline sc-PLA possessed extremely higher melting point (∼230 °C) than PLLA and PDLA homopolymers (∼170 °C) [[42], [43], [44]] with high tensile strength and modulus [45]. For example, Tsuji et al. studied PLA films made by solution casting, and concluded that the mechanical strength of the sc-PLA film was approximately 60% higher than that of PLLA [46]. Li et al. also prepared a shape memory polymer by blending sc-PLA as crosslinks and PDLLA as switching segments, presenting dramatic shape recovery (∼100%) with the high tensile storage modulus (∼3.1 GPa) [47]. Additionally, Purnama et al. proposed a new concept to enhance the melt stability of sc-PLA macromolecules by introducing CL components as a soft fragment to accelerate the chain movement of PDLA fragments to interact with PLLA chains [48]. Controlling Ttrans of SMPs is extremely important for the biomedical applications of the SMPs. Ttrans must be above room temperature to maintain the temporary deformed shape of the SMPs for the usage of the materials at room temperature. The Ttrans between room temperature and body temperature could realize spontaneous shape recovery of SMPs when they are implanted into the body. If Ttrans is set above body temperature, the SMP can start shape recovery, e.g. by heating with external media [49]. Adjusting Ttrans of SMPs at various temperatures can be achieved by controlling Tg of the switching-segment polymers. Previously, it was reported that the random copolymerization was a convenient method to change the Tg of the polymers, determined by the ratio of the two different monomers in consideration of the Tg of the respective homopolymers (Tg,A and Tg,B) [50].

Biodegradable polymer blends and composites are used in applications such as biomedicine, packaging, and agriculture. Controlling the degradation rates of the overall material is essential and was achieved by biodegradable additives, both polymers, and fillers, as outlined below. There is much interest in polymer blends for tissue engineering, because of their adjustable mechanical properties and their ability to adjust the degradation rates to the regrowth of a specific tissue. For this application, a high control of biodegradation is important, e.g., when the speed of bone reconstruction completion is quicker than the time of bone scaffolds degradation to be more suitable for the repair of bone defects or for other tissue.[23, 24] Currently, often porous polymers are used in tissue engineering applications if the polymer matrix can be suitable as a scaffold for tissue growth and can serve as a provisional aid for the cell growth during the regeneration of the target tissue. The polymer can be implanted into the body via minimal operations using small equipment. A small cross-sectioned polymer can be intercalated into the body via a small incision through a catheter. When in the demanded anatomy, with the aid of the body heat, this can be deployed into a greater preordained shape.[23, 24] A promising biocompatible base polymer, of which the biodegradation can be controlled by blending, is PLA.[25] PLA has been used in various biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability in vivo. However, PLA's degradation rate is often too slow,[26] and was accelerated by blending with various polymers and will be discussed in this review. Biodegradable composites were, for example, used by Huang et al. for bone tissue engineering.[23] The authors prepared composites using fibers of nano-hydroxyapatite in a matrix of polymers with different degradation rates. Scaffolds demonstrated preferred structural integrity for constant growth of new bone, however, if scaffold biodegradation occurs too fast it causes a loss in cellular orientation out of a loss in adhesion or cell viability. The result of this study can help to simulate the dynamic microenvironment of biological processes. In another study, Alan et al. studied PLA scaffolds filled with conductive and magnetic fillers obtained by fused filament fabrication (3D printing).[27] It was shown that especially the PLA with conductive fillers (carbon fibers and graphene nanoplatelets) enhanced the bioactivity of the composites and accelerated its biodegradation. It was suggested that these materials could act as potential candidates for tissue engineering such as a scaffold for bone replacement and regeneration. Also, interesting research was reported by Liu et al.[28] they aimed at scaffold preparation using PGS/PCL blends, as the PGS alone would limit an application in tissue engineering because the time needed for its biodegradation is less than the time needed for cartilage regeneration. Thus, they blended PCL with PGS to adjust the time of biodegradation and enhance the mechanical strength of the final material.
Biodegradability of pristine polymer and IPN materials were evaluated by the solid burial tests [27]. The specimens (10 mm × 10 mm × 1 mm) were buried in the fertile soil with the distance of 10 cm. The places of burial were noted with the relative humidity around 60% for 30 days. Finally the specimens were taken out and treated with dry air to remove the sticky soil on the surfaces. The optical images of degraded pristine polymers and IPNs after 30 days of burial test were shown in Fig. 7 (a-f) and their weight loses were shown in Fig. 8. It is observed that the biodegradability of IPN polymers are superior to the pristine polymers and it is in-accordance with their weight loss results. It confirms the biodegradable resins accelerating the biodegradation of IPN polymers. It is an efficient method to construct biodegradable, functional and enhanced mechanical strength polymers, which can be used as ecofriendly and sustainable environmental applications. The blending of monomer styrene and methyl methacrylate with pristine resins derived from natural plant oils for the formation of IPNs is successfully employed. The IR and XRD spectra of IPNs show no evidence for the chemical bonding in the polymeric matrix and the polymer formation was mainly due to the interpenetration through the efficient blending. The optimized ratio of monomers with the pristine resins yields the polymeric sheets in the glass mold after curing. The as-prepared virgin and IPNs polymers show the enhanced mechanical and thermal properties and confirms the interpenetration of one or two pristine resins on the polymeric matrix which formed by the cross-linking of monomers. The IPN polymers exhibit the nature of biodegradability even though it was blended with the polymeric matrix. These classes of plant oils based pristine resins integrated with monomers for flexibility and transparency pave the fabrication of biocompatible protection for sustainable environmental applications.
Collectively, this set of data suggests that our IPNs form suitable environments for cell infiltration and remodeling. Additionally, even though SA was incorporated as an enzymatically degradable entity, the biomaterials seemed to remain intact up to 1 month following implantation, suggesting slow biodegradation. This could be attributed to the presence of poly(methyl methacrylate) segments within the polymer network, which are known to poorly degradable in vivo.15,75 Various strategies could be investigated to make these IPN constructs more prone to biodegradation.76 One strategy could be to use biodegradable PEG-based block copolymers (e.g., PEG-co-polyglycolic acid) which contain hydrolysable ester bonds.43,77 Lastly, signs of tissue remodeling were observed with host fibroblasts, de novo synthesis of collagen and early stages of angiogenesis (i.e., neovascularization) within the explanted constructs, indicating good biointegration.14 Therefore, these constructs have great potential for dermal tissue regeneration and wound healing applications.4,5,41,78 However, follow-up validation studies with relevant wound healing models are recommended.

Biodegradable and biocompatible polymers, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA),6 poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL),7 and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB),8-10 are widely used in the biomedical field. These plastic polymers are aliphatic polyesters that can be degraded by hydrolysis and their degradation products are non-toxic. Among the polymers, PCL is slowly degraded in about two to three years and has good flexibility and extensibility compared to the other polymers.7 On the other hand, PHB belongs to the family of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) that are entirely synthesized by microorganisms. PHB is a highly crystalline polymer, which is more brittle and difficult to process.8-11 The copolymers of PHB with poly(3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHV) or poly(3-hydroxyheptanoate) (PHH) may reduce the crystallinity and increase the toughness of PHB. Besides, the lower melting point allows the copolymers to be easily processed.12,13 The copolymers show better cytocompatibility than the pure PHB, with respect to fibroblasts,14 osteoblasts,14,15 bone marrow cells,16 and chondrocytes.17 PU also represents a category of shape memory polymers (e.g. DiAPLEX®, SMP Technologies Inc.).18 Shape memory polymers can be temporarily fixed under a certain condition and recovered to the original shape by temperature, moisture, water/solvent, ions, or pH changes.19 The shape memory effect usually arises from the molecular chain entanglement, crystalline domain, chemical crosslinking, or interpenetrated network.20-23 Thermoplastic PUs are generally elastic and do not possess shape memory. When the crystallinity of PUs increases, they may have shape memory behavior because of the increased fixation effect below Tg.22
Implants required for a limited time period, such as intended for tissue regeneration or drug release, are beneficially composed of degradable polymers so that after the required time the material is eliminated from the body.1 The majority of degradable polymers, such as polyesters, show a bulk degradation behavior,2, 3 i.e. the rate of diffusion of water participating in bond hydrolysis is faster than the rate of hydrolysis. For such polymers, molecular weight and material properties change over the course of degradation. In hydrophobic polymers, it often has been observed that while initially only a gradual change is observed, at a certain time point a sudden fragmentation of the material occurs.4 In degradable polymer networks, in contrast, a more controlled change of material properties can be realized.5 Some polymers, such as polyanhydrides and polyorthoesters display a surface erosion mechanism,6 i.e. here the rate of hydrolysis is faster than the rate of water diffusion, which leads to mass loss without much change of material properties, although because of e.g. thinning of structures, the overall mechanical stability will reduce over time. Surface eroding polymers have been attracting attention for drug release,7 as here the release and degradation can be directly coupled, and can be used also for pulsatile8 or consecutive release.9 As for surface erosion, the rate of diffusion needs to be low, and the rate of hydrolysis needs to be high; polymer design requires the use of repeating units with high hydrophobicity and high susceptibility for hydrolysis. The natural environment of cells, their extracellular matrix, is a complex nanostructured hydrogel. Biomimetic design is based on the hypothesis that resembling structure and properties of biological structures enables also to realize their functions.10 Successful examples for such a strategy comprises the guidance of stem cell differentiation in vitro,11 material-induced bone regeneration,12 as well as on a basic level the high biocompatibility of hydrogels in biological applications.13 When hydrogels are based on biopolymers such as proteins or polysaccharides, they will degrade over time under physiological conditions.14 Likely, because of the high diffusion of water molecules in a hydrogel, a bulk degradation should be expected. However, to predict material behavior in applications, a thorough analysis of material properties during the degradation is a prerequisite.15, 16 Furthermore, it is of interest to investigate whether in the presence of enzymes,17 resembling the in vivo situation, the degradation mechanism stays the same. It would somehow be a trivial finding to observe surface degradation when the enzyme is too large to enter the polymer mesh, which indeed has been shown especially for hydrophobic polymers.18, 19 Therefore, here the hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of gelatin-based hydrogels crosslinked with diazides in a copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition with different crosslinking density, and crosslinker types were investigated. In all cases, the mesh size of the hydrogels as determined from rheological experiments was selected to be larger than the hydrodynamic radius of the enzyme employed, Clostridium histolyticum collagenase (CHC, radius = 4.5 nm).20 In contrast to tissue collagenases, CHC makes multiple scissions per chain21 so that a fast and complete degradation is expected. In the following, the hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation studies are presented, discussing especially the mass loss as well as changes of water uptake and mechanical properties, enabling the development of models for the degradation mechanism.
Nowadays, macromolecular design, blending, and additives are being considered to alter the conditions for biodegradation of synthetic polyesters.[38] In terms of polymer structure, the main factors affecting the abiotic and biotic degradation rate of polymers are the monomer structure, crystallinity, hydrophilicity, Mw, and density of the susceptible hydrolyzable chemical groups such as ester or ether. To increase the degradation rate, low crystallinity, low Mw, high density of ester groups (this means short-chains aliphatic monomers), and high hydrophilicity for microbial adhesion (associated with high surface roughness) are desired.[39] Abiotic methods to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers include modifications of the bulk properties (Mw, crystallinity, increase of chain mobility, catalysis of chemical hydrolysis, among others), and surface properties (roughness, surface energy, and alteration of hydrophilic/hydrophobic balance). Besides these methods, reduction of the polymer size by mechanical action also allows the acceleration of biodegradation by increasing the surface area or surface-to-volume ratio available for water (abiotic) or biotic (enzymatic) attack. Treatments such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, plasma, microwave, alteration of the surface of the polymer by acidic/alkaline immersion, incorporation of specific additives (plasticizers or surfactants), copolymerization, reactive blending, composites, and nanocomposites have been reported to enhance biodegradation at some extent (Table 2). Since thermal properties of biodegradable polymers, reflected in transition temperatures such as glass transition temperature (Tg) and melting temperature (Tm), are expressed in a wide range, a pre-treatment of a mix of plastic waste involving the use of elevated temperatures presents some challenge. Temperatures around the Tg of PLA are already at the Tm of PHAs or PCL. It is conceivable that biodegradable polymers with low Tg and Tm have more susceptible biodegradable structures and higher biodegradation rates. However, other factors such as polymer crystallinity and surface properties also play a crucial role.

Exposure of polymers to high-energy irradiation initiates a process known as chain scission, in which the covalent bonds within the polymer backbone are broken. This results in the formation of shorter polymer chains, known as oligomers, leading to a significant decrease in molecular weight [16]. Oxidative degradation catalyzed by irradiation and oxygen proceeds via a free radical mechanism, forming unstable hydroperoxides that decompose into reactive species and introduce hydrophilic terminal groups such as carboxylic acids (-COOH), hydroxyl (-OH), or carbonyl (C═O) groups [17]. Meanwhile, hydrolysis involves the cleavage of PBS ester bonds upon contact with water, resulting in smaller molecular fragments. These chemical changes increase the polymer's polarity and create an environment conducive to microbial colonization. Low-molecular weight polymers are more accessible and easier for microorganisms to metabolize [18]. Additionally, the hydrophilic nature of the irradiated surface helps retain moisture, further facilitating microbial adhesion and enzymatic degradation. Notably, hydrolysis enhances oxidative vulnerability by increasing hydrophilicity, while oxidation promotes hydrolysis through the formation of polar functional groups. This interplay accelerates the polymer degradation in soil environments and reduces the accumulation of plastic waste. Figure 1 shows the schematic illustration of the synergistic degradation mechanisms of polymers via irradiation and soil burial conditions, where irradiation induces radical formation and oxidation, enhancing hydrolysis and microbial degradation during soil exposure. For bioplastic, the free radicals are formed in C-H aliphatic bonds on PBS molecules when subjected to irradiation. Radicals (i) and (ii) are likely formed through the abstraction of hydrogen atoms from methane groups in the polymer backbone, as shown in Figure 2a. Meanwhile, radicals (i), (ii), and (iii) are formed through the breaking of C-O-C and C-C main chain bonds as depicted in Figure 2b due to the exposure to high irradiation dose [19]. The breaking of C-O-C bonds in the polymer backbone is the dominant effect of biodegradable polymers when exposed to irradiation [20]. According to a previous study, the irradiated bioblend films of polylactic acid (PLA) and starch showed an enhancement in thermal and mechanical properties due to an increase in interfacial adhesion between components, subsequently having the potential to replace conventional plastics [21]. It is necessary to investigate the influence of EB irradiation on the properties of polymer blends to ensure that they can maintain their integrity and serve their utilization purpose with the application of irradiation. Results representing the effects of irradiation with different LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blend compositions on structural, mechanical, thermal, and degradation properties are analyzed and reported to conclude the irradiation doses to these effects. Based on a previously published article [22], the researchers focused on the development of LDPE/PBS blends (10-50 wt% PBS) enhanced with a PE-g-MA compatibilizer (3-5 phr) to improve mechanical, thermal, and morphological properties for sustainable packaging applications. In the current study, the researchers investigate the degradation behavior of LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blends (10-30 wt% PBS, 5 phr PE-g-MA) subjected to EB irradiation and soil burial, aiming to accelerate environmental breakdown through oxidative degradation and microbial attack. In general, the former study aimed to improve the durability and performance of partially biodegradable blends, while the latter focused on promoting their environmental degradability by using irradiation as a pretreatment. Particular attention is given to the synergistic effect of irradiation-induced chain scission and biodegradation during soil exposure. As packaging materials must be nontoxic, biodegradable, and exhibit properties comparable to conventional plastics, the irradiated LDPE/PBS/PE-g-MA blends demonstrate promising potential as eco-friendly alternatives for commercial packaging.

However, non-thermal plasma treatment (a related surface modification technique) is described as improving surface properties of biodegradable polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL) in the following ways:

1.  **Incorporation of Oxygen-Containing Functional Groups:** Plasma treatment incorporates polar oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., -OH, -COOH, C=O) onto the polymer surface, either directly or via post-oxidation [4].
2.  **Increased Surface Energy and Wettability:** The added polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability (hydrophilicity) of the polymer [4].
3.  **Enhanced Protein Adsorption and Cytocompatibility:** The increased surface energy and hydrophilicity improve the adsorption of proteins (without denaturing them) and enhance cell affinity, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and proliferation [4].
4.  **Surface-Specific Modification:** Crucially, plasma treatment modifies only the top few nanometers of the polymer surface, significantly altering surface properties while preserving the bulk mechanical properties (e.g., structural strength, elasticity) [4].
5.  **Improved Biocompatibility for Implants:** This surface modification positively influences the adhesion and proliferation of specific cell types (e.g., human foreskin fibroblasts, mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts), enhancing biocompatibility for tissue engineering applications [4].
6.  **Sterilization Compatibility:** Plasma treatment offers a potential sterilization method that requires evaluation to ensure it maintains the introduced beneficial surface properties post-sterilization [4].

Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is a quasi-neutral gas in which protons and neutrons are ionized. Plasma is generated by the collision of electrons and photons with neutral gas. Gases that generate plasma include oxygen, nitrogen, argon, and helium, and their effects may vary depending on the gas injected [16,17]. Plasma is a simple and well-known method of surface modification and can be used to modify polymer surfaces by generating it. Surface plasma-modifying strategies for polymers include plasma treatment, plasma polymerization, plasma syn-irradiation, and plasma post-irradiation grafting. Plasma treatment implants hydroxyl (O-H), carbonyl (C=O), and carboxyl (COOH) groups on the polymer surfaces [18,19]. In addition, hydrophobic surfaces become hydrophilic through changes in wettability, surface energy, and roughness of the polymer surfaces. Therefore, several studies have been conducted to improve the degradation rate of biodegradable polymers via plasma treatment. Although many studies have investigated the use of plasma treatment to accelerate the degradation of electrospun biodegradable polymers [9,20,21], few have systemically examined the effect of plasma treatment time on the degradation rate of electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes. In this study, atmospheric-pressure non-thermal argon plasma, which is clinically applicable, was applied to electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes. By varying the plasma treatment time, we evaluated the differences in degradation after 1, 4, and 12 weeks. The aim of this study is to regulate the degradation rate of electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes for GBR by controlling the plasma treatment time. Electrospun biodegradable polymer membranes were fabricated using biodegradable polymers: PCL (Mn: 80,000, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), PLA (Mw: 193,300, GoodFellow, Seoul, Korea), and PLGA (lactide:glycolide = 75:25, Mw: 66,000-107,000, Sigma-Aldrich, U.K.). These polymers have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and are biocompatible and biodegradable. The solvents used were Chloroform (CF, Sigma-Aldrich, U.K.), N,N-Dimethylformamide(DMF, Tokyo Chemical Industry, Chuo-ku, Japan), and Acetone(AC, DUKSAN, Korea); PCL and PLA used a mixture of DMF and CF, and PLA used a mixture of DMF and AC. Each Polymer was dispersed within proper solvents and stirred magnetically at 60 ℃ and 600 rpm overnight. The prepared solution was loaded into a 5 mL syringe (KOVAX, Seoul, Korea) with a 23 G metal nozzle (NanoNC, Seoul, Korea). The membranes were fabricated using an electrospinning machine (ESR200RD, NanoNC, Seoul, Korea). As shown in Table 1, the flow rate of all polymer solutions was maintained at 2 mL/h, the voltages of PCL and PLA were 15 kV and PLGA was 9.5 kV; the distance between syringe and collector was 14 cm for PCL, and that between syringe and collector was 12 cm for PLA and PLGA. The fabricated membrane was dried overnight in a vacuum dryer (ilShinBioBase Lab Co. Ltd., Dongducheon, Korea) to remove any residual solvent.
The surfaces of poly(l-lactic acid) (PLA), poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx), and their cast-film blends were activated using low-temperature argon plasma to confirm the possibility of improved microbial adhesion and biodegradation rate using soil microflora as a degrading medium. Radio frequency (RF) plasma systems selectively altered the surface characteristics of PLA/PHBHHx blend cast films without significantly affecting their bulk properties. Notably, Ar-etching (12 min, 50 W) promoted a strong hydrophilic behavior (up to 25 ± 2°), surface energy (up to 48 ± 5%), and surface roughness by ∼4-fold. The increased wettability on plasma-treated samples could be linked to the introduction of polar groups (C-O and O═C-O) and formation of distinct rough topographical structures, which provide a conducive microenvironment for the initial microbial attachment and subsequent biofilm formation. The enhanced wettability favors abiotic hydrolysis by promoting biofilm formation (30 ± 5%), which in turn stimulates the biodegradation rate by 1.1-1.5-fold. These findings indicate that surface activation by argon plasma is a sustainable and viable strategy to enhance cell-surface interactions and biodegradation of biopolymers. Unconstrained usage and gradual accumulation of polymer waste are major concerns of the modern age. However, the broadened public awareness and modification in legislation have introduced a new class of polymers, i.e., biodegradable polymers. (1) Thermoplastic biopolymers such as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) and poly(l-lactic acid) (PLA) can overturn the negative impacts associated with conventional plastics and are considered the main promoters for creating biopolymer demand in the market. Plasma technology is an optimal method for surface modification that can be applied quickly and easily with fewer external physical and chemical influences than chemical methods or laser irradiation [19, 20]. In this study, material surface modification was carried out through the gas-phase plasma process at atmospheric pressure, which has been used in various fields for a long time, and its safety and effectiveness have been verified [21-23]. Many studies on modifying polymer surfaces using plasma techniques have already been reported. Most of these studies presented results focused on surface treatment of polymers to achieve specific goals such as promoting bone regeneration [24, 25]. Research on controlling the drug delivery ability of polymers through plasma treatment has also been reported [26, 27], but it just was presented the drug release rate and did not propose verification of drug holding ability in the polymer surface and efficacy of the drug released. Recently, research on polymers as substitutes for metals has been actively conducted for implantable materials. These studies considered the essential duration of the material’s existence in the body, importance of the interface between the material and tissue, biocompatibility, and mechanical properties such as elasticity, flexibility and strength. In particular, in the case of dental or orthopedic applications, the difference in stiffness, shear stress, or elastic modulus between the implanted material and the surrounding tissue can cause the implant to fall out of the placement location or decrease its adhesion to living tissue due to physical movement or external forces. PLA (Mw ∼60 kDa) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) and dissolved in chloroform (5%, w/v) with stirring at 140 °C. Since the last century, plastic industry has developed so fast that plastic products have gained universal application in many fields. However, most of the plastic products are not biodegradable, and this causes serious environmental pollution. Therefore, developing biodegradable polymers is necessary and it is important to solve this problem. It is well known that aliphatic polyesters are the most promising polymers among the biodegradable plastics. Among aliphatic polyesters, poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) has relatively higher melting temperature and other excellent properties. However, the insufficient mechanical properties of PBS have prevented it from being used in diverse applications. Thus, various techniques, such as physical blending1-5 and copolymerization,6-11 have been explored to improve these weaknesses. Crosslinking is another effective method to improve the properties of PBS.12-20 Up to now, there are mainly two different ways to attain a three-dimensional network. One is irradiation by electron-beam or γ-ray,12-18 and the other is by thermal process.19, 20 Irradiation is an effective technique to induce crosslinking. Kamarudin et al.12 studied the crosslinking of PBS by electron-beam irradiation. They found that the crosslinking introduced by irradiation improved the melt strength of PBS effectively. As a result, the foams could be produced. Moreover, a series of studies have been done by the research group of Fumio Yoshii.15, 16, 18 They investigated the effects of polyfunctional monomer (PFM) and inorganic material on the gel formation during irradiation. The results demonstrated that the presence of PFM and inorganic material in PBS had positive influence on the gel formation. Besides, they studied irradiation of the composite synthesized by PBS and glass fiber. All the articles suggested that the heat stability or mechanical property of PBS was improved, and the materials were still biodegradable in enzymatic degradation or soil burial test. Nevertheless, the equipment investment for irradiation is large. Furthermore, to prevent pollution caused by γ-ray or electron beam, rigorous safeguarding is needed. As a result, it is difficult to apply irradiation on a large scale. In addition, degradation of polymer may also occur during irradiation.

Therefore, the prediction of long-term polymer behaviour in such a mechanically complex bio-environment is indeed difficult. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. In particular, polycaprolactone (PCL) has received considerable attention due to its excellent mechanical and structural properties, and tuneable degradation kinetics. Moreover, the non-immunogenicity of PCL, combined with the possibility of using it as an interporous scaffold material, has resulted in better tissue ingrowth [2-4]. The above-mentioned benefits, in addition to the inexpensive production routes of PCL, have encouraged many research groups to investigate its potential applications in numerous fields of tissue engineering [2, 5]. However, the bioactivity of the tissue-engineered constructs is threatened by the hydrophobic nature of PCL [4, 6-8]. In general, it is known that a moderate surface hydrophilicity allows for an increased adsorption of proteins without modifying their natural conformation. In turn, this increases the cell affinity towards the surface, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and cell proliferation [9, 10]. As a consequence, PCL hydrophobicity negatively impacts cell-material interactions [1]. In order to overcome this issue, surface modification is required. Several approaches have previously been investigated, including wet-chemical treatments, and ion beam, x-ray and gamma radiation. However, the wet-chemical treatment route generates large amounts of hazardous chemical waste and often impacts on bulk properties such as structural strength and elasticity, while most radiation methods can cause severe degradation of the polymer [11]. As an alternative, non-thermal plasma treatment has shown to be a promising method because it is highly versatile, only modifying the top few nanometer layers of the polymer without altering the bulk properties [4, 6, 12, 13]. By choosing an appropriate working gas, this treatment incorporates oxygen-containing functional groups, either directly or via post-oxidation [14]. These polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability and thus improve protein adsorption and cytocompatibility [7, 12]. Many studies have shown that plasma treatment of PCL performed at low pressure enhances the adhesion and proliferation of a wide variety of cell types [4, 8, 12, 15, 16]. As an alternative to low-pressure plasma treatments using expensive vacuum equipment, a few authors have reported that atmospheric pressure plasma treatment is also effective, giving rise to high cellular adhesion and proliferation [7, 17, 18]. Medium pressure plasma is rarely used to treat PCL, despite its potential to easily acquire a larger volume of plasma compared to atmospheric pressure plasma treatments, with relatively cost-effective pumping systems [19]. Therefore, our research group has previously used a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD), operating in different gases at medium pressure, in order to modify PCL surface properties. Both air and argon plasmas introduce oxygen-containing functionalities onto the PCL surface and thus increase its wettability, positively influencing the adhesion and the proliferation of human foreskin fibroblasts and mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts [3, 20]. Once an efficient surface modification is accomplished, a crucial and final prerequisite for the use of PCL in vitro and in vivo is required: the material sterility [21, 22]. Consequently, after sterilization, PCL should maintain the introduced surface properties that determine to a large extent the success of the implant. Despite the importance of the material properties, the impact of sterilization on the PCL structure and surface is largely overlooked in the literature, as the majority of studies solely focus on the microbial activity to check for the sterilization efficacy [23].
Biodegradable polymers are degraded into natural metabolites by simple hydrolysis or enzyme action under physiological conditions.1, 2 Compared with metal materials and nondegradable polymer materials, biodegradable polymers have the advantage of not requiring secondary surgery.3 In recent decades, polylactic acid,4 polycaprolactone,5 polyglycolic acid,6 and other absorbable polymer materials are increasingly favored by researchers.7, 8 Poly (1,3-trimethylene carbonate) (PTMC) is an absorbable, flexible, and amorphous elastomer.9 Unlike other aliphatic polyesters, PTMC is degraded by enzymatic surface erosion.10 It can achieve zero-order release of drugs.11 PTMC hydrolyzes relatively stable in water or buffers solution (pH = 1-13) in vitro.12 There are no acidic products in the degradation process and should not cause serious inflammation.13 PTMC has great potential in biomedical applications, such as drug delivery systems,14-16 soft tissue engineering,17, 18 vascular prostheses,19, 20 or nerve regenerative systems.21-23 However, linear PTMC has very low modulus and low tensile strength.24 The amorphous structure and lower glass transition temperature result in poor dimensional stability of PTMC, and it is prone to creep at room temperature.25 This limits any practical application of PTMC. Therefore, it is necessary to obtain a rubber-like biodegradable elastomer network through crosslinking. The crosslinking of PTMC can be performed through nonionizing radiation such as ultraviolet radiation,25 and ionizing irradiation such as gamma rays26 and electron beams.27 Irradiation technology has gradually become an important method in the study of polymer material modification due to its advantages such as environment friendly, simple operation, less damage to substrate and high accuracy. UV irradiation needs a double bond moiety in the polymer structure, PTMC containing photoinitiators and crosslinking aids can be exposed to ultraviolet light for photocrosslinking.28 However, the low energy of ultraviolet light can only excite particles, forming PTMC networks with low network density. In the absence of initiators, strong ionizing irradiation can cause chemical changes in the polymer structure by forming ions, free radicals, and excited states.9 Meanwhile, high-energy radiation can effectively destroy micro-organisms and viruses. Compared with other sterilization methods, ionizing radiation has a high sterilization efficiency for materials (such as porous scaffolds) whose sterilizers are difficult to penetrate. However, ion and electron beam radiation rapidly attenuate and deposit more energy on the sample surface, potentially causing damage.29 Irradiation with an electron beam causes an essential change in the hole of the scaffold, resulting in partial melting of the scaffold's surface.27 Thus, we chose gamma rays to prepare cross-linked PTMC networks. The crosslinking reaction is also dependent on conditions including irradiation atmosphere, irradiation dose, and temperature. The free radicals generated during the irradiation can react with nearby oxygen, leading to autocatalytic oxidative degradation.30 The compressed molded films were vacuum-sealed and irradiated at room temperature.
In the biomedical fields, replacing materials implanted into a human body with biodegradable polymers has the potential to reduce the burden on the human body. As the candidates for such biomedical materials, aliphatic polyesters such as poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) have been actively investigated [[29], [30], [31], [32], [33], [34], [35], [36]]. Due to their hydrolytically-degradable polymer backbones, such polyesters can degrade and be absorbed in the human body, preventing adverse effects on the human body and unwanted second surgery for the removal of the materials. For example, in the previous study, Lendlein et al. developed a helical stent with the original outer diameter of 3.45 mm composed of biodegradable PCL-based shape-memory polymers with self-expandable properties. Xue et al. also reported a degradable suture for wound closure, exhibiting good shrinkage behavior on animal skin at relatively high temperature [16,37]. Among the biodegradable polymers, PLA has attracted much attention, because PLA can be synthesized from renewable feed stocks, possessing biocompatibility, superior mechanical properties (Young's modulus: ∼1.5-2.0 GPa), and thermal properties (melting point: ∼170 °C) [38,39]. PLA have isomers, such as semi-crystalline poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), and amorphous poly(d,l-lactide) (PDLLA). It is also known that unique crystal morphology called stereocomplex crystals could form in the PLLA/PDLA blend [40,41]. In the stereocomplex polylactide (sc-PLA) crystals, the molecular chains of PLLA and PDLA were packed side by side, where the L-chains and the D-chains could generate strong interaction as compared with the interaction produced by identical PLA due to the van der Waals interaction between C-H⋯OC and CH3⋯OC. The resulting high-density crystalline sc-PLA possessed extremely higher melting point (∼230 °C) than PLLA and PDLA homopolymers (∼170 °C) [[42], [43], [44]] with high tensile strength and modulus [45]. For example, Tsuji et al. studied PLA films made by solution casting, and concluded that the mechanical strength of the sc-PLA film was approximately 60% higher than that of PLLA [46]. Li et al. also prepared a shape memory polymer by blending sc-PLA as crosslinks and PDLLA as switching segments, presenting dramatic shape recovery (∼100%) with the high tensile storage modulus (∼3.1 GPa) [47]. Additionally, Purnama et al. proposed a new concept to enhance the melt stability of sc-PLA macromolecules by introducing CL components as a soft fragment to accelerate the chain movement of PDLA fragments to interact with PLLA chains [48]. If Ttrans is set above body temperature, the SMP can start shape recovery, e.g. by heating with external media [49]. Biodegradable polymer blends and composites are used in applications such as biomedicine, packaging, and agriculture. Controlling the degradation rates of the overall material is essential and was achieved by biodegradable additives, both polymers, and fillers, as outlined below. There is much interest in polymer blends for tissue engineering, because of their adjustable mechanical properties and their ability to adjust the degradation rates to the regrowth of a specific tissue. For this application, a high control of biodegradation is important, e.g., when the speed of bone reconstruction completion is quicker than the time of bone scaffolds degradation to be more suitable for the repair of bone defects or for other tissue.[23, 24] Currently, often porous polymers are used in tissue engineering applications if the polymer matrix can be suitable as a scaffold for tissue growth and can serve as a provisional aid for the cell growth during the regeneration of the target tissue. The polymer can be implanted into the body via minimal operations using small equipment. A small cross-sectioned polymer can be intercalated into the body via a small incision through a catheter. When in the demanded anatomy, with the aid of the body heat, this can be deployed into a greater preordained shape.[23, 24] A promising biocompatible base polymer, of which the biodegradation can be controlled by blending, is PLA.[25] PLA has been used in various biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability in vivo. However, PLA's degradation rate is often too slow,[26] and was accelerated by blending with various polymers and will be discussed in this review. Biodegradable composites were, for example, used by Huang et al. for bone tissue engineering.[23] The authors prepared composites using fibers of nano-hydroxyapatite in a matrix of polymers with different degradation rates. Scaffolds demonstrated preferred structural integrity for constant growth of new bone, however, if scaffold biodegradation occurs too fast it causes a loss in cellular orientation out of a loss in adhesion or cell viability. The result of this study can help to simulate the dynamic microenvironment of biological processes. In another study, Alan et al. studied PLA scaffolds filled with conductive and magnetic fillers obtained by fused filament fabrication (3D printing).[27] It was shown that especially the PLA with conductive fillers (carbon fibers and graphene nanoplatelets) enhanced the bioactivity of the composites and accelerated its biodegradation. It was suggested that these materials could act as potential candidates for tissue engineering such as a scaffold for bone replacement and regeneration. Also, interesting research was reported by Liu et al.[28] they aimed at scaffold preparation using PGS/PCL blends, as the PGS alone would limit an application in tissue engineering because the time needed for its biodegradation is less than the time needed for cartilage regeneration. Thus, they blended PCL with PGS to adjust the time of biodegradation and enhance the mechanical strength of the final material.

Biodegradable and biocompatible polymers, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA),6 poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL),7 and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB),8-10 are widely used in the biomedical field. These plastic polymers are aliphatic polyesters that can be degraded by hydrolysis and their degradation products are non-toxic. Among the polymers, PCL is slowly degraded in about two to three years and has good flexibility and extensibility compared to the other polymers.7 On the other hand, PHB belongs to the family of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) that are entirely synthesized by microorganisms. PHB is a highly crystalline polymer, which is more brittle and difficult to process.8-11 The copolymers of PHB with poly(3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHV) or poly(3-hydroxyheptanoate) (PHH) may reduce the crystallinity and increase the toughness of PHB. Besides, the lower melting point allows the copolymers to be easily processed.12,13 The copolymers show better cytocompatibility than the pure PHB, with respect to fibroblasts,14 osteoblasts,14,15 bone marrow cells,16 and chondrocytes.17 PU also represents a category of shape memory polymers (e.g. DiAPLEX®, SMP Technologies Inc.).18 Shape memory polymers can be temporarily fixed under a certain condition and recovered to the original shape by temperature, moisture, water/solvent, ions, or pH changes.19 The shape memory effect usually arises from the molecular chain entanglement, crystalline domain, chemical crosslinking, or interpenetrated network.20-23 Thermoplastic PUs are generally elastic and do not possess shape memory. When the crystallinity of PUs increases, they may have shape memory behavior because of the increased fixation effect below Tg.22

question: Why is Polyglycolic acid (PGA) often used for surgical sutures but rarely for long-term tissue scaffolds?
ground_truth: PGA has high tensile strength (6–7 GPa modulus) but degrades rapidly via hydrolysis, losing ~50% of its strength within 2 weeks and resorbing completely in 6–12 months. This rapid degradation is ideal for sutures that need to hold tissue only until healing occurs but is too fast for scaffolds requiring long-term structural support.

Preparation of highly interconnected porous poly(ε‐caprolactone)/poly(lactic acid) scaffolds via supercritical foaming Tissue engineering has attracted more and more attention in recent years.1-4 The preparation of scaffold materials is the foundation of tissue engineering.5, 6 For bone tissue, the pore size larger than 300 μm in the scaffold is conducive to intramembrane osteogenesis and angiogenesis during bone regeneration. The small pores of about 100 μm are helpful for cell migration and osteochondral formation. At the same time, the existence of pores of 1-50 μm is conducive to the transfer of nutrients and metabolites.7, 8 In addition, the mechanical properties of the scaffold material should match the implanted bone parts of the human body.9 Therefore, the preparation of tissue engineering scaffolds with multi-modal cell structure, high porosity, and good mechanical properties has become the goal pursued by researchers. At present, the polymers for tissue engineering scaffolds mainly included polyhexalactone (PCL),10, 11 polylactic acid (PLA),12, 13 and poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA).14 PLGA is formed by copolymerization of lactic acid and glycolic acid, which has controllable degradability and good biocompatibility. PLGA has been widely used as the scaffold material for bone tissue engineering and has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for clinical research.15 Supercritical carbon dioxide (Sc-CO2) foaming is believed as a green technology to prepare bone tissue engineering scaffolds. During the Sc-CO2 foaming process, the introduction of nucleating agents can effectively enhance heterogeneous nucleation by reducing the nucleation barrier and surface tension.16 Hydroxyapatite,17 montotonite,18 calcium carbonate,19 and polyethylene glycol20 are all used as nucleating agents in the foaming process to enhance the nucleation behavior during the process.21 Some researchers prepared iteroparous bioactive glass (MBGS) particles /polylactic acid composite scaffolds with appropriate mechanical and degradation properties and in vitro biological activity. They found that MBGS could not only promote nucleation, make the porosity of the scaffolds up to 73%-85%, but also significantly promote bone differentiation.22 Nejaddehbashi23 found that sulfonymine silver (SSD) played a role in accelerating wound healing in the SSD/polyhexantone composite scaffolds. At the same time, how to use Sc-CO2 foaming technology to prepare the scaffold with multi-modal cell structure was still a challenge. Some researchers used Sc-CO2 as a physical foaming agent to prepare foamed polymer by using constant temperature and varying-temperature modal (VTM). They found that the scaffold formed multi-modal cell structure after foaming at VTM.24, 25 Xu et al.24 prepared PS foaming materials with bi-modal pore distribution using batch foaming method via first heating and then depressurization. Li et al.25 obtained polypropylene foaming material with a bi-modal structure by synergistic cooling and depressurization. Therefore, changing the foaming process or adding a nucleating agent that promotes the performance of the scaffold is an effective way to prepare the multi-mode cell structure scaffold with high porosity.

First published on 8th January 2013 Porous scaffolds composed of polypeptides and polysaccharides have remarkable biocompatibility and potential to mimic an extracellular matrix for tissue engineering. This study presented a novel design of polyelectrolyte complex porous scaffolds of a synthetic polypeptide poly(L-glutamic acid) (PLGA) and a natural polysaccharide chitosan (CS) using a freeze drying method. The microstructure of the porous scaffolds could be adjusted by changing the freezing temperature and solid content of the reacting polymer. PLGA/CS scaffolds fabricated from 2% solid content and at a freezing temperature of −20 °C exhibited an interconnected porous structure with average pore size between 150 and 200 μm. The contact angle of less than 75° and high swelling ratio of more than 700% showed the excellent hydrophilic performance of these scaffolds. Degradation of the PLGA/CS composite scaffolds could be modified and more CS content contributed a higher resistance to biodegradation. The mechanical properties of the scaffolds could be controlled by varying the PLGA/CS molar ratio and solid content. The scaffolds exhibited good elastic behavior in wet state. In vitro culture of rabbit adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) indicated that the selected PLGA/CS porous scaffolds supported cell attachment and growth. In summary, the PLGA/CS porous scaffolds show excellent properties, such as an interconnected porous structure, mechanical strength, hydrophilicity, biodegradability and biocompatibility. The successful repair of articular cartilage defects showed the potentiality of using PLGA/CS scaffolds in cartilage tissue engineering. Poly(L-glutamic acid) (PLGA), a novel synthetic polypeptide, is unique in that it is composed of naturally occurring L-glutamic acid that were linked together through amide bonds. PLGA shows good hydrophilicity and biodegradability and is absent of antigenicity and immunogenicity.4,5 These features make PLGA an ideal biomedical material as evidenced by its successful application in drug delivery systems.5 However, few reports showed that PLGA served as a scaffold in tissue engineering. Since PLGA is water-soluble, it is crucial to crosslink it for shape forming and processing of scaffold precursor in aqueous solution. Also, cross-linking of PLGA based scaffolds is an effective method to modify the biodegradation rate and to optimize the mechanical properties. In our previous study, we have crosslinked PLGA with chitosan (CS), a natural cationic polysaccharide, using EDC and NHS as activator.6 Chemically cross-linked PLGA/CS scaffolds showed high porosity, hydrophilic nature and good cell attachment. However, in such a preparation process, chemical cross-linking agents and organic solvent were left along with the scaffolds, which may trigger a cytotoxicity reaction to cells seeded within the scaffold.
Polylactic acid (PLA) is a polymer derived from lactic acid, and it exhibits excellent biocompatibility with non-toxic degradation by-products [204]. When introduced into the living body, it undergoes hydrolysis, breaking down into its fundamental component of α-hydroxy acid, which is then incorporated into the body’s tricarboxylic acid cycle and ultimately excreted [204]. Due to these favorable properties, polylactic acid has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in biomedical applications [205]. Because polylactic acid has antibacterial properties, non-cytotoxic, strong biocompatibility, biodegradability, and moisture management properties, it may accelerate wound healing through angiogenesis, collagen deposition, wound area repair, and cell activity [205]. However, the degradation of PLA can lead to the formation of lactic acid and oligomeric fragments, which may cause a temporary local increase in acidity, which could lead to inflammatory response [206]. Liu et al. introduced rosmarinic acid and graphite oxide into polylactic acid in addition to polyethylene glycol, resulting in a nanofibrous membrane with strong antibacterial properties and wound-healing effects [207]. Fan and Daniels studied the use of polylactic acid with the addition of triterpene extract, which showed promising properties for future wound therapy applications [208]. IIomuanya et al. utilized biomimetic PLA electrospun fibers and hyaluronic acid-valsartan hydrogel scaffolds, which increased re-epithelization that accelerate wound healing [209]. It is a highly crystalline simplest linear polymer and exists only in one form [202, 210]. Its high degree of crystallinity makes it insoluble in most organic solvents. When polyglycolic acid (PGA) is broken down physiologically, it produces glycolic acids, which can enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle and leave the body as CO2 and water, so its biodegradation products are non-toxic [211]. Due to its promising properties, polyglycolic acid is broadly used in the biomedical fields due to hydrophilicity, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and nontoxicity [212]. It is used with other biopolymers in wound-healing applications [213,214,215]. Fang et al. investigated the use of nanofibers with poly(γ-glutamic acid) (γ-PGA) core and PLA shell materials prepared via coaxial electrospinning, which showed favorable biocompatibility in cell culture and re-epithelialization in vivo, suggesting a promising material for tissue engineering and wound healing [216]. Canton et al. developed a highly biodegradable fibrous PLA/PGA with ibuprofen dressing for wound repair which showed reduced inflammation and pain and enhanced cell attachment and proliferation [217]. Polylactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) is a random copolymer synthesized via ring-opening polymerization of lactide and glycolide monomers, resulting in a linear chain of lactic acid and glycolic acid units. After hydrolyzing and rupturing its ester bonds, PLGA produces monomers of lactic and glycolic acids that are readily broken down by the Krebs cycle [218]. Because of its good mechanical properties, high cell adhesion, predictable degradation rates, and lack of toxicity, it is a highly biocompatible polymer [219]. It is one of the best polymers for supplying lactate which is needed to speed up wound healing and reparative angiogenesis [220]. Due to its properties, it is used in biomedical applications especially wound healing [220,221,222].
