Wang et al. studied electrospun PLGA nanofibers loaded with zinc oxide nanoparticles and vascular endothelial growth factors, which showed antibacterial properties, mechanical behavior, and great potential for in vivo wound healing, making them a promising solution for managing infectious wounds [225].
Synthetic biomaterials such as PCL, poly lactic acid, poly glycolic acid, and PLGA have been used to prepare the scaffolds for enhanced tissue regeneration [36]. In particular, PLGA is used for the reconstruction of various tissues owing to its high cytocompatibility [36, 48, 49]. However, scaffolds composed only of PLGA do not maintain their shapes either in the in vitro or in vivo environments owing to their brittle property and rapid resorption [34, 50]. In contrast, PCL has comparatively less cell affinity than PLGA, but it has excellent mechanical properties that prevent early fractures of the scaffold [39] and its degradation rate is slower than the rate of bone regeneration [51]. Thus, blended PCL/PLGA scaffolds exhibit biological and mechanical advantages obtained during the PCL and PLGA mixing processes that complement their respective weaknesses [36]. In addition, as β-TCP was added to the blended PCL/PLGA for the fabrication of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membrane, their elastic modulus was enhanced and their surface roughness was increased [1, 52, 53]. In the SEM images of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes prepared in this study, the rough surfaces generated by the incorporated β-TCP were confirmed (figure 7). During cellular testing with fibroblasts and preosteoblasts, early cell attachment and differentiation were higher in collagen, but the difference of proliferation and differentiation had disappeared when examined on day 7 and day 14, respectively. In contrast, fibroblasts aggregated and were detached from the membrane when maintained until day 14 (data not shown). This was in line with the results of a previous paper [40] and is an indication of the membrane’s ability to inhibit the ingrowth of soft tissues. We next applied the GBR to an in vivo implant model utilizing beagle dogs and performed histological analyses after sacrifice at 8 weeks. The histologic and histomorphometric analyses in this study showed that the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP group did not differ significantly from the collagen group; furthermore, in particular among the histometric measurements, the new bone area (%) and bone-to implant contact (%) of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP group were significantly higher than those of the collagen group (P < 0.05). These findings indicated that the group receiving PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes showed levels of new bone formation and regeneration in the defect area comparable with those induced by collagen membranes, confirming that the biocompatibility of the PCL/PLGA/β-TCP membranes as well as their ability to maintain migration and proliferation of surrounding tissue and to support osteogenic differentiation to ultimately induce bone formation are comparable to those of collagen.
Sutures, tissue adhesives, and surgical staples provide means for inosculation of surgical sites, and sutures, in particular, are widely used in inosculation and fixation of skin, muscle, and blood vessels. In addition, the applications of surgical sutures have expanded to hard tissues and to reconstruction of damaged ligaments. Sutures can be categorized as absorbable or non-absorbable. Natural absorbable sutures are composed of collagen extracted from animal intestines; however, their use is declining due to high infection rates, low tensile strength, and foreign body reactions [1]. Synthetic absorbable sutures based on poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) were developed during the early 1970s, and followed by the invention of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) sutures, which are now replacing conventional collagen sutures (catgut) [2, 3]. Biodegradable filament sutures are available as monofilament or multi-filament (braided) types. Multi-filament sutures have good handling properties and provide greater frictional force at suture sites; however, they are associated with higher risk of bacterial infection. On the other hand, monofilament sutures have weaker knot strength and lower internal breaking strength [4, 5]. PGA sutures, which are widely used nowadays, can only be degraded by simple hydrolysis, which can be accelerated by enzymes, such as esterase, trypsin, and chymotrypsin [6]. A recent study on absorbable sutures focused on development of soft monofilament sutures with controlled degradation properties that incorporated therapeutic agents in order to reduce infection rates in surrounding tissues. The recently developed poly(p-dioxanone) (PDO) monofilament suture is widely applicable due to its low toxicity, improved hydrolysis, and good tensile strength and knot properties [7, 8]. However, its low melting point, plasticity, and pyrolysis during the spinning process leave room for improvement [9].
AbstractIn this paper we created novel poly(ester urethane)s (PESUs) designed specifically for tissue engineering. The PESUs were derived from oligomeric α,ω-dihydroxy(ethylene-butylene adipate) (dHEBA), 1,4-butanediol (BDO) and aliphatic 1,6-hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) and modified with l-ascorbic acid to improve their biocompatibility. In addition, we determined their mechanical properties (such as tensile strength, elongation at break and hardness). To determine how these materials may potentially behave after implementation in tissue, we estimated the degradation behavior of obtained PESUs in various chemical environments, which were exemplified by canola oil, saline solution, distilled water and phosphate buffered saline (PBS). Finally, the PESU biocompatibility and hemocompatibility tests were carried out. Biocompatibility was determined with a MTT assay and it was performed with 3T3 cell line. The results showed satisfactory mechanical properties, good hemocompatibility and improved biocompatibility, which let us to conclude that PESUs modified with ascorbic acid might find an application in biomedical field of soft tissues engineering. IntroductionPolyurethanes have found very strong position in the medical market for the last years. Some polyurethanes (PUs) with the commercial names like Pellethane, Tecoflex, Elasthane, BioSpan found the application in medicine as very good biostable materials for long term implants. They are based mostly on aromatic diisocyanates. However, new medical-grade polyurethane materials continue to be developed and obtained expand their use in medicine [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6].There is great interest in designing new types of polyurethanes for regenerative medicine, in particular to obtain a tissue scaffold [7], [8], [9]. Such scaffolds are intended to serve as a place for air and nutrients exchange as well as the template for cells that proliferate, migrate and differentiate to form new functional tissue.In the procedure of this type of regeneration a scaffold material should be biodegradable upon the growth of new cells.Requirements of template are suitable mechanical, physicochemical and biological properties such as biocompatibility, hemocompatibility and biodegradability. Tissue scaffold biocompatibility means that the implanted material may serve its function with an appropriate host response, without forming prominent system inflammation [10].Properly designed polyurethanes may meet all these requirements, due to the possible changes in the chemistry of segmented structure consisting of specific hard and soft segments, which allow the adjustment of PU properties in a wide range.PU scaffolds are mostly obtained from polyester polyols, aliphatic diisocyanates, low molecular weight chain extenders [11], [12], [13] and other components, called modifiers, to improve polyurethanes' biocompatibility and biodegradability [1], [2].There are several examples in the literature, describing the modification of PU with the use of natural polymers such as chitosan [14], [15], starch [16], cellulose [17], gelatin [18], [19] and collagen [20] leading to the desired changes in biodegradation rate of the material, as well as contributing to improving its biocompatibility [1], [2].Also known are modifications of polyurethanes with other compounds that improve biocompatibility or degradability.Interesting examples are phospholipid copolymer modification of PU [21], elastin cross-linked peptide [22] or poly(ethylene glycol) methacrylate [23], [24].There are also literature data reporting addition of biologically active substances such as vitamin E or vitamin C [3], [4], [25] to increase biocompatibility of synthetic polymers.Vitamin C (also known as ascorbic acid) is particularly interesting because of its antioxidant properties and high impact on tissue regeneration [26], [27], [28], [29], [30].The stimulatory effect of ascorbic acid (AA) on cell proliferation was recognized by Zhang et al. and Cetina-Diaz et al. which received polyurethane materials modified with ascorbic acid for use in bone tissue engineering [3], [4], [31]. For comparison, unmodified poly(ester urethanes) were obtained. Both types of PESUs were tested to determine their tensile strength, elongation at break, permanent set and hardness. The samples were also subjected to the standard procedure of degradation [36], [37] in three different defined media: canola oil, saline, distilled water and phosphate buffered saline (PBS). An ideal graft for in situ tissue engineering should be readily available for implantation, compliant, durable, and biologically active to support arterial regeneration and ensure long-term patency [12]. This material’s ability to bind various cell-adhesive and functional ligands via photoclickable ‘thiol-ene’ chemistry makes it an excellent candidate for bioengineered scaffolds that regulate cellular activities. Recently, there has been a lot of research on a technology known as tissue engineering that can help with tissue regeneration and functional recovery [1]. Tissue engineering is a method that combines engineering and biological science principles to develop biologically active substitutes to heal damaged tissues and enhance their capabilities. A scaffold that can support the spread and growth of the cells that will form the new tissue acts as the basis for engineered tissue [2, 3]. Providing a favorable environment for cell growth, proliferation, infiltration, differentiation, and migration is the primary function of scaffolds in tissue engineering. Therefore, tissue engineering scaffolds must have properties like biocompatibility, good mechanical properties, degradability, and porous morphology [4]. Bones, blood vessels, muscles, and nerves are just a few examples of organs and tissues that can be repaired and regrow organs and tissues that can be repaired and regrown through the application of tissue engineering. Consequently, the preparation and design of tissue engineering scaffolds using biomimicry are becoming increasingly important [5, 6]. Due to their structural resemblance to extracellular matrix, and other properties, electrospun scaffolds are suitable candidates for wound dressing [7]. Many biopolymers such as alginate [8], collagen [9], chitin [10], and PLA [11] were incorporated into electrospun membranes for use as wound dressing materials. Among this, Poly lactic acid (PLA) is a well-researched biodegradable polymer, it is used as a scaffold material in tissue engineering and medical implant device manufacturing [12]. The US Food and Drug Administration-approved clinical research, the outstanding biocompatibility of PLA, and the important production of harmless byproducts after biodegradation are some of the elements contributing to its attraction [13]. Non-exhaustive uses of PLA include the development of antimicrobial products, bone tissue engineering, the development of 3D-printed scaffolds, surgical suturing, and the manufacture of food and beverages, in addition to its use as drug carrier agents [14]. Another significant issue is the development of ROS (reactive oxygen species) on the surfaces of biomaterial scaffolds that have been implanted [15]. ROS is a byproduct of regular oxygen metabolism that is formed in the body and plays a significant role in cell signaling, wound healing, and inflammatory responses. In the body, free radicals like peroxy (R-COO•) and hydroxyl (OH•) that are often short-lived and extremely reactive are produced when ROS oxidizes and releases molecules like superoxide anions (O−2) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) [16]. The occurrence of diseases including cancer, diabetes, and inflammation can cause a significant increase in ROS levels, which may damage the structure of cells [17]. Therefore, using antioxidant materials in combination with biomaterials is essential for avoiding excessive production of ROS, which could lead to irritation and, eventually, implant failure [18]. Numerous plant compounds have strong antioxidant properties, which may be crucial for the healing of wounds. One of the first known medicinal plants is fenugreek, also known as methi, and is a member of the Leguminosae family. Due to its strong aroma and flavor, it is primarily used in food preparations. Fenugreek seeds have anti-ulcerogenic, hypocholester olaemic, and hypoglycemia properties [19, 20]. In healthy and diabetic erythrocytes, fenugreek seeds may have antioxidant abilities and reduce oxidative damage induced by H2O2 [21]. Fenugreek has been utilized as an additive by Ivy and co-workers to create collagen-based biomaterials, and it has been shown to change the physicochemical characteristics of collagen [22]. These characteristics suggest that adding fenugreek to the PLA matrix is a novel way to develop biodegradable scaffold materials with enhanced bio performance. Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum L.) is an annual herb that belongs to the family Leguminosae widely grown in Middle Eastern countries. The seeds contain the alkaloid trigonelline along with mucilage, tannic acid, yellow coloring matter, fixed and volatile oils, a bitter extractive, diosgenin, gitogeni, a trace of trigogenin, and vitamin A. The seeds are also rich in protein and contain a unique major free amino acid 4-hydroxy isoleucine, characterized as one of the active ingredients in fenugreek seeds [].
Many synthetic polymers, such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic) acid and polycaprolactone (PCL), have been extensively studied as potential scaffold materials for tissue engineering. The use of a well characterized synthetic material has potential advantages for such applications including avoiding the need for donor tissue with autografts and immunological rejection with allografts, as well as supply and reproducibility challenges that can occur in using natural polymers. For skin tissue engineering, these polymers serve as the scaffold supporting cell functions and resisting contraction to allow the tissue to regenerate. Ideally, natural tissue is formed and fills the space and function of the polymer matrices that eventually degrade under the environment created by biological processes. Therefore, the matrices need to support functions (such as adhesion, proliferation and differentiation) of appropriate cells (such as fibroblasts) and have mechanical and degradation characteristics suitable for skin regeneration applications. However, the hydrophobic nature of many polymers such as PCL makes them non-ideal for adsorption of important adhesive proteins (such as fibronectin, vitronectin) in their native conformation. The hydrophobic surfaces tend to cause protein denaturation and subsequent foreign body reactions to the implants in vivo. This in turn limits the functions of adherent cells including fibroblasts [1-4]. This hydrophobic nature of polymers such as PCL also results in very slow degradation, often requiring 1 year or more for complete degradation in the case of PCL [5-7]. In skin tissue engineering applications where tissue formation takes place in the first several months following the surgery, a faster degradation rate is desirable. Therefore, in this study, we demonstrated that by simply altering the wetting properties of the model polymer PCL, we have (1) enhanced its interaction with fibroblasts and (2) accelerated its degradation. PCL is a biodegradable polyester polymer synthesized by ring-opening polymerization reaction of ε-caprolactone [8]. Its biodegradability is attributed to non-enzymatic hydrolysis of the ester bonds in the polymer chains in the physiological environment [5, 9, 10]. Reports in the literature have demonstrated methods such as hydrolysis using concentrated NaOH to make polymers such as PCL more hydrophilic for cell interactions [11-13]. However, these methods tend to only alter the wetting properties of the surface of the materials and can lead to etching; therefore, they may not be ideal.

This study compared PEGDA and polycaprolactone (PCL) nanofiber matrix (NFM) coated PEGDA, referred to as PCL-PEGDA, scaffolds for their application in multiple tissue repair such as articular cartilage, nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc (IVD). We examined each scaffold morphology, porosity, swelling ratio, degradation, mechanical strength, and in vitro cytocompatibility properties. A defect was created in Sprague Dawley rat tail IVD by scraping native cartilage tissue and disc space, then implanting the scaffolds in the disc space for 4 weeks to evaluate in vivo efficacy of multi-tissue repair. Maintenance of disc height and creation of a new cell matrix was assessed to evaluate each scaffold’s ability to repair the tissue defect. Although both PEGDA and PCL-PEGDA scaffolds showed similar porosity ∼73%, we observed distinct topographical characteristics and a higher effect of degradation on the water-absorbing capacity for PEGDA compared to PCL-PEGDA. Mechanical tests showed higher compressive strength and modulus of PCL-PEGDA compared to PEGDA. In vitro cell studies show that the PCL NFM layer covering PEGDA improved osteoblast cell adhesion, proliferation, and migration into the PEGDA layer. In vivo studies concluded that the PEGDA scaffold alone was not ideal for implantation in rat caudal disc space without PCL nanofiber coating due to low compressive strength and modulus. In vivo results confirm that the PCL-PEGDA scaffold-maintained disc space and created a proteoglycan and collagen-rich new tissue matrix in the defect site after 4 weeks of scaffold implantation. However, its rapid degradation rate leads to premature loss of structural integrity, making it unsuitable for long-term tissue scaffolds that require sustained mechanical support over months [5]. Additionally, PGA's degradation produces acidic byproducts (e.g., glycolic acid), which can lower local pH, induce inflammatory responses, and hinder tissue regeneration—critical drawbacks for scaffolds needing prolonged biocompatibility [5], [14]. In contrast, sutures benefit from PGA's quick absorption and sufficient initial strength, while scaffolds often rely on slower-degrading polymers like PCL or PLGA blends to match tissue regeneration timelines and avoid adverse pH effects [8], [13], [14].

Sutures, tissue adhesives, and surgical staples provide means for inosculation of surgical sites, and sutures, in particular, are widely used in inosculation and fixation of skin, muscle, and blood vessels. In addition, the applications of surgical sutures have expanded to hard tissues and to reconstruction of damaged ligaments. Sutures can be categorized as absorbable or non-absorbable. Natural absorbable sutures are composed of collagen extracted from animal intestines; however, their use is declining due to high infection rates, low tensile strength, and foreign body reactions [1]. Synthetic absorbable sutures based on poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) were developed during the early 1970s, and followed by the invention of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) sutures, which are now replacing conventional collagen sutures (catgut) [2, 3]. Biodegradable filament sutures are available as monofilament or multi-filament (braided) types. Multi-filament sutures have good handling properties and provide greater frictional force at suture sites; however, they are associated with higher risk of bacterial infection. On the other hand, monofilament sutures have weaker knot strength and lower internal breaking strength [4, 5]. PGA sutures, which are widely used nowadays, can only be degraded by simple hydrolysis, which can be accelerated by enzymes, such as esterase, trypsin, and chymotrypsin [6]. A recent study on absorbable sutures focused on development of soft monofilament sutures with controlled degradation properties that incorporated therapeutic agents in order to reduce infection rates in surrounding tissues. The recently developed poly(p-dioxanone) (PDO) monofilament suture is widely applicable due to its low toxicity, improved hydrolysis, and good tensile strength and knot properties [7, 8]. However, its low melting point, plasticity, and pyrolysis during the spinning process leave room for improvement [9].
Surgical sutures are wound closure filaments manufactured in different shapes. These sutures secure tissues in position until the wound naturally heals and gives enough tissue strength. The U.S. Federal Drug Administration (FDA) has approved PLA for utilizing as a suture material due to its advantageous features such as biocompatibility, bioresorbability, and biodegradability with non-toxic degradation products. But, the inherent properties of PLA like high crystallinity (around 40%), and slow rate of degradation, impose restrictions on its application as material for suture. Because of this, copolymerization of lactic acid (LA) with biodegradable monomers, like glycolic acid (GA), is done to obtain the PGA/PLA copolymer, which has better properties than PLA for suture applications. PGA/PLA copolymer with 90:10 mol ratio of GA: LA has been commercialized as Vicryl by Ethicon. This amorphous copolymer has lower glass transition temperature (Tg) and higher degradation rate than that of PLA and has been found very much useful as a suture material [111, 139]. A stent is a small mesh tube used to hold open passages in the human body, such as weak or narrowed arteries. There exist three major kinds of stents: (a) bare-metal stents, (b) drug-eluting stents, and (c) biodegradable / bioresorbable stents. Bare-metal stents and drug-eluting stents may leave residues in the body that can affect further treatment and recovery process, whereas bioresorbable stents, providing both mechanical support and drug delivery to the vessel wall, can be fully absorbed by the body, and therefore, permits better vascular remodeling and decreases the triggering of persistent inflammation. In reconstructive medicine there is a tremendous need for suitable biomaterials to allow the repair and regeneration of damaged or diseased tissue [1]. A large range of injectable gel scaffolds have been investigated, developed and subsequently applied in tissue engineering because their structure and properties can be easily varied and eventually optimised [2]. The injectable scaffolds intended for use in regenerative medicine should be (i) biocompatible; (ii) injectable, the scaffold formulation should be sufficiently fluid and not undergo premature solidification; (iii) biodegradable, the scaffold should degrade at a rate comparable to that of new tissue regeneration and (iv) of sufficient mechanical strength and tissue adhesivness. Although a large amount of work has been carried out in this area, injectable scaffolds/cell suspensions are still not used clinically. The scaffold design parameters must be fully optimised and controlled before such scaffolds can become a clinical reality. Linear aliphatic polyesters such as poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), polylactide (PLA) and polyglycolide (PGA) have recently attracted attention in biomaterials science because of their biodegradability and biocompatibility [3], [4]. Notably, PCL has been approved by the FDA for use as a surgical suture. However, the hydrophobic and semicrystalline nature of PCL, as well as the absence of utilisable functional groups on the polymer backbone, have limited its practical applications [4]. A wide variety of PCL-based biomaterials that exhibit desirable properties have been developed by appropriate selection of co-monomers to be polymerised with ε-caprolactone [5]. For example, injectable, porous thermo-responsive scaffolds based on poly(ethylene glycol)-block-poly(ε-caprolactone) (PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG) [6] and hyperbranched polycaprolactone-click-poly(N-vinylcaprolactam) (HBPCL-click-VPCL) [7] have been used for tissue regeneration. The scaffolds were able to support the proliferation and differentiation of the embedded cells and promote tissue growth. Despite such encouraging results, there are still many challenges that need to be overcome in the future, in order that the PCL-based biomaterials be successfully utilised in reconstruction medicine [8]. Hydrophilic hyperbranched polyglycidol (HBPG) polymers have emerged as a new promising platform in tissue engineering applications because of their strong biocompatibility, [9] desirable mechanical properties, high transport capacity, and multiple pendant hydroxyl-groups which can be used as attachment sites for targeting biological cells and tissues [10], [11]. In addition, oligoglycidols are approved as food and pharmaceutical additives by the FDA. Recently, the chemical modification of the surface of biomaterials with methyl and hydroxyl functional groups has shown promise in enhancing the ability of a material to support mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) adhesion and differentiation [12]. We propose that the presence of numerous hydroxyl groups in HBPG will be therefore able to promote the cellular attachment and differentiation without exogenous biological stimuli.
A poly(lactide-co-glycolide)/hydroxyapatite composite scaffold with enhanced osteoconductivity Tissue engineering represents a powerful approach toward bone regeneration through the surgical implantation of a biodegradable scaffold, i.e., a porous structure mimicking the properties of the native extracellular matrix. The scaffold can be either directly implanted in the tissue defect site or previously cultured with the appropriate cell type and combined with bioactive substances promoting tissue regeneration, such as growth factors and signaling molecules.[1] Poly(α-hydroxy acids) are among the most widely investigated synthetic polymers for tissue engineering since they are approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for drug delivery and other clinical applications.[2] They include poly(lactide) (PLA), poly(glycolide) (PGA), and their copolymers poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), linear aliphatic polyesters degraded in physiological environments through the hydrolysis of their ester linkages into non-toxic molecules removed by natural metabolic pathways.[3] Depending on the application, PLGA can be preferred to the two relevant homopolymers (i.e., PLA and PGA), since its hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance and the resulting degradation kinetics can be tailored by varying the molar ratio between the two comonomer units.[4] Indeed, PLGA has been studied for tissue engineering applications since the 1990s.[5, 6] However, even though the mechanical properties of PLGA scaffolds can be engineered to be comparable to those of trabecular bone, their stiffness is much lower than that of cortical bone. For this reason and to enhance their osteoinductive properties,[4] PLGA is often loaded with bioactive calcium phosphate ceramics, including hydroxyapatite (HA)[7-11] and β-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP).[12-16] Increasing the compatibility between a polymer phase and an inorganic filler represents one of the main challenging issues in composite material development and mechanical properties optimization.[17] In particular, the interface adhesion strength between HA and poly(α-hydroxy acid) matrices is typically low, compromising the structural stability of the resulting composite material.[18] HA particle surface modification through polymer grafting can be exploited to increase compatibility and achieve effective mechanical stress transfer between the two phases. In this way, it is possible to reduce inter-phase stress concentration and improve material mechanical properties.[19] “Grafting from” approaches involve polymer synthesis directly on the surface of HA particles,[15] often after ceramic functionalization through covalent linking monomers that act as initiators.[20, 21] These methods have some disadvantages, including poor control over PLGA comonomeric unit ratio and the possibility of grafting only short polymeric chains.[22] For this reason, a “grafting to” approach based on covalent bonding of preformed aliphatic polyesters on the surface of HA particles, was explored in this study to develop additively manufactured composite materials.

The use of polymers in tissue engineering has been growing in the last decades. They emerged as an alternative to frequently limited autografts, allografts, and xenografts.[1-5] The replication of these conventional grafts in the laboratory is a huge challenge, but there are many synthesis pathways to come up with advanced biomaterials that solve specific tissue diseases.[6, 7] If they are used to produce temporary grafts or scaffolds, they need to be non-only biodegradable, but also biocompatible and resorbable.[8-10] With this purpose, many resorbable polymers such as collagen,[11] chitosan,[12] or polyesters such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(glycolic acid) (PGA), and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) have been utilized either alone or in combination with other biomaterials delivering promising results.[13] In particular, PLA has proven to be one of the best candidates due to its versatility. This polyester is usually synthetized by the ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of lactide.[14] As this monomer has two enantiomeric species (l-lactide and d-lactide), then isotactic poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) or poly(d-lactide) can be produced. Otherwise, by using a mixture of both enantiomers or the meso form, heterotactic poly(d,l-lactide) can be prepared.[15-17] Physical properties of PLA can be modified by the control of stereoregularity. It directly influences the crystallinity, which afterward affects the hydrolytic degradation[18, 19] and, to a lesser extent, the mechanical properties.[20] PLA has been used in medical devices for tissue regeneration that are already available in the market. Biotrak (Acumed), Rapidsor (Depuy Synthes), and Bioscrew (ConMed) are some examples. However, they are not temporary grafts as such, but instead they are used for the fixation of autografts, allografts or osteochondral defects. Temporary grafts must be prepared as porous scaffolds to allow bone growth, and nutrients and waste exchange through the pores promoting the healing process.[21-25] But porosity weakens scaffolds,[26] which is critical when using a rigid and brittle polymer such as PLA.

In general, the crystallization process of polymers consists of two main stages: nucleation and crystal growth. A primary nucleation process can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous. Homogeneous nucleation stems from the statistical fluctuations of polymer chains in the melt and is characterized by a constant rate. While the heterogeneous one occurs at relatively low supercooling due to the presence of foreign bodies in the polymer melt which increase the crystallization rate by acting as heterogeneous nuclei and reducing the free energy needed for the formation of a critical nucleus. These additives, which have high performance in the acceleration of nucleation, are called “nucleating agents (NAs).”14 It has been demonstrated that the addition of an NA is effective to accelerate the crystallization of polymers.15 By adding an NA, the crystallization rate of a polymer can be enhanced due to the increasing of the nucleation density and the decreasing of the spherulite size. Recently, the crystallization of poly(L-lactide) (PLLA), one biomass-derived, biodegradable and biocompatible bioplastic, is reported to be significantly accelerated by the incorporation of zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn).24 PPZn is one kind of metal phosphonate which is a synthetic inorganic/organic hybrid material with a layered structure similar to montmorillonite clay. It has been used widely in the fabrication of metal phosphonate reinforced polymeric composites.25-28 Besides, metal phosphonates can also find applications in the field of biomaterials due to the natural occurring nature of phosphate. According to Pan et al.,24 the crystallization of PLLA has been significantly accelerated and the tensile and storage moduli of PLLA have been reinforced by the incorporation of PPZn. IntroductionPoly(lactic acid) (PLA) is a biopolymer from renewable agricultural resources which is on the expectation to substitute petroleum-based polymers, due to its physico-chemical properties such as high modulus, strength, thermoplasticity, as well as the easy processability to create various types of products. However, the fact that PLA is brittle due to its slow crystallization behavior, the improvement of PLA-based product is still required. As the crystallization of PLA in terms of the rate and the extent of crystallization can be enhanced by nucleating agents, the mechanical properties can be improved whereas the cycle period in injection molding processes becomes shorten [1], [2]. Nucleating agents are typically either low molecular weight organic or inorganic additives. Talc is a good inorganic nucleating agent for crystallization of polycaprolactone [3], [4], poly(ethylene terephthalate) [5], and PLA [6], [7], [8], as evidenced from a decrease of crystallization temperature upon heating as well as a decrease in spherulite size. Jiang et al. [9] investigated the crystallization behavior of PLA nanocomposites with montmorillonite clay and found the crystallization temperature (Tc) was shifted to lower temperature leading to an enhanced crystallinity. For organic nucleating agents, Nam et al. [10] reported that aliphatic amide such as N,N′-ethylenebis(12-hydroxystearamide) increased an overall crystallization rate of PLA whereas the average spherulite size was found to decrease as the number of nuclei increased. Blending PLA with other polymers can also modify the crystallization behavior. For example poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) [11], poly(butylene succinate) [12], and poly(ethylene oxide) [13] shifted the cold crystallization temperature of PLA to lower temperature and increased the crystallization rate. Stereocomplexation between PLLA and PDLA is accepted as the most effective methods to enhance the thermal properties of PLA-based materials [14], [15], [16]. An effective nucleating agent must be compatible and well dispersed within the PLA matrix, whilst also promoting crystallization.22 To address the brittleness of PLA, flexible polymers are commonly employed as toughening agents, which can be melt blended with PLA to achieve targeted mechanical properties.23 However, incorporating such agents can reduce heat resistance and hardness, making it necessary to carefully adjust both the composition and molecular weight of nucleating and toughening agents to concurrently enhance mechanical and thermal properties. Currently, the nucleating agents used for sc-PLA typically include inorganic nanoparticles, organometallic complexes and regenerated cellulose.24-29 Recently, porous microspheres (MSs), racemic PLA (i.e. poly(d,l-lactic acid) or PDLLA) and carbon nanotubes were also demonstrated as effective nucleating agents for encouraging the formation of sc-PLA.30-32 Another approach to improving PLA crystallization is to increase molecular chain mobility through plasticization. For instance, adding poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) can enhance chain mobility, thereby improving PLA crystallization. PEG can serve both as an efficient nucleating agent and a plasticizer in PLLA/PDLA blends.33-35 Phuangthong et al. systematically examined the effects of different molecular weights and concentrations of PEG on the crystallization behaviors of sc-PLA in PLLA/PDLA blends. Low molecular weight PEG at low concentration can effectively increase the mobility of the PLLA/PDLA chain, lowering the energy barrier for crystallization. Conversely, PEG with high molecular weight has limited solubility in PLLA/PDLA blends and thus penetrates the matrix less effectively.36 Moreover, Song et al. synthesized PDLA-PEG block copolymers that, when mixed with PLLA solutions, exhibited a higher propensity for stereocomplex crystallization and a faster crystallization rate than conventional PLLA/PDLA blends.37-42 Despite these advancements, sc-PLA samples often still exhibit inherent brittleness and low heat-distortion temperature, restricting their broader applications.43-49 While melt blending with flexible polymers can toughen PLA, it often exacerbates its poor heat resistance and mechanical strength.30, 31, 50-53 For example, Srithep et al. blended PLLA/PDLA with thermoplastic starch and a chain extender to enhance thermal and mechanical properties. Based solely on the provided evidence, nucleating agents like talc and zinc phenylphosphonate (PPZn) play the following roles in the injection molding of PLA:

1.  **Accelerate Crystallization Rate:** They significantly increase the crystallization rate of PLA, evidenced by a dramatic reduction in crystallization half-time (t1/2). 2.  **Reduce Cycle Time (tcycle):** By accelerating crystallization, these nucleating agents enable shorter cycle times in injection molding processes [1][9][10][12]. Faster crystallization allows the molded part to solidify more quickly, improving productivity.

3.  **Increase Crystallinity:** The addition of nucleating agents like talc and PPZn increases the overall degree of crystallinity (χc) achievable in PLA parts [3][7][10][12][14]. Higher crystallinity generally improves mechanical properties and heat resistance.

4.  **Improve Heat Resistance:** Enhanced crystallization, particularly with talc, significantly increases the Heat Distortion Temperature (HDT) of PLA. For instance, using 1µm talc at 10 wt% raised the HDT from 58°C to a maximum of 139°C, allowing the molded parts to resist thermal deformation at higher temperatures [7][9].

Talc addition most rapidly reduced Tc between 128°C and 107°C at 1 wt% [7].

6.  **Increase Nucleation Density:** They act as heterogeneous nuclei, increasing the nucleation density and reducing the spherulite size within the PLA matrix [2][3][4][10][12][14]. This dense nucleation is fundamental to accelerating the overall crystallization kinetics.

7.  **Potential Trade-offs:** While enhancing crystallinity and heat resistance, the evidence indicates that talc can make PLA composites more brittle, reducing tensile elongation at break and impact strength, especially at higher loadings like 10 wt% [7][12].

Previous studies have found that the crystallization properties of materials are inseparable from heat resistance, so that increasing crystallization rate and crystallinity is considered to be a most effective way to improve the heat resistance of PLA [23, 24]. In regard to this matter, adding nucleating agents has been recognized as a most economic manner to modulate the crystallization behavior of PLA [25]. Three types of nucleating agents have been commonly utilized in practice, including inorganic nucleating agents, organic nucleating agents, and polymer resins. Common inorganic nucleating agents comprise talc [26, 27], nanostructure carbons [28,29,30], calcium carbonate [31], and montmorillonite [32, 33]. In the process of melt crystallization, these nucleating agents provide heterogeneous nucleation sites for PLA and thus improve its crystallization ability. Shakoor et al. reported the fabrication of a PLA/Talc composite via melt blending [27]. They found that, after adding 20 wt% talc, the cold crystallization temperature (Tc) decreased from 127 to 96 °C, while the crystallinity of PLA increased from 2.0 to 25%. However, as a large amount of inorganic filler is applied, it tends to agglomerate, resulting in a destruction of the mechanical properties of PLA-based blends. Compared with inorganic counterparts, organic nucleating agents with a better interfacial compatibility usually show more significant nucleation induction for PLA. At present, common organic nucleating agents consist of amides [34,35,36,37], phthalimide [38], phenyl phosphates [39,40,41], and hydrazide compounds [42, 43]. Plastics are synthetic polymer compounds made substantially from petrochemical materials extracted from coal, oil, and natural gas.[1] In general, fossil fuel plastics achieve high mechanical and fluid barrier properties by packing their chains into specific crystalline and amorphous regions. However, its hydrophobic and long-chain structural features make it lack bio-accessible organic chemical groups, limiting the ability of microorganisms to break them down.[2] The accumulation of fossil fuel plastics in the environment has severely affected soil quality, the aquatic environment, flora, and fauna.[3] The depletion of fossil fuels and environmental pollution have prompted researchers to develop eco-friendly biodegradable polymers to replace petrochemical-based polymers. In this context, bioplastics appear as a promising alternative. A bioplastic is often considered bio-based and/or biodegradable material[4, 5] such as polyvinyl alcohol, polylactic acid, polybutylene succinate, as well as carbohydrate derivatives and blends based on protein, starch, chitin, and cellulose. The global market size for bioplastics is considered to burgeon every day. The global production capacity of bioplastics in 2023 was ≈2.18 million tonnes, which is projected to expand to 7.43 million tonnes by 2028.[6] This shows that bioplastics have great application value and development prospects in various fields of modern society. Currently, PLA is the most important among the biobased biodegradable plastics because of its zero toxicity, biodegradability, and good mechanical attributes.[7] PLA is produced by the polymerization of lactides or lactic acid monomers fermented from starch, mainly used in 3D printing, food packaging, transport, agriculture, and textile industries.[8] Upon biodegradation, PLA releases CO2, water, and decomposed organic matter without leaving any visible and toxic residues.[7] These substances are absorbed by plants, thus imparting less carbon footprint. Although, compared to fossil fuel plastics, neat PLA has some disadvantages such as brittleness and low crystallization rate, which restricts commercial usage.[9] The mechanical performance of PLA is greatly affected by the crystallinity degree, which depends on the source and processing conditions.[10, 11] For example, the oriented samples of PLA were prepared by being heated and mechanically drawn, the tensile strength and crystallinity increased significantly with the increase in draw ratio.[12] In addition, there is also a study on increasing the crystallinity of PLA by adding nucleating agents (Zinc PhenylPhosphonate, Ecopromote, and EcopromoteHD) to improve its mechanical properties.[13] Heterogeneous nucleation is a frequently encountered phenomenon in the crystallization of composite systems.[14] By adding inorganic compounds,[15] polysaccharide polymers,[16] carbon-based materials,[17] and other substances[18] as nucleation sites, the heterogeneous nucleation rate of the matrix can be effectively promoted.[19] For instance, lignin was used as a heterogeneous nucleating agent to increase the crystallinity of PLA, which also results in the enhancements of PLA tensile strength and gas barrier properties.[20] However, the heterogeneous nucleation effect of proteins as nucleating agents is rarely reported. Blending the protein with biodegradable synthetic polymers has been shown to be an effective strategy to improve performances,[21-23] but whether this is related to nucleation effects still remains unclear. Polylactide (PLA) is a bio-based and biodegradable polymer receiving much attention because of its versatility in many applications as packaging and disposal bottles/cutlery3 or biomedical materials and drug delivery systems.4 Properties as good processing capacity and the ability to biodegrade under specific conditions minimize its environmental print with respect to conventional polymers. One of its limits is its poor mechanical stability, exhibiting less than 10% elongation at break and relatively poor impact strength (1.9-2.6 KJ/m2)5 that it is surpassed by the addition of reinforcements as natural6, 7 or glass fibers8 in the polymeric matrix. Another limit remains the relatively little knowledge about degradation behavior in different aqueous environments and the combined effect with the degradation temperature. Previous works have dealt with the aging of PLA-based biocomposites. PLA was immersed in distilled9 and sea water10, 11 at room temperature, where natural aging was characterized by a slow degradation rate even after 10 weeks of immersion time. Temperature was employed to accelerate aging by Deroine et al.,12 who immersed PLA samples in distilled water and seawater at temperatures up to 50°C to evaluate its influence on the kinetics of degradation observing a deviation from Fickian behavior and morphological changes of the samples at higher temperatures.12 Gil-Castell et al.13 tested the hydrothermal aging of PLA/sisal biocomposites below and above the glass transition (around 70°C) and observed that at tests below 70°C the polymer chains maintained their morphology and structure whereas above this temperature some changes in the internal structure of the biocomposite might occur.13 Few works can be found testing the stability of PLA after immersion on different media (acidic and alkaline solutions) as shown in the review by Gorrasi and Pantani,14 where tests at varying pH and their influence on the degradation mechanisms are described. Elsawy et al. showed that pH, temperature, and the autocatalytic behavior of PLA were the key parameters controlling the PLA degradation process.15 PLA was tested at different pH and temperatures mimicking biomedical applications16 obtaining high degradation rates in extreme alkaline conditions. For this work, the PLA-based biocomposite was designed and tested as food and beverage container, and thus at a specific range of pH and temperatures, to the knowledge of the author not tested before. Several reinforcing agents have been traditionally included in the biopolymeric matrix to increase their required performance.17, 18 In this work, ArcBiox™ degradable glass fibers were used as reinforcing agent. The fabrication of degradable glass fibers can be done in a similar manner than that of conventional glass fibers, although the thermal characteristics of degradable silicate glasses make their drawing into fibers very challenging.23 In terms of processing, the glass is heated to fiber drawing temperatures and drawn into fibers. The production of continuous glass fiber made by melting and subsequent fiber drawing typically requires a sizing step on the glass fiber during the manufacturing process. This sizing step has mainly two functions: it provides protection to the filaments during the production process and enhances the fiber's adhesion properties so it firmly bonds with the polymer matrix. In this sense, the developed degradable glass fibers were optimized on their sizing for their use in polyester matrices, as polylactic acid (PLA).

The development of sustainable and environmentally benign polymers from renewable feedstocks is important to reduce the dependence of most engineering and commodity plastics on fossil-based resources [[36], [37], [38]]. Moreover, the global shift from reusable containment and packaging to single-use contributed to an extraordinary growth in the plastics market [39]. For instance, the global plastic production reached about 407 million tonnes in 2017 [39]. The most extensively produced commodity plastics such as low density poly (ethylene) (LDPE), linear low density poly (ethylene) (LLDPE), high density poly (ethylene) (HDPE), poly (propylene) (PP), poly (ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly (styrene) (PS) and poly (vinyl chloride) (PVC) constitute close to 70% of the overall production as shown in Fig. 3a [39]. Overall, about 38% of all plastics produced are employed in packaging applications (Fig. 3b), mainly because of the appealing cost structure and excellent packaging attributes of plastics [40] over other materials such as metals or glasses. In addition to their prevalent use, the stable carbon - carbon bond in the backbone of most of these polyolefin and polyolefin derivative plastics that withstand biodegradation, resulted in a tremendous increase in the share of plastics in municipal solid waste. In middle - and high income - countries, plastic waste increase was estimated from less than 1% in 1960 to more than 10% by 2005 [39,41]. The geographic distribution limitation and unstable and unpredictable prices of fossil fuel feedstock for such plastics coupled with the alarming waste accumulation and pollution associated with non-biodegradable plastic caused an increasing research interest in sustainable polymers. In the quest for an alternative raw material to fossil derived resources, agricultural feedstock such as polysaccharides, proteins, chitosan, lignin, algae, glycerol, and lipids are being extensively studied [11,[42], [43], [44], [45]]. More recently, research and development efforts in catalysis, process development, and polymer science and engineering put a spotlight on CO2 based polymers. However, the kinetic and thermodynamic stability of CO2 has limited its extensive utilization as a feedstock for polymers. Many reactions pathways for the conversion of CO2 into useful polymers involve positive change in enthalpy (ΔH) and thus they are endothermic. Consequently, a substantial input of energy, effective reaction conditions, and often active catalysts, are necessary for such conversions [46]. Despite these challenges, methods to overcome the high energy barriers based on reduction, oxidative coupling with unsaturated compounds on low valent metal complexes, and increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon are being developed [23].

Synthetic polymers have higher mechanical properties and are used in various industry applications like automotive, aerospace, electronics, sports materials, etc [3, 4]. Natural materials, or agro-by-products are easily available in plenty; they are eco-friendly materials to the environment that are utilized for multiple products manufacturing; they slowly replace the traditional products [5] and control the pollution caused by the traditional materials [6]. Poly Lactic Acid (PLA) is produced from renewable sources such as sugar, beet, corn, and potato, and also the degradation process of PLA is easier [7]. PLA produces 25%-55%, a lesser amount of energy compared with petroleum-based polymers [8]. PLA is used for commercial purpose materials like packaging of products, electronics, housing for computers and automotives [8], and biomedical applications such as scaffolds, bone fixators, dental implants, and wound dressings [9, 10]. PLA is a thermoplastic polymer with a higher strength and modulus, and it is considered a biodegradable and compostable polymer [11]. The biopolymers can be processed easily in injection molding, compression molding, extrusion, and additive manufacturing methods. Harussani et al [12] state that the main merit of using PLA is reduced production cost and waste disposal cost, by adding natural fillers, the polymer composites can be easily disposed off through landfilling, incineration or by the pyrolysis method.
Plastics produced from fossil resources through petroleum refinery processes have played a key role in modern society over the past decades. However, our heavy dependency on fossil resources and derived products has led to serious issues such as extreme climate change, global warming, increasing the carbon-footprints, and the rapid depletion of fossil resources, which pose a threat not just to humans but also to the entire planet.[1-4] To cope with these global challenges, there is an urgent need to substitute fossil-based plastics with environment-friendly and bio-based plastics from renewable resources.[5] Among various available bioplastics, polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) have received more attention in both academic and industrial research fields because of their biodegradability in soil and marine environment at ambient conditions,[6, 7] and have shown great potential as a green replacement for fossil-based plastics.[8-10] Notably, emerging PHAs bioplastics with green features are continued to make incursions into the commercial market, which is expected to be worth USD 28 billion tons by 2025.[11] The current market volume occupied by PHAs is 23 000MT, at a compound annual growth rate of 6.28% from the last 4 years.[12] The Food and Drug Administration of the United States (US-FDA) has approved permission to the use of PHAs bioplastics for food contact and biomedical applications because of their biocompatibility and nontoxic nature.[13, 14] In addition, the demand for PHAs is gradually increasing in various industrial applications. Although PHAs are environment-friendly and biocompatible polyesters, their high selling price (4 to 5 € kg−1) in comparison to fossil-based plastics (less than 1 € kg−1) limits their competition with fossil-based plastics in the commercial market or their broader applications as commodity plastics.[15-17] The high selling price of PHAs is associated with the use of expensive carbon substrates, which accounted for 50% of its overall costs of production. To overcome such a challenge, intensify research efforts have focused on the increased utilization of renewable and inexpensive carbon sources for PHAs production.[18] In this context, the biotransformation of lignocellulosic biomass to PHAs has acquired immense attention in both academic and industrial sectors because these raw materials are abundant, carbon neutral, nonedible, and low-cost carbon sources.[19]
Public awareness of the environmental impact of plastic waste has led to initiatives aimed at reducing its negative effects on natural resources and CO2 emissions [26, 27]. Due to insufficient disposal capacity and environmental concerns, the focus is now on recycling waste goods [28, 29]. Recycling plastic materials presents challenges such as diverse polymer composition, desirable features, and advanced technology requirements, making the process complex and time-consuming [30]. Traditional plastic composite [31] recycling releases particulate matter and toxic gases (CO2, NOx, and SOx) into the atmosphere [26]. Bioplastic misconceptions persist, as the final product may not naturally biodegrade due to bio-related feedstock [32]. Recyclable and bio-based plastics are eco-friendly polymers, albeit they sometimes have different basic notions. Biodegradable and bio-based plastics are examples of eco-friendly polymers [33]. In contrast with conventional plastics produced from fossil resources, bio-based materials are derived from renewable resources. They include some fully biodegradable ones and others to some degree [30]. Bio-based materials are entirely or partially biodegradable, unlike conventional plastics derived from fossil fuels and non-renewable natural resources [30]. Bioplastics are made from bio-based polymers from renewable resources, including corn, sugarcane, and cassava. The name "bio-based" describes the technique of making these materials, even if not all bio-based polymers are biodegradable [34]. Cellulose is the most utilized commercial biodegradable polymer with billions of kilograms sold per year.18 However, due to its highly crystalline structure and difficult processability, cellulose has limited use in traditional plastic applications. Synthetic cellulose derivatives have been developed as attractive options for replacement of conventional plastics.19 Here, ester or ether groups are bound to the hydroxyl groups of the glucose repeat units allowing for control of the polymer thermomechanical properties. Cellulose triacetate (CTA) is one of the most common cellulose derivatives, where at least 92% of the hydroxyl groups are acetylated, resulting in a typical degree of substitution (DS) of greater than 2.72.20 Typically, increasing DS increases solubility, while decreasing DS increases water absorptivity and plasticity.21 As a rigid polymer, CTA has significant tensile strength and high storage modulus, but low elongation at break.22 It is commonly used in LCD displays, packaging and solution-cast plastic films.21, 23

Most synthetic polymers exhibit a substantial trade-off between rigidity (elastic modulus) and extensibility (strain at failure). Hard synthetic polymers such as composite resins have superb elastic moduli (E ≈ 1-10 GPa), but lack extensibility (εmax < 20%).1, 2 In contrast, soft synthetic polymers (elastomers) offer superior extensibility (up to 650%),3 but have much lower moduli (≈1-100 kPa).4 Because of the ubiquitous challenges in designing load-bearing materials, there is a great demand to improve-or at least maintain-high stiffness without significant detriment to elongation. Inspiration can be taken from nature, wherein several materials have this ability.5-8 The byssus of marine mussels, for example, is used as a holdfast that anchors to rocky surfaces in the hostile intertidal zone.6-8 The byssal thread (Figure 1A,B) is comprised of a soft, collagenous fiber-bundle core and a hard, 5-10 µm-thin protective cuticle. With this combination of stiffness (E ≈ 800 MPa) and extensibility (ε > 100%),6, 7 the thread allows for significant degree of tensile movement, preventing from being torn off under the high loads from waves and wind. The previous works have presented that this protective coating strategy can be endowed by (but not limited to) granular microstructure of the cuticle and catechol-iron coordination chemistry.6, 7 Inspired by this natural protective coating strategy, we here desire to mimic the mitigation of core-cuticle delamination to quantify its possible viability to increase overall material toughness through a simple gradient layering technique in a most common synthetic polymer (acrylate polymer). Synthetic polymers that utilize the similar heterogeneous structure to emulate such a unique stress-strain relationship have shown promise as a mechanism for improved load distribution such as traditional polymer composites containing organic/inorganic fillers. More recently, double-network architectures of synthetic polymers have been attained via interpenetrating one network to another to dissipate the strain energy by sacrificing one network upon tension.8-11 Dual physically cross-linked (DPC) hydrogels of acrylic polymers with primary cross-links of laponite nanoparticles and secondary cross-links of Fe3+ (ferric) ion coordination complexes were also introduced, which significantly improved both elastic modulus and extensibility of DPC hydrogels over non-DPC.11 However, these methods involve multi-step processes of network penetration, wherein a soft network is swollen in aqueous solution, followed by cross-linking with another polymer network.4, 6, 12 These approaches, therefore, are limited to hydrogels or polymers that swell in water such as polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based networks.6, 12 Additionally, high localization of stress in similar polymer matrices often causes failures in areas of localization and asymmetric cross-linkage, endowing high initial rigidity but resulting in premature fracture at only fractions of maximum strain.12, 13 Therefore, these moisture-sensitive materials cannot be applied for more general load-bearing applications which are mostly prepared from hydrophobic polymer networks.14 A heterogeneous bilayer or sandwich architecture of polymers can be a candidate to overcome these limitations, but since most bilayers laminate a rigid coating onto a flexible substrate, it results in trade-off between rigidity and elongation.15-17 The resulting extreme modulus mismatches can cause high interfacial stress localization, which intensifies until strain energy exceeds the critical strain energy release rate, causing the rigid coating to fracture or delaminate.16

Stress relaxation, one of the basic characteristics of polymeric materials in long-term loadings, is a viscoelastic material behavior that must be defined in a material model to determine all behaviors of these materials. As a basic principle, in stress relaxation tests, constant strain is applied to polymeric materials that are subjected to loadings such as compression, tension, and flexural at certain strain rates and constant temperature. Under this constant strain, the force, applied to the material to maintain the strain, does not remain constant over time and decreases. As a result, the stress decreases, and stress relaxation occurs in the material. Stress relaxation is a time-dependent behavior and is an indication of the rate-dependency of the deformation. Stress relaxation behavior occurs with zero strain rate.19 Determining this behavior is critical to detect the problems such as damage and fracture that may occur in polymeric materials during long-term loading and determine the material's service life. For this reason, a material model that can predict the time-dependent behavior of polymeric materials and the behaviors mentioned above is needed for structural analysis. Experimental studies determine the stress relaxation behavior of polymers at different strain levels.20-22 However, when the studies on the prediction of stress relaxation behavior are reviewed, it is seen that there are a limited number of modeling studies with constitutive equations consisting of standard spring and damper elements. Yun et al. predicted the stress relaxation behavior of carbon black-epoxy composites at different temperatures with an empirical-rheological model. Considering the microstructure of the epoxy, they used the Kelvin model to simulate the viscoelastic behavior of amorphous chains in epoxy and the spring model to simulate the elastic behavior of cross-linked chains. The simulation results revealed the effect of the additives on the material properties.23 Papanicolaou et al. modeled the flexural stress relaxation behavior of the starch powder-epoxy composite with three different models. They stated that depending on the applied deflection and the weight ratio of the additive, the residual property model (RPM) more accurately predicted this behavior of the composite.24 Tamrakar et al. experimentally determined the relaxation time and equilibrium stress of DER 353 epoxy and estimated the uniaxial compression stress relaxation behavior with an incremental approach when the strain rate drops to zero at different constant strain levels.25 In this study, a wide range of material behaviors of epoxy (Araldite LY 564) are modeled using the cooperative-VBO model. These behaviors are storage modulus, quasi-static compression at different strain rates, high strain rate behavior, and stress relaxation behaviors (at two different constant strains) at room temperature. To the best of our knowledge, in the literature, no single modeling work depicts all the behaviors mentioned above in one paper. The simulation results of the cooperative VBO model are compared to experimental data obtained from Bakbak et al.26 It is shown that the cooperative VBO model is capable of modeling the quasi-static behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, strain softening, and strain hardening) and high strain behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, and thermal strain softening) of epoxy. Also, the model prediction of the epoxy stress relaxation behavior at 1.E-1 /s strain rate agrees with the experimental results. The model reasonably predicted the changes in the long-term stress relaxation modulus, and the model results were consistent with the experimental results depending on the strain level. In addition, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was performed to determine the viscoelastic behavior of the epoxy. The storage modulus, which changes depending on the temperature above and below the glass transition temperature, is also modeled with the cooperative VBO model. The outcome of this work is important since it shows that the cooperative VBO model is capable of modeling all viscoelastic and viscoplastic behaviors mentioned above.
There are several theoretical models that capture the interesting strain hardening response of semiflexible and flexible networks.[47] For flexible chains, classical rubber elasticity has been used to model polymer network mechanical behavior based on the entropy of the chains and cross-links of an isotropic network as a function of small strains.[1, 48, 49] Flory and Rehner extended this model to predict that the modulus of a gel would decrease as a function of swelling as the chains are stretched to accommodate the solvent.[50-52] To capture the effects of large strains, Yeoh and Fleming included finite extensibility of the network chains.[53] Mackintosh et al.[54] developed a model for cross-linked gels and entangled solutions of semiflexible biopolymers to explain the concentration dependence of the storage modulus and yield strain. This model assumes that chains are nearly straight and results in viscoelasticity having a dependence on the bending modulus. A later study also breaks the mechanical behaviors into two regimes, affine and nonaffine deformation, as a function of cross-link density and filament rigidity.[55] Dobrynin and Carrillo[20] took this theoretical analysis further and used molecular dynamics simulations to relate the strain-hardening behavior to the molecular parameters of the network chains. They found a universal relationship that captures the strain hardening response of flexible and semiflexible networks, by using an extension parameter, β, that relates the initial end to end vector of the network to the maximum stretch, . Carrillo et al.[56] expanded this model further to include the bending modulus of discrete chains and improve modeling of strain hardening segments of the gel network. These theoretical efforts capture the key parameters that can predict response of nonlinear networks, such as swelling, initial state of the chains, and maximum extension in the network. Control of the strain-hardening behavior in materials is important for both biological systems and synthetic materials. Matsumoto et al.[57] synthesized PLL hydrogels with large swelling ratios. These hydrogels were shown to undergo a structural change as a function of pH. A later study by Matsumoto et al.[58] uses this structural transition to functionalize the hydrogels as drug carriers of a model drug. Methylcellulose is a synthetically modified polysaccharide that forms fibrils spontaneously and gels with thermal treatment.[59] The moduli of the methylcellulose gels are an order of magnitude higher than would be expected for a flexible polymer gel at the same concentration because of this fibril structure.[60] Gkikas et al. synthesized poly-l-proline hydrogels that have higher shear modulus upon heating from 5 to 35 °C because of a change in chain conformation from a compact right-handed helix to a stretched left-handed helix.[61] Kouwer et al.[46] and Pochan and co-workers[62, 63] have created polyisocyanopeptide hydrogels formed from bundled chains and β-hairpin hydrogels formed from an exchangeable strand domain that transitions to a beta hairpin upon heating. These materials are being investigated as wound dressings[64] and injectable therapies.[65] To determine the onset of strain hardening of model polypeptide hydrogels, we have cross-linked PLL, a polypeptide which has a well-known random coil-helix transition as a function of the pH environment, as shown in Figure 1. We investigate the mechanical properties of the hydrogel network as a function of helicity and cross-link density with small and large amplitude oscillatory shear and dynamic light scattering. We compare the small amplitude and nonlinear response of these materials as a function of the percent helicity of the network. As the network chains form helical structure, a transition from strain softening to strain hardening occurs, which we are able to model with Dobrynin and Carrillo's[20] model at large strains. Using these model systems, we observe the transition to strain hardening as a function of chain structure, which occurs in various biological systems, and can possibly be used to store stresses and generate mechanical forces in the material.

This study initially investigates the use of solid-state stretching technology to physically modify polymer foam materials for the development of wood-mimicking materials. The resulting material demonstrated a tensile strength exceeding 30 MPa in the stretching direction, which approaches the intrinsic tensile strength of polybutylene succinate (PBS) and is comparable to that of balsa wood. This enhancement in tensile strength is directly correlated with the transformation of the foam's cell and cell wall structures, which tend towards a "tubular cell with highly oriented and reinforcing crystals alternating in orderly arrangement." Furthermore, the solid-state stretching process increases the degree of crystallinity and orientation of the cell walls, significantly contributing to the improved tensile properties of the foam. Structural simulations conducted using ANSYS software further validate the theoretical feasibility of this processing method. These simulations also explored the variation in tensile properties across different stretch ratio models, highlighting the impact of the pure cellular structure on tensile strength enhancement. Consequently, this processing technology holds substantial promise for future polymer foam modification and processing endeavors. Stress concentration refers to the phenomenon that the stress at defects will increase sharply to a value much higher than the average stress of the material when the material has defects internally. In general, stress concentration is not desired, because it can lead to the premature cracking of material due to overload. Notably, for rubber-toughened plastics, one main toughening mechanism is to generate crazes in stiff polymers, namely inducing plastic deformation based on stress concentration in glassy-state polymers [18,19]. The plastic deformation can not only increase the elongation at break of stiff polymers through local deformation, but also benefit the further deformation of stiff polymer via transferring excessive local stress and promoting the rearrangement of chain structure due to the capability of dissipating energy. The rubber phase with smaller size can produce more small stress concentration-induced plastic deformation in the matrix, resulting in better toughness [[20], [21], [22]]. Besides, the high deformability of rubber phase, which can terminate the development of microcracks, also contributes to the high toughness of rubber-toughened plastics. Herein, what attracts us is that stress concentration can induce plastic deformation in stiff polymer matrix and benefits the toughness of polymers. Since stress concentration can induce plastic deformation in glassy-state polymers, it is promising to toughen stiff polymers while maintaining the high stiffness. In fact, some nanofiller-reinforced stiff polymer can also show improved deformability due to stress-induced plastic deformation [[23], [24], [25]]. In this case, the excellent dispersion of nanofiller, which can generate plentiful small stress concentration points, is required. However, the increment in elongation at break is very limited due to the limited chain-segment movability. Therefore, it is difficult to obtain stiff polymer with high toughness by stress concentration-plastic deformation alone. Herein, plasticized polymer with balanced stiffness and toughness is achieved based on commercially available plasticizers, and a novel mechanism that integrates plasticization and stress concentration-induced plastic deformation is proposed. Specifically, poly(lactic acid) (PLA), a bio-based and biodegradable stiff polymer, is selected as the matrix and three organic compounds [triethyl phosphate (TEP), tributyl phosphate (TBP) and trioctyl phosphate (TOP)] with different solubility parameters are selected as plasticizers. The effects of the plasticizer-PLA compatibility on the mechanical properties, microstructure, deformation mechanism and energy dissipation of plasticized PLAs were systematically investigated. TBP, the plasticizer with a moderate compatibility to PLA, is found to endow the plasticized PLA with optimal stiffness and toughness. The excellent performances of PLA/TBP15 cannot be exceeded via tuning the content of plasticizer with the best compatibility to PLA (TEP). The mechanism is revealed to originate from the combined moderate plasticization and stress concentration-induced plastic deformation. Moderate plasticization can promote the chain-segment movability while maintaining a high stiffness, where the deformability is usually limited. The stress concentration-induced plastic deformation can impart good deformability to PLA with moderate plasticization. We envision that this work can enrich the methods of manipulating the mechanical properties of plasticized polymers and contribute to the industrial preparation of plasticized polymers with balanced stiffness and toughness. Under this condition, the magnitude of the tensile strength (or other mechanical properties) is predicted as a mathematical function of the constituent volume fractions and influential factors (like bubble traps, cellulose content, etc.), combined with the rule of mixture [1].

In essence, the isostrain condition enables the use of the rule of mixture for initial predictions but often leads to overestimation of tensile strength because it fails to incorporate the detrimental effects of poor interfacial adhesion and ineffective stress transfer between the matrix and reinforcement [1], and homogenizes the response of structurally distinct networks only at small strains [5].

Stress relaxation, one of the basic characteristics of polymeric materials in long-term loadings, is a viscoelastic material behavior that must be defined in a material model to determine all behaviors of these materials. As a basic principle, in stress relaxation tests, constant strain is applied to polymeric materials that are subjected to loadings such as compression, tension, and flexural at certain strain rates and constant temperature. Under this constant strain, the force, applied to the material to maintain the strain, does not remain constant over time and decreases. As a result, the stress decreases, and stress relaxation occurs in the material. Stress relaxation is a time-dependent behavior and is an indication of the rate-dependency of the deformation. Stress relaxation behavior occurs with zero strain rate.19 Determining this behavior is critical to detect the problems such as damage and fracture that may occur in polymeric materials during long-term loading and determine the material's service life. For this reason, a material model that can predict the time-dependent behavior of polymeric materials and the behaviors mentioned above is needed for structural analysis. Experimental studies determine the stress relaxation behavior of polymers at different strain levels.20-22 However, when the studies on the prediction of stress relaxation behavior are reviewed, it is seen that there are a limited number of modeling studies with constitutive equations consisting of standard spring and damper elements. Yun et al. predicted the stress relaxation behavior of carbon black-epoxy composites at different temperatures with an empirical-rheological model. Considering the microstructure of the epoxy, they used the Kelvin model to simulate the viscoelastic behavior of amorphous chains in epoxy and the spring model to simulate the elastic behavior of cross-linked chains. The simulation results revealed the effect of the additives on the material properties.23 Papanicolaou et al. modeled the flexural stress relaxation behavior of the starch powder-epoxy composite with three different models. They stated that depending on the applied deflection and the weight ratio of the additive, the residual property model (RPM) more accurately predicted this behavior of the composite.24 Tamrakar et al. experimentally determined the relaxation time and equilibrium stress of DER 353 epoxy and estimated the uniaxial compression stress relaxation behavior with an incremental approach when the strain rate drops to zero at different constant strain levels.25 In this study, a wide range of material behaviors of epoxy (Araldite LY 564) are modeled using the cooperative-VBO model. These behaviors are storage modulus, quasi-static compression at different strain rates, high strain rate behavior, and stress relaxation behaviors (at two different constant strains) at room temperature. To the best of our knowledge, in the literature, no single modeling work depicts all the behaviors mentioned above in one paper. The simulation results of the cooperative VBO model are compared to experimental data obtained from Bakbak et al.26 It is shown that the cooperative VBO model is capable of modeling the quasi-static behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, strain softening, and strain hardening) and high strain behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, and thermal strain softening) of epoxy. Also, the model prediction of the epoxy stress relaxation behavior at 1.E-1 /s strain rate agrees with the experimental results. The model reasonably predicted the changes in the long-term stress relaxation modulus, and the model results were consistent with the experimental results depending on the strain level. In addition, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was performed to determine the viscoelastic behavior of the epoxy. The storage modulus, which changes depending on the temperature above and below the glass transition temperature, is also modeled with the cooperative VBO model. The outcome of this work is important since it shows that the cooperative VBO model is capable of modeling all viscoelastic and viscoplastic behaviors mentioned above.
