Stress relaxation, one of the basic characteristics of polymeric materials in long-term loadings, is a viscoelastic material behavior that must be defined in a material model to determine all behaviors of these materials. As a basic principle, in stress relaxation tests, constant strain is applied to polymeric materials that are subjected to loadings such as compression, tension, and flexural at certain strain rates and constant temperature. Under this constant strain, the force, applied to the material to maintain the strain, does not remain constant over time and decreases. As a result, the stress decreases, and stress relaxation occurs in the material. Stress relaxation is a time-dependent behavior and is an indication of the rate-dependency of the deformation. Stress relaxation behavior occurs with zero strain rate.19 Determining this behavior is critical to detect the problems such as damage and fracture that may occur in polymeric materials during long-term loading and determine the material's service life. For this reason, a material model that can predict the time-dependent behavior of polymeric materials and the behaviors mentioned above is needed for structural analysis. Experimental studies determine the stress relaxation behavior of polymers at different strain levels.20-22 However, when the studies on the prediction of stress relaxation behavior are reviewed, it is seen that there are a limited number of modeling studies with constitutive equations consisting of standard spring and damper elements. Yun et al. predicted the stress relaxation behavior of carbon black-epoxy composites at different temperatures with an empirical-rheological model. Considering the microstructure of the epoxy, they used the Kelvin model to simulate the viscoelastic behavior of amorphous chains in epoxy and the spring model to simulate the elastic behavior of cross-linked chains. The simulation results revealed the effect of the additives on the material properties.23 Papanicolaou et al. modeled the flexural stress relaxation behavior of the starch powder-epoxy composite with three different models. They stated that depending on the applied deflection and the weight ratio of the additive, the residual property model (RPM) more accurately predicted this behavior of the composite.24 Tamrakar et al. experimentally determined the relaxation time and equilibrium stress of DER 353 epoxy and estimated the uniaxial compression stress relaxation behavior with an incremental approach when the strain rate drops to zero at different constant strain levels.25 In this study, a wide range of material behaviors of epoxy (Araldite LY 564) are modeled using the cooperative-VBO model. These behaviors are storage modulus, quasi-static compression at different strain rates, high strain rate behavior, and stress relaxation behaviors (at two different constant strains) at room temperature. To the best of our knowledge, in the literature, no single modeling work depicts all the behaviors mentioned above in one paper. The simulation results of the cooperative VBO model are compared to experimental data obtained from Bakbak et al.26 It is shown that the cooperative VBO model is capable of modeling the quasi-static behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, strain softening, and strain hardening) and high strain behaviors (elasticity modulus, yield stress, and thermal strain softening) of epoxy. Also, the model prediction of the epoxy stress relaxation behavior at 1.E-1 /s strain rate agrees with the experimental results. The model reasonably predicted the changes in the long-term stress relaxation modulus, and the model results were consistent with the experimental results depending on the strain level. In addition, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was performed to determine the viscoelastic behavior of the epoxy. The storage modulus, which changes depending on the temperature above and below the glass transition temperature, is also modeled with the cooperative VBO model. Stress concentration refers to the phenomenon that the stress at defects will increase sharply to a value much higher than the average stress of the material when the material has defects internally. In general, stress concentration is not desired, because it can lead to the premature cracking of material due to overload. Notably, for rubber-toughened plastics, one main toughening mechanism is to generate crazes in stiff polymers, namely inducing plastic deformation based on stress concentration in glassy-state polymers [18,19]. The plastic deformation can not only increase the elongation at break of stiff polymers through local deformation, but also benefit the further deformation of stiff polymer via transferring excessive local stress and promoting the rearrangement of chain structure due to the capability of dissipating energy. The rubber phase with smaller size can produce more small stress concentration-induced plastic deformation in the matrix, resulting in better toughness [[20], [21], [22]]. Besides, the high deformability of rubber phase, which can terminate the development of microcracks, also contributes to the high toughness of rubber-toughened plastics. Herein, what attracts us is that stress concentration can induce plastic deformation in stiff polymer matrix and benefits the toughness of polymers. Since stress concentration can induce plastic deformation in glassy-state polymers, it is promising to toughen stiff polymers while maintaining the high stiffness. In fact, some nanofiller-reinforced stiff polymer can also show improved deformability due to stress-induced plastic deformation [[23], [24], [25]]. In this case, the excellent dispersion of nanofiller, which can generate plentiful small stress concentration points, is required. However, the increment in elongation at break is very limited due to the limited chain-segment movability. Therefore, it is difficult to obtain stiff polymer with high toughness by stress concentration-plastic deformation alone. Herein, plasticized polymer with balanced stiffness and toughness is achieved based on commercially available plasticizers, and a novel mechanism that integrates plasticization and stress concentration-induced plastic deformation is proposed. Specifically, poly(lactic acid) (PLA), a bio-based and biodegradable stiff polymer, is selected as the matrix and three organic compounds [triethyl phosphate (TEP), tributyl phosphate (TBP) and trioctyl phosphate (TOP)] with different solubility parameters are selected as plasticizers. The effects of the plasticizer-PLA compatibility on the mechanical properties, microstructure, deformation mechanism and energy dissipation of plasticized PLAs were systematically investigated. TBP, the plasticizer with a moderate compatibility to PLA, is found to endow the plasticized PLA with optimal stiffness and toughness. The excellent performances of PLA/TBP15 cannot be exceeded via tuning the content of plasticizer with the best compatibility to PLA (TEP). The mechanism is revealed to originate from the combined moderate plasticization and stress concentration-induced plastic deformation. Moderate plasticization can promote the chain-segment movability while maintaining a high stiffness, where the deformability is usually limited. The stress concentration-induced plastic deformation can impart good deformability to PLA with moderate plasticization. We envision that this work can enrich the methods of manipulating the mechanical properties of plasticized polymers and contribute to the industrial preparation of plasticized polymers with balanced stiffness and toughness. The 'isostrain' condition in polymer blends assumes uniform strain across all phases during deformation. This condition leads to mechanical models that overpredict tensile strength when real-world imperfections exist, as they inherently assume perfect stress transfer and interfacial bonding [1]. Specifically:

-   Models based on isostrain conditions (e.g., rule of mixtures) treat composite properties as a mathematical function of constituent volume fractions and factors like interfacial strength. However, discrepancies arise when interfacial bonding is imperfect or defects (e.g., bubbles, fiber damage) are present, as these factors degrade stress transfer efficiency [1].
-   When adhesion is poor (e.g., no filler-matrix bonding), models like Nicolais-Narkis underpredict strength because they assume filler reduces the load-bearing cross-section without reinforcement. Isostrain models fail to capture this without incorporating adhesion parameters [4][5].
-   Improved predictions (e.g., Halpin-Tsai model) only align with experimental tensile strength when good adhesion exists (e.g., chemical interactions like amine groups on silane-grafted nanocellulose), as this condition better satisfies the isostrain assumption of effective stress transfer [4][5].
-   Phase morphology (e.g., domain size in blends) critically influences deformation mechanisms (crazing vs. shear yielding), which isostrain models ignore. This leads to prediction errors if dispersed phases do not uniformly share strain [3].
-   Fiber degradation during processing (e.g., manual mixing) reduces longitudinal integrity, violating the isostrain assumption and causing strength reductions not captured by idealized models [1].

question: What is the primary environmental risk associated with the degradation of biodegradable polymers in anaerobic landfills?
ground_truth: In anaerobic landfill conditions, the microbial degradation of biodegradable polymers (like PLA or PHAs) generates methane (CH4) rather than just CO2. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential ~25-30 times higher than CO2, necessitating methane capture systems to mitigate climate impact.

The big question is whether the biodegradation of biodegradable polymer blends and composites raises concerns regarding the degradation of by-products and their potential environmental impact. While biodegradation offers the advantage of reducing the accumulation of plastic waste in landfills and oceans, concerns have been raised about the potential of releasing harmful substances. Under controlled industrial or laboratory conditions, assessing biodegradation based on standard procedures is simpler than in real-life contexts including soils and oceans, which have varying microbial populations.301 According to Ali et al.,302 because biodegradation involves a mixture of identified and unidentified substances that may be hazardous to animals and soil health, it can both pose challenges and offer advantages in complex ecosystems. Unknown substances with roughly 32% cytotoxicity, 23% anti-androgenicity, 42% oxidative stress, and 67% baseline toxicity in bioassays have been shown to be present in bioplastics according to some studies. These compounds have the potential to negatively impact soil and animal health. Ecotoxicity assessments play a crucial role in evaluating the environmental implications of biodegradable polymer blends and composites. These assessments involve evaluating the potential toxicity resulting from the degradation of various organisms in aquatic and terrestrial environments. Such testing includes a focus on endpoints such as reproductive effects, acute and chronic toxicity, and bioaccumulation potential. To be deemed environmentally benign, these polymers, their blends, and composites must pass toxicity testing and break down into fragments within a given amount of time. However, one of the major setbacks in assessing the ecotoxicity of biodegradable polymers is the lack of standardized testing procedures and regulatory frameworks, unlike the biodegradation and compostability of plastics that have standardized and established testing procedures with clearly outlined regulatory requirements.303 Unlike biodegradation and controlled composting, there seems to be no specific standard for assessing the ecotoxicity of these materials in different environments. In fact, two ASTM standards, i.e., ASTM D5152-91; practice for water extraction of residual solids from degraded plastics for toxicity testing304 and ASTM D5951-96(2002); standard practice for preparing residual solids obtained after biodegradability standard methods for plastics in solid waste for toxicity and compost quality testing305 were withdrawn in 1998 and 2011, respectively, with no replacements. Hence the assessment of the ecotoxicity of biodegradable materials presents unique complexities as a result of their various compositions and degradation pathways. The multifaceted complexities in the assessment of the ecotoxicity of polymer blends and composites require ecotoxicity testing procedures suited for biodegradable polymers for understanding the possible environmental problems that may be associated with them. A study by Palsikowski et al.306 on ecotoxicological assessment of PLA, PBAT, and their compatibilized blend in soil found that the biodegradable materials and their blends did not exhibit phytotoxic (adverse effects on plant growth, physiology, or metabolism), cytotoxic (quality of being toxic to cells), genotoxic (damaging to DNA or genetic material), or mutagenic (causing genetic mutations) effects on the meristematic cells of Allium cepa, except for a chromosomal aberration index observed in one experiment with the blend 25/75. Sforzini et al.307 used biotests to evaluate the ecotoxicity impact of Mater-Bi, a biodegradable plastic, on soil organisms. The ecotoxicity tests on Mater-Bi biodegradable plastic showed no harmful effects on soil organisms, including autotrophic organisms, Daphnia magna, and Eisenia andrei. In their discussion of the environmental fate and ecotoxicity assessment of biodegradable polymers, Farachi et al.308 emphasized the importance of assessing the possible ecological dangers that may be connected to biodegradable materials. Carteny et al.309 hypothesized that in marine environments, biodegradable microplastics may accumulate more contaminants than conventional microplastics, despite emitting fewer additives. Life cycle analyses (LCAs) are the most complete tools to evaluate the entire lifecycle of recyclable polymers, blends and their composites, starting from the raw material stage to the final disposal stage or end of life. Through LCAs, factors such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and ecotoxicity potential are evaluated. These analyses help identify challenges and opportunities to enhance the sustainability of biodegradable materials.

Despite advancements in plastic waste management strategies including mechanical and chemical recycling, thermal treatments, and microbial biodegradation a substantial fraction of plastic waste continues to be openly burned or relegated to landfills without adequate treatment. Open burning releases carbon monoxide and other hazardous pollutants, exacerbating air quality issues [68]. Ecotoxicity assessments play a crucial role in evaluating the environmental implications of biodegradable polymer blends and composites. These assessments involve evaluating the potential toxicity resulting from the degradation of various organisms in aquatic and terrestrial environments. Such testing includes a focus on endpoints such as reproductive effects, acute and chronic toxicity, and bioaccumulation potential. To be deemed environmentally benign, these polymers, their blends, and composites must pass toxicity testing and break down into fragments within a given amount of time. However, one of the major setbacks in assessing the ecotoxicity of biodegradable polymers is the lack of standardized testing procedures and regulatory frameworks, unlike the biodegradation and compostability of plastics that have standardized and established testing procedures with clearly outlined regulatory requirements.303 Unlike biodegradation and controlled composting, there seems to be no specific standard for assessing the ecotoxicity of these materials in different environments. In fact, two ASTM standards, i.e., ASTM D5152-91; practice for water extraction of residual solids from degraded plastics for toxicity testing304 and ASTM D5951-96(2002); standard practice for preparing residual solids obtained after biodegradability standard methods for plastics in solid waste for toxicity and compost quality testing305 were withdrawn in 1998 and 2011, respectively, with no replacements. Hence the assessment of the ecotoxicity of biodegradable materials presents unique complexities as a result of their various compositions and degradation pathways. The multifaceted complexities in the assessment of the ecotoxicity of polymer blends and composites require ecotoxicity testing procedures suited for biodegradable polymers for understanding the possible environmental problems that may be associated with them. A study by Palsikowski et al.306 on ecotoxicological assessment of PLA, PBAT, and their compatibilized blend in soil found that the biodegradable materials and their blends did not exhibit phytotoxic (adverse effects on plant growth, physiology, or metabolism), cytotoxic (quality of being toxic to cells), genotoxic (damaging to DNA or genetic material), or mutagenic (causing genetic mutations) effects on the meristematic cells of Allium cepa, except for a chromosomal aberration index observed in one experiment with the blend 25/75. Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].

Natural and synthetic biodegradable polymers comprise of several advantages such as tissue compatibility, biodegradability, low toxicity, sustained release property with specific target-oriented delivery approaches [7], [8], [9]. The multifarious applications of biodegradable polymers cover an enormous area in novel drug delivery system and oral vaccination. Such kind of strategies have been employed in water borne diseases like cholera and auto immune diseases like atrophic rhinitis [13], [14]. Bioavailability is a major concern for various therapeutic molecules delivered through oral route [15]. Oral bioavailability problem of drugs arises due to their poor solubility and less permeability through biological membranes [16]. However, the pre-systemic metabolism also can significantly affect the bioavailability of therapeutic molecules along with these two parameters (solubility and permeability) [17]. Orally administered drugs (except drugs intended through buccal and sublingual route) generally have to pass through the intestinal wall and portal circulation of liver before they reach to systemic circulation [18], [19]. Intestinal and hepatic enzymes significantly metabolise drugs and may result in poor bioavailability due to inadequate plasma concentration required for the desired therapeutic response [20]. The importance and comparison of the role of hepatic and intestinal enzymes in the bioavailability of various therapeutic molecules are also studied. The reports suggest the predominant role of intestinal enzymes in pre-systemic metabolism over hepatic enzymes because there is relatively high blood supply in liver as compared to intestine. Thus, the residence time of therapeutic molecules in intestine is relatively high as compared to liver as a result drugs remain in contact with intestinal enzyme for more time and ultimately lead to higher metabolism and poor bioavailability [21], [22]. The biodegradable polymers have shown various promising applications in improving the bioavailability of such therapeutic molecules with poor bioavailability. Curcumin obtained from turmeric (Curcuma longa) possesses several medicinal properties but low aqueous solubility limits its therapeutic efficacy [23], [24]. Due to its hydrophobicity, curcumin is poorly bioavailable. Bioavailability of curcumin has been effectively modified by encapsulating it in biodegradable polymer preparations like PLGA-curcumin (poly lactic acid-co-glycolic acid curcumin) [25] and cyclodextrin encapsulated curcumin [26]. Several bioactive molecules effective in number of diseases have been successfully encapsulated using biodegradable polymers in order to obtain improved bioavailability, controlled release, targeted delivery and reduced side effects. Gomez-Gaete et al. encapsulated dexamethasone into biodegradable poly (D, L-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) nanoparticles to avoid side effects arise in systemic administration of the drug alone into the vitreous cavity. The developed nanoparticulate delivery system provided improved drug retention in the vitreous cavity as well as improved targeting efficiency [27]. Oral bioavailability of daunorubicin (DAUN) was 10-fold improved when chitosan coated DAUN-PLGA nanoparticles were given to wister rats as compared to free DAUN [28]. Mady and Shaker enhanced oral bioavailability of ellagic acid (EA) (naturally occurring bioactive in cancer therapy), formulating ellagic acid-nanoparticles (EA-NPs) using poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) as the biodegradable polymer. In vivo study revealed 3.6-fold increase in area under the curve for EA-NPs as compared to EA alone [29]. When therapeutic molecules are incorporated into polymeric systems, some major criteria are taken into consideration such as encapsulation efficiency, retention time which ultimately lead to the improvement in bioavailability of therapeutic molecules [30]. It has also been observed that the drug conjugated with biodegradable polymer is much superior with respect to therapeutic impact and also in terms of controlled and targeted delivery [31], [32]. Further, improvement in therapeutic efficacy and targeted delivery may be influenced by particle size, hydrophobicity, surface charge and surface modification of conjugated system [33]. The size, shape and structure of nanoparticles control their physico-chemical properties which play very important role during their transportation across the biological membranes [34]. It is generally agreed that decrease in particles size increases absorption of particulate systems [35]. Surface charge is also important for absorption of therapeutic molecules across the biological barrier and generally it also determines the interaction of molecules with charged biological membranes [36], [37]. Lipophilicity is another important parameter to ascertain bioavailability of the drugs and in nutshell, smaller particle size with proper hydrophilic-lipophilic balance is always preferable to get desired therapeutic response. In this context, polymeric nanoparticles have done considerably better job to improve the bioavailability of numerous drugs. In some disease conditions like cancer, it is also desirable that drug concentration should be constant and continuous at the targeted site in single dose formulation [38], [39]. Sometimes chemotherapy with drug alone leads serious side effects due to higher concentration at a particular site and such condition may be completely avoided by incorporating the therapeutic molecule in conjugated system with biopolymers [40], [41]. In recent time, polymeric micro-/nano-particulate systems such as microspheres [42], [43], microparticles [44], [45], [46] and nanoparticles [47], [48], [49], [50] have gained much importance not only for the delivery of synthetic or natural drug molecules but also for the delivery of the therapeutic protein, peptide and oligonucleotides through oral route.

The polymer is capable of prolonged release of a thrombolytic agent Designing systems for the controlled drug delivery which are based on biodegradable polymers is one of the most promising and rapidly developing areas of chemical technology [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. Such polymers are used to manufacture nano- and micro-particles, membranes and coatings. Nano- and micro-particles are usually used as carriers [6]. Membranes are used to make isolating materials and bandages [7]. Coatings are applied to implants - e.g., prostheses, pins and stents, medical devices used to expand narrowed hollow organs [8]. Local release of drugs from biodegradable polymers can solve a number of potential postoperative complications at the site of implantation. Accordingly, the problems actively studied today are (1) the search for materials that can make a basis for biodegradable coatings and (2) the search for pharmaceuticals that retain their chemical structure upon incorporation into polymer coatings and can diffuse from them in a controlled manner, depending on the external conditions [10]. The main advantage of controlled drug delivery systems is their ability to maintain the required level of a preparation in tissues and biological fluids for a long time - long enough to complete the therapy [11]. The effectiveness of controlled drug delivery systems is largely determined by the properties of the materials that the systems are made of. [12]. In addition to the key ability to release pharmaceutical preparations in a controlled manner, such materials should be biocompatible, biodegradable and atraumatic - and should also have a number of necessary physicochemical and mechanical properties [13]. A promising material for controlled drug delivery systems is considered to be poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [14]. It is usually synthesized from lactic and glycolic acids or obtained by enzymatic fermentation of carbohydrates. In both cases, renewable raw materials of biological origin are used to produce PLGA [15]. The physicochemical properties of PLGA are determined by the molar ratio and the sequential arrangement of lactic and glycolic acids in the polymer chain. PLGA copolymers can be obtained with different molecular weights and structure, making it possible to vary the degree of interaction between macromolecules [16]. Hence, the physicochemical properties of PLGA can vary quite a lot depending on the composition of the polymer. PLGA polymers are known to be biodegradable and biocompatible. [17]. They are already used in medicine to manufacture surgical sutures and subcutaneous implants [18], as well as to treat the surface of dental implants [19]. PLGA polymers are also used in orthopedy and cosmetology [20]. It is already possible to make PLGA-based systems for the controlled delivery of low molecular weight pharmaceuticals [21]. PLGA-based matrices can also be used to incapsulate enzymes [22]. The possibility of using PLGA-based systems for the controlled delivery of high molecular weight compounds - systems which would have all the necessary physicochemical properties - is yet to be confirmed though. In this work, we offer a number of technological solutions for the synthesis of PLGA-based polymer membranes and coatings with necessary mechanical properties. Our objective was to create biodegradable PLGA-based coatings for stents, which would be capable of prolonged release of the antithrombotic agent streptokinase. Upon entering the bloodstream, streptokinase interacts with plasminogen (profibrinolysin) and forms an “activator complex”, which catalyzes the conversion of blood plasminogen and blood clots into plasmin (fibrinolysin) [23]. Plasmin, a proteolytic enzyme, cleavages fibrin filaments of blood clots and catalyzes degradation of fibrinogen and other plasma proteins, including V (accelerin) and VII (convertin) coagulation factors [24]. Thus, streptokinase dissolves blood clots, acting both on their surface and from the inside [25]. It is most effective for dissolving fresh clots of fibrin (before retraction). The enzyme restores patency of thrombosed blood vessels and is inactivated by the antibodies circulating in the blood [26]. The novelty of this work lies in the synthesis and testing of a range of biodegradable PLGA-based polymer membranes, possessing the necessary mechanical properties and capable of a directional and sustained release of biomacromolecules with high molecular weight. To synthesize PLGA-based membranes, copolymers of PLGA (50:50) (Creative Biolabs, USA) of various molecular weights (45, 90, and 180 kDa) were used. Since it is not quite correct to apply the concept of molecular weight to a polymer product, hereafter we shall use the term molar mass (kg/mol). Preliminary experiments showed that solutions with the concentration of PLGA in the range of 2.8-3.2% are most suitable for the formation of membranes. The solutions of 3% PLGA (Creative Biolabs, USA) in chloroform (Irea 2000, Russia) were prepared by stirring for 1 h at 57°С, until homogeneity. To incorporate streptokinase into the membrane, a colloidal solution of streptokinase in phosphate-buffered saline (15 mM, pH = 7.4) was added to the homogeneous PLGA solution. The resulting mixture was poured into 12-mL plastic molds (85 mm in diameter). The PLGA-based membranes were prepared by the method of casting of the polymer solution followed by a two-step solvent evaporation [27]. The first evaporation step was carried out for 3 h at a pressure of 50 Torr; the second step, for 5 h at 3 Torr. After solidification, the membranes were deposited for 1 day at the atmospheric pressure and temperature of 40 °C.

question: How does the molecular weight (Mn) of PLA influence its transition from a ductile to a brittle material during degradation?

When the number-average molecular weight (Mn) drops below a critical entanglement molecular weight (typically ~40,000 Da), the polymer chain entanglements are insufficient to sustain plastic deformation, causing the material to lose structural integrity and become brittle.

Many researches have been carried out to improve the brittleness of PLA. These researches can be classified into 3 groups, which are small-molecule plasticizers, flexible co-polymers and elastomeric toughening agents. Examples of small-molecule plasticizers include citrate esters, triacetine and low molecular weight poly (ethylene glycol) (Mw = 300-400 g/mol) [[5], [6], [7], [8], [9]]. Poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) was the most studied plasticizer for PLA, where low molecular weight PEG possessed better plasticizing effect and could accelerate the spherulite growth rate of PLA [5]. However, PEG and other small-molecule plasticizers were not suitable for long-term usage due to the blooming problem [[10], [11], [12]]. Flexible co-polymers used to blend with PLA were usually block- or graft- copolymers, such as random aliphatic copolyesters, ethylene/n-butyl acrylate/glycidyl methacrylate (EBAGMA) [13], and ring opening of δ-valerolactone (VL) and ε-caprolactone (CL) [14]. Some of these polymers could improve the toughness of PLA, but their synthesis methods were complicated leading to high cost. The last alternative was by blending with toughening agents such as commercial natural and synthetic rubbers, as well as thermoplastic elastomers. This method is interesting as it could avoid complicated synthesis processes without a blooming problem. Bitinis et al. (2011) found that the optimal NR content to improve the brittleness of PLA was 10 wt%, where the tensile tests of the samples showed a drastic increase in the average elongation at break from 5% to 200% [2]. Kowalczyk and Piorkowska researched on mechanisms of plastic deformation in biodegradable polylactide/poly(1,4-cis-isoprene) blends and found that incorporation of only 5 wt% of rubber could significantly increase the strain at break of compression molded film during uniaxial drawing, and could improve its tensile strength by 80% [15]. Petchwattana and Covavisaruch studied the toughness improvement of poly (lactic acid)/ rubber wood sawdust composite by using acrylic core-shell rubber (CSR). They found that 5% of CSR could improve the impact strength of the composite by more than five times with improved tensile elongation at break [16].Rui-lei et al. (2014) studied the improvement in toughness of polylactic acid by melt blending with bio-based polyurethane elastomer (TPU). They found that 15 wt% of TPU had the highest improvement in impact strength from 4 kJ/m2 to 9 kJ/m2 [17]. Sachiko et al. [18] studied toughening of PLA by melt blending with various rubbers, which were ethylene-propylene copolymer (EPDM), ethylene-acrylic rubber (ACM), acrylonitrile-butadiene rubber (NBR), and isoprene rubber (IR) in an effort to toughen PLA. They found that PLA/NBR (20%wt) possessed the highest impact strength (250 J/m); however, their impact strength of referenced PLA (150 J/m) was much higher than those reported in other literatures (25-35 J/m). This means NBR can only improve the impact strength of PLA by 1.6 times. Desa et al. [19] studied rubber toughened PLA using NR, epoxidized natural rubber (ENR) and CSR. Therefore, it is of interest to investigate the performance of different rubbers as impact modifiers in PLA based on their structures and functional groups. The rubbers included in this research were isoprene rubber (IR), acrylic rubber (AR), acrylic core-shell rubber (CSR), thermoplastic polyester (TPE) and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). Nowadays, the importance of bio-based polymers is emerging due to environmental issues. Among biopolymers, poly(lactic acid), PLA, is one of the most studied biodegradable polymers. PLA is biodegradable and biocompatible, and above all, it has great potential for industrial applications due to its excellent processability.1-10 However, PLA has a serious limit for use in industrial applications because it is brittle due to its slow crystallization.1-5 Thus, it is critical to overcome this limitation of PLA for its use in future applications. PLA has a high tensile strength, but it is brittle. Thus, it is important to impart ductility to PLA. Ductility has been induced with plasticizers11, 12 or by blending with a rubbery elastomer.13-21 Among these methods, blending is known to be economical. Natural rubber (NR),13, 22, 23 polycaprolactone (PCL),24, 25 ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA),26, 27 and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT)28, 29 are among the representative examples of elastomers that are blended with PLA for toughening. The toughening mechanism of the polymer blend has been widely studied. The main toughening mechanisms are crazing (fine cracks and fibril formation) and shear-yielding (chain slippage).26, 30, 31 The dominant mechanism for dissipating energy varies depending on the nature of the main matrix polymer.24, 30-33 However, the critical dispersed phase size or the distance between dispersed phases for blend toughening exists under the assumption that the interfacial adhesion within the blend is constant. Therefore, when using a blend system composite in which a third phase (particles, polymers, etc.) is added to the blend, the properties of the polymers or the blend interface changes due to the additives dispersed within the blend.34 Therefore, it is not possible to determine the toughening mechanism by considering the morphological effect alone.

As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. Blending PLA with another immiscible or miscible polymer with higher melt viscosity is perhaps a less expensive and practical alternative way to prepare a variety of useful composites and alloys. Blends of PLA with PCL,11, 12 atactic poly[(R, S)-3-hydroxybutyrate],13 poly(ethylene succinate),14 hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol),15 poly(methyl methacrylate),16 poly(ethylene glycol),17 and poly(vinylphenol),18 have been investigated. Most of the above studies revealed that blending PLA with other polymers can substantially modify the mechanical and thermal properties, degradation rate, and permeability, but few distinct evidence of the improvement for melt viscosity can be found in these blends. Recently, Jiang et al.19 showed that the melt elasticity of the biodegradable PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends increased with the concentration of PBAT increasing via blending process, but the viscosity increase is limited. Carboxyl-ended polyester (CP) and solid epoxy (SE) have been widely used in polyester powder coating because they can form a crosslinking structure, and the viscosity of PLA will increase after in situ crosslink if CP and SE are added into the PLA matrix. In this article, CP and SE are used as the modifier of PLA to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA. Compared with the above-mentioned methods (increasing molecular weight, branching/crosslinking and incorporating new functional groups into PLA backbone), this method with CP/SE as the modifier has some outstanding advantages. For instance, the reaction temperature of CP/SE is close to the processing temperature of PLA; CP/SE has a high melt viscosity after reaction, and abundant functional end groups, which are easily accessible. With the unique crosslinking structure after reaction, CP/SE results in the different dispersion phase size and stereo hindrance for the linear polymer. Furthermore, the abundance of hydroxyl end groups attached to CS/SE may have some H-bonding interactions with PLA.20 Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the incorporation of CP/SE into PLA may bring about either the improved melt viscosity or the increased strength.
In the development of sustainable or eco-friendly materials, polylactic acid (PLA) stands out because of its good stiffness and strength, which have enabled it to compete with some commodity plastics.1, 2 However, the inherent brittleness of PLA is a bottleneck that limits its use in engineering applications.3, 4 Although the addition of plasticizers such as poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) will overcome the brittleness of PLA, it comes with a loss of stiffness or decreased elasticity modulus, which is an important property for semi-structural applications.2, 4, 5 A typical goal of the blending of PLA with other polymers is to increase elongation at break and toughness without adversely affecting the tensile strength and tensile modulus of the resulting material. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. Depending on the crystallization conditions, PLA exhibits rich polymorphism with various ordering degrees, namely α, α’, β and γ-forms [5]. Among them, the low-ordered α’ and β-forms PLA are recognized to have a lower mechanical modulus but higher ductility due to the loose chains packing in crystal lattices [[27], [28], [29]]. 1.  **Molecular weight reduction drives degradation:** PLA degradation involves hydrolytic chain scission, significantly reducing its molecular weight (Mn) over time [1, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12].

3.  **Loss of entanglement and interchain interactions:** Polymers with lower Mn have fewer intramolecular entanglements and weaker interchain interactions [4]. Evidence [11, 12] further supports that a drastic decrease in Mn correlates with rapid property deterioration.
5.  **Mn controls degradation rate and thus transition timing:** Lower initial Mn PLA degrades faster due to fewer entanglements and interactions making water penetration easier [4, 5]. Therefore, the transition from ductile to brittle occurs more rapidly compared to higher initial Mn PLA, which degrades slower and retains its entanglements/properties longer [4, 5, 10, 11, 12].

Polylactic acid (PLA) is a bio-based and biodegradable polyester synthesized from renewable resources such as corn starch and sugarcane. Due to its excellent mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and thermal stability, PLA has been widely utilized in applications ranging from disposable packaging to biomedical implants [1]. However, despite being classified as biodegradable, PLA degradation in natural environments is significantly slow, primarily relying on hydrolysis followed by microbial assimilation [2]. This slow degradation rate limits its large-scale application in sustainable materials, necessitating effective strategies to enhance its biodegradability. Enzymatic degradation has emerged as an effective and eco-friendly approach to accelerate PLA breakdown. Among various hydrolytic enzymes, lipases have demonstrated promising results in catalyzing ester bond hydrolysis in polyesters. In particular, Candida rugosa lipase has shown high efficiency in degrading PLA by targeting its ester linkages, promoting rapid depolymerization under controlled conditions [3-5]. Recent studies suggest that embedding C. rugosa lipase directly into PLA films enhances self-degradation, offering a novel strategy for improving polymer biodegradability. Furthermore, research on enzyme concentration effects and degradation kinetics has provided insights into optimizing lipase-assisted PLA breakdown under various environmental conditions [6, 7].
Till now, biodegradable synthetic polymers have very promising applications in the biomedical field, including tissue engineering, drug controlled release, gene delivery, wound dressing, post-operative anti-adhesion, etc [1], [2]. Among the synthetic polymers, aliphatic polyesters such as polyglycolide (PGA), polylactide (PLA) and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), have generated an enormous amount of research and interest owing to their biodegradability and biocompatibility [3], [4], [5]. As one of the most important aliphatic polyesters, PCL has been used in several FDA approved products due to its facile accessibility, good solubility, low melting temperature and excellent blend-compatibility [5], [6], [7]. The enzymatic and hydrolytic degradation of PCL has been widely investigated [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Three kinds of lipase, i.e. Rhizopus delemer lipase, Rhizopus arrhizus lipase and Pseudomonas lipase, have been reported as capable of effectively accelerating the hydrolytic degradation of PCL [13], [14], [15], [16]. Highly crystalline PCL was reported to totally degrade in several days in the presence of Pseudomonas lipase [17], while hydrolytic degradation required several years at 37 °C [18]. Recently, further studies have been focused on the properties modification of PCL polymers, by introducing hydrophilic/hydrophobic segment by blend or copolymerization techniques.
Numerous studies and patents have been published on the enzymatic depolymerization of biodegradable aliphatic polyesters, often utilizing enzymes such as lipase or Proteinase K [120]. This process involves the initial breakdown of polymers into oligomers and further depolymerization into monomers. Lipases can increase the depolymerization rate by up to 30%, even at lower temperatures, thus reducing enzyme degradation. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that enzyme Immobilization on solid supports can enhance enzyme stability and recyclability, potentially increasing the number of recycling cycles from 3 to 10. Enzymes such as cutinase, lipases, and proteases, as well as specialized enzymes like PETase, play a crucial role in biodegradation by breaking down bioplastic polymers into simpler, eco-friendly monomers that microbes can metabolize. Microorganisms like Pseudomonas, Bacillus, Aspergillus, and Penicillium secrete these enzymes, driving the decomposition process, which typically takes three to six months to degrade substrates (Fig. 8). However entirely, challenges persist such as the enzyme instability under extreme conditions (temperature, pH), poor substrate binding affinity, and susceptibility to proteolytic degradation limit their efficiency in industrial settings [115]. Advancements in protein engineering and immobilization techniques have been pivotal. Protein engineering utilizes tools such as machine learning and artificial intelligence to optimize enzyme structures, thereby enhancing thermostability, substrate specificity, and catalytic efficiency. Complementary strategies include novel high-throughput screening methods to identify superior enzyme variants and reinforcement of enzyme surfaces to improve substrate binding (highlighted in the “Bioengineered proteins for bioplastic degradation” framework). Immobilization techniques further enable enzyme reuse and stability by anchoring enzymes to solid supports, mitigating degradation risks. Modern bioengineering methods, such as gene cloning and metagenomics (Fig. 8), have expanded the discovery of novel enzymes and microbial producers. For instance, microbial consortia exhibit synergistic effects by combining multiple species with complementary enzymatic activities, accelerating degradation kinetics. Species like Bacillus and Aspergillus are particularly promising due to their robust secretion of lipases and proteases, while Pseudomonas demonstrates versatility in degrading complex polymer blends. Despite progress, scaling up enzyme production while maintaining cost-effectiveness, ensuring long-term stability in industrial waste streams, and optimizing microbial co-cultures for consistent performance remain key hurdles. Continued innovation at the intersection of enzyme engineering, microbial ecology, and integrated waste management systems is essential to fully harness the potential of biodegradable plastics, aligning with the circular economy model depicted in the bioplastic lifecycle framework [115]. For instance, lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds of polyesters having a relatively large number of methylene groups such as PCL, PESu, PBSu and PBSA, but cannot catalyze degradation reactions in polyesters having optically active carbons [324]. Such optically active polyesters with high melting temperature; i.e. PLLA, P3HB and P3HV, require the use of proteinase-like enzymes or PHB-depolymerases [315], [325]. Since the discovery of the conversion of starch into sugars by diastase in 1833, the role of enzymes as biocatalysts has been deeply investigated [326]. Enzymes are proteins formed by many different amino acids with a peculiar three-dimensional structure and become essential to support life as they are responsible of catalyzing in vivo metabolic reactions in living cells [329], [330], [331]. The specific region where the catalytic reactions takes place within enzymes is known as the active site, whose activity is determined by the spatial arrangement and the electrostatic properties of the amino acids that surround this site [332], [333]. Enzymes could be classified into 6 main classes according to Enzyme Commission (EC) number: oxidoreductases (EC.1), transferases (EC.2), hydrolases (EC.3), lyases (EC.4), isomerases (EC.5) and ligases (EC.6) [334]. Cutinases are multifunctional enzymes with good stability in the 20-50 °C temperature range and pH 8-11 which are able to hydrolyze ester bonds of cutin [338].

Percolation threshold in nanocellulose composites was shown to be dependent on the size, shape and orientation of the particles, and on interactions among them.83 Models determined for rod-shape particles in composites show that C* is inversely proportional to the particle aspect ratio.83,84 For instance, C* in CNC systems ranges from 1% (v/v) for tunicate CNCs (5 nm wide, 1000 nm long) and 5.9% (v/v) for cotton CNCs (∼15 nm wide, ∼172 nm long).83 For BC (5-50 nm wide, 100-1000 nm long), the reported C* is 6% (v/v).83 Based on a model for fibre percolation in composites and Monte Carlo simulations, C* was shown to be influenced by fibre orientation, particularly when the aspect ratio is lower than 100.85 For fibres with aspect ratios of 50, the determined C* was ∼20 and ∼10% (v/v) in anisotropic and isotropic assemblies, respectively.85 Based on similar models for each cellulose building block in dispersions, or solutions, it would be possible to control ρapp and to predict the lowest value that a system can offer. Controlling density is thus fundamental to achieve most target properties, as described in the following sections, and also to reduce the amount of cellulose required to build the material. The reason for choosing compressive over tensile testing is likely to be practical: porous structures of cellulose can be easily compressed (stress as low as 1 kPa),88 such that the specimen would be deformed if gripped for typical tensile testing. Impact properties are regularly determined in porous materials, though the main target applications (sorbents,24 tissue scaffolds,89 heat insulation,2,90 and sound-absorbing boards)5,11 do not involve impact. Generally, designing particle-reinforced polymer matrix composites is concerned with the maximum efficiency for polymer property improvement and the maximum loading level of particles in the matrix.21 Establishing percolation networks of particles within the polymer matrix is a primary cut-off criterion for the composite performance.22-25 Percolation describes the dispersion of particles in a random system to form larger connected clusters spanning across the entire system at a certain critical volume fraction, referred to as the percolation threshold.26 Numerous literatures showed that the percolation threshold of nanosized rod-like cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) varies among different polymer matrices.27-33 Santamaria-Echart et al.30 evaluated the CNC percolation threshold in a waterborne polyurethane matrix by measuring the tensile and thermomechanical properties of the resulting nanocomposites. In this study, enhancements in tensile stress at yield (36%), tensile modulus (16%), and thermomechanical stability were observed at the CNC percolation threshold (3 wt.% CNC). Sheets of styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) reinforced with varying levels of CNC from 0.5 to 8 wt.% (based on rubber weight) were fabricated by a solution casting process.28 The tear strength and maximum work required to tear the sheets increased at CNC loading level above 4 wt.% in the SBR latex, at which point the percolation of CNC occurred. Two CNC percolation thresholds at around 0.8 and 1.5 wt.% in poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) matrix were revealed and the mechanical and hydrolytic properties of CNC-PBS nanocomposites showed significant changes at the threshold.29 As discussed above, CNC particles in solution or latex can building a continuous rigid network through hydrogen bonds at the percolation threshold, thereby dramatically improving the performance of polymer composites.33 However, for SDCNC particles, the particle size (microscale), morphologies, and surface energy differs dramatically from CNC on a nanoscale, which are the factors influencing the threshold.19, 33-37 In addition, hydrogen-bonded SDCNC particle networks cannot be built in the melt compounding process as the networks are established during the solution casting process by the solvent drying process.38 Therefore, the effect of percolation threshold on composite performance is entirely different for SDCNC particles in a thermoplastic matrix manufactured using a melt compounding process. In more detail, the contact point between SDCNC particles could function as a discontinuity surface rather than forming strong hydrogen bonds, facilitating composite failure under external stress. Surpassing the percolation threshold could also potentially lead to SDCNC particle agglomeration, inducing stress concentration points and weakening the effective stress transfer from SDCNC to the polymer matrix.39 Hence, research on evaluating the percolation threshold of SDCNC particles in polymer matrix is beneficial for developing high-performance SDCNC PP composites.

Based on the provided evidence, the percolation threshold in conductive biodegradable nanocomposites refers to the critical concentration (volume or weight fraction) of conductive filler required to form a continuous, interconnected network within an insulating biodegradable polymer matrix. This network enables electrical conductivity through the composite by establishing conductive pathways across the material. Key aspects include:

1.  **Definition and Significance:** It marks the insulator-to-conductor transition, where a sharp decrease in electrical resistance occurs due to the formation of the first continuous conductive pathway. Near this threshold, the composite exhibits high sensitivity to external stimuli (like strain), making it crucial for applications such as piezoresistive sensors [4].
2.  **Threshold Values in Biodegradable Systems:** Reported values vary significantly depending on the filler, matrix, and processing method. Examples include:
    *   ≈ 0.47 vol% for MWCNTs in biodegradable polybutylene succinate (PBS) [14].
    *   As low as 0.049 vol% in MWCNTs/PVB/PBS composites utilizing a double percolation structure [14].
    *   ≈ 0.48-0.50 vol% in systems like rGO/PHB and CB/TPU foam prepared via specific methods [11].
    *   ≈ 3 vol% for CNTs in polylactic acid (PLA) nanofiber membranes [8].
3.  **Influencing Factors:**
    *   **Filler Aspect Ratio:** Higher aspect ratio fillers (e.g., long, thin rods like CNTs or CNCs) lower the percolation threshold (`C*` is inversely proportional to aspect ratio) [1][4][13].
    *   **Filler Dispersion and Alignment:** Uniform dispersion is essential. Preferential alignment of nanocellulose substrates can create anisotropic conductive networks, significantly impacting piezoresistive sensitivity [4][13]. Agglomeration above the threshold can disrupt networks and increase the threshold [2][3][14].
    *   **Processing Method:** Solution casting or latex assembly generally facilitates better network formation through hydrogen bonding (for CNC) and lower thresholds compared to melt compounding, where network formation is hindered [2][3][4]. Specialized methods like aerogel formation combined with foaming [11] or double percolation structures [14] can drastically reduce the threshold.
    *   **Nanocellulose Additives:** Nanocellulose (e.g., CNCs) can act as "percolation directors," significantly reducing the percolation threshold of conductive fillers like CNTs (e.g., from 7.0 vol% to 1.6 vol%) by assisting in building hierarchical conductive structures [4].
    *   **Matrix-Filler Interactions:** Compatibility modifiers (e.g., PVB in PBS) can improve dispersion and enable double percolation, lowering the threshold [14]. Poor interfacial bonding can lead to higher thresholds [13].
4.  **Impact on Biodegradability:** While not directly defined by the threshold, the filler content (which relates to achieving percolation) influences biodegradability. Optimal nanofiller dispersion can slow biodegradation by creating a denser structure resistant to microbial/moisture ingress. Agglomeration or high filler content can accelerate degradation by creating weak points [9][12]. Nanofillers can sometimes inhibit biodegradation in complex systems [12].

Impact properties are regularly determined in porous materials, though the main target applications (sorbents,24 tissue scaffolds,89 heat insulation,2,90 and sound-absorbing boards)5,11 do not involve impact. Generally, designing particle-reinforced polymer matrix composites is concerned with the maximum efficiency for polymer property improvement and the maximum loading level of particles in the matrix.21 Establishing percolation networks of particles within the polymer matrix is a primary cut-off criterion for the composite performance.22-25 Percolation describes the dispersion of particles in a random system to form larger connected clusters spanning across the entire system at a certain critical volume fraction, referred to as the percolation threshold.26 Numerous literatures showed that the percolation threshold of nanosized rod-like cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) varies among different polymer matrices.27-33 Santamaria-Echart et al.30 evaluated the CNC percolation threshold in a waterborne polyurethane matrix by measuring the tensile and thermomechanical properties of the resulting nanocomposites. In this study, enhancements in tensile stress at yield (36%), tensile modulus (16%), and thermomechanical stability were observed at the CNC percolation threshold (3 wt.% CNC). Sheets of styrene butadiene rubber (SBR) reinforced with varying levels of CNC from 0.5 to 8 wt.% (based on rubber weight) were fabricated by a solution casting process.28 The tear strength and maximum work required to tear the sheets increased at CNC loading level above 4 wt.% in the SBR latex, at which point the percolation of CNC occurred. Two CNC percolation thresholds at around 0.8 and 1.5 wt.% in poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) matrix were revealed and the mechanical and hydrolytic properties of CNC-PBS nanocomposites showed significant changes at the threshold.29 As discussed above, CNC particles in solution or latex can building a continuous rigid network through hydrogen bonds at the percolation threshold, thereby dramatically improving the performance of polymer composites.33 However, for SDCNC particles, the particle size (microscale), morphologies, and surface energy differs dramatically from CNC on a nanoscale, which are the factors influencing the threshold.19, 33-37 In addition, hydrogen-bonded SDCNC particle networks cannot be built in the melt compounding process as the networks are established during the solution casting process by the solvent drying process.38 Therefore, the effect of percolation threshold on composite performance is entirely different for SDCNC particles in a thermoplastic matrix manufactured using a melt compounding process. In more detail, the contact point between SDCNC particles could function as a discontinuity surface rather than forming strong hydrogen bonds, facilitating composite failure under external stress. Surpassing the percolation threshold could also potentially lead to SDCNC particle agglomeration, inducing stress concentration points and weakening the effective stress transfer from SDCNC to the polymer matrix.39 Hence, research on evaluating the percolation threshold of SDCNC particles in polymer matrix is beneficial for developing high-performance SDCNC PP composites.

Graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) are promising conductive nanofillers due to their high aspect ratio and exceptional electrical and thermal properties [4]. GNP have the potential to form 3D conductive networks at much lower concentrations than 3D nanofillers, significantly reducing the percolation threshold in CPCs [5]. Numerous studies have reported enhanced electrical conductivity in polymers upon the addition of small amounts of graphene. For example, the incorporation of 0.52 vol% graphene into an epoxy matrix resulted in a conductivity of 10−2 S/m, 0.1 vol% graphene yielded 10−5 S/m in polystyrene (PS), and 0.47 vol% graphene led to a conductivity of 7.4 × 10−2 S/m in poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) [6]. However, GNP also exhibit a strong tendency of self-agglomeration, limiting their dispersion and raising the percolation threshold. One of the strategies to tailor the distribution of nanofillers within a polymer matrix is to introduce immiscible polymer blends with a cocontinuous morphology as a matrix for CPCs, where selective localization of the nanofillers at the polymer-polymer interface can dramatically lower the percolation threshold [7-9]. By localizing nanofillers at the interface, the amount of filler required for percolation is significantly lowered, improving both the material's performance and its processability. However, localization of the nanofiller in one phase has also been shown to reduce the percolation threshold through the double percolation effect [10, 11]. Double percolation in polymer nanocomposites refers to a structural phenomenon whereby two interconnected percolation networks are formed: one from a conductive filler within a polymer phase and another from the cocontinuous morphology of a polymer blend. This dual-network structure significantly enhances electrical or mechanical properties while reducing the filler content required for percolation [12, 13]. The localization and migration of nanofiller during melt compounding of polymer blends are significantly influenced by kinetic factors such as the compounding sequence [8, 14], melt viscosity of the individual polymers [14], mixing time [8, 15], and shear rate [16]. Several studies have demonstrated strategies to optimize these parameters. Mun et al. [9] reported that by controlling the mixing time and mixing sequences during melt blending, an ultralow percolation threshold of graphene (<0.1 vol%) was achieved in high-density polyethylene (HDPE)/polylactic acid (PLA) cocontinuous blends. Bai et al. [8] reported cocontinuous PLA/PS blends and interfacially localized reduced graphene oxide (r-GO) using kinetic control, achieving an ultralow percolation threshold of 0.028 vol%. Additionally, thermal annealing has been shown to promote nanofiller localization at the interface, as demonstrated in linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE)/ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) blends with GNP, achieving percolation at 0.5 vol% [17]. Based solely on the provided context evidence, the percolation threshold in conductive biodegradable nanocomposites is defined as follows:

1.  **Critical Filler Concentration**: It is the minimum critical volume or weight fraction of conductive filler (e.g., carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, carbon black) dispersed within an insulating biodegradable polymer matrix (e.g., polylactic acid (PLA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), natural rubber (NR), thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), nanocellulose) where a continuous, interconnected conductive network first forms throughout the material [1][2][3][4][5][7][9][10][13].
2.  **Insulator-to-Conductor Transition**: At this threshold concentration, the composite undergoes a percolative transition from being an electrical insulator to becoming a conductor, as the conductive pathways span the entire material [1][3][4][5][7][13].
3.  **Key Factor for Sensing**: Near the percolation threshold, the electrical resistance becomes highly sensitive to external stimuli (like strain), as small deformations readily disrupt the continuous conductive network, resulting in significant resistance changes crucial for piezoresistive sensors [1].
4.  **Influencing Factors**: The threshold value depends on:
    *   **Filler Characteristics**: Aspect ratio (higher ratio lowers threshold), shape, surface modification [1][8][9][10][11].
    *   **Matrix & Processing**: Polymer type, dispersion quality, alignment/orientation of fillers or matrix components (e.g., aligned nanocellulose enhances anisotropic sensing) [1][3][7][9][10].

Global environmental concerns have led to a progressive trend in producing and applying biobased and biodegradable polymers for various purposes. Nowadays, the principal approach of the packaging industry for waste management relies on adopting sustainable materials and developing eco-friendly packaging alternatives. One of the alternatives to petroleum-based plastics is the polylactic acid/polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PLA/PBAT) blends. These blends are often used in the production of biodegradable and compostable materials. It is worth mentioning that both blend components are biodegradable and bio-based polymers derived from renewable resources.1-3 Following a specific duration or exposure to stimuli such as moisture, UV light, biological microorganisms, and so on, these biodegradable plastics break down into basic chemicals, ideally comprising naturally occurring, non-toxic molecules.4 The biodegradability, compostability, and flexibility of the PLA/PBAT blend have led to significant commercial growth and broad application of this material in manufacturing packaging materials, disposable stuff, agriculture films, and textiles.5-7 As the main component of PLA/PBAT blend, PLA is a linear aliphatic polyester used extensively in biomedical applications due to its high modulus, significant strength, and excellent biocompatibility.8-10 The processing potential of PLA is predominantly constrained by its low melt strength, low heat deflection temperature, and high brittleness. PBAT is a promising choice for blending with PLA to produce blends with improved melt strength, toughness, ductility, and processability. The plastic market is dominated by petroleum-based products for single use applications, which take years to decompose. One viable solution involves the development of bio-composites, utilizing biodegradable polymers infused with abundant and underutilized bioderived material. Polyesters, particularly polylactic acid (PLA), have comparable physical and mechanical properties (high visibility, barrier properties, high modulus, and strength) to those of other thermoplastics namely, high density polyethylene (HDPE), polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET).1, 2 For this reason, PLA is mostly used in many applications such, as packaging, automotive, biomedical and so forth.3, 4 Nonetheless, PLA encounters inherent limitations that impede its use in specific applications.
