The thermal stability of the shorter linear and branching PLLs was lower than that of the longer linear PLL. In another work about Joncryl® ADR 4368, Wutisart [17] found that this chain extender can improve morphology and enhance mechanical characteristics of polybutylene succinate (PBS) and polycaprolactone (PCL) blend. However, Joncryl® ADR 4368 need to process at high temperature, therefore it is not appropriate to PCL which has very low melting temperature. They illustrated that when processing temperatures were increased, the processed PLA’s molecular weight (Mw) tended to decrease, and its molecular weight distribution (MWD) shifted towards to lower molecular weights zone, whereas Mw of chain extended PLA increased, and MWD displayed bimodal distribution and shifted slightly towards to higher molecular weight zone. The hydrolysable ester bonds offer potential for biodegradation in the environment, especially for polyesters that are susceptible to non-enzymatic hydrolysis at a moderate rate at ambient temperature. Their hydrolysis does not rely on enzymes, so degradation is likely to still take place under unfavourable conditions for biodegradation, such as in the deep sea. Therefore, non-enzymatically hydrolysable polyesters contribute to reducing plastic accumulation in the environment, especially for marine environments. Commercialisation of such polyesters may also reduce the effects of MNPs. Large quantities of biodegradable polyesters entering the environment can be considered as an input of carbon, which might affect the carbon and nitrogen dynamics.101-103 Some microbial species could be enriched by biodegradation and result in the change of microbial communities, which might decrease the biodiversity.102 For instance, lactic acid could facilitate the growth of lactic acid bacteria, which will generate toxic substance for other microbes and fungi.104 Therefore, qualitative and quantitative investigation into the biodegradation products and their interactions with (micro)organisms and the environment is necessary. Although the sensitivity to non-enzymatic hydrolysis will reduce the service life of the polymers/plastics (“plastics with an expiry date”), the benefits of environmental biodegradation not requiring specific hydrolase enzymes should outweigh the disadvantages. For many applications, we must consider the trade-off between convenience and reduction in environmental risk. Similar to the variety of thermal and mechanical properties, polyesters also show great potential for designing their biodegradability by selection of building blocks, even though this does require the development of novel synthetic approaches and copolymerisation. Generally, incorporation of cyclic monomers as rigid building blocks, including aromatic and aliphatic compounds, improves certain thermomechanical properties of polyesters. For hydrocarbon-based monomers, this typically leads to a regression in the biodegradation and/or non-enzymatic hydrolysis rate, which becomes worse with higher molar ratio of these cyclic monomers. This could be the result of (1) the decrease in the flexibility of the polymer chain, which decreases the probability of hydrolysis via enzymes with deep active-sites; and/or (2) the steric hindrance/hydrophobicity of the cyclic structure. As far as the problem of polymeric waste accumulation and disposal is concerned, two subcategories of related issues gravitate around the material typologies: the non-biodegradable and the biodegradable ones [1]. Indeed, especially in the textile sector (for apparel, upholstery, or technical applications), where massive and widely differentiated materials are discarded [2], it is commonly reported that non-biodegradable synthetic fabrics cause pollution if indiscriminately dispersed in the environment and, alternatively, they are difficult to recover completely, since they need complex procedures of separation and recycling, both from a mechanical and chemical point of view [3,4]. Even biological systems involving engineered enzymes have been developed as a novel solution to face this issue [5]. However, also biodegradable fabrics composed of biodegradable polymers (i.e., polylactic acid - PLA, poly-ε-caprolactam - PCL, polybutylene succinate - PBS, etc.) or natural biopolymers (i.e., cellulose, lignocellulose, keratin, fibroin) [[6], [7], [8], [9]] may present criticalities. In the case of biodegradable polymers, recent literature reports that during the biodegradation process, the materials can undergo only partial deterioration [10,11], not ensuring their sustainability and the absence of environmental risks (formation of debris, microplastics, toxic intermediates, etc.) [12,13]. Instead, textile materials based on biopolymers have complete inherent biodegradability. For instance, cotton (derived from the plant genus Gossypium L.) is composed of cellulose that, in turn, is constituted of glucose monomers linked by β-glycosidic bonds [14]. When cotton undergoes a biodegradation process, the involved enzymes (often endoglucanases and exoglucanases) induce cellulose structural amorphization and depolymerization up to the mineralization and the formation of non-toxic products (namely carbon dioxide and water, if occurring in an aerobic environment) [15,16]. Despite this theoretical end-of-life, biopolymer-based fabrics (not only cotton, but also silk and wool) can cause problems depending on their chemical finishing [2,17,18]. The finishing treatments, which are aimed at imparting specific functional properties [19,20] and include waterproofing, dyeing, softening and the conferring of antimicrobial properties and flame resistance, can inhibit biodegradation, prolonging the environmental half-lives of fibers [21]. The reasons lie in the specific nature of finishing, but also in the new bonds that are formed with the textile substrate [[21], [22], [23]]. Additionally, the release or the simultaneous degradation of the finishing compounds can be detrimental, potentially inducing the formation of toxic substances [8,24]. Among others, commonly used synthetic dyes', if leached, become recalcitrant pollutants [25] and can trigger soil erosion, deteriorate soil fertility, and destroy wildlife [26]. However, a recent article -almost countercurrent with respect to the general concern about the use of finishing products- has pointed out the possibility of treating the leather with substances that are not necessarily biodegradable but, above all, able to improve the soil characteristics, particularly plant germination and growth [27]. In this context, the present work focuses on the chitosan finishing effect on the biodegradability of cotton, alone or in combination with a natural dye. Chitosan is a random copolymer made by β-(1 → 4)-linked 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-d-glucopyranose and 2-amino-2-deoxy-d-glucopyranose units, obtained by the N-deacetylation of chitin, naturally occurring in the exoskeletons of crustaceans, insect cuticles and cell walls of some fungi [28,29]. Chitosan possesses unique properties that are mainly aroused by the presence of primary amino groups and it is generally considered a low-toxic, non-immunogenic and biodegradable polysaccharide [30,31]. The applications of chitosan fall in several technological fields: food industry (as a thickening and gelling additive), environmental remediation (as a flocculant, coagulant and adsorbent), agriculture (as a biocontrol agent for controlling diseases in plants), pharmaceutical and cosmetics (in drug delivery and as a formulation excipient), tissue engineering (as a scaffold and wound healing agent), packaging sector (as a bioplastic and bioactive component) and energy production (as a catalyst and electrolyte in fuel cells) [28,[32], [33], [34], [35], [36], [37]]. One of the main characteristics of chitosan that has made it so popular is its antimicrobial activity against microorganisms (fungi, bacteria and yeasts) [38,39]. The basilar mechanism relies on the electrostatic attraction between the positive NH3+ sites of chitosan and the cell membranes of microbes (negatively charged), whose interaction alters the permeability of the microbial cell, causing the release of intracellular components, impeding normal metabolic processes and finally resulting in cell death [40,41]. By virtue of these properties, chitosan has also attracted a lot of attention in the textile sector [[41], [42], [43], [44], [45]]. Beyond its employment to impart antimicrobial properties to textile materials, chitosan finishing has also been selected to improve anti-odor, anti-wrinkle and anti-felting characteristics and to act as a carrier and linker for further fabric modifications [43,46,47]. One of the uses as a linker concerns the dyeing process [[48], [49], [50]]. Anionic dyes have a low affinity to cellulose-based fibers due to charge repulsion in water. In these cases, chitosan can be used as an electrolyte, such as the widely used sodium chloride or sodium sulfate (salt effect), and is a safer alternative to cationizing agents [47] or metal-based mordants [51]. In fact, at a proper pH, NH3+ chitosan sites act as a cationic bridge, promoting the binding of cellulose with the dye [52]. Following this rationale, in a previous paper, some of us successfully combined Carmine Red with chitosan to dye cotton and polyamide 6,6 [53]. Indeed, Carmine Red is a natural colorant derived from the Cochineal insect crushing, whose composition is basically carminic acid (anthraquinone structure, anionic dye), which generally implies the use of mordants to be fixed on fabrics [54,55]. The fabrics obtained in [53] showed enhanced characteristics: stability, washing fastness and quick antibacterial properties (the fabric cotton-chitosan+Carmine Red abated in 12 min 94.2 % of Escherichia coli and 97.1 % of Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, respectively). The textile materials used in the present work have been produced as in [53], since they are considered established and known systems (also see Fig. S1 for a schematization of fabric components' interactions).

As illustrated in Figure 7, the life cycle of biodegradable aliphatic polyesters begins with the preparation of raw materials, where monomers are extracted from fossil fuels or plants. These raw materials are processed into products and manufactured into commercial items before being distributed. Common biodegradable aliphatic polyester-based products include drug delivery systems, wound dressings, skin tissue materials for biomedical purposes, grow bags, mulch films, and nets for agricultural practices.[23, 123, 131, 135] The widespread use of these products eventually leads to their disposal in landfills. Once disposed of, exposure to open areas and soil influences the biodegradation rate, allowing the waste to decompose into carbon dioxide, water, and methane, which ultimately become nutrients for plant growth. Poly (lactic acid) polymers (PLA) belong to the bioplastic family of polymers entirely derived from renewable resources. Finally, the effect of the chain extender was evaluated by adding the additive directly during the cast extrusion of slabs made with 100% post-process material. The results showed that the twin-screw compounding process induces a lower degradation in the material compared to the cast extrusion process. Based solely on the provided evidence, chain extenders play a multifaceted role in the recycling of biodegradable polyesters, primarily by counteracting degradation and restoring properties:

1.  **Rebuilding Molecular Weight:** Chain extenders react with carboxyl (-COOH) and hydroxyl (-OH) end groups generated by chain scissions during biodegradation or thermal processing. This reconnects broken chains, enhancing the molecular weight of the recycled polyester. This is essential for maintaining material properties [7][11][14].
2.  **Counteracting Property Loss:** Biodegradable polyesters are sensitive to thermal-hydrolytic degradation during processing (e.g., extrusion, thermoforming), leading to chain scission and reduced molecular weight. Adding chain extenders during recycling processes helps mitigate this degradation, maintaining or improving viscosity, melt strength, and tensile properties. This allows for repeated processing cycles using post-process waste material [6][7][14].
3.  **Improving Processability:** By increasing molecular weight and melt viscosity, chain extenders reduce the melt flow index of the recycled polyester. This enhances the material's processability in subsequent manufacturing steps like cast extrusion or blow film extrusion [6][7][14].
4.  **Enabling Compatibilization:** In blends involving biodegradable polyesters (e.g., PLA/PBAT, PLA/starch), chain extenders can improve compatibility between phases. This enhances interfacial adhesion, leading to better morphology, thermal stability, and mechanical properties (such as modulus, tensile strength, impact strength, and fracture strain) in the recycled blend [7][15].
5.  **Addressing Biodegradation Sensitivity:** While specifically focused on recycling, the evidence highlights that chain extenders are used to counteract the inherent tendency of biodegradable polyesters like PLA to degrade during thermal processing, which is a prerequisite for recovering post-process waste material effectively [14]. This degradation sensitivity is often linked to the hydrolysable ester bonds that also enable biodegradation [8][15].

Chitosan is a random copolymer made by β-(1 → 4)-linked 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-d-glucopyranose and 2-amino-2-deoxy-d-glucopyranose units, obtained by the N-deacetylation of chitin, naturally occurring in the exoskeletons of crustaceans, insect cuticles and cell walls of some fungi [28,29]. The fabrics obtained in [53] showed enhanced characteristics: stability, washing fastness and quick antibacterial properties (the fabric cotton-chitosan+Carmine Red abated in 12 min 94.2 % of Escherichia coli and 97.1 % of Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, respectively). The textile materials used in the present work have been produced as in [53], since they are considered established and known systems (also see Fig. S1 for a schematization of fabric components' interactions).

Based solely on the provided evidence, the role of chain extenders in the recycling of biodegraded polyesters is to counteract the degradation-induced reduction in molecular weight and improve material properties for reprocessing. Specifically:

1.  **Reconnect cleaved chains:** Biodegradation and thermal processing cause chain scissions in polyesters, lowering molecular weight and negatively impacting properties like viscosity and mechanical strength. Chain extenders are di- or poly-functional compounds that react with the terminal groups (e.g., carboxyl or hydroxyl) of the broken polymer chains, reconnecting them and increasing the molecular weight [2].
2.  **Increase viscosity and melt strength:** By reconnecting chains and increasing molecular weight, chain extenders significantly enhance the melt viscosity of the recycled polyester. This is evidenced by reduced melt flow indices and improved elongational viscosity, which is crucial for processing like extrusion or blow film molding [1], [2], [6].
3.  **Mitigate property degradation:** Adding chain extenders during recycling helps restore or improve key properties of the biodegraded/reprocessed polyester:
    *   **Mechanical Properties:** They can enhance tensile strength, modulus, fracture strain, and impact strength in recycled blends like PLA/PBAT (Ecovio) and PLA/PA6 [1], [2].
    *   **Thermal Properties:** Chain extenders influence the glass transition temperature (Tg), crystallization behavior, melting temperature (Tm), and thermal stability, often shifting these properties compared to the degraded material without extension [1], [2].
    *   **Processability:** The increased viscosity and melt strength improve the material's processability during recycling steps like extrusion or thermoforming [1], [5], [6].
4.  **Enable recycling of sensitive biopolymers:** Biodegradable polyesters like PLA are particularly sensitive to thermal degradation during processing and recycling. Chain extenders are specifically highlighted as an additive strategy to mitigate this degradation, allowing for the recovery and reuse of post-process waste material (e.g., scrap from thermoforming) by preventing severe molecular weight loss and property deterioration [3], [5].

The use of supercritical fluids has recently appeared as an innovative way to improve clay dispersion leading to new “clean and environment friendly” processes. Supercritical carbon dioxide (sc-CO2) is often used because it is non-toxic, non-flammable, chemically inert, and its supercritical conditions are easily reached [11]. Sc-CO2 has also more favourable interaction with polymers compared to other inert gases and it has the ability to dissolve in large quantities and to act as a plasticizer, which modify drastically polymer properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, etc.). In addition, the dissolved sc-CO2 can act as a foaming agent during processing [12]. It is therefore possible to master pore generation and growth by controlling the operating conditions [13], and to generate low density porous structures of interest for lighter packaging or as carriers of active ingredients, e.g. for drug release applications. PHB and its copolymers have already exhibited good compatibility with sc-CO2. The solubility of PHB in supercritical carbon dioxide can reach several g/L [14] and a high sorption degree can be achieved [15]. Moreover, the authors have shown that an increase from 8% to 12% of the HV content in the copolymer results in an increase in the sorption degree because HV blocks induce higher molecular mobility. All these features make sc-CO2 also able to modify the nanoparticles dispersion inside polymer matrices, which in turn has an effect on the foam structure. Improved dispersion of clays and modified porous structures have been obtained with sc-CO2, mainly in batch processes via the in-situ intercalation method, with various nanocomposite systems such as polydimethysiloxane (PDMS)/clays [16], polystyrene (PS)/clays [17] and recently polylactic acid (PLA)/clays [18]. As an alternative to batch processes, continuous processes such as sc-CO2 assisted extrusion or injection are very promising since they are more easily adaptable for an industrial scale-up. Incorporating sc-CO2 in continuous processes is also of great interest because its plasticization capacity decreases the viscosity of molten polymers and allows to limit the mechanical stresses and the operating temperatures during processing [13]. This is particularly interesting for polymers having a limited thermal stability as biopolyester. For instance, it has been shown that the melting temperature of PHB and PHBV decrease respectively from 178 to 151 °C and from 171 to 137 °C for pressures up to 35 MPa [19]. In the same work, melt processing of PHB and PHBV, which are prone to thermal degradation upon melting in ambient atmosphere, was achievable without degradation in CO2 medium. The interactions with other polymers could also been modified by the presence of sc-CO2. Jenkins et al. [20] have studied the PHBV-PCL blend system by the use of mechanical blending in the presence of supercritical CO2. They showed that PHBV-PCL blends produced by mechanical means were immiscible and degraded, whereas the same blends produced using supercritical methods were found to be miscible over the lower wt% PHBV compositions and less degraded. Recently, efforts have been made to produce high-expanded PLA foams from sc-CO2 assisted extrusion [21], [22], [23], [24]. A growing number of studies also reported on the preparation of nanocomposites systems with clays nanoparticles by sc-CO2 assisted continuous processes. Different processing methods were used e.g. two-step extrusion process [25], [26], [27], sc-CO2 assisted single-screw extrusion [28], single-screw extrusion with prior preparation of exfoliated nanocomposites by in-situ polymerization [29] or the injection of sc-CO2/clays mixtures in the extruder [30]. In most cases, the authors obtained an increased cell density, a smaller cell size and improved performances with exfoliated nanocomposite foams. More recently, the effect of nanoclay on the foamability of PLA was investigated [31], [32]. The results showed that both the cell density and the expansion ratio were greatly promoted with increased clay content. Zhao et al. [33], [34] have investigated the possibility to use a supercritical nitrogen (sc-N2) assisted injection molding process to develop microcellular PLA/PHBV clay nanocomposites. The results showed a decrease of the average cell size and an increased cell density with the addition of clays in PLA/PHBV blends. Rheological behaviour of the PLA/PHBV/clays nanocomposites suggests a good dispersion of the clays within the matrix. Javadi et al. [35] have also used sc-N2 to foam PHBV-poly (butylene adipate co-terephthalate) (PBAT)-hyperbranched-polymer (HBP)-nanoclay (NC). Microcellular nanocomposites exhibited a mixture of exfoliated and intercalated structures. Moreover, dispersed clays improved the thermal stability, reduced the cell size and increased the cell density of the foams.
An alternative method for incorporation using supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) as the solvent has been reported by many researchers.10-12 Guney and Akgerman reported incorporation of 5-fluorouracil and β-estradiol in the biodegradable polymer, poly(DL-lactide-co-glycolide), using scCO2 as the DDS preparation method.10 Natu et al. conducted experiments using poly(ε-caprolactone)/poly(oxyethylene-b-oxypropylene-b-oxyethylene) and poly(ε-caprolactone)/poly(ethylene-vinyl acetate) as base materials for the DDS.11 In addition, Varona et al. reported incorporation of lavandin (Lavandula hybrida) essential oil in starch under scCO2.12 A previous attempt was made to impregnate the polymers poly(L-LA), poly(L-LA-ran-CL) (CL: ε-caprolactone), poly(L-LA-ran-2,2-DTMC) (2,2-DTMC: 2,2-dimethyltrimethylene carbonate), poly(L-LA-ran-TEMC) (TEMC: tetramethylene carbonate), and poly(L-LA-ran-DXO) (DXO: 1,5-dioxepan-2-one) with low-boiling organic compounds using scCO2.13,14 Supercritical fluids have unique properties such as liquid-like dissolving capability and transportation properties similar to a gas. Carbon dioxide, a nontoxic fluid with a relatively low critical point (Tc = 31 °C, Pc = 7.376 MPa), is widely used as a supercritical fluid. The scCO2 is considered a “green solvent” and has been used in food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and plastics industries. In the plastics industry, scCO2 has been used for various polymer-processing purposes, such as polymer blending,15,16 additive impregnation,17,18 plastic foaming,19-21 and preparation of microcapsules.22-26 To impregnate oil extracted from Japanese cypress into poly(L-LA) random copolymers, the influence of impregnation degree and release properties of the copolymers were examined. Until now, various techniques have been developed to build three-dimensional (3D) open pore structures, such as electrospinning,9 particle leaching,10 phase separation,11 3D printing,12 and gas foaming.13 Among them, supercritical fluid microcellular foaming, one kind of gas foaming, is attracting more and more attentions due to being free of organic solvents and eco-friendly characters.14 In this technology, supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) is served as blowing agent as its inexpensive, nontoxic, recoverable, and highly dissolvable in polymer. scCO2 process is normally limited by the variety of pore size, as well as their uncontrollable shape and distribution nonuniformly. Since expansion force of CO2 is too small to overcome the strength of the polymer matrix, low interconnectivity among pores is easily obtained.15 Various approaches have been exploited to improve the open-cell content of pores, including heterogeneous melt structure,16-18 homogeneous melt rupture,19 particle leaching,20, 21 ultrasound treatment,22 and co-continuous blend.23 The immiscible nature of the hard/soft blends can lead to open-cell porous structures formation by creating debonding points within the cells walls and struts.10, 20, 21 Unlike the big viscoelastic difference between the two phases of immiscible blends, the completely or partially compatible blends can endow similar viscoelastic property and poor heterogeneous nucleation effect during scCO2 progress. PLCL and PCL are completely compatible without phase separation for low level (up to 30%) of PLCL in PCL matrix.25 PLCL combines the high elasticity and modulus, which make it possible to produce vascular scaffolds with tunable mechanical property.26 Another advantage of PCL/PLCL blend is that the melt strength of matrix PCL can be strengthened by adding PLCL, allowing the improvement of cell nucleation and cell growth during scCO2 foaming process. Biodegradable polymers have attracted great attention from both industrial and academic areas, since they are environmentally benign and able to be degraded into carbon dioxide, water, biomass and humic matter by microorganisms [1]. In particular, biodegradable polymers in the form of foams have drawn interest from both engineers and researchers, because these biodegradable polymer foams can be widely used in many applications, such as acoustic and thermal insulation, impact resistance and scaffolds for tissue engineering [2-4]. A large number of reports have been published on the preparation of biodegradable polymer foams including poly(epsilon-caprolactone) (PCL) [5, 6], polylactide (PLA) [7, 8], poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) [9, 10] and poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) [11] by using supercritical carbon dioxide (sc-CO2) as the blowing agents. As compared to these traditional physical blowing agents, the sac-CO2, which is chemically inert, non-toxic and environmentally friendly, has been gradually widely used. Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is a biodegradable and biocompatible aliphatic polyester with excellent mechanical properties, good thermal resistance and melt processability [12]. It can be synthesized through condensation polymerization of 1,4-butanediol and succinic acid [13]. In light of its biodegradability and harmless degradation products, PBS has been used as a novel biomaterial for tissue engineering [14-17] and drug delivery [18-20]. However, there are few reports focusing on the preparation of PBS foams. Bahari et al. [21] formed PBS foams with cross-linked structures by irradiating the PBS with electron-beam irradiation, and then blends with different chemical blowing agents. Lim et al. [22-24] mixed PBS with carbon nanofiber, organoclay and multi-walled carbon nanotube, respectively, and then studied the effects of the processing methods, nanofiller content and foaming conditions on the cell morphology of the expanded PBS foams. The cell morphology observations exhibited that a small amount of nanofillers could increase the cell density. Li et al. [25] improved the viscosity of PBS with dicumyl peroxide (DCP) and trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate (TMPTA), and finally foamed PBS with a chemical blowing agent named azodicarbonamide (AC). The result showed that a well-closed cell structure of PBS foam could be produced with appropriate content of DCP and AC. Zhang et al. [26] prepared PBS foams by using ammonium bicarbonate as the chemical blowing agent and obtained the smallest cell size of pristine PBS foam with the addition of 5 wt.% ammonium bicarbonate. Xu et al. [27] and Son et al. [28] prepared PBS microcellular foams with sc-CO2, and studied the effects of processing parameters, including foaming temperature, saturation pressure and depressurization step and rate on the morphology of PBS foams. The results revealed that higher saturation temperature and lower depressurization rate contributed to an increment in cell size. It is well known that the nanofillers loaded into a polymer matrix can act as a homogenous nucleating agent to facilitate the cell nucleation process. Compared with the neat polymer foams, polymer nanocomposite foams show higher cell density, smaller cell size and narrower cell size distribution [29, 30]. However, few work about preparing PBS nanocomposite foams using sc-CO2 as a physical blowing agent have been reported.
To be used as a scaffold, its matrix should meet the following requirements: (a) biocompatibility with the tissues, (b) biodegradability at the ideal rate corresponding to the rate of new tissue formation, (c) non-toxicity and non-immunogenicity, (d) optimal mechanical properties, and (e) adequate morphology and porosity for mass transfer both intra-scaffold and inter-scaffold and also with its local environment [1]. Many biodegradable polymers are either chemically or physically modified to meet these requirements, and much attention has been given to a natural biopolymer, chitosan (CS) [2-6]. Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide composed of randomly distributed β-(1-4)-linked d-glucosamine (deacetylated unit) and N-acetyl-d-glucosamine (acetylated unit). Chitosan is produced commercially by deacetylation of chitin, which is the structural element of the exoskeleton of crustaceans (crabs, shrimp, etc.) and cell walls of fungi. Chitosan is widely employed as an excipient for drug delivery in the pharmaceutical industry and as a scaffold for tissue culture in tissue-engineering applications [4-8]. Chitosan is a renewable, biocompatible, biodegradable, antibacterial, and non-toxic biomaterial. It can be fabricated into the desired shapes of the scaffolds, and can be molded to porous structures. Based solely on the provided context evidence, the specific advantages of using supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO₂) in processing biodegradable scaffolds include:

1.  **Lower Processing Temperatures:** scCO₂ acts as a plasticizer, reducing viscosity and lowering the melting temperature of biodegradable polymers (e.g., PHB from 178°C to 151°C, PHBV from 171°C to 137°C at 35 MPa), enabling melt processing without thermal degradation for thermally sensitive biopolyesters [1].
2.  **Solvent-Free Pore Generation:** scCO₂ serves as a non-toxic, environmentally friendly ("clean and environment friendly", "green solvent") physical blowing agent to create porous structures via microcellular foaming, eliminating the need for organic solvents ("free of organic solvents") [1][3][4].
3.  **Controlled Pore Structure:** The operating conditions (temperature, pressure, depressurization) can be mastered to control pore generation, growth, cell size, and cell density ("master pore generation and growth by controlling the operating conditions"), which is crucial for scaffold morphology, mass transfer, and cell seeding [1][3][4]. Adding nanofillers like clay further enhances nucleation, increasing cell density and reducing cell size [1][3][4].
4.  **Improved Nanoparticle Dispersion:** scCO₂ can enhance the dispersion of nanoparticles (e.g., clays) within the polymer matrix, which subsequently improves the resulting foam structure and properties [1].
5.  **Solvent-Free Impregnation:** scCO₂ acts as a solvent for impregnating active ingredients (e.g., drugs, essential oils, repellent oils) into polymers without using traditional organic solvents, enabling the creation of drug delivery systems (DDS) or functionalized scaffolds [2][10].
6.  **Enhanced Blend Compatibility:** scCO₂ can promote miscibility in otherwise immiscible polymer blends (e.g., PHBV-PCL), preventing degradation and improving blend properties compared to mechanical blending without scCO₂ [1].

Supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) foaming technology is a green, efficient, and controllable method that enables the production of low-density, high-porosity foams with tunable properties through precise control of process parameters.[21-24] By combining the excellent properties of PBST with the advantages of scCO2 foaming, the development of biodegradable foam materials holds significant theoretical and practical value. During the production of PBST microcellular foams using scCO2 technology, dimensional stability remains a critical technical challenge. Although the initial expansion ratio of PBST foams can reach up to 40, the shrinkage rate of pure PBST foams can be as high as 80%.[25] This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the slower rate of air diffusion into the foam compared to the rate at which CO2 escapes from the foam cells, resulting in the development of negative pressure within the cells. Additionally, PBST has a glass transition temperature of −29 °C, and at room temperature, the foam cell walls lack sufficient rigidity, leading to significant shrinkage under negative pressure.[26] To address the dimensional stability issue of polymer foams, researchers have explored various strategies. Among these, the use of mixed gases as blowing agents, chain extension techniques,[27, 28] and polymer blending[29, 30] have become the main approaches. For example, Xue et al[31] incorporated PBS into PBST and used a CO2 and N2 mixed gas system as the foaming agent, achieving foams with an expansion ratio of 10.6 and good dimensional stability. Le Moigne et al[32] employed scCO2-assisted single-screw extrusion to prepare PHBV/nano-clay biocomposite foams with a porosity of 40-50%. Long et al[33] studied the effect of adding PLA and epoxy chain extender ADR4368 to PBAT, producing biodegradable foams with high expansion ratios and improved foam stability. Despite the progress made in these studies, significant challenges remain in practical applications. First, while modifying PBST through chain extension or branching can alter foam morphology and reduce shrinkage, it may negatively impact the material's biodegradability.[34] Second, controlling the gas concentration in mixed gas foaming of PBST foams presents difficulties in achieving precise control.[35] Therefore, polymer blending modification remains the simplest and most practical method to enhance the foamability of PBST. This study focuses on improving the dimensional stability of PBST-based foam without compromising its biodegradability through the incorporation of biodegradable polymer particles. To this end, a polymer exhibiting suitable compatibility with PBST was carefully selected and employed as the dispersed phase for blend modification. During the supercritical fluid foaming process, the micro/nano-scale polymer crystalline particles were uniformly distributed in the PBST matrix and played a dual role during the nucleation and growth of foam cells: they served as nucleation sites, promoting uniform foam cell formation, and acted as stress concentrators, inducing localized fracture during foam growth to form an open-cell structure.[36-38] This open-cell mechanism effectively alleviated the pressure difference between the interior and exterior of the foam cells, significantly reducing the material's tendency to shrink.

Long et al[33] studied the effect of adding PLA and epoxy chain extender ADR4368 to PBAT, producing biodegradable foams with high expansion ratios and improved foam stability. Despite the progress made in these studies, significant challenges remain in practical applications. First, while modifying PBST through chain extension or branching can alter foam morphology and reduce shrinkage, it may negatively impact the material's biodegradability.[34] Second, controlling the gas concentration in mixed gas foaming of PBST foams presents difficulties in achieving precise control.[35] Therefore, polymer blending modification remains the simplest and most practical method to enhance the foamability of PBST. This study focuses on improving the dimensional stability of PBST-based foam without compromising its biodegradability through the incorporation of biodegradable polymer particles. To this end, a polymer exhibiting suitable compatibility with PBST was carefully selected and employed as the dispersed phase for blend modification. During the supercritical fluid foaming process, the micro/nano-scale polymer crystalline particles were uniformly distributed in the PBST matrix and played a dual role during the nucleation and growth of foam cells: they served as nucleation sites, promoting uniform foam cell formation, and acted as stress concentrators, inducing localized fracture during foam growth to form an open-cell structure.[36-38] This open-cell mechanism effectively alleviated the pressure difference between the interior and exterior of the foam cells, significantly reducing the material's tendency to shrink.
The use of supercritical fluids has recently appeared as an innovative way to improve clay dispersion leading to new “clean and environment friendly” processes. Supercritical carbon dioxide (sc-CO2) is often used because it is non-toxic, non-flammable, chemically inert, and its supercritical conditions are easily reached [11]. Sc-CO2 has also more favourable interaction with polymers compared to other inert gases and it has the ability to dissolve in large quantities and to act as a plasticizer, which modify drastically polymer properties (viscosity, interfacial tension, etc.). In addition, the dissolved sc-CO2 can act as a foaming agent during processing [12]. It is therefore possible to master pore generation and growth by controlling the operating conditions [13], and to generate low density porous structures of interest for lighter packaging or as carriers of active ingredients, e.g. for drug release applications. PHB and its copolymers have already exhibited good compatibility with sc-CO2. The solubility of PHB in supercritical carbon dioxide can reach several g/L [14] and a high sorption degree can be achieved [15]. Moreover, the authors have shown that an increase from 8% to 12% of the HV content in the copolymer results in an increase in the sorption degree because HV blocks induce higher molecular mobility. All these features make sc-CO2 also able to modify the nanoparticles dispersion inside polymer matrices, which in turn has an effect on the foam structure. Improved dispersion of clays and modified porous structures have been obtained with sc-CO2, mainly in batch processes via the in-situ intercalation method, with various nanocomposite systems such as polydimethysiloxane (PDMS)/clays [16], polystyrene (PS)/clays [17] and recently polylactic acid (PLA)/clays [18]. As an alternative to batch processes, continuous processes such as sc-CO2 assisted extrusion or injection are very promising since they are more easily adaptable for an industrial scale-up. Incorporating sc-CO2 in continuous processes is also of great interest because its plasticization capacity decreases the viscosity of molten polymers and allows to limit the mechanical stresses and the operating temperatures during processing [13]. This is particularly interesting for polymers having a limited thermal stability as biopolyester. For instance, it has been shown that the melting temperature of PHB and PHBV decrease respectively from 178 to 151 °C and from 171 to 137 °C for pressures up to 35 MPa [19]. In the same work, melt processing of PHB and PHBV, which are prone to thermal degradation upon melting in ambient atmosphere, was achievable without degradation in CO2 medium. The interactions with other polymers could also been modified by the presence of sc-CO2. Jenkins et al. [20] have studied the PHBV-PCL blend system by the use of mechanical blending in the presence of supercritical CO2. They showed that PHBV-PCL blends produced by mechanical means were immiscible and degraded, whereas the same blends produced using supercritical methods were found to be miscible over the lower wt% PHBV compositions and less degraded. Recently, efforts have been made to produce high-expanded PLA foams from sc-CO2 assisted extrusion [21], [22], [23], [24]. A growing number of studies also reported on the preparation of nanocomposites systems with clays nanoparticles by sc-CO2 assisted continuous processes. Different processing methods were used e.g. two-step extrusion process [25], [26], [27], sc-CO2 assisted single-screw extrusion [28], single-screw extrusion with prior preparation of exfoliated nanocomposites by in-situ polymerization [29] or the injection of sc-CO2/clays mixtures in the extruder [30]. In most cases, the authors obtained an increased cell density, a smaller cell size and improved performances with exfoliated nanocomposite foams. More recently, the effect of nanoclay on the foamability of PLA was investigated [31], [32]. The results showed that both the cell density and the expansion ratio were greatly promoted with increased clay content. Zhao et al. [33], [34] have investigated the possibility to use a supercritical nitrogen (sc-N2) assisted injection molding process to develop microcellular PLA/PHBV clay nanocomposites. The results showed a decrease of the average cell size and an increased cell density with the addition of clays in PLA/PHBV blends. Rheological behaviour of the PLA/PHBV/clays nanocomposites suggests a good dispersion of the clays within the matrix. Javadi et al. [35] have also used sc-N2 to foam PHBV-poly (butylene adipate co-terephthalate) (PBAT)-hyperbranched-polymer (HBP)-nanoclay (NC). Microcellular nanocomposites exhibited a mixture of exfoliated and intercalated structures. Moreover, dispersed clays improved the thermal stability, reduced the cell size and increased the cell density of the foams.
Until now, various techniques have been developed to build three-dimensional (3D) open pore structures, such as electrospinning,9 particle leaching,10 phase separation,11 3D printing,12 and gas foaming.13 Among them, supercritical fluid microcellular foaming, one kind of gas foaming, is attracting more and more attentions due to being free of organic solvents and eco-friendly characters.14 In this technology, supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) is served as blowing agent as its inexpensive, nontoxic, recoverable, and highly dissolvable in polymer. scCO2 process is normally limited by the variety of pore size, as well as their uncontrollable shape and distribution nonuniformly. Since expansion force of CO2 is too small to overcome the strength of the polymer matrix, low interconnectivity among pores is easily obtained.15 Various approaches have been exploited to improve the open-cell content of pores, including heterogeneous melt structure,16-18 homogeneous melt rupture,19 particle leaching,20, 21 ultrasound treatment,22 and co-continuous blend.23 The immiscible nature of the hard/soft blends can lead to open-cell porous structures formation by creating debonding points within the cells walls and struts.10, 20, 21 Unlike the big viscoelastic difference between the two phases of immiscible blends, the completely or partially compatible blends can endow similar viscoelastic property and poor heterogeneous nucleation effect during scCO2 progress. So achieving porous structures with high open-cell content is still a challenge. Biodegradable and biocompatible polymers are usually used in artificial blood vessels, such as polycaprolactone (PCL), polylactic acid (PLA), polylactic acid-glycolic acid (PLGA), polyglycolic acid (PGA), and so forth. PCL is one of the most promising candidates for fabricating biodegradable scaffold. PCL has good cytocompatibility, no obvious toxicity to cell growth, and high elongation at break (>1100%).24 Due to relatively low mechanical property and long degradation time (>3 years), PCL is normally blended physically or copolymerized chemically with other polymer, such as PLA, resulting in controllable properties. However, PLA has a high rigid performance, limiting the application in soft tissue such as blood vascular. Poly(L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone) (PLCL) is a copolymer from PCL and PLA. PLCL and PCL are completely compatible without phase separation for low level (up to 30%) of PLCL in PCL matrix.25 PLCL combines the high elasticity and modulus, which make it possible to produce vascular scaffolds with tunable mechanical property.26 Another advantage of PCL/PLCL blend is that the melt strength of matrix PCL can be strengthened by adding PLCL, allowing the improvement of cell nucleation and cell growth during scCO2 foaming process. To the best of the author's knowledge, only few investigations have been reported that PCL/PLCL porous scaffolds can be obtained by 3D bioprinting27 and solid-liquid phase separation methods.25 No prior researches on the fabrication of PCL/PLCL foams via scCO2 foaming technology used in tissue engineering field. In this study, PCL and PLCL were melt blended with various composition ratio to fabricate small-diameter tubular porous scaffolds using solid-state scCO2 foaming technology. The effects of PLCL content on rheological property and pore morphology of tubular scaffold were investigated. The ϕ 4 mm tubular porous PCL/PLCL scaffolds were fabricated successfully. Moreover, pore structures, such as pore size, pore density, and open-cell content were measured quantitatively. Related wettability, tensile property, radial compliance, and biocompatibility were also explored.
Biodegradable ϕ4 mm tubular porous poly(ε-caprolactone)/poly(L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone) (PCL/PLCL) scaffolds are fabricated successfully via one-step microcellular supercritical carbon dioxide foaming process. The effect of blending ratio on the rheology, pore structures, mechanical property, wettability, and biocompatibility of PCL/PLCL blends tubular scaffold are reported. Rheological results show that PCL matrix and PLCL dispersed phase has good compatibility. The melt strength of PCL can be enhanced obviously by adding PLCL. With an increase of PLCL content from 10 to 30 wt%, the pore size increases from 7.6 to 24.9 μm due to the homogeneous nucleation effect. The maximum open-cell content can reach 77% for PCL/PLCL foamed sample. Cyclical tensile and compliance tests show that few content of dispersed PLCL (10-20 wt%) improves the flexibility and recoverability. Cell viability results demonstrate that human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) cultured on all PCL/PLCL porous scaffolds exhibit a typical spindle-like cell morphology. Moreover, HUVECs have a higher density and spreading areas on surface of 10% PLCL scaffold. The results gathered in this paper may open a new perspective for the fabrication of small-diameter vascular tissue engineering scaffold. Biodegradable polymers have attracted great attention from both industrial and academic areas, since they are environmentally benign and able to be degraded into carbon dioxide, water, biomass and humic matter by microorganisms [1]. In particular, biodegradable polymers in the form of foams have drawn interest from both engineers and researchers, because these biodegradable polymer foams can be widely used in many applications, such as acoustic and thermal insulation, impact resistance and scaffolds for tissue engineering [2-4]. A large number of reports have been published on the preparation of biodegradable polymer foams including poly(epsilon-caprolactone) (PCL) [5, 6], polylactide (PLA) [7, 8], poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) [9, 10] and poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) [11] by using supercritical carbon dioxide (sc-CO2) as the blowing agents. As compared to these traditional physical blowing agents, the sac-CO2, which is chemically inert, non-toxic and environmentally friendly, has been gradually widely used. Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is a biodegradable and biocompatible aliphatic polyester with excellent mechanical properties, good thermal resistance and melt processability [12]. It can be synthesized through condensation polymerization of 1,4-butanediol and succinic acid [13]. In light of its biodegradability and harmless degradation products, PBS has been used as a novel biomaterial for tissue engineering [14-17] and drug delivery [18-20]. However, there are few reports focusing on the preparation of PBS foams. Bahari et al. [21] formed PBS foams with cross-linked structures by irradiating the PBS with electron-beam irradiation, and then blends with different chemical blowing agents. Lim et al. [22-24] mixed PBS with carbon nanofiber, organoclay and multi-walled carbon nanotube, respectively, and then studied the effects of the processing methods, nanofiller content and foaming conditions on the cell morphology of the expanded PBS foams. The cell morphology observations exhibited that a small amount of nanofillers could increase the cell density. Li et al. [25] improved the viscosity of PBS with dicumyl peroxide (DCP) and trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate (TMPTA), and finally foamed PBS with a chemical blowing agent named azodicarbonamide (AC). The result showed that a well-closed cell structure of PBS foam could be produced with appropriate content of DCP and AC. Zhang et al. [26] prepared PBS foams by using ammonium bicarbonate as the chemical blowing agent and obtained the smallest cell size of pristine PBS foam with the addition of 5 wt.% ammonium bicarbonate. Xu et al. [27] and Son et al. [28] prepared PBS microcellular foams with sc-CO2, and studied the effects of processing parameters, including foaming temperature, saturation pressure and depressurization step and rate on the morphology of PBS foams. The results revealed that higher saturation temperature and lower depressurization rate contributed to an increment in cell size. It is well known that the nanofillers loaded into a polymer matrix can act as a homogenous nucleating agent to facilitate the cell nucleation process. Compared with the neat polymer foams, polymer nanocomposite foams show higher cell density, smaller cell size and narrower cell size distribution [29, 30]. However, few work about preparing PBS nanocomposite foams using sc-CO2 as a physical blowing agent have been reported.
In this study, we propose an alternative new process for the acetylation of plant cellulose fiber using supercritical carbon dioxide (sc-CO2) as a reaction medium. The peculiar properties of supercritical conditions, such as low viscosity, high diffusion, easy separation, and no surface tension, have attracted a lot of interest and led to applications that include extraction [9], dyeing [10], foaming [11], and organic/polymer synthesis [12]. With relevance to cellulose, supercritical water is reported to be useful for hydrolysis and gasification [13], [14]. Supercritical ammonia has been used for the crystal transformation from cellulose I to IIII [15], [16], and supercritical methanol has been utilized for CA fiber formation [17]. Nanoporous cellulose aerogels were obtained by sc-CO2 drying [18], [19]. Recently, Yin et al. reported the application of sc-CO2 for the synthesis of cellulose carbamate from cotton [20]. They employed severe sc-CO2 conditions such as a 140 °C temperature and 18 MPa of pressure, for a total period of 9.5 h; however, the degree of substitution (DS) was limited to 1.3 per glucose unit. On the contrary, we reported here the preparation of cellulose acetate with a higher DS from natural plant fiber (ramie) using shorter and milder sc-CO2 conditions. The structure and mechanical properties of CA fiber were investigated. In particular, the space distribution of acetyl groups in a chemically modified single fiber was analyzed using synchrotron microbeam X-ray diffraction and nano-Raman scattering. The plant cellulose fiber used in this study was refined ramie supplied by Toyobo Co.Ltd. Prior to acetylation, the fiber was pretreated by immersing it in glacial acetic acid containing 5% w/w of ZnCl2 at 25 °C for 24 h [21]. The pretreated fibers were pressed between filter paper to remove the pretreatment solution, then they were fixed at both ends to a rectangular shaped metal frame (60 mm × 20 mm). The fibers were sealed in a high pressure reactor (inner volume: 138 ml) with acetic anhydride (5 ml), then subjected to 9.8 MPa of pressure with CO2 at 70 °C. During the reaction, the fibers were kept separated from the liquid phase of acetic anhydride. After the designated time, the temperature and pressure were reduced to ambient levels. The fibers were rinsed with running water, then with distilled water to neutralize them. Finally, they were dried at room temperature and further dried in a vacuum at 60 °C for 12 h. For comparison, a vapor phase process was also carried out in the presence of acetic anhydride at 70 °C under reduced pressure of 2 × 10−3 Pa.
To be used as a scaffold, its matrix should meet the following requirements: (a) biocompatibility with the tissues, (b) biodegradability at the ideal rate corresponding to the rate of new tissue formation, (c) non-toxicity and non-immunogenicity, (d) optimal mechanical properties, and (e) adequate morphology and porosity for mass transfer both intra-scaffold and inter-scaffold and also with its local environment [1]. Many biodegradable polymers are either chemically or physically modified to meet these requirements, and much attention has been given to a natural biopolymer, chitosan (CS) [2-6]. Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide composed of randomly distributed β-(1-4)-linked d-glucosamine (deacetylated unit) and N-acetyl-d-glucosamine (acetylated unit). Chitosan is produced commercially by deacetylation of chitin, which is the structural element of the exoskeleton of crustaceans (crabs, shrimp, etc.) and cell walls of fungi. Chitosan is widely employed as an excipient for drug delivery in the pharmaceutical industry and as a scaffold for tissue culture in tissue-engineering applications [4-8]. Chitosan is a renewable, biocompatible, biodegradable, antibacterial, and non-toxic biomaterial. It can be fabricated into the desired shapes of the scaffolds, and can be molded to porous structures. It also contains amino and hydroxyl groups which can be reacted and functionalized [9, 10].

ground_truth: PHB forms large, spherulitic crystals with a high degree of crystallinity (50–80%). These large spherulites often contain inter-spherulitic cracks and amorphous regions that are constrained by the rigid crystals. In recent years, biodegradable plastics have attracted attention due to their environmental compatibility. Poly[(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate], P[(R-HB], appears to nearly ideally to meet such criteria.1-3 It is produced biologically from renewable resources.4 It is stable under normal usage conditions, but degrades rapidly on composting conditions. Additionally, PHB is the basis for biocompatible materials, and its degradation yields valuable stereoregular building blocks for organic synthesis. However, the shortcoming of brittleness and narrow processability window has limited the wide applications of PHB. These are mainly related to its relatively high melting temperature and high crystallinity.5-7 Many approaches have been reported to improve the brittleness of PHB, for example, incorporation of other 3-hydroxyalkanoate units such as 3-hydroxyvalerate in the backbone of P[(R)-HB],8-10 addition of plasticizers and nucleating agents,11-13 blending with flexible polymers,14 and copolymerization with flexible synthetic biodegradable components such as poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), poly(butylene adipate) (PBA), poly(diethylene glycol adipate) (PDEGA), or poly(ethylene glycol).15-24 The advantage of the obtained copolymers over the other kinds of PHB material is that their segmented and domain structure can be easily controlled by a selection of the monomer units for building the segments, their relative proportions and the length of segments. Meanwhile, the crystalline structure and morphology are also greatly influenced by the thermal history.25-32 Therefore, the crystallization kinetics study should be paid enough attention, since it is not only affects the crystalline structure and morphology of semi-crystalline polymers, but also affects the final mechanical and physical properties and biodegradability. Crystallization during polymer processing occurs non-isothermally, except for some special cases. In order to reach optimizing condition in an industrial process and to obtain a product with desired properties, it is necessary to have some quantitative evaluations of the non-isothermal process. However, aging is a serious problem for the semi-crystalline PHA. PHB, PHBV and PHBHHx age rather quickly over time even at room temperature, exhibiting reduction of ɛb due to increase of brittleness [4], [5], [6], [7]. Furthermore, the introduction of 3HV or 3HHx monomers results in significant reduction on the crystallization rate and on the degree of crystallinity, which is disadvantageous for their processing including injection molding, film blowing and fiber spinning. Recently, a microbial terpolyester PHBVHHx containing 3HB, 3HV and 3HHx monomers was synthesized by recombinant Aeromonas hydrophila 4AK4 harboring phbA and phbB (phaAB) genes encoding β-ketothiolase and acetoacetyl-CoA reductase of Ralstonia eutropha [8], [9]. It was reported that simultaneous incorporation of 3HV and 3HHx improved the ductility and rigidity of the polyester compared with PHBV and PHBHHx with similar comonomer contents. For example, the cast film of poly(3HB-co-5.4 mol% 3HV-co-11.7 mol% 3HHx) terpolyester showed a rather high elongation at break up to 340%, and the tensile strength was still maintained at about 15.7 MPa. Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA's) are bacterial polyesters that are fully biodegradable in natural conditions and can be produced from renewable sources, including organic wastes, by a variety of microorganisms [[1], [2], [3]]. Among PHA's, the most commonly investigated and easiest to produce is the homopolymer poly-3-hydroxybutyrate (PHB). However, its high crystallinity and glass transition temperature result in fairly stiff and brittle materials [4], limiting its use as a general-purpose plastic substitute (i.e. elongation at break is about 2% compared to up to 400% for some polyolefins). An approach to address this problem is the incorporation of 3-hydroxyvalerate units (HV units) in the molecular structure of PHB to produce poly[R-3-hydroxybutyrate-co-(R-3-hydroxyvalerate)] copolymers (PHBV). Indeed, the resulting decrease of overall crystallinity and glass transition temperature is likely to lead to a better processability and a significant improvement of the material ductility [5]. PHBV-based materials display contrasting functional properties depending on their macromolecular and crystalline structures, which are strongly related to their HV content, the comonomer compositional distribution, the molar mass and the sample purity [6,7]. The macromolecular and crystalline structures can also be strongly affected by the processing conditions such as melting and cooling temperatures and rates [8]. As a consequence, even if the synthesis and macromolecular structure of PHBV have been optimized (i.e. increased HV content), its final functional properties can be limited due to inadequate processing conditions. Defining optimal processing conditions that would allow maximizing the copolymer's final technical performance thus appears as a critical and necessary step for their implementation in general-purpose plastic applications. In particular, the impact of HV content on the thermal sensitivity towards processing conditions is still unclear and thus deserves more consideration. Surprisingly, while the influence of the cooling/heating rate and the holding time in the melt on the overall crystallinity and final mechanical properties has already been studied for PHB [8], this subject is not documented for PHBV copolymers with varying HV contents.

Among the mentioned methods, the use of nucleating agents is demonstrated to be easy and effective on enhancing the crystallization rate and toughness of PHB. The nucleating agents studied included both inorganic and organic compounds, e. g., boron nitride, talc, clay, mica, calcium carbonate, terbium oxide, lanthanum oxide, hydroxyapatite, Zn-Al nitrate, zinc phenylphosphonate monohydrate, graphite nanoplatelets, saccharin, nanocrystalline cellulose, ammonium chloride, sodium salts/carboxylic salts of metals of Group 1 and 11 of the Periodic Table, lignin, α-cyclodextrin, cyclodextrin-complex, organophosphorous, thymine, melamine, behenamide, cyanuric acid, orotic acid, nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic compound (pyridine, pyrimidine, pyrazine, pyridazine, triazine, or imidazole), poly(vinyl alcohol), etc. [14-41]. [6] indicated that the mechanical properties of PHB were improved by introduction of two kinds of commercial montmorillonites (MMTs). ans_rerank: The crystalline structure of PHB contributes to its brittleness through multiple interrelated mechanisms. First, PHB’s high crystallinity (>50%) and slow crystallization kinetics lead to large spherulites with inter-spherulitic cracks, creating structural weaknesses that propagate under stress [1, 8]. Secondary crystallization during storage further increases crystallinity and rigid amorphous fraction (RAF), which restricts chain mobility in the amorphous regions adjacent to crystals, amplifying brittleness over time [1, 2, 6]. The RAF, coupled with PHB’s glass transition temperature (Tg) near room temperature, locks the amorphous phase in a glassy state at ambient conditions, reducing ductility [1, 2, 7]. Additionally, the absence of impurities or nucleating agents in pure PHB results in low nucleation density, favoring large spherulite formation and exacerbating crack susceptibility [1, 8]. These factors collectively limit the material’s ability to deform plastically, leading to low elongation at break (typically <5%) [1, 6, 7].

Recent research has suggested that PBS could be produced solely from renewable sources, the succinic acid can be produced by fermenting lignocellulosic sugars, and 1,4-butanediol feasible be produced by hydrocracking starches and sugars [16,17,18]. Catalysts play a key role in synthesis of PBS by traditional melt polycondensation. Using excess succinic acid to react with 1,4-butanediol in the absence of a catalyst. Matthieu G. et al. synthesized PBS of weight-average molecular weight (Mw) ranging from 4.0 × 103 to 1.8 × 105 g mol−1 with varying amounts of tetrabutyltitanate catalyst [19]. The focus of this paper is to control the synthesis of high molecular weight PBS through different catalysts. Cui C.N. et al. provided a kind of green and efficient synthesis method for high molecular weight PBS. It was synthesized via using 1, 4-butanediol with succinate as starting material then titanic acid ester and acetate as catalyst. What's more tried to improve PBS via changing end-group to carboxyl, hydroxyl and chlorine, the Mw was 1.3 × 105 g mol−1. Furthermore, PBS governed end-group had finer thermal properties [20]. Han. et al. prepared the high molecular weight linear or branched PBS. The Mw of the prepared linear or branched PBS was in the extent of 1.0 × 105-2.2 × 105 g mol−1. The Tm with thermal stability of high molecular weight linear or branched PBS was slightly higher than those of ordinary PBS [21]. Velmathi S. et al. was synthesis PBS with 1,1,3,3-tetrabutyldistannoxane being catalyst in the CEM models focused microwave synthesis system. It a Mw about 2.35 × 104 was gotten in a short time of 20 min [22]. Gkountela C. et al. utilized immobilized candida antarctica Lipase B (Novozym 435) to do catalyst, isooctane was adopted as organic solvents [23]. In the end PBS have Mw at 5.0 × 103 g mol−1. In order to improve the thermal and mechanical property of PLA, biodegradable PBS with certain toughness and high crystallinity was selected for blending modification [24]. Therefore, it is important to studies have been carried out on the properties of PLA/PBS blends. Saowaroj et al. found that the PLA/PBS blends revealed a PBS dose-dependent enhance in the impact strength, elongation at break, degree of crystallinity and thermal stability contrasted to the PLA. The highest impact strength of about 96.3% and elongation at break of about 4.0% were found after adding 30.0 wt% PBS to PLA [25]. Hassan et al. researched the properties of PLA/PBS blend fibers, it showed that increased crystallinity of PLA after addition different content of PBS, the degree of crystallinity of PLA in the blend raised from 30.0 to 40.0% [26]. Importantly, it is observed that the sample varied from brittle fracture of neat PLA to ductile fracture of the blends, the elongation at break of PLA/PBS in the blend raised from 18.0 to 30.3%. Deng Y. et al. analyzed the ductility and phase inversion effects of PLA/PBS blend. The findings indicate that a clear improvement in ductility with 10 wt% of PBS, elongation at break over 250% [27]. The improved ductility was taken on account of a co-continuous phase morphology of blends, it was dominant by the relative viscosities of the components [28]. In this study, a higher molecular weight and small dispersion PBS was synthesized by two-step method. Different contents of PBS were used to increase the toughness of the PLA and thus expand its range of applications [29]. The PLA/PBS blends were investigated by means of mechanical property, thermal property, crystallization, rheological behavior and micromorphology, and the toughening mechanism of blends was clearly elucidated in terms of microscopic morphology.

Luque et al. proved that the selectivity of the formation of these products can be tuned by the suitable choice of the catalyst.48 The production of polybutylene terephthalate (PBT) (Table 2) is the second largest use of 1,4-BDO. Recently, there are over 50 companies engaged in the production of PBT. Among these companies, Toray has recently manufactured a partially bio-based PBT using 1,4-BDO made with Genomatica's bio-based process technology. PBT exhibits excellent thermal stability, high strength, high chemical resistance and good durability. It is also easily made into yarn which has a natural stretch similar to Lycra®. These characteristics of PBT polyester resins and yarns lead to its many uses. A great deal of effort has also been devoted to further broaden its current applications by changing its crystallinity and crystallization rate.240 In terms of ring opening polymerization (ROP), poly(4-hydroxybutyrate) (P4HB) (Table 2) is produced from GBL. However, the polymerization reaction gives low molecular weight products.241 Nonetheless, the copolymers of GBL with L-lactide, glycolide, β-propiolactone, δ-valerolactone and ε-caprolactone were reported. It was stated that the use of GBL as a monomer for the synthesis of biodegradable polymer materials offers distinct advantages.242,243 P4HB polyester belongs to the polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) family (Section 5.16). So, another and more efficient production route for the production of P4HB is the fermentation process, in which a much higher molecular weight, strong and flexible plastic can be derived. For instance, Tepha Inc. currently produces PHA4400, the commercial product of P4HB, for medical applications using a proprietary transgenic fermentation process.244 Unlike GBL, the ROP of THF has attracted much more attention. The resulting linear polymer of the ring opening process is poly(tetramethylene oxide) (PTMO). The most important difunctional derivative of PTMO is PTMEG (Table 2), an α,ω-dihydroxy-terminated polymer. PTMEG has turned out to be a large-scale commercial product and the main use of this polymer is to make thermoplastic elastomers.245 In this manner, it can be either reacted with diisocyanates to produce thermoplastic polyurethane elastomers or reacted with diacids or their derivatives to produce thermoplastic polyester elastomers. Thermoplastic elastomers contain two different types of blocks or chain segments to form a hard and a soft segment.246 In particular, PTMEG is often applied as polyol because compared to other soft segments, it renders low temperature flexibility, low content of extractable substances, microbial resistance and hydrolytic stability.247 For instance, the main use of PTMEG is to make spandex (Elastane, Lycra), a highly elastic synthetic fiber. PTMEG based spandex is typically produced by first making a prepolymer of PTMEG and methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI). Later on, the prepolymer is extended via a diamine extension process in which ethylenediamine is often preferred.248 Other examples of PTMEG based commercial thermoplastic elastomers include Arnitel (DSM), Hytrel (DuPont) and Pibiflex (SOFTER). Through reductive amination of succinic acid by using amine, ammonium or ammonia and optionally alcohol, 2-pyrrolidone can be synthesized (Fig. 2a).51 2-Pyrrolidone can undergo an anionic ROP. The corresponding polymer, PA-4, has been known to be difficult to synthesize and process due to its thermal instability. Its melting and decomposition points are very close and when melted it reverts to its thermodynamically stable monomer.249 Although it has not been commercially produced due to its insufficient thermal stability, PA-4 membranes show interesting dialysis properties which are comparable to those of commercial cellophane and cellulose acetate membranes.238
