Ester bonds play a fundamental role during the degradation process because they can undergo hydrolytic scission more easily than other chemical bonds. The urethane and urea linkages are less sensitive to hydrolysis than the ester bonds.29 An initially homogeneous sample undergoes hydrolysis, with consequent cleavage of the ester bonds confirmed by a decrease in the mass. On the FTIR spectra shown in Figures 12 and 13, a very broad absorbance band develops in the 3300-3000 cm−1 area during the first half of the composting experiment. This can probably be associated to the presence of carboxylic acid groups resulting from hydrolytic chain scissions. The velocity of the hydrolysis is determined by the “concentration” of reaction partners, water, and labile bonds.30 From water uptake tests NE elastomers resulted to be more hydrophilic (7.1%) than the E elastomers (2.3%), and, after 10 days, the absorption peaks of ester bonds substantially decreased. This is in accordance with the larger weight loss occurred to nonenergetic binders. The inherent more hydrolytic resistance of the energetic polyurethane must be attributed to the presence of the azide group in the backbone chains. The final hydrolysis products of the polyesters will be degraded by microorganisms to smaller end products after they are released in a natural environment. But, at this stage of the work, no ecotoxicity tests were conducted. In summary, FTIR-PAS spectra have shown that the combination of the hydrolytic and bacterial attack in the compost was more efficient in the case of nonenergetic binders. This work aimed to produce an energetic biodegradable polyurethane elastomer. The first step was devoted to the production of a low-molecular-weight prepolymer. The synthesized azide polyol was suitable for being modified by an azidation reaction and being included in polyurethane elastomer formulation. Copoly(ester/ethers) of PECH and SA were prepared by two standard polycondensation methods to evaluate the appropriate operation conditions. First, direct polycondensation of PECH with SA was conducted in toluene using a Dean Stark apparatus. Even if different reaction conditions and catalysts were tried, a copolymer of satisfactory molecular weight was not produced. On the other hand, pyridine-promoted polycondensation of PECH with SC resulted in producing copolymers of higher molecular weight (6000-25,000 g/mol, relative to polystyrene standard). Biodegradable cross-linked energetic and nonenergetic polyurethanes (binders) were prepared from PCL and copolymers of PECH and SC as soft segments and LDI as hard segments. The cross-linked elastomers showed good biodegradability in the compost. The rate of weight loss was significantly higher for the nonenergetic binders with respect to energetic ones. This was due to the presence of the chlorine group in the molecular chains on nonenergetic binder. The ether/ester bonds of the energetic polyurethane were found to be less susceptible to hydrolysis, probably because the azide group affecting the steric hindrance reduced the possibility of cleavage of the molecular chains. These biodegradable binders with elastomeric properties may be used in military applications where more environmentally acceptable products are sought. Future work includes the optimization of the mechanical properties of these novel materials. Saponification, or de-esterification, typically describes the hydration reaction (hydrolysis) that breaks the ester bonds by either free hydroxides or acids. Such side reactions may happen to some extent among the complex heterogenous mixture (slurry) of hemp fibers and pectin under highly acidic or basic conditions. Under highly acidic conditions, such side reactions may happen and yield free carboxylic acids on the pectin. The free carboxylic acids of pectin can reform ester bonds with the hydroxyl groups on the hemp fibers. However, under high basic conditions, any saponification (or de-esterification) will yield free carboxylates, but the basic conditions cannot catalyze the re-formation of ester bonds with hydroxyl groups because the byproducts, hydroxide ions, are not good leaving groups. Thus, for the methyl carboxylate groups of pectin to react with hydroxyl groups on the fiber surface to produce robust biocomposite as we observed in our experiment, transesterification, though slow, is expected to happen. In other words, most of these methyl carboxylate groups probably do not hydrolyze under the basic conditions evaluated in our experiments. It is important to note that when the pH of the crosslinking reaction was adjusted in the fabrication process to either 1-2 or 12-14, only a few milliliters of the aqueous pectin solution were used for a reaction with 4 grams of hemp fibers. The total numbers of moles of acids or bases were relatively small when compared to the amount of hemp fibers used in the fabrication process. Also, our heating process at 70°C for 2 h and then at 100°C for 10 h will deplete most of the water needed for saponification and hence promote the formation of ester bonds by shifting the equilibrium. Though the transesterification reaction is relatively slow, we believe that sufficient crosslinking can happen due to such reaction mechanisms. Otherwise, we would not observe the V-shape compressive strength trend in Figure 10. In addition, the common method to measure the degree of methylation of pectin is by de-esterification of pectin with a 3× to 10× strong base (such as aqueous NaOH solution (pH = 13-14) mixed 50/50 with isopropanol).85 Even under such harsh conditions, a minimum of 2 h is recommended for complete esterification. This indicates that the de-esterification process is not too fast compared to our reaction period. Hence, the reaction time used in our method is expected to be sufficient for significant crosslinking via transesterification to happen. In this paper, a one-step water-based process to valorize hemp fiber was reported to fabricate hemp fiber composites with pectin. In our composite fabrication methodology, we highlighted the valorization approach to efficiently use surplus hemp fibers by crosslinking them using pectin into green and sustainable biocomposites. Unlike other synthetic polymers such as polyurethane, epoxy, and other petroleum-based products used in conventional composite fabrication,6, 20 we used pectin for crosslinking the hemp fibers in our process because pectin was a plant-based biopolymer extracted from fruit peel. This allowed these hemp fiber composites fabricated using this approach to be sustainable and biodegradable. This green approach further overcame the major shortcomings of the conventional fabrication methodologies for hemp fiber composite materials, which considerably relied on the heavy use of organic solvents.86 In addition, the one-way ANOVA study followed by Tukey's HSD test revealed that the mass ratios of pectin to hemp fibers showed that these mass ratios had statistically significant interaction effects on the compressive strength and bulk density of the hemp fiber composites. Furthermore, the versatility of our demonstrated fabrication process under different acidic or basic pH conditions offered flexibility to accommodate different industrial production processes with other fiber materials such as flax, sisal, coir, kenaf, and jute that possess free hydroxyl surface functional groups. The illustrated carbohydrate chemistry was generalizable and could be easily applied to incorporate and functionalize other bio-based macromolecules such as gelatin, agar, alginic acid, and chitosan into polymer composite materials.

Currently, the most widely used method for synthesizing polymer hydrogels revolves around utilizing a diverse range of dynamic interactions. These interactions contain reversible covalent bonds such as Diels-Alder, disulfide, borate ester, and imine reactions, as well as supramolecular interactions including host-guest interactions, metal coordination, ionic interactions, and hydrogen bonding. The borate ester (B-O) bond is a hexagonal or pentagonal ring [16], [17] when boric acid reacts with cis-1,3- or 1,2-diol. This structure is reversible and dependent on the pH and temperature of the environment [18], [19]. The B-O bond easily forms in water-based solutions that contain water-soluble polyols or other substrates with electron-donating groups [20]. Therefore, B-O bond cooperation is widely employed as a network strategy in the synthesis of hydrogel materials [21], [22], [23]. He et al. reported an extremely flexible hydrogel with self-healing properties and a double cross-linked network. This network is achieved through the formation of boric acid ester bonds via polyvinyl alcohol and borax, as well as acylhydrazone bonds formed by aldehyde-based nanocellulose and adipic acid dihydrazide-modified alginate [24]. The incorporation of dynamic acylhydrazone bonds notably enhanced the hydrogel's flexibility, leading to a substantial increase in elongation from 480 % to around 1440 %. Li et al. developed a polyethylene-based flexible hydrogel crosslinked with borax, utilizing sodium alginate (SA), tannic acid (TA), and alcohol (PVA) [25]. The toughness of the hydrogel prepared via a simple one-pot method reached 587.1 KJ m−1. Du et al. developed a double-network supramolecular hydrogel by combining phenylboronic acid, galactomannan (GG), tannic acid (TA), metal ion Al3+ and polyacrylamide (PAM) chains. This unique combination results in the formation of borate ester bond dynamic crosslinks and MBA (N, N′-methylene bisacrylamide) covalent crosslinks [26]. The dynamic nature of the borate ester bond facilitates controlled modulation of the catechol group, achieving a reversible transition between viscosity and debonding. This dual-network architecture establishes a robust electron transport pathway for aluminum ions, resulting in a conductivity of 4.9 mS·cm−1. Most borate-based hydrogels exhibit rapid self-healing characteristics, allowing the healing hydrogel to effectively recover its mechanical strength [27], [28], [29]. However, these borate-based hydrogels often exhibit poor mechanical strength, facing a challenge to balance the performance between strength and toughness [30], [31], [32]. The toughness of these hydrogels is usually weak, with toughness values at the kilojoule level [33], [34], which limits their application as strain sensors. Additionally, conductive hydrogels using pure water as the dispersing medium will freeze and lose their original conductivity below zero degrees Celsius [35], [36], [37]. Therefore, improving mechanical properties such as stress, strain, flexibility, and conductivity under different conditions (room temperature and low temperature) while maintaining strong self-healing abilities remains a critical issue for borate ester bond hydrogels used as strain sensors. The decrease in conductivity of hydrogels at lower temperatures is primarily attributed to an increase of hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Two main strategies exist to reduce the hydrogen bonding between water molecules. The first method is to introduce polyelectrolyte or zwitterionic polymer to construct intrinsic antifreeze hydrogels. The second method is to introduce polyols (ethylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, etc.) or to add ions [38], [39]. Considering the conductivity of the hydrogel, the incorporation of ions is currently the most feasible and low-cost method for obtaining antifreeze hydrogels. Lithium chloride is an excellent water retention agent and antifreeze. It can not only be used as an antifreeze to reduce the freezing point of water, but also as an electrolyte to provide conductive ions and improve the conductivity of the gel.

Under basic conditions, the carbonate linkage of the LPEEC polymer can readily hydrolyze to form the alcoholate ion and polymers with an Eo repeating unit. A chain scissions mechanism is proposed for LPEEC polymer, as shown in Fig. 6(a), when a carbonate group in the backbone of LPEEC is attacked by the alcoholate anion [20]. The chain scissions model can be described by the kinetic equation d(Ec)p/dP = k (Ec)p/P - 1, as demonstrated in Fig. 6(b) and in Appendix A. In Fig. 6(b), P stands for the LPEEC polymer proportional to the Mn (Table 3), and (Ec)p stands for the split component containing the Ec subunit after LPEEC chain scissions by the attack of the alcoholate anion. It is assumed that (Ec)p is proportional to the molar percentage of Ec in LPEEC (i.e., Mp,Ec in Table 5). Since the (Ec)p/P ratio can be close to a constant because of the pseudo-steady state of the (Ec)p generation and elimination during the chain scission reaction (Fig. 6(b)), it is further assumed that the d(Ec)p/dP ratio is proportional to d(Mp,Ec)/d(Mn) that may also close to a constant. To prove these assumptions, a linear relationship between Mp,Ec and Mn, based on the data in Table 3, Table 5, is shown in Fig. 7. The linear regression equation is Mp,Ec = 2.212 × 10−5 Mn + 0.169 with a good linear correlation coefficient r = 0.982. The mechanisms in Fig. 7 result in the chain cleavage of LPEEC and explain the decrease in Ec content, which is consistent with the faster decrease in x values in Table 3. According to the mechanisms in Fig. 5, Fig. 6, a full procedure for LPEEC synthesis and chain cleavage is proposed. We assumed that the proper molecular structure of LPEEC after the chain scission reaction helped to penetrate the molecular regions of steric hindrance between the starch and PBAT molecules and then strengthen the intermolecular structure and enhance mechanical properties (Fig. 4). A specific length (Mn) of LPEEC is also needed to provide sufficient interactions between LPEEC, starch, and PBAT molecules. Using polyethylene glycol (PEG 2000) of a moderate molecular weight as a plasticizer in the polylactic acid (PLA) and starch blends has been discussed [24]. The migration and miscibility of PEG 2000 have resulted in better water resistance and mechanical properties for composite plastics. The possible interactions of LPEEC with the other components in the compounded plastics are proposed in the following section. Yeh and co-workers prepared DCN hydrogels with imine and borate ester bonds using the amine and phenylboronic acid groups of phenylborate-modified PEI (PBA-PEI) and the aldehyde and diol groups of OSA (Figure 16).[152] Zhao et al. proposed phenylboronic-modified chitosan and ODex to prepare injectable DCN hydrogels based on crosslinking of imine and borate ester bonds.[153a] Due to the pH sensitivity of imine bonds and to the fact that borate ester bonds can be dissociated using another competitive diol (such as glucose), these DCN hydrogels have pH- and glucose-triggered drug release capabilities. Hydrogels also exhibited good biocompatibility and can be used to culture and proliferate cells. Based on the same crosslinking mechanism, the same team also reported that phenylboronic-modified chitosan together with PVA and PEG end-capped with benzaldehyde groups (PEG-DA) can form both borate ester and imine bonded DCN hydrogels.[153b] The obtained DCN hydrogels also showed pH/glucose triggered release of protein drugs and live cells, and demonstrated self-healing properties. DCN hydrogels crosslinked with both borate ester bonds and reversible C═N bonds show once again that two dynamic bonds can retain their respective stimuli-responsiveness even incorporated in a DCN. In addition to two polymeric building blocks, DCN hydrogels can also be prepared from various (more than two) polymeric precursors. An example of a three-component fabrication of DCN hydrogels crosslinked by imine and borate ester bonds was presented by Tao and co-workers using multifunctional PEG bearing both a benzaldehyde group and a phenylboronic acid group at the each ends of the linear chain.[154] This multifunctional PEG as a polymeric crosslinker can form DCN hydrogels within seconds by creating imine bonds with glycol chitosan (GC) and borate ester bonds with PVA. By adjusting the concentration of GC and PVA, the ratio of crosslinking types can be easily adjusted. For example, SCN hydrogels crosslinked by single borate ester or imine bonds can be obtained by selectively adding only PVA or GC to the multifunctional PEG, respectively. Due to the different formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability of borate ester and imine bonds, the borate ester-crosslinked SCN has a shorter gelation time and weaker mechanical strength than the imine-crosslinked SCN. The gelation time and mechanical properties of DCN hydrogels can hence be adjusted by varying GC/PVA. Compared to the two SCN hydrogels, these DCN hydrogels have enhanced strength and mucosal adhesion capacity. It indicates that DCN can not only have enhanced performances, but the performance can be tuned by the thermodynamics and kinetics of the two crosslinking bonds. These DCN hydrogels also have self-healing properties, biocompatibility and biosafety, and can be used as injectable drug carriers. Tan and co-workers synthesized phenylboronic- and ketone-functionalized diblock copolymers P(N-isopropyl acrylamide-co-N-acryloyl-3-aminophenylboronic acid)-b-(N-isopropyl acrylamide-co-diacetone acrylamide) (PAD) for both acylhydrazone and borate ester crosslinked DCN hydrogels.[155] As shown in Figure 17a, the addition of PVA was used for forming borate ester bonds with PAD, and the ADH was employed as crosslinker to react with the ketone groups of PAD to form acylhydrazone-crosslinked subnetwork. Based on the respective stimuli-responsiveness of these two dynamic bonds, DCN hydrogels showed pH-triggered (HCl/NEt3) reversible gel-sol transition, and irreversible gel-to-sol transition due to the addition of an excess ADH or fructose. Interestingly, the more dynamic borate ester linkage endows the DCN hydrogel with fast gelation kinetics and self-healing ability, and the stable acylhydrazone linkage imparts the hydrogel with enhanced mechanical properties. The single borate ester-crosslinked SCN hydrogel had a typical frequency-dependent behavior, and the acylhydrazone-crosslinked SCN hydrogel showed almost frequency-independent behavior (Figure 17b). The DCN hydrogel also demonstrated frequency-dependent behavior, especially at low frequency. Compared to the two SCN hydrogels (33 and 28 kPa), the DCN hydrogel (55 kPa) exhibited higher stress at break (Figure 17c). The DCN has higher mechanical strength, but a limited deformability compared to one of the SCNs crosslinked by a single dynamic bond (as shown in Figure 17c, the rupture strain of DCN is between the two SCNs). These results suggest that the stress relaxation behavior of a DCN hydrogel constructed from two reversible bonds with different dynamics is primarily linked to the bond with the faster kinetics. Based solely on the provided context evidence, the mechanism of chain scission during hydrolysis of ester bonds involves the cleavage of ester linkages in the polymer backbone through a hydrolytic reaction with water. Specifically:

1.  **Hydrolysis causes cleavage**: Ester bonds undergo hydrolytic scission more readily than other bonds like urethane or urea linkages. This cleavage results in a decrease in the polymer's molecular mass [1], [2].
2.  **Formation of carboxylic acid groups**: The hydrolysis reaction cleaves the ester bonds, generating carboxylic acid end groups. This is evidenced by the appearance of a broad FTIR absorbance band in the 3300-3000 cm⁻¹ region [1], [2].
3.  **Nucleophilic attack (specific mechanism for carbonate esters)**: For carbonate ester linkages in polymers like LPEEC (Linear Poly(ether-ester-carbonate)), chain scission proceeds under basic conditions via nucleophilic attack by an alcoholate anion on the carbonate group in the polymer backbone. This reaction cleaves the polymer chain [11].
4.  **Kinetics and products**: The rate of hydrolysis depends on the concentration of water and the labile (ester) bonds. The cleavage products, such as carboxylic acids, can be further degraded by microorganisms in the environment [1], [2], [3], [4]. Enzymatic degradation (e.g., by lipase) can also cleave ester bonds within polymers [7].

Saponification, or de-esterification, typically describes the hydration reaction (hydrolysis) that breaks the ester bonds by either free hydroxides or acids. Such side reactions may happen to some extent among the complex heterogenous mixture (slurry) of hemp fibers and pectin under highly acidic or basic conditions. Under highly acidic conditions, such side reactions may happen and yield free carboxylic acids on the pectin. The free carboxylic acids of pectin can reform ester bonds with the hydroxyl groups on the hemp fibers. However, under high basic conditions, any saponification (or de-esterification) will yield free carboxylates, but the basic conditions cannot catalyze the re-formation of ester bonds with hydroxyl groups because the byproducts, hydroxide ions, are not good leaving groups. Thus, for the methyl carboxylate groups of pectin to react with hydroxyl groups on the fiber surface to produce robust biocomposite as we observed in our experiment, transesterification, though slow, is expected to happen. In other words, most of these methyl carboxylate groups probably do not hydrolyze under the basic conditions evaluated in our experiments. It is important to note that when the pH of the crosslinking reaction was adjusted in the fabrication process to either 1-2 or 12-14, only a few milliliters of the aqueous pectin solution were used for a reaction with 4 grams of hemp fibers. The total numbers of moles of acids or bases were relatively small when compared to the amount of hemp fibers used in the fabrication process. Also, our heating process at 70°C for 2 h and then at 100°C for 10 h will deplete most of the water needed for saponification and hence promote the formation of ester bonds by shifting the equilibrium. Though the transesterification reaction is relatively slow, we believe that sufficient crosslinking can happen due to such reaction mechanisms. Otherwise, we would not observe the V-shape compressive strength trend in Figure 10. In addition, the common method to measure the degree of methylation of pectin is by de-esterification of pectin with a 3× to 10× strong base (such as aqueous NaOH solution (pH = 13-14) mixed 50/50 with isopropanol).85 Even under such harsh conditions, a minimum of 2 h is recommended for complete esterification. This indicates that the de-esterification process is not too fast compared to our reaction period. Hence, the reaction time used in our method is expected to be sufficient for significant crosslinking via transesterification to happen. In this paper, a one-step water-based process to valorize hemp fiber was reported to fabricate hemp fiber composites with pectin. In our composite fabrication methodology, we highlighted the valorization approach to efficiently use surplus hemp fibers by crosslinking them using pectin into green and sustainable biocomposites. Unlike other synthetic polymers such as polyurethane, epoxy, and other petroleum-based products used in conventional composite fabrication,6, 20 we used pectin for crosslinking the hemp fibers in our process because pectin was a plant-based biopolymer extracted from fruit peel. This green approach further overcame the major shortcomings of the conventional fabrication methodologies for hemp fiber composite materials, which considerably relied on the heavy use of organic solvents.86 In addition, the one-way ANOVA study followed by Tukey's HSD test revealed that the mass ratios of pectin to hemp fibers showed that these mass ratios had statistically significant interaction effects on the compressive strength and bulk density of the hemp fiber composites. The illustrated carbohydrate chemistry was generalizable and could be easily applied to incorporate and functionalize other bio-based macromolecules such as gelatin, agar, alginic acid, and chitosan into polymer composite materials.

Based solely on the provided context evidence, the mechanism of chain scission during ester bond hydrolysis involves the cleavage of ester linkages through nucleophilic attack by water (hydrolysis), acids, or bases. This cleavage reduces polymer molecular weight and generates chain-end functional groups:

1.  **Under basic conditions**, hydroxide ions attack the carbonyl carbon of the ester bond. This nucleophilic substitution breaks the C-O bond, producing a carboxylic acid salt (carboxylate) and an alcohol fragment. This process is saponification or de-esterification [1][2][6]. The basic conditions prevent re-formation of ester bonds because hydroxide is a poor leaving group [1][2].
2.  **Under acidic conditions**, protonation of the ester carbonyl oxygen makes the carbon more electrophilic. Subsequent nucleophilic attack by water cleaves the C-O bond, yielding a carboxylic acid and an alcohol [1][2][4][5].
3.  **Kinetics and Products**: Hydrolysis cleaves ester bonds more readily than urethane or urea linkages [4][5][6]. The reaction rate depends on water concentration, labile bond concentration, and pH [4][5]. Cleavage is confirmed by mass loss and the appearance of FTIR absorbance bands (3300-3000 cm⁻¹) corresponding to carboxylic acid groups formed [4][5][9]. For carbonate esters (a specific ester type), chain scission occurs when an alcoholate anion attacks the carbonate group in the polymer backbone [3].
4.  **Factors influencing rate**: The density of ester bonds and polymer crystallinity significantly impact hydrolysis rates; higher ester bond density generally increases degradation rate, while higher crystallinity slows it down [7]. Base catalysis typically degrades ester bonds faster than acid catalysis [6].

question: Why are 'zinc' or 'magnesium' alloys sometimes grouped with biodegradable materials for implants?
ground_truth: Zinc and Magnesium alloys are biodegradable metals. They corrode/degrade in the physiological environment to form non-toxic ions ($Mg^{2+}$, $Zn^{2+}$) that are metabolized or excreted. They provide higher initial load-bearing capacity than polymers for orthopedic applications (bone screws) and degrade as the bone heals.

Nowadays, the study of innovative degradable biomaterials is one of the most interesting research topics in biomaterials. Degradable biomaterials have been proposed from polymers, ceramics, and metals. Metals are more mechanically interesting compared to polymers for load-bearing implants, such as internal bone fixation screws/pins and plates and for coronary stents, which require high strength to bulk ratio [7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17,18,19,20,21]. The most promising candidates for designing biodegradable metallic implants are magnesium, zinc, and iron alloys. Among these, Mg-based alloys and Fe-based alloys are the most widely explored [3, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 19, 22]. Magnesium and its alloys have already been successfully tested in vivo and in clinical studies (Fig. 1) [15, 23, 24]. Most of the studies on Mg-based implants reported a rapid degradation rate in physiological environments accompanied by the evolution of considerable amounts of hydrogen [14, 15, 25]. Excessive rate of degradation can lead to undesired loss of mechanical integrity of the implant; therefore, various methods have been used to control it [26]. An alloying with other elements (Al, Zn, Ca, Ag, Ce, Th) and the preparation of composites were used to improve mechanical properties of Mg-based biomaterials [27]. The main challenge for both Mg and Fe materials is the successful implementation of long-term in vivo experiments. A look at the status of Mg-based metals shows that it is very complicated to develop the material that would be load-bearing, biodegradable, and biocompatible. Metallic implant materials, such as stainless steels, Ti alloys and Co-Cr-Mo alloys have been widely used to support the injured bones during the healing process. Because of the remarkable difference between the elastic modulus of these implants and the cortical bone, a decrease in bone density and thickness takes place over time, causing bone weakening through the well-known shielding effect. This effect is more pronounced for the permanent implants having high elastic modulus, so that they need to be removed from the body via a second surgery. In contrast, biodegradable magnesium implants can reduce the stress shielding effect due to their similar elastic modulus and yield stress to those of the cortical bone [1,2], and thus, they do not need to be removed from the human body. Furthermore, on the account of insufficient strength of other biodegradable materials such as polymeric implants [3], excellent biocompatibility of Mg alloys [4], and the necessity of Mg element in bone generation process [5], researchers have recently turned their attention toward Mg alloys as new materials for biodegradable implants. Pure magnesium is degraded very fast, even before the healing process completes [6]. This early corrosion brings about the premature integrity loss and mechanical failure. Accordingly, researchers have focused on methods to control the degradation rate of Mg alloys through surface coating [7] and also to improve their mechanical properties by alloying [[8], [9], [10]], pre-processing treatments such as extrusion [11,12] and severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques [13]. Among Mg alloys, the Mg-Gd-Zn alloys seem to be promising candidates for biomedical applications, as they provide excellent room temperature ductility and formability [14], along with good corrosion resistance [15], due to the entrapment of impurities in the Gd-containing intermetallic compounds [16]. Moreover, the presence of Zn results in strength and corrosion resistance improvements [17]. Addition of Mn results in grain refinement [18], tensile strength enhancement [19], and improvement in the corrosion resistance by reducing the impurities [20], and the formation of Mn-containing oxides, such as MnO on the surface of the corroded samples [21]. Adding 0.8 wt% Mn to a solution treated Mg-15Gd-1Zn (GZ151) alloy led to an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) improvement from 218 to 272 MPa [22], whereas adding 0.5 wt% Mn to an extruded Mg-2Gd alloy increased its charge transfer resistance from 449.4 to 1590 Ω cm2, due to impurity removal [23]. Similarly, adding 1 wt% Mn to an Mg-10Gd alloy improved its corrosion resistance by forming a compact and passive film [24]. Substituting Mn for Zr in an Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy resulted in enhanced mechanical properties [25]. Gu et al. asserted that the improved ductility and yield stress of an extruded Mg-4Gd alloy after 0.8 wt% Mn addition was mainly due to the lower texture intensity and grain refinement of the resulting alloy [26]. After adding trace amounts of Mn and Zr elements to an extruded Mg-2Gd-1.2Y-0.5Zn alloy, Xu et al. reported higher UTS and yield stress (YS) values for the Mn-containing alloy in comparison with the Zr-containing one [27]. They concluded that Mn was a better choice for the enhancement of mechanical properties in this alloy. Recently, it has been shown that addition of up to 1 wt% Mn to an Mg-4Zn alloy results in grain refinement, texture modification and enhanced mechanical properties and corrosion resistance [28].
Biomedical metallic materials that are currently used can be harmful to the human body in the long term due to metallic particles that are released and accumulated by means of degradation and corrosion of the material. Therefore, metallic materials for temporary implants must have excellent biocompatibility and bifunctionality, adequate load capacity, high wear resistance, low density, and a gradual and controlled biodegradation rate that allows once the bone is healed; then, reabsorption of the biodegradable material is completed [60]. Appropriate selection of biodegradable materials reduces the health risks associated with the use of implants and a second surgery to remove the implant after the tissue has healed [97]. Zinc-based metal alloys have good biocompatibility, high bioabsorbability (up to 15 mg/day [98]), ideal corrosion rate in vitro (approximately 0.022 mm/year [99]) and relatively low Young's modulus (80-90 GPa, see Fig. 2). Zinc is essential for the normal operation of human body; for instance, it is indispensable for heart functioning and protects endothelial cells [100]. Zinc alloys do not produce harmful gases during biodegradation, and the corrosion products are biocompatible and harmless [100]. The low melting temperature of these alloys and the low reactivity during melting allow successfully casting components [98, 100]. All these advantages justify the successful use of the zinc alloys as biodegradable implant material. However, zinc alloys implants are limited in size, because they are brittle, have low mechanical properties and show poor ductility under compression loading. In addition, production costs are relatively high for these alloys due to the high purity elements that are required in the fabrication process of the zinc alloys [98, 101].

However, the corrosion rate of commercially pure magnesium is high and does not match the rate of regeneration of bone tissues. In this work, magnesium alloys containing zinc and cerium, either alone or in combination, were investigated and compared with commercially-pure magnesium as biomaterials. The microstructure, mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and response of osteoblasts in vitro were systematically assessed. Results reveal that alloying with Ce results in grain refinement and weakening of texture. The tensile test revealed that the ternary alloy offered the best combination of elastic modulus (41.1 ± 0.5 GPa), tensile strength (234.5 ± 4.5 MPa), and elongation to break (17.1 ± 0.4%). The ternary alloy was also the most resistant to corrosion (current of 0.85 ± 0.05 × 10−4 A cm−2) in simulated body fluid than the other alloys. The response of MC3T3-E1 cells in vitro revealed that the ternary alloy imparts minimal cytotoxicity. Interestingly, the ternary alloy was highly efficient in supporting osteogenic differentiation, as revealed by the expression of alkaline phosphatase and calcium deposition. In summary, the extruded Mg alloy containing both Zn and Ce exhibits a combination of mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and cell response that is highly attractive for engineering biodegradable orthopedic implants. Thus, the development of biodegradable implants that can perform the human body’s required function and self-degrade timely is a promising approach that eliminates the need for secondary surgery and facilitates the healing process. Compared to polymeric materials, which are also widely used as biodegradable implants, metals have higher mechanical strength and release inert ions during biocorrosion, thereby are not capable of causing local pH reduction and introducing an allergic reaction [1, 9]. The idea of degradable metal usage has brought more attention to temporary implants’ materials. Thus, several key issues should be extensively explored, including the choice of alloying elements, adjusting microstructural and mechanical properties, biodegradation mechanisms, their influence on the human body, controlling the rate of decomposition and metabolism of the degradation products, and the biocompatibility of metals. The biodegradable metal implants should satisfy the following characteristics: biocompatibility of materials themselves and products of their degradation, ability to corrode with appropriate degradation rates, stability for several months before it is fully bioabsorbed [10, 11]. Among the most commonly used metals are iron (Fe), magnesium (Mg), zinc (Zn), and various alloy combinations [12]. Magnesium, one of the most studied biodegradable materials, is a light metal with a high corrosion rate, which requires mandatory alloying with biocompatible elements to increase mechanical strength. Also, magnesium tends to release hydrogen during degradation, which leads to an undesirable increase in pH value in tissues [13]. Compared to magnesium, zinc has a low corrosion rate and no hydrogen evolution, but at the same time, low mechanical strength and a tendency to age hardening. Iron is a fairly strong, ductile, and easily processed material but has a low degree of corrosion compared to Mg and Zn. For the first time, pure iron was used as a biodegradable implant for peripheral stent construction and showed a low degradation rate [14-16]. Alloying iron with other elements can accelerate the degradation process; for example, an implant consisting of Fe-Mn [17] and Fe-Mn-Si [18] alloys and doped with Co, W, S, or C showed a higher decomposition rate than pure iron. At the same time, Fe-Mn-Pd [19] and alloys with Al and B did not show significant changes in the degradation rate. Alloying iron with other elements not only affects the rate of degradation, but also modification of structure and morphology by the method of fabrication [20]. 3D printing technology can accelerate the degradation of iron due to the presence of pores, changing the grain size and properties of boundaries, or by adding additional alloying elements [21-23]. Moreover, additive manufacturing is actively used to create metal implants with complex geometric shapes, sizes, customizable designs, and a certain degree of porosity [4]. When processing biodegradable metals such as zinc and magnesium, significant losses of matter and porosity can be observed [24]; therefore, we turned our attention to iron. In this work, we investigated a porous scaffold based on an iron-silicon (Fe-Si) alloy fabricated by 3D printing technology. As an alloying additive, silicon is a biocompatible element that can increase the strength of iron and reduce its corrosion rate, which can lead to the creation of stronger framework structures required for solid implants for bone grafting. Meanwhile, by forming the porosity and grain structures [25] using additive technologies, it is possible to control the biodegradation rate by increasing the area of the implant’s inner surface, which contact with tissue and reducing the difference in mechanical properties between bones and metals. Printed FeSi scaffolds were analyzed for mechanical properties and biocompatibility using cytotoxicity, and immunotoxicity tests.
Biodegradable metals with good mechanical properties, excellent degradability and biocompatibility have recently been suggested as a class of promising metallic biomedical materials for orthopedic implants, attracting a great amount of interest.4-11 Magnesium and its alloys have attracted much attention as biodegradable metals for implants owing to their similar mechanical properties to those of the body's natural bone and the biocompatibility of magnesium ions.4-7 Nevertheless, one of the most significant risks of Mg-based biodegradable devices is that they are corroded so rapidly. It has generally been acknowledged that Mg-based biodegradable metals with a very low corrosion potential (−2.36 VSCE), which exhibit a rapid corrosion rate in physiological environments, cannot offer effective support and their mechanical integrity is compromised prior to recovery after implantation in the body.4,7,10 Compared with Mg-based alloys, Zn and its alloys might be considered to be interesting candidates owing to their higher electrode potential and similar mechanical properties.12 Furthermore, Zn element is generally considered to be an essential element for humans, playing an important role in the metabolic processes of the human body.13 After these factors were considered, Zn and its alloys were suggested as new members of the family of biodegradable materials. However, preliminary studies have demonstrated that pure Zn had poor mechanical properties and hardness (the tensile strength of as-cast pure Zn was only 20 MPa, its elongation was 0.3% and its hardness was approximately 25 HV9,14), which might not offer sufficient support for implanted devices. Therefore, as an indispensable strengthening process, alloying has been adopted to improve their mechanical performance. Many novel types of zinc alloys have been designed and developed, with the main concentration on Zn-Mg,9,14-19 Zn-Ca,19 Zn-Sr,19 Zn-Mg-Ca,20,21 Zn-Mg-Sr,20-22 Zn-Ca-Sr20 and Zn-Mg-Mn alloys.23 As an effective alloying element in zinc alloys, Mg was found to prominently improve their mechanical performance, and the addition of 0.93 wt% or 1.55 wt% Mg to pure Zn provided superior tensile strength and hardness.9,14 Nevertheless, the maximum elongation of Zn-Mg alloys was approximately 1.5%, which might be suggested as indicating poor ductility for implanted devices. However, advanced processing technology such as extrusion,16,18-20 rolling19,20,22,23 and high-pressure torsion (HPT)24 could be employed to greatly improve the mechanical properties of Zn-based biodegradable metals, which were significantly superior to those of the well-known Mg-based biodegradable metals that have been developed.23,25 In the present work, Zn-1.2Mg alloy has been designed and, in consideration of its effective composition between Zn-1Mg alloy and Zn-1.5Mg alloy, its development as a biodegradable metal and its feasibility for implants were evaluated, in particular after hot extrusion. Its microstructure, mechanical properties, in vitro degradation behavior, in vitro hemocompatibility and cytotoxicity were tested to investigate its feasibility as a new biodegradable material.
Magnesium alloys have shown potential as body-implanted materials for orthopedic application compared with the traditional implanted materials, due to its excellent biocompatibility (no toxicity), good biodegradability, low density (1.74-2.0 g cm−3) and moderate Young’s modulus (41-45 GPa) close to the human bone (3-20 GPa) [1, 2]. Due to poor corrosion rate, it is difficult to maintain enough strength before the bone is healed [3]. It is required to possess certain properties for biodegradable Mg alloys such as in cardiovascular application [4], including: (1) excellent mechanical properties (ultimate tensile strength > 250 MPa, fracture elongation > 15%), (2) homogeneous degradation during tissue recovery (12-24 months) and (3) good biocompatibility. Therefore, the main emphasis of developing new biodegradable Mg alloys exhibits high mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. The alloying is one of the most effective methods to improve the corrosion and mechanical properties. Researchers try to develop magnesium alloys with non-toxic or low toxic alloying element for orthopedic applications, such as Mg-Zn (Zn, Ca, Sr) [5,6,7,8,9], Mg-Zn-X (Ca, Sr, Mn) [10,11,12,13,14,15,16], Mg-Ca-X (Sr, Bi) [17,18,19] and Mg-Zn-Mn-Ca [20,21,22]. Zn as an element in human body can improve the strength and corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [1]. Zirconium (Zr) is a grain refiner to improve mechanical properties of Mg alloys [23]. Besides, rare-earth elements (RE) have been used in Mg biological alloys to improve mechanical properties and corrosion resistance in recent years, such as Mg-X (La, Ce, Nd, Sc, Dy) [24,25,26], Mg-Zn-X (Gd, Sc, Nd) [27,28,29], Mg-Dy-Gd-Zr [26] and Mg-Nd-Zn-Zr [30]. The researches show that the RE elements can penetrate into the corrosion film and enhance the film compactness to protect the Mg matrix [31]. Though alloying can improve the corrosion and mechanical properties, the as-cast alloys cannot meet enough mechanical properties requirements in physiological environment. The thermal deformations such as extrusion are considered as one of the most effective methods to improve mechanical and corrosion properties for magnesium alloys. Li et al. [14] have reported that a biodegradable Mg-Zn-Zr-Sr alloy reaches a high strength (ultimate tensile strength up to 376 MPa, elongation up to 16.6%) and moderate corrosion resistance (4.07 mm/y) after extrusion. Zhao et al. [8] have studied Mg-Sr binary alloys as biodegradable implant materials; the as-extruded alloys exhibited high strength (270 MPa for ultimate tensile strength and 11% for elongation) and low corrosion rate.
Cobalt-based alloys, stainless steels and titanium (Ti) alloys have been widely used as hard tissue implants such as plates, screws and pins for orthopaedic applications [1]. Since these implants are not biodegradable in the human body and may cause long-term complications, a subsequent surgical procedure may be necessary to remove these implants from the human body after the tissues heals. For such applications, it is desirable to use biodegradable implants. Although biodegradable polymeric materials have been used for a long time, these polymeric materials are not suitable to be orthopaedic implants due to their poor mechanical strength. Therefore, it is necessary to develop biodegradable metallic implant materials with appropriate mechanical properties. Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys for biodegradable implants have extensively attracted attentions because they exhibit suitable mechanical properties and can degrade in the human body. The previous studies on using Mg alloys as biomaterials mainly focused on Mg-Al and Mg-RE alloy systems [2-4] and the existing Mg and its alloys corrode rapidly in the human body fluid [3-5]. It can result in loss of mechanical integrity before the tissue heals and hydrogen production near the implants, which retard the healing process [3, 5]. Hence, it is necessary to develop novel biodegradable Mg alloys that would corrode at acceptably low rates to ensure Mg alloy implants with the function of loading-bearing through their service lives and reduce hydrogen bubbles in the healing process. Element alloying is an effective method to enhance corrosion resistance. Zinc (Zn), manganese (Mn), calcium (Ca) and rare earth elements (RE) are regarded as suitable alloying elements for the development of biodegradable Mg alloys [5]. So far, some Mg alloys such as Mg-Zn, Mg-Zn-Mn, Mg-Zn-Mn-Ca, Mg-Zn-Y, Mg-Si-Ca-Zn and Mg-Ca alloys have been studied for biomedical applications [6-12]. Other than Zn and aluminium (Al), zirconium (Zr) is also a very effective alloying element in improving both the corrosion resistance and strength in Al-free Mg alloys [3, 13, 14], though it has been reported that the presence of Zr is associated with some illnesses [5]. However, recent studies [13, 15] have verified the biocompatibility of Mg alloys with a small amount of Zr, hence the Mg-Zr-based alloys with low Zr content may be promising candidates for biomedical applications. Up until now, there are a few reports on biomedical Mg-Zr-based alloys [13, 15, 16]. In this study, Mg-Zr-based alloys were chosen as an experimental model to screen for the potential use in biomedical applications. Since Ca is an essential element in the human body, and a minor addition of Ca (below 2 wt %) can enhance the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [12, 13], it has also been chosen as an alloying element. To the best knowledge of the authors, Mg-Zr-Ca alloys have not been systematically studied for orthopaedic applications.
Biodegradable metal implants are gaining attention over traditional bio-inert/bio-stable implants owing to the fact that most of the clinical problems need only short-term support while healing. These implants deteriorate by releasing metallic components that the body metabolizes and are finally replaced by bone tissue [1,2,3]. Performing a secondary surgery to remove the implant is unnecessary because biodegradable implants are designed to provide initial mechanical support and gradually dissolve in the body without causing any harm. The temporary implant experiences a gradual decrease in mechanical strength and integrity due to deterioration. This process also allows for a gradual transfer of load from implant to bone, hence reducing the stress shielding effect [4, 5]. Zinc, iron and magnesium are the biodegradable metals that have been studied the most. Notably iron has been identified as suitable material with high strength, formability and slow corrosion rate. However, degradation rate can be improved by fabrication of porous scaffolds [6, 7]. The optimal daily dosage of zinc is approximately 40 mg; however, temporary amounts of up to 100 mg do not result in any health issues. Zinc is reported to have good biocompatibility, making it a potential biodegradable implant material [8, 9]. Zn could be combined with Fe to produce a composite biomaterial to overcome the demerits of both the metals and harness the beneficial properties resulting to the development of a more suitable biomaterial. Bioceramics can be added in low concentrations to facilitate bone ingrowth and ensure an effective bond between bone and implant material. The implant surface must possess bioactive properties that encourage the growth of bone cells and the formation of biological apatite, hence enhancing osteoconductivity [10, 11]. Hydroxyapatite (HAp) is commonly employed in the biomaterials sector as a bone bioactive substitute and coating material. This is because it possesses remarkable biocompatibility and closely resembles the mineral composition of human bones, which primarily consist of calcium and phosphorous [12,13,14,15,16]. HAp is reported to enhance the bioactivity of titanium dental and orthopaedic implants; magnesium and iron biodegradable implants in various studies [17,18,19,20,21].
Thus, zinc metal, with its ZnO nanotube structures, can facilitate drug delivery, including antibiotics to prevent early infections and anticancer drugs to suppress cancer cell growth. Biodegradable metals and their alloys have found numerous applications in orthopedic and cardiovascular fields, prompting extensive research to enhance their performance. Biodegradable alloys must be non-toxic, be biologically compatible, and exhibit low corrosion rates in the body.65,66 Materials classified as biodegradable implants interact with damaged tissues within the human body, directly impacting human life. Consequently, it is critical that these materials exhibit unquestionable biocompatibility and biosafety to prevent adverse reactions with host tissues and minimize the release of corrosive by-products. As previously noted, alloying is essential for utilizing zinc in load-bearing biomedical applications. Alloying elements should enhance mechanical properties while positively influencing biodegradation and biological behavior. Incubation of MG-63 bone cells with undiluted pure zinc extracts in indirect cellular assays revealed cytotoxic effects, with insufficient biocompatibility at high Zn2+ concentrations repeatedly documented.67 In recent years, research has shifted toward alloying zinc to improve its mechanical properties, enabling its use in bone tissue engineering scaffolds. Key alloying elements include zirconium,34 lithium,35 aluminum,45 titanium,37 magnesium and calcium,30 magnesium and strontium,31 and copper and iron,33 among others. The enhancement of mechanical properties and control of corrosion rates in zinc-based alloys depend primarily on the choice, quantity, and distribution of alloying elements within the zinc matrix. These elements can be categorized into three groups: those with negligible or no solubility (e.g., iron, magnesium, and calcium), those with low or limited solubility (e.g., copper, aluminum, and lithium), and those with high solubility (e.g., silver) in zinc. Alloys of the first two categories may exhibit poor ductility and premature failure, which could be unacceptable for stent applications. However, severe plastic deformation techniques can adjust the mechanical properties of these alloys for specific uses.64 For cardiovascular stents, an ultimate tensile strength of ∼300 MPa is required, whereas pure zinc exhibits a tensile strength of only 20-120 MPa.68,69 Thus, developing zinc alloys with adequate strength and biocompatibility remains an area requiring further exploration with diverse alloying elements beyond those currently reported.
Recently, various biodegradable implant materials as interim implants generated intense interest for their diverse medical uses. They became useful for abrogating the requirement of second removal surgery, circumventing the adverse impacts of enduring implantations [1], [2]. Compared to the ceramics and polymers, biodegradable metals offer higher strength performance, wear resistance, ductility, as well as toughness [3]. These properties make them an appealing candidate in orthopedics as load-bearing and fixation device applications including the replacements of joints, bone-plate, screws, dental implants, pacers, suture wires, and coronary stents [4], [5], [6], [7]. Engineers and scientists have constantly been improving the mechanical and degradation characteristics of these biodegradable metallic implants. Pure iron (Fe), pure magnesium (Mg), pure zinc (Zn) and their alloys are widely studied to evaluate their implantation potentials [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. Numerous animal experiments and clinical trials show that these biodegradable metals are safe and feasible as implants [17], [18]. They have good biocompatibility despite their differences in degradation rate. The degradation rate of pure Fe is very slow [19], while the degradation rate for Mg is very rapid [20]. Pure Zn exhibits an intermediate degradation rate [21]. The advantage of using ferroalloys (Fe-based alloys) is that they have a higher tensile strength compared to Mg and Zn alloys. For example, Fe alloys can achieve a tensile strength of up to 433 MPa, whereas Mg alloys are limited to around 186 MPa [22]. While having a similar modulus of elasticity to human bone and could promote bone growth, Mg alloys suffer from mechanical integrity issues due to their rapid corrosion rate. Zn alloys show tunable mechanical properties with an intermediate corrosion rate but generally have lower strength than Fe alloys [21].

Biodegradable implant materials, which could satisfy clinical requirements for mechanical properties, degradation rate, and requisite biocompatibility [1-3]. However, among these biodegradable, Fe-based materials exhibited an excessively low degradation rate, which can not meet the clinical requirement of total degradation in 2 years after implantation [6]. Also, the degradation products of Fe-based materials were nonabsorbable and hard to excrete from the human body. On the other hand, Mg-based materials have proven effective in clinical applications with good biocompatibility and osteogenic capability, while the excessively high degradation speed restricted the application of Mg-based as biodegradable implants [7, 8]. Further, hydrogen generation during the degradation process of Mg-based implants could cause the hydrogen accumulation around the implant, inducing pain and inhibiting wound healing [9, 10]. Zn, as a widely distributed essential trace element, plays a significant role in enzyme synthesis, DNA replication, transcription, and expression [11-13]. More importantly, Zn can promote osseointegration and osteoinduction during the bone healing process, indicating the great potential of Zn-based materials as a biofunctional orthopedic implant [14, 15]. Moreover, elemental Mg, as a major essential dietary element participates in many biochemical reactions and enzyme reactions in the human body. From the perspective of biosafety, Mg should be an ideal alloying element for the Zn matrix to develop a biocompatible and biofunctional Zn-based alloy [16, 17]. Moreover, Mg is a critical factor for glucose metabolism and the cellular respiratory system and a stabilizing function of DNA and RNA [18, 19]. A previous study revealed that Zn-1Mg alloy lead to no side effect on cell multiplication and no cytotoxicity to MG63 osteoblasts, exhibiting improved cytocompatibility [20]. This extension was attributed to forming a work-hardened layer with submicron-sized SiC fragments, enhancing support for the tribological layer on the wear surface. Delamination wear is observed at moderate loading conditions, influenced by hard particles as nucleation sites for crack propagation. The coefficient of friction ranged from 0.25 to 0.45, reaching minimums at critical speeds and loads. Despite considerable progress, these passive strategies cannot address the following three challenges. First, it is immensely challenging to achieve a desired combination of degradation time and mechanical strength solely through alloy engineering.[26] Second, individual variations of the recovery time of patients cannot be taken into account after implantation. question: What is the role of 'plasticizers' like Citrate esters in PLA formulations?
ground_truth: Plasticizers (e.g., Acetyl Tributyl Citrate) insert themselves between polymer chains, increasing free volume and chain mobility. For PLA, this lowers the glass transition temperature (Tg), reduces brittleness, and improves flexibility and elongation at break, making the material suitable for flexible films.

Plasticizers increase flexibility and reduce the glass transition temperature. In PLA, common plasticizers include citrate esters like acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) and triethyl citrate (TEC), glycerides, polyethylene glycol (PEG), and lactic acid esters. While these plasticizers enhance flexibility, they present several disadvantages. They can migrate from the polymer to the surface or environment, reducing their effectiveness [11]. Certain plasticizers may have toxic or allergic effects on humans and animals, especially in medical or food packaging applications [12]. Additionally, not all plasticizers are fully compatible with PLA, possibly resulting in non-uniform distribution and adverse mechanical and optical properties [13]. Research focuses on bio-based plasticizers for PLA to find alternatives that offer better performance without the associated disadvantages of traditional plasticizers [14], [15]. Alternatively, blending PLA with other polymers like polycaprolactone (PCL) and polybutylene succinate (PBS) can enhance flexibility and processability but presents challenges. Incompatibility can cause phase separation, negatively affecting mechanical properties and appearance. Optimizing processing conditions for each polymer combination increases costs and manufacturing complexity. Adding certain polymers may also affect PLA's biodegradation rate and mode, undesirable for ecological applications [16], [17]. Phenethyl esters are compounds of great interest due to their unique chemical properties formed by esterification of carboxylic acids with different chain length with phenol [18]. Both products involved can be obtained from natural resources, a sustainable route for the obtention of biobased material with low impact for the environment [19]. The ideal plasticizer is proposed to possess a combination of structural features, including aliphatic chains that act as spacers to increase the free volume and consequently lower the glass transition temperature, ester groups that contribute to molecular cohesion, and aromatic rings that enhance compatibility with the polymer matrix, thereby promoting miscibility [20]. In this context, phenethyl esters represent a promising alternative, as they incorporate all the aforementioned functional groups, facilitating the development of an effective plasticizer. As part of the ongoing search for high-performance plasticizers, the use of naturally derived compounds containing ester functionalities has previously been explored [21]. Importantly, these phenethyl esters have not been previously used as plasticizers for PLA, confirming the novel opportunity to explore their potential in enhancing the mechanical and processing properties of the polymer. Phenethyl esters have diverse applications, due to their chemical and sensory properties [22]. Phenethyl propionate serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, including steroid hormones used in hormonal therapies [23]. As described, these esters generally have a favorable safety profile, making them suitable for use in products with direct skin, food, or medical contact.
The effect of plasticizer on PLA blending was also studied by several researchers. The blending of origin PLA or mixing with other nanofillers produced brittle product. The plasticizer acts as a processing aid in flow improvement, mostly for films and cables. Instead of reducing the ductility, the plasticizer also functions in the mechanical and thermal properties enhancement. Plasticizers work by embedding themselves between the chains of polymers, spacing them apart, and thus, significantly lower the T g for the plastic and makes it softer. A list of ester-like plasticizers for PLA has been studied, such as glucose monoesters, partial fatty acids, citrates, glycerol esters, and dicarboxylic esters [174-180]. Unfortunately, the low molecular weight plasticizers have the problem of migrating, owing to their high mobility within the PLA matrix. Therefore, the high molecular weight plasticizers with low mobility are suitable, such as poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG) [174, 181, 182], poly(propylene) glycol (PPG) [183], and atactic poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (a-PHB) [184]. Besides lowering the T g, they do not crystallize and miscible with PLA. Table 6 shows the recent studies using plasticizers, mostly PEG in PLA blends and their thermal analysis. The choice of plasticizer used as a modifier for PLA is limited by legislative or the applications. On the other hand, the plasticizer has to be biodegradable, non-toxic for food contact (for packaging), and biocompatible (for medical applications). Commonly, the amount of plasticizers that range from 10 to 20 % is required to provide both a substantial reduction of T g of the PLA matrix, and adequate mechanical properties. In environmental issues, the biodegradable or bioresorbable; and non-volatile plasticizer is preferred, with a relatively low molecular weight to produce the desired decrease of the Young’s modulus value. Additionally, the ranging amount between 20 and 30 % of plasticizer in PLA matrix leads to phase separation. It must be remembered that the percentage of plasticizer determines the plasticization of PLA blend.
External plasticization is an effective strategy to enhance the processability and flexibility of polylactic acid (PLA). The success of this approach largely depends on the miscibility and diffusion of the plasticizer within the polymer matrix, ensuring long-term material stability. Conventional plasticizers, often phthalate-based and synthetically derived, pose environmental and health risks due to their carcinogenic nature and tendency to leach at ambient temperatures. In this study, ricinoleic acid-based esters were synthesized as bio-based alternatives for PLA plasticization. Two esters icinoleic ester (RE) and benzoic ricinoleic ester (BRE) were synthesized using ricinoleic acid, benzoic acid, and trimethylolpropane. The extent of esterification was verified by acid value analysis, FTIR spectroscopy, and 1H NMR. PLA was plasticized with varying loadings of RE and BRE, and the resulting materials were characterized using DSC, TGA, FTIR, UTM, and rheological analysis. Both plasticizers exhibited thermal stability at PLA processing temperatures, with BRE showing superior miscibility and plasticization efficiency. A loading of 10 phr was found optimal, resulting in significant Tg reduction and improved flexibility. The findings suggest that BRE, in particular, offers a promising bio-based plasticizer for enhancing the performance of PLA without compromising its inherent properties.
Fibers have also been used to enhance the mechanical properties of PLA. Glass fibers (GF) and carbon fibers (CF) are some of the most popular ones. Natural fibers are also being studied, such as jute, abaca, hemp or flax fibers [10,11]. In spite of the fact that some of these fibers are quite rigid, they are capable of improving the toughness and general mechanical properties of PLA. Incorporation of plasticizers is an effective technical solution to provide improved ductility to PLA. In general, plasticizers increase flexibility and toughness. A wide range of plasticizers have been proposed, including monomeric plasticizers such as citrates, malonates, glycerol esters, oligomers of lactic acid, adipates, among others. Polymeric plasticizers have also given interesting properties to PLA. It is worthy to highlight the use of poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), among others, as polymeric plasticizers for PLA, thus leading to binary/ternary blends with full or partial miscibility, depending on the polymeric plasticizer [[12], [13], [14]]. In general, monomeric plasticizers offer exceptional plasticization performance, but the migration is higher than plasticized PLA formulations containing polymeric plasticizers due to a lower molecule size. With the aim of broadening the industrial applications of PLA without compromising the biobased nature, new alternative plasticizers are continuously being proposed. Llanes et al. [15] reported the potential of malonate and fumarate isomers as environmentally friendly plasticizers for PLA with a noticeable decrease in glass transition temperature (Tg) from 58 °C (neat PLA) down to 22 °C for the plasticized formulation containing 12 wt% dimethyl fumarate (DMF). Recently, Barandarian et al. [16] have reported the exceptional plasticization efficiency of different cinnamate esters with a noticeable increase in elongation at break from 3.9 % (neat PLA) up to values comprised between 250 and 339 % with 20 wt% cinnamate esters, which was also reflected by a decrease in Tg from 61.7 °C (neat PLA) to values below 40 °C. Ivorra-Martinez et al. [17,18] have shown the extraordinary plasticization efficiency of dibutyl itaconate (DBI) as environmentally friendly plasticizer for PLA. They reported an increase in elongation at break from 4.6 % (neat PLA) up to 322 % with just 10 wt% DBI. Brüster et al. [19] explored the effect of conventional and reactive extrusion (REX) on the plasticization efficiency of terpene-based plasticizers. Other natural terpenes, such as geraniol or linalool have also been reported to possess excellent plasticizing properties, especially when they are reacted with carboxylic acids to form esters [20]. Geraniol esters have shown interesting plasticization properties on poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) as reported in a previous work [21] Nevertheless, despite the solubility parameters of P3HB and geraniol esters suggest good miscibility and hence, good plasticization, the overall plasticization effects of geranyl esters are not exceptional, due to the intrinsic difficulty to plasticize crystalline P3HB.
This study demonstrates the potential of different cinnamate esters, namely methyl trans-cinnamate (MC), isobutyl cinnamate (IBC), allyl cinnamate (AC), and ethyl cinnamate (EC), as environmentally friendly plasticizers for polylactide (PLA). Plasticized PLA formulations with a constant nominal wt% of 20 of each plasticizer are compounded in a twin-screw co-rotating extruder and subsequently processed by injection molding. The results show exceptional plasticization efficiency of AC with an increase in elongation at break from 3.9% (neat PLA), up to 339.4% and a remarkable increase in impact strength, thus showing great potential to overcome the main drawback related to PLA intrinsic brittleness. The incorporation of cinnamates in a PLA matrix leads to a decrease in Tg from 61.7 °C down to 36.1 °C for the plasticized PLA formulation containing 20 wt% AC. Thermogravimetry analysis reveals that a slight plasticizer loss occurs during processing, as it happens with other monomeric plasticizers, but this phenomenon does not limit their plasticization efficiency. Therefore, the results obtained in this study confirm the suitability of a new family of organic compounds derived from the esterification of cinnamic acid as green plasticizers for PLA with improved toughness, with comparable, or even superior, ductile properties of typical plasticizers for PLA. In the last decade, aliphatic polyesters have attracted much attention due to the increasing concern about the environment. Aliphatic polyesters can undergo biodegradation under compost conditions due to the hydrolysis of ester groups, which represents a clear advantage from an environmental point of view. Among these polymers, it is possible to find petroleum-based polyesters such as polybutylene succinate (PBS), polyglycolide (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate-co-adipate (PBSA). In fact, currently, some of these polyesters can also be fully or partially synthesized from different biobased building blocks.[1-4] Nevertheless, biobased polyesters, such as polylactide (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), have received much attention due to their environmental advantages and represent a sound alternative to petroleum-derived polymers.[5-7] PLA is an aliphatic polyester that is usually obtained by ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of lactide, which is obtained by fermentation of starch-rich plant sources such as rice, corn, cassava (tapioca), and sugarcane, among others.[8-10] PLA offers rather good balanced properties (mechanical, thermal, biodegradation, transparency, barrier, and so on) and processability.[11] Nevertheless, one of its main drawbacks is related to its intrinsic brittleness, due to poor ductile behavior, which hinders its massive use, mainly in the packaging industry. Hence, much research on PLA has focused on improving toughness.[12-16] To overcome this, physical blending with flexible polymers and plasticization have been proposed.[17, 18] It has been widely reported in the literature the remarkable improvement in ductile and impact strength properties of PLA by binary and ternary blends with flexible polymers such as PBS,[19-21] PCL,[22] PBSA,[23] polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (PBAT),[24-26] and thermoplastic starch,[27] among others, with or without using compatibilizers.[28, 29]
Numerous techniques have been explored to enhance the ductility of PLA without compromising its environmentally friendly potential. One such approache is blending PLA with other more ductile polymers, such as poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [8], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [9], or thermoplastic starch (TPS) [10]. Despite the appeal this approach offers, in some instances the poor miscibility between PLA and the other polymers reduces its viability. Thus, another more frequent strategy to improve the ductility of PLA involves the use of plasticizers, low molecular weight compounds that are incorporated into the PLA polymeric chains and mitigate the intensity of the polymer-polymer chain interactions, thus enhancing the processability and flexibility of the polymer [11]. Plasticization is very simple and cost-effective as it involves de addition of the plasticizer during the processing. However, the plasticizer must be compatible with PLA. Some environmentally friendly plasticizers that have been extensively studied include citrates [12], modified vegetable oils [13], esters of cinnamic acid [14], esters of geraniol [15] and esters of linalool [16], among others. All these plasticizers allow PLA to boost its elongation at break from a very low value (5 %) to values between 200 and 500 %. More recently, attention is being given to tartaric acid (TA) derivatives as potential plasticizers for PLA. Plasticizers derived from TA are sourced from natural origins and are biodegradable, so they preserve the biodegradability of PLA. Tartaric acid can be obtained from grapes [17] or tamarind [18]. These derivatives, which include several tartrates, show high compatible with PLA, as most widely used citrates [19]. Previous studies have shown that diethyl-l-tartrate (DET) is a highly effective plasticizer for PLA, delivering elongation at break exceeding 550 % for a DET content of 20 wt% and a reduction of the glass transition temperature of PLA from 60 down to 23 °C for a 50 wt% DET content. Zawada et al. [20] have shown the potential of 13 different tartrate compounds as “double green” biobased plasticizers for PLA. Despite they reported exceptional plasticization properties of various synthesized tartrates, most of them are not commercially available which can limit their industrial use. Although they observed good plasticization properties of diethyl tartrate (DET), they concluded the exact composition of the mixture needs further optimization to improve the overall performance, as well as the use of processing conditions similar to industrial processes. On the other hand, Gomez-Caturla et al. [19], demonstrated that a plasticizer content of 20 wt% DET, gives optimum balanced mechanical and thermal properties on plasticized PLA. Therefore, the potential of other commercially available tartrates as biobased plasticizers for PLA could be of interest. Another promising group of plasticizers yet to be explored are α-tocopherol based plasticizers. α-tocopherol is considered one of the most biologically active compounds in the phenol family. It exhibits significant antioxidant potential and has been used in several studies to enhance the food preservation capacity of polymeric materials, such as chitosan/zein mixtures [21], polyolefins [22] or polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) films [23]. Esters derived from α-tocopherol have also been used in medical applications, such as the treatment of acne [24], or the production of bi-layer membranes of α-tocopherol acetate for wound healing and skin regeneration [25]. These esters offer significant potential as plasticizers for PLA, which could additionally give this polymer antioxidant properties and other features. An additional huge advantage of α-tocopherol and its derivatives is their natural origin and environmentally friendly nature, as they are non-toxic organic, biodegradable and biocompatible compounds. Esters of α-tocopherol offer a unique chemical structure which could provide multifunctional properties to PLA since it has been demonstrated to provide melt stabilization during polyolefin processing [26], as well as antioxidant properties to PLA [27]. On the other hand, the plasticization properties of α-tocopherol, has been described by Kangarlou et al. [28], in ethyl cellulose films, therefore corroborating the potential of α-tocopherol as biobased plasticizer in polymer formulations.
Citrate esters triethyl citrate, tributyl citrate, and acetyl tributyl citrate were used as plasticizers for amorphous poly(D,L-lactide) (PDLLA). The resultant compositions were analyzed by means of differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), dynamic mechanical thermal analysis, and tensile testing to investigate the properties of the blends. Glass transition temperatures (Tgs) obtained by DSC were also compared to theoretically calculated Tgs. Increasing plasticizer content decreased the resultant Tg of the blend with plasticizer efficiency enhanced as the molecular weight of the citrate ester increased. However, in blends with high plasticizer content, a lack of miscibility also occurred with increased molecular weight. Theoretical results were comparable with those obtained experimentally at compositions, which were miscible. Increasing plasticizer content increased the ductility and decreased the strength of the polymer.
