Three-dimensional (3D) printing has long been a powerful technology to fabricate complicated biomimetic microstructures.24,25 Among diverse 3D printing technologies, extrusion-based 3D bioprinting26 is widely used to generate well-designed microstructures with high resolution and fidelity for biomimetic scaffolds and flexible sensors. Polymer hydrogels have been widely used as 3D bioprinting inks for extrusion-based printing. Usually, hydrogel precursor solutions with high viscosity are extruded from the nozzle to deposit on the substrate and immediately cured by freezing27 or UV light.28 In many cases, the dilemma of printability and fidelity severely limits the stability and resolution of printed constructs. Novel hydrogels are needed to achieve both printability and fidelity, as well as mechanical stability against cyclic loadings, under mild conditions. Microgels have emerged as promising materials for 3D printing. Microgel assemblies have been used as a supporting bath to create artificial tissues and organs.29,30 But the obtained constructs are usually weak and fragile, and need post-printing treatment to cure and improve the strength and stability. On the other hand, microgel assemblies are widely used as inks for extrusion-based 3D printing. Microgels can self-assemble through inter-particle dynamic bonds and are used as bioinks to achieve high printability, shape fidelity and cellular activity.31 Hydrogel microparticles with extensive inter-particle hydrogen bonding and geometric jamming are developed by crushing chitosan methacrylate/polyvinyl alcohol hydrogels. The microparticles assemble into hydrogels with thixotropy and excellent creep resistance, which enables direct 3D printing at room temperature to fabricate biomimetic scaffolds with high resolution and fidelity.27 However, the printed microgel constructs with weak inter-particle interactions cannot survive periodic loadings in practical applications. It remains a great challenge to improve the mechanical properties of the printed microgel constructs to meet the demand of hydrogel sensors on high toughness and sensing stability. Herein, we demonstrate 3D printing of highly sensitive and tough microstructured flexible sensors based on a microgel-reinforced double network (MRDN) hydrogel for biomechanical and tracking applications. Rigid polyelectrolyte microgels have been utilized as building blocks and sacrificial units to dissipate energy, increase resistance against crack propagation and build special network topologies, and thus significantly improve the strength and toughness of hydrogels.32,33 Here, we massively synthesize polyelectrolyte poly(2-acrylamido-2-methylpro-panesulfonic acid) (PAMPS) microgels by emulsion polymerization, and then mix them with acrylic acid (AAc) monomers to produce a viscous ink for direct 3D printing of well-designed microstructures with high resolution and fidelity. Subsequent UV curing results in in situ formation of a second network interpenetrating throughout the microgels, yielding microstructured MRDN constructs with high strength and toughness (Fig. 1). The obtained hierarchical structures improve the pressure sensitivity by a factor of 50, with outstanding stability against cyclic loadings. An array of MRDN hydrogels is assembled into a wearable shoe-pad with eight-channel pressure sensors to monitor the foot biomechanics during gaiting. Moreover, we demonstrate a dependence of sensitivity on the geometry of microstructures, including pyramids, semispheres, and cubes, and thus fabricate a flexible sensor array with well-designed in-plane distribution of different microstructures and sensitivities to track the trajectory of a moving animal (e.g., a tortoise) on the surface. This study provides a promising method to fabricate microstructured hydrogel sensors with high sensitivity and stability by 3D printing of curable microgel inks. This novel strategy is promising for the development of high-performance hydrogel pressure sensors for application in wearable intelligent medical devices.
Hydrogels are cross-linked three-dimensional (3D) networks of water-soluble polymers and large amounts of water, and structural similarities to some human soft tissues. [11] The hydrophilic networks allow the diffusion of glucose and nutrients, thereby promoting cell growth [12,13]. They have suitable properties as 3D bioinks, with good printability at low pressures, controllable swelling properties and contraction, and excellent biocompatibility. However, the successful 3D bioprinted hydrogels, are usually fragile, with limited mechanical integrity [14,15] and such properties are frequently tailored by polymers' mixing or crosslinking. For extrusion-based printing, the hydrogels shear thinning properties facilitate the flow through fine nozzles [16,17]. Chemical crosslinking leads to ingrowth biomechanical properties of hydrogels, excellent mechanical strength, but low stretchability and self-healing ability [18]. Natural and synthetic polymers have been explored in the field of soft hydrogel and hyaluronic acid, agarose, alginate, chitosan, collagen type I and gelatin have been printed either alone or together with other polymers as components of bioinks [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23]]. Collagen, and its derivative gelatin, typically extracted from animal tissues and containing cell adhesion sites, has physiological and biochemical properties similar to the normal tissues, as well as excellent biodegradability. However, their mechanical properties and three-dimensional stability of printed tissue are usually critical [24]. Skardal et al. studied the effect of poly(ethylene glycol) - PEG on the bioinks viscosity and Yu et al. studied matrices from methacrylated gelatin(GelMA) - based bioinks in order to optimize the mechanical properties [17,25]. Gelatin forms networks able of interaction with various fluids, enzymatic degradation response and non-toxicity [26]. However, gelatin hydrogels are thermal reversible with limitations for in vivo applications [27]. Methacrylated gelatin (GelMA), is a light-curing polymer, consisting of gelatin with functional methacrylate groups, suitable for tissue engineering. The biopolymer contains a large number of functional side chains that favor subsequent changes [28,29]. GelMA application in biomedical field is based on its tunable physicochemical shape-forming ability, cytocompatibility and fast polymerization properties [30], and includes 3D hydrogels, electrospun fibrous membranes, 3D printed scaffolds [31]. Combined with other polymers, growth factors or small molecules of drugs, it can meet the conditions for engineering the soft tissues repairs (skin repairs, cornea, blood vessels) [32,33].
Biohybrid hydrogels comprising of cell-adhesive proteins and synthetic polymers have been considered as the ideal biomaterials as they can not only retain their good printability and mechanical property but also enhance bioactive characteristics for promoting cellular activities.[22] Various studies have investigated on the developments of the biohybrid hydrogels for printing biologically functional 3D scaffolds, including polyurethane (PU)/gelatin, PEG/gelatin/arginyl-glycyl-aspartic acid (RGD), MA-BSA (methacrylate bovine serum albumin)/PEGDA, PEGDA/Silk Methacrylate (SilMA), etc. Hsieh et al. synthesized a biohybrid hydrogel composed of PU and gelatin, which had excellent stacking ability (up to 80 printed layers), high-resolution printability (through an 80-µm nozzle), and threefold increase in compressive modulus after CaCl2 treatment.[23] Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) embedded in PU/gelatin scaffolds showed high cellular mobility, good viability, and ≈300% increase in proliferation after 10 days in vitro. Piluso et al. reported a novel PEG-based biohybrid inks by incorporating low-molecular-weight gelatin fragments that enabled to fabricate various architectures, including kite-like, star, mesh, and multilayer tubular while maintain the high viability of 3T3 fibroblasts (>90%) and continuous proliferation (7 days).[24] The authors further improved the biofunctionality of PEG/Gelatin biohybrid inks with addition of cell-adhesive RGD ligands, allowing to transform the embedded cells from spindle-like elongated morphology to spread-out shape.[24] Smith and colleagues demonstrated, for the first time, formulation of MA-BSA and PEGDA as photocurable biohybrid hydrogel that can be utilized for fabrication of complex geometries (lattice and honeycomb) with good resolution (250 µm).[25] The printed scaffolds showed long-term biocompatibility (21 days) with excellent cell viability (>95%) due to the presence of BSA in the backbone chain, promoting the cell adhesion of matrix protein such as fibronectin. Bandyopadhyay et al. prepared PEGDA/SilMA biohybrid hydrogel with desirable printability, structural and mechanical stability for chondrogenesis.[26] The 3D-printed PEGDA/SilMA constructs successfully maintained at high chondrocytes viability (>95%) and facilitated the accumulation of cartilaginous matrix (aggrecan and collagen type II) after 2-week culture. Those studies indicate that the hybridization of cell-adhesive proteins and synthetic polymers endows the hydrogel inks with desirable bioactive characteristics and mechanical sustainability postprinting for tissue engineering applications. In this study, we have focused on the development of tough biohybrid hydrogels comprised of MPLE gel and cell-adhesive proteins (gelatin and albumin), with optimal concentration ratios, enabling to utilize benefits of each component for tissue engineering applications. Both the proteins are FDA approved and cover a broad spectrum of cellular functional mechanisms to enhance proliferation, while MPLE gel would provide the outstanding printability, stacking ability, and physical strength of the scaffolds with high resolution. Additionally, subcutaneous implantation was evaluated in mice to demonstrate the excellent biocompatibility in vivo and tunable mechanical properties for synergistically regulating cell behaviors (Figure 1). Our previous report has demonstrated that the fine-tuned viscosity of poly(maleate-propylene oxide)-lipoate-poly(ethylene oxide) (MPLE) gel allowing for high-resolution printability was acquired via condensation polymerization of biocompatible monomers (maleic acid, lipoic acid, and poly(propylene glycol) diglycidyl ether) and then radical graft-polymerization with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEDGA) for printability control. The MPLE gel also possesses good mechanical strength and high cytocompatibility for load-bearing tissue reconstruction. However, its cellular interactivity and bioactive property needed for fabricating biologically functional 3D scaffolds are still major concerns due to the bioinertness of polymeric constituents in the gel system. Moreover, the long-term biosafety and tunable biodegradability also needed to be addressed for in vivo experiments. We first hypothesized that incorporation of cell-adhesive proteins (gelatin and albumin) into the MPLE gel can facilitate the cellular proliferation and bioactivity while maintaining the great printability to ensure the successful fabrication of cell-laden structures. To realize this purpose, various ratios of Gelatin-and Albumin-MPLE gels were selected for preliminary investigation as shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information). The incorporation of gelatin and albumin provided the adequate biological properties (bioactivity, biofunctionality, and cytocompatibility) of the hydrogel inks, whereas the addition of PEGDA offered suitable viscosity for 3D-printing process that could ensure the high-resolution pattern and the stability of the printed constructs. Permanent chemical cross-linking of the prepared hydrogels was achieved by exposing 3D-printed scaffolds under UV-light to stabilize the integrity and strength of the stacked patterns. During the preparation step, protein polymer hydrogels were preliminarily tested to achieve optimal printability for biofabrication. The conditions at 10% (w/v) for both Gelatin-MPLE gel and Albumin-MPLE gel were found to be satisfied the above requirements and thus were employed for further characterization and analysis throughout the study.
Hydrogels have good biocompatibility and large water content (around 90%), which are similar to extracellular matrix structures. Therefore, hydrogel is widely regarded as the most attractive material in bioprinting process [3,4]. In the last decade, various approaches, including inkjet printing using microdrops [5], microextrusion printing using continuous liquid inks [6] and stereolithography using UV photopolymerization [7] have been proposed and well developed to print hydrogels. Compared to other methods, extrusion printing is an improved FDM technology, which constructs a three-dimensional layered structure by extruding continuous liquid ink. Because of its high unit density, large material range and good balance between printer cost and printing quality, FDM is considered as the best strategy for bioprinting [6,8]. However, low printing resolution limits its application in the biomedical field. To overcome this drawback, this study adjusted the rheological characteristics of the printing ink to obtain 3D printing structures with high precision. Natural polymers, such as collagen [9], hyaluronic acid (HA) [10], chitosan [11] and alginate [1], are able to maintain the shape of 3D structure after printing through cross-linking,which are commonly used as bioink. Crosslinking can be divided into two forms: physical and chemical. Generally, physical crosslinking is caused by temperature change [9,12] and ionic crosslinking [13,14], while chemical crosslinking is formed by polymerization [15]. Sodium alginate (SA), as an anionic polymer, can be separated from brown algae and has the ability of auxiliary crosslinking by bivalent or trivalent [16]. SA has the advantages of hydrophilicity, high biocompatibility and biodegradability under normal physiological conditions. As a kind of instant gel material, it has attracted more and more attention in tissue engineering. For 3D printing hydrogel, due to the low viscosity of hydrogels, the shape of printing often collapses. In order to improve the viscosity of SA solution, researchers proposed various methods, such as changing its concentration and molecular weight [17], combining with other materials including nanocellulose [1] or gelatin [4], printing with supportive sacrifice polymers [18], and partially crosslinking with calcium ions [19]. However, minimizing the Barus effect of bioink to achieve shape fidelity during printing have not been sufficiently investigated [20]. Moreover, most of 3D printed hydrogels exhibit inferior mechanical property and poor interfacial property between layers. In order to improve the printing resolution and adhesion property, the thermo-responsive agar and ionic-responsive alginate were combined to prepare the mixed ink. Agar increased the viscosity of ink, thus further improved the rheological properties, making it suitable for precision printing. Alginate, which was crosslinked by calcium ions, linked different layers, resulting in good interface in 3D printing constructs. By using alginate/agar mixed ink and thermal-controlled method, the 3D printed gel stripes own high resolution and the width of gel stripes is similar with the width of needle. After printing, a soft polyacrylamide (PAAm) network is introduced into 3D printed hydrogel with rigid calcium alginate network to minimize the interfacial defects by using double network hydrogel mechanism. These 3D printed tough hydrogels are produced with superior mechanical properties, high printing resolution and low cytotoxicity, which can be considered a potential candidate for artificial tissues in biomedical field.
First published on 8th March 2023 Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting is an emerging manufacturing technology to print materials with cells for tissue engineering applications. In this study, we prepared novel ternary soft segment-based biodegradable polyurethane (tPU) using waterborne processes. The ternary soft segment included poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), polylactide, and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB). tPU2 with a soft segment of PCL, poly(D,L-lactide), and PHB in a molar ratio of 0.7:0.2:0.1 demonstrated lower stiffness (∼2.3 kPa) and a greater tanδ value (∼0.64) and maintained good vitality (91.3%) of neural stem cells (NSCs) among various tPUs. The bioprinted tPU2 constructs facilitated cell proliferation (∼200% in 7 days) and neural differentiation of NSCs. Meanwhile, tPU2 formed double network composite hydrogels with gelatin or agarose, and the composite hydrogels showed good biocompatibility and achieved high-resolution (∼80 μm nozzle) bioprinting. In addition, a new series of double network polyurethane-chitosan composite (PUC) hydrogels were developed by combining tPU2 with a self-healing chitosan hydrogel. The PUC hydrogel demonstrated self-healing properties and bioprintability without the need for a post-crosslinking process. The bioprinted PUC composite hydrogel promoted cell proliferation (∼300% in 7 days) and neural differentiation of NSCs better than the tPU2 bioink. This study revealed new formulae of a polyurethane bioink and a polyurethane-chitosan composite bioink for 3D bioprinting and tissue engineering applications. Several natural hydrogels are employed in 3D bioprinting, such as chitosan, alginate, agarose, and collagen.25-27 In general they lack appropriate mechanical properties and often need chemical modification or crosslinking to enhance their printability. The additional chemical processes may cause cytotoxicity.28,29 Synthetic hydrogels made of polyethylene glycol (PEG) have been used in bioprinting.30-32 The PEG-based hydrogels are not biodegradable and have low biological activities.33 Meanwhile, many bioprinted hydrogels are cured by UV light with photoinitiators before cell encapsulation. Either free radicals generated during the UV curing process or the residual photoinitiators may be harmful to cells.34,35 Therefore, it remains an interesting research topic to synthesize novel biodegradable materials with suitable mechanical properties and cytocompatibility for 3D bioprinting.
Biohybrid hydrogels comprising of cell-adhesive proteins and synthetic polymers have been considered as the ideal biomaterials as they can not only retain their good printability and mechanical property but also enhance bioactive characteristics for promoting cellular activities.[22] Various studies have investigated on the developments of the biohybrid hydrogels for printing biologically functional 3D scaffolds, including polyurethane (PU)/gelatin, PEG/gelatin/arginyl-glycyl-aspartic acid (RGD), MA-BSA (methacrylate bovine serum albumin)/PEGDA, PEGDA/Silk Methacrylate (SilMA), etc. Hsieh et al. synthesized a biohybrid hydrogel composed of PU and gelatin, which had excellent stacking ability (up to 80 printed layers), high-resolution printability (through an 80-µm nozzle), and threefold increase in compressive modulus after CaCl2 treatment.[23] Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) embedded in PU/gelatin scaffolds showed high cellular mobility, good viability, and ≈300% increase in proliferation after 10 days in vitro. Piluso et al. reported a novel PEG-based biohybrid inks by incorporating low-molecular-weight gelatin fragments that enabled to fabricate various architectures, including kite-like, star, mesh, and multilayer tubular while maintain the high viability of 3T3 fibroblasts (>90%) and continuous proliferation (7 days).[24] The authors further improved the biofunctionality of PEG/Gelatin biohybrid inks with addition of cell-adhesive RGD ligands, allowing to transform the embedded cells from spindle-like elongated morphology to spread-out shape.[24] Smith and colleagues demonstrated, for the first time, formulation of MA-BSA and PEGDA as photocurable biohybrid hydrogel that can be utilized for fabrication of complex geometries (lattice and honeycomb) with good resolution (250 µm).[25] The printed scaffolds showed long-term biocompatibility (21 days) with excellent cell viability (>95%) due to the presence of BSA in the backbone chain, promoting the cell adhesion of matrix protein such as fibronectin. Bandyopadhyay et al. prepared PEGDA/SilMA biohybrid hydrogel with desirable printability, structural and mechanical stability for chondrogenesis.[26] The 3D-printed PEGDA/SilMA constructs successfully maintained at high chondrocytes viability (>95%) and facilitated the accumulation of cartilaginous matrix (aggrecan and collagen type II) after 2-week culture. Those studies indicate that the hybridization of cell-adhesive proteins and synthetic polymers endows the hydrogel inks with desirable bioactive characteristics and mechanical sustainability postprinting for tissue engineering applications. In this study, we have focused on the development of tough biohybrid hydrogels comprised of MPLE gel and cell-adhesive proteins (gelatin and albumin), with optimal concentration ratios, enabling to utilize benefits of each component for tissue engineering applications. Both the proteins are FDA approved and cover a broad spectrum of cellular functional mechanisms to enhance proliferation, while MPLE gel would provide the outstanding printability, stacking ability, and physical strength of the scaffolds with high resolution. Additionally, subcutaneous implantation was evaluated in mice to demonstrate the excellent biocompatibility in vivo and tunable mechanical properties for synergistically regulating cell behaviors (Figure 1). Our previous report has demonstrated that the fine-tuned viscosity of poly(maleate-propylene oxide)-lipoate-poly(ethylene oxide) (MPLE) gel allowing for high-resolution printability was acquired via condensation polymerization of biocompatible monomers (maleic acid, lipoic acid, and poly(propylene glycol) diglycidyl ether) and then radical graft-polymerization with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEDGA) for printability control. The MPLE gel also possesses good mechanical strength and high cytocompatibility for load-bearing tissue reconstruction. However, its cellular interactivity and bioactive property needed for fabricating biologically functional 3D scaffolds are still major concerns due to the bioinertness of polymeric constituents in the gel system. Moreover, the long-term biosafety and tunable biodegradability also needed to be addressed for in vivo experiments. We first hypothesized that incorporation of cell-adhesive proteins (gelatin and albumin) into the MPLE gel can facilitate the cellular proliferation and bioactivity while maintaining the great printability to ensure the successful fabrication of cell-laden structures. To realize this purpose, various ratios of Gelatin-and Albumin-MPLE gels were selected for preliminary investigation as shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information). The incorporation of gelatin and albumin provided the adequate biological properties (bioactivity, biofunctionality, and cytocompatibility) of the hydrogel inks, whereas the addition of PEGDA offered suitable viscosity for 3D-printing process that could ensure the high-resolution pattern and the stability of the printed constructs. Permanent chemical cross-linking of the prepared hydrogels was achieved by exposing 3D-printed scaffolds under UV-light to stabilize the integrity and strength of the stacked patterns. During the preparation step, protein polymer hydrogels were preliminarily tested to achieve optimal printability for biofabrication. The conditions at 10% (w/v) for both Gelatin-MPLE gel and Albumin-MPLE gel were found to be satisfied the above requirements and thus were employed for further characterization and analysis throughout the study.

One of the most important factors for the successful fabrication of 3D printed scaffolds is the choice of the material to be printed, or bioink. The bioink has to be suitable for the printing technology adopted and has to display the right mechanical properties (e.g. viscosity, stiffness, shear thinning behaviour) to allow both the 3D deposition of the ink and stability of the obtained constructs, but, more importantly, must be biocompatible to ensure cell survival during and after printing.11-13 Due to their chemical and physical properties, high water content, biodegradability and capability to mimic the natural environment of cells, hydrogels are ideal candidates as bioinks for 3D bioprinting.12 These materials can incorporate more than 99% water and can be obtained from cross-linked polymer gelators (PGs) or via the self-assembly of low molecular weight gelators (LMWGs) in aqueous media.14 So far, due to their ease of gelation, simple manipulation and highly tuneable mechanical properties, a wide variety of polymeric hydrogels have been studied as bioinks. The majority of them are based on natural molecules, such as collagen (ca. 26% of the reported bioinks) and alginate (ca. 24%) or their composites with other polymers.15 Further bioinks reported in literature are based on other natural and synthetic polymers including hyaluronic acid, gelatin, cellulose, soy protein, fibrinogen, chitosan, dextran, starch, polylactic acid (PLA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic) acid (PLGA), polyethylene glycol (PEG), polycaprolactone (PCL).15 Alginate is a natural polymer that can easily form hydrogels by simple mixing with divalent cations. Being biocompatible and very versatile, it is an ideal candidate for 3D bioprinting. Since this field has seen a rapid expansion in the last few years, the number of research articles on novel bioink formulations is dramatically increasing. For this reason, when approaching this research field, it can be difficult to acquire a clear idea of the available formulations and their applications. This review focuses on alginate-based bioinks prepared using pure alginate or in combination with other polysaccharides. The main goal is to update the reader on the latest developments in this field, providing a simple guide on available formulations, their compositions and biological applications. We hope that this article will simplify the identification of the main types of alginate-based polysaccharidic bioinks and inform the design of novel formulations. By developing a series of ‘design principles’ for bioprinted alginate gels, we hope that this review will facilitate the development of new formulations with additional functionality and further promote uptake of these fascinating gel-phase materials in high-tech applications.
Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting is an emerging layer-by-layer approach for engineering patient-specific custom scaffolds with high shape fidelity and porous architecture [1, 2]. Hydrogel based bioinks such as alginate, gelatin and gellan gum are commonly used for 3D bioprinting of tissue engineered constructs due to advantages such as high water content, good biocompatibility, and smooth viscosity transitions (i.e. shear thinning) [3-5]. Recently, use of collagen-based bioinks for 3D printing has garnered significant interest because of superior biocompatibility, presence of cell adhesion sites, and ability to print biomimetic constructs that resemble native tissue extracellular matrix (ECM) properties [6, 7]. However, constructs printed using low concentrations of collagen bioinks tend to collapse and deform under their own weight resulting in significant loss in print fidelity. Further, gelation of collagen is a thermally driven time-dependent process, which limits its use as an ink for 3D printing applications. To address these limitations, Hinton et al reported on a new freeform reversible embedding of suspended hydrogels (FRESH) printing technique that employs a thermo-reversible support bath comprised of gelatin microparticles which hinders the spreading of the bioink post printing and allows for 3D printing of soft hydrogel-based constructs by integrating the printed layers without clogging the nozzle [8]. Further, methacrylation of collagen enables in situ photochemical crosslinking of the printed construct in the FRESH bath to improve the physical and mechanical properties of collagen constructs [9]. We have recently shown that it is feasible to print pure collagen constructs with good print fidelity and high cell viability using low concentration methacrylated collagen (CMA) bioink (i.e. 3 mg ml−1) and the FRESH printing technique [10]. The goal of the current study is to employ the FRESH printing technique to generate collagen-based hybrid constructs that resemble the organic and inorganic composition of native bone for use in bone tissue engineering (BTE) applications. These biomimetic constructs may provide key compositional cues to direct and control cellular function (i.e. osteogenic differentiation, matrix mineralization) and thereby enable enhanced bone regeneration. Bioglass 45S5 (BG) is an osteostimulative biomaterial that can chemically bond to hard and soft tissue [11, 12]. Combination of collagen and BG has been extensively used for the generation of viable tissue scaffolds for BTE applications [13]. However, most existing scaffold fabrication methodologies are associated with limitations that deter the clinical translation of BG incorporated collagen constructs. For example, freeze-drying yields highly porous BG incorporated collagen scaffolds but weak mechanical properties of freeze-dried scaffolds are a concern. Plastic compression entails the application of a fixed compressive load onto a BG incorporated collagen hydrogel in order to densify the collagen microstructure and improve the stiffness of the collagen hydrogels [14]. However, lack of porosity and little control over scaffold shape are possible limitations. Therefore, there is a need for an alternative biofabrication methodology for the generation of mechanically viable BG incorporated collagen scaffolds with better control of scaffold shape and architecture. Use of mechanically viable scaffolds can aid in seamless implantation of the scaffold, enable earlier mobilization of the injured site, and expedite the bone healing process [15]. In addition, matrix elasticity of the initial scaffold is an important parameter known to guide stem cell differentiation [16].
Innovative bioink with multifunctional properties are vastly researched in three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting field. Bioinks used in 3D bioprinting should have adequate printability and mechanical integrity during printing as well as post-printing stages in addition to their biocompatibility and biodegradability [1-4]. Especially, the bioinks with multiple crosslinking abilities are highly explored for their post-printing stability in the recent time. Different bioink constituents have been proposed and used in 3D bioprinting for the tissue engineering and regenerative medicine [1, 3, 5, 6]. In spite of numerous advancements in the field of 3D printing-based tissue engineering; yet, several challenges remain in the development of tangible bioinks with desired physio-chemical, biological and self-standing properties [4]. Hence, the development of appropriate bioinks with ideal characteristic required for the regeneration of desired tissues and organs is the need of the hour [3]. The desirable properties of the bioinks include high resolution printability, biodegradability, biocompatibility, post-printing stability with self-standing ability, and mechanical properties matching those of the desired tissue or organ. Also, with the ability to accommodate bioactive molecules and cells; especially, without affecting their native structures and cell viability [7, 8]. Amongst the reported materials for the 3D bioprinting applications, hydrogels are the most preferred biomaterials owing to their exceptional properties comparable to those of the tissues. Particularly, the water content, softness, biodegradation, nutrient transport properties which are similar to the extracellular matrix (ECM) 3D environment present in the organs and tissues [2, 3]. Further, the hydrogels can be tuned as per the necessities of the tissue by varying the cross-linking degree and methods as well as combination of different polymers such as natural, synthetic, pH-sensitive, temperature-sensitive, ion-sensitive polymers, etc [7-11]. As an example, sodium alginate or alginic acid (Alg), a polysaccharide with β-D-mannuronic acid and α-L-guluronic acid units, obtained from seaweeds has been employed as a key bioink polymer [3, 12-14]. They are used exclusively in 3D printing, because of its suitable printability and ionic cross-linking ability [12, 13]. Several works on alginate-based gels are reported frequently for various tissue engineering applications [15-18]. The cross-linking occurs mainly with the help of the ionic interactions between the anionic carboxyl groups (-) of alginate and the multivalent cations present in the cross-linking solutions (e.g. Ca2+, Al3+ and Mg2+) [13, 19]. This takes place at normal physiological conditions and also favors the inclusion of biomolecules or cells during gel formation before 3D bioprinting. However, calcium ion crosslinking alone has several disadvantages; where the ionic crosslinking is uncontrolled and loss of Ca2+ ions will lead to heterogeneous gel matrix at different areas of the 3D printed construct [20, 21]. Also, other biological, mechanical/physical properties including swelling ratio and degradation are very hard to control [22]. Pre-crosslinking using Ca2+ ions will lead to heterogeneous gelation and clogging of nozzles while 3D printing [23]. One of the primary reasons for the uncontrolled mechanical properties of these printed scaffolds are due to the loss of multivalent ions when exposed to different mono-ionic solutions [24]. Once these mono-ions replace the multivalent ions, they lose the mechanical properties largely [23, 24]. Hence, the printed structures may lose the shape fidelity, leading to collapse of its structure even before the actual application in animal or human [23, 24]. To address these limitations, several researchers tried to incorporate chemical modifications on alginate side chains using various strategies including methacrylate, catechol groups or even some chemical crosslinkers [12, 13, 21, 23]. Further, they varied the Ca2+ concentrations to get optimal properties of the scaffolds [25]. Even though many of these strategies increased the stability of the 3D printed scaffolds, the bioactivity and mechanical properties along with self-standing ability and post-printing stability of the 3D bioprinted scaffolds require to be improved further for better tissue regeneration. This should be achieved without affecting the other properties such as biocompatibility, printability, processing, gelation, crosslinking ability and layer to layer bonding. Hence, addition or crosslinking of ECM-based polymer to the alginate makes it more suitable for tissue regeneration as well as 3D bioprinting. Direct addition of hyaluronic acid (HA) like polymers were also reported for tissue engineering applications without chemical modifications or with simple crosslinking [25-30]. Again, their stability is not controlled due to ionic crosslinking and in some cases, the gels do not have dynamic self-healing ability between printed layers or within the gel which is highly required for 3D bioprinting applications [31, 32]. This property helps to increase the layer-to-layer interactions after extrusion and prevents the cells or biomolecules from damaging with increased flexibility than the covalently crosslinked rigid gel networks. Using hydrazone-based or Schiff’s base reaction is one way to obtain such dynamic bonds in the hydrogel [33, 34]. However, they may be inferior in mechanical properties after 3D bioprinting. Recently, Thanh et al [35], have reported an alginate, HA and silk fibroin based bioink crosslinked using ethylenediamine and aldehyde modifications [35]. This gel forms Schiff’s base linkages, and the study emphasizing highly on hydrogel characterization and evaluation only. Large 3D bioprinted constructs were neither printed nor studied in detail. Apart from the dynamic linking before 3D printing, the 3D printed constructs need other crosslinking mechanisms, especially, like crosslinking with varying ionic concentrations to attain desired mechanical properties after printing [33, 34]. Even though, ECM-based polymers are used for cell adhesion and proliferation; yet, adding other polymers like alginate will increase the versatility of the bioink. Because, alginate has exceptional printability, mechanical properties and crosslinking abilities; Likewise, alginate serves as a model polysaccharide with high versatility in much easier crosslinking and chemical modifications. Hence, we selected alginate along with HA for the bioink combination.

Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting is an emerging tissue engineering approach that aims to develop cell or biomolecule-laden, complex polymeric scaffolds with high precision, using hydrogel-based “bioinks”. Hydrogels are water-swollen, highly crosslinked polymer networks that are soft, quasi-solid, and can support and protect biological materials. However, traditional hydrogels have weak mechanical properties and cannot retain complex structures. They must be reinforced with physical and chemical manipulations to produce a mechanically resilient bioink. Over the past few years, we have witnessed an increased use of nanoparticles and biological moiety-functionalized nanoparticles to fabricate new bioinks. Nanoparticles of varied size, shape, and surface chemistries can provide a unique solution to this problem primarily because of three reasons: (a) nanoparticles can mechanically reinforce hydrogels through physical and chemical interactions. This can favorably influence the bioink's 3D printability and structural integrity by modulating its rheological, biomechanical, and biochemical properties, allowing greater flexibility to print a wide range of structures; (b) nanoparticles can introduce new bio-functionalities to the hydrogels, which is a key metric of a bioink's performance, influencing both cell-material and cell-cell interactions within the hydrogel; (c) nanoparticles can impart “smart” features to the bioink, making the tissue constructs responsive to external stimuli. Responsiveness of the hydrogel to magnetic field, electric field, pH changes, and near-infrared light can be made possible by the incorporation of nanoparticles. Additionally, bioink polymeric networks with nanoparticles can undergo advanced chemical crosslinking, allowing greater flexibility to print structures with varied biomechanical properties. Taken together, the unique properties of various nanoparticles can help bioprint intricate constructs, bringing the process one step closer to complex tissue structure and organ printing. In this review, we explore the design principles and multifunctional properties of various nanomaterials and nanocomposite hydrogels for potential, primarily extrusion-based bioprinting applications. We illustrate the significance of biocompatibility of the designed nanocomposite hydrogel-based bioink for clinical translation and discuss the different parameters that affect cell fate after cell-nanomaterial interaction. Finally, we critically assess the current challenges of nanoengineering bioinks and provide insight into the future directions of potential hydrogel bioinks in the rapidly evolving field of bioprinting. Among the different types of materials, hydrogels have been suitably used as bioinks for extrusion-based tissue printing applications.11-13 Hydrogels are water-retaining, crosslinked, polymeric chains that closely resemble macromolecular-based structures in the body.14-16 Hydrogels are excellent candidates for biomedical applications, including 3D bioprinting, because of their bio-friendly material properties.17 Biopolymers, such as polysaccharides and polypeptides, derived from plant and animal sources are crosslinked either physically or chemically to form natural hydrogels.18 Natural hydrogels are easily degradable and form desirable scaffolds for cell encapsulation and adhesion. Because of these favorable biological properties, natural polymer-based hydrogels are often selected for 3D bioprinting.19 However, hydrogels made from purely natural polymers find limited applications.20 Hydrogels originating from natural sources like gelatin, sodium alginate and chitosan exhibit inferior mechanical properties. This is particularly problematic for in vivo tissue engineering applications. Premature wearing-out of hydrogels can lead to the early degradation of the scaffold and unnecessary formation of cracks at the site of application. Degraded scaffolds can even fall prey to harmful opportunistic microorganisms.21 Different strategies to modify the polymer chemistry and enhance the applicability of such materials have been investigated over the past decade. Some of the examples include the use of double-network hydrogels,22 multi-network hydrogels,23 click chemistry-based hydrogels,24 and supramolecular hydrogels.25 However, they are currently limited by one or more of the following parameters - mechanical resilience, printability, shape fidelity, proper mechanical energy dissipation mechanism, biocompatibility, cell-instructive, or biofunctional properties. Introducing nanoparticles into the polymeric network of hydrogels (also known as nanocomposite hydrogels) has the potential to address the current drawbacks of conventional bioinks.26,27 In fact, reinforcing hydrogels with nanoparticles can offer unique advantages over earlier discussed strategies.28Fig. 1 summarizes some of the crucial functionalities that can be imparted by the appropriate use of nanoparticles. The figure also highlights some possible areas of application of these bioinks. Unique properties, such as photo-responsiveness,29 magnetic field-responsiveness,30 and so on, can be integrated by functionalizing the hydrogels with nanoparticles. Different types of nanomaterials are being considered for the functionalization process. For example, carbon-based nanomaterials, such as carbon nanotubes and carbon dots, can make hydrogels electroconductive, thermally conductive, optically active, and mechanically strong.31,32 Bioactive inorganic nanoparticles have also been studied for designing nanocomposite hydrogels. Inorganic materials like silicon, calcium, magnesium, and many more, are essential to the proper functioning of the body.33 Nanoparticles synthesized with these minerals can impart properties unique to such nanomaterials. For instance, nanosilicates, also known as nanoclay/LAPONITE®® silicate nanoplatelets, can be added to hydrogels to introduce osteogenic properties.34 Nanosilicates can also enhance the mechanical properties of hydrogels and help in modulating the release of drugs.35,36 Metal and metal oxide nanoparticles are also commonly used for fabricating nanocomposite hydrogels.37 Silver-based nanoparticles show antimicrobial properties that are often used to design nanocomposite hydrogels to counter antibiotic-resistant bacteria.38 Gold nanospheres can introduce photothermal-responsiveness in hydrogels.39 These unique nanocomposite hydrogels are being implemented as drug delivery devices, biosensors, bioactuators, tissue engineering scaffolds and so on. An emerging application of these materials is in the field of 3D bioprinting where they serve as the bioinks.26,40,41Fig. 2A-D display injectable nanocomposite hydrogels that have the potential to become bioinks.36,42-44 However, it should be noted that there are strict process requirements for 3D bioprinting, which will be discussed in section 2. The examples presented in Fig. 2 can become biomaterial inks only when such rigorous process standards are met. In this review, we will focus primarily on the material properties of different nanocomposite hydrogels that are essential to generate the next generation of biomaterial inks and/or bioinks for diverse biomedical applications. Additionally, the review will also provide an insight into the future of these newly formulated bioinks and nanocomposite hydrogels.

3D bioprinting utilizes biodegradable hydrogels as bioinks to fabricate scaffolds or constructs with tailored structures for tissue engineering and drug delivery. These hydrogels, often derived from natural polymers like gelatin, alginate, or chitosan, are selected for their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM) [1, 3, 4, 9]. Key functionalities include:  

1. **Printability and Structural Integrity**: Hydrogels are engineered to exhibit shear-thinning behavior, enabling extrusion through nozzles while rapidly recovering viscosity post-printing to maintain shape fidelity [5, 9, 15]. For example, alginate-gelatin hydrogels achieve this via temperature-dependent gelation and ionic crosslinking with Ca²⁺ [1, 4].  

2. **Crosslinking Mechanisms**: Biodegradability and stability are modulated through ionic (e.g., Ca²⁺ for alginate), chemical (e.g., glutaraldehyde for gelatin), or enzymatic crosslinking. Dual crosslinking (ionic + covalent) enhances mechanical strength and degradation control [1, 3, 8].  

3. **Bioactivity and Functionality**: Additives like mesoporous bioactive glass nanoparticles (MBGNs) or platelet lysate (HPL) improve mineralization, cell adhesion, and growth factor release in bone tissue scaffolds [3, 6]. Hybrid systems (e.g., alginate-hyaluronic acid) introduce dynamic self-healing bonds (e.g., Schiff’s base) for layer-to-layer cohesion [5, 13].  

4. **Cell Compatibility**: Hydrogels support cell encapsulation, proliferation, and differentiation. For instance, ternary polyurethane (tPU) hydrogels promote neural stem cell growth, while chitosan-alginate composites enhance cytocompatibility [2, 8, 12].  

5. **Degradation Control**: Adjusting polymer ratios (e.g., alginate-HA) or incorporating hydrolytically stable bonds (e.g., N-acyl-hydrazone in HA-CMC hydrogels) tailors degradation rates to match tissue regeneration timelines [13, 15].  

6. **Responsive Systems**: pH- or temperature-sensitive hydrogels (e.g., PEO-PPO-PEO triblocks) enable controlled drug release or 4D structural changes post-printing [7].  

These strategies address challenges in mechanical stability, bioactivity, and print resolution, positioning biodegradable hydrogels as versatile materials for creating functional, patient-specific constructs [4, 10, 14].

PLA is a bio-based, biodegradable, and biocompatible polyester, which has strength and elastic modulus comparable to those of conventional petroleum-based polymers such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) and polystyrene [1]. PLA has attracted increasing attention in recent years as the environmentally benign and biomedical materials usable for agriculture, automobile, diary commodities, tissue engineering and controlled drug delivery etc. [2]. However, it exhibits brittle fracture behavior. It has also a low heat distortion temperature due to the low glass transition temperature (T g) (ca. 60 °C), and no back-up of the elastic modulus above T g due to a low rate of crystallization. Therefore, a great deal of efforts has been made to modify the properties of PLA in both industry and academia [3, 4]. Melt blending of PLA with some flexible biodegradable polyesters, such as poly(butylene succinate) [5-7], poly(butylene succinate-co-L-lactate) [8, 9], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [10-14] and poly(butylene adipapte-co-terephthalate) [15, 16] is an effective way to improve the ductility of PLA. Unfortunately, all the blending inevitably leads to a dramatic deterioration in originally poor heat resistance of PLA, which is not acceptable for many commercial applications. Interestingly, Oyama found the annealing induced crystallization of PLA matrix for the blends of PLA and poly(ethylene-glycidyl methacrylate) improves both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness [17]. Bai also reported the improvement of both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness for PLA/PCL blend is capable by the control of the PLA matrix crystallization and PCL particle size [18]. On the other hand, PLA-based polymer networks and semi-interpenetrating polymer networks (semi-IPNs) are promising strategies to improve the thermal and mechanical properties of PLA. Koo et al. reported that a crosslinked PLA by UV irradiation exhibits a little higher tan δ peak temperature and a higher toughness by 22.5 % in spite of a little lower elongation at break than PLA [19]. He et al. reported tough semi-IPNs composed of PLA and the crosslinked polyurethane prepared by reacting 4,4’-methylenediphenyl diisocyanate with poly(ethylene glycol) and glycerol [20]. In the past studies, simultaneous improvements of T g, toughness and ductility for the PLA-based polymer network and semi-IPNs compared with those of PLA have not been accomplished.

There are many strategies to improve the intrinsic brittleness of PLA including chemical copolymerization, plasticization and melt blending. Hillmyer and his team11, 12 synthesized PLA graft copolymers consisting of 1,5-cyclooctadiene fraction and they found that the elongation at break was increased by 18 times and the tensile toughness was increased by 14 times compared to those of pristine amorphous PLA. Lan et al.13 synthesized PLA and poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) copolymers by a cross-coupling reaction using 1,3-dicyclohexylcarbodiimide as coupling agent and 4-(dimethylamino)pyridine as catalyst. They found that the elongation at break and tear strength of the PLA-PBS copolymer can be increased to 64.4% and 114.3 N mm−1, which are over three times higher than those of virgin PLA. Even though PLA modification by copolymerization is a powerful technique to create a new material with outstanding properties, the copolymerization procedure is quite complicated and requires hazardous solvent and expensive catalyst.14 Therefore, copolymerization of PLA has not been commercially available in the industrial market. Moreover, the flexibility and processability of PLA can be improved by incorporation of low molecular weight plasticizers, e.g. polyethylene glycol (PEG),15 acrylated PEG,16 epoxidized soy bean17 and acetyl tributyl citrate.18 However, the major disadvantage of a plasticizer is the migration of plasticizer molecules from the bulk of the finished product onto the surface as time passes due to the incompatibility between plasticizer and polymer matrix. The migration of plasticizer during use or aging decreases the flexibility and softness of plasticized polymeric products, eventually decreasing their mechanical performance. For instance, epoxidized soybean oil plasticized PLA films were kept at room temperature for 90 days and it was found that the plasticized PLA films became less flexible and the elongation at break and tensile toughness gradually decreased because of plasticizer migration to the film surface.17 Melt blending with soft and flexible polymers is the most cost-effective method which has been extensively and industrially used to reduce cost, enhance processability, and improve optical, mechanical, thermal and gas permeation properties of the polymer blends. Toughening of PLA can be achieved by incorporation of commodity thermoplastics, biodegradable thermoplastics and elastomers. Balakrishnan et al.19 reported that the impact strength of injection molded PLA was increased 53% with the addition of 10 wt% linear low density polyethylene. Yemisci and Aytac20 found that blending PLA with 10 wt% polycarbonate (PC) provided a maximum elongation at break of 70%; however, the elongation at break gradually decreased as PC loading increased which was attributed to the low compatibility between PLA and PC. Yao et al.21 presented slight increases in elongation at break of PLA from 3.6% to 10.1% and tensile toughness from 1.5 to 3.1 MJ m−3 by incorporating 30 wt% poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC). Besides, enhancing the compatibility of the PLA/PPC blends by adding 0.3 wt% maleic anhydride further increased the elongation at break and tensile toughness to 59.3% and 13.4 MJ m−3 respectively, because maleic anhydride increased the interfacial adhesion between the PLA and PPC phases. Jiang et al.22 blended PLA with biodegradable poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) and reported that PLA exhibited ductile fracture behavior in which the elongation at break of the blends remarkably increased from 4% (pristine PLA) to 115% and 200% at PBAT contents of 5 and 20 wt%, respectively. Persenaire et al.23 suggested that incorporating 20 wt% low viscosity PBS gave higher elongation at break (242%) than high viscosity PBS because low viscosity PBS can be well dispersed and forms a smaller domain size in the PLA matrix. Lascano et al.24 reported an increment of elongation at break of PLA from 9.2% to 29.7% when 20 wt% poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) was added. Moreover, the elongation at break further increased to 121.2% when the PLA/PBSA blends were compatibilized by the addition of a chain extender at 0.5 phr. Adding acrylic impact modifier (ACR) into the PLA blends increased impact strength about four times and elongation at break about three times over those of virgin PLA. Furthermore, the tensile, flexural and impact properties of the PLA/ACR blends strongly depended on the soft/hard ratio of ACR.25 Thermoplastic starch (TPS) plasticized by glycerol/sorbitol mixtures increased the elongation at break of PLA about 100% compared with neat PLA; however, the PLA/TPS blends showed reduced impact strength by about 30% which was attributed to a weak inherent strength of the TPS phase and a poorly bonded interfacial area.26 An addition of elastomer is also an interesting technique to increase the toughness of thermoplastics. Elastomer is a loosely crosslinked polymer that has an amorphous structure with excellent elasticity and flexibility since its glass transition temperature is very low and normally below the service temperature. Elastomers can be natural rubber (NR) obtained from natural rubber latex3, 27, 28 or synthetic rubbers such as epoxidized natural rubber,29 cis-1,4-polyisoprene,30 liquid polybutadiene (LPB),31 ethylene propylene diene (EPDM),32 acrylonitrile butadiene rubber (NBR),33, 34 silicone rubber35 and so on. The overview of toughening PLA by elastomers has been well reported by Alias and Ismail.36 Most polymer pairs, however, are thermodynamically immiscible, leading to heterogeneous morphologies. For more details, the fundamental aspects of the morphological evolution and applications of immiscible polymer blends (e.g. rheology of the blends, breakup and coalescence mechanisms, physical and reactive compatibilizations) have been highlighted by Mural et al.37 Owing to the weak interfacial strength and poor mechanical properties of immiscible blends, modification of interfacial adhesion is a crucial key for acquiring greater performance of the polymer blends. There has been much effort in recent years to improve the compatibility of binary polymer blends. A physical compatibilizer is a premade graft or block copolymer intentionally added to improve the interfacial interaction of PLA and another phase. Chavalitpanya et al.38 found that adding 7.5 phr of polyethylene glycol-block-polypropylene glycol (PEG-PPG) copolymer into PLA/polycaprolactone blends drastically increased the elongation at break from 2% to 74%. Moreover, the incorporation of 3 wt% synthesized PLA-PEG-PLA triblock copolymer gave an elongation at break of PLA/PBAT blends eight times more than that of the uncompatibilized blends.39 Physical compatibilizers will show an optimal result when they diffuse into the interface of two polymers in order to stabilize the blend morphology and facilitate the interfacial adhesion. Therefore, a highly efficient mixing condition as well as a similar affinity between copolymers and the two main polymers are greatly necessary to achieve the best compatibilization efficiency. Otherwise, these added premade copolymers will phase separate into micelles, which are less effective for compatibilization. Conversely, for reactive compatibilization the copolymer is produced from a reaction specifically taking place at the boundary of two immiscible polymers.40 Reactive compatibilization can be done by functionalizing one of the two polymers in the blends; therefore, it can promptly couple with the functional groups of another polymer (e.g. grafting maleic anhydride onto NR to react with the hydroxyl and carboxylic endgroups of PLA).41 Another approach is addition of a third component that can chemically bond two polymers during melt mixing directly. Dynamic vulcanization is a melt blending process in which the elastomer phase is forced to crosslink whereas the thermoplastic phase remains uncrosslinked, leading to a crosslinked elastomeric dispersed phase in the uncrosslinked thermoplastic continuous matrix. Moreover, dynamic vulcanization can be considered as a compatibilization technique in the attempt to increase the compatibility of immiscible thermoplastic/elastomer blends. Dynamically vulcanized blends have been recognized as new outstanding materials combining good processability of thermoplastics and the unique elastic behavior of elastomers together, such as the potential to be recyclable, improved ultimate tensile strength, high strain recovery, high fatigue resistance, high oil resistance and high melt strength.42, 43 High density polyethylene (HDPE)/ethylene vinyl acetate blends were dynamically vulcanized using dicumyl peroxide (DCP) as a free radical initiator and it was found that the shear viscosity of the vulcanized blends was higher than that of unvulcanized blends, in particular at low shear rates, because of the predominant crosslinking of the rubber phase.44 George et al.45 examined the effect of dynamic vulcanization in a sulfur system, a peroxide system and a combination system on the rheological behavior, morphology and physical properties of HDPE/NBR blends. They observed that the peroxide system provided the highest shear viscosity because peroxide was capable of crosslinking both polymer phases unlike the sulfur system which can crosslink only the rubber phase. Further, the peroxide-cured blends had comparatively stronger carbon-carbon linkages than the sulfur-sulfur linkages in the sulfur-cured blends. Increasing the DCP content increased the shear viscosity as a result of higher crosslink density. Furthermore, dynamic vulcanization by DCP gave higher tear strength, tensile strength and elongation at break than dynamic vulcanization by sulfur, which can be explained by the change in morphology of the blends. NBR was inadequately crosslinked in the sulfur curing system, causing phase separation and weak interfacial strength. Besides, the ingredients in the sulfur curing system (e.g. activator and accelerator) acted as lubricants, inhibiting the breakup of rubber dispersed domains. Conversely, the peroxide can readily be well mixed with polymers and the crosslinked rubber domains can easily break up into finer particles. Thus, the fine and uniformly distributed crosslinked NBR particles in the HDPE matrix and the improved compatibility between phases contributed toward an enhancement of mechanical properties.46, 47 Chen and his team48-51 proposed novel supertoughened biobased material of PLA/NR blends prepared via dynamic vulcanization by DCP. It was clearly seen that the PLA blends with 35 wt% of a continuous net-like structure of crosslinked NR phase exhibited greatly enhanced elongation at break of 200% and Izod impact strength of 58.3 kJ m−2, i.e. approximately 40 and 21 times respectively those of the neat PLA. This mechanical property improvement was attributed to the compatibilization effect of PLA grafted onto NR, which increased the interfacial strength between phases. A similar improvement in mechanical properties was also reported for dynamically vulcanized PLA/epoxidized NR blends.29, 52 Deetuam et al.3 also supported the effective interfacial compatibilization effect of PLA-NR copolymer formed during melt blending on the improved tensile toughness of PLA/NR blends at low DCP loading; however, the tensile toughness eventually dropped at higher DCP concentration mainly attributed to the large content of highly crosslinked NR gel. Krishnan et al.53, 54 dynamically vulcanized PLA blends containing synthesized biobased polyester elastomers and found that the impact strength increased about two to three times compared to that of the neat PLA. Zhao et al.55 toughened PLA by dynamic vulcanization with biomass-derived castor oil polyurethane using 4,4′-diphenylmethane diisocyanate as crosslinking agent. With an addition of 5 wt% castor oil polyurethane, the elongation at break increased from 7.5% to 338% and Izod impact strength increased from 33.9 to 52.8 J m−1. Toughening of PLA was achieved by an addition of PBAT and in situ compatibilization using DCP as a free radical initiator. The dynamically vulcanized blends showed a decrease in PBAT domain size and improved interfacial adhesion. Shear yielding of the PLA matrix occurring during stretching was the dominant toughening mechanism affecting the improved ductility of the vulcanized PLA/PBAT blends, leading to increases of elongation at break from 4% to 300% and notched Izod impact strength from 28 to 110 J m−1.56 Lim et al.31 reported that an incorporation of DCP into the PLA/LPB blends showed smaller polybutadiene particles distributed in the PLA matrix and also prominently increased the elongation at break by more than 1500% compared to pristine PLA. Henceforth, the primary aim of this research was to improve the properties of PLA/NBR blends via peroxide-induced dynamic vulcanization. The relationship between different acrylonitrile contents of NBR and the degree of dynamic vulcanization on the morphology, thermal and tensile properties of PLA/NBR blends has been established. We consider that PLA/NBR blends have potential as barrier films for food packaging and investigations will be reported in a future publication.
Enhancing the toughness of PLA is a challenging task, often involving the blend of PLA with other polymeric materials. Researchers have continuously explored feasible methods to toughen PLA, including polymer blending, plasticization, and copolymerization. (26−28) Chemical copolymerization can efficiently enhance PLA’s ductility but may reduce its strength, melting temperatures, and increase costs. (29) On the contrary, blending is a more cost-effective technique that requires less reaction and processing time. Plasticization, while effective, often necessitates higher quantities of plasticizers (approximately 15 to 20%) to enhance tensile toughness in composite systems. (30,31) For instance, adding 15 wt % glyceryl triacetate can increase PLA’s elongation at break by 11 to 233%, albeit at the cost of a 29 MPa decrease in tensile strength and a 0.59 GPa decrease in elastic modulus from 65 MPa and 1.02 GPa, respectively. (32) This may be attributed to the poor durability of plasticizers, leading to polymer migration from the bulk area to the surfaces. (33,34) In comparison, blending with elastic or flexible polymers offers a feasible approach to improving tensile properties in composite systems, with comparatively lower reductions in tensile strength and modulus compared to plasticization. (26) For example, adding 20 wt % poly(ethylene glycol) can increase elongation at break by over 200% despite a slight decrease in tensile strength (approximately 41%) and modulus (approximately 29%). (35) A report demonstrates that (36) incorporating 10 wt % of polymeric plasticizer (polylimonene ether) significantly enhances PLA properties, including flexibility, thermal stability, and hydrophobicity, making it a promising material for applications such as food packaging and agricultural mulch films. In a previous study, we used poly(butylene 2,5-furan dicarboxylate) (PBF) for blending with PLA and observed improved toughening without significant deterioration. (37) Moreover, by incorporating compatibilizers, such as reactive or reactive extrusion modifiers, the interfacial adhesion between PPF and PLA can be improved, leading to enhanced compatibility and potentially influencing the mechanical and thermal properties of the blends. (38−41) The presence of biobased plasticizers enhances the hydrophilicity of PLA, increases the microbial accessibility, and accelerates its breakdown in natural environments. Hence, the use of PLA may be limited in applications where high elongation or plastic deformation at high impact rates are required.[8, 9] A widespread and cost-effective method to overcome the drawback of the mechanical properties is to blend PLA with ductile polymers.[7, 10] Poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is a ductile semicrystalline aliphatic polyester, with Tg and Tm ≈−60 °C and 55-70 °C, respectively.[1, 11] Although it is a nonbiobased polymer, PCL is biodegradable and biocompatible, as well as PLA. In terms of packaging area, the tensile toughness is used to judge whether the film is tough or not, because it is always destructed by pulling apart. As a typical polymer material, PLA has various structural units, which can be defined as matrix and reinforcements, respectively. Due to the longer molecular chain structure, multiple motion units coexist in PLA, which contains side groups, chain units, chain segments and whole chains in the scale between around 1 nm and 10 nm. Besides, crystalline regions can be constructed by chain segments, which are in the scale range of 0.1-1 mm. In general, the arrangement of chains in crystals is closer than that in non-crystalline regions. The barrier properties of the PHBVs and their nanocomposites were evaluated by measuring the water and oxygen permeability at high relative humidity, to approach the conditions found in real food packaging systems. The results gathered in Table 6 evidence that the hydroxyvalerate content, the presence of plasticizer, and the addition of BCNW considerably affected the barrier performance of PHBVs.
Then, summarizing the general trends: stress and strain at break were shown to depend on filler content, particle surface properties, and fiber/matrix interfacial adhesion, while Young's Modulus was mainly affected by the intrinsic properties of each component as well as on the aspect ratio of fibers. Moisture storage conditions impact biocomposites mechanical properties, thus limiting their use as food packaging to dry products. Numerous studies have also been devoted to study the water damage on natural fiber composite materials.93-95 When fibers are exposed to mild humidity, water molecules can have a plasticizing effect, thus affecting the strength and the rigidity of fibers. Studied have also evidenced that moisture can seriously jeopardize the fiber-matrix adhesion, leading to the deterioration of the stress transfer efficiency from matrix to reinforcement.94, 96 The degradation process starts with the swelling of the cellulose fibers, causing microcracking of the matrix around the swollen fibers.94, 97 Nevertheless, few authors took interest in the influence of fiber moisture content at the moment of composites processing and its resultant impact on structure and properties.98, 99 Main results displayed a decrease of flexural strength and modulus, in relation to a decrease of interfacial shear strength, which was attributed to the poor interfacial bonding formed at the high relative humidity conditions.98, 99 It is worth noting that fiber treatments were widely and successfully experimented in order to reduce both the moisture level and the rate of absorption very significantly.10, 44-48 Another possible impact of environmental moisture is the degradation of the polymer matrix, which has been notably studied in the case of PHBV.100 However, since huge changes of atmosphere relative humidity can occur in a single day, a week, a season, a year and over a number of years, up-scaling the preparation of biocomposites from lab scale to industrial scale should also take this aspect into account, especially in the case of moisture sensitive polymers, such as PHBV. To our knowledge, no paper has been yet devoted to study the impact of fiber moisture content, at the moment of processing, on the relationships between the structure and the mechanical properties of PHBV-based biocomposites. A forthcoming paper101 aims at studying the impact of initial moisture content on the structure/mechanical properties relationships of PHBV/wheat straw fibers biocomposites. It is shown that fiber/matrix adhesion was visually not affected by the initial fiber moisture content, while PHBV molecular weight decreased with increasing fiber moisture content, which was attributed to hydrolysis reactions induced by residual water molecules, inducing a increase in the overall material crystallinity. In spite of structural differences, tensile properties were similar for all composites, leading to the conclusion that the initial fiber moisture content was not a predominant factor for controlling the mechanical properties of PHBV/wheat straw fibers composites. Since no impact on fiber/matrix adhesion was spotted, such a stability in mechanical properties toward fiber moisture content could be explained either by the fact that structural changes were not sufficient to alter the bulk mechanical properties, or by the occurrence of competitive phenomena. Such assumptions should be deepened and may be system dependant. Similar studies should be conducted by selecting a polymer matrix that would be less sensitive to moisture, e.g., a polyolefin.104

[Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.interscience.wiley.com.] In this article, we investigated the in vitro degradation of PHBV with varying HV composition in phosphate buffer medium. Mass loss results show that the mol % of HV in the PHBV copolymer influences the extent to which PHBV degrades in phosphate buffer medium. We noticed slower degradation of PHBV film for up to 7 weeks beyond which there was a steady degradation of PHBV film. The HV content in the copolymer was found to decrease upon extended exposure to hydrolytic medium. The biggest drop in HV content of the copolymer was noticed for PHBV12 film, as ascertained by 1H-NMR measurements. The initial slow degradation of PHBV followed by its steady degradation at pH 7 and 37°C suggests that PHBV-based biomaterials may remain intact for several weeks before degrading in physiological environments, Moreover, this degradation property makes PHBV an ideal material for orthopedic surgical implants that require stability for a short period of time. Additionally, the biocompatibility study showed marginal enhancement in osteoblast-like cell attachment and proliferation. This increase in cell growth is due to the increase in the HV copolymer content of PHBV film and/or the collagen presence in the PHBV matrix. The ability of osteoblast cells to proliferate on the PHBV matrix and the initial stability of the matrix are useful characteristics which makes PHBV a suitable candidate for orthopedic applications.

Activation energy versus extent of mass loss for 50/50 w/w PHBV/PCL with 3 wt% TiO2 Gaseous degradation products formed during the thermal or biodegradation of polyesters contain water and carbon dioxide in addition to other volatiles, where CO2 is formed by the decarboxylation of carboxylic acid end groups. Water comes from the condensation reactions of hydroxyl and/or carboxylic acid functional groups formed as the temperature increases [48-51]. It has been reported that the presence of moisture in biodegradable polymers causes hydrolysis of the carboxylic acids, which results in the early thermal degradation of polymers [47]. Water is one of the degradation products of PHBV, as indicated by the presence of the 967 and 3577 cm−1 (O-H vibration) bands in Fig. 9a. Since PHBV degrades first when heating a PHBV/PCL blend, the released moisture may accelerate the degradation of PCL, which could have contributed to the decrease in activation energy of the PCL phase in the neat blend. In the presence of TiO2 nanoparticles, the activation energy was significantly higher than that in the blend, and observably increased during the PCL degradation phase (Fig. 10). The higher activation energy for the degradation of the PHBV phase indicates that the influence of blending, as discussed earlier, has been offset by the retardation of volatilization through interaction with the nanoparticles. This is probably also the reason why the PCL phase shows an increase in activation energy compared to the decrease observed for the neat blend. This is in line with the higher degradation temperatures observed for both polymers in Fig. 7b.
Degradation of PHBV involves chain scission of ester bond through hydrolytic attack by water molecules and shortening the main chains into oligomer fragments and soluble monomers. During this process, aliphatic polyester is degraded faster in amorphous domains than crystalline ones.47 Because of hydrophobic nature and high degrees of crystallinity, it is difficult for water molecules to diffuse into PHBV freely, so that its hydrolytic degradation is a very slow process. The modified PHBV films had increasing wettability with hydrophilic chains on the surface, through which water molecules can be absorbed to accelerate in situ degradation. The weight loss should increase as the relative crystallinity being estimated from the enthalpies of the melting endotherms decrease. Amine-PHBV had the maximum weight loss at 50 days of incubation, perhaps mainly owing to its highest WSP among the modified PHBV films. After 50 days of incubation, the irregular weight loss may relate to chelation formation between nitrogen of amine groups and electron-deficient metal ions, which might further attract counterions of PBS to initiate inorganic nucleation. The thermal properties and in vitro degradation of amide-, amine-, and collagen-PHBV were studied. The thermal decomposition temperatures of PHBV were lower than amide-PHBV but much higher than amine- and collagen-PHBV. The Avrami-Erofeev equation with n = 2/5 was the probable kinetic function (correlation coefficient > 0.98) while using the Friedman method to study thermal decomposition kinetics of PHBV component in the films, and the corresponding mechanism was controlled by random nucleation and growth process. E of PHBV was lower than that of amide-PHBV but higher than that of amine- and collagen-PHBV. The weight loss of the modified PHBV films increased compared with that of PHBV, which was influenced by films' wettability and crystallinity. The approximately neutral pH of the degradation fluids will not catalyze the hydrolysis degradation. With an initial aim to construct cytocompatible surface, the modified PHBV films with different functional groups offered biomaterials with various biodegradation.
WAXD profiles of PHBV, amide-PHBV, amine-PHBV, and collagen-PHBV. Weight loss for pyrolysis of the films as a function of temperature is shown in Figure 5. At the heating rate of 10°C/min, PHBV showed a one-step thermal decomposition within 263.2-284.5°C. Usually, PHB and PHBV are known to degrade thermally in one step by a random chain scission process, which includes a six-member transition producing unsaturation at the chain ends. This type of scission reaction might cause a gradual decrease in molecular weight.34, 35 The thermal decomposition of amide-PHBV presented two main stages. It underwent massive thermal degradation with about 78% weight loss below 300°C, mainly due to the degradation of PHBV; within 370-430°C, the weight loss might be the decomposition of neighboring acrylamide groups to nitrile and final carbonization of PAM. There was no more distinct weight loss above 430°C. Amine-PHBV showed weight loss from the beginning because of its strong water absorption. In the range of 223.3-247.8°C, nearly 67% of total weight loss was observed, which might be the thermal decomposition of PHBV. The weight loss continuously increased in linear below 440°C, perhaps owing to the main thermal degradation of polyvinylamine and unreacted PAM.36 There was not any distinct weight loss above 440°C. Collagen-PHBV showed about 8% weight loss below 140°C. Usually, collagen denatures above 40°C, where H-bonds and hydrophobic bonds collapse and the triple-helix fails. When the temperature increases up to 60°C, some covalent bonds collapse and collagen starts thermal degradation. Over 125°C, amino acid residues destroy with release of ammonia and water.37 Within 239.2-266.3°C PHBV decomposed quickly with weight loss of 42%, and the remaining polyvinylamine degraded below 360°C. The second distinct weight loss (nearly 24% weight loss) fell in the range of 360-430°C, and no more significant weight loss was observed above 430°C. The residual weight percentage at 800°C was 3.20, 6.10, 11.20, and 10.20% for PHBV, amide-, amine-, and collagen-PHBV, respectively.
