As shown in Fig. 2, the mechanical properties of the bioplastic films produced with this improved process were similar, in the dry state, to the mechanical properties measured in our previous work. To study the effect of absorbed moisture on the mechanical properties of the bioplastics, samples were measured after conditioning at different RH: 11%, 44%, 84%, 100%. The results, shown in Fig. 2A, are summarized in Fig. 2B. Once conditioned at different humidity the bioplastics behaved noticeably different: at low RH films were brittle, whereas at high RH films were softer and more stretchable. This behavior was transient and could be completely reversed after storing the films at a different RH. This effect is very similar to that of a plasticizer in a conventional polymer, in which the plasticized material has higher extensibility and lower stiffness. A glass transition influenced by the water content was described for pectin [24,25,36] but in the carrot bioplastic, pectin constitutes about 40% of the material [14], so it was noteworthy to see a plasticizing effect of this magnitude on the bioplastic. The effect is also more pronounced than what was measured in films produced by our group with a similar procedure, starting from different plant wastes [37]. To estimate the amount of water absorbed by the bioplastic films, a thermal gravimetric analysis was performed on samples conditioned at different humidity. Results are reported in Fig. S3 and Fig. S4 and summarized in Table S1. Data show that the water content changes significantly in the different samples: only 2.2% water was found in the sample conditioned at 11% RH, while 13.5% water was incorporated in the sample conditioned at 84% RH. A steep increase to 38% water was found in the sample conditioned at 100% RH. The water absorption was higher than what was reported for cellulose, the main component of the bioplastic, and similarly to what was reported for pectin, the absorption was found to be non linear with the relative humidity conditioning [17,[22], [23], [24], [25],36]. The water absorption kinetic, reported in Fig. S4, showed that the carrot bioplastic samples equilibrate with the surrounding atmosphere within 16 h. The effect of water-induced softening was exploited to develop protocols for manipulation and processing of the developed vegetable bioplastic films. Features such as folds and narrow corners (found in dishes, trays, boxes, etc.) were created not only at a macroscopic level, but at the sub-millimiter scale as well, as can be seen in Fig. 3. Once conditioned at a humidity higher than 60% (ambient humidity), films with thickness between 15 μm and 50 μm were flexible enough to be folded and create origami, such as the crane origami showed in Fig. 3A. The shape was retained for several weeks even when the samples were stored at lower humidity and the material became stiffer. This transient moisture-induced softening was further exploited to create even micrometer-scale features via compression molding.
Thermal properties of the different PHBV grades and their nanocomposite films were investigated by DSC analyses and the main estimated parameters are gathered in Table 5. The pure PHBVs presented a two-step melting behavior, consisting of a sharp melting peak followed by a melting shoulder. The appearance of two melting peaks has been reported for several PHBV grades and it has been attributed to several factors. While some studies hypothesized that more defective or smaller crystals are able to re-crystallize after melting, forming more perfect crystals which subsequently melt at higher temperatures,13 other works pointed out to the existence of different crystalline phases (HB-rich and HV-rich domains associated to the high- and low-temperature melting processes, respectively).37 In this work, the ratios of the melting enthalpies corresponding to each peak were clearly not related to the HV content of the samples. Thus, the first hypothesis, implying that a small amount of crystals were able to re-crystallize into a more perfect phase, seemed more feasible. Increasing the HV content from 3 to 9-16 mol % gave rise to lower melting and glass transition temperatures, as well as reduced overall melting enthalpy. The reduced enthalpy might be related to a crystallinity reduction caused by the higher hydroxyvalerate content, but it might also be a consequence of the slight hydrolytic degradation suffered by the higher valerate PHBVs. On the other hand, the incorporation of PEG into the PHBV3 did not reduce the overall crystallinity of the material, but prevented the creation of more perfect crystals after the first melting process, thus showing only one melting peak. The incorporation of BCNW led to a drop in the melting temperature of both the first and second melting peaks. Additionally, the overall melting enthalpy was reduced only for those samples in which the nanofiller dispersion was very high, i.e., the samples incorporating 1 wt % BCNW through electrospinning. This behavior was also reported for PHBV8 composites incorporating bamboo pulp fibers by melt compounding38 and is likely due to the cellulose nanofillers acting as obstacles for the crystallization of PHBV under the rapid cooling conditions applied after melt compounding. Additionally, the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PHBV3 increased with the incorporation of BCNW. This effect has been previously related to a reduced mobility of the PHBV molecular chains in the presence of dispersed cellulose nanocrystals.12, 15 Conversely, the addition of BCNW did not seem to have a significant effect on the Tg values of the PHBV9 and PHBV16 matrices, which may be indicative of weaker matrix-filler interactions, despite the relatively homogeneous dispersion of BCNW observed by SEM. This distinct behavior is likely to be related to the presence of a certain amount of hydrophilic impurities in these two latter PHBV grades. Although the materials were subjected to a purification step which prevented thermal degradation during melt processing, they presented a marked decrease in the Tg as compared with the commercial PHBV3. In fact, Tg values typically reported for non-purified PHBV grades are even lower (−2.4 and −4.9°C for PHBV1911 and −2.7°C for PHBV716), hence confirming that the amount of impurities remaining in the material has a strong impact in the corresponding Tg. If some impurities remain in the material, the BCNW are expected to interact preferentially with these due to their strong hydrophilic behavior, creating separate domains and thus, hindering the interaction between the nanofiller and the hydrophobic PHBV matrix. This hypothesis of weaker BCNW-PHBV interactions for the PHBV9 and PHBV16 is further supported by the barrier and mechanical properties described in the following sections. Table 4 summarizes the mechanical properties of the neat PHBV matrices and of their nanocomposites. From these results, it may be deduced that the mechanical properties were affected by both the hydroxyvalerate content of the PHBV and the presence of plasticizer, whereas the incorporation of low loadings of BCNW did not lead to significant changes.

Wet chemical reaction is a direct method to give the desired groups via chemical etching or chemical initiating graft polymerization. Chemical treatments break the ester bonds on the surfaces to produce functional groups, altering the surface chemical states, free energy, and morphology of PHAs. An alkaline treatment modified the PHB membranes by creating carboxylic groups on the surface. Importantly, the alkaline-treated PHB enhanced the proliferation of human osteoblasts, and inhibited S. aureus growth more than 60% after 48 h of culture, showing its potential application as an antibacterial and osteoconductive membrane for numerous orthopedic and dental tissue engineering applications.46 After being incubated in the 5 × SBF (simulated body fluid), NaOH-treated PHBHHx films (Figure 2a) presented an increased mass by ≈15% over its original value, and the growth rate had a close relationship with the increasing carboxyl and hydroxyl groups. MC3T3-E1 cell attachment and proliferation enhanced significantly on surface-hydrolyzed PHBHHx.47 KOH-treated PHBV film showed the decreasing water contact angles that reached an almost constant value after 2 h. The adsorption of albumin, collagen, and fibronectin was almost 100 times higher on the hydrolyzed PHBV films than the native surface.48 Chemical etching in the form of aminolysis introduced amino groups on PHAs surface (Figure 2b). Short treatment of ethylenediamine to PHBHHx was able to decrease the hydrophobicity without a significant alteration of the mechanical properties.49 Lipase (Lipolase 100T, Lipolase Ultra 50T, and Lipoprime 50T) treatment increased the viable cell number on the PHB film from 107 to 201 times than the untreated PHB film, compared with 25 times for NaOH treated-PHB film. The surface of the PHB film had many pores with sizes range of 1-5 µm, which reduced to less than 1 µm after the lipase treatment.50 The major advantages of the chemical etching are its simplicity and low cost. But the functionality available usually depends on many factors, such as reagents concentration, reaction time, and crystallinity of the substrate.51 Chemical initiating-graft polymerization of vinyl monomers onto PHBV film has been studied by using benzoyl peroxide (BPO) as an initiator (Figure 2c). The free-radical fragments from the peroxides may abstract the methine protons of PHBV, the most acidic protons, to generate the macroradicals that initiate the graft polymerization of acrylamide (AM) and 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA), along with the unavoidable homopolymerization. It should be noted that the grafting of polyacrylamide occurred well inside the film either, not just being limited to the film surface, but the film surface had a higher polyacrylamide content. The film treated with monomer and initiator prior to the graft polymerization yielded a slightly higher graft percentage due to the swelling of the base film to increase the inclusion of monomer and initiator.52, 53 Different vinyl monomers could be grafted onto the films to provide diverse functional groups on the surface with tunable thickness of the layer. But the macromolecular chains may also be introduced into the films to influence the bulk properties if the monomer concentration or reaction time increased. Moreover, the branch or crosslinking structure being formed during the chemical initiating-graft polymerization should be reduced to avoid deteriorate the mechanical properties. This modification method provides an opportunity to adapt the grafting strategy to a chosen wettability and functionality of PHAs.
Measurements most often reference the location and depth of the sample in the soil, and in rare cases identify the microorganism community. However, the characteristics of the soil not only affect the conditions, but also how the conditions will change over the duration of the experiment. For example, PHBV (8% HV) powder tested in sand (dry silica with low organic material) achieved 80% biodegradation after 600 days,176 which is significantly longer than most soil biodegradation tests. The poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is a natural, nontoxic, semicrystalline, linear chain copolymer, with fewer hydroxyvalerate (HV) units than hydroxybutyrate units. Furthermore, it is biodegradable, biocompatible, has a high degree of polymerization.1-3 Its high crystallinity provides good barrier properties1 and as a rigid and brittle material, it bears low deformations. Its compatibility with biological systems and biodegradability allows the PHBV to be applied in controlled drug delivery and tissue engineering.4, 5 It also can stimulate bone tissue growth and be used for biodegradable packaging.6 Many studies propose the combination of PHBV with other polymers or reinforcing agents, forming polymer blends, composites and nanocomposites in order to improve its properties.6-12 The plasticizers are considered processing additives and properties modifiers, because they change processing parameters and the thermal and mechanical properties of polymers. These additives are selected in order to enhance polymer attributes, such as processability, elongation capacity, flexibility and can even lower the glass transition temperature and tensile modulus.13-15 Plasticizers make the polymers flow easier when they are melted, due to lower viscosity, and the higher the plasticizer concentration, the lower the hardness, tensile strength and modulus, and the higher the elongation at break.13, 16, 17

Based on the provided evidence, the Shape Memory Effect (SME) in biodegradable polyurethanes refers to their ability to be deformed from an original ("permanent") shape into a temporary shape under specific conditions, and then recover the original shape upon exposure to an external stimulus. This effect arises from their unique molecular architecture:

1.  **Molecular Mechanism**: SME relies on a segmented structure where **crystalline domains** (often derived from biodegradable polyester soft segments like poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL)) act as reversible molecular switches. These domains soften/melt upon heating above their transition temperature (e.g., PCL melting temperature, T~m~), allowing deformation. Upon cooling below the transition temperature, the domains harden/crystallize, "fixing" the temporary shape. Reheating above the transition temperature melts/softens these domains again, allowing elastic recovery forces from the **crosslinked network** (formed by hard segments via physical interactions like hydrogen bonding or covalent bonds) to drive the material back to its permanent shape [1, 3, 4, 5, 9].
2.  **Stimuli**: The recovery stimulus is most commonly **heat** (thermal-responsive SME), where the transition temperature of the crystalline switching domain (e.g., T~m~ of PCL) triggers recovery [1, 3, 4, 5, 9]. Other stimuli like light or pH changes are also possible [3, 4, 7].
3.  **Performance Metrics**: SME is quantified by **shape fixity** (ability to retain the temporary shape, often >95%) and **shape recovery** (ability to return to the permanent shape, often >90%) [2, 15]. These properties can be tailored by adjusting the polymer chemistry, such as the hard segment content or switching segment type/crystallinity [2, 5].
4.  **Biomedical Relevance**: Crucially for biodegradable polyurethanes, the SME transition temperature (e.g., T~m~ of PCL) can be designed near **human body temperature (~37°C)**, enabling applications like self-tightening sutures or deployable stents within the body [2, 4, 12]. The shape memory effect of PLA is a crucial property for functionalized PLA constructs. That said, a major limitation with shape memory effects is that the polymer tends to have low actuation stress and long memory cycle time, limiting practical robotic/biomedical applications unless the shape memory polymer is supported by functional additives [9]. PLA as a thermoplastic polymer for 3D printing has shown great interest, with comparable mechanical properties to commodity thermoplastics such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), with the additional attraction of biodegradability and being derived from renewable resources [12]. Shape memory polyurethane (SMPU) is a typical shape memory polymer widely used in biomaterials,1, 2 such as bone tissue engineering,3orthodontic,4 closure device,5 and self-expandable stents.6 The shape memory behavior, typically remembering a temporary shape and returning to its original shape, can be stimulated by pH, temperature, humidity, electricity, magnetism, electromagnetism, and so on.7 The most important specie among them is thermal responsive polyurethane.8, 9 The semicrystalline poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is popularly used as soft segments of SMPU because of its nontoxicity, low melting temperature, and biodegradability.10-13 The main aspect in designing PCL-based SMPU is the transition temperature of the soft segment, which controls the transition between temporary and permanent shape. The transition temperature is glass transition or melting temperature according to the molecular weight14 and the degree of microphase separation between the hard and soft segments.15 Most PCL-based SMPU was designed to recover at or slightly below body temperature according to its biomedical application. At present, researchers generally believe that shape memory polymers have a two-phase structure, namely a stationary phase (permanent) and a reversible phase (temperoary) [8]. Its main function is to remember and restore the permanent shape, that is, to define the permanent shape and store energy during the deformation process; the reversible phase can be a partially crystalline phase that produces reversible changes during crystalization and crystal melting, or a phase structure that undergoes a reversible transition between glassy and rubbery states. Cellulose is one of the most abundant and renewable biopolymers from nature and has been studied broadly in both academic and industrial areas. The advantages of cellulose include low cost, low density, high stiffness, renewable nature, and biodegradability.24 Enormous research has focused on the composites reinforced with cellulose fiber. As for microcrystalline cellulose, in structure, cellulose chains aggregate to form micro-fibrils, long threadlike bundles of molecules stabilized laterally by hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups and oxygens of adjacent molecules. The arrangement of cellulose molecular chain in micro-fibrils is sufficiently regular to form monocrystalline cellulose domains. There is also an amount of cellulose in amorphous state within the micro-fibril.25 Because of the different original resource, including the plants and some sea animals,26 the cellulose micro-fibrils possess diameters ranging from 2 to 20 nm and the lengths that can be several tens of microns. The micro-fibril is a string of cellulose whiskers, assembled by the amorphous domains. The modulus of micro-fibrils can be close to the perfect crystal of native cellulose (estimated to 150 GPa). The amorphous domains as the defect can be removed from the micro-fibrils, so as to obtain the short microcrystals, i.e., cellulose whiskers. Dong et al. revealed that the hydrolysis condition, such as temperature and time, together with the subsequent ultrasonic treatment can be used to prepare the cellulose microcrystallites.27 The length of prepared cellulose microcrystallites can be 75-107 nm evaluated from TEM images. The 'Shape Memory Effect' in biodegradable polyurethanes refers to their ability to return from a deformed temporary shape to their original permanent shape upon exposure to an external stimulus, typically heat near body temperature (37°C). This behavior arises from a two-phase structure: (1) a **stationary phase** (hard segments, often crosslinked networks or crystalline domains) that retains the permanent shape through physical/chemical interactions, and (2) a **reversible phase** (soft segments, e.g., poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) or poly(lactic acid) (PLA)) that undergoes thermal transitions (melting/glass transition) to fix/release temporary shapes [1], [5], [7].  

When heated above the transition temperature (e.g., PCL’s melting point), the reversible phase softens, allowing deformation. Cooling fixes the temporary shape via crystallization or vitrification of the soft segments [4], [7]. Subsequent reheating melts or softens the reversible phase, enabling entropy-driven recovery to the original shape via the elastic network of the stationary phase [5], [9]. Adjusting hard/soft segment ratios or incorporating additives (e.g., PEG, cellulose whiskers) tunes transition temperatures, mechanical properties, and biodegradability [1], [10], [12]. Biodegradability stems from hydrolyzable ester bonds in soft segments (e.g., PCL, PLA), which degrade into non-toxic byproducts [2], [7], [10]. These properties make biodegradable polyurethanes suitable for medical implants and devices [1], [7], [15].

3D printing technology is also known as additive manufacture and has been more and more promoted because of convenient processing and high operability. It can be used to produce parts or products used in many industries. PLA is a very popular raw material used in melt deposition molding (FDM) 3D printing technology [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. Combining stereo-complexation with 3D printing technologies and toughening the 3D printed stereo-complexed PLA (SC-PLA) materials are two major objectives that need to be fulfilled in the future, which will effectively promote the development of 3D printing and expand the applications of PLA materials. However, only limited numbers of reports were available on the toughening of SC-PLA. These reports mainly include melt blending of non-biodegradable elastomers [[19], [20], [21]] or bio-degradable elastomers [22], radiation crosslinking [23] and structure control by solvent [24]. However, these methods are not satisfactory solutions to brittleness of SC-PLA due to several reasons, including limited improvement in breaking elongation (ranging from 6 to 12 times of increase), substantial loss in tensile strength (ranging from 20% to 45% of loss), use of non-biodegradable tougheners (such as poly (ethylene methyl acrylate glycidyl methacrylate), rubber and polyurethane), and poor adaptiveness to 3D printing. Other methods to improve toughness of traditional PLLA could be expanded to plasticizing with small molecules [25,26], block or graft copolymerization [[27], [28], [29]] and reinforcing with nanoparticles [[30], [31], [32]]. Nevertheless, these methods also have their defects. Low-molecular-weight plasticizers are easy to migrate to surface of the products, leading to loss of ductility. Copolymerization requires complicated process. Nanoparticles tend to agglomerate and are expensive. Among all above methods, blending PLA with elastomers is a simple and effective way to enhance product properties, especially with the help of compatibilizer. Blending PLA with biodegradable elastomer poly (butyleneadipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is one of the most potential and environmentally sustainable methods to achieve good ductility [33]. However, traditional PLA and PBAT have large difference in their solubility parameters (PLA: 10.1 (cal/cm3)1/2；PBAT: 22.95 (cal/cm3)1/2) [34,35]. They are incompatible and have weak interfacial adhesion, which cannot effectively transfer the interphase stress. Such incompatibility greatly limits the toughening of PLA by PBAT. Therefore, enhancing compatibility between the two components becomes necessary. Previous research mainly includes non-reactive compatibilization and reactive compatibilization of traditional PLLA and PBAT. Such two types of compatibilization uses polar substances that do not react but interact with the compatibilized substances (via hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole forces, etc.) and reactive substances with highly reactive groups, respectively. Reactive substances mainly come from the epoxy [36,37], isocyanate [38] and peroxide [39] families. However, controlling the reactivity degree in several heating processes becomes the biggest obstacle to use reactive compatibilizers in 3D printing of PLLA/PBAT. One example is the work of Chen et al. [40]. the compatibilization of SC-PLA/PBAT was achieved by grafting reaction in the melt blending process. If such a recipe was applied to 3D printing, epoxy groups SG (poly (styrene)-co-(glycidylmethacrylate) easily react with PLA and PBAT components during the filament preparation. Such a structural change hinders the subsequent melt 3D printing. Increase in printing temperature might favor the melting of the crosslinked blends, but also increase the risk of thermal degradation of PLA. In addition, the preparation of SG (poly (styrene)-co-(glycidylmethacrylate) compatibilizer was complex and costly. PMMA compatibilizer, with a large availability on the market, is a convenient, low cost and high efficiency alternative. Therefore, using non-reactive compatibilizers in 3D printing of PLLA/PBAT seems more feasible than using reactive compatibilizers.

Preparation and Properties of 3D-Printed Hydrogel-Embedded PLA Composite Scaffolds Tissue engineering aims to repair damaged tissues and organs using structure known as scaffolds, which are pre-defined replaceable temporary supports to serve as carriers for cell cultures and control their growth.1, 2 This means that as cells grow, there is a gradual biodegradation of the support material, leading to the formation of a new tissue with the desired shape and properties. Because of this, scaffolds are developed using biodegradable materials to guarantee their appropriate disintegration after forming a new tissue.1, 3 Furthermore, the biocompatibility and non-toxicity properties are crucial to prevent possible bodily rejection and inflammatory responses.2, 4 Besides those characteristics, scaffolds for tissue engineering should present a good porosity percentage rate,5 satisfactory mechanical properties,6 and pore size corresponding to the tissue replaced.7 To facilitate indirect interactions between cells across the scaffold, the pore size must be sufficiently large to support cellular nutrition but not too large to inhibit cell migration. So, to obtain a satisfactory scaffold, it is necessary to develop a material with an appropriate morphology and microstructure based on adequate porosity, pore size, pore shape, and interconnectivity.6 In this sense, materials currently used in this field are available in several types: entirely synthetic materials, which the most popular polymers are linear aliphatic polyesters, such as polyglycolic acid (PGA) and polylactic acid (PLA); natural materials, such as collagen, proteoglycans, alginate-based substrates and chitosan, ceramics such as hydroxyapatite and tri-calcium phosphate, as well as their combinations.7, 8 On the other hand, some of these materials present drawbacks: ceramics are stiff, some synthetic polymers can be non-biodegradable, and natural polymers might have poor mechanical properties.6 Therefore, the big challenge of tissue engineering is finding the best combination of materials available and improving scaffold biocompatibility.

The addition of some amounts of the D-stereoisomer to the L-chain results in a significant reduction of the crystallinity compared to the pure PLLA [8,9]. Usually, for biomedical applications, Poly(L-co-D,L-lactic acid) (PLDLA) is produced with up to 30 % of d,l-lactic acid content, which has been shown to improve the biocompatibility of the material [9,10]. The ampoules were immersed in an oil bath at 130 °C for 48 h under vacuum. Understanding the properties of 3D-printed scaffolds is critical for facilitating their proper modeling and efficient design. Surface topography, chemistry as well as mechanical properties have been shown to significantly influence scaffolds’ biological functionalities including cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation [9-11]. Each method of characterization has its own advantages and disadvantages and often they complement rather than replace each other. Conventional means of classical mechanical characterization of tissue engineering scaffolds, often require destructive testing or means that can compromise the sterility of the samples [12]. In contrast, ultrasonic techniques offer a cost-effective, non-invasive and non-destructive characterization without lengthy prior preparation [13, 14]. Furthermore, it can directly probe the elastic and viscous properties of a material by measuring the speed of ultrasound and its attenuation. Such acoustic characterization has been performed for biological tissues [15-17] as well as a number of synthetic polymeric constructs made of PLGA [18], Silicone [19], Polyvinyl alcohol [15], Agar gel [19] and polyacrylamide gel [20] for their possible use as human tissue substitutes. A few studies that have investigated the role of microstructure such as porosity and pore size on ultrasonic properties of bone mimicking phantoms [21-24] focused on biomaterials fabricated by conventional techniques and therefore suffered from irregular surface patterns with no control over pore size and porosity. Based on the provided evidence, 'stratification' (interpreted as phase separation) plays a critical role in accelerating the degradation of PCL/PLA blends by facilitating the penetration of degradation agents into the material matrix. Specifically:

1.  **Enhanced Penetration Pathways**: Phase separation within PLA/PCL blends creates distinct domains and interfacial boundaries. This morphology allows water and enzymes (e.g., lipases, esterases) to penetrate more easily into the blend compared to a homogeneous structure [1, 2].
2.  **Accessibility to PCL-Rich Regions**: The phase-separated structure creates localized PCL-rich domains. PCL's aliphatic ester bonds are highly susceptible to enzymatic hydrolysis, accelerating the breakdown of these regions, especially in blends with higher PCL content [1, 2].
3.  **Influence on Crystallinity & Amorphous Regions**: Higher PCL content disrupts polymer chain packing, reducing the overall crystallinity of the blend (as supported by DSC data). The resulting increase in amorphous regions is more accessible to hydrolytic and enzymatic attack, further accelerating degradation. The phase separation enhances this effect by concentrating amorphous regions within domains [1, 2].
4.  **Synergistic Degradation Dynamics**: The interplay between the degrading amorphous regions (faster degradation) and the more stable crystalline regions (slower degradation) within the phase-separated morphology creates a dynamic system that maintains a consistent degradation rate across the material while overall mass loss increases [1, 2].
5.  **Hydrophilicity & Water Interaction**: While not directly mentioned for PCL/PLA, evidence regarding hydrophilic additives like TPS/cotton in PLA highlights that structures promoting water affinity (potentially via interfaces created by phase separation) lower surface energy and favor water retention, increasing material fragility and hydrolysis susceptibility [8, 15]. This principle likely extends to the interfaces formed between PLA and PCL phases.

The gas barrier property of the polymers (i.e. oxygen permeability) is another critical requirement for their use in practical applications. For example, the packaging sheets for food storage should possess low oxygen permeability. For this purpose, we measured the oxygen permeabilities of the PLAPU-2, PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 samples (Figure 4). These thin-film samples were prepared in pieces with an area of 5 × 5 cm2 and a thickness of about 1 mm using a hot press at 100 °C under a pressure of 1450 psi, after which their oxygen permeabilities were measured. The PLAPU-2 sample had the highest oxygen permeability of 782.7 cm3 mm m−2 day−1. In contrast, PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 had dramatically reduced oxygen permeabilities of 35.0 and 9.2 cm3 mm m−2 day−1, respectively. It is well known that the gas permeabilities of thermoplastic elastomers based on PU are affected mainly by changes in crystallinity, chain density and molecular weight.34, 35 Therefore, the low gas permeabilities of PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 polymers were probably due to the lower free volumes in the PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 samples caused by the presence of higher molecular weight chains.36, 37 In addition, it should be noted that PLAPU-4 showed much lower permeability (9.2 cm3 mm m−2 day−1) than the previously reported value of 777 cm3 mm m−2 day−1 for pure PLA with comparable Mw = 160 kg mol−1.36 Therefore the incorporation of longer PCL segments has a critical role in enhancing oxygen barrier properties and also in improving the flexibility and entanglement of PLAPUs. To demonstrate the feasibility of PLAPU polymers for use in biodegradable packaging materials, hydrolytic degradation tests were performed in PBS.37 For this purpose, PLAPU-2, PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 polymers were molded into samples with thicknesses of 1 mm using the same conditions that were used for the mechanical tests. Then the samples were weighed (about 0.1 g) and inserted into vials. During the degradation process, the PLAPU samples were treated continuously in PBS at 35 °C for 30 days. Figure 5 shows the weight loss of the PLAPU-2, PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 polymers as a function of treatment time in the PBS. Because PLA is highly biodegradable,38 all of the PLAPU specimens were degraded continuously by PBS hydrolysis, but the degradation rate was dependent on the content of PCL in the polymers. For example, PLAPU-2 which had a higher PLA:PCL ratio of 1:1 showed a higher weight loss (30%) after 30 days than PLAPU-3 (26%) and PLAPU-4 (14%). The higher degree of chain entanglements in the high molecular weight PLAPU-3 and PLAPU-4 could suppress the chain mobility significantly, thereby decreasing the degradation rate compared with that of PLAPU-2. In this study, we successfully developed high molecular weight PLAPU polymers with high elongation properties, low gas permeabilities and biodegradability. Four different PLAPU polymers were prepared with different composition ratios of hard PLA to soft PCL segments. By tuning the PLA:PCL ratios from 1:1 to 1:5, we determined that the optimum ratio was 1:3. PLAPU-3 exhibited a sharply increased elongation at break of 1053% with a relatively high Young's modulus of 51.8 MPa. In addition, the morphological study indicated good agreement with the results of the mechanical properties. The gas permeabilities of the PLAPU polymers were strongly influenced by the content of soft PCL segments and chain entanglement in the high molecular weight PLAPU polymers. In addition, all the PLAPU polymers were biodegradable, but the degradation rate depended on the PLA content. PLAPU polymers can be prepared using this method to obtain enhanced flexibility, low gas permeability and good biodegradability by easily controlling the PLA:PCL ratio. These improved properties of PLAPU polymers show that they have high potential for use in environmentally friendly packaging materials.

Although significant after three measurements, the increase is very small, because, from a technological point of view, a relevant effect includes the change of an order of magnitude in permeability. We propose two hypotheses for our findings. First, although the DSC and DMA results clearly show the crystallinity of the recrystallized PLA, no apparent spherulites are observed with a microscope under cross-polarized light, which is in contrast to the observations of Solarski et al.21 or Tsuji and Ikada.35 The morphology can be explained by the low recrystallization temperature used in this work to obtain small spherulites. Therefore, we suggest that the spherulites in our film samples might be too small to create a more tortuous path for the oxygen molecules and thus to decrease the gas permeability. It has been described for PET that an increase in the size of the superstructure in the crystalline phase decreases the gas permeability due to an increase of the tortuosity.32 A second hypothesis might be the de-densification of the amorphous phase which counteracts the decrease of the quantity of permeable amorphous phase due to crystallization. De-densification of the amorphous phase in PET has been shown by Liu et al.36 to be responsible for the higher oxygen permeability of bottle walls processed under conditions of higher thermal exposure, although the treatment led to an increase in the volume fraction of impermeable crystals. A decrease in the permeable amorphous phase density causing an increase of gas permeability through heat-set PET was also shown by Qureshi et al.37 It has been shown for poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), in comparison to PET, that there is an important decoupling between crystalline and surrounding amorphous phase.24, 38, 39 This behaviour is attributed to the high flexibility of the macromolecular chain, which is able to fold easily on the crystal surface. The result would be less tied molecules between amorphous and crystalline phase,38 a factor limiting the possibility of de-densification of the amorphous phase. To this end, commercial PLA/biodegradable polyester blends were mixed with talc at different loadings (0-5 wt%). Polymer filler interactions should be enhanced in order to improve the mechanical properties. Other filler types can be considered in future studies.

question: How does 'enzymatic recycling' of PET (and potentially bio-polyesters) contribute to the circular economy?
ground_truth: Enzymatic recycling (e.g., using engineered PETase) breaks down polymers into their constituent monomers (TPA and EG) with high purity, even from mixed or contaminated waste streams. These monomers can be re-polymerized to create virgin-quality plastic, closing the loop indefinitely, unlike mechanical recycling which leads to down-cycling.

Another concept coming into focus and integrated into sustainability discussions is the circular economy, an economic system based on resource efficiency and the reuse and regeneration of materials or products.309 In a bio-based economy, economic activity involves the use of biological resources, technologies, processes and methods to provide value-added products, goods, services and energy in a sustainable manner to all economic sectors.310 In a circular bioeconomy, natural capital is renewable and sustainably sourced, produced, managed, recovered and reused as much as possible across its entire life cycle.311 Circular biopolymers are one probable pathway for decoupling economic growth from the consumption of finite resources by sustainably sourcing feedstocks and building end-of-life recovery pathways that recapture polymer material value after use.312 This approach includes bio-based material innovations sourced from renewable feedstocks that are waste byproducts and coupling material innovations with complementary end-of-life “waste” management and recycling systems that create added value in organics processing infrastructure. Controlling the biopolymer morphology (aspect ratio), degree of polymerization, and orientation, allows tuning of their interactions at the molecular- and nano-scales, which ultimately governs the macroscopic behavior and fracture of those entirely biobased materials. Structural biopolymers are obtained from biomatter through extraction and homogenization processes, which often require excessive chemical and thermo-mechanical treatments, which need to be taken into consideration when discussing the environmental impact of such materials. In addition, the effects of each processing step on the composition and morphology of the extracted biopolymers are critical, and should be carefully evaluated. For example, we discussed literature-reported results which demonstrate that extraction processes effectively reduce the polymer chain length and aspect ratio, which leads to inferior performance, compared to the native biopolymer state.

Polyolefins (Fig. 2), such as polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS), are the most widely used petroleum-based polymer materials, with a global market size of USD 240 billion in 2020. Generally, polyolefin monomers are joined by C-C bonds, with the monomer skeleton structure also composed of C-C bonds. Thus, the selective recovery of monomers by polyolefin depolymerization is challenging under moderate reaction conditions, as the bond energies of the different C-C bonds are basically the same.11,17 Although some recent advances have been made in polyolefin depolymerization, with the capture of fuel additives such as alkanes and aromatics through the catalytic pyrolysis of waste polyolefins, this cannot solve the recycling issue.17,18 Therefore, there is still a need to produce new plastic from non-renewable resources including petroleum and coal.19 Moreover, if plastic waste is converted to fuel, the carbon atoms in the plastic will still end up in the atmosphere, which is not conducive to carbon neutrality in terms of carbon footprint. Compared with polyolefins, polyesters can be more easily depolymerized to their monomers via highly selective breakage of the ester bonds.20-23 More importantly, most polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(ethylene-2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF), and PET, can be produced from a variety of sources, including non-renewable and renewable resources, and have become more attractive due to their good thermal and mechanical properties, processing versatility, and degradability (Fig. 2).24-27 Among these, PET is the most important and abundant one, and is widely used as thermoplastic polymers with excellent properties, including thermal stability, transparency, high strength, low density, chemical resistance and low cost.28 PBT and PEF are structurally and functionally similar to PET, and possess unique advantages in physicochemical properties.29,30 For example, PBT can be a viable substitute for the crystalline thermoplastics (e.g., PE and nylon) because of its lower melting point, lower strength and stiffness, lower glass transition temperature, and better impact resistance. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is a semi-aromatic polyester with excellent mechanical, thermal and barrier properties, and is widely used in packaging, textile and composite applications. However, the robustness of this polymer also serves as a double-edged sword since PET is highly resistant to degradation in a normal aqueous environment and may persist for hundreds or thousands of years.[1-3] This creates a burden for effective handling of this polymer in a circular life cycle, as such a significant portion of used PET articles are accumulating on land and in water. This is particularly the case for PET fibers, films, and composites where the economics of recycling is considered to be low.[1, 4] Although aliphatic polyesters such as polylactic acid, polycaprolactone, and hydroxybutyrate are biodegradable under normal outdoor conditions, the mechanical strength and barrier properties of these polymers cannot match with those of PET. These biodegradable polyesters are also much more expensive to produce. Therefore, a method for degrading PET in a natural environment, if found, would revolutionize the polymer industry. Is PET biodegradable? A question like this by itself is a paradox. Scientifically speaking, PET is biodegradable; there are natural enzymes such as cutinase promoting the biodegradation of PET.[3, 5, 6] Actually, a group of researchers[7] recently found that a bacterial species called Ideonella sakaiensis secrets two types of enzymes, PETase and MHETase, to degrade and assimilate PET into monomeric units. Practically speaking, biodegradation of PET is a rather difficult process, and a person with a normal life span most likely would not see a PET bottle naturally degrade in an outdoor environment. The biodegradation of a polymer is expected to be dependent on many factors, especially crystallinity, hydrophobicity, and geometrical size,[8] yet the accrued evidences for PET biodegradation (even extremely slow) are mostly demonstrated for amorphous PET at miniature sizes. Of course, we hold a promise for new developments in this area, which at a future time may lead to a viable bioengineering process for PET degradation. Every problem can be multifaceted, so is the degradation of PET. Rather than finding a biological process, one may look for a chemical route. Indeed, it is well known that the hydrolysis of PET in an aqueous environment can be promoted by various chemical moieties including alkaline, acid, and alcohol. Particularly, the activation energy of hydrolysis is found to be greatly lowered by strong bases such as sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide.[9] Previous studies[10, 11] have demonstrated that PET can be effectively dissolved in strong alkaline solutions such as sodium hydroxide solution at moderate temperature below 100°C. These results may promote one to consider a potential method for promoting the degradation of a PET article by inclusion of a source for high basicity in the material formulation. One simple way is to mix a metal hydroxide as a filler material in PET matrix. However, direct incorporation of a metal hydroxide into PET is difficult since PET is normally processed in its melt state at high temperature. Melt mixing of PET with a metal hydroxide can bring about significant polymer degradation and as a result, poor mechanical properties. Existing research[12] has already shown that melt mixing of PET with a metal hydroxide such as sodium or potassium hydroxide leads to strong hydrolysis of PET. Therefore, a different approach for rendering high basicity should be sought after because enhanced hydrolysis is only desired at end of life cycle.

1.  **Direct Monomer Recovery for Repolymerization:** Enzymes like PETase (from *Ideonella sakaiensis*) and thermostable variants of leaf-branch compost cutinase (LCC) selectively depolymerize PET into its monomers, terephthalate (TA) and ethylene glycol, at high efficiency (up to 16.7 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹). These monomers can be purified and repolymerized into virgin-quality PET, enabling closed-loop recycling and reducing reliance on fossil feedstocks. [[13], [15]]
2.  **Biological Upcycling into Higher-Value Products:** Enzymatically derived monomers, particularly TA, serve as feedstocks for engineered biological pathways to synthesize valuable chemicals. For example, TA can be converted into vanillin (>79% conversion) via enzymatic cascades in engineered *E. coli*, transforming plastic waste into a high-demand commercial product instead of downcycling it. [[13]]
3.  **Synthesis of Novel Functional Materials:** Enzymatic or chemically assisted depolymerization products (e.g., from aminolysis) can be used as building blocks for new materials. PET waste monomers have been used to synthesize antimicrobial cationic polyionenes and biodegradable poly(ester amide)s suitable for demanding applications like biomedical coatings and bone tissue regeneration scaffolds, demonstrating high-value upcycling. [[14]]
4.  **Mild Condition Processing & Environmental Compatibility:** Enzymatic degradation operates efficiently at relatively low temperatures (ambient to 72°C) in aqueous conditions, offering an energy-efficient alternative to harsh chemical recycling methods. Furthermore, any unrecycled material can potentially biodegrade microbially into inorganic carbon, integrating into the natural carbon cycle. [[13], [15]]
5.  **Integration within the Circular Bioeconomy Framework:** Enzymatic recycling facilitates the "design-for-recycling" principle and contributes to circular biopolymer pathways by sustainably sourcing feedstocks (waste plastic) and creating end-of-life recovery systems that recapture material value. It exemplifies connecting R&D with downstream applications to keep materials in circulation at economic value. [[1], [3]]

Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(trimethylene terephthalate) (PTT) are examples of polyesters with partial biobased content, produced by combining fossil-derived terephthalic acid (TA) with renewable components such as 1,3-propanediol (PDO) or ethylene glycol. Although PET is typically regarded as non-biodegradable or non-compostable, studies have shown that certain enzymes can naturally break it down, albeit at a very slow rate [81]. This bacterium produces PET-hydrolyzing enzymes, such as PETase, which facilitate the breakdown of PET. This discovery presents new possibilities for the bio-recycling of PET, potentially leading to more efficient and environmentally friendly methods of recycling this widely used plastic. Polyamides (PAs) are a class of condensation polymers characterized by repeating amide groups in their molecular chains [56]. These amide groups facilitate the formation of inter-chain hydrogen bonds, which contribute to the material’s ordered microstructure and high degree of crystallinity. This structural feature underlies the polyamides’ excellent mechanical properties, including strong impact resistance, high hardness, and good abrasion resistance.

The recycling of bioplastics: advantages and Obstacles The sustainability of plastics, regardless of their origin or compostability, heavily depends on their inclusion in recycling systems. While non-biodegradable plastics are commonly viewed as recyclable, biodegradable bioplastics are often considered suitable only for biodegradation [84]. However, bioplastics like PLA and PHA degrade slowly under natural conditions, limiting their environmental benefits as they might not break down fast enough to reduce pollution [128]. Improving recycling infrastructures, such as adopting chemical recycling, can mitigate these issues. Chemical recycling converts bioplastics into their basic monomers, which can be repolymerized into new plastics, maintaining material quality and reducing environmental impacts [94]. The biodegradation of plastics in landfills can release methane, a potent greenhouse gas that exacerbates climate change. Thus, bioplastics should ideally degrade in controlled composting environments to minimize methane emissions [87]. However, premature disposal of bioplastics wastes valuable raw materials, such as lactic acid in PLA, which could be preserved through chemical recycling. This process transforms waste bioplastics into new monomers and compounds, conserving renewable resources and reducing the reliance on virgin materials [121]. Enzymatic and catalytic processes in chemical recycling are also improving, enhancing the efficiency of converting bioplastics into valuable raw materials (Table 1).
The establishment of infrastructure, such as commercial composting facilities, along with customer involvement in appropriate waste sorting, are prerequisites for the success of these initiatives. Moreover, new chemical recycling techniques are being developed that may decompose polymers into their monomers, providing a means of repurposing biodegradable waste to make new materials and thereby closing the loop. Many studies have focused on the significance of product design, effective utilization, waste management, and reuse. As a step toward a circular economy, sustainable woody-like composites derived from recycled Tetra Pak cellulose and poly(butylene succinate) were fabricated.320 McKeown et al.321 concentrated on PLA chemical recycling, highlighting how end-of-life disposal strategies of biobased polymers are vital for a successful transition to a sustainable circular economy. In the framework of a circular economy, the utilization of waste coffee trash as a renewable source for creating sustainable PBS biocomposites was highlighted.322 The creation of sustainable polymer materials in a way that improves sustainability through material design, waste management, renewable energy sources, biodegradability, biotechnological approaches, and enzymatic recycling within the framework of an international circular (bio)economy can foster efficient resource utilization and management.323 Biodegradability, while valuable in open environmental contexts where plastic leakage is inevitable, may not offer the same benefits in structured waste management systems lacking industrial composting infrastructure. In fact, in the hierarchy of circularity, recyclable materials are often prioritized because they better support long-term material retention and reuse.327,328 To align polymer blend development with circular economy goals, future strategies must go beyond traditional property enhancement. This includes designing blends with recyclability in mind through reversible chemistries, dynamic covalent networks, or advanced compatibilization techniques that allow effective reprocessing without compromising performance. Additionally, the concept of ‘design-for-recycling’ should be embedded from the outset, ensuring that material formulations account for their entire lifecycle, not just their immediate utility or degradability.328

There are different approaches to realizing the proposed circular material streams. One part of the solution is the production of biodegradable polymers, which will ideally decompose instead of persisting and accumulating in the environment. Finally, biodegradation is usually less effective compared to technical chemical processes and the material is at least temporarily lost at the end of life, not contributing to the circular economy. Polyolefins (Fig. 2), such as polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS), are the most widely used petroleum-based polymer materials, with a global market size of USD 240 billion in 2020. The quantities of plastics recycled and recovered vary geographically, according to plastic type and application.4 Most of the recycling and recovery of post-consumer plastic waste takes place either through mechanical recycling or energy recovery.5 Thermoplastics are typically suitable for mechanical recycling. However, chemical recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) has been more successful than that of polyolefins due to more simple processes and milder process conditions.4, 6 In 2014, the highest recycling rates in the United States for different plastics in the municipal waste were for PET, high density polyethylene (HDPE), and low density polyethylene (LDPE)/low density and linear low density polyethylenes (LLDPE) (19.1%, 10.5%, and 5.8%, respectively).7 PET bottles and HDPE bottles/containers are in most cases easier to identify and to separate from the waste stream. However, large amounts of plastics are still accumulating in landfills and in natural habitats. Space for landfills is soon becoming scarce with contamination risks of soil and groundwater.8, 9 Recycling is the process of using recovered material to manufacture a new product, and it is one potential way to reduce the negative impacts of plastics waste.4 Plastics can be recycled in four ways: (1) primary mechanical reprocessing (re-extrusion or closed-loop recycling) of the scrap material into a similar product, (2) secondary (mechanical) reprocessing into products requiring lower properties, (3) tertiary chemical recovery of constituents, and (4) quaternary recovery of energy by combustion.4, 10 By 2020, solid waste streams should be diverted toward thermal and/or mechanical treatment and energy recovery in the EU. Primary recycling is practical when the main constituent can be separated from contaminants or stabilized against degradation during reprocessing and subsequent use. Primary recycling is only feasible with semi-clean scrap. Pre-consumer plastic waste is currently recycled to a greater extent than post-consumer packaging, as it is relatively pure and readily available in higher volumes. The volumes of post-consumer waste are up to five times larger than those generated in commerce and industry.11 Primary recycling can also involve the re-extrusion of post-consumer plastics. Recycling plastics waste mechanically involves a number of preparation steps. In some instances recovered plastic is used to make a new plastic product displacing all, or a proportion of virgin resin. Major challenges are immiscibility between recyclate and virgin polymer, degradation of recyclate due to various stresses during prior processing and use, and differences in processing requirements. Cellulose nanofibril (CNF), also referred to as nanocellulose, is one of the most promising candidate for use as a sustainable barrier material in packaging industry. J Appl Polym Sci, 2012 The growing demands to substitute petroleum-based products have increased the focus on biopolymers or biopolymers composites. Biodegradable polymers like poly(lactic acid) (PLA), a corn-based polymer, have been the subject of many studies during the past decade.1-3 And it is a polymer of lactic acid and commonly produced by ring-opening polymerization of the cyclic lactide dimer.4 PLA provides good strength and easy process ability with perfect degradable in most products. However, poor heat distortion temperature (HDT) and other low physical properties of PLA limit its applications.2, 3
Taking into consideration differences in composition and experimental methodology, the annealed HDT values are comparable with literature. Nagarajan et al. conducted studies with PLA and LAK, finding that a 1 wt% loading of LAK and exposure to a heated injection mold at 90 °C for 60 s resulted in an HDT of 65 °C [71]. More substantial changes in HDT (>85 °C) have been recorded for higher mold temperatures exceeding 110 °C [71]; however, such mold conditions can compromise the mechanical properties of the material as was observed for the annealing temperature of 120 °C in this work (Figs. 8 and 10). In addition to being derived from bio-based, renewable materials, PLA is also considered to be biodegradable, under certain conditions. The hydrolytic degradation behaviour of PLA is strongly dependent on parameters such as molecular weight, crystallinity, geometry, and surrounding environment (temperature, moisture, pH, presence of micro-organisms, etc) [72]. Given the influence of crystallinity on degradation behaviour (Fig. 2), it is of interest to investigate the effects of higher crystallinity on the degradation of PLA. In this section we investigate the effect of annealing at 100 °C on the long-term hydrolytic degradation profile of neat and modified PLA. Fig. 12 shows the mass loss of the PLA samples as a function of degradation time. All samples show the same principal erosion behaviour; the matrices start to lose mass after an induction period of minimal mass loss. However, the time at which mass loss sets in is quite different between the compression molded and annealed samples. The original PLA sample showed an initial period of minimal mass loss of about 70 days, followed by rapid mass loss toward the end of the degradation period. The delay in the onset of mass loss coupled with immediate and rapid loss in molecular weight was attributed to a bulk erosion mechanism that is prevalent in these samples [38].
Figure 12 shows the heat deflection temperature (HDT) of PLA and the polymer blends. PLA showed an HDT of around 53°C, a value close to that reported in the literature.91 Incorporating 30% AES into the PLA matrix did not increase the HDT, producing a similar value of 52.6°C. Although the acrylonitrile in the AES molecular structure often confers thermal and chemical resistance, it did not improve HDT. Therefore, the structural stability of the PLA matrix was maintained in the PLA/AES blend. Similarly, the 0.2 phr DCP did not improve the HDT of the PLA/AES/DCP blend. In the 0.4-1 phr DCP range, the HDT results of the PLA/AES/DCP blends stabilized between 53.2 and 53.8°C, a minor and insignificant improvement. Even though the degree of crosslinking increased in PLA/AES/DCP blends, it could not significantly increment the HDT. The annealed PLAT, PL/AEST, and PLA/AES/DCPT samples presented an increment of around 11°C in HDT. This behavior suggests that PLA and the polymer blends gained structural stability upon annealing, explained by the higher degree of crystallinity shown in XRD and DSC. The effect of crosslinking on PLA/AES/DCPT blends was insignificant, bearing that the HDT of all samples was within the margins of experimental error. The most prominent factor positively influencing HDT was the development of higher crystallinity in the PLA matrix. The HDT results of the PLA/AES/DCP blends are of technological relevance, especially for the composition containing 0.8 phr of DCP that retained a high impact strength. For the first time in the literature, AES has been applied as an impact modifier to PLA under the combined effect of the crosslinking and annealing heat treatment. The direct addition of AES improved PLA's ductility and impact strength, possibly due to polar interactions. Crosslinking increased proportionally to the DCP content used in PLA/AES blends, as evidenced by torque rheometry, resulting in higher molecular entanglement in the PLA/AES/DCP blends, increased viscosity, and reduced fluidity according to MFI. However, the 0.2 DCP could not effectively crosslink the PLA/AES blends, giving similar results to the non-crosslinked base system. Adding 0.8 phr of DCP maximized the impact strength and elongation at break, with gains of 505.6% and 264.8%, respectively, compared to PLA. From the standpoint of annealing, FTIR and XRD showed the formation of crystalline materials for PLA and the polymer blends. The infrared spectra presented bands at 1208 and 921 cm−1, evidencing a high degree of crystallinity and the formation of large crystals, which had a deleterious effect on impact strength and elongation at break. Heat deflection temperature (HDT) is important for materials because it determines the highest temperature a material can withstand before deformation.7 It is well known that PLA exhibits rather low HDT (∼55 °C) and the addition of PLA normally leads to a decrease of HDT of blends.8 In this study, the addition of 35% PLA did not weaken the HDT of PHBV dramatically. The binary blend exhibits a rather high HDT of ∼135 °C (similar value to pure PHBV), as shown in Fig. 3. This mainly resulted from the high crystallinity of PHBV in the blend. As expected, the addition of thermoplastic elastomer, PPC, resulted in reduction of HDT of the binary blends. The HDT reduced more with increasing PPC content, from 100 °C (20% PPC) to 72 °C (40% PPC). The HDT of the flexible sample (PLA-PHBV-PPC (20:40:40)) with 40% PPC was much higher than that of pure PLA, which will benefit the application of this biopolymer blend at higher temperature. In summary, the biodegradable blends can be tailored to form stiffness-HDT-toughness balanced materials by adjusting the composition ratios appropriately. With 40% PPC added, the ternary blends of PLA-PHBV-PPC (20:40:40) exhibited high stiffness with modulus of 2.7 GPa, acceptable HDT of 72 °C and high flexibility with elongation at break of 215%. The designed ternary blend (PLA-PHBV-PPC (20:40:40)) is expected to be used in different applications to substitute for petroleum-based plastics. To reveal the mechanism behind the thermal-mechanical performance of ternary blends, the crystallization, thermal degradation, and morphology were evaluated and analysed and are discussed in the following sections. Because of the slow crystallization rate, PLA exhibits cold crystallization in the following heating cycles, as shown in Fig. 5(b). The cold crystallization peak at 110 °C for PLA disappeared in the ternary blends, indicating that the crystallization rate of PLA had been improved with the addition of PHBV and PPC. If there is sufficient chain and surface mobility, as seen in binary44 and ternary blends,26 PHBV can act as nucleating centres to enhance PLA crystallization. Specifically, the phase interface has a strong effect in determining nucleation enhancement.44 The interface between phase domains must be taken into account in order to properly evaluate rate of crystallization in melt blended polymers.45,46 Differing terminal and bulk biopolymer functionality of small molecules that contain an abundance of shorter chain ends encourages free mobility of biopolymer chains to the interface, as well as being oriented, where localized alignment could promote crystalline growth.45,47,48

PLA is a cornstarch-based biodegradable polymer and exhibits mechanical properties comparable to those of polystyrene. However, PLA shows poor heat resistance with a heat deflection temperature (HDT) of around 50-60 °C. Though some grades of PLA are semi-crystalline, they generally crystallize slowly during processing, resulting in PLA products of low crystallinity [1], [2], [3], [4]. Therefore, HDT is largely dictated by the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PLA. The low HDT limits the current applications of PLA to those disposable goods that do not require high heat resistance. Apparently, it is essential to enhance the HDT of PLA to expand its applications at elevated temperatures [5]. Various methods have been explored to improve the HDT of PLA. One method is to incorporate heat-resistant reinforcing fillers into PLA to increase the HDT. Additions of wood fiber [6], [8], glass fiber [7], cellulose fiber [9], wheat straw [10], [11], corn stover and soy stalks [11] to PLA, were all noted to increase HDT; however, the improvement in HDT is limited (within 20 °C). Another method is to add a nucleating agent to increase the crystallinity and hence improve the heat resistance of PLA. Talc [12], montmorillonite [13], and bismaleimide [14] were studied as nucleating agents for PLA, and behaved differently in improving the HDT of PLA. While addition of 9.1 wt% talc brought about an increase of 1 °C in the HDT of PLA [12], incorporation of 8 wt% montmorillonite to PLA resulted in an increase of 28 °C in HDT [13]. A further increment is limited mainly due to aggregation of the nucleating agents.
Shih and Huang8 showed that the heat deflection temperature (HDT) for neat PLA was 62°C, and it was increased to 130°C, when PLA was reinforced with banana fibers. This finding can however not be supported by the results in the present study, which shows that the thermal sensitivity of the mechanical properties of PLA is not improved by reinforcement with natural fibers, only the elastic modulus and maximum stress of the PLA composites are at a higher level, due to the reinforcement effect of the fibers. From this study it is observed that the temperature impact is seen gradually, rather than taking place at a well-defined temperature interval. The HDT and the glass transition temperature cannot be used as the sole thermal sensitivity parameters for determining the gradual change in mechanical properties of polymers and composites. As already mentioned, the results show that the elastic modulus for neat PLA does not change at temperatures from 5 to 45°C, whereas the elastic modulus of the jute/PLA composite is reduced gradually in the same temperature interval. This points toward that the reinforcement efficiency of the jute fibers changes as a function of temperature. The cell wall of jute fibers is consisting of cellulose, lignin and hemicellulose, which all have glass transition temperatures well above 100°C.16 In addition, a previous study of jute fiber composites17 estimated that the elastic modulus of the fibers barely changes within the temperature range used in present study. Thus, based on these previous findings, it is indicated that the reduction of the elastic modulus seen for the jute/PLA composite, but not seen for neat PLA, are not caused by the fibers themselves. Instead, it is indicated that the reinforcement efficiency of the fibers is reduced due to changes in the interaction between matrix and fibers within the composite. Even though the matrix sustains a constant elastic modulus, the ability of the matrix to transfer the forces to the fibers is apparently reduced when the temperature is increased. To validate this hypothesis, further investigations are needed of the thermal induced change of interface bonding properties in natural fiber composites with biopolymeric matrices. AbstractInjectable biodegradable copolymer hydrogels, which exhibit temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition, have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials such as drug delivery, cell implantation, and tissue engineering. These injectable hydrogels can be implanted in the human body with minimal surgical invasion. Temperature-responsive gelling copolymers usually possess block- and/or branched architectures and amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as polylactide, poly(lactide-co-glycolide), poly(ε-caprolactone), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and biocompatibility. Copolymers of PEG with other hydrophobic polymers such as polypeptides, polydepsipeptides have also been recently reported as injectable hydrogels. IntroductionIn situ gel forming polymer systems have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials for minimally invasive therapy [1], [2], [3]. In particular, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers, which show sol-to-gel transition between room temperature and body temperature upon heating, are expected to be useful for injectable polymer gel (IPG) systems in biomedical applications. These polymer solutions are in sol state in the syringe at room temperature and become gel in situ after injection into the body, without requiring any toxic cross-linkers. Such systems can easily entrap pharmaceutical agents or cells and form a depot by a simple syringe injection at a target site, where the depots acts as sustained drug delivery devices or a cell-growing scaffolds for tissue engineering [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. To exhibit a temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition in aqueous solutions, such polymers should possess amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance [11]. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments of thermo-gelling polymers due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as poly(l-lactide) (PLLA), poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), poly(dl-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and relatively good biocompatibility [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Since pioneering research on biodegradable IPG systems using triblock copolymer of PEG and PLLA, PEG-b-PLLA-b-PEG, by Kim et al. in 1997 [11], many kinds of biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers have been developed by combining PEG and aliphatic polyesters with various molecular architectures including linear-type and star-shape block as well as graft topologies [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. In addition, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers containing amino acids as building blocks of the hydrophobic segments have been recently developed [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. Biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers reported can be categorized into block copolymers including linear-type and/or star-shaped diblock, triblock, and multiblock architectures, and graft copolymers from the view point of molecular architectures, as summarized in Table 1. These copolymers exhibits various properties based on the molecular architectures and nature of the components.In this article, brief history and recent advances in biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers as IPGs are reviewed especially focusing on the relationship between polymer structure and their properties. Moreover, the applications of these IPGs for biomedical use such as DDS and tissue engineering are also reviewed.

Synthetic polymer-based injectable hydrogels including triblock copolymers consisting of biodegradable poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), which is bioinert and has relatively high biocompatibility,11 showed a thermal responsive sol-gel transition.12, 13 Therefore, triblock (PEG-PLLA-PEG) copolymers are injectable at 45 °C and form a gel at body temperature (37 °C).12, 13 However, a high concentration of the degradation products due to hydrolysis exhibits cytotoxicity.14 Alternately, naturally derived polymers extracted from animals or plants have higher biocompatibility. Collagen and gelatin, a denatured collagen, are widely studied for tissue engineering because of their good biocompatibility and biodegradability. Cells cultured with the injectable hydrogel composed of carbohydrazide-modified gelatin and aldehyde-modified hyaluronic acid showed excellent viability, migration, and angiogenic properties, but this hydrogel has a relatively low storage modulus compared with that of soft tissues and organs.15 Moreover, injectable hydrogels composed of two types of alginate derivatives, benzylamino tetrazine or norbornene-modified alginate, abbreviated as Alg-T and Alg-N, respectively, have been reported.16 Alg-T and Alg-N react through tetrazine-norbornene click chemistry and can form a hydrogel under the skin. This phenomenon could be due to the hexanoyl group inducing weak inflammation in the tissue, resulting in the secretion of inflammatory cytokines or growth factors.19 We hypothesized that the hydrophobic group induces weak inflammation and promotes protease secretion, which enhances degradation of the ApGltn network and allows cells to migrate into the hydrogel.
