In situ forming hydrogels are systems responsive to the environmental stimuli, such as change of temperature, pH, photo intensity, ionic strength, etc.14, 15 They have been divided into two types, one is chemical in situ gels and the other is physical in situ gels. Chemical in situ gels, also called “permanent” gels, are hydrogels containing covalently cross-linked networks. They are irreversible polymeric networks via the use of cross-linkers or enzymes.16 Physical in situ gels, or “reversible” gels, are those networks held together by molecular entanglements and secondary forces such as hydrogen bonding, ionic, hydrophobic forces.17, 18 Usually these weak and reversible bonds formation depends on external stimulation to form cross-linking, which makes temperature, pH, lights, or ions sensitive reversible hydrogels possible.19-22 In situ delivery systems have an upper hand compared with conventional systems, because they take longer time for in situ system to finish releasing drug at targeted site. Particularly, a temperature responsive hydrogel, namely thermogel, is a reversible physical cross-linking system, forming upon heating up temperature until critical temperature. The properties of thermogel offer opportunities in therapeutic application because of several reasons.23-25 An injectable thermogel system has simplicity of pharmaceutical formulation by mixing of drug below sol-gel transition temperature. Large scale surgery for implantation is not needed. After injection, body temperature will stimulate sol-gel transition, viscous solution will change into a drug delivery depot. The high percentage water content makes thermogel highly competitive with the injection site. Also, peptides are kept at low temperature before application, which makes sure no denaturalization due to organic solvent interaction or dissolution triggered by high temperature. Currently, there are only two types of commercial polymeric thermoresponsive hydrogel products available in the market. One is Poloxamer, and the other is poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAAm). When using Poloxamer based hydrogel, two conditions, polymer critical micelle concentration (CMC) and critical micelle temperature (CMT), must be reached to promote sol-gel transition. For Poloxamer, it includes Amphipathic Poloxamer and Pluronic F127. Amphipathic Poloxamer, a FDA-approved triblock polymer, composes of hydrophobic poly(ethylene oxide) and hydrophilic poly(propylene oxide) components.26 Hydrogel based on this has been widely used in both therapeutic and consumer applications. Although Amphipathic Poloxamer has proven to be biocompatible and able to perform drug delivery,27 degradation of it based hydrogels does not support sustainable process. The degradation period, 4 h, has severely limited targeted or long-termed drug release application.12 Meanwhile, Pluronic F127, with CMT of human body temperature (37 °C) and longer degradation period, has higher CMC, which limits its bioapplications. Commercial PNIPAAm is another typical amphipathic thermoresponsive polymer, which was first synthesized in the 1950s.28-30 Hydrogel based on this can undergo reversible phase change by changing the temperature of aqueous environment. However, poor mechanical and nonbiodegradable properties, teratogenicity and carcinogenicity of its residual monomers, and toxicity of degradation products of isopropyl amine limit its biomedical applications.31-34 After drug delivery process, PNIPAAm based hydrogel needs to be removed by extra surgery, which goes against the advantage of thermogel by avoiding surgery on patients and will not bring convenience and ease to therapeutic application. Being one of the earliest and most studied biomaterials, polyester has its irreplaceable place among all polymer materials.35-41 Compared with other biomaterials, polyester has three great advantages-biodegradation, biocompatibility, and synthetic versatility.42-48 The application of hydrogel based on this as scaffold for cell transplantation has already benefitted thousands of people every year.49 Being the only biodegradable polymer with high molecular weight, polyester is able to undergo hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation. This is due to its highly hydrolysable ester linkages in the polymer backbone and good fitness to enzyme's active site, respectively.24, 41, 50-52 Controllable degradation gives polyester based hydrogel the advantage of application in periodic and targeted drug release.53 The end result of degradation also brings no harm to human body as it will be transformed into carbon dioxide and water, released out of human body by metabolism eventually. Besides, human body contains 70% of water and it is important for any material used in human body to also largely contain water to achieve good biocompatibility. Polyester based hydrogel is able to trap large amount of water in aqueous environments including body fluids. Another uniqueness of polyester based biodegradable hydrogel is its synthetic versatility, including polycondensation of combinations of diols and dicarboxylic acids, self-polycondensation of hydrogel acids, and ring-opening polymerization of lactones and lactides.54, 55 An ideal polymeric thermogelling system for biomedical application should have near physiologically temperature responsive range, reasonable biodegradation rate, enough mechanical strength, great biocompatibility, good targeting specificity in therapeutic delivery, and synthetic versatility for property tuning. According to the literature, polyester based thermogelling system is one of the best candidates to satisfy most requirements. Hence, in this review, the polyester based thermogelling systems are described and classified by different components. Moreover, their applications in biomedical area including drug delivery and tissue engineering are also introduced and discussed. PLA based biopolymer materials have been very popular among new biomedical materials.35, 43, 47, 48 It has great biocompatibility and biodegradability for medical use, besides, it is also a sustainable material, a good alternative to replace conventional fossil fuel based polymers.47 The constitutional unit of PLA is lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid, HOCH3CHCOOH), which is a chiral molecule existing as two enantiomers, l-lactic acid and d-lactic acid. As there are two stereocenters of lactic acid monomer, a large number of different combinations of chains and crystal structures have been discovered.42 The polymorphism of PLA gives scientists freedom to blend different PLA isomers and adjust their composition ratios to get modulation of the crystallinity for any specific application. Among them, stereoisomerism has been extensively studied for determining the physicochemical properties of PLA. Stereocomplexes of poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) and poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA) are reported, and they are highly crystalline isotactic polymers. The investigation shows that they have better physical properties than enantiomeric counterparts, poly(d,l-lactic acid) (PDLLA), which is amorphous atactic polymer, such as higher melting point, stronger mechanical properties.47, 42 Besides, thermoreversible sol-gel transition is made possible by stereocomplexes, such as their respective copolymers with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG).47
The sol-gel transition time of the SF-GMA-EPL hydrogels was also investigated using rheology analysis to determine the point at which the pre-hydrogel solution started to form a hydrogel when exposed to UV light. At a constant strain of 0.1% and frequency of 1 rad s−1, the time required for sol-gel transition was determined as 1 s, 2 s, and 3 s for SF-GMA(L)-EPL, SF-GMA(M)-EPL and SF-GMA(H)-EPL, respectively (figure 10(C)). When a hydrogel undergoes a sol-gel transition in seconds, it becomes suitable for use as an injectable hydrogel. A previous study investigated the potential of a hydrogel composed of Pluronic F127-bis-(acryloyloxy acetate) and methacrylated hyaluronic acid as an injectable hydrogel for wound healing purposes. The study focused on evaluating the therapeutic effects of the hydrogel, which demonstrated a rapid transition to a gel state within a short duration of 2 s [91]. Thus, all the SF-GMA-EPL hydrogel formulations reported in this study exhibited promising outcomes in promoting wound healing. In this study, as a combination of SF-GMA and EPL-GMA, three novel SF-GMA-EPL hydrogels were developed. These hydrogels incorporating 20% EPL-GMA demonstrated strong activity against P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae, and moderate activity against MRSA. On the hydrogels, growth of Hs68 and Balb/3t3 cells was supported for 21 d, demonstrating that this material can promote long-term cell attachment and proliferation. Regarding antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effectiveness, the hydrogels have a 69%-74% •OH radical scavenging ability and a 60% ability to remove LPS. Slow and gradual degradation, non-cytotoxicity of the degradation products, porous internal morphology, moderate swelling behavior, and elastomeric properties of the hydrogels were also determined. Because of its favorable biological and physical properties, the SF-GMA-EPL hydrogels hold great potential for a wide range of biomedical applications, including wound healing, tissue engineering, and drug delivery

In situ injectable hydrogels can be formed by either chemical or physical crosslinking methods. Chemically crosslinked hydrogels, prepared through photopolymerization [4], disulfide bond formation [5], or reaction between thiols and acrylate or sulfones [5], undergo significant volume changes during the phase transition. In contrast to chemical hydrogels, physically crosslinked hydrogels, formed by the self-assembly of polymers in response to environmental stimuli (for example, temperature, pH, or both) display sol-gel transitions without marked volume changes. The hydrogels systems are relatively low viscosity aqueous solutions (sol state) prior to injection, but rapidly convert into a gel under physiological conditions post-injection [1], [6], [7]. Physical hydrogels have several advantages over chemical hydrogels, because they do not require photo irradiation, use of organic solvents or crosslinking agents, and do not release heat at the gelation site, which may denature incorporated proteins and damage embedded cells and surrounding tissues. Thus, the physical systems have recently attracted increased attention. For use in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering, hydrogels should be low-viscosity solutions (free-flowing) prior to subcutaneous injection, and should rapidly gel in the human body, where ultimate degradation of the hydrogels is desired. Injectable hydrogels that are sensitive to temperature are useful for both in vitro and in vivo applications, because temperature control is generally easy. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)/Polyester copolymers, as an injectable biodegradable temperature-sensitive physically crosslinked hydrogel, of hydrophilic biocompatible PEG with biodegradable biocompatible aliphatic polyesters, for example polylactide (PLA) [8], [9], poly(d,l-lactic acid-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [10], [11], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [12], [13], or poly[(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate] (PHB) [14], have received increasing attention as promising biomaterials. Among those thermogelling systems, block copolymers of PLGA and PEG are very important owing to their high adjustability of biodegradation and good properties to encapsulate and release biological substances [15], [16], [17], [18]. However, the appropriate composition region, such as block ratio and block length, is narrow, which limits its application to a large extent. Recently, Yu’ group has found a facile approach to prepare a thermogelling system by simply blending two similar block copolymers with different block ratios [19], [20]. One specimen was water-soluble and the other was just a precipitate in a broad temperature region. Although neither specimen possessed the thermogelling property, the aqueous solution of the copolymer mixture with a certain mix ratio showed a reversible sol-gel transition with the increase of temperature. On the basis of this good idea, thermogelling property of mixed star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels is investigated by us in order to develop applications of pure star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels. Our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers for designing injectable biomaterials. In this paper, a new kind of copolymer, 3-arm or 4-arm star-shaped poly(d,l-lactic-co-glycolic acid)-b-methoxy poly(ethylene glycol)(3sPLGA-mPEG or 4sPLGA-mPEG), is synthesized via the arm-first method rather than the core-first method reported in the literature [21], [22], [23]. We will present a systematic study of sol-gel transition behavior, micellization behavior and degradation behavior of the two-component thermogelling mixture and examine their in vitro and in vivo biocompatibility. Comparing with plenty of reports of biodegradable biomaterials, the detailed research of the degradation profiles of injectable temperature-sensitive hydrogels, particularly of physical hydrogels, is very limited. As such, our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers and puts forward a new strategy to design injectable biomaterials.
First published on 4th August 2025 Herein, we report the design and synthesis of bio-degradable porous polyurethane hydrogels by a green, solvent-free, one-pot technique that can withstand physiological mechanical loads and aid in tissue regeneration. The hydrophilic/hydrophobic nature of the hydrogel was tuned using diols such as polycaprolactone diol (PCL) and polycarbonate diol (PCD), in combination with polyethylene glycol (PEG, MW ≈ 4000 g mol−1), 4,4′-methylene bis(cyclohexyl isocyanate) (H12MDI) and hexanetriol (HT), which served as crosslinking agents. The structural characterizations of the hydrogels were performed using FT-IR as well as 1H and 13C high resolution magic angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance (HR-MAS) spectroscopy. The utilization of various diols in the synthesis of the hydrogels enabled precise control over crystallinity, pore sizes, and customization of mechanical and degradation properties. These hydrogels exhibited tensile strength in the range of 0.22-1.48 MPa, while their compressive strength varied from 0.92 to 29.3 MPa. In vitro degradation profiles in the presence and absence of the enzyme Amano lipase PS revealed that the degradation process is contingent upon the specific diol present in the hydrogel. Furthermore, preliminary in vitro biological experiments confirmed the biocompatibility of the gels, indicating their potential as suitable substrates for drug delivery applications. This diverse library of gels can be shaped into specific forms, highlighting their promising applications as scaffolds and implants in drug delivery systems and tissue engineering. Even though hydrogels have received high acceptance for biomedical applications, the requirement of extreme load-bearing capability of hydrogels similar to that of tissues has challenged researchers to engineer hydrogels that are tough and have a capability akin to tissue's that can withstand physiological mechanical loads. In contrast to natural hydrogel-like biological tissues, such as cartilage, tendons, and muscles, which exhibit remarkable mechanical toughness, conventional hydrogels are often brittle and demonstrate inadequate mechanical performance. This characteristic poses a challenge for their application as effective biomaterials, highlighting the need for advancements in hydrogel technology to improve their mechanical properties and broaden their usability in biomedical applications. This has attracted great interest in the development of polyurethane-based hydrogels because of their excellent biocompatibility, chemical versatility, and superior mechanical properties.24-26 Besides other applications in adhesives, coatings, synthetic leather, etc., polyurethanes (PUs) have been extensively investigated for biomedical applications, including cardiovascular devices such as vascular prostheses, intra-aortic balloons, cardiac valves, membranes for dialysis, craniofacial reconstruction, and breast implants.27-32
Hydrogels have been applied in different industries, e.g., medicine, biomedical engineering, and agriculture, due to their high water absorption capacities. In agriculture, hydrogels have mainly been used for soil water retention,8, 9 as slow-release materials for fertilizer,10, 11 and heavy metal remediation.12 Thus, they have a wide utility in agriculture as soil amendments. However, there has been a debate on the pros and cons of using synthetic and bio-based hydrogels as amendments regarding their biodegrability. Despite the arguments supporting a shift to bio-based hydrogels (i.e., hydrogels made from natural polymers), few/no studies have compared the biodegradability of synthetic (i.e., hydrogels made from synthetic polymers) and bio-based hydrogels in agricultural soils. Biodegradation refers to a type of degradation catalyzed by microorganisms leading to the reduction of organic material into carbon, CO2, water, and new microbial biomass.13 Biodegradability is thus the property of a material that allows the materials to undergo biodegradation. Biodegradable materials are organic (i.e., plant and animal matter), derived from living organisms or synthetic materials similar to plants and animals, so microorganisms can act on them.14 According to Lucas et al.,15 biodegradation can be divided into four main stages: biodeterioration, biofragmentation, assimilation, and mineralization. Biodeterioration occurs when microbial communities, other decomposers, and/or abiotic factors fragment biodegradable materials into smaller pieces.15 Biofragmentation involves the cleavage of polymeric molecules, reducing their molecular weights and generating oligomers, dimers, and monomers.15 Assimilation is when energy, new biomass, and other primary and secondary metabolites are produced in the cytoplasm of microorganisms. Finally, mineralization involves the oxidation of simple and complex metabolites into CO2, N2, CH4, and H2O in the environment.15 Scientists are interested in how polymers biodegrade in the soil as the byproducts of degradation have implications for the environment. The structure of carbon bonds in materials entering the soil determines the rate at which those materials will be decomposed into soil organic matter. In the same way, the type of carbon bonds in the backbone material used to synthesize a hydrogel will determine the rate at which it biodegrades in soil, if it degrades at all. For example, carbohydrates have linear, branched chains, making them easy to break down by soil microbes16 compared to lignin with recalcitrant carbon bonds. Some researchers have synthesized biodegradable hydrogels by cross-linking cellulose derivatives using difunctional molecules as cross-linkers capable of binding different polymers into three-dimensional hydrophilic networks.17 By modifying hydrogels with natural polymers, new, more biodegradable materials may be produced.18
Implanted hydrogels should ideally have tunable biodegradation kinetics profiles to either match the rate of neo-tissue regeneration,[59] or to degrade in a controlled manner after completion of their initial objective (i.e., imaging, drug delivery).[60, 61] To evaluate the biodegradation properties of Si-HA hydrogels, various gel formulations (DS = 13.5-57.7%) were injected in the subcutis of immunocompetent mice under aseptic conditions, and submitted to two volume assessment methods after 7 and 21 d. This model is particularly useful to obtain general information on degradation rates and inflammatory response following hydrogel injection, in anticipation of future applications in vascularized tissues.[62] As a first semiquantitative approach, a daily palpation test was performed to assess the in vivo erosion of hydrogels over time (Figure 4A,C). On day 0, all the formulations tested led to gels that could be manually detected, confirming the successful in situ formation of Si-HA gels. For a DS of 13.5%, gels could no longer be detected by palpation after 4-14 days postinjection (Figure 4B), indicating rapid biodegradation in agreement with the limited stability observed in vitro. Increasing the DS to 21.8% yielded more stable hydrogels in vivo, with first signs of biodegradation occurring after 14 d. Gels from highly silanized components (i.e., 40.0% and 57.7%) were still intact after 21 d. To further assess their in vivo behavior, gels were explanted for μCT analysis at 1 and 3 weeks after injection (Figure 4D). The volume of explanted samples after 7 and 21 d was calculated and compared to the initially injected volume of 250 µL. Low silanized HA (DS = 13.5%) showed a volume reduction of 23.5% ± 7.8% after 7 d, and were completely degraded after 21 d, in agreement with the palpation-based assessment method. Silanized HA with DS of 21.8% and 40.0%, showed continuous swelling in vivo, reaching 253% ± 12% and 163% ± 56% after 21 d, respectively. On the contrary, highly silanized HA (DS = 57.7%) did not significantly swell or degrade over the same time period. These results show a tendency similar to that of the in vitro experiments, and demonstrate that the crosslink density determines the in vivo swelling and degradation behavior of Si-HA gels. Interestingly, as compared to in vitro, Si-HA from DS of 21.8% and 40.0% swelled in vivo by a factor of 2.2 and 1.4, respectively. This discrepancy may be attributed to the gelation of Si-HA gels that need a few hours to reach completion (Figure S3, Supporting Information), which may facilitate initial fluid adsorption. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the use of μCT for the rapid evaluation of the volume of explanted hydrogels. This strategy is easy to implement, and allows a precise determination of hydrogel volume. However, it also requires that the hydrogel does not initially contain proteins negatively stained by the opacifying agent (e.g., fibrins, collagens). Altogether, these results demonstrate that the biodegradation rate and swelling profile of in situ forming Si-HA hydrogels can be tuned by controlling the crosslink density. As a final characterization step, we evaluated the biocompatibility of Si-HA hydrogels following in vivo implantation. At 7 and 21 d after hydrogel implantation, the inflammatory response was evaluated by histomorphometric analyses (i.e., type of infiltrate, cell counting, measures of the periprosthetic tissue thickness) on hematoxylin, eosin and Safran (HES)-stained samples. All Si-HA formulations triggered an initial inflammatory response upon injection, characterized at day 7 by a cell population composed of fibroblasts, macrophages, and a few lymphocytes[63] (Figure 5A; and Figure S6, Supporting Information). Similar cell densities (≈400 cells per Mpixel2) were observed for all injected formulations (Figure 5B), as well as a thick, but loose, fibroinflammatory capsule (from 64 to 153 µm, for DS = 40.0% and 21.8%) surrounding the materials (Figure 5C). This type of initial inflammatory response is commonly reported for implanted biomaterials, and may result from the injury caused by the injection procedure.[63-65] Infiltrated cells were also noticed within Si-HA gels with DS of 13.5% and 21.8%, whereas highly silanized HA (DS = 40.0% and 57.7%) showed limited to no cell infiltration. Consistent with these observations, Ehrbar et al. noticed in vivo cell infiltration in low-density polyethylene glycol gels, which was otherwise inhibited in stiffer networks.[66] Si-HA gels have a theoretical mesh size smaller than the typical diameter of a cell (i.e., 1-20 µm), and result from the formation of irreversible covalent bonds. Thus, cell infiltration is probably driven by the erosion mechanism of the gel, as previously observed for similar systems.[67] In low-silanized gels, rapid enzyme and water uptake and subsequent bulk erosion of the gel occurs, facilitating cell infiltration. Conversely, the limited diffusivity of highly silanized HA gels only allows for surface erosion, which ultimately impairs cell infiltration. After 21 d, no polymorphonuclear cells could be detected, indicative of a resorption of the acute phase and an absence of pyogenic infection.[64] No residual inflammation was observed in the fully-degraded samples (DS = 13.5%, Figure S5, Supporting Information), showing that a normal wound healing process occurred after Si-HA degradation. In samples where the hydrogel was still detectable after 21 d, a significant decrease in the peri-implant cell density (from 400 to 200 cells per Mpixel2) was observed, as well as a significant diminution (p < .0001) of the periprosthetic fibrous tissue. These results indicate a resorption of the initial inflammation caused by the injection, and highlight the biocompatibility of Si-HA gels. Interestingly, a newly secreted collagenous matrix was observed in the Si-HA gels with a DS of 21.8%, showing that cells are able to colonize the hydrogel. Further immunohistochemical detections of the pan-macrophage marker CD68 revealed the vast majority of infiltrated cells were macrophages, indicating their central role in inducing hydrogel degradation (Figure 5D; and Figure S4, Supporting Information). In the slow-degrading gels (DS = 40.0% and 57.7%), an absence of infiltrated cells was noticed and CD68+-macrophages only formed a thin layer around the implants. Some multinucleated giant cells were also visible, indicative of a foreign body reaction typically observed for slow-degrading materials.[68] In agreement with previous reports,[63, 69] our results suggest that the extent of the foreign body response is correlated to the degradation rate of the hydrogels, and thus to the crosslink density. Although beyond the scope of this article, further investigations of the macrophage polarization to a pro- (M1) or anti- (M2) inflammatory phenotype could be performed to elucidate how the interactions between the material and macrophages influence the inflammatory response. In this study, we successfully designed for the first time in situ forming Si-HA hydrogels using the hybrid inorganic-organic silanization chemistry. By tuning the DS and MW of Si-HA, we showed that single-polymer gels can be formed under physiological conditions of pH and temperature, with tunable gelation time and stiffness. We confirmed the cytocompatibility of Si-HA hydrogels with 3 different cell types (i.e., murine L929 fibroblasts, human BMSCs, and ASCs), and demonstrated their in situ forming ability and biocompatibility. We finally showed that their degradation profiles can be tuned from days to weeks in vivo. Future experiments should evaluate the ability of Si-HA gels to favor tissue regeneration in tissue engineering applications.

IntroductionIn situ gel forming polymer systems have recently drawn much attention as promising biomedical materials for minimally invasive therapy [1], [2], [3]. In particular, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers, which show sol-to-gel transition between room temperature and body temperature upon heating, are expected to be useful for injectable polymer gel (IPG) systems in biomedical applications. These polymer solutions are in sol state in the syringe at room temperature and become gel in situ after injection into the body, without requiring any toxic cross-linkers. Such systems can easily entrap pharmaceutical agents or cells and form a depot by a simple syringe injection at a target site, where the depots acts as sustained drug delivery devices or a cell-growing scaffolds for tissue engineering [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. To exhibit a temperature-responsive sol-to-gel transition in aqueous solutions, such polymers should possess amphiphilicity with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance [11]. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has typically been used as hydrophilic segments of thermo-gelling polymers due to its biocompatibility and temperature-dependent dehydration nature. Aliphatic polyesters such as poly(l-lactide) (PLLA), poly(d-lactide) (PDLA), poly(dl-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and their modified copolymers have been used as hydrophobic segments based on their biodegradability and relatively good biocompatibility [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].Since pioneering research on biodegradable IPG systems using triblock copolymer of PEG and PLLA, PEG-b-PLLA-b-PEG, by Kim et al. in 1997 [11], many kinds of biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers have been developed by combining PEG and aliphatic polyesters with various molecular architectures including linear-type and star-shape block as well as graft topologies [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. In addition, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers containing amino acids as building blocks of the hydrophobic segments have been recently developed [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. Biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers reported can be categorized into block copolymers including linear-type and/or star-shaped diblock, triblock, and multiblock architectures, and graft copolymers from the view point of molecular architectures, as summarized in Table 1. These copolymers exhibits various properties based on the molecular architectures and nature of the components.In this article, brief history and recent advances in biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers as IPGs are reviewed especially focusing on the relationship between polymer structure and their properties. Moreover, the applications of these IPGs for biomedical use such as DDS and tissue engineering are also reviewed. Since pioneering research on biodegradable IPG systems using triblock copolymer of PEG and PLLA, PEG-b-PLLA-b-PEG, by Kim et al. in 1997 [11], many kinds of biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers have been developed by combining PEG and aliphatic polyesters with various molecular architectures including linear-type and star-shape block as well as graft topologies [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. In addition, biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers containing amino acids as building blocks of the hydrophobic segments have been recently developed [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. Biodegradable thermo-gelling polymers reported can be categorized into block copolymers including linear-type and/or star-shaped diblock, triblock, and multiblock architectures, and graft copolymers from the view point of molecular architectures, as summarized in Table 1. These copolymers exhibits various properties based on the molecular architectures and nature of the components.
Implanted hydrogels should ideally have tunable biodegradation kinetics profiles to either match the rate of neo-tissue regeneration,[59] or to degrade in a controlled manner after completion of their initial objective (i.e., imaging, drug delivery).[60, 61] To evaluate the biodegradation properties of Si-HA hydrogels, various gel formulations (DS = 13.5-57.7%) were injected in the subcutis of immunocompetent mice under aseptic conditions, and submitted to two volume assessment methods after 7 and 21 d. A novel approach to tissue regeneration is the use of injectable in situ crosslinkable hydrogels as a carrier for the delivery of therapeutic agents and cells [1], [2]. Less invasive injectable gels coupled with minimally invasive arthroscopic techniques are an attractive alternative to implantation of pre-formed polymers for treating irregularly shaped or inaccessible defects [3], [4], [5], [6]. Furthermore, diffusivity of nutrients [7], [8] and proteins [9], [10] in hydrogels is 4-5 orders of magnitude higher than solid polymers, thus providing a supportive matrix for differentiation, proliferation, and maturation of seeded cells into the desired tissue [11]. In addition, hydrogels can be reinforced with calcium phosphate nanoparticles to produce injectable cements for hard tissue applications [1], [12], [13]. Biodegradable polymers are widely used as a supportive carrier in tissue engineering and drug delivery [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Among them, poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is the most widely used biodegradable polymer because its degradation products (lactic and glycolic acid) are resorbed through metabolic pathways [19], [20]. PLGA and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) polymers have been copolymerized with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) to produce amphiphilic macromers that form thermally-induced physical gels [21], [22], [23]. Studies concerning the effect of macromer structure on water content and modulus [22], [24] demonstrate that physically crosslinked gels are significantly weaker than those that are chemically crosslinked [25], [26], limiting them for use in non-load bearing biomedical applications. In addition, degradability of chemically-crosslinked gels can be controlled independent of gelation by the molecular weight and ratio of hydrophobic/hydrophilic domains [21], [27], [28]. To control the hydrogel water content (and therefore mechanical strength), degradation rate and the rate of crosslinking, our laboratory has previously developed a poly(lactide-co-ethylene oxide fumarate) (PLEOF) macromonomer consisting of low molecular weight poly(l-lactide) (LMW-PLA) and PEG blocks linked by unsaturated fumarate units [6], [26]. The water content of the PLEOF hydrogel could be adjusted by the ratio of hydrophilic PEG to hydrophobic PLA blocks and by PEG molecular weight [26]. Degradation rate of the network could be controlled by the ratio of PLA to PEG blocks or by the molecular weight of PLA segments [26]. However, due to steric hindrance of the fumarate groups along the chain and their lower reactivity (compared to acrylates and methacrylates) [26], [29], [30], the gelation kinetics depended strongly on UV initiator and small molecule monomer concentrations [26]. It is well established that the viability of cells encapsulated in synthetic gels is largely determined by the fraction of small-molecule initiators and monomers that cross the cell membrane [31], [32]. Terminal reactive groups at chain ends are less sterically hindered compared to those along the macromonomer chain. The reactivity of acrylates is an order of magnitude higher than fumarates [6], [26], [33]. In addition, star macromonomers have lower shear viscosity than linear ones at the same molecular weight [34], resulting in the onset of gelation at higher conversions and a higher extent of crosslinking. We hypothesized that a multi-arm star amphiphilic poly(ethylene oxide-co-lactide-glycolide) based macromonomer each arm terminated with an acrylate group would significantly increase the rate of crosslinking, thus reducing the minimum required concentration of initiator/monomer to produce robust networks. The objective of this work was to synthesize a novel star poly(ethylene oxide-co-lactide-glycolide acrylate) (SPELGA) macromonomer and investigate the effect composition had on gelation kinetics and degradation of the hydrogels. In this work, SPELGA macromonomer was synthesized by ring-opening polymerization of lactide and glycolide monomers using hydrophilic pentaerythritol ethoxylate or poly(ethylene glycol) initiators, followed by acrylation of the chain ends with acryloyl chloride. The structure of the synthesized macromonomers was characterized by 1H-NMR and GPC. The kinetics of photopolymerization of the SPELGA macromonomers in aqueous solution was investigated by rheometry. The SPELGA hydrogels were characterized with respect to sol fraction, swelling and degradation.

Based on the provided context evidence, the 'sol-gel' transition in injectable biodegradable hydrogels refers to a **temperature-dependent physical transformation** where a polymer solution (sol) converts into a gel network upon exposure to physiological conditions. Key characteristics include:

1.  **Injectable Liquid State (Sol)**: The polymer exists as a free-flowing aqueous solution at or below room temperature, enabling syringe injection [1][3][4][6][7].
2.  **Gelation Triggered by Body Temperature**: Upon injection into the body (~37°C), the solution undergoes a reversible phase transition to form a semi-solid gel network *in situ* without requiring toxic chemical cross-linkers [1][3][4][6][7][13].
3.  **Physical Crosslinking Mechanism**: The transition is driven by physical interactions (e.g., hydrophobic associations, micelle formation/packing, molecular entanglements) rather than covalent bonds. This is facilitated by the amphiphilic nature of the polymers, typically composed of hydrophilic blocks (e.g., PEG) and biodegradable hydrophobic blocks (e.g., PLA, PLGA, PCL) [1][2][4][6][7][13].
4.  **Biomedical Function**: The resulting gel acts as a depot for sustained drug delivery or a scaffold for cell implantation and tissue engineering, providing structural support at the target site with minimal surgical invasion [1][3][4][6][7][13].

Typical thermogelled hydrogels include natural or seminatural polymers such as chitosan and gelatin and synthetic polymers like poloxamer 407. Qi et al. (69) have reported a kind of chitosan-heparin hydrogel, which is cross-linked with heparin by physical entanglement and electrostatic attraction. In this work, the sol precursor could transform to gel at 37 °C in 15 min. Additionally, Zhang et al. (70,71) reported a kind of 17β-estradiol heparin-poloxamer thermosensitive hydrogel, of which the viscosity suddenly increased at elevated temperature. This poloxamer hydrogel could form a gel state when heating to body temperature and turn to a sol state after cooling, as shown in Figure 2. Moreover, host-guest supramolecular hydrogels based on macrocyclic molecules such as cyclodextrin are also popular in the biomedical field. (64) Li et al. (72) described a hydrogel based on the self-assembly of inclusion between α-CD and PEO blocks in Pluronic and the aggregation of PPO blocks, which exhibited thixotropic and reversible properties and could be applied as injectable drug delivery system. However, due to the noncovalent and reversible nature of the cross-linkers in the polymer network, hydrogels formed by these weak interactions could be affected by temperature, pH, ionic strength, solvent composition, and the imposed mechanical stress, causing a burst release of encapsulant and further limiting their uses in endometrial repair. (73) Polymeric hydrogels formed by chemical cross-linking have also been developed for endometrium repair, in which the cross-linked networks are provided by the covalent bonds, forming the stronger and more stable hydrogels. Covalently bonded hydrogels are usually achieved by cross-linking the mixture of precursors in vitro, as shown in Figure 3. Samantha et al. (74) have modified the gelatin with methacrylic anhydride to synthesize methacrylate functionalized gelatin (GelMA). The precursor solution of GelMA was mixed with a photoinitiator, and then the hydrogel was obtained by the photopolymerization under UV light. Similarly, Cheng et al. (75) have prepared HA hydrogel by the method of photoinitiation, in which methacrylate modified HA was obtained by the reaction of HA and methacrylic anhydride. The encapsulation of therapeutic agent is also critical for the hydrogel delivery system, which is related to the cross-linking method of hydrogel. Figure 3 shows the general preparation process of hydrogel delivery system for endometrium repair. For covalent-cross-linked hydrogel, the incorporation of therapeutic agent by adsorption may be time-consuming and inefficient, while in situ loading of the therapeutic agent may lead to its inactivation during the cross-linking process. (76) Instead, the loading efficiency and content of therapeutic agent could be improved by promoting the interaction between therapeutic agent and hydrogel network. (77,78) For example, Wu et al. (77) reported a new drug encapsulation strategy to achieve the sustain release of small molecule ionic drug from hydrogel platform. In their strategy, arginine-based unsaturated poly(ester amides) (Arg-UPEAs) and alginate were introduced into the Pluronic hydrogel by UV photo-cross-linking method. The presence of polyelectrolytes improved the electrostatic interaction and affinity of ionic drugs with the hydrogel network. Furthermore, in situ loading of therapeutic agent is also attractive for the noncovalent cross-linked hydrogel. In this case, the therapeutic agent is uniformly mixed with the precursor solution and then encapsulated within the network matrix during the formation of the hydrogel. (31,74,79)
Orthogonally Crosslinked Gelatin‐Norbornene Hydrogels for Biomedical Applications For cell transplantation, a cell suspension is injected into the target site, such as the heart or ischemic limbs, to promote organ or tissue regeneration.1-4 However, the survival rate and retention time of injected cells are low because of the extruding of injected cells from the target site, lack of interaction with host tissue, and insufficient supply of oxygen and nutrients through host blood vessels.5-9 To overcome these challenges, injectable gels have been studied to promote the survival rate and prolong retention time of injected cells.10 The main components of these injectable hydrogels can be classified into three types: synthetic polymers, naturally derived polymers, and their hybrids. Synthetic polymer-based injectable hydrogels including triblock copolymers consisting of biodegradable poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), which is bioinert and has relatively high biocompatibility,11 showed a thermal responsive sol-gel transition.12, 13 Therefore, triblock (PEG-PLLA-PEG) copolymers are injectable at 45 °C and form a gel at body temperature (37 °C).12, 13 However, a high concentration of the degradation products due to hydrolysis exhibits cytotoxicity.14 Alternately, naturally derived polymers extracted from animals or plants have higher biocompatibility. Collagen and gelatin, a denatured collagen, are widely studied for tissue engineering because of their good biocompatibility and biodegradability. Cells cultured with the injectable hydrogel composed of carbohydrazide-modified gelatin and aldehyde-modified hyaluronic acid showed excellent viability, migration, and angiogenic properties, but this hydrogel has a relatively low storage modulus compared with that of soft tissues and organs.15 Moreover, injectable hydrogels composed of two types of alginate derivatives, benzylamino tetrazine or norbornene-modified alginate, abbreviated as Alg-T and Alg-N, respectively, have been reported.16 Alg-T and Alg-N react through tetrazine-norbornene click chemistry and can form a hydrogel under the skin. However, cell migration into the hydrogel was hindered because of the tight network of chemical cross-linking.16 Furthermore, synthetic and naturally derived hybrid hydrogels composed of thiolated hyaluronic acid (HA-SH) and poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) cross-linked by Michael addition exhibited excellent host cell migration into the hydrogel.17 However, the thiol group of HA-SH and acrylate group of PEGDA induced inflammation, and accumulation of inflammatory cells at the injection site after 1 month was confirmed, indicating chronic inflammation.17 In short, previously reported hydrogels exhibit limited biocompatibility and cell migration into the hydrogel. Therefore, the aim of this study was to develop in situ chemically cross-linkable hydrogels with enhanced cell migration. In this study, we chose Alaska pollock-derived gelatin (ApGltn) as a base material because ApGltn has a low sol-gel transition temperature (<13.8 °C) due to its low imino acid content (<150 units per 1000 residues) and does not require pre-heating before use.18 We previously reported that a porous membrane composed of hexanoyl group-modified porcine gelatin and trisuccinimidyl citrate enhanced angiogenesis in vivo. This phenomenon could be due to the hexanoyl group inducing weak inflammation in the tissue, resulting in the secretion of inflammatory cytokines or growth factors.19 We hypothesized that the hydrophobic group induces weak inflammation and promotes protease secretion, which enhances degradation of the ApGltn network and allows cells to migrate into the hydrogel. Therefore, ApGltn was modified with the hexyl group as a hydrophobic group (C6-ApGltn) to enhance cell migration. C6-ApGltn was then cross-linked with biocompatible PEG-based four-armed cross-linker, pentaerythritol poly (ethylene glycol) ether tetrasuccinimidyl glutarate (4S-PEG), which is already used clinically.20 We evaluated cell migration behavior into the C6-ApGltn hydrogel in vitro and in vivo and elucidated the relationships of physicochemical parameters such as mechanical strength and water absorption properties.
In situ injectable hydrogels can be formed by either chemical or physical crosslinking methods. Chemically crosslinked hydrogels, prepared through photopolymerization [4], disulfide bond formation [5], or reaction between thiols and acrylate or sulfones [5], undergo significant volume changes during the phase transition. In contrast to chemical hydrogels, physically crosslinked hydrogels, formed by the self-assembly of polymers in response to environmental stimuli (for example, temperature, pH, or both) display sol-gel transitions without marked volume changes. The hydrogels systems are relatively low viscosity aqueous solutions (sol state) prior to injection, but rapidly convert into a gel under physiological conditions post-injection [1], [6], [7]. Physical hydrogels have several advantages over chemical hydrogels, because they do not require photo irradiation, use of organic solvents or crosslinking agents, and do not release heat at the gelation site, which may denature incorporated proteins and damage embedded cells and surrounding tissues. Thus, the physical systems have recently attracted increased attention. For use in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering, hydrogels should be low-viscosity solutions (free-flowing) prior to subcutaneous injection, and should rapidly gel in the human body, where ultimate degradation of the hydrogels is desired. Injectable hydrogels that are sensitive to temperature are useful for both in vitro and in vivo applications, because temperature control is generally easy. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)/Polyester copolymers, as an injectable biodegradable temperature-sensitive physically crosslinked hydrogel, of hydrophilic biocompatible PEG with biodegradable biocompatible aliphatic polyesters, for example polylactide (PLA) [8], [9], poly(d,l-lactic acid-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [10], [11], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [12], [13], or poly[(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate] (PHB) [14], have received increasing attention as promising biomaterials. Among those thermogelling systems, block copolymers of PLGA and PEG are very important owing to their high adjustability of biodegradation and good properties to encapsulate and release biological substances [15], [16], [17], [18]. However, the appropriate composition region, such as block ratio and block length, is narrow, which limits its application to a large extent. Recently, Yu’ group has found a facile approach to prepare a thermogelling system by simply blending two similar block copolymers with different block ratios [19], [20]. One specimen was water-soluble and the other was just a precipitate in a broad temperature region. Although neither specimen possessed the thermogelling property, the aqueous solution of the copolymer mixture with a certain mix ratio showed a reversible sol-gel transition with the increase of temperature. On the basis of this good idea, thermogelling property of mixed star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels is investigated by us in order to develop applications of pure star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels. Our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers for designing injectable biomaterials. In this paper, a new kind of copolymer, 3-arm or 4-arm star-shaped poly(d,l-lactic-co-glycolic acid)-b-methoxy poly(ethylene glycol)(3sPLGA-mPEG or 4sPLGA-mPEG), is synthesized via the arm-first method rather than the core-first method reported in the literature [21], [22], [23]. We will present a systematic study of sol-gel transition behavior, micellization behavior and degradation behavior of the two-component thermogelling mixture and examine their in vitro and in vivo biocompatibility. Comparing with plenty of reports of biodegradable biomaterials, the detailed research of the degradation profiles of injectable temperature-sensitive hydrogels, particularly of physical hydrogels, is very limited. As such, our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers and puts forward a new strategy to design injectable biomaterials.
Stimuli-sensitive injectable hydrogels, composed of biodegradable copolymers, have emerged as prominent candidate materials for the sustained delivery of therapeutic drugs. In this study, we developed a biodegradable and temperature-sensitive injectable hydrogel system based on heparin-bearing poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (Hep-PCLA) as the carrier system for lysozyme. Hep-PCLA conjugates are capable of undergoing temperature-induced sol-to-gel transitions in an aqueous solution. The gelation rate, mechanical strength, and viscosity of Hep-PCLA conjugates are controllably tunable by varying the graft density of PCLA copolymers to heparin. The gel window in which Hep-PCLA forms a gel covers the physiological conditions (37 °C), i.e., free flowing Hep-PCLA in aqueous solutions (25 °C) could form a hydrogel at body temperature. Using an in vitro cytotoxicity test, Hep-PCLA conjugates were found to be non-toxic to fibroblast cells, even at high concentrations. Lysozyme, chosen as a model protein, was effectively loaded into Hep-PCLA conjugates using ionic and hydrophobic interactions. The lysozyme-loaded conjugates readily formed a hydrogel when implanted in the back of Sprague-Dawley rats, and retarded the initial burst of lysozyme release, exhibiting sustained release. Our results show that biodegradable, temperature-sensitive injectable Hep-PCLA hydrogels can be used as sustained protein carriers. In recent years, numerous injectable hydrogels have been developed that are responsive to various stimuli including temperature, pH, and enzymes.10-13 Stimuli-responsive injectable hydrogels, also termed smart hydrogels, are able to switch sol-to-gel phase transitions in response to various stimuli. Of these stimuli, temperature is the most widely used stimulus in injectable hydrogels.14,15 Polymers exhibiting lower critical solution temperatures (LCSTs) with ideal phase transitions between room and body temperatures are attractive candidate materials for injectable formulations.16,17 Such polymers are soluble at room temperature and form hydrogels after administration. For instance, various copolymers including Pluronic, poly(phosphazene), and poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) exist in the sol state at room temperature and transform into gels at body temperature.14,18-20 Although these copolymers exhibit sharp temperature-responsive transitions, their biological usage has been limited due to non-degradability and limited biocompatibility. To surmount these issues, poly(ester)-based biodegradable and biocompatible polymers that are capable of exhibiting LCSTs have been developed.21 In particular, poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (PCLA)-based copolymer hydrogels are promising candidates for injectable delivery systems.22 In addition to the PCLA copolymers, thermosensitive injective hydrogels based on poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG) have been developed for biomedical applications.23 The PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG-based thermosensitive gels combined with curcumin have been proven to enhance anti-tumor activity in a colorectal peritoneal carcinomatosis model as well as wound healing in an excision wound model.24,25 Furthermore, PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG/acellular bone matrix composite hydrogels have been used for bone regeneration in cranial defects.26 Although PCLA-based amphiphilic copolymer hydrogel systems could load proteins and enable their sustained release, the neutral nature of hydrogels severely restricts the loading of some proteins, as most therapeutic proteins are ionically charged.27,28 It is noteworthy to mention that the integration of the PCLA-based polymers with cationic or anionic charged polymers may provide a useful hydrogel system for the delivery of ionically charged proteins. Natural polysaccharide-based ionic polymers including hyaluronic acid, heparin, chitosan, and dextran derivatives have been extensively investigated in biomedical applications mainly because of their biocompatibility, non-immunogenicity, biodegradability and cell-adhesion properties.29-37 Among the variety of natural polysaccharides, heparin is a negatively charged linear polysaccharide composed of alternating units of sulfated glucuronic acid and glucosamine derivatives.38 Heparin is clinically used as an anticoagulant. The presence of negatively charged functional groups (sulfate and carboxylate) endows a high negative charge to heparin, which facilitates ionic interaction and complexation with various proteins, growth factors, and chemokines.39 Given its unique structure, hydrogels and nanoparticles composed of heparin exhibit attractive properties in biomedical applications.40 For example, photo-cross-linked alginate-heparin hydrogels allowed the sustained release of various therapeutic proteins.41,42 It is known that heparin could form complexes with various growth factors.43 The heparin present in the photo-cross-linked hydrogels binds to various growth factors and allows the sustained release of growth factors.44 Although numerous attempts have been made to develop heparin-based hydrogels, no significant attempt has been made to develop heparin-based biodegradable and injectable hydrogels for protein delivery.
Such temperature-responsive IP systems exhibit rapid sol-to-gel transitions to form hydrogels by the physical (non-covalent) cross-linking (aggregation) of polymers. However, one of the practical problems for these temperature-responsive gelation systems is the short duration time of the gel state in the body. The formed hydrogel tends to revert to the sol state within a short period (typically less than 24 h) where a large amount of water or body fluid exists, such as in the intraperitoneal space and interior of blood vessels, because the main driving force of gelation in these systems is a non-covalent hydrophobic interaction and gel formation is an equilibrium process. This property might be a disadvantage for the application of biodegradable IP systems as implant biomedical materials. Alternatively, in situ gelation systems by chemical (covalent) cross-linking such as polymerization systems and coupling reaction systems have been reported.26-30 The covalent gelation systems have advantages of a longer duration time of the gel state and a relatively high mechanical strength of the obtained hydrogels, but also have several problems. In polymerization systems, how and when the polymerization starts is the issue. UV irradiation and photoinitiators are potentially toxic, and polymer chains produced by polymerization are not biodegradable. In coupling reaction systems, it is generally difficult to control the gelation time, and a special syringe for mixing of two solutions is needed. Therefore, biodegradable IP systems having the advantages of both the temperature-responsive physical gelation system and the covalent bond formation system are desired to achieve favourable gelation times, longer duration times of the gel state and biodegradability. Block copolymers of PEG and polycaprolactone (PCL)20-22,31 or stereocomplex (SC) formation of polylactide (PLA) blocks32-34 were reported to show irreversible gelation and provided some solutions to these issues by crystallization of the PCL block and SC formation of PLLA and PDLA. However, the duration times of the gel state were still not very long. A biodegradable IP system with a longer and controllable duration time of the gel state should have a great advantage as implantable biomedical materials. For example, the sustained release of drugs from the hydrogel during the desired period may be achieved if the drug release occurred in a degradation-dependent manner. An ideal drug releasing period depends on the kind of drug. The IP hydrogel with a controllable degradation period must be useful for application as a drug releasing depot. Moreover, as a scaffold for regenerative medicine, the ideal degradation periods and moduli were different for the kind of tissue to be regenerated and the cell growth rate, such as bone, cartilage or soft tissues. The IP hydrogel systems with controllable degradation periods and moduli can provide wide varieties of scaffolds for the regeneration of different tissues.
Gelatin gels form a strong, three-dimensional structure at low temperatures due to interconnected polymer chains37 and hydrogel exhibits predominant elastic behavior (G′ ≫ G″). As temperature increases, these chains loosen, resulting in disruption of the ordered arrangement of gelatin polymers inside hydrogel matrix38 and unwind into a random coil-like structure, causing the gel to transition into a liquid-like state, resulting in gel-to-sol transition. At T ≫ Tgel-sol (gel-to-sol transition temperature), temperature-assisted mobility of random coils of gelatin polymers leads to hydrogel in a viscous liquid state and exhibits (G′ < G″).38 The thermoresponsive behavior of gelatin makes it a promising candidate for bioprinting applications where temperature-controlled material properties are desired.39 The gel-to-sol transition temperature, Tgel-sol, for our samples was investigated using a temperature sweep test [Fig. 3(c)]. The critical Tgel-sol, was found to be around 34.5 ± 0.5 °C for the pure gelatin hydrogel. Interestingly, we do not observe any change in Tgel-sol for composite samples and it was found to be independent of PAuNR composition (Fig. S2b). The Tgel-sol of a hydrogel is influenced by the concentration of gelatin polymers40 and the presence of new interactions between gelatin and the nanocomponents used as fillers.5,41 The nearly same Tgel-sol for gelatin and composite hydrogel at fixed gelatin concentration (5%) indicates the physical entanglement of gelatin polymers is solely responsible for the thermal stability of the hydrogel and is unaffected by the nanorod composition. The flow behavior of gelatin hydrogel is characterized by analyzing the viscosity profile in the shear rate range of 0.1-500 s−1. Shear thinning behavior is evident for pure and composite hydrogel as viscosity decreases with an increase in shear rate [Fig. 3(d)]. The observation of shear thinning behavior suggests that the rate of disentanglement of the polymer network due to applied shear stress is higher than the reconstruction rate of the network.42 Interestingly, in the intermediate shear rate (≈1-20 s−1), we measure a deviation from the shear-thinning behavior. This suggests a possible interplay between two opposing effects: shear-induced thinning and localized shear thickening. The localized thickening behavior might be attributed to the application of shear rate disrupting and opening polymeric clusters within the hydrogel. This disruption exposes hidden bonding sites, facilitating the formation of new networks between polymer chains and leading to a temporary thickening effect.43 In Fig. S3, local shear thickening behavior is shown for the observed range of shear rate. The local shear thickening effect is found to diminish with increasing composition of PAuNR suggesting the presence of PAuNR hinders the reconstruction of new network formation between polymers. In Fig. 4(a), we show the estimates of critical yield strain, γo, and viscosity, η, for pure gelatin and composite samples at various added PAuNR compositions. It is evident that the composite samples exhibit lower values, suggesting sample softening due to the presence of PAuNR. These observations suggest a potential disruption in network formation between gelatin polymers caused by the incorporation of PAuNRs within the matrix. To further analyze the mechanical properties of the gelatin and gelatin composite hydrogels, uniaxial compression tests were conducted using a rheometer (Anton Paar MCR 702) on cylindrical hydrogel samples with an 8 mm diameter and 4 mm height, using an 8 mm parallel plate geometry (supplementary material). The compression strength and fracture strain of the gelatin and gelatin composite hydrogels, as presented in Fig. S2(d), were determined from the stress-strain curve shown in [Fig. S2(c)]. The pure gelatin hydrogel exhibited a compression strength of 0.0243 MPa and a fracture strain of 80.53%. In contrast, the incorporation of PAuNR led to a decrease in both compression strength and fracture strain, with GNC4 showing the lowest values of 0.0107 MPa and 67.20%, respectively. This reduction is attributed to the decreased entanglement between gelatin polymers due to the presence of PAuNR.44 These findings are consistent with the results from shear rheology tests, indicating a decrease in mechanical stability with PAuNR incorporation. As for future applications, the shear thinning behavior of this gelatin composite hydrogel system makes it suitable for extrusion-based 3D-bioprinting as well as for easier surgical placement.45
A general feature of the thermosensitive hydrogel is that the polymer should be amphiphilic, having a hydrophobic segment and a hydrophilic segment.17,29-32 A delicate balance between hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity is imperative for the temperature-dependent sol-gel transition to occur for polymer aqueous solutions. A too large hydrophilic segment will result in no sol-gel phase transition, and a too large hydrophobic segment will lead to insolubility in aqueous solution at physiologically relevant temperature range.33 Polyesters such as polylactide (PLA), polyglycolide (PGA), and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) continue to be widely investigated in the biomedical field as they all have been approved by the FDA for in vivo use, and many products based on these polymers are commercially available.34 Not surprisingly, several injectable and thermosensitive hydrogels based on these polyesters have been reported including diblock PLGA-PEG, triblock PEG-PLGA-PEG, and grafted PLGA-g-PEG copolymers.17,29-31,35-37 These systems combine the biocompatibility and biodegradability of PLGA with the injectability of an aqueous sol. Degradation products of PLA/PLGA, however, can induce an acidic environment that may be a problem for some tissues and perhaps detrimental to incorporated drugs or proteins.38 In addition, our earlier reported PLGA-g-PEG polymers have relatively weak mechanical properties and a paste-like morphology and their dissolution in water or buffer solution can take up to several days.35,37,39-41 Polycaprolactone (PCL), meanwhile, has recently regained great attention in the biomedical field particularly with its use for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and medical devices.42 As with PLA and PGA, PCL based polymers have superior biocompatibility as evidenced by several drug-delivery devices and sutures fabricated with PCL that have been approved by the FDA. Due to its increased degree of crystallinity and hydrophobicity versus PLA, PGA, and PLGA, PCL-based polymers have superior rheological properties and a solid morphology resulting in a significant improvement in terms of handling and transfer.11,27,42 Moreover, unlike PLA and PGA, PCL degradation product is less acidic and typically takes much longer time to degrade than PLA and PGA; these two properties have led other authors to believe that PCL degradation essentially will not lead to an acidic environment.43,44 Indeed, to take advantage of the benefits offered by PCL, thermosensitive hydrogels of block copolymers consisting of PCL or PCLA (poly(caprolactone-co-lactide)), and PEG have been reported and summarized.33,43-47 However, to our knowledge, injectable and thermosensitive hydrogels based on polycaprolactone (PCL) grafted with polyethylene glycol (PCL-g-PEG) have not yet been reported. Grafted copolymers such as PCL-g-PEG and PLGA-g-PEG can offer more versatility and latitude as the hydrophilicity of the polymers can be modulated by both PEG length and number of PEG grafts, whereas only PEG length can be utilized to tune hydrophilicity for block thermosensitive copolymers. Here we report versatile hydrogel of PCL-g-PEG, which is structurally comparable to our previously developed PLGA-g-PEG with the difference being that the PLGA segment is replaced by PCL. The rheological properties, sol-gel transition mechanisms, and enzymatic degradation by lipase of the PCL-g-PEG hydrogel were investigated and their potential biomedical applications were discussed in this study. The test tube inversion method has also been used to judge sol or gel states for thermosensitive polymer aqueous solutions.28,39,53 The sol and gel states of PCL-g-PEG aqueous solution at 5 wt% at 0 °C and 37 °C are shown in Fig. 3. The test tube inversion method showed that a polymer aqueous solution of 5 wt% formed a hydrogel at 37 °C. However, a polymer solution at 2 wt% did not form a hydrogel at 37 °C. This suggests that the critical gelation concentration is between 2 wt% and 5 wt% at 37 °C. Such a low critical gelation concentration is much lower than that of a triblock PCL-PEG-PCL aqueous solution (∼13 wt%)33 and a PLGA-g-PEG aqueous solution (∼19%).39 A low gelation concentration indicates that gels with high water content can be prepared, which may be valuable for tissue engineering applications because it would facilitate the transport of nutrients, oxygen, soluble metabolites and wastes generated by incorporated cells.54 Indeed, a limited permeability of an injectable gel has been reported to be responsible for the decreased viability of incorporated osteoblast cells.24 Furthermore, as drug release rate is most likely gel permeability dependent, a large gelation concentration window at physiological temperature is advantageous and versatile to tune drug release profiles.
The sol-gel transition of chitosan in the alkaline system is irreversible. Chitosan (CS), a linear polysaccharide composed of randomly distributed β-(1 → 4)-linked d-glucosamine and N-acetyl-d-glucosamine, is mainly obtained by deacetylation of chitin [[1], [2], [3]]. Because of its good biocompatibility, biodegradability, and non-toxicity, antimicrobial activity, and low immunogenicity, chitosan has been widely studied as a promising biomaterial and attracted significant interests in the areas of tissue engineering [[4], [5], [6], [7], [8]], drug delivery [[9], [10], [11], [12], [13]], wound dressing [[14], [15], [16]], and gene therapy [17,18]. However, many of these applications require chitosan to be constructed into hydrogels. As compared to chitosan hydrogels fabricated by chemical crosslinking, physically crosslinked chitosan hydrogels are more favored because they can avoid the potential toxicity from chemical crosslinking agents [[19], [20], [21]]. The conventional fabrication of physical chitosan hydrogel is to solubilize chitosan powder in an acidic aqueous solution, and then chitosan chains can be entangled to form a three dimensional gel network by immersing in an alkaline coagulating bath [22]. Thus, the pH-dependent solubility of chitosan provides it with a convenient way to the fabrication of a physical hydrogel. However, poor mechanical properties of chitosan physical hydrogels formed from an acidic aqueous solution seriously impede its practical applications. In recent years, breaking the limitation of using an acidic aqueous solution to dissolve chitosan, a new solvent system, alkali/urea (referred to as an alkaline system), has been designed and used to dissolve chitosan via the freezing-thawing method [23,24]. Subsequently, an as-prepared chitosan alkaline solution is able to undergo a sol-gel transition upon heating, and further constructs a robust physical hydrogel by immersing the formed chitosan alkaline hydrogel in DI water to remove alkali and urea. Duan and coworkers thought that the dissolution of chitosan in the KOH/LiOH/urea aqueous solvent should be attributed to the formation of complexes between chitosan and alkali/urea molecules due to the hydrogen bonding. However, heating dissociates the complexes of chitosan and solvent molecules, and leads to the regeneration of chitosan chains into nanofibrils. At high chitosan concentrations, the generated chitosan nanofibrils could entangle and crosslink with each other through intermolecular hydrogen bonds to form a three dimensional gel network [25]. On the basis of fluorescent analysis, Wang and coworkers investigated the gelation process of chitosan in a LiOH/urea aqueous solvent, and found that the gelation of chitosan at the elevated temperatures should be attributed to the formation of the embryonic structure and crystalline structure [26]. It is well known that a gelling solution changes its state from a liquid to a solid in the vicinity of a critical value of a gelling parameter (e.g. temperature or concentration) which is referred to as the gel point. For a chitosan alkaline solution, the transition from a fluidic state to a viscoelastic solid state depends not only on temperature but also chitosan concentration. However, the gelation of chitosan in an alkali/urea aqueous solution has not been studied in depth.
In situ forming hydrogels are systems responsive to the environmental stimuli, such as change of temperature, pH, photo intensity, ionic strength, etc.14, 15 They have been divided into two types, one is chemical in situ gels and the other is physical in situ gels. Chemical in situ gels, also called “permanent” gels, are hydrogels containing covalently cross-linked networks. They are irreversible polymeric networks via the use of cross-linkers or enzymes.16 Physical in situ gels, or “reversible” gels, are those networks held together by molecular entanglements and secondary forces such as hydrogen bonding, ionic, hydrophobic forces.17, 18 Usually these weak and reversible bonds formation depends on external stimulation to form cross-linking, which makes temperature, pH, lights, or ions sensitive reversible hydrogels possible.19-22 In situ delivery systems have an upper hand compared with conventional systems, because they take longer time for in situ system to finish releasing drug at targeted site. Particularly, a temperature responsive hydrogel, namely thermogel, is a reversible physical cross-linking system, forming upon heating up temperature until critical temperature. The properties of thermogel offer opportunities in therapeutic application because of several reasons.23-25 An injectable thermogel system has simplicity of pharmaceutical formulation by mixing of drug below sol-gel transition temperature. Large scale surgery for implantation is not needed. After injection, body temperature will stimulate sol-gel transition, viscous solution will change into a drug delivery depot. The high percentage water content makes thermogel highly competitive with the injection site. Also, peptides are kept at low temperature before application, which makes sure no denaturalization due to organic solvent interaction or dissolution triggered by high temperature. Currently, there are only two types of commercial polymeric thermoresponsive hydrogel products available in the market. One is Poloxamer, and the other is poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAAm). When using Poloxamer based hydrogel, two conditions, polymer critical micelle concentration (CMC) and critical micelle temperature (CMT), must be reached to promote sol-gel transition. For Poloxamer, it includes Amphipathic Poloxamer and Pluronic F127. Amphipathic Poloxamer, a FDA-approved triblock polymer, composes of hydrophobic poly(ethylene oxide) and hydrophilic poly(propylene oxide) components.26 Hydrogel based on this has been widely used in both therapeutic and consumer applications. Although Amphipathic Poloxamer has proven to be biocompatible and able to perform drug delivery,27 degradation of it based hydrogels does not support sustainable process. The degradation period, 4 h, has severely limited targeted or long-termed drug release application.12 Meanwhile, Pluronic F127, with CMT of human body temperature (37 °C) and longer degradation period, has higher CMC, which limits its bioapplications. Commercial PNIPAAm is another typical amphipathic thermoresponsive polymer, which was first synthesized in the 1950s.28-30 Hydrogel based on this can undergo reversible phase change by changing the temperature of aqueous environment. However, poor mechanical and nonbiodegradable properties, teratogenicity and carcinogenicity of its residual monomers, and toxicity of degradation products of isopropyl amine limit its biomedical applications.31-34 After drug delivery process, PNIPAAm based hydrogel needs to be removed by extra surgery, which goes against the advantage of thermogel by avoiding surgery on patients and will not bring convenience and ease to therapeutic application. Being one of the earliest and most studied biomaterials, polyester has its irreplaceable place among all polymer materials.35-41 Compared with other biomaterials, polyester has three great advantages-biodegradation, biocompatibility, and synthetic versatility.42-48 The application of hydrogel based on this as scaffold for cell transplantation has already benefitted thousands of people every year.49 Being the only biodegradable polymer with high molecular weight, polyester is able to undergo hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation. This is due to its highly hydrolysable ester linkages in the polymer backbone and good fitness to enzyme's active site, respectively.24, 41, 50-52 Controllable degradation gives polyester based hydrogel the advantage of application in periodic and targeted drug release.53 The end result of degradation also brings no harm to human body as it will be transformed into carbon dioxide and water, released out of human body by metabolism eventually. Besides, human body contains 70% of water and it is important for any material used in human body to also largely contain water to achieve good biocompatibility. Polyester based hydrogel is able to trap large amount of water in aqueous environments including body fluids. The 'sol-gel' transition in injectable biodegradable hydrogels is a temperature-responsive physical change where a polymer solution transforms from a low-viscosity liquid state (sol) to a semi-solid gel state upon heating. This occurs specifically between room temperature and body temperature (approximately 37°C) [1][2]. The transition enables minimally invasive implantation: the polymer solution remains injectable (sol state) in a syringe at room temperature but rapidly forms a gel *in situ* after subcutaneous injection into the body [1][2][8][10].

The mechanism relies on amphiphilic copolymers with a delicate hydrophobic/hydrophilic balance. Heating triggers dehydration of hydrophilic segments (typically poly(ethylene glycol), PEG) and aggregation of hydrophobic segments (e.g., aliphatic polyesters like PLA, PLGA, or PCL) via hydrophobic interactions, leading to physical cross-linking without toxic chemical cross-linkers [1][2][12][14]. This physical gelation is reversible upon cooling [6][8].

Biodegradability arises from hydrolytically or enzymatically cleavable segments (e.g., polyester blocks [1][12][14] or polypeptides [4][9]). The resulting hydrogel acts as a depot for sustained drug delivery or a scaffold for tissue engineering [1][2][10].

Its biodegradability, coupled with favorable water vapor barrier properties, makes it particularly attractive for food packaging applications [111]. Nevertheless, TPS does present certain limitations, including lower mechanical strength, heightened sensitivity to moisture, and reduced processing compatibility compared to synthetic polymers [23]. To this end, starch is one of the most promising biopolymers due to its natural origin from renewable sources, economically competitive and biodegradable. Native starch is not a thermoplastic polymer in a natural way, due to its degradation temperature is lower than the temperature required for plasticization. However, in the presence of a suitable plasticizer, under temperature and shear conditions, it is converted in a thermoplastic starch (TPS) able to be processed as the conventional thermoplastic polymers [1]. Plasticizers for starches must be small molecules capable of diffusing between the starch molecules and they must own groups capable of forming hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups of starch molecules. Glycerol is, among the polyols, the most used plasticizer for starch due to its low cost, high boiling point and no toxicity. However, the interaction between glycerol and starch is not strong enough, so the starch often recrystallizes after being stored for a period of time. Isosorbide is a bicyclic compound obtained from the glucose dehydration, characterized by having two OH groups and two oxygen atoms intercalated in the double carbon ring. Recently, isosorbide has been tested as a novel, effective and green plasticizer for starch due to its biodegradability and no toxicity, which prevents the starch retrogradation [4,5]. During the gelatinization process, semicrystalline starch granules undergo a change of state from an ordered to a completely or partially disordered structure [5]. Wang et al. [7] have studied the nature of structural changes during processing of starches granules from different sources. Some of the most studied and reported TPS plasticizers in the literature include polyols such as glycerol, glycol, sorbitol, xylitol, maltitol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, butanediol;107,110,111 sucrose, fructose, mannose,112 fatty acids (such as myristate or palmitate),113etc. It is also necessary to note that water is a good plasticizer of starch. The replacement of conventional petroleum-based polymers by other more environmentally friendly polymers has been focused research in recent times. Although the studies about the use of isosorbide as a plasticizer for starches are scarce at the moment, its use is revealed as an interesting strategy to obtain more durable materials that do not present the disadvantages generated by retrogradation processes. The TPS have two main disadvantages compared to the common thermoplastic polymers including poor mechanical properties and a low moisture resistance. A strategy widely used in recent years to overcoming the TPS drawbacks consists of the incorporation of biodegradable micro or nanoparticles used as a filler in the TPS matrix. Some fillers used were clays and silicates [6], starch nanoparticles [7], talc nanoparticles [8], cellulose nanofibers [9] and cellulose nanocrystals [10].
