Starch, characterized by its abundant source, low cost, renewability and complete biodegradability,20 is considered one of the most promising fillers for PBAT. However, due to the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in starch molecules, the melting temperature of starch is higher than its decomposition temperature, rendering it unsuitable for melt processing. To address this, a substantial amount of plasticizer must be added to starch under high temperature and shear to facilitate plasticization, resulting in thermoplastic starch (TPS) with melt processability. Common plasticizers for TPS include glycerol,21 citric acid,22 glycerol triacetate,23 formamide, water and small molecules of poly(vinyl alcohol),24-27 with glycerol being the most commonly used and effective. However, the low mechanical strength of TPS and the issue of plasticizer migration and exudation contribute to a significant reduction in the mechanical strength of PBAT/TPS blend materials. Additionally, the strong hygroscopicity of glycerol leads to increased water absorption in PBAT/TPS blend materials. Therefore, improving the mechanical strength of TPS and addressing plasticizer migration and exudation are essential to effectively produce low-cost PBAT/TPS blend films with high starch content. Excess sorbitol solidifies after processing, preventing plasticizer exudation and migration. Nevertheless, TPS still has limited applications due to its moisture sensitivity, poor thermal resistance, and low strength and resilience.7 Several attempts have focused on enhancing these drawbacks by melt blending TPS with a hydrophobic and flexible polymer such as PE.8, 9 However, melt blending of these two polymers often results in immiscible blends due to the high interfacial tension between the nonpolar PE and the highly polar TPS.10 To overcome this problem, several alternatives have been investigated, including: (i) chemically modifying starch11, 12 and PE1, 13-15 and (ii) incorporating chemical compatibilizers into the PE/TPS blend.9 Sailaja12 and Bikiaris and Panayiotou13 reported that introduction of poly(ethylene-co-glycidyl methacrylate) and poly(ethylene-grafted-maleic anhydride) improved the miscibility between PE and TPS. Alternatively, nano/micro inorganic fillers such as organoclay and zeolite could be used to improve the miscibility of polymer blends, in addition to enhancing the mechanical properties of polymers17, 18 and polymer blends.19-21 Several studies have reported the compatibilizing effect of organoclay in polymer blends20-22; however, thus far only Djoumaliisky and Zipper19 have reported on the compatibilizing effect of an activated natural zeolite in a recycled polymer blend. Zeolites are nanoporous crystalline aluminosilicate materials, with pore sizes ranging from ∼ 3 to 15 Å.18 The structures of zeolites comprise three-dimensional frameworks of SiO4 and AlO4 tetrahedra. Exhibiting thermoplastic behavior, TPS can be processed using conventional plastic manufacturing techniques, including extrusion, injection molding, and film blowing. Due to its renewable origin and inherent biodegradability, TPS has emerged as a promising material for environmentally sustainable packaging solutions [111]. Despite these challenges, TPS continues to gain prominence globally. Hydrogen bonds hold the starch chains together, making them insoluble in cold water. Additionally, these hydrogen bonds lead to a high glass transition temperature, which makes starch difficult to process. This disadvantage can be overcome by converting raw starch into thermoplastic starch (TPS). This conversion is achieved through a process called “gelatinization,” which is performed in the presence of excess water, using a plasticizer and heat. As a result of this irreversible process, the crystalline structure in the starch granules is eliminated, resulting in a completely amorphous structure [6, 7]. The selection of plasticizers plays a pivotal role in determining the mechanical, thermal, and biological properties of TPS. Among various options, the combination of glycerol and D-sorbitol offers significant advantages over conventional plasticizers such as urea, glycols, and citrate esters [7-9]. Glycerol, due to its high hydrophilicity, disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains, thereby improving processability. In contrast, D-sorbitol, with its longer molecular structure, contributes to enhanced thermal stability and water resistance [10]. Furthermore, its low volatility reduces plasticizer migration, thus improving the long-term stability of the material [11]. The synergistic use of these two plasticizers can effectively address common issues associated with TPS, including starch retrogradation, plasticizer migration, brittleness, and elevated glass transition temperatures, while allowing for precise tuning of water resistance and mechanical performance [9, 10]. Li and Huneault [7] reported that while glycerol alone produced TPS with low thermal stability and excessive hydrophilicity, the incorporation of sorbitol improved expansion resistance by 30%. Similarly, Sanyang et al. [10] found that combining glycerol and sorbitol doubled the Young's modulus of palm starch films compared to systems plasticized with glycerol alone. However, these studies primarily focused on corn or potato starch, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the plasticization behavior of wheat starch-a variant particularly rich in amylose. In a recent study in which glycerol was used as a plasticizer, it was reported that the tensile strength and Young's modulus of TPS films obtained from wheat starch were higher than those of other conventional starches [4]. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to systematically investigate the physicochemical properties and cellular interactions associated with varying glycerol-to-sorbitol ratios in wheat starch-based TPS formulations. TPS can be processed using conventional plastic processing techniques, such as injection molding, extrusion, and solvent casting [6]. However, owing to the inherently poor mechanical properties of starch, TPS is often blended with biodegradable or non-degradable synthetic polymers for biomedical applications [12-21]. For example, Carmona et al. [20] reported that polycaprolactone (PCL)/poly (lactic acid) (PLA) blends exhibited 40% lower fibroblast proliferation compared to starch-containing composites. The relative hydrophilicity of starch, attributed to its abundant hydroxyl groups, enhances protein adsorption and promotes cell adhesion [18]. Moreover, in contrast to synthetic polymers-which may generate acidic and potentially cytotoxic degradation products-starch degrades into glucose chains that can serve as an additional nutrient source for cells [19]. Emerging evidence suggests that optimized TPS formulations may support superior fibroblast proliferation compared to their synthetic counterparts, likely due to starch's intrinsic bioactivity and biocompatible degradation profile.

Glycerol functions as a plasticizer in the production of thermoplastic starch (TPS) by disrupting the strong intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonds between starch molecules. This enables the starch to undergo thermoplastic processing (e.g., extrusion, injection molding) under heat (90–180°C) and shear without thermal degradation [2][3][4][5][11]. Specifically, glycerol forms hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups on starch chains, reducing the glass transition temperature (Tg) and gelatinization temperature, thereby enhancing chain mobility and processability [1][12][14][15].  

Glycerol is widely used due to its low cost, non-toxicity (suitable for food/medical applications), and high boiling point (292°C), which minimizes volatilization during processing [1][7][12]. However, it can leach out over time or under high humidity, leading to starch retrogradation (recrystallization) and embrittlement [1][2][11]. Its high hydrophilicity also increases moisture sensitivity and water absorption in TPS, limiting mechanical performance [5][15].  

While glycerol improves elongation at break in TPS [1], its limitations have driven research into alternative plasticizers (e.g., sorbitol, isosorbide) or plasticizer blends to enhance stability and reduce migration [12][14][15].

question: What is the 'lag phase' in the biodegradation of plastics in compost?
ground_truth: The lag phase is the initial period where no significant mineralization (CO2 evolution) occurs. During this time, microorganisms colonize the surface and secrete extracellular enzymes to begin fragmenting the polymer chain. Only after the molecular weight drops sufficiently to produce water-soluble intermediates does rapid assimilation and mineralization begin.

Composting is a controlled biological aerobic process that transforms organic waste into carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), heat, minerals, biomass, and humus, all of which are beneficial for plant growth [54]. This transformation is driven by microorganisms that decompose organic matter into stable, nutrient-rich soil amendments. It is crucial to distinguish between compostable plastics and other biodegradable plastics, as this distinction has a significant impact on waste management and environmental impact. Compostable plastics, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered to decompose under industrial composting conditions, typically within a few weeks to months. These conditions include specific temperature, humidity, and microbial activity levels that facilitate the rapid breakdown of these materials into carbon dioxide, water, and biomass without leaving toxic residues [98]. Biodegradable plastics refer to a broader category that includes materials capable of breaking down through natural processes into water, carbon dioxide, and biomass [121]. However, the rate and conditions under which this degradation occurs can vary widely. Some biodegradable plastics may require specific environments, such as high-temperature industrial composting facilities, to degrade effectively. Others may take years to break down in natural environments and may not fully degrade in landfill conditions, where oxygen levels are low. Compostable polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered with ester or glycosidic bonds that hydrolyze under industrial composting conditions (58-65 °C, high humidity, and microbial consortia). PLA, a polyester derived from corn starch, undergoes microbial enzymatic degradation (proteinases and lipases) to produce CO₂, water, and biomass. However, incomplete degradation leaves behind oligomers (lactic acid dimers), which exhibit persistence and toxicity in soil ecosystems, as evidenced by genotoxic effects on earthworms (Eisenia fetida) at concentrations > 5%. This aligns with findings that weathering of biodegradable plastics releases oligomers resembling persistent organic pollutants (POPs), raising concerns about bioaccumulation and ecosystem disruption [64]. The distinction between compostable and biodegradable plastics has significant implications for waste management and environmental sustainability. Compostable plastics, when disposed of correctly in composting facilities, can contribute to the production of nutrient-rich compost, enhancing soil quality and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizers. However, suppose compostable plastics are not separated correctly from non-compostable waste. In that case, they can contaminate recycling streams or fail to decompose properly in landfills, where conditions are not conducive to composting [146]. Moreover, not all biodegradable plastics can be treated in industrial composting facilities due to the potential release of harmful substances or the requirement for prolonged degradation times. This necessitates clear labeling and consumer education to ensure proper disposal and treatment of these materials. Mismanagement can lead to increased pollution and undermine the environmental benefits that these materials are intended to provide [31].
Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].
It should be also obvious that the environment is not a dumping ground for plastic waste, and no environmentally biodegradable polymer will be developed with the aim of throwing and dumping into the environment after use. However, the property of biodegradability can be beneficially used for managing plastic waste originating especially from specific sectors such as food packaging as a managed end-of-life cycle option in controlled industrial compost (i-compost) plants. Packaging is one of the biggest sectors both using plastics and generating waste. Lot of plastic food packaging based on polyolefins and PET lands up in composting plants when food items are discarded together with packaging. New i-compostable biodegradable polymers with fast biodegradation and suitable mechanical and gas-barrier properties as a substitute for polyolefins used presently would be a promising solution for MPs generated from packaging. This will also be advantageous for disposable items used for only a short period of time. This is in accord with the E.U. strategy for circular economy utilizing organic recycling of such polymers in compost plants. At present, ASTM D-6400 (Standard Specification for Labeling of Plastics Designed to be Aerobically Composted in Municipal or Industrial Facilities) and the test procedure described in ASTM 5338 is used for testing the composting capability of plastics. According to the method, the sample is labeled positive (compostable in industrial facilities) in the case it fulfills the combined requirements: 1) after 12 weeks, not more than 10% of fragments more than 2 mm in size should be left; and 2) 90% of the organic carbon must be converted to CO2 in 180 days (24 weeks). The problem is that real composting times in industrial compost plants are much shorter than the procedure allows. Most of these plants already distribute compost after 8-12 weeks. In some other compost plants, the time of composting is still shorter. This implies that the plastic with slow biodegradation in compost (biodegradation in compost not completed till the compost is ready in plants say in 8-12 weeks but which might be completed in 24 weeks) will also have the label of i-compostable biodegradation but will certainly be a source of MP as it will contain plastic fragments at the time of distribution. Composting is a controlled biological aerobic process that transforms organic waste into carbon dioxide (CO2), water (H2O), heat, minerals, biomass, and humus, all of which are beneficial for plant growth [54]. This transformation is driven by microorganisms that decompose organic matter into stable, nutrient-rich soil amendments. It is crucial to distinguish between compostable plastics and other biodegradable plastics, as this distinction has a significant impact on waste management and environmental impact. Compostable plastics, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered to decompose under industrial composting conditions, typically within a few weeks to months. These conditions include specific temperature, humidity, and microbial activity levels that facilitate the rapid breakdown of these materials into carbon dioxide, water, and biomass without leaving toxic residues [98]. Biodegradable plastics refer to a broader category that includes materials capable of breaking down through natural processes into water, carbon dioxide, and biomass [121]. However, the rate and conditions under which this degradation occurs can vary widely. Some biodegradable plastics may require specific environments, such as high-temperature industrial composting facilities, to degrade effectively. Others may take years to break down in natural environments and may not fully degrade in landfill conditions, where oxygen levels are low. Compostable polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and thermoplastic starch (TPS), are engineered with ester or glycosidic bonds that hydrolyze under industrial composting conditions (58-65 °C, high humidity, and microbial consortia). PLA, a polyester derived from corn starch, undergoes microbial enzymatic degradation (proteinases and lipases) to produce CO₂, water, and biomass. However, incomplete degradation leaves behind oligomers (lactic acid dimers), which exhibit persistence and toxicity in soil ecosystems, as evidenced by genotoxic effects on earthworms (Eisenia fetida) at concentrations > 5%. This aligns with findings that weathering of biodegradable plastics releases oligomers resembling persistent organic pollutants (POPs), raising concerns about bioaccumulation and ecosystem disruption [64]. The distinction between compostable and biodegradable plastics has significant implications for waste management and environmental sustainability. Compostable plastics, when disposed of correctly in composting facilities, can contribute to the production of nutrient-rich compost, enhancing soil quality and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizers. However, suppose compostable plastics are not separated correctly from non-compostable waste. In that case, they can contaminate recycling streams or fail to decompose properly in landfills, where conditions are not conducive to composting [146]. Moreover, not all biodegradable plastics can be treated in industrial composting facilities due to the potential release of harmful substances or the requirement for prolonged degradation times. This necessitates clear labeling and consumer education to ensure proper disposal and treatment of these materials. Mismanagement can lead to increased pollution and undermine the environmental benefits that these materials are intended to provide [31].
Biological waste treatments tailored for biodegradable plastics represent sophisticated end-of-life management strategies. These treatments can be implemented under aerobic conditions (with oxygen, such as composting) or anaerobic conditions (without oxygen, such as anaerobic digestion). Composting, which utilizes a diverse microbial community including fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes, can occur at psychrophilic temperatures (below 35 °C for home composting) or thermophilic temperatures (50-60 °C for industrial composting) [11]. For example, kitchen scraps and garden waste are commonly composted in home settings, while large-scale operations might process municipal organic waste. This process reduces waste and produces valuable compost, rich in nutrients and beneficial for soil health. It can also be used in agriculture and landscaping. Similarly, anaerobic digestion, exclusively facilitated by bacteria, can be performed under mesophilic (below 35 °C) or thermophilic (50-60 °C) conditions. This method is often applied in wastewater treatment plants and livestock farms, where organic materials such as food waste, manure, and sewage sludge are digested [108]. The primary factor determining a bioplastic’s suitability for specific waste Management methods is its duration for complete degradation. International standards for biodegradability, such as those set by ISO and ASTM, define a Material as biodegradable if it fully decomposes within 56 days in aquatic environments or within two years in soil. However, these standards often rely on elevated temperatures that surpass typical conditions found in unmanaged natural environments, leading to a disparity between laboratory results and actual biodegradation in the real world. This highlights the importance of aligning biodegradation standards with actual environmental conditions when developing policies for managing plastic waste. Additionally, the design of plastic products must account for potential end-of-life scenarios, ensuring they align with the degradation timelines and processes of intended waste management systems. A cohesive strategy integrating policy, standards, and design is key to crafting practical and reliable solutions for bioplastic waste [101]. The study of biodegradation kinetics and carbon fate of bioplastics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions offers valuable insights, but it also highlights critical limitations in their practical applications. While PHB and PHBV exhibit versatility by biodegrading under both conditions, PCL’s reliance on aerobic environments restricts its utility in anaerobic waste systems [99]. Integrating carbon balance analysis adds depth by tracking carbon sinks, such as gases, biomass, and soluble compounds; however, its complexity and resource demands may hinder scalability in industrial contexts. Additionally, the observed enhancement of mineralization rates with smaller particle sizes, though beneficial for assay duration, is impractical for real-world waste management, where uniform particle reduction is challenging and costly. Combining carbon balance with kinetic analysis provides a promising framework for testing and improving biodegradable materials, but the feasibility of implementing such rigorous methods at scale remains questionable. Addressing these challenges by focusing on scalable, realistic conditions and simplifying analytical methodologies will be critical to translating these findings into effective waste management solutions [99].

Biodegradation under composting conditions is a process widely used as end-of-life (EoL) option for organic waste such as manure, food, and yard waste. The composting process allows the biological stabilization of organic waste, producing a stable material that can be diverted to agricultural activities at a large scale, urban areas at a smaller scale and also gardening at home.[1] Additionally, compostable plastic products, including packaging, can be collected and diverted along with organic waste. At present, although many materials are certified compostable, their biodegradation rate and disappearance in compost facilities may vary. Hence, the presence of compostable plastics during the collection of organic waste (mostly food waste and its associated packaging) has created a challenging situation for compost facilities since times required for ultimate biodegradation of biodegradable plastics may be longer than for organic waste such as food. Extensive research has been conducted at laboratory scales. Successful biodegradation of polymers in thermophilic simulated composting conditions has been reported, mainly for aliphatic and aliphatic/aromatic polyesters such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV), poly(hydroxyoctanoate) (PHO), poly(caprolactone) (PCL), poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), and natural polymers such as starch and cellulose.[2-5] However, laboratory studies involve mostly the use of polymers in their neat state (i.e., pellets, sheets, or films) or with one or two additives; whereas the final products to be discarded after post-consumer stage can be complex structures with several layers to fulfill product protection needs and consumer preferences. Furthermore, laboratory conditions offer a controlled environment where parameters, such as temperature, airflow, moisture content and even biotic population, are carefully tailored; and materials under biodegradation can also be conditioned to powder of homogenous thickness to make it the preferred substrate for the microbial population. However, in real conditions such as industrial or home composting facilities or soil environments, more variability is observed where a material under biodegradation may not be homogenous in type and shape, and they may not be the preferred available source of nutrients and energy for the microbial population.[6, 7] Besides studies at the laboratory scale, field tests are also conducted to certify that these structures can fully disintegrate at the commercial composting facility scale.[8-10] Laboratory tests are conducted under specific national and international standards. Both standards are based on the evolution of the percentage of biodegradation of the samples. These polyesters are formed as intracellular carbon storage compounds and energy reserves in bacteria such as Ralstonia eutropha (Alcaligenes eutrophus), Bacillus megaterium, Azotobacter chroococcum, etc. and have a wide range of values for properties such as elongation at break, strength and modulus.6-8 These advantages of PHAs render them potential substitutes for polyolefins. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) are the most important PHAs. It has been reported that PHB is a highly crystalline polymer with high melting point and brittleness. To overcome the shortcomings of PHB, copolymers have been developed. PHBV (Figure 1) is a copolymer of PHB having randomly arranged 3-hydroxybutyrate (HB) group and 3-hydroxyvalarate (HV) groups. The copolymer has higher flexibility and processability than PHB. Generally, the melting point and brittleness of the copolymer decreases with increases in the valerate content. Singh et al.9 have reported the low strength, low modulus and slow cooling rate of PHBV. To improve these properties of PHBV, its blends with poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), polyetherimide (PEI) thermoplastic starch (TPS), 4,4′-dihydroxydiphenylpropane (BPA) and p-tert-butylphenol (TBP), etc. have been studied.10-13
Many attempts were carried out to improve the performances of PHB, mostly by copolymerization of PHB with other monomers such as β-hydroxyvalerate (β-HV), 4-hydroxybutyrate (4-HB) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3-HHx). Alternatively, another approach by blending PHB with other (co)polymers such as ethylene propylene rubber (EPR) [13], poly(ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) (EVA) [14], epoxidized natural rubber (ENR) [15], poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) [16], poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) [17, 18], poly(propylene) (PP) [19], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [20] and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [21, 22] was applied in literature. Among these polymers, the PVAc, PEO and EVA with >85 wt% of vinyl acetate were reported to be miscible with PHB while the others are immiscible with PHB. Another polymer used to blend with PHB is poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), which is biodegradable under aerobic conditions and is a condensation polymer of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol [23]. Commercial grade of PBS, currently, is synthesized from oil-based feedstock, however, both of the two monomers, i.e. succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, can be derived from renewable resources via fermentation [24, 25]. Thus, PHB/PBS blends can potentially retain both biocompostable and renewable characteristics. Qiu et al. [26, 27] blended poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) with PHB and PHBV in solution. They reported that PHB and PHBV were immiscible with PBS except the PHB/PBS (20/80) blend which showed limited miscibility. The incorporation of PBS restricted the crystallization of PHB and PHBV to a certain extent. In our previous work, the toughness and the strength of the PHB and PHBV were remarkably enhanced by incorporation of PBS in combination with an in situ compatibilization using dicumyl peroxide as a free radical initiator [28]. However, to the authors’ knowledge, the morphology and crystallization behavior of melt-blended PHB/PBS which are more environmentally friendly and more industrial feasible have not been widely studied yet. The prime objective of this paper is to increase the over all crystallization of the PHB by melt blending with PBS. The results of an investigation concerning of the phase morphology of the blends, the crystallization and melting behavior of the PHB in the presence of PBS are discussed.

In this paper, the biodegradability of PHBV containing 3 mol% of hydroxyvalerate (HV) was tested under composting conditions on both a pilot and a laboratory scale. In the pilot-scale composting conditions, parameters such as pH value, temperature and the amounts of oxygen and CO2 produced were determined periodically. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) homopolymer and related copolymers are biologically produced semicrystalline biodegradable polymers which have attracted considerable attention as potential substitutes for petrochemical plastics. Because of its biodegradability, various applications of PHB to functional materials have been extensively studied. The mechanical properties of PHB are comparable to those of conventional fuel-based polymers. However, the usefulness of PHB is limited by its fragility. Melt temperature (ca. 172 °C) of PHB, which happens to be close to thermal decomposition temperature (ca. 200 °C), and a relatively high degree of crystallinity (it sometimes exceeds 50%) are major obstacles to its practical applications [1], [2], [3], [4]. To resolve these limitations, many research groups developed copolymers of PHB with longer side chains monomeric units like 3-hydroxyvalerate (3-HV) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3-HHx) [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (P(HB-co-HV)) was commercialized by ICI Ltd. In 1987 Doi et al. reported that P(HB-co-HV) with a wide range of 3HV content from 0 to 95 mol% are produced in A. eutrophus using pentanoic and butyric acids as carbon sources [6], [7], [8]. The resultant P(HB-co-HV) has lower crystallinity, higher flexibility, and therefore, it is less brittle than homopolymer PHB. Due to these characters, P(HB-co-HV) is used for various applications, giving a positive impact on research and commercial. Chemical structures of PHB, PHV, and P(HB-co-HV) are shown in Fig. 1.
Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a class of natural polyesters that are produced as carbon/energy or reducing-power storage material by numerous micro-organisms with an essential growth-limiting component such as nitrogen, phosphate, sulfur, oxygen, or magnesium.1, 2 Two commercial PHA polymers, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB, Figure 1a) and poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV, Figure 1b), have been studied most in recent years. PHB, being discovered in 1925, is characterized as a thermoplastic macromolecule of high crystallinity and narrow window of processability owing to potential degradation to crotonic acid through a β-scission reaction at temperatures little higher than the melting temperature.3 The processability and toughness of PHB can be improved by incorporating hydroxyvalerate (HV) monomers in the fermentation process. PHBV with a more HV content shows higher flexibility, lower crystallinity and crystallization rate. Novel PHAs with a variety of compositions have been successfully developed by using both genetic engineering and new fermentation techniques, such as poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate) (P3HB4HB, Figure 1c), poly(3-hydroxyoctanoate) (PHO, Figure 1d), and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx, Figure 1e).4 Owing to the biocompatibility, biodegradability, and thermoplasticity, PHAs have recently attracted much attention on their potential biomedical applications, including the surgical wound dressings, controlled drug-release carriers, blood vessel, and tissue engineering scaffolds.5-7 Once PHAs are implanted in vivo, it is the surface that interacts with the host (e.g., cells, bacteria, etc.). Accordingly, surface properties are extremely important as they determine the interactions at the biomaterial-biological environment.8, 9
The interest towards the polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) as materials for biomedical applications is continuously and remarkably growing, since PHAs have been found to be adequate as substrates for the cells proliferation, suggesting a high possibility to further develop these material for tissue replacement and regeneration as well as in tissue engineering [1]. The PHAs constitute a class of natural, microorganisms derived, biodegradable and biocompatible thermoplastic polyesters. Among them poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) have been extensively investigated [2] and their in vitro cytotoxicity has been assessed with various cell lines, i.e. osteoblasts, epithelial cells, and ovine chondrocytes [3], [4], fibroblasts [3]. In particular, the copolymer PHBV is the most explored due to its improved flexibility and processability [5]. However, PHBV shows some drawbacks, such as poor mechanical performance, limited by its high crystallinity degree and inherent rigidity [6] intrinsic hydrophobicity, and poor blood compatibility, leading to platelet adhesion and subsequent thrombi formation [7], [8]. These shortcomings prevent its application in some biomedical fields [6], since it is well known that the key step of cells adhesion on biomaterials, preliminary to their migration and/or proliferation [9], strongly depends on the interactions between the cells and the seeding substrates, as postulated by the recognized mechanochemical transduction phenomenon [10]. The cells adhesion on a support is quite a complex process, involving several factors [11], such as the chemical groups types present on the polymer surface, its relative hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity ratio [12], the electrical charge interactions, the H-bonds, the electrostatic forces [13], the mechanical properties and the surface roughness [1].

Biodegradable polyesters have received much attention because of the eco-friendly properties and potential use as industrial and biomedical materials in the last two decades.1 Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is a biodegradable and biocompatible thermoplastic polymer, which can be produced by Alcaligenes eutrophus using pentanoic and butyric acids as the carbon sources.2, 3 The melting point of PHBV decreases from 178°C to 108°C with increasing 3-hydroxyvalerate (3HV) component from 0 to 95 mol%, and has a minimum value at 70°C when the 3HV content is 40 mol%.4 The decrease of melt point means that the processing window becomes broad that would benefit the processing in industry. The crystallinity of PHBV is only slightly decreased when the 3HV content increase from 0 to 25 mol % because of the isodimorphism of PHBV.5, 6 However, PHBV is still too brittle to apply in industry when the HV content is low. Meanwhile, poly (3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate) (P3/4HB) was fermented successfully by A. eutrophus from the 4-hydrobutyric and butyric acid.7, 8 The physical property of P3/4HB is from semi-crystallization to amorphous elastomer depending on the 4-hydroxybutyrate (4HB) content.4 The PHBV may be too rigid and brittle and lack of superior mechanical properties, which are required for biomedical and packaging film applications. In contrast, P3/4HB is elastomeric but has very low elastic modulus.9 Several modifications have been proposed to improve their mechanical properties and processing of PHBV and P3/4HB, such as chemical modification and physical blending, in which blending is preferred because of the easy, fast, and low-cost working techniques. Many researches have been done to study the miscibility and the crystallization property of PHBV to expand the potential applications in industry. On one hand, previous researchers revealed that PHBV was miscible with poly(vinylidene fluoride), poly(epichlorohydrin-co-ethylene oxide), and cellulose acetate butyrate.10-12 On the other hand, PHBV was known as immiscible with other common type biodegradable polyesters such as poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(L-lactic acid), poly(butylene succinate), and poly(ethylene succinate).13-17 However, the mechanical property have not been significantly enhanced. Moreover, some functional monomers or polymers for example 4,4′-dihydroxydiphenyl propane, poly(p-vinyl phenol), and epoxidized natural rubber were used to blend with PHBV to study the crystallization property.18-20 The hydrogen bonding was formed between the functional group and the carbonyl of PHBV in these blends systems. These functional materials acted as a physical cross-linked agent, herein reducing the crystallization rate of PHBV.
Biopolymers are envisioned as the potential substitute of petroleum-based polymers. The growing cost of petroleum, alarming overuse of landfill sites and concerns for the environment are the factors stimulating the interest in biopolymers.1, 2 Furthermore the renewable resource origin of biopolymers and their biodegradability or compostability gives an advantage over conventional polymers.3, 4 These biopolymers are produced by the help of biological systems or biological materials.5 Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a group of bioplastics produced in nature by bacterial fermentation of sugars and lipids. These polyesters are formed as intracellular carbon storage compounds and energy reserves in bacteria such as Ralstonia eutropha (Alcaligenes eutrophus), Bacillus megaterium, Azotobacter chroococcum, etc. and have a wide range of values for properties such as elongation at break, strength and modulus.6-8 These advantages of PHAs render them potential substitutes for polyolefins. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) are the most important PHAs. It has been reported that PHB is a highly crystalline polymer with high melting point and brittleness. To overcome the shortcomings of PHB, copolymers have been developed. PHBV (Figure 1) is a copolymer of PHB having randomly arranged 3-hydroxybutyrate (HB) group and 3-hydroxyvalarate (HV) groups. The copolymer has higher flexibility and processability than PHB. Generally, the melting point and brittleness of the copolymer decreases with increases in the valerate content. Singh et al.9 have reported the low strength, low modulus and slow cooling rate of PHBV. To improve these properties of PHBV, its blends with poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), polyetherimide (PEI) thermoplastic starch (TPS), 4,4′-dihydroxydiphenylpropane (BPA) and p-tert-butylphenol (TBP), etc. have been studied.10-13
Many attempts were carried out to improve the performances of PHB, mostly by copolymerization of PHB with other monomers such as β-hydroxyvalerate (β-HV), 4-hydroxybutyrate (4-HB) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3-HHx). However, the copolymerization route compromises on the strength and E-Modulus of PHB, and results in even slower crystallization of the copolymerized materials. Alternatively, another approach by blending PHB with other (co)polymers such as ethylene propylene rubber (EPR) [13], poly(ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) (EVA) [14], epoxidized natural rubber (ENR) [15], poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) [16], poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) [17, 18], poly(propylene) (PP) [19], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [20] and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [21, 22] was applied in literature. Among these polymers, the PVAc, PEO and EVA with >85 wt% of vinyl acetate were reported to be miscible with PHB while the others are immiscible with PHB. Another polymer used to blend with PHB is poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), which is biodegradable under aerobic conditions and is a condensation polymer of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol [23]. Commercial grade of PBS, currently, is synthesized from oil-based feedstock, however, both of the two monomers, i.e. succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, can be derived from renewable resources via fermentation [24, 25]. Thus, PHB/PBS blends can potentially retain both biocompostable and renewable characteristics. Qiu et al. [26, 27] blended poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) with PHB and PHBV in solution. They reported that PHB and PHBV were immiscible with PBS except the PHB/PBS (20/80) blend which showed limited miscibility. The incorporation of PBS restricted the crystallization of PHB and PHBV to a certain extent. In our previous work, the toughness and the strength of the PHB and PHBV were remarkably enhanced by incorporation of PBS in combination with an in situ compatibilization using dicumyl peroxide as a free radical initiator [28]. However, to the authors’ knowledge, the morphology and crystallization behavior of melt-blended PHB/PBS which are more environmentally friendly and more industrial feasible have not been widely studied yet. The prime objective of this paper is to increase the over all crystallization of the PHB by melt blending with PBS. The results of an investigation concerning of the phase morphology of the blends, the crystallization and melting behavior of the PHB in the presence of PBS are discussed.
The polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) is the mostly studied biosynthesis material among all polyhydroxyalkanoates because of its early appearance in the 1920’s and particular biodegradation/biocompatibility properties [1-8]. Many applications of PHB have been proposed to take advantage of the mentioned bio-properties, but the wide acceptance of PHB is generally blocked by its relatively high cost, low toughness, and inferior thermal stability. As known, PHB usually has a high crystallinity, but a slow crystallization rate and significant post secondary crystallization whereas which could form irregular pores in the material, impair the flexibility of amorphous chains, and then decrease the toughness. A lot of methods such as annealing the molded PHB at a high temperature, cold-drawing of PHB, blending PHB with thermoplastics (e. g., cellulose, polyethylene, polyesters, poly(vinyl chloride), poly(methyl methacrylate), poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(lactic acid), poly(cis-1,4-isoprene), poly(vinyl acetate), poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(vinylidene fluoride), poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(ethylene oxide), epoxidized natural rubber, etc.), adding low molecular weight plasticizers/nucleating agents into PHB, and copolymerizing PHB with flexible constituents (e. g., 3-hydroxyvalerate and 3-hydroxyhexanoate) were proposed to change the crystallization behaviors and subsequently improve the toughness of PHB [6-16].

The development of biobased and biodegradable polymers as potential substitutes for plastics from fossil resources is an emerging field of research and development. In recent years, different types of biodegradable polymers have attracted much attention for developing various new polymeric materials with reduced environmental impacts [1], [2]. Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are derived from renewable resources and are fully biodegradable thermoplastics [3]. They are aliphatic biopolyesters naturally produced via a microbial process on sugar-based medium, and act as a source of carbon and energy storage for microorganisms [4], [5]. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is one of the most widely studied PHA polymers due to its potential use in packaging, automotive, biomedical, and agricultural applications because of its natural origin, biocompatibility, and thermoplastic behavior [6]. However, PHBV shows some drawbacks such as its high crystallinity and brittleness [7]. Moreover, its degradation temperature close to its melting temperature [8] makes it difficult to process. Various solutions have been proposed to solve the above problems, including physical blending, or block copolymerization [9]. Blending PHBV with other polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [4], [10], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) [11], [12], poly(propylene carbonate) [13], poly(caprolactone) (PCL) [14] and poly(ethylene succinate) (PES) [15] represent interesting routes to control the properties of PHBV. Another polymer that can be used to blend with PHBV is poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [16], [17], [18]. PBS is a thermoplastic polyester synthesized through the polycondensation reaction of 1,4-butanediol with succinic acid. This polymer has high flexibility, excellent impact strength, thermal and chemical resistance [19]. It can be processed easily and it is thus a good candidate for blending with PHBV. In this respect, Qiu et al. [16] blended PHBV with PBS in solution using chloroform. They reported that PHBV and PBS are immiscible and the crystallization rate of PHBV was decreased by adding PBS, although its crystallization mechanism did not change significantly. Ma et al. [17] studied the in-situ compatibilization of PHBV/PBS and PHB/PBS blends in the presence of dicumyl peroxide (DCP). During processing, DCP initiated a free-radical reaction between PHBV and PBS (and also PHB and PBS) forming PHBV-g-PBS copolymers which subsequently acted as compatibilizer and partially cross-linked networks in the blends. The size of PBS particles in PHBV or PHB decreased significantly accompanied by an improvement of the interfacial adhesion. Consequently, the mechanical properties of the PHBV/PBS and PHB/PBS blends were significantly improved. Many strategies were developed to compatibilize polymer blends. An interesting one is the use of targeted and modified inorganic micro and nano-fillers. The effects of fillers on the morphology and structural properties of the blends vary depending on their geometry, chemical composition and modification which influence significantly their location in the blend microstructure [20]. Zembouai et al. [21] studied the effect of organomodified montmorillonite (OMMT) Cloisite 30B (C30B) with and without compatibilizer, maleic anhydride-grafted-PHBV (PHBV-g-MA), on the morphology and properties of PHBV/PLA blends prepared by melt mixing. The results showed that C30B enhances the thermal stability and improves the tensile properties of the blends such as Young’s modulus. Further, a synergistic effect of compatibilizer and C30B was highlighted, leading to an improved miscibility of the two blend components. Bittmann et al. [22] investigated the properties of PHBV/PBAT blends as well as the effect of C30B on the morphology and thermal behavior of the blends. The results revealed a good dispersion of C30B in the polymer blend. They also showed that C30B enhances the thermal stability, delays the crystallization of PHBV and accelerates its melting and increases the crystallinity of PHBV. Mofokeng et al. [23] studied the morphology, thermal stability and thermal degradation kinetics of melt-mixed PHBV/PCL blends filled with titanium(IV) oxide (TiO2) nanoparticles. They showed a well dispersion of TiO2 in both polymers with the presence of some aggregates. They found that the presence of TiO2 enhanced the thermal stability of PHBV and PCL.
Poly (Butylene Adipate‐Co‐Terephthalate) (PBAT) - Based Biocomposites: A Comprehensive Review Many efforts have been made to develop sustainable bio-based and biodegradable polymers for packaging, automotive, electrical & electronics, household, agriculture, and biomedical application. Commercially available poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) has gained much attention due to its comparable mechanical properties as compared to polyolefin along with excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability.1-5 As one of the members of the PHA family, PHBV is a copolymer of PHB with randomly arranged 3-hydroxybutyrate (HB) groups and 3-hydroxyvalarate (HV) groups and synthesized by various microorganisms.6, 7 It can be efficiently degraded into carbon dioxide and water by microorganisms in the most biologically active environment.8, 9 Consequently, PHBV has been considered to be one of the good alternatives for petroleum-based synthetic polymers. However, the applications of PHBV are limited by its brittleness, low impact strength, low thermal stability, and low melt elastic strength.10-13 The mechanical properties of PHBV need to be improved to widen its applications. Many attempts and strategies have been conducted to modify PHBV to improve its mechanical properties without affecting its biodegradability. PHBV is this material produced from renewable feedstock and demonstrates excellent biodegradability. Resolving the brittleness of PHBV without sacrificing its biodegradability is a great challenge. The shortage of the mechanical properties of PHBV can be effectively balanced by melt compounding with tough components. Blending PHBV with other bio-based and biodegradable polymers is an alternative approach to enhance its properties, which exhibit superior thermal and mechanical properties over pure PHBV. Studies have been carried out on compounding PHBV with PBS,14, 15 thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU),16 poly lactides (PLA),17 poly (propylene carbonate) (PPC),18 poly (ethylene succinate) (PES),19 and Poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG).20 While the effects on the toughness of the PHBV blends were far from satisfactory.
Most studies that have been published on obtaining a polyhydroxyalkanoate bionanocomposite involve the copolymer poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV), which has a processing window larger than that of PHB, and its properties are very similar to those of polyethylene. With respect to the PHB bionanocomposite, the results show that there is a nucleation effect depending on the different organically modified clays studied (Na-montmorillonite and 30B-montmorillonite) that increases the elastic modulus of PHB according to the melt-blending method.20 In other work, bionanocomposites were obtained by the film-casting method, and it was determined that there is a minimal effect on the degree of crystallization and melting temperature when PHBV is used to work with clays like Na-montmorillonite and modified montmorillonite (Cloisite 15A and C93A).16 Another way to improve the properties of polyhydroxyalkanoates is by blending them with other polymers. The best candidate for polymer blending with PHB is starch, as it is widely available, inexpensive, and biodegradable.21, 22 Starch is mostly composed of linear amylase and branched amylopectin; both are composed of α-D(1,4′)-glucan repeating units, but amylopectin has a large number of α-1,6′-linked branch points.23 However, starch itself is unfavorable in terms of processing ability and mechanical properties. Therefore, native starch is submitted to thermal and mechanical treatment to obtain thermoplastic starch (TPS).21 Studies regarding blends of PHB with TPS show that it can produce an elastic modulus with a wide range of values, providing the concentration of starch or TPS granules is less than or equal to that of PHB.24 The thermal degradation of the blend is similar to that of PHB, and the degree of crystallinity increases compared to PHB at lower TPS concentrations (less than 20% wt/wt).24 The only way to obtain significant improvement of the PHB properties is to improve the interaction between PHB and starch. This can be achieved by obtaining a bionanocomposite of PHB with starch and clay, as some studies state that montmorillonite improves the interfacial adhesion between PHBV and starch, thus improving the mechanical properties and increasing the biodegradability with respect to PHBV.25

The semicrystalline, bacterially synthesized polymer, poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), is a member of the polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) family, which contains ester functional groups in the main chain (Fig. 1(a)) [1]. PHB has received keen interest because of its environmentally friendly properties [[2], [3], [4]]. PHB is a 100% biodegradable material; it can be broken down into small sections over a wide range of temperatures, even at low temperatures around 60 °C with a moisture level of 55% [5]. PHB is a biocompatible material for medical applications because it is stored in the cell envelope eukaryotes [[6], [7], [8]]. However, PHB also has some undesirable properties, such as high rigidity due to a high degree of crystallinity of approximately 60-80%, and limited operating temperature, which is a stumbling block to its production [5,9,10]. Therefore, in order to mitigate such undesirable properties and improve the physical properties of PHB, many efforts have been invested, such as toward the development of polymer blends including PHB. Numerous studies on polymer blends containing PHB have been continuously reported over the decades [[11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]]. One of the most interesting blends is between PHB and poly(4-vinylphenol) (PVPh) (Fig. 1(b)). PVPh is an amorphous polymer, which has been identified as an OH-group-containing polymer that reduces the crystallinity of PHB [17]. By confirming the single glass transition temperature (Tg) and the negative values of the equilibrium melting point for various blending ratios, the PHB/PVPh blends were shown to be a miscible system [11].
The blending effect of PVAc in the PHBV ring-banded spherulite was discussed. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) is known as a biodegradable semicrystalline polyester and has attracted much attention in ring-banded spherulite studies due to its very large spherulitic dimensions [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. However, owing to its mechanical fragility, it has not been used extensively as an industrial material. 3-Hydroxyvalerate (3HV) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3HHx), as a comonomer, have been introduced into PHB for overcoming its brittleness and displaying a broad range of thermal and mechanical properties by varying its comonomer content [6], [7], [8]. Within a certain temperature range, PHB, poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV), and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co- 3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx) spherulites all exhibit double extinction ringed patterns observed under a polarized optical microscope (POM) [1], [3], [4], [9], [10], [11], [12]. The width and regularity of its band spacing strongly depend on the crystallization temperature (Tc). Furthermore, regarding X-ray diffraction analyses, PHBV random copolymers show high crystallinity (>50%) in all compositions from 0 to 95 mol% 3HV. PHBV copolymers crystallize in the lattice same as PHB homopolymer (orthorhombic lattice with a = 0.576 nm, b = 1.320 nm, c = 0.596 nm) with compositions from 0 to 37 mol% 3HV while it crystallize in the lattice of poly(3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHV, orthorhombic lattice with a = 0.950 nm, b = 1.010 nm, c = 0.556 nm) with compositions higher than 53 mol% 3HV, and in between these two ranges mixed crystals of PHB and PHV lattices are generated, respectively [6], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]. Cocrystallization behavior and isomorphism of PHBV have also been confirmed by solid-state NMR analyses [18], [19]. VanderHart et al. reported that the PHB and PHV type lattice structures were detected in as-received 27 mol% 3HV PHBV samples [19]. There are several published works concerning the physical properties of PHB and PHBV (with 3HV composition less than 27 mol%) banded spherulites [1], [3], [4], [5], [20], [21]. We give below a very brief survey of some of the principal findings of previous workers as they relate to this study. Ring-banded spherulites growing on the glass plate show alternating circular ridges and valleys in radial direction at the surface [21]. The a-axis of the crystal unit cell is radial oriented in the whole banded spherulites and the b- and c-axes are oriented to the tangential direction of the banded spherulite at the valley and ridge areas, respectively [1], [3], [4], [5], [20]. After the healing and reorganization of the bone in the fracture gap, common implants made from stainless steel or titanium alloys have to be removed in a second surgery [2-4]. In addition, stress-shielding effects can lead to an implant-induced osteopenia and an increase in cortical porosity [5]. To avoid or reduce both negative aspects of conventional materials, the development of biodegradable implant materials based on magnesium alloys has been the focus of research in recent years [6, 7], as common degradable polymers are not suitable for load-bearing applications due to insufficient mechanical stability [8]. In contrast, magnesium alloys, with an elastic modulus closer to natural bone, exceed the stability and Young's modulus of polymers [9] and therefore are promising implant materials for this application [10-14]. The degradation rate of the implant has to be consistent with the bone healing processes. A first stable initial fixation under a functional load should be replaced by a predictable step-by-step degradation of the material and a substitution with bone in the cortical area. Magnesium as a co-factor for many biological functions [15] is considered to be relatively safe [10]. While high-purity magnesium shows the slowest degradation [16, 17], the degradation rate of Mg-alloys depends on the alloy composition [18, 19]. The most commonly used magnesium alloys include zinc (Zn) [13, 20-24] or rare earths (RE) [12, 19, 25, 26] as alloying elements, although their innocuousness is not definitively proven [27-29]. Within Mg-alloys, Zn and RE improve strength and, depending on the alloy's composition, reduce the corrosion rate [30, 31]. In recent studies, various RE- or Zn-containing alloys showed good biocompatibility [12, 19, 24, 25, 30, 32]. The magnesium alloy ZEK100 contains Zn and RE as alloying elements; ZEK100-plates have already been evaluated in a Hanks' balanced salt solution in vitro [33] and ZEK100-pins intramedullary in rabbit tibia in vivo [34, 35] as a potential biodegradable implant material for osteosynthesis due to their good mechanical characteristics. However, their biocompatibility was not finally approved, because an increased bone reactive capacity was observed in the implant surrounding of the ZEK100-pins after a 6 month implantation period [36]. Subsequent investigations by Dziuba et al did not recommend ZEK100 for biomedical use as these intramedullary implanted pins induced adverse host reactions after 9 and 12 month investigation periods [35]. However, these investigations consider intramedullary implantation [36, 35]. Their degradation properties, as well as host responses like inflammatory reactions or removal of degradation products, might be different in other locations. Relating to a surgical procedure, initiation, resolution and organization as first sign of the acute host response are normally followed by the immigration of immuno-inflammatory cells, which infiltrate the implant adjacencies. Furthermore, various cellular and tissue responses can be associated with an implanted degrading biomaterial [37, 38]. These reactions in the implant surrounding have to be examined to assess the implant's biocompatibility, and can differ depending on the implant location [36, 39].

Environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, UV exposure, and the presence of microorganisms further influence the rate and extent of biodegradation. Abiotic processes, driven by environmental conditions like heat and sunlight, cause polymer fragmentation into smaller particles. However, complete mineralization into CO2, H2O, and biomass requires microbial activity (biotic degradation), which involves enzymatic depolymerization of bioplastics. This distinction is critical, as abiotic processes alone can leave persistent particles in the environment. The evaluation of biodegradability employs various methods, including CO2 evolution, CH4 production, and weight loss. These metrics highlight the need for standardized protocols that better reflect real-world degradation conditions. ground_truth: Bioactive glass particles release ions (Ca, P, Si) as they degrade. These ions interact with physiological fluids to form a hydroxyapatite layer on the scaffold surface, which bonds to bone. Additionally, the ions (especially Si) can stimulate osteoblast gene expression, actively promoting bone regeneration (osteoconduction and osteoinduction).

Based solely on the provided evidence, bioactive glass fillers enhance biodegradable bone scaffolds through several key mechanisms:

1.  **Ion Release and Bioactivity:** Bioactive glass degrades over time, releasing soluble ions (e.g., calcium, silica). These ions promote bone formation by activating bone growth and stimulating osteoprogenitor cells at the genetic level. Importantly, they induce a specific reaction forming a hydroxyapatite (HA) layer on the scaffold surface, enabling direct bone bonding (osteoconduction) and integration [1, 5, 8, 11, 14]. This osteoconductive ability is lacking in many polymers alone [1, 8].

2.  **Mechanical Reinforcement:** Incorporating bioactive glass particles or fibers into biodegradable polymer matrices (like PCL, PLA, chitosan, gelatin) significantly enhances the composite scaffold's mechanical properties, including compressive strength and modulus, making them more suitable for load-bearing applications compared to the weaker polymers alone [1, 3, 4, 8, 13]. 3.  **Degradation Control:** The dissolution rate of bioactive glass can be tailored based on its composition (e.g., silicate vs. phosphate glasses) and structure (e.g., sol-gel glasses have inherent nanoporosity increasing surface area), influencing the overall scaffold degradation kinetics to better match bone healing rates [2, 5, 11, 14]. Phosphate glasses offer highly controllable degradation rates [2]. Nanopores in sol-gel glasses accelerate degradation via increased cellular interaction [5].

4.  **Enhanced Biocompatibility and Osteogenesis:** The dissolution products and the bioactive surface created by bioactive glass improve cell response. Bioactive glass enhances cell adhesion, proliferation, migration, differentiation (particularly of stem cells and osteoblasts), and extracellular matrix mineralization [1, 3, 11, 14, 15]. Nanoscale particles further enhance cell adhesion and biological properties due to mimicking bone's nanostructure [5, 13].

Moreover, ensuring biological compatibility and biofunctionality is critical. Although nanocellulose possesses inherent biocompatibility, the inclusion of modifications and additives during the fabrication process of nanocellulose-based hydrogels can disrupt its interactions with cells and tissues. This disruption can have significant effects on cell viability, proliferation, and differentiation in the hydrogel matrix, which are essential factors for successful tissue regeneration. Additionally, nanocellulose-based hydrogels should degrade at a rate compatible with tissue regeneration while maintaining structural integrity during the healing process. Balancing biodegradation and stability is challenging and requires precise control over hydrogel composition, crosslinking density, and degradation kinetics. Rapid degradation may lead to premature loss of mechanical support, while slow degradation can impede tissue remodeling and integration. Calcium release from BG can be temporarily stored in polymers like alginate, achieving controlled ion release [13].

Plastics are synthetic polymer compounds made substantially from petrochemical materials extracted from coal, oil, and natural gas.[1] In general, fossil fuel plastics achieve high mechanical and fluid barrier properties by packing their chains into specific crystalline and amorphous regions. However, its hydrophobic and long-chain structural features make it lack bio-accessible organic chemical groups, limiting the ability of microorganisms to break them down.[2] The accumulation of fossil fuel plastics in the environment has severely affected soil quality, the aquatic environment, flora, and fauna.[3] The depletion of fossil fuels and environmental pollution have prompted researchers to develop eco-friendly biodegradable polymers to replace petrochemical-based polymers. In this context, bioplastics appear as a promising alternative. A bioplastic is often considered bio-based and/or biodegradable material[4, 5] such as polyvinyl alcohol, polylactic acid, polybutylene succinate, as well as carbohydrate derivatives and blends based on protein, starch, chitin, and cellulose. The global market size for bioplastics is considered to burgeon every day. The global production capacity of bioplastics in 2023 was ≈2.18 million tonnes, which is projected to expand to 7.43 million tonnes by 2028.[6] This shows that bioplastics have great application value and development prospects in various fields of modern society. Currently, PLA is the most important among the biobased biodegradable plastics because of its zero toxicity, biodegradability, and good mechanical attributes.[7] PLA is produced by the polymerization of lactides or lactic acid monomers fermented from starch, mainly used in 3D printing, food packaging, transport, agriculture, and textile industries.[8] Upon biodegradation, PLA releases CO2, water, and decomposed organic matter without leaving any visible and toxic residues.[7] These substances are absorbed by plants, thus imparting less carbon footprint. Blending the protein with biodegradable synthetic polymers has been shown to be an effective strategy to improve performances,[21-23] but whether this is related to nucleation effects still remains unclear. In recent decades, biobased polymers have drawn attention from both academia and industry to find more sustainable alternatives to replace conventional dominant fossil-based polymers[1], [2]. Biobased polymers are derived from renewable resources such as agricultural products and organic waste streams[3]. Generally, biobased polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and bioethylene-based polymers, have a lower carbon footprint, in terms of greenhouse gas emission, compared to their fossil based alternatives[4]. However, greenhouse gas emissions are not the only current threat to fossil-based commodity plastics. Polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride, polyurethanes and polyethylene terephthalate take account for 75 % of the plastic production worldwide and are resistant to biodegradation [5], [6], [7]. Improper waste management or dumping of these plastics in landfills can therefore lead to marine, fresh water and soil pollution [8], [9], [10]. However, their accumulation in the environment is not the main pitfall of their resistance to biodegradation since adequate waste handling and recycling of these materials could limit this. A growing concern of nonbiodegradable polymers is the formation of microplastics. These environmental contaminants are smaller than 5 mm and originates from different sources, including personal care products, paints, washing wastewater, rubber tires, and macroplastics (>5 mm), such as bottles and bags, which can break into smaller pieces[11], [12]. These microplastic have properties similar to those of their original products, i.e., high stability and long residence time, and might end up in the food chain and lead to exposure to toxic contaminants and additives[13]. This means that even during use and proper waste management, plastic particles might still end up in the environment and could lead to serious threats. Therefore, an optimum should be found between polymer performance, durability and the rate of biodegradation. Aliphatic polyesters are a class of polymers that can be enzymatically hydrolyzed and some polymers are prone to biodegradation[14], [15]. Examples include polybutylene succinate (PBS) and polycaprolactone (PCL), which are used for agricultural and biomedical applications [16], [17], [18]. However, aliphatic polyesters are prone to hydrolytic degradation, have generally limited thermal and mechanical properties, require additives or need to be blended with other polymers, although it is dependent on the application [16], [19].

These strategies can potentially be utilized in industries associated with polymeric fiber applications to positively impact its business. For instance, corn starch which is a significant ingredient used in the manufacture of biodegradable plastics, can be easily broken down when in contact with water in a matter of weeks.[110]
Petroleum-based polymers are extensively used in packaging, automobile industries, and construction [3]. The excessive use of these polymers has created environmental problems, such as the “plastic plague” and an increase in greenhouse gas emissions. To address environmental issues resulting from the excessive use of petroleum-based plastic and societies’ transition from the single-use economy to a circular economy, researchers are developing bio-based sustainable materials that can be alternative to petroleum-based plastics. PLA is the most commonly used thermoplastic biopolymer produced from glucose derived from corn-starch, sugarcane, and sugar beets [[2], [3], [4], [5]]. It is a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer widely used for 3D printing applications primarily because of the lower glass transition and melting temperature compared to common thermoplastic polymers used for 3D printing and its non-adherence to printing surfaces [4,[6], [7], [8]]. Despite useful features, its brittle nature, low toughness, moisture sensitivity, and comparatively higher cost limit its broader applications [3,6]. On the other hand, lignin is the second most abundant biomaterial after cellulose. It is available in relatively large amounts as a byproduct from pulp and paper and potentially from the 2nd generation bioethanol industries [[9], [10], [11]]. A large portion of annually produced lignin is burnt to generate energy [9]. Due to lignin's heterogeneous-complex structure, and properties like low-purity standard, odor, and color issues, and the need for some form of physical and chemical modifications before its use, only 2% of annually produced lignin is used for preparing carbon fibers, chemicals, adhesives, plastics, and composites. However, most of those applications still lack successful commercialization [6,9,12]. Blending PLA with lignin to produce composite filaments for 3D printing is a promising bio-based option that could increase lignin utilization other than burning for energy. The use of lignin as a feedstock in the biopolymer manufacturing helps its valorization. Additionally, incorporating lignin in PLA decreases its (PLA) amount being used and reduces filaments' overall cost. It was found that adding 15 wt% rice straw (US$ 0.28/kg) in ABS filament decreased the overall cost of the filament production that included additional processing costs [13]. Several studies were carried out regarding incorporating lignin in the PLA matrix to form composite filaments for 3D printing making it evident that lignin's addition often leads to a decrease in tensile strength and elongation [3,6,9]. Filaments with poor properties will be the death of successful commercialization efforts. There is still a lack of studies done regarding the enhancement of PLA-lignin composite filaments' properties. Various strategies were found from literature to be applied for enhancing the properties of polymer-lignin composite filaments, such as modifying lignin, adding plasticizers, and carbon fibers [1,12,14].
