The improved PLA has wider applications in the electronics and automotive fields. IntroductionThe severity and range of the impacts of global climate change on our lives are not yet fully realized. Plastic consumption is one of several factors affecting global climate change. The life cycle of plastic and plastic waste mismanagement generate enormous amounts of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. When exposed to sunlight, discarded plastic wastes emit GHG i.e., methane and ethylene etc. and also decompose to microplastics that contaminate soil, air, and water resources [1]. In several countries around the world, disposing of plastic waste by burning it in the open is a common practice that produces serious air pollution in the form of carbon dioxide, black carbon, and fine particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5). The mismanagement of plastic waste has now become a major and urgent development challenge. To solve these problems, bio-circular-green (BCG) approaches are needed. The replacement of conventional plastics with fully biodegradable polymers should be seriously supported by all public and private enterprises [2]. One of the most promising biodegradable plastics for use in packaging, medicine, textiles, and automotive production is polylactide (PLA) [3].PLA has outstanding properties in terms of high modulus and stiffness, transparency, easy processing, excellent biocompatibility, and full biodegradability in a few weeks [4,5]. However, for some applications, PLA also has limitations, such as poor ductility, low impact resistance, high cost compared to conventional plastics, low thermal stability, and slow crystallization rate [6,7]. PLA also has poor flame retardancy and generates heavy melt dripping during the burning process, leading to fire-spreading hazards [8]. The fire resistance of PLA has been improved by numerous studies up to this point. Since IFR systems are effective and free of halogens, the majority of them are concentrating on employing them. An acid supply, a blowing agent, and a carbonization source make up the IFRs' typical main three components. By forming char as a result of the interaction of these components, PLA's flammability is decreased since the char shields the underlying materials from heat and oxygen. Furthermore, certain other flame retardants, such as additives containing silicon, inorganic materials, and phosphorus, were combined with PLA. However, adding flame retardants, particularly IFRs, typically results in PLA having worse mechanical and processing properties. In order to increase the flame retardancy of PLA, Zhang et al. [8] studied the intumescent flame retardant system employing ammonium polyphosphate (APP) and urea-modified lignin. They claimed that while the urea-modified lignin and APP composites had outstanding flame retardancy and thermal stability, the mechanical characteristics had been significantly reduced due to the weak interfacial adhesion between the PLA and IFR. More intumescent flame retardants added to an IFR system typically result in greater incompatibility with the polymer and worse mechanical qualities. To improve the flame resistance of polymers, a flame retardant alone needs to be used at a reasonably high percentage, which has an impact on other properties. This is a research gap that needs to be filled immediately. Additionally, these limitations prevent PLA from being widely used in the home décor, electronics, and automotive industries [9,10]. The materials' ability to resist fire is significantly improved by the addition of these flame retardants, but the mechanical and processing qualities are severely compromised. Therefore, a compromise between the flame retardant and mechanical properties of PLA must be found, and this is the main goal of this research. This will be a different approach to enhancing PLA's flame retardant qualities and substituting for the IFR system.To overcome the disadvantages of PLA, various research efforts have focused on three effective routes: (1) chemical modification of the polymeric structure of PLA; (2) blending PLA with other biodegradable polymers such as poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [11,12], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) [13], polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) [14], and polycarbonate (PC) [15]; and (3) combining PLA with additives, such as plasticizers [[16], [17], [18]], fibers [19], activated biochar [20], and microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) [21]. Compared to the chemical modification route, blending and/or combining PLA with additives are practical and inexpensive techniques that enhance the relevant properties. Based on our previous works, an effective way of striking a balance between desirable mechanical performance and flame retardancy is to combine PLA with a bio-based reinforcing filler and an appropriate additive [13]. Specifically, in this study, we enhance the fire resistance and impact toughness of PLA by using tricresyl phosphate (TCP), which acts as both flame retardant and plasticizer, combined with a bio-filler of MCC.MCC is the particulate form of cellulose extracted from several cellulosic resources such as bagasse [22], pineapple [23,24], soybean [25], flax and hemp [26], and oil palm empty fruit bunch (OPEFB) [27]. Oil palm is one of the most important crops in Thailand and is the raw material for the palm oil industries. Oil palm production processes generate large quantities of waste in the form of palm kernel shells, oil palm trunks, and OPEFB that cannot be easily disposed of. OPEFB is composed of 41-47 % cellulose, 25-34 % hemicellulose, and 28-32 % lignin [27]. Thus, the OPEFB waste in Thailand is potentially a cheaper source of MCC than other feedstocks and was selected as a raw material in this study.Using MCC as a bio-filler for PLA composite supports the BCG economic model in several ways and can help solve the mismanagement of waste. MCC offers high mechanical strength, low density, low cost, non-toxicity, renewability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability [28]. On the other hand, the high polarity of MCC, due to the many hydroxyl groups in its chemical structure, is an obstacle to properly combining PLA and MCC. The difference between more polar MCC and less polar PLA caused phase separation and poor compatibility, which led to a final product with worse properties than pure PLA [29]. Therefore, surface modification must be done before mixing MCC with PLA. Polyelectrolytes, physical surfactant adsorption, graft polymerization, and chemical coupling processes can all be used to surface-modify MCC [30], but chemical treatments are more efficient than physical ones [[31], [32], [33]]. According to Zhou et al. [33], cellulose was successfully chemically altered employing reactive chemicals as feasible adsorbents. In an oil bath at a high temperature, the cellulose and reactive chemical were heated in a 1:10 ratio while adding the polar solvent dimethylacetamide (DMA). Without solvents and at high temperatures in the reaction media, most chemical treatments of MCC are challenging to complete, but solvents pose additional challenges and have a higher negative impact on the environment due to their toxicity, flammability, and ease of volatilization. An alternative method of chemically modifying MCC without a solvent is necessary for an eco-friendly and sustainable process. The solvent-free chemical modification of MCC can be done with maleic anhydride (MA), due to its low melting point at about 45 to 50 °C [32]. The hydroxyl groups in MCC covalently bond with anhydride in MA, forming strongly reactive ester linkages.As a result, MCC from OPEFB waste (OPMC) was chemically altered in this work using molten MA via a solvent-free and low temperature heating technique and employed as a bio-based reinforcing filler in PLA composite with a TCP addition. The physical and morphological properties of MAMC were characterized and compared to those of OPMC. In terms of scalability, the solvent-free, low-temperature heating approach is the most effective for creating MAMC. The influences of TCP content and the ratio of TCP and MAMC on the properties and flame retardancy of the PLA composite are investigated. The combined usage of these materials can develop an eco-friendly prototype product, support effective waste management, and help reduce plastic consumption. In the recent years, the excess use and disposals of petroleum derived polymeric composites becomes a serious threats to the environment. The preparation of sustainable composites from the renewable resources, use of biodegradable polymers which can replace the nondegradable materials are the effective methods to minimise the problems. The use of PLA in the preparation of the composites is an ideal alternatives and have gained the significant interest due to its multiple advantages like biodegradability, biocompatibility and bio-absorbable nature [1,2,3,4,5,6]. The most advantageous part of the PLA is that it is one of the renewable resources that can be used in the preparation of the composites which can replace the synthetic polymers [7]. The PLA based composites exhibited better mechanical strength and easy processability compared to other natural polymeric based composites [8, 9]. However, the major drawbacks of PLA based composites are higher cost and brittle character which limits its use for many advanced applications [10]. Different effort has been made for developing the overall properties of the PLA based composites and reduce the cost of the production [11]. Among the different methods, physical blending with the natural fiber is an effective method to improve the properties and reduce the cost. Incorporation of natural fiber into the PLA matrix is one of the significant method to upgrade the properties of the composites [12,13,14,15]. Also, the usage of these natural resources in the preparation or modification of the composites has gained significant attention due to the increase environmental issue. Incorporation of natural fibers like bamboo fiber or wood fiber with the thermosets or thermoplastics results superior mechanical properties [16]. Among different natural fibers, bamboo fibers are the extensively used structural material because of its gradient structure in the radial direction, easy availability, cost effective and advanced materialistic properties [9, 17, 18]. The bamboo fiber mainly composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin which can be used as the reinforcing agent. These are biodegradable, nonabrasive, having high specific properties like high modulus, high strength high toughness and load bearing capacity which significantly increases its application potential [19,20,21]. These low cost bamboo species are abundant in the North-Eastern region of India and can be fully exploit in the preparation of PLA composites which can significantly decreases the cost of PLA based composites without compromising the properties [22].
Traditional petroleum-based plastics, polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC), are widely used in various fields due to their low manufacturing cost, high mechanical strength, and good processability [1], [2], [3]. These high molecular weight polymers with strong hydrophobicity and stable chemical properties are not degraded easily by microorganisms. To ensure the ultraviolet radiation does not damage the polymer's performance during its service life, they are often provided with a protective coating, making them very durable. However, the process allows them to persist and accumulate in large quantities in nature over time, resulting in “white pollution” [4], [5]. Degradable plastics, including thermoplastic starch (TPS), polylactic acid (PLA) and polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT), can be oxidized and decomposed into environmentally harmless CO2 under the action of enzymes and H2O2. The commercial production capacity of biodegradable plastics worldwide is increasing annually, and its output value accounted for about 25-30 % of the entire plastics market in 2020. Replacing petroleum-based plastics with biodegradable plastics is a green alternative in line with human development [6], [7]. PLA is a high-molecular polymer formed by polycondensation of small-molecule lactic acid obtained from microbial fermentation of biomass raw materials such as corn or sugar cane. PLA has non-toxicity, good biocompatibility, and excellent machinability that can be applied in drug carriers, food packaging, and optoelectronic devices [8]. However, PLA also has inherent poor toughness, high brittleness, poor heat resistance, and high preparation cost, which limits its application market. Modification treatment, including the introduction of fillers, plasticizers and flexible polymer materials for blending or copolymerization, is an effective method to improve the performance of PLA [9], [10]. In addition, adding gelatin, nanoparticles, mixed oxides, and further regulating the nanostructure of the composites can also achieve highly functional applications in the fields of antibacterial, photocatalysis and pollution control [32], [33], [34], [35], [36]. Adding fiber fillers to PLA produces composites with controllable cost and excellent performance [37], [38], [39]. However, the bonding of untreated plant fibers and the PLA matrix interface is poor, so pretreatment methods for plant fibers are required, including acidic, alkaline, oxidative and enzymatic hydrolysis treatments [11], [12], [13], [16]. Oxidation treatment changes the chemical composition of plant fibers using oxidants such as ozone, hydrogen peroxide, and hypochlorite. Cellulose is reacted to obtain oxidized cellulose, while oxidized lignin and hemicellulose are partially removed. The functional groups are also changed during the oxidation reaction. The hydroxyl groups on the molecular chain are oxidized to aldehyde, ketone, or carboxyl groups, brings bleaching effects since removing some chromophoric groups. The oxidized wood fibers and oil palm mesocarp fibers are proved to improve the stiffness of the composites [14], [27], but the problems remain including high brittleness and poor toughness. The biodegradable elastomers polyanhydrides (PSA), polybutylene succinate (PBS), and polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) is expected to improve the toughness of PLA. PLA can break through its own limit and further elongate when subjected to tensile force after blended with the biodegradable elastomers, showing good elongation at break and impact strength. In addition, they also affected the crystallization process of PLA and changed the compositional structure of the composites [15], [43], [44]. The interfacial compatibility is poor resulting in a significant decrease in the tensile strength of the composite however, and it is necessary to add an expensive coupling agent to improve the performance when the two polymers are blended, such as titanate, maleic anhydride, and silane coupling agent [45], [46].

Issues related to the disposal of plastic waste derived from fossil fuels have determined a growing interest from scientific and industrial research in the development of materials with greater environmental sustainability. In order to tackle the waste disposal emergency, the European Commission has implemented a series of policies and introduced regulations that limit or prohibit the marketing of objects made with plastics derived from fossil fuels. Disposable objects such as straws, plates, cotton sticks, and cutlery will be completely banned from the market, starting from 2021. These products shall be made exclusively with low environmental impact materials.1 In this perspective, bioplastics are a potential alternative. These materials, as reported in recent EU communications on waste disposal may represent a valid strategy for waste reduction. Among biopolymers potentially suitable for the replacement of common plastic materials, poly (lactic acid) polymers (PLA) stand out. Compared to other biopolymers, PLA has good mechanical strength, good toughness and moderate thermal characteristics. In terms of availability on the market, it is characterized by the greater variety and availability of commercial grades. Although this material has a lower market price than most biopolymers, the comparison with common fossil-fuel plastics is unforgiving and strongly discourages the use of PLA. It should also be noted that some processing technologies, such as cast extrusion and thermoforming used for the manufacturing of disposable objects have an important percentage of process waste. Recovery of post-process materials (i.e., the waste from the production process), in combination with the virgin polymer is a common practice for fossil-fuel plastics, and properties of the final product are not altered in the process. Liu et al.13 studied the use of a chain extender with PLA. This study showed that the chemical reaction between the functional groups of the additive and the polymeric matrix increased the molecular weight and viscosity of the polymer. This approach allows to restore rheological properties of the material affected by processability loss due to thermo-degradation phenomena.

In recent decades, biobased polymers have drawn attention from both academia and industry to find more sustainable alternatives to replace conventional dominant fossil-based polymers[1], [2]. Biobased polymers are derived from renewable resources such as agricultural products and organic waste streams[3]. Generally, biobased polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and bioethylene-based polymers, have a lower carbon footprint, in terms of greenhouse gas emission, compared to their fossil based alternatives[4]. However, greenhouse gas emissions are not the only current threat to fossil-based commodity plastics. Polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride, polyurethanes and polyethylene terephthalate take account for 75 % of the plastic production worldwide and are resistant to biodegradation [5], [6], [7]. Improper waste management or dumping of these plastics in landfills can therefore lead to marine, fresh water and soil pollution [8], [9], [10]. However, their accumulation in the environment is not the main pitfall of their resistance to biodegradation since adequate waste handling and recycling of these materials could limit this. A growing concern of nonbiodegradable polymers is the formation of microplastics. These environmental contaminants are smaller than 5 mm and originates from different sources, including personal care products, paints, washing wastewater, rubber tires, and macroplastics (>5 mm), such as bottles and bags, which can break into smaller pieces[11], [12]. These microplastic have properties similar to those of their original products, i.e., high stability and long residence time, and might end up in the food chain and lead to exposure to toxic contaminants and additives[13]. This means that even during use and proper waste management, plastic particles might still end up in the environment and could lead to serious threats. Therefore, an optimum should be found between polymer performance, durability and the rate of biodegradation. Aliphatic polyesters are a class of polymers that can be enzymatically hydrolyzed and some polymers are prone to biodegradation[14], [15]. Examples include polybutylene succinate (PBS) and polycaprolactone (PCL), which are used for agricultural and biomedical applications [16], [17], [18]. However, aliphatic polyesters are prone to hydrolytic degradation, have generally limited thermal and mechanical properties, require additives or need to be blended with other polymers, although it is dependent on the application [16], [19].

Typical parameters are energy demand (ED), fossil resource depletion (FRD), agricultural land occupation (ALO), climate change (CC), human toxicity (HT), global warming impact (GWI), ozone depletion (OD), photochemical ozone formation (POF), freshwater ecotoxicity (FE), Ionizing radiation (IR), photochemical oxidant formation (POF), terrestrial acidification (TA), marine ecotoxicity (ME), freshwater, marine and terrestrial eutrophication (FEU, MEU, TEU) as well as particulate matter (PM), abiotic depletion potential(ADP), acidification potential (AP) [25]. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most important bioplastics on the global market and accounts for 20.5% of the total amount of bioplastics produced annually.1 Despite good mechanical properties and high availability, the use is inhibited by the high price compared to polyolefins. One way to solve this problem is to add low-cost fillers such as native starch.2 The use of starch is accompanied by a change in the mechanical, thermal, and structural properties, but also leads to an improvement in the carbon footprint.3 By saving PLA, not only costs can be reduced, but also the energy that must be expended for the synthesis. Starch, on the other hand, already binds CO2 during the plant growth phase.2, 4 Composites of starch types from different origins have already been produced. In addition to potato starch, rice, tapioca and corn starch were also used.5-18 The addition of native starch to a PLA matrix leads to an embrittlement and thus a decrease in tensile strength and elongation at break, with an increasing effect with rising starch content.3, 13 Due to their properties, PLA starch composites are suitable for a wide range of applications, which are currently mainly limited to plastic trays, loose-fills, cutlery, and writing instruments.2, 19 During use, components are exposed to numerous environmental influences such as temperature, humidity, and UV radiation. These influences, in turn, cause complex aging phenomena, which become noticeable in the properties of the composites. In particular, starch can increase the causes of aging such as water absorption, and therefore promote aging processes.20 This is based on the polar groups of the starch, which lead to hydrogen bondings and thus form the strongly hydrophilic character of starch.2 For PLA, which is known to be a material prone to hydrolysis, the increased water absorption is accompanied by a change in properties.21-25 In 2003, Wang et al.26 investigated the physical aging of composites of PLA and starch and observed a deterioration of the mechanical properties as a result of storage at 25°C and 50% humidity. In addition, the microstructure of the composites also changed and showed an increasing ductility of the matrix with continued physical aging and a simultaneous deterioration of the bond between the starch and the matrix, which in turn caused a decrease in tensile strength. Yew et al.27 and Gáspár et al.28 also showed a reduction in mechanical properties as a result of humid storage. Yew et al.27 showed a clearly stronger and accelerated water absorption of PLA through the addition of hygroscopic starch, whereby the samples with 20% starch absorbed 5 times as much water as pure PLA samples. It is assumed that the absorbed water leads on the one hand to hydrolysis of the PLA and on the other hand to a deterioration of the adhesion between PLA and starch and thus to a reduction in the mechanical properties. Similarly, artificial weathering of PLA starch composites led to a reduction in tensile strength, although the reduction was less for starch-containing samples than for pure PLA. The reason for this is the UV-shielding effect of the starch particles, which slows down the UV-induced chain degradation.6 In addition to starch-filled PLA, there are also numerous studies on LDPE that have been filled with starch: Danjaji et al.29 showed a decrease in the tensile strength of starch-filled LLDPE as a result of significantly increased water absorption. The improved PLA has wider applications in the electronics and automotive fields. IntroductionThe severity and range of the impacts of global climate change on our lives are not yet fully realized. Plastic consumption is one of several factors affecting global climate change. The life cycle of plastic and plastic waste mismanagement generate enormous amounts of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. When exposed to sunlight, discarded plastic wastes emit GHG i.e., methane and ethylene etc. and also decompose to microplastics that contaminate soil, air, and water resources [1]. In several countries around the world, disposing of plastic waste by burning it in the open is a common practice that produces serious air pollution in the form of carbon dioxide, black carbon, and fine particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5). The mismanagement of plastic waste has now become a major and urgent development challenge. To solve these problems, bio-circular-green (BCG) approaches are needed. The replacement of conventional plastics with fully biodegradable polymers should be seriously supported by all public and private enterprises [2]. One of the most promising biodegradable plastics for use in packaging, medicine, textiles, and automotive production is polylactide (PLA) [3].PLA has outstanding properties in terms of high modulus and stiffness, transparency, easy processing, excellent biocompatibility, and full biodegradability in a few weeks [4,5]. However, for some applications, PLA also has limitations, such as poor ductility, low impact resistance, high cost compared to conventional plastics, low thermal stability, and slow crystallization rate [6,7]. PLA also has poor flame retardancy and generates heavy melt dripping during the burning process, leading to fire-spreading hazards [8]. The fire resistance of PLA has been improved by numerous studies up to this point. Since IFR systems are effective and free of halogens, the majority of them are concentrating on employing them. An acid supply, a blowing agent, and a carbonization source make up the IFRs' typical main three components. By forming char as a result of the interaction of these components, PLA's flammability is decreased since the char shields the underlying materials from heat and oxygen. Furthermore, certain other flame retardants, such as additives containing silicon, inorganic materials, and phosphorus, were combined with PLA. However, adding flame retardants, particularly IFRs, typically results in PLA having worse mechanical and processing properties. In order to increase the flame retardancy of PLA, Zhang et al. [8] studied the intumescent flame retardant system employing ammonium polyphosphate (APP) and urea-modified lignin. They claimed that while the urea-modified lignin and APP composites had outstanding flame retardancy and thermal stability, the mechanical characteristics had been significantly reduced due to the weak interfacial adhesion between the PLA and IFR. More intumescent flame retardants added to an IFR system typically result in greater incompatibility with the polymer and worse mechanical qualities. To improve the flame resistance of polymers, a flame retardant alone needs to be used at a reasonably high percentage, which has an impact on other properties. This is a research gap that needs to be filled immediately. Additionally, these limitations prevent PLA from being widely used in the home décor, electronics, and automotive industries [9,10]. The materials' ability to resist fire is significantly improved by the addition of these flame retardants, but the mechanical and processing qualities are severely compromised. Therefore, a compromise between the flame retardant and mechanical properties of PLA must be found, and this is the main goal of this research. This will be a different approach to enhancing PLA's flame retardant qualities and substituting for the IFR system.To overcome the disadvantages of PLA, various research efforts have focused on three effective routes: (1) chemical modification of the polymeric structure of PLA; (2) blending PLA with other biodegradable polymers such as poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) [11,12], poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) [13], polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) [14], and polycarbonate (PC) [15]; and (3) combining PLA with additives, such as plasticizers [[16], [17], [18]], fibers [19], activated biochar [20], and microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) [21]. Compared to the chemical modification route, blending and/or combining PLA with additives are practical and inexpensive techniques that enhance the relevant properties. Based on our previous works, an effective way of striking a balance between desirable mechanical performance and flame retardancy is to combine PLA with a bio-based reinforcing filler and an appropriate additive [13]. Specifically, in this study, we enhance the fire resistance and impact toughness of PLA by using tricresyl phosphate (TCP), which acts as both flame retardant and plasticizer, combined with a bio-filler of MCC.MCC is the particulate form of cellulose extracted from several cellulosic resources such as bagasse [22], pineapple [23,24], soybean [25], flax and hemp [26], and oil palm empty fruit bunch (OPEFB) [27]. Oil palm is one of the most important crops in Thailand and is the raw material for the palm oil industries. Oil palm production processes generate large quantities of waste in the form of palm kernel shells, oil palm trunks, and OPEFB that cannot be easily disposed of. OPEFB is composed of 41-47 % cellulose, 25-34 % hemicellulose, and 28-32 % lignin [27]. Thus, the OPEFB waste in Thailand is potentially a cheaper source of MCC than other feedstocks and was selected as a raw material in this study.Using MCC as a bio-filler for PLA composite supports the BCG economic model in several ways and can help solve the mismanagement of waste. MCC offers high mechanical strength, low density, low cost, non-toxicity, renewability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability [28]. On the other hand, the high polarity of MCC, due to the many hydroxyl groups in its chemical structure, is an obstacle to properly combining PLA and MCC. The difference between more polar MCC and less polar PLA caused phase separation and poor compatibility, which led to a final product with worse properties than pure PLA [29]. Therefore, surface modification must be done before mixing MCC with PLA. Polyelectrolytes, physical surfactant adsorption, graft polymerization, and chemical coupling processes can all be used to surface-modify MCC [30], but chemical treatments are more efficient than physical ones [[31], [32], [33]]. In several countries around the world, disposing of plastic waste by burning it in the open is a common practice that produces serious air pollution in the form of carbon dioxide, black carbon, and fine particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5). To ensure the ultraviolet radiation does not damage the polymer's performance during its service life, they are often provided with a protective coating, making them very durable. However, the process allows them to persist and accumulate in large quantities in nature over time, resulting in “white pollution” [4], [5]. Degradable plastics, including thermoplastic starch (TPS), polylactic acid (PLA) and polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT), can be oxidized and decomposed into environmentally harmless CO2 under the action of enzymes and H2O2. The interfacial compatibility is poor resulting in a significant decrease in the tensile strength of the composite however, and it is necessary to add an expensive coupling agent to improve the performance when the two polymers are blended, such as titanate, maleic anhydride, and silane coupling agent [45], [46].

Issues related to the disposal of plastic waste derived from fossil fuels have determined a growing interest from scientific and industrial research in the development of materials with greater environmental sustainability. In order to tackle the waste disposal emergency, the European Commission has implemented a series of policies and introduced regulations that limit or prohibit the marketing of objects made with plastics derived from fossil fuels. Disposable objects such as straws, plates, cotton sticks, and cutlery will be completely banned from the market, starting from 2021. These products shall be made exclusively with low environmental impact materials.1 In this perspective, bioplastics are a potential alternative. These materials, as reported in recent EU communications on waste disposal may represent a valid strategy for waste reduction. Among biopolymers potentially suitable for the replacement of common plastic materials, poly (lactic acid) polymers (PLA) stand out. Compared to other biopolymers, PLA has good mechanical strength, good toughness and moderate thermal characteristics. In terms of availability on the market, it is characterized by the greater variety and availability of commercial grades. Although this material has a lower market price than most biopolymers, the comparison with common fossil-fuel plastics is unforgiving and strongly discourages the use of PLA. It should also be noted that some processing technologies, such as cast extrusion and thermoforming used for the manufacturing of disposable objects have an important percentage of process waste. Recovery of post-process materials (i.e., the waste from the production process), in combination with the virgin polymer is a common practice for fossil-fuel plastics, and properties of the final product are not altered in the process. The recycling and recovery of biopolymer post-process waste, instead, is highly compromised by the tendency to thermo-hydrolytic degradation of these materials. Large scale deployment of PLA in processing technologies involving significant percentage of process waste is, therefore, limited both by the cost of the raw material itself and by the costs related to the difficult recovery of the post-process waste. Numerous literature studies report how thermo-hydrolytic degradation of PLA and the consequent loss of rheological characteristics of the material affect processability. Badía et al.,2 Pillin et al.,3 and Żenkiewicz et al.4 observed a significant loss of mechanical properties and a reduction in the molecular weight of the polymer following multiple processing cycles, that is, the reprocessing of the material in subsequent processing steps. Yarahmadi et al.5 found an 80% increase in the Melt Flow Rate (MFR) of PLA after six extrusion cycles, while Sirin et al.6 observed a correlation between thermal stability of a PLA/TPS blend and the number of repeated processing cycles. Strategies aimed at limiting the sensitivity of biopolymers to thermal treatments and allow multiple re-processing (i.e., recovery of post-process material) are mainly based on the design of formulations involving the use of additives which modify properties and behavior of the material in subsequent processing cycles. Optimal formulation of the compounds, besides reducing sensitivity to the degradation phenomena, allows to effectively customize the material according to properties required in the specific application. For example, the increase in the tenacity of PLA can be pursued by introducing a secondary flexible polymeric phase. This strategy, extensively investigated in literature, has demonstrated the effectiveness of using succinic acid polymers. Bathia et al.7 found an increase in elongation at break of about 300% in PBS:PLA blends (10:90) compared to as-is PLA. A similar study was conducted by Chuayjuljit et al.8 who have observed a correlation between the increase in impact resistance and elongation at break with the PBS content in PLA/PBS blends. To limit thermal degradation of PLA, the use of organic and inorganic fillers has been thoroughly investigated. Tesfaye et al.9 studied the effect of silk nanocrystals (SNCs) on the properties of PLA subjected to multiple extrusion cycles (i.e., extruding the same material multiple times) observing a slower degradation of the composite material. Similarly, Botta et al.10 have observed the increase in thermal stability of PLA by adding nano graphene sheets. The results showed that the addition of GnP to PLA reduces the degradation rate of the composite compared to the as-is PLA. The use of talc in combination with PLA has shown a reduction in thermal degradation of the material.11, 12 Another approach concerns the possible use of additives that act by restoring the molecular weight of the polymer phase. Liu et al.13 studied the use of a chain extender with PLA. This study showed that the chemical reaction between the functional groups of the additive and the polymeric matrix increased the molecular weight and viscosity of the polymer. This approach allows to restore rheological properties of the material affected by processability loss due to thermo-degradation phenomena.

Another requirement regarding food packaging materials, is to provide antimicrobial protection.23 Focusing on PLA specifically, several studies investigate its antimicrobial activity on a variety of nanocomposite systems, or following the modification/treatment of its surface.24-32 In the latter case, there are quite a few methods followed in the literature, providing modification of the surface of the samples under study, either in the category of physical (e.g., sputtering, ion plating etc) or chemical (pyrolysis, plasma-enhanced, etc) vapor deposition,33-35 aiming to improve barrier properties and enhance antimicrobial activity. The growing demand for biodegradable and renewable materials has led to a resurgence of interest in natural polymers, particularly starches, as sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based polymers. Starch is a polysaccharide abundantly present in many plant organs, including seeds, tubers, and fruits, and has long been valued for its low cost, biodegradability, and film-forming properties. It is composed mainly of two glucose polymers: amylose, a linear polymer, and amylopectin, a highly branched polymer. These two components and their structural arrangements define the physicochemical behavior of starch, including its gelatinization, pasting, and thermal degradation profiles. These characteristics make starch a promising candidate for various industrial applications, including packaging, food, pharmaceutical, and biomedical fields. However, conventional starch sources such as corn, wheat, and potato are increasingly being criticized due to food-versus-material concerns and their associated environmental burdens [1, 2]. Conventional starch sources such as corn, wheat, potato, and cassava have been widely studied [3], but the need to diversify sources is increasing due to the rising global demand and geographical constraints [4].
Starch is considered as stored energy obtained from plants. It is called native starch unless it undergoes chemical modification, in this case, it is termed derived starch. Starch is modified to achieve particular features. The starch matrix is composed of 10-20% linear amylose macromolecules and 80-90% of branched amylopectin macromolecules. The percentages are correlated to the origin of starch [1]. The position of the branch on the main substrate is likely to be on the C6 forming α-D-(1,6)-glycosidic linkages [2]. Starch is partially soluble in water which limits its adjustment to industrial applications. Thus, to get benefit from its useful properties such as biodegradability and its natural availability, the chemical modification was suggested. Vinyl monomers like styrene [3] and acrylamide [4] were grafted onto starch, using free radical or ionic initiators. A free radical is the most used mechanism. The starch free radical reacts with the vinyl monomers leading to the formation of macro free radicals [1].
Characterization of Residues from Partially Hydrolyzed Potato and High Amylose Corn Starches by Pancreatic α‐Amylase There is growing global impetus for a transition away from fossil fuel-based materials to enhance sustainable development, protect ecosystems, and reach net-zero targets. Synthetically derived, non-renewable polymers such as polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyvinyl chloride are particularly problematic due to their poor biodegradability,1 and carbon-intensive production methods. Biomaterials such as starch are essential for the transition towards sustainably produced polymer products. Starch is a highly abundant,2, 3 renewable and biodegradable polymer. It is the primary energy storage in all green plants, and can be found in staple crops such as corn, potatoes, wheat and rice.2, 4 Its low cost, versatility and bio-compatibility makes it an ideal material to replace petroleum-based products.5, 6 Industrially, starch is an important raw material used in a wide range of industries ranging from food and packaging to pharmaceuticals and biofuels.5, 7 According to Copeland et al.,7 60 million tonnes of starch are extracted annually, of which 60% is used in the food industry-either as a food product or additive (e.g., thickener, gelling-agent, stabilizer, preservation agent, or quality enhancer). Starch is the second-most abundant natural polymer after cellulose. It is produced as a storage polymer in several granular plants such as corn, cassava, cereal, rice and potato. It is an odorless and tasteless white powder, and insoluble in cold water or alcohol. Starch is a semi-crystalline polymer, with a crystallinity varying from 15 % to 45 % depending on the plant species from which it originates (Vall zabala, 2020). Morphologically, starch is composed of mostly microscopic spherical granules with diameters ranging from 2 to 100 μm, depending on the botanical origin. Chemically, starch molecules are composed of two main macromolecular components: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose has a linear or slightly branched structure consisting of 2 × 105-106 glucose units per molecule, which are joined together by ∼99 % α-D (1 → 4) glucosidic bonds and ∼1% α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic linkages. Amylopectin has a highly branched structure with approximately 106 glucose units per molecule, which are connected with α-D (1 → 4) linkages and 5-6% of α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic side chains (Wu et al., 2018). Generally, amylose and amylopectin constitute ∼20-25 % and ∼75-80 % of a starch granule, respectively. There are three reactive hydroxyl groups on the glucose unit of the starch chain: one primary and two secondary hydroxyl groups. These hydroxyl groups serve as anchoring platforms for surface modifications or cross-linking reactions (Ojogbo, Ogunsona, & Mekonnen, 2020). Starch molecules have two critical features that make them a unique and promising material for the production of composites. First, starch is naturally biodegradable in soil and water and can be easily degraded into sugars and organic acids, which is of utmost importance from an environmental viewpoint. Second, owing to its unique chemical characteristics, starch is amenable to a variety of chemical and enzymatic modifications that provide many opportunities to confer new functionalities on starch polymers. To meet the necessary requirements of green chemistry, renewable resources are increasingly in demand to enable the manufacture of sustainable composites. Starch, which seems to meet these expectations, can be employed as a green polyol component for the synthesis of PU-based materials. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) has also attracted considerable attention during the past two decades as an interesting alternative to synthetic polymers (Gironès et al., 2012). PUs are a diverse class of polymeric materials that possess urethane linkages within their backbone. PUs are generally composed of hard and soft segments. The soft segment consists of a polyol, such as a polyester or polyether, which renders flexibility to the PU’s structure; the hard segment is composed of a wide variety of isocyanate-based components that impart mechanical strength to the PU network. The use of a varying range of hard and soft segments with different chemistries gives rise to the development of PUs with a broad range of physical and mechanical properties (Costa et al., 2015; Sáenz-Pérez, Laza, García-Barrasa, Vilas, & León, 2017). For example, PUs can be either thermoplastic or irreversibly thermoset depending on the ratio of hard and soft segments in their structure. The versatile PU chemistry and its ability to form different types of molecular architectures enable PUs to meet the highly diversified demands of modern technologies, including coatings, adhesives, foams and thermoplastic elastomers (Dandeniyage et al., 2018; Kausar, 2018). It is worth mentioning that almost all traditional PUs are non-degradable; however, they can be specifically designed to show some degrees of degradation. Biodegradable PUs have recently gained great interest because of their sustainable features and potential for use in different biomedical applications. Biodegradable PUs can be devised with a simple manipulation of PU structure and/or its composition, particularly modification of the soft segment (Dou et al., 2019). Soft segments, which are composed of polyester or polyether polyols with a hydrolysable backbone, are more susceptible to microbial attack. Thus, the incorporation of a biodegradable unit (particularly an ester group) into the PU backbone is a pragmatic approach to impart higher susceptibility to microbial action under natural environmental conditions. The potential to introduce biodegradability and tailor a multitude of structures and mechanical properties makes PUs versatile polymers for developing starch-PU composites or hybrids (Mahajan & Gupta, 2015). Conventional PUs are synthesized through a step-growth polymerization reaction between isocyanate and polyol molecules in the presence of either a catalyst or UV light irradiation (Fig. 1a). Polyols that are commonly used for PU synthesis often have two or more OH groups. Isocyanates are another essential component for PU synthesis. They are often di-functional in nature, containing two NCO groups per molecule. They can be classified as aliphatic or aromatic isocyanates. Aromatic isocyanates, such as toluene diisocyanate (TDI) and diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI), tend to be more reactive towards polyols than their aliphatic counterparts, such as isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI) and hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Isocyanates can react with OH groups to produce PUs at room temperature (and up to 50 °C), while, they generate allophanate, biuret, and isocyanate linkages at higher temperatures above 100 °C. If linear PUs are desired, the use of the low temperature is required. If high cross-linked PUs are desired, higher temperatures (100-150 °C) are indeed required (Engels et al., 2013). Synthesis of PUs can be carried out as one- or two-step reactions. In one-step synthesis, all required ingredients are mixed at the beginning; in two-step synthesis, the polyols are first reacted in excess with a diisocyanate component to prepare NCO-terminated PU prepolymers, after which a chain extender is added to produce a final long-chain PU (Janik, Sienkiewicz, & Kucinska-Lipka, 2013). The two-step reaction method is generally preferred because it allows more control over the reaction, and yields PUs with well-defined structural and physical properties (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Even though these PU materials are highly durable and safe, the main drawback of classic PU synthesis is the use of isocyanates, which are classified as carcinogenic and mutagenic. Prolonged exposure to isocyanate substances in the workplace can have dramatic impacts on health, such as asthma, dermatitis and acute poisoning. Therefore, despite the continuous efforts of the PU industry to improve the quality of PU raw materials (e.g., using bio-based diisocyanates derived from natural resources), the need for more environmentally friendly processes that address both the renewability of the starting material and the sustainability of the synthesis is urgent (Llevot & Meier, 2019). NIPUs, which are mainly synthesized through a ring-opening reaction between poly(cyclic carbonates) and polyamines, have been shown to have substantial green credentials (Fig. 1b). The phosgene-free and isocyanate-free reactions represent a suitable greener alternative for PU synthesis, with structures comparable to those produced by the polyaddition of diisocyanates and polyols (Ghasemlou, Daver, Ivanova, & Adhikari, 2019). The isocyanate-free reactions can be carried out at ambient temperatures although a moderately high temperature (ca. 60-80 °C) can achieve high conversion rate of NIPU (Cornille et al., 2016). More importantly, due to their hydrophilic nature, NIPUs tend to be more compatible with hydrophilic native starch in composites. We have recently reviewed the various green routes that have been used to synthesize NIPUs and their precursors to pave the way for their application in the PU industry (Ghasemlou et al., 2019a).

The enzymatic degradation of starch primarily involves glycoside hydrolases that hydrolyze α-glycosidic bonds in the polymer backbone. α-Amylase initiates the process by cleaving long starch chains into shorter fragments, which are further hydrolyzed by enzymes such as β-amylase, glucoamylase, and α-glucosidase [1][2][3]. These enzymes specifically target α-1,4-glycosidic linkages in amylose and amylopectin [3][7][9]. Additionally, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs) contribute by catalyzing oxidative cleavage of glucose linkages [1][2].  

Microorganisms facilitate this degradation by secreting extracellular enzymes (e.g., amylases), which depolymerize starch into oligomers, dimers, or monomers. These smaller molecules are subsequently assimilated and mineralized into CO₂, H₂O (aerobic), or CH₄, CO₂ (anaerobic) [4][8]. The efficiency of enzymatic degradation depends on starch’s botanical origin, granule morphology (size, surface area), and amylose/amylopectin ratio, as these factors affect enzyme accessibility to α-(1,4) bonds [7][10]. Higher water uptake in starch-based materials enhances degradation by promoting enzyme penetration [9][12].

The 3D printing techniques have advantages over other fabrication routes, such as reduced waste, cost-effectiveness, rapid prototyping, and the ability to fabricate parts with complex geometries.37 Among the various 3D printing methods, fused deposit modeling (FDM) has been widely reported in studies investigating the feasibility of the process in the design and fabrication of thermoplastic polymer-based parts. The FDM mainly functions on the extrusion of thermoplastic polymer filaments that may lead to low-cost and rather accurate single-step fabricated parts.38 One of the major challenges in FDM printing is the limited availability of multifunctional engineering materials of specific performance in the form of filament. Another challenge to be addressed is the 3D processing of the environmentally friendly polymer compounds exhibiting suitable mechanical properties.39 Numerous studies have reported 3D printing of bio-based biodegradable polymer blends and the overall mechanical and physical properties of the parts fabricated. Kuo et al. succeeded in fabricating biodegradable printable filaments by combining acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and TPS filled with titanium oxide and carbon black.40 A printable composite containing PLA and microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) was prepared by Murphy and Collins.41 The results showed that increasing the cellulose content increased the crystallinity and the dynamic mechanical behavior of the fabricated composites. Wang et al.42 reinforced PLA with micro/nano-cellulose to be used in the FDM process. Coppola et al. developed a class of nanocomposite filament by incorporating nanoclay into PLA,43 showing the enhancement in the thermal stability, crystallinity, and mechanical performance of the specimens compared to those exhibited by the reference neat parts. A PLA-based bio-filament blended with polyethylene glycol and birch fiber as the reinforcement was developed by Rafiee et al.44 The study showed that the ultimate tensile strength of specimens decreased with the addition of fiber into PLA associated with the brittleness of the samples and nozzle clogging. Tekinalp et al. extruded filaments and compression-molded PLA-based parts reinforced with cellulose nanofibril (CNF).45 Their findings represented that the ultimate tensile strength in the case of molded and FDM processed specimens improved 60% and 51% at 40 wt% of CNF, respectively. As understood from the literature, only a few studies have reported the mechanical and thermal performance of FDM processed biodegradable PLA-based composites reinforced with nanoclay. Moreover, no study has so far revealed the feasibility and performance of PLA/TPS nanocomposites blends filled with nanoclay fabricated by the FDM process. As mentioned earlier, melt mixing techniques such as extrusion-injection molding has been broadly utilized to fabricate biodegradable nanocomposites. Nevertheless, to better understand the effect of the processing method on the overall mechanical and thermal behavior of PLA/TPS-based nanocomposites, the properties of the extruded-injection molded PLA/TPS nanocomposites need to be addressed with respect to the behavior of FDM processed nanocomposites. Besides this, it is further highlighted that there is a gap in the literature to be addressed concerning the processing and overall behavior of nanoclay/PLA/TPS nanocomposites processed through injection molding. To give a better insight into the performance and processability, this study, thus, aims at the performance of FDM and injection molding processed PLA/TPS blends reinforced with 1, 3, and 5 wt% of nanoclay. The research examines the mechanical response of the fabricated parts, such as the tensile and flexural behavior and impact resistance, as well as the thermal and structural properties of the specimens to understand better the interplay among the process-structure-property characteristics of the fabricated parts. The findings of this work illustrate two leading melt processing routes based on biodegradable binary systems filled with an accessible nanofiller applicable in the development of engineered biodegradable nanocomposites targeting specific applications.

Fused deposition modeling (FDM)-one kind of additive manufacturing (AM), rapid prototyping (RP), and solid free-form fabrication (SFF) technique-is one out of many trendy three-dimensional printing (3DP) techniques1, 2 that can construct bulk products from elements of dimension scale of sub-millimeter (0.1 mm). With FDM, one can print objects with exotic topological structure (e.g., metamaterial with negative Poisson's ratio3) in an additive way with great freedom but little manufacturing time, which is difficult or impossible for traditional manufacturing methods.
The expansion of global markets for additive manufacturing (AM), also referred to as 3D printing, is expected to grow at a very large and rapid pace over the next few years [1]. The ability to produce complex and customizable designs at a low production cost has become the main attraction of this technology [2]. From aerospace to biomedical as well as electronic packaging and household products, everything can be fabricated through computer-aided design (CAD) before being “printed” into 3D objects without the need to manufacture the mold first, reducing production time, cost, and material expenses [3, 4]. Among the various 3D printing techniques, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is widely used because it is conceptually basic, easy to handle, and economically affordable [5, 6]. The FDM manufacturing technique is effortless because the thermoplastic filament, acting as the “ink,” is continuously fed into the extrusion chamber at a predefined temperature. The material melts to form a highly viscous fluid and is deposited on the printing bed, solidifying after printing [7, 8]. Therefore, the development of the filament with excellent mechanical properties is crucial, in order to improve and broaden the functionality of 3D printing applications6. Previously, polylactic acid (PLA) has been used as filaments in 3D printing due to the material's sustainability, biocompatibility, and nontoxic properties, which make it a suitable candidate for many applications [9, 10]. The printability of PLA is undeniable since it possesses a low melting temperature, good adhesion to the printing bed, and a low degree of warpage and delamination [11, 12]. However, PLA has some serious drawbacks that limit its application, such as its inherent brittleness, low deformation at breaking, poor impact resistance, and slow degradability [13, 14]. Several approaches have been studied to overcome these disadvantages, particularly to improve the toughness and degradability of PLA. The addition of additives, copolymerization, and blending are among the methods which have been proposed by researchers [15, 16]. The melt blending technique is the most preferred method, as it is more economical and easier to implement, requiring only an instrument similar to an industrial plastic mixer. Blending PLA with elastomeric materials, such as rubber, is a promising approach for improving the ductility and rate of degradation of PLA [14, 17]. Rubber toughening is a viable method to enhance the mechanical properties of PLA by incorporating rubber particles into the polymer matrix. The rubber particles that disperse in the polymer matrix act as stress concentration spots, which initiate crazes or shear bands in the matrix and this prevents premature cracking. A large amount of energy is dissipated during the deformation process; thus, the toughness of the materials is enhanced [18, 19]. One of the toughening mechanisms involved when rubber particles are present in the polymer matrix is known as “interfacial adhesion.” Strong bonds between the rubber particles and the polymer matrix ensure the efficient load transfer when stress is applied, improving the toughness of the materials. In addition, the distribution of rubber particles is important, to make certain that the optimum toughening effect takes place, thus liquid natural rubber (LNR) is regarded as an ideal elastomer due to its liquid form, which improves the polymer mixing and processing.

Among the different 3D printing methods, fused deposition modeling (FDM) technology stands out, mainly due to its ease of use and the availability of raw materials; but also, because it allows the addition of reinforcement fibers continuously during the manufacturing process of the parts [4], [5]. FDM is a technique that dates back to the 80's [6] and its operation process consists of passing a filament through a head containing a hot extruder. This filament is melted and reaches the nozzle in a semi-liquid state. In order to carry out the printing, the movement of the head is in an XY plane, and the deposition base (bed) moves in the Z (vertical) direction to form a part layer by layer. The printer generates a 2D shape in the XY plane by the movement of the head; whereas, the vertical displacement movement (Z direction) of the bed recreates the 3D shape [7]. The whole process of the printing machine is regulated by numerical control software that is based on a series of parameters that will significantly affect the set of characteristics and mechanical properties of the printed part. Some of these parameters of importance that have been studied are the geometric pattern of the layer, nozzle and bed temperature, layer thickness, infill percentage, feed rate, number of part contours, build time, moisture content, among others. However, based on these studies, it has been defined that the parameters that mostly affect part properties using 3D printing technology are layer height, lattice orientation and geometric pattern, build or deposition orientation, and infill density [8]. Similarly, the type of material used to produce the part should be considered, as the effect of these parameters on the mechanical properties can vary depending on the raw materials used [5]. Due to their melting temperature and ease of printing, polymeric materials have been preferred over other materials for processing 3D printed parts under the FDM technique. Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polylactic acid (PLA) and nylon (N) are examples of this. Based on the principle of layered manufacturing and layer-by-layer stacking, 3D printing, also known as, “additive manufacturing,” is a nontraditional advanced manufacturing technology, which is capable of constructing products with arbitrarily complex structures. The shape of 3D printed products can be transformed over time, achieving 4D printing. In this work, poly(lactic acid) (PLA)/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) blends are fabricated via fused deposition modeling (FDM). The thermoresponsive shape memory effects (SMEs) of 3D printed blends are investigated by stress-controlled dynamic mechanical analysis in tension mode. The SME mechanism is clarified in detail, along with the crystallization and melting behaviors, dynamic mechanical properties, and morphologies of PLA/PCL blends. It is confirmed that the crystallinity of reversible phase PCL, the glass transition behavior of fixed phase PLA and the two-phase interfaces have important effects on the shape memory performance. Furthermore, the SME can be tuned by optimizing printing parameters. In the field of advanced manufacturing industry, 3D printing is one of the most promising manufacturing techniques.[1] For manufacturing the products with complicated structures, 3D printing technologies have great advantages over traditional manufacturing processes.[2, 3] The selection of 3D printing techniques is based on the nature of raw materials and the performance requirements of final products.[4] Among the available 3D printing technologies, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is the most commonly used and cost-effective.[5, 6] However, the printing materials suitable for FDM are generally limited to thermoplastics. The printing anisotropy and printing orientation in FDM process attracted great interest. Chen et al. prepared thermoplastic polyurethane/poly(lactic acid) (PLA)/graphene oxide nanocomposites via FDM, and found that the mechanical properties of nanocomposites were highly dependent on printing direction.[7] Tekinalp et al. reported that acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS)/carbon fiber composites by FDM had both higher fiber orientation and higher molecular orientation compared to those by conventional techniques.[8] Jia et al. used FDM technology to make graphite sheets vertically oriented in polyamide 6 (PA6) polymer matrix, resulting in composites with high through-plane thermal conductivity.[9] It was reported that the performance of FDM products was closely related to their construction methods.
3D printing is an emerging method that forms 3D scaffolds by successively laying down layer upon layer of viscous or solid materials to obtain a desired geometry by computer-aided design models.[1, 2] 3D scaffolds produced by this method exhibit adequate pore size and interconnected porous structure to enhance cell attachment, migration, and proliferation required for biomedical applications.[3-5] Several 3D printing techniques are being used in the biomedical field, including laser-assisted deposition, extrusion, fused deposition modeling (FDM), and inkjet printing, particularly for bone regeneration and wound healing approaches.[6-8] Among them, FDM is a low-cost, high-speed, and convenient method that involves the extrusion of melted thermoplastic polymers.[6] Various thermoplastic polymers, such as polyvinyl chloride, polyacrylamide, polycaprolactone (PCL), polyethylene, and polylactic-co-glycolic acid, have been investigated for fabricating 3D scaffolds by the FDM method.[9, 10] PCL is one of the most commonly used linear-aliphatic polyesters for the 3D printing process due to its excellent processability, good biocompatibility, and high mechanical properties compared to natural polymers.[2] Hutmacher et al.[11] fabricated 3D-printed PCL scaffolds using the FDM method. Their results demonstrated that different layer-down patterns change the mechanical behavior of scaffolds. The in vitro studies conducted with primary human fibroblasts showed that in the first 2 weeks, 0/60/120° layer-down pattern had higher in vitro cell proliferation than 0/72/144/36/108°.[11] In another study, Teo et al.[12] investigated gentamicin sulfate-incorporated- PCL/tricalcium phosphate 3D-printed scaffolds for wound healing applications. The authors reported that PCL/tricalcium phosphate 3D-printed scaffolds incorporated with 15 wt% gentamicin sulfate reduced Staphylococcus aureus bacterial viability within 2h, while the scaffolds were not cytotoxic for normal human dermal fibroblast (NHDF) cells.[12] Electrospinning is a versatile, cost-efficient, and conventional technique for forming non-woven fibrous mats from micro- to nanoscale.[13-15] Such electrospun mats mimic the extra cellular matrix (ECM) structure and promote cellular attachment, proliferation, and differentiation.[14, 16] So far, various synthetic and natural polymers have been spun and engineered for wound dressing applications.[17-21] For instance, cashew gum polysaccharide- poly (vinyl alcohol) electrospun nanofibers were fabricated by Rojara et al.[22] for scarless wound healing. Their in vivo wound healing results showed that the electrospun nanofibers have the potential to accelerate tissue regeneration and the healing process.[22] Recently, Anaya Mancipe et al.[23] successfully fabricated core-shell nanofibers containing a hydrophobic PCL core with a hydrophilic Type I collagen/poly(vinyl alcohol) shell for chronic wound treatment.[23]
The main goal of this study is to develop PVA for 3-dimensional printing (3D printing). 3D printing is a rapidly developing technology that is quick inexpensive and can produce complex parts without geometry limitations.14 Fused deposition modeling (FDM), an important type of 3D printing that uses layer-by-layer deposition of extruded filament to build up a part, has been widely studied because it is fast, safe, inexpensive, and simple to operate.15 FDM has been utilized for tissue engineering such as fabricating scaffolds with controllable pore shapes and sizes.16-19 However, the multi-hydroxyl groups lead to strong inter and intra-molecular hydrogen bonding in PVA, narrowing the gap between the melting point of PVA and its decomposition temperature; thus, products fabricated from this material cannot be prepared by melt processing. Therefore, FDM of PVA scaffold remains a significant challenge. Previous studies have shown that intermolecular complexion and plasticization are effective to realize melt-processing of PVA.20-22 To meet the requirements for use with thermal processing equipment or improving the thermal processability and mechanical properties of PVA, complex plasticizers were chosen. Chen23 used an amide containing group(Ac) combined with water to realize the PVA melt spinning. Wang24 used glycerol/caprolactam/water as a plasticizer for PVA to retard water evaporation, which is beneficial to the melt-processing of PVA. Jiang25 examined using urea/ethanolamine as a high-efficiency plasticizer to produce PVA products with excellent mechanical properties. Zhou26 used glycerol/urea to improve the rheological and mechanical properties of PVA/starch products. In this research, glycerol is chosen as a blend plasticizer for PVA, as it is product of metabolism and is nontoxic. Water is the key plasticizer as it enhances the plasticization effect and inhibits the precipitation of the other components in the plasticizer. Our earlier research proved that, to achieve smooth FDM processing without buckling, the feedstock material should possess an appropriate compressive modulus and viscosity.27 By adjusting the composition of the plasticizers, different mechanical and rheological properties can be obtained for PVA. Thus, PVA filament feedstock with appropriate properties and suitable for FDM processing can be successfully prepared. It is believed that this work will not only provide an effective strategy for thermally processing PVA but also a novel FDM-compatible material for use in the biomedical field.
The 3D printing techniques have advantages over other fabrication routes, such as reduced waste, cost-effectiveness, rapid prototyping, and the ability to fabricate parts with complex geometries.37 Among the various 3D printing methods, fused deposit modeling (FDM) has been widely reported in studies investigating the feasibility of the process in the design and fabrication of thermoplastic polymer-based parts. The FDM mainly functions on the extrusion of thermoplastic polymer filaments that may lead to low-cost and rather accurate single-step fabricated parts.38 One of the major challenges in FDM printing is the limited availability of multifunctional engineering materials of specific performance in the form of filament. Another challenge to be addressed is the 3D processing of the environmentally friendly polymer compounds exhibiting suitable mechanical properties.39 Numerous studies have reported 3D printing of bio-based biodegradable polymer blends and the overall mechanical and physical properties of the parts fabricated. Kuo et al. succeeded in fabricating biodegradable printable filaments by combining acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and TPS filled with titanium oxide and carbon black.40 A printable composite containing PLA and microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) was prepared by Murphy and Collins.41 The results showed that increasing the cellulose content increased the crystallinity and the dynamic mechanical behavior of the fabricated composites. Wang et al.42 reinforced PLA with micro/nano-cellulose to be used in the FDM process. Coppola et al. developed a class of nanocomposite filament by incorporating nanoclay into PLA,43 showing the enhancement in the thermal stability, crystallinity, and mechanical performance of the specimens compared to those exhibited by the reference neat parts. A PLA-based bio-filament blended with polyethylene glycol and birch fiber as the reinforcement was developed by Rafiee et al.44 The study showed that the ultimate tensile strength of specimens decreased with the addition of fiber into PLA associated with the brittleness of the samples and nozzle clogging. Tekinalp et al. extruded filaments and compression-molded PLA-based parts reinforced with cellulose nanofibril (CNF).45 Their findings represented that the ultimate tensile strength in the case of molded and FDM processed specimens improved 60% and 51% at 40 wt% of CNF, respectively. As understood from the literature, only a few studies have reported the mechanical and thermal performance of FDM processed biodegradable PLA-based composites reinforced with nanoclay. Moreover, no study has so far revealed the feasibility and performance of PLA/TPS nanocomposites blends filled with nanoclay fabricated by the FDM process. As mentioned earlier, melt mixing techniques such as extrusion-injection molding has been broadly utilized to fabricate biodegradable nanocomposites. Nevertheless, to better understand the effect of the processing method on the overall mechanical and thermal behavior of PLA/TPS-based nanocomposites, the properties of the extruded-injection molded PLA/TPS nanocomposites need to be addressed with respect to the behavior of FDM processed nanocomposites. Besides this, it is further highlighted that there is a gap in the literature to be addressed concerning the processing and overall behavior of nanoclay/PLA/TPS nanocomposites processed through injection molding. To give a better insight into the performance and processability, this study, thus, aims at the performance of FDM and injection molding processed PLA/TPS blends reinforced with 1, 3, and 5 wt% of nanoclay. The research examines the mechanical response of the fabricated parts, such as the tensile and flexural behavior and impact resistance, as well as the thermal and structural properties of the specimens to understand better the interplay among the process-structure-property characteristics of the fabricated parts. The findings of this work illustrate two leading melt processing routes based on biodegradable binary systems filled with an accessible nanofiller applicable in the development of engineered biodegradable nanocomposites targeting specific applications.

This article presents research results showing that the property of fused deposition modeling (FDM) products is obtained jointly by careful control of processing parameters, structure of products, and the composition of material. In this manuscript, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) was incorporated with graphene or carbon nanotube (CNT) through repeated melt blending. Filament of the PLA/graphitic nano-filler was prepared and used in FDM. Rheological and thermal analysis were conducted to assess the suitability of the composite as FDM feedstock, and mechanical and electrical property were tested subsequently. Research results demonstrate that filament diameter-regarded as processing-related parameter-was positively correlated with mechanical stiffness and strength of FDM products. Tensile elongation at break of FDM products exhibited significant increase at a raster angle of 45° compared with the filament before FDM, showing in certain cases, material property depends more on the structure than the composition. And when incorporated with graphene or CNT, the electrical conductivity of the PLA-based composite increased drastically. Fused deposition modeling (FDM)-one kind of additive manufacturing (AM), rapid prototyping (RP), and solid free-form fabrication (SFF) technique-is one out of many trendy three-dimensional printing (3DP) techniques1, 2 that can construct bulk products from elements of dimension scale of sub-millimeter (0.1 mm). With FDM, one can print objects with exotic topological structure (e.g., metamaterial with negative Poisson's ratio3) in an additive way with great freedom but little manufacturing time, which is difficult or impossible for traditional manufacturing methods.
The expansion of global markets for additive manufacturing (AM), also referred to as 3D printing, is expected to grow at a very large and rapid pace over the next few years [1]. The ability to produce complex and customizable designs at a low production cost has become the main attraction of this technology [2]. From aerospace to biomedical as well as electronic packaging and household products, everything can be fabricated through computer-aided design (CAD) before being “printed” into 3D objects without the need to manufacture the mold first, reducing production time, cost, and material expenses [3, 4]. Among the various 3D printing techniques, fused deposition modeling (FDM) is widely used because it is conceptually basic, easy to handle, and economically affordable [5, 6]. The FDM manufacturing technique is effortless because the thermoplastic filament, acting as the “ink,” is continuously fed into the extrusion chamber at a predefined temperature. The material melts to form a highly viscous fluid and is deposited on the printing bed, solidifying after printing [7, 8]. Therefore, the development of the filament with excellent mechanical properties is crucial, in order to improve and broaden the functionality of 3D printing applications6. Previously, polylactic acid (PLA) has been used as filaments in 3D printing due to the material's sustainability, biocompatibility, and nontoxic properties, which make it a suitable candidate for many applications [9, 10]. The printability of PLA is undeniable since it possesses a low melting temperature, good adhesion to the printing bed, and a low degree of warpage and delamination [11, 12]. However, PLA has some serious drawbacks that limit its application, such as its inherent brittleness, low deformation at breaking, poor impact resistance, and slow degradability [13, 14]. Several approaches have been studied to overcome these disadvantages, particularly to improve the toughness and degradability of PLA. The addition of additives, copolymerization, and blending are among the methods which have been proposed by researchers [15, 16]. The melt blending technique is the most preferred method, as it is more economical and easier to implement, requiring only an instrument similar to an industrial plastic mixer. Blending PLA with elastomeric materials, such as rubber, is a promising approach for improving the ductility and rate of degradation of PLA [14, 17]. Rubber toughening is a viable method to enhance the mechanical properties of PLA by incorporating rubber particles into the polymer matrix. The rubber particles that disperse in the polymer matrix act as stress concentration spots, which initiate crazes or shear bands in the matrix and this prevents premature cracking. A large amount of energy is dissipated during the deformation process; thus, the toughness of the materials is enhanced [18, 19]. One of the toughening mechanisms involved when rubber particles are present in the polymer matrix is known as “interfacial adhesion.” Strong bonds between the rubber particles and the polymer matrix ensure the efficient load transfer when stress is applied, improving the toughness of the materials. In addition, the distribution of rubber particles is important, to make certain that the optimum toughening effect takes place, thus liquid natural rubber (LNR) is regarded as an ideal elastomer due to its liquid form, which improves the polymer mixing and processing.
