Among the different 3D printing methods, fused deposition modeling (FDM) technology stands out, mainly due to its ease of use and the availability of raw materials; but also, because it allows the addition of reinforcement fibers continuously during the manufacturing process of the parts [4], [5]. FDM is a technique that dates back to the 80's [6] and its operation process consists of passing a filament through a head containing a hot extruder. This filament is melted and reaches the nozzle in a semi-liquid state. In order to carry out the printing, the movement of the head is in an XY plane, and the deposition base (bed) moves in the Z (vertical) direction to form a part layer by layer. The printer generates a 2D shape in the XY plane by the movement of the head; whereas, the vertical displacement movement (Z direction) of the bed recreates the 3D shape [7]. The whole process of the printing machine is regulated by numerical control software that is based on a series of parameters that will significantly affect the set of characteristics and mechanical properties of the printed part. Some of these parameters of importance that have been studied are the geometric pattern of the layer, nozzle and bed temperature, layer thickness, infill percentage, feed rate, number of part contours, build time, moisture content, among others. However, based on these studies, it has been defined that the parameters that mostly affect part properties using 3D printing technology are layer height, lattice orientation and geometric pattern, build or deposition orientation, and infill density [8]. Similarly, the type of material used to produce the part should be considered, as the effect of these parameters on the mechanical properties can vary depending on the raw materials used [5]. Due to their melting temperature and ease of printing, polymeric materials have been preferred over other materials for processing 3D printed parts under the FDM technique. Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polylactic acid (PLA) and nylon (N) are examples of this. A comparative study between PLA and ABS parts demonstrated the adequate service life under dynamic loads of both materials, highlighting the performance of PLA. Likewise, it has been found that the use of carbon fibers (CF) as continuous reinforcement in a PLA and nylon matrix can increase the tensile strength by 14 % and 300 %, with respect to a matrix reinforced with ground fibers added during filament manufacture and without fibers, respectively. In addition, fibers were observed to promote greater stability to the finished part during the printing process [5], [9]. However, there is no comparative study between these three types of materials in terms of design parameters and tensile strength. Such a comparative analysis may be useful because each material has specific advantages depending on the application in which it will be used. Similarly, there are no reports of other engineering properties such as physical ones and their relationship to mechanical properties for 3D printed parts; in particular studies that show that the UTS of a printed part can be higher than that of the filament. On the other hand, the determination of the influence of 3D printing parameters on the mechanical properties of the parts has been evaluated by means of ANOVA or Taguchi's fractional factorial design [5]. However, further research is needed to obtain relevant information about the effect of printing parameters and to define robust manufacturing processes with statistical significance, as well as to optimize parameters to predict with sufficient certainty the mechanical properties of each type of material, all this with a relative degree of simplicity. Likewise, it is necessary to establish in the literature a strategy or algorithm to systematically analyze the different materials and parameters simultaneously in order to select the appropriate performance based on the application. These are some of the advantages of using a DOE to design parts by 3D printing, in addition to the fact that it allows minimizing the number of tests and experimental specimens to obtain results that describe the trend of the variables or processes, as well as their optimization in a statistically valid and representative way, which obviously has an impact on the costs of research and manufacturing of components.
There are various types of 3D printing technology have been introduced, for instance, fused deposition modelling (FDM), stereo lithography (SLA), and selective laser sintering. Each process has a different physical principle, process parameters, and a range of available materials [4]. Among them, the FDM method is extremely popular due to its simplicity and efficiency. The FDM process employs machines equipped with a stock feed material that extrudes in a semi-solid state via a temperature-controlled nozzle. The nozzle moves in the XY horizontal direction and deposits the building material on the machine build platform that moves in the vertical Z direction based on a 3D model. The printing software allows the manipulation of different printing parameters. The FDM process is complex because many contradictory parameters influence the component quality and material properties to its properties. The printing parameter affects mechanical properties, quality, volume, printing time, and finally the cost of the printed part. Many authors have surveyed the impacts of printing parameters on the mechanical properties of 3D printing products. To date, these studies mainly concentrate on examining the infill density, raster pattern, number of contours, number of shells, layer thickness, raster orientation, raster width, air gap, and part orientation. Other principal parameters such as printing speed, traveling speed extruder temperature, and build plate temperature are also reported. Gomez-Gras et al [5] analysed the fatigue response of the PLA part’s influence on four factors (layer height, fill density, nozzle diameter, and velocity). Travieso-Rodriguez et al [6] investigated the influence of six manufacturing factors (layer height, filament width, fill density, layer orientation, printing velocity, and infill pattern) on the flexural resistance. Melenka et al [7] evaluated and forecasted the tensile properties of continuous fibre-reinforced 3D printed structures. Lumpe et al [8] investigated the tensile strength of multi-material interfaces in 3D printing parts. Wittbrodt and Pearce [9] studied the influence of PLA colour on the material properties of 3D printed components. Azadi et al [10] found that PLA specimens had better fatigue lifetimes than ones of ABS samples. Also, Doshi et al [11] reviewed the printing parameters directly influencing the mechanical properties such as tensile strength, stress, and Young’s modulus on the parts produced by FDM. Surprisingly, few researchers have explored the effect of various parameters on the flexural strength and fatigue strength of 3D printing parts. Alshamrani et al [12] examined the effects of printing layer thickness on the flexural strength of a 3D-printed resin. Vaezi and Chua [13] studied the impact of layer thickness and binder saturation on the 3D printing process. Most recently, Gad and Fouda [14] systematically investigated the factors affecting the flexural strength of 3D-printed resins. Atakok et al [15] narrowed their focus to parameters like filament, layer thickness, and occupancy rate’s impact on the three-point bend strength of printed polylactic acid (PLA) and recycled PLA. Nugroho et al [16] studied the effect of layer thickness on the flexural properties of PLA through 3D printing. Ezeh and Susmel [17] conducted quantitative research on the fatigue behaviour of additively manufactured polylactide (PLA). Afrose et al [18] investigated the fatigue behaviour of PLA parts in three (X, Y, and 45°) different build orientations. Recently, through experiment design, the impact of FDM production factors on the shape memory effect (SME) has been examined by Rahmatabadi et al [19]. Three combinations of PLA 50, 70, and 90 weight per cent were studied to examine the impact of temperature, programming deformation, and loading mode on the SME [20]. The infill density determines the amount of plastic used inside the print. A higher infill density results in more material within the print, leading to a stronger object but also increasing the time to complete the print. Moreover, 3D printing infill refers to the internal structure of a 3D-printed part. This internal structure can be produced using many different shapes. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. In particular, polycaprolactone (PCL) has received considerable attention due to its excellent mechanical and structural properties, and tuneable degradation kinetics. Moreover, the non-immunogenicity of PCL, combined with the possibility of using it as an interporous scaffold material, has resulted in better tissue ingrowth [2-4]. The above-mentioned benefits, in addition to the inexpensive production routes of PCL, have encouraged many research groups to investigate its potential applications in numerous fields of tissue engineering [2, 5]. However, the bioactivity of the tissue-engineered constructs is threatened by the hydrophobic nature of PCL [4, 6-8]. In general, it is known that a moderate surface hydrophilicity allows for an increased adsorption of proteins without modifying their natural conformation. In turn, this increases the cell affinity towards the surface, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and cell proliferation [9, 10]. As a consequence, PCL hydrophobicity negatively impacts cell-material interactions [1]. In order to overcome this issue, surface modification is required. Several approaches have previously been investigated, including wet-chemical treatments, and ion beam, x-ray and gamma radiation. However, the wet-chemical treatment route generates large amounts of hazardous chemical waste and often impacts on bulk properties such as structural strength and elasticity, while most radiation methods can cause severe degradation of the polymer [11]. As an alternative, non-thermal plasma treatment has shown to be a promising method because it is highly versatile, only modifying the top few nanometer layers of the polymer without altering the bulk properties [4, 6, 12, 13]. By choosing an appropriate working gas, this treatment incorporates oxygen-containing functional groups, either directly or via post-oxidation [14]. These polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability and thus improve protein adsorption and cytocompatibility [7, 12]. Many studies have shown that plasma treatment of PCL performed at low pressure enhances the adhesion and proliferation of a wide variety of cell types [4, 8, 12, 15, 16]. As an alternative to low-pressure plasma treatments using expensive vacuum equipment, a few authors have reported that atmospheric pressure plasma treatment is also effective, giving rise to high cellular adhesion and proliferation [7, 17, 18]. Medium pressure plasma is rarely used to treat PCL, despite its potential to easily acquire a larger volume of plasma compared to atmospheric pressure plasma treatments, with relatively cost-effective pumping systems [19]. Therefore, our research group has previously used a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD), operating in different gases at medium pressure, in order to modify PCL surface properties. Both air and argon plasmas introduce oxygen-containing functionalities onto the PCL surface and thus increase its wettability, positively influencing the adhesion and the proliferation of human foreskin fibroblasts and mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts [3, 20]. Once an efficient surface modification is accomplished, a crucial and final prerequisite for the use of PCL in vitro and in vivo is required: the material sterility [21, 22]. Consequently, after sterilization, PCL should maintain the introduced surface properties that determine to a large extent the success of the implant. Despite the importance of the material properties, the impact of sterilization on the PCL structure and surface is largely overlooked in the literature, as the majority of studies solely focus on the microbial activity to check for the sterilization efficacy [23].

Since the early 2000s, there has been an increasing interest in biodegradable polymers and materials based on them in regenerative medicine [1]. Unlike biologically inert implants, these biomaterials are designed for controlled degradation and promote the growth of new tissues or support the growth of the body’s own cells [2,3,4,5,6,7]. In addition to biodegradability, materials for tissue engineering should have biocompatibility, i.e., they should be incorporated into the body without causing adverse clinical implications [4, 8], and biological potency, such as antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor potency [9, 10]. Two classes of biodegradable polymers should be distinguished: synthetic and natural. The former are produced from raw materials obtained from oil resources (non-renewable), and the latter are produced from biological resources (renewable). As a rule, natural polymers are inferior in physical and mechanical properties to synthetic ones [11]. However, the properties that make synthetic polymers more preferable for many practical applications lead to difficulties in their utilization, prolonged biodegradation, and, consequently, environmental accumulation [11, 12].
In recent years, regeneration of damaged or lost tissue by tissue engineering is of intense interest to biomedical materials science researchers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) is an approach whereby cells are cultivated on temporary scaffolds at the site of damaged or lost tissue for regeneration of the tissue [6], [7]. For this purpose, biodegradable polymers exhibiting controllable degradation behavior, good cell attachment, and excellent biocompatibility are desirable materials for scaffolds. Such scaffolds are used to supply cells to a desired location in the body and to provide a space for cell growth and tissue formation. It is well known that some growth factors improve the early healing process and regeneration of damaged tissue [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), transforming growth factor (TGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) are known to exhibit functions such as regulation of proliferation, chemotaxis and differentiation of various pluripotent cells [12], [13]. Aliphatic polyesters such as polyglycolide (PGA), poly-l-lactide (PLLA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and their copolymers have been frequently applied as implantable carriers for drug delivery systems and for surgical repair due to their good biodegradation properties, relatively high biocompatibility, high mechanical strength, and excellent shaping and molding properties [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Biodegradable polymer blends and composites are used in applications such as biomedicine, packaging, and agriculture. Controlling the degradation rates of the overall material is essential and was achieved by biodegradable additives, both polymers, and fillers, as outlined below. There is much interest in polymer blends for tissue engineering, because of their adjustable mechanical properties and their ability to adjust the degradation rates to the regrowth of a specific tissue. For this application, a high control of biodegradation is important, e.g., when the speed of bone reconstruction completion is quicker than the time of bone scaffolds degradation to be more suitable for the repair of bone defects or for other tissue.[23, 24] Currently, often porous polymers are used in tissue engineering applications if the polymer matrix can be suitable as a scaffold for tissue growth and can serve as a provisional aid for the cell growth during the regeneration of the target tissue. The polymer can be implanted into the body via minimal operations using small equipment. A small cross-sectioned polymer can be intercalated into the body via a small incision through a catheter. When in the demanded anatomy, with the aid of the body heat, this can be deployed into a greater preordained shape.[23, 24] A promising biocompatible base polymer, of which the biodegradation can be controlled by blending, is PLA.[25] PLA has been used in various biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability in vivo. However, PLA's degradation rate is often too slow,[26] and was accelerated by blending with various polymers and will be discussed in this review. The result of this study can help to simulate the dynamic microenvironment of biological processes. It was suggested that these materials could act as potential candidates for tissue engineering such as a scaffold for bone replacement and regeneration. Also, interesting research was reported by Liu et al.[28] they aimed at scaffold preparation using PGS/PCL blends, as the PGS alone would limit an application in tissue engineering because the time needed for its biodegradation is less than the time needed for cartilage regeneration. However, biodegradable polymers have limited application due to their low mechanical strength versus that for non-degradable polymers [11,12]. To overcome this limitation, much research has been done to improve the mechanical properties of biodegradable polymers [[13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]]. The strategies investigated can be largely divided into two methods. One method utilizes a hybrid material prepared by mixing the matrix polymer with additional matter, such as a nucleating agent, plasticizer, and filler. In the other method, secondary processing is used for modifying the physical properties and crystal structure of the original material; this secondary processing requires heat and a solvent. Although the first method is a relatively simple process, because of a material that is composed of more than two components, the desired chemical properties of the original material may not be retained [[22], [23], [24]]. On the contrary, a neat material composed of a single component may be prepared using the second method. The mechanical strength of the material may be dramatically improved through modification of the crystal structure of the crystalline phase [14,[25], [26], [27]]. Industries have commonly utilized the second method, which includes extrusion, injection molding, and spinning; these have both the effect of strengthening and shape forming the material [[28], [29], [30], [31]]. One of the most common methods is melt extrusion because, not only is it a simple and accessible process, it has the ability to improve the mechanical properties of the polymeric scaffold. The principle of this method when used for strengthening the scaffold is as follows: the repulsive force that arises from a screw inside the extruder is converted into a shear force at the outlet of the nozzle, and the shear force can induce chain orientation and crystal growth in the polymeric scaffold. However, in spite of its simplicity, the efficacy of extrusion for strengthening is moderate; it does not impact an exceptional level of strength compared with other methods. A vascular scaffold based on a biodegradable polymer and fabricated by injection molding has been generally unavoidable, because conventional extrusion leads to the fabrication of a rod or filament-shaped product rather than a tubular-shaped product [[32], [33], [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], [40]]. However, this type of scaffold has inferior resistance to circumferential stress and, as a consequence, has been the origin of negative clinical outcomes including vessel shrinkage, collapse, thrombosis, and restenosis of medical devices.

Unfortunately, bioactive molecules are usually rapidly released by desorption and diffusion though the material, which consequently inactivates the polymer matrix. In this context, covalent incorporation of biomolecules into biomaterials is a strategy of choice when sustained bioactivity is required. Numerous studies focused on the functionalization of degradable polymers with peptides exploring many chemical pathways [13], [14]. Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS Using biodegradable polymers as biomaterials has contributed to significant advancements in the fields of regenerative medicine and tissue engineering [1]. In particular, polycaprolactone (PCL) has received considerable attention due to its excellent mechanical and structural properties, and tuneable degradation kinetics. Moreover, the non-immunogenicity of PCL, combined with the possibility of using it as an interporous scaffold material, has resulted in better tissue ingrowth [2-4]. The above-mentioned benefits, in addition to the inexpensive production routes of PCL, have encouraged many research groups to investigate its potential applications in numerous fields of tissue engineering [2, 5]. However, the bioactivity of the tissue-engineered constructs is threatened by the hydrophobic nature of PCL [4, 6-8]. In general, it is known that a moderate surface hydrophilicity allows for an increased adsorption of proteins without modifying their natural conformation. In turn, this increases the cell affinity towards the surface, leading to stimulated cell adhesion and cell proliferation [9, 10]. As a consequence, PCL hydrophobicity negatively impacts cell-material interactions [1]. In order to overcome this issue, surface modification is required. Several approaches have previously been investigated, including wet-chemical treatments, and ion beam, x-ray and gamma radiation. However, the wet-chemical treatment route generates large amounts of hazardous chemical waste and often impacts on bulk properties such as structural strength and elasticity, while most radiation methods can cause severe degradation of the polymer [11]. As an alternative, non-thermal plasma treatment has shown to be a promising method because it is highly versatile, only modifying the top few nanometer layers of the polymer without altering the bulk properties [4, 6, 12, 13]. By choosing an appropriate working gas, this treatment incorporates oxygen-containing functional groups, either directly or via post-oxidation [14]. These polar groups increase the surface energy and wettability and thus improve protein adsorption and cytocompatibility [7, 12]. Many studies have shown that plasma treatment of PCL performed at low pressure enhances the adhesion and proliferation of a wide variety of cell types [4, 8, 12, 15, 16]. As an alternative to low-pressure plasma treatments using expensive vacuum equipment, a few authors have reported that atmospheric pressure plasma treatment is also effective, giving rise to high cellular adhesion and proliferation [7, 17, 18]. Medium pressure plasma is rarely used to treat PCL, despite its potential to easily acquire a larger volume of plasma compared to atmospheric pressure plasma treatments, with relatively cost-effective pumping systems [19]. Therefore, our research group has previously used a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD), operating in different gases at medium pressure, in order to modify PCL surface properties. Both air and argon plasmas introduce oxygen-containing functionalities onto the PCL surface and thus increase its wettability, positively influencing the adhesion and the proliferation of human foreskin fibroblasts and mouse calvaria pre-osteoblasts [3, 20]. Once an efficient surface modification is accomplished, a crucial and final prerequisite for the use of PCL in vitro and in vivo is required: the material sterility [21, 22]. Consequently, after sterilization, PCL should maintain the introduced surface properties that determine to a large extent the success of the implant. Despite the importance of the material properties, the impact of sterilization on the PCL structure and surface is largely overlooked in the literature, as the majority of studies solely focus on the microbial activity to check for the sterilization efficacy [23].

By addressing these properties diligently, it becomes possible to develop medical devices that not only exhibit sustainability and biodegradability but also fulfill the functional requirements for effective medical applications.[5, 6]

Since the early 2000s, there has been an increasing interest in biodegradable polymers and materials based on them in regenerative medicine [1]. Unlike biologically inert implants, these biomaterials are designed for controlled degradation and promote the growth of new tissues or support the growth of the body’s own cells [2,3,4,5,6,7]. In addition to biodegradability, materials for tissue engineering should have biocompatibility, i.e., they should be incorporated into the body without causing adverse clinical implications [4, 8], and biological potency, such as antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor potency [9, 10]. Two classes of biodegradable polymers should be distinguished: synthetic and natural. The former are produced from raw materials obtained from oil resources (non-renewable), and the latter are produced from biological resources (renewable). As a rule, natural polymers are inferior in physical and mechanical properties to synthetic ones [11]. However, the properties that make synthetic polymers more preferable for many practical applications lead to difficulties in their utilization, prolonged biodegradation, and, consequently, environmental accumulation [11, 12].
In recent years, regeneration of damaged or lost tissue by tissue engineering is of intense interest to biomedical materials science researchers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) is an approach whereby cells are cultivated on temporary scaffolds at the site of damaged or lost tissue for regeneration of the tissue [6], [7]. For this purpose, biodegradable polymers exhibiting controllable degradation behavior, good cell attachment, and excellent biocompatibility are desirable materials for scaffolds. Such scaffolds are used to supply cells to a desired location in the body and to provide a space for cell growth and tissue formation. It is well known that some growth factors improve the early healing process and regeneration of damaged tissue [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), insulin-like growth factor (IGF), transforming growth factor (TGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) are known to exhibit functions such as regulation of proliferation, chemotaxis and differentiation of various pluripotent cells [12], [13]. Aliphatic polyesters such as polyglycolide (PGA), poly-l-lactide (PLLA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and their copolymers have been frequently applied as implantable carriers for drug delivery systems and for surgical repair due to their good biodegradation properties, relatively high biocompatibility, high mechanical strength, and excellent shaping and molding properties [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Polydepsipeptides are copolymers consisting of amino acids and hydroxy acids that possess biodegradability similar to that of aliphatic polyesters and functionality as polypeptides. We previously synthesized biodegradable copolymers of depsipeptide and lactide, poly(depsipeptide-co-lactide)s, by ring-opening copolymerization of l-lactide (LA) with cyclodepsipeptides consisting of glycolic acid (Glc) and aspartic acid (Asp) or lysine (Lys) to give poly[(Glc-alt-Asp)-co-lactide] (PGDLA) and poly[(Glc-alt-Lys)-co-lactide] (PGKLA) (Fig. 1) with reactive (hydrophilic and ionic) side-chain groups [19], [20], [21], [22]. The poly(depsipeptide-co-lactide)s obtained exhibited higher non-enzymatic degradability compared to PLLA depending on the depsipeptide unit content of the copolymers [20]. We investigated the cell attachment and growth on films and porous sponges composed of PGDLA and PGKLA and reported the potential utility of these copolymers as scaffolds for tissue regeneration [23], [24]. Other works on tissue engineering using biodegradable matrices containing amino acids or proteins have also been reported [25], [26], [27], [28], [29], [30]. To achieve efficient cell growth and cell differentiation, sustained release of growth factors from depots or matrices is effective [31], [32], [33], [34], [35]. In this study, to evaluate the utility of PGDLA and PGKLA as biodegradable scaffolds exhibiting the sustained release of growth factors, the entrapment and release of proteins into and from the matrices were investigated. We employed three types of growth factors, basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), epidermal growth factor (EGF) and nerve growth factor (NGF), which stimulate the proliferation of mesenchymal-derived cells, including fibroblasts and ligament cells. Three typical proteins (lysozyme, insulin and lactoferrin) with similar physicochemical characteristics to these growth factors (molecular weights and isoelectric points) were additionally chosen as model proteins for the growth factors. We then prepared biodegradable matrices (films and sponges) entrapping these model proteins or growth factors by a water in oil (w/o) emulsion method and investigated the release behavior of the proteins and the cell growth on the matrices.
First published on 25th February 2016 Phosphorylated polymers are promising for bone regeneration because they may recapitulate the essence of the phosphorylated bone extracellular matrix (ECM) to build an instructive environment for bone formation. However, most of the existing synthetic phosphorylated polymers are not fully biodegradable; thus, they are not ideal for tissue engineering. Here, we designed and synthesized a new phosphorylated polymer, poly(sebacoyl diglyceride) phosphate (PSeD-P), based on the biodegradable osteoconductive backbone PSeD. To our knowledge, PSeD-P is the first polymer to integrate the osteoinductive moiety β-glycerol phosphate (β-GP). PSeD-P shows good biodegradability and can be readily fabricated on 3D porous scaffolds. It has a porous structure with interconnected macropores (75-150 μm) and extensive micropores (several microns). PSeD-P promotes the adhesion, proliferation, and maturation of osteoblasts more effectively than poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA). Furthermore, PSeD-P induces a significantly higher expression of osteogenic biomarkers and ALP activity in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) compared to its non-phosphorylated precursor, PSeD. The level of improvement is comparable to free β-GP in culture medium. More importantly, without using β-GP, the typical mineralization promoter in osteogenic culture media, PSeD-P substantially induces the mineralization of the ECM in MSCs, which is totally absent using PSeD under identical culture conditions. PSeD-P provides a new strategy to integrate bioactive phosphates via β-GP into biomaterial, and has promise for bone regeneration applications. In addition, the synthetic method is versatile; both the backbone and the side phosphate groups could be readily tailored to generate a family of phosphorylated polymers for a wide range of biomedical applications. Herein, we report a new phosphorylated polymer, poly(sebacoyl diglyceride) phosphate (PSeD-P), for bone regeneration (Fig. 1). Nowadays, macromolecular design, blending, and additives are being considered to alter the conditions for biodegradation of synthetic polyesters.[38] In terms of polymer structure, the main factors affecting the abiotic and biotic degradation rate of polymers are the monomer structure, crystallinity, hydrophilicity, Mw, and density of the susceptible hydrolyzable chemical groups such as ester or ether. Besides these methods, reduction of the polymer size by mechanical action also allows the acceleration of biodegradation by increasing the surface area or surface-to-volume ratio available for water (abiotic) or biotic (enzymatic) attack. Treatments such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, plasma, microwave, alteration of the surface of the polymer by acidic/alkaline immersion, incorporation of specific additives (plasticizers or surfactants), copolymerization, reactive blending, composites, and nanocomposites have been reported to enhance biodegradation at some extent (Table 2). Since thermal properties of biodegradable polymers, reflected in transition temperatures such as glass transition temperature (Tg) and melting temperature (Tm), are expressed in a wide range, a pre-treatment of a mix of plastic waste involving the use of elevated temperatures presents some challenge. Temperatures around the Tg of PLA are already at the Tm of PHAs or PCL. It is conceivable that biodegradable polymers with low Tg and Tm have more susceptible biodegradable structures and higher biodegradation rates. However, other factors such as polymer crystallinity and surface properties also play a crucial role.

Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is among the most commonly used thermoplastic polymers in various industries, such as textiles, packaging, construction, and marine engineering [1]. Historically, antimony compounds have been the most commonly used catalysts in PET production. However, antimony is a suspected carcinogen and is able to migrate to the aqueous environment when using PET products [2]. In view of the increasing daily production and usage of PET, it is imperative to find an environmentally friendly catalyst to avoid the risk of antimony pollution. Titanium-based catalysts are attractive alternatives due to their high catalytic activity, low cost, and pollution-free features, and show promising potential for PET production [[3], [4], [5], [6]]. On the other hand, PET, especially that produced using titanium compounds as catalysts, is susceptible to thermal oxidation through radical reactions during its synthesis and post-processing at elevated temperatures, which can remarkably degrade its properties and color [[7], [8], [9]]. With a view to enhancing the thermal stability of PET, its thermal oxidation behavior has been extensively studied by means of various analytical methods, such as thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometry, and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS) [8,[10], [11], [12]]. Although several reasonable mechanisms have been postulated on the basis of results obtained by the above techniques, direct information on the radical intermediates generated in PET is still lacking. In this context, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) accompanied by spin-trapping methods is evolving as a feasible approach for identifying short-lived radical intermediates during the thermal oxidation of polymers [[13], [14], [15], [16]]. Recently, Sono et al. [17,18] gained great insight into the thermal degradation mechanism of another versatile polyester, poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT), and a related co-polymer elastomer, poly(butylene terephthalate)-co-poly(ethylene oxide) (PBT-co-PEO), through temperature-controlled EPR with spin trapping. Spin reagents were introduced into polymers by a solution-casting method and hydrogen abstraction was found to initialize thermal degradation at relatively low temperature (110 °C); α-carbon radicals, -O−•CH−, were subsequently detected, and the main chain decomposition occurred by β-scission at the ester linkage [17]. Likewise, the thermal degradation process of PBT-co-PEO was studied over four weight-loss stages. Alkoxy radicals -O−•CH-CH2− and alkyl radicals −•CH2− were trapped during the first decomposition stage, which was accompanied by random degradation and gelation. In the second and third stages, thermo-oxidative degradation was successively observed for PEO segments and PBT units [18]. In addition to these analyses of PET thermo-oxidative phenomena, stabilizers such as anti-oxidants are also used to minimize oxidation reactions and discoloration [[19], [20], [21]]. Among them, sterically hindered phenol derivatives (Irganox 1010, Irganox 1222, Irganox 1098, etc.) are regarded as the most promising anti-oxidants for PET, and are widely applied to improve long-term stability [[22], [23], [24]]. For example, Irganox 1010 and Irganox 1222 have been separately studied with regard to their effects on PET synthesis, and it was found that an appropriate concentration of anti-oxidant permits a higher polycondensation rate and leads to good stability with low DEG content [25]. Freitas et al. [26] noted a synergistic effect when anti-oxidant Irganox B561 (a mixture of Irganox 1010 and Irgafos 168) was introduced into recycled PET, imparting a superior intrinsic viscosity. The calcium complex Irganox 1425 is another efficient phenolic anti-oxidant, which bears phosphonic acid ethyl ester groups to improve the thermal stability of polymer melts [27,28]. It has been used to prevent transesterification or thermo-oxidative degradation during the production of PC/PET blends, and also shows activity for catalyzing solid-state polycondensation [29,30].

Toxicologic pathology is the art of assessment of potential adverse effects at the tissue level in pre-clinical studies. In the case of biomaterials and medical devices, the toxicologic pathologists assess the safety (biocompatibility) and efficacy (conditions of the use) of the implantable materials. Proper assessment of biocompatibility of biomaterials is of utmost importance, since it helps to determine their safety after implantation in humans. Biomaterial-related toxicity can be attributed to several factors, including for example leachable compounds from the material leading to thrombosis or carcinogenesis, or biodegradation of the material causing changes in its physical and compatibility properties. Evaluation of biocompatibility and biofunctionality involves assessment of cytotoxicity, allergic responses, irritation, inflammation and systemic and chronic toxicity. In many of these assessments, the toxicologic pathologist has an important role in determining product safety and potential toxicity. In this article, we review the special needs for proper toxicologic pathology assessment of biomaterials and degradable polymers. We review common adverse effects expected with biomaterials and describe their pathological picture and their clinical relevance. We also introduce a novel compact MR imaging technology as a tool for assessing biocompatibility and efficacy of implanted biodegradable materials, since it allows for the longitudinal imaging and quantification of inflammation in vivo caused by the device implantation, and enabling general inspection of shape, location and integrity of the device in vivo. Since the MR imaging technique is non-invasive, the effects of the implantable device can be monitored longitudinally in the same animal without perturbation of the pathology. PLGA copolymers can be prepared by either the direct polycondensation of lactic acid and glycolic acid or ring-opening copolymerization (ROCOP) of the related cyclic lactide (LA) and glycolide (GA). Compared to the step-growth polycondensation approach, in which only PLGA copolymers with low molar masses can be obtained,8 the ROCOP of LA and GA represents a more efficient strategy considering the advantages of atomic economy, controllable molar masses, low dispersities and well-defined chain-ends. The most widely investigated and used catalyst for the preparation of PLGA is stannous octanoate both in academia and industry.9-11 With the increasing concern about the health safety risk of stannous octanoate, some other low toxic metal-based catalysts were later developed for the ROCOP of LA and GA, including bismuth subsalicylate,12 zinc lactate,13 zirconium acetylacetonate14 and dimethyl(salicylaldiminato) aluminum compounds.15 Due to the much higher reactivity of GA compared to LA, PLGA copolymers with truly random microstructures were not directly achieved with the abovementioned organometallic catalysts.12-16 Although long glycolidyl blocks can be randomized to shorter ones by transesterification, product discoloration resulting from the high reaction temperature (typically above 140 °C) as well as metal residues still hamper the applications of resultant PLGA copolymers in biomedical technologies. Although it was reported that residual phosphazene catalysts also showed considerably cytotoxicity,17 organocatalysts have been intensively investigated as sustainable alternatives to metal-based catalysts in the past decades due to their easy preparation, easy manipulation, good stability and facile removal from products, especially for biomedical, electronic and food packaging applications, in which catalyst residues are undesired.18-23 A series of aliphatic polyesters, including poly(lactide), poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(δ-valerolactone) and poly(γ-butyrolactone), have been successfully achieved with organocatalysts.24-29 Despite the great successes achieved with organocatalysts in the ROP of cyclic lactones or lactides, the organocatalytic preparation of PLGA copolymers has been scarcely explored. Satoh and coworkers achieved the organocatalytic regioselective ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of optically active methylglycolides (MGs) to produce highly alternating PLGAs using an organophosphazene base tBu-P2 as the catalyst.30 But the MG monomers are not commercially available and the preparation needs several steps and tedious purification. To the best of our knowledge, the only organocatalytic ROCOP of lactide and glycolide was reported by Hoye and coworkers, in which GA was continuously added in a controlled manner to a mixing solution of LA, poly(ethylene glycol) macroinitiator and 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene (DBU) catalyst.31 Though PLGA copolymers with random microstructures were obtained with this semi-batch strategy, a sophisticated technique was necessary to control the addition rate of GA. This approach was also limited by the low LA conversion (ca. 50%) due to the much higher reactivity of GA relative to LA. The organocatalytic ROCOP of GA with LA needs to solve the dilemma that the reactivity of GA is generally much higher than LA. Otherwise, long glycolidyl blocks will form in the propagating chain due to the preferred incorporation of glycolyl units, resulting in the precipitation of the obtained PLGA copolymers in common solvents before full conversions of LA and GA monomers. Therefore, it is highly demanding to develop or discover new catalysts that have extremely high activity to both GA and LA monomers. We have developed a new organophosphazene base (CTPB) and demonstrated its high activity toward the ROP of LA.26 The (thio)urea anionic organocatalysts developed by Waymouth et al. exhibited high activity and good control over the ROP of lactides, lactones and cyclic carbonates.32-34 In the framework of our research interest in the organocatalytic ROP of cyclic esters, we recently reported the controlled ROP of low strained γ-butyrolactone and its derivatives with organophosphazene base/urea binary catalysts.35-37 In these studies, the urea anions can effectively activate cyclic lactones and lactides through hydrogen bonding as evidenced by the accelerated polymerization rate compared to a single base as the catalyst. It is supposed that organophosphazene/urea binary catalysts may significantly improve the reactivity of LA and reduce the reactivity difference between LA and GA. These findings inspire us to explore the ROCOP of LA and GA using CTPB/urea binary catalysts. In this contribution, we explored the one-pot organocatalytic ROCOP of LA and GA to produce PLGA copolymers with random microstructures at ambient temperature. The CTPB/urea showed high catalytic activity over the ROCOP of LA and GA. Full conversions of GA and LA were achieved within a few seconds, indicating ultrafast copolymerization kinetics. In contrast to the previous catalytic systems, in which GA exhibited much higher reactivity than LA, the CTPB/urea binary catalyst herein led to similar reactivity of LA and GA, producing random PLGA copolymers with tunable monomer sequence lengths.

Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is among the most commonly used thermoplastic polymers in various industries, such as textiles, packaging, construction, and marine engineering [1]. Historically, antimony compounds have been the most commonly used catalysts in PET production. However, antimony is a suspected carcinogen and is able to migrate to the aqueous environment when using PET products [2]. In view of the increasing daily production and usage of PET, it is imperative to find an environmentally friendly catalyst to avoid the risk of antimony pollution. Titanium-based catalysts are attractive alternatives due to their high catalytic activity, low cost, and pollution-free features, and show promising potential for PET production [[3], [4], [5], [6]]. On the other hand, PET, especially that produced using titanium compounds as catalysts, is susceptible to thermal oxidation through radical reactions during its synthesis and post-processing at elevated temperatures, which can remarkably degrade its properties and color [[7], [8], [9]]. With a view to enhancing the thermal stability of PET, its thermal oxidation behavior has been extensively studied by means of various analytical methods, such as thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometry, and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS) [8,[10], [11], [12]]. Although several reasonable mechanisms have been postulated on the basis of results obtained by the above techniques, direct information on the radical intermediates generated in PET is still lacking. In this context, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) accompanied by spin-trapping methods is evolving as a feasible approach for identifying short-lived radical intermediates during the thermal oxidation of polymers [[13], [14], [15], [16]]. Recently, Sono et al. [17,18] gained great insight into the thermal degradation mechanism of another versatile polyester, poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT), and a related co-polymer elastomer, poly(butylene terephthalate)-co-poly(ethylene oxide) (PBT-co-PEO), through temperature-controlled EPR with spin trapping. Spin reagents were introduced into polymers by a solution-casting method and hydrogen abstraction was found to initialize thermal degradation at relatively low temperature (110 °C); α-carbon radicals, -O−•CH−, were subsequently detected, and the main chain decomposition occurred by β-scission at the ester linkage [17]. Likewise, the thermal degradation process of PBT-co-PEO was studied over four weight-loss stages. Alkoxy radicals -O−•CH-CH2− and alkyl radicals −•CH2− were trapped during the first decomposition stage, which was accompanied by random degradation and gelation. In the second and third stages, thermo-oxidative degradation was successively observed for PEO segments and PBT units [18]. In addition to these analyses of PET thermo-oxidative phenomena, stabilizers such as anti-oxidants are also used to minimize oxidation reactions and discoloration [[19], [20], [21]]. Among them, sterically hindered phenol derivatives (Irganox 1010, Irganox 1222, Irganox 1098, etc.) are regarded as the most promising anti-oxidants for PET, and are widely applied to improve long-term stability [[22], [23], [24]]. For example, Irganox 1010 and Irganox 1222 have been separately studied with regard to their effects on PET synthesis, and it was found that an appropriate concentration of anti-oxidant permits a higher polycondensation rate and leads to good stability with low DEG content [25]. Freitas et al. [26] noted a synergistic effect when anti-oxidant Irganox B561 (a mixture of Irganox 1010 and Irgafos 168) was introduced into recycled PET, imparting a superior intrinsic viscosity. The calcium complex Irganox 1425 is another efficient phenolic anti-oxidant, which bears phosphonic acid ethyl ester groups to improve the thermal stability of polymer melts [27,28]. It has been used to prevent transesterification or thermo-oxidative degradation during the production of PC/PET blends, and also shows activity for catalyzing solid-state polycondensation [29,30].

Starch is a reproducible resource that can be isolated from many natural substances such as wheat, corn, paddy, potato, and other agricultural products. Native starch has a high water-holding capacity but does not efficiently remove heavy metal ions. However, when starch is grafted with a variety of vinyl monomers, such as acrylic amide (AM), acrylic acid (AA), acrylonitrile, methylacrylonitrile, alkylmethacrylates, vinyl ketones, and 2-(dimethylamino) ethylacrylate, it can be used to remove heavy metal ions without sacrificing its biodegradable nature.17 Cassava starch is among the most important starches in industry, especially in countries like India, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam.18 Since the tubers lack lipids and other extraneous compounds, the extraction of starch is easier, and the yield is very high compared to cereal and other tuber starches.18 The polymer matrix of a native starch granule consists of two kinds of polymers, amylose and amylopectin.17 While the amylopectin in the cassava starch structure accounts for 83%, it is more suitable for a grafting reaction with a vinyl monomer. The application of modified starch, which works by chelating organic compounds, has emerged as a strong area of interest due to its low cost and biodegradability.19, 20 The starch derivatives that contain various functional groups have the potential to remove heavy metal ions because of their chelating functional groups, and this can be considered an unconventional and economic approach to these processes.17 Starch-based superabsorbent polymer (SAP) is a copolymer that results from grafting starch with vinyl monomers, and it has an outstanding water absorption and holding capacity due to its loosely crosslinked network structure and hydrophilic side groups.21 These polymers have been widely used in agriculture, horticulture, bioengineering, biomedicine, water purification, and food storage.22-24 Moreover, their adsorption properties for heavy metal ions from solutions have attracted much attention due to their excellent biodegradability and biocompatibility.25-28 Lu et al.17 synthesized acrylic acid-grafted corn starches for Cu2+ ion adsorption, and the functions of pH, water holding capacity, the content of NaCl, and the initial Cu2+ concentration were all investigated. Zheng et al.29 prepared a series of starch-g-poly (acrylic acid)/sodium humate (St-g-PAA/SH) hydrogels in order to adsorb Cu2+ from aqueous solution. In another work,30 hydrogels of two biopolymers (starch and dextrin) with different acrylamide monomers crosslinked with methylenebisacrylamide were prepared to extract three transition metal ions, Fe2+, Cr6+, and Cu2+. Ramasubramaniam et al.25 revealed that the chitosan/starch polymer blend was an excellent adsorbent for Cd2+ ion removal. However, most of these starch-based SAPs have a relatively low adsorption capacity for heavy metals. For cassava starch-based superabsorbent polymers (CST-SAPs), many studies have focused on their synthesis, characterization, and swelling behavior.18, 31, 32 There are comparatively fewer reports on Cd2+ ion adsorption. Hence, we prepared a CST-SAP, and the morphologies and structures of the CST, CST-SAP, and CST-SAP-Cd2+ were investigated and compared using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The adsorption capacity, adsorption isotherm, and kinetics of the CST-SAP were evaluated. Furthermore, the effects of contact time, contact temperature, initial solution pH, initial Cd2+ concentration, and adsorbent dosage on the removal of Cd2+ were all studied in detail. Based solely on the provided evidence, the specific role of oxidized maize starch (OMS) as a binder in 3D printing is **not explicitly described**.

However, the evidence provides relevant context regarding starch in 3D printing and oxidation:

1.  **Starch in 3D Printing:** Starch-based materials are primarily used in 3D printing (specifically Fused Deposition Modeling, FDM) as composite systems blended with polymers like polylactic acid (PLA) or acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) copolymers. The starch component contributes renewability and degradability to these composites [2].
2.  **Oxidation of Starch:** Oxidation modifies the structure of maize starch. It introduces carbonyl and carboxyl groups onto the starch molecules at carbons 2, 3, and/or 6 during treatment with oxidizing agents like sodium perborate (SPB). This oxidation process also cleaves glycosidic bonds, reducing molecular weight. The extent of oxidation dictates the degree of functional group formation [9], [11].
3.  **Effect of Oxidation on Properties:** Oxidation alters the morphology of starch granules, making their surfaces rough and edges more defined compared to native starch [9]. It also affects thermal stability [9].

**Conclusion:** While the evidence confirms oxidized maize starch exists and details its production chemistry, morphology, and thermal properties [9], [11], and establishes that starch is used in polymer blends/composites for 3D printing [2], it **does not explicitly state or describe the mechanism by which OMS functions specifically as a "binder"** within the context of 3D printing processes or materials.

Starch is a naturally abundant polysaccharide which is available at low cost for preparation of various functional polymers. In general, starch is widely used not only in food but also in nonfood industrial applications such as food packaging, pharmaceutical, and thickener agent in the printing past of the reactive dyes.11-15 The modification of starch is one of the interesting processes for required properties such as low viscosity, low gelatinization temperature, and good solubility in cold water. Recently, various chemical modifications of starches including carboxymethyl starch (CMS)15-18 dialdehyde starch,19 and starch acetate20 have been of interests due to the insertion of bulky hydrophilic group on polysaccharide chains to reduce retrogradation (recrystallization) of starch and increase cold water solubility. The incorporation of starches or modified starches into rubbers to form composites has been paid attention by many researchers. Angellier et al.21 have prepared the starch nanocrystal/NR nanocomposite films by casting the mixture of waxy maize starch (MS) nanocrystals suspension. The NR latex was loaded with 0-50 wt % waxy MS nanocrystals, which were hydrolyzed using sulfuric acid. It was found that the swelling phenomenon was due to the formation of starch nanocrystals network through hydrogen linkages between starch nanoparticles clusters and the favorable interactions between the matrix and the starch. The nanocomposite film loaded with 20 wt % starch nanocrystal showed the highest tensile strength value (14.4 MPa) whereas nanocomposite film with 10 wt % starch nanocrystal was claimed to give similar stiffness value to the composite film loaded with 26.6 wt % CB.22 Rajisha et al.23 have reported homogenously dispersed starch nanocrystals in NR matrix. The starch nanocrystals could be used to improve the mechanical properties in terms of tensile strength and modulus in nanocomposites film. Wang et al.24 have prepared starch xanthate/NR composite by blending starch xanthate in the range of 0-25 phr in NR latex. It was found that starch xanthate loading increased thermal stability and mechanical properties of NR vulcanizates whereas unmodified starch loading decreased thermal stability of NR vulcanizates. Khalaf and Sadek25 have studied the effect of compatibilizers including maleic acid anhydride (MAH) and glycidyl methacrylate (GMA) on sulfur-cure characteristics and physicomechanical properties of NR/MS vulcanizates. The physicomechanical properties based on tensile strength and elongation at break of NR/MS (90/10) vulcanizates with GMA at 1 phr were found to be higher than those of NR/MS vulcanizates with MAH at the same amount whereas Young's modulus and hardness were found to be lower than those of the NR/MS vulcanizates with MAH at all loading content. ans_rerank: Based on the provided context evidence, oxidized maize starch (OMS) serves as a binder in 3D printing primarily by enhancing compatibility with synthetic polymers through chemical modification. Oxidation introduces carbonyl and carboxyl groups ([3], [4], [14]), which reduces starch's intermolecular hydrogen bonding and decreases agglomeration ([6]). This structural change improves interfacial adhesion when blended with polymers like polylactic acid (PLA) or acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) in filament formulations ([1], [6]). The carbonyl groups in OMS form hydrogen bonds with synthetic polymer matrices ([6]), facilitating uniform dispersion during melt processing and layer deposition in techniques like Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) ([1]). Additionally, OMS exhibits higher thermal stability due to its oxidized groups ([3], [4]), which is critical for maintaining structural integrity during the 3D printing process where temperatures typically reach 70–160°C ([1]). However, challenges related to printability and material safety remain unresolved ([1]).

Regarding the first factor, Young's modulus strongly depends on the highest carbonization temperature. For example, Johnson et al. In the present work, the highest carbonization temperature that we could achieve was 1500 °C. Typically, carbonization is performed at 350-1700 °C, followed by graphitization wherein fibers are further heated in an inert atmosphere to temperatures above 2000 °C to improve orientation of the basal planes and to increase stiffness [32]. Regarding the second factor, simultaneous stretching and heating of fibers during formation and carbonization are known to improve fiber orientation, thereby increasing Young's modulus. In the present work, the fibers were hand drawn, and they were not stretched during aromatization or carbonization. We did not use fiber-spinning equipment that would allow simultaneous heating and stretching during the aromatization and carbonization steps, due to the small scale of the study. PLA/natural fiber composites have been investigated by numerous researchers. Du et al.7 studied the properties of PLA/cellulosic natural fiber composites produced by film stacking method. The natural fibers were hardwood high yield pulp, softwood high yield pulp, and bleached kraft softwood pulp fibers. They investigated the mechanical and thermal properties of the composites. They showed that the incorporation of pulp fibers increased the composite storage modulus significantly, and improved the tensile modulus and the tensile strength. They reported that the highest composite tensile strength achieved was nearly onefold higher than that of the neat PLA. Huda and coworkers8 investigated the effect of fiber surface treatments on the properties of laminated biocomposites from PLA and kenaf fibers. Kenaf fiber reinforced PLA laminated composites were prepared by compression molding using the film stacking method. The kenaf fibers were alkaline treated and silanized prior to composite preparation. They reported that both silane-treated fiber (FIBSI) reinforced composite and alkali-treated fiber (FIBNA) reinforced composite offered superior mechanical properties compared to untreated fiber-reinforced composite. The heat deflection temperature (HDT) of the PLA laminated composites was found to be significantly higher than that of neat PLA resin. They concluded that standard PLA resins were suitable for the manufacture of kenaf fiber reinforced laminated biocomposites with useful engineering properties. In other study, a commercial PLA was converted to film and then used in combination with jute fiber mats to generate composites by a film stacking technique.9 It was highlighted that the tensile properties of composites produced at temperatures in the 180-220 °C range were significantly higher than those of PLA alone. They observed that the composites fractured in a brittle nature under tensile load. Size exclusion chromatography revealed that only minor changes in the molecular weight distribution of the PLA occurred during the process. In a recent study, Porras and Maranon10 focused on the development and characterization of a laminate composite material from PLA and woven bamboo fabric. The results showed that the strength of the plain-woven bamboo fabric in the weft direction was greater than in the warp direction. question: How does 'gamma-irradiation' affect the molecular weight of PCL?
ground_truth: Gamma irradiation causes random chain scission in the amorphous regions of PCL. This leads to a dose-dependent decrease in molecular weight ($M_n$ and $M_w$). While PCL is more radiation-resistant than degradable polyethers, high doses (>25 kGy) used for sterilization can still significantly compromise its mechanical toughness.

Our study shows that irradiation doses of 10 and 25 kGy, which are commonly used for sterilization of medical devices, practically do not change the structural features of the hybrid wound dressing's layers. If a higher dose of 35 kGy is needed, the sterilization process can be safely performed in a L.N. environment, which practically does not change the structure of the PDLGA layer and even that of the more sensitive collagen layer. Based on the results described above a schematic representation of a qualitative model can be presented, describing the effect of the irradiation dose (at room temperature) on the physical and on the mechanical properties of the dressing and its performance (Fig. 9). A sign of a wide arrow in a box represents a case when an increase in the irradiation dose results in a decrease in the specific property. In all other cases, an increase in irradiation dose increases the property. As shown in the schematic model, the weight loss and the WVTR are increased while the water uptake is decreased with the increase in the irradiation dose. As expected, higher weight loss of the collagen layer mainly, which results from degradation, enables higher WVTR and lower water uptake. An increase in the radiation dose also resulted in an increase in both, tensile strength and modulus and a decrease in the maximal strain. These changes probably occur because of crosslinking of the collagen layer and result in stronger but more brittle wound dressings. An exception is the case of irradiation dose of 50 kGy which results in a collapse of the microstructure of both, collagen and PDLGA layers, leading to very low WVTR, strength and strain. It is important to note that all described above changes are much smaller when the irradiation is performed in liquid nitrogen, because of smaller changes in degradation and chain scission of both polymers. This study enabled us to assess the effect of the sterilization using gamma irradiation on the physical and mechanical properties of our newly developed hybrid wound dressing. We showed that irradiation at R.T. affect the relevant properties and function of the wound dressing, but when a dose of 25 kGy is used, which is standard for medical devices, the changes are not so dramatic in most properties, and enable function similar to that of non-sterilized samples. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. In addition, it releases antibiotics and pain killers in a controlled desired manner to the wound. Therefore, performing an appropriate sterilization process for this new system will enable to use it in the clinic. Exposure of polymers to high-energy irradiation initiates a process known as chain scission, in which the covalent bonds within the polymer backbone are broken. This results in the formation of shorter polymer chains, known as oligomers, leading to a significant decrease in molecular weight [16]. Oxidative degradation catalyzed by irradiation and oxygen proceeds via a free radical mechanism, forming unstable hydroperoxides that decompose into reactive species and introduce hydrophilic terminal groups such as carboxylic acids (-COOH), hydroxyl (-OH), or carbonyl (C═O) groups [17]. Meanwhile, hydrolysis involves the cleavage of PBS ester bonds upon contact with water, resulting in smaller molecular fragments. These chemical changes increase the polymer's polarity and create an environment conducive to microbial colonization. Low-molecular weight polymers are more accessible and easier for microorganisms to metabolize [18]. Additionally, the hydrophilic nature of the irradiated surface helps retain moisture, further facilitating microbial adhesion and enzymatic degradation. Notably, hydrolysis enhances oxidative vulnerability by increasing hydrophilicity, while oxidation promotes hydrolysis through the formation of polar functional groups. This interplay accelerates the polymer degradation in soil environments and reduces the accumulation of plastic waste. However, in the absence of further surface modification, the lack of functional moieties on the PCL chain results in non-ideal surface properties of such scaffolds, especially in terms of the inability to tailor the presentation of functional ligands for directed cell adhesion and growth. question: What is the 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films?
ground_truth: Most biodegradable polymers (PLA, starch, PBAT) have relatively poor gas and water vapor barrier properties compared to conventional laminates. Improving biodegradability (hydrophilicity) often intrinsically reduces water barrier performance. This trade-off is often managed via multilayer structures or high-barrier coatings (like SiOx or nanoclays).

First published on 5th April 2024 This review article provides a thorough overview of barrier coating materials that have been used in food packaging with a focus on biodegradable (bio-based or petroleum-based) materials, such as lipids, proteins, polysaccharides, agriculture waste and polyesters. The goal is to provide an opportunity to acknowledge progress made in this field, focusing on modifications made to coatings. These modifications aim to address the shortcomings of biodegradable substrates (either plastic or paper) and improve their performance, enabling them to compete with traditional petroleum-based food packaging materials. This includes their barrier against water vapor and oxygen, mechanical and surface characteristics (sealability and adhesion), as well as antimicrobial properties. The barrier of most biodegradable polymers underperforms in comparison with petroleum-based non-biodegradable polymers, which possess either high water vapor barrier or high oxygen barrier. Coating technology is a promising solution particularly in barrier improvement of biodegradable polymers. Currently, there are only metallized, or inorganic nanosheet coatings available for biodegradable films that meet food packaging requirements. There are some challenges in this field, for example, being able to retain the coating's biodegradability despite applied modifications to improve it's performance, the large-scale fabrication of biodegradable coatings, the coating's delamination and heat-sealability during service time, and the migration of the coating into the packaged food. Moreover, green chemistry and its sustainability needs in biodegradable polymeric coatings are also discussed regarding new ideas and possible directions for widespread application of coatings in food packaging. This is the first review that specifically summarizes biodegradable coatings on plastic and paper substrates with a focus on coating modifications to improve the performance of the base substrate to meet the required properties for food packaging applications.

For this reason, methods other than physical attachment technique could be more effective in this matter [3, 4]. In the packaging area, mainly synthetic films are used, due to their high tensile strength, low permeability and low cost [10]. One major disadvantage in the synthetic film is the biodegradability, and the non-biodegradability will contribute to the environmental disposal issue. This issue steered the interest in natural-based films [10]. The alternative film is expected to be a new horizon for creating new markets for natural products and contributes to solving environmental pollution. One solution is the use of biodegradable film made from polysaccharides such as cellulose. The use of natural products such as cellulose for making films is restricted by several drawbacks, like their hydrophilicity which cause the natural-based films to have high permeability to water vapor [11,12,13].
Packaging material is crucial for containing and protecting commodities, especially perishable food and beverages. Until the 1950s, petroleum-based polymers are majorly utilized material to fabricate for the development of packaging thin films. Unlike synthetic polymeric materials, biodegradable or biobased films are trending today because of their sustainability and eco-friendliness. Synthetic polymers have superior overall performance regarding the flexibility, thermal, mechanical, and convenience of use for different classes of products. In contrast, biodegradable material lacks mechanical and barrier properties compared to synthetic ones. The major disadvantage of these biopolymers is lacking heat sealability, which limits their application for specific applications such as pouches, bags, sachets, or packets to contain powdered or liquid substances such as seasoning and flavoring material for instant food, coffee, milk powders, and other food products [1]. The films' good sealability and durable seal strength are prominent for a successful heat-sealed package.
