However, their non-biodegradable nature contributes to severe environmental challenges, including pollution and resource depletion. Ecosystems are seriously threatened by the buildup of plastic garbage in landfills and the ocean, and sustainability issues are made worse by the industry's reliance on fossil fuels for manufacturing [5]. Biodegradable materials, which can naturally decompose into non-toxic components through microbial activity, present a sustainable alternative to conventional plastics. Biopolymers such as chitosan, cellulose, and PLA have gained significant attention due to their ability to minimize environmental impact while ensuring food safety and quality. These materials break down under natural conditions, reducing long-term waste accumulation and lowering the carbon footprint of packaging. Chitosan, derived from chitin, exhibits antimicrobial properties that enhance food preservation, while cellulose-based materials offer excellent biodegradability and mechanical strength. PLA, a biopolyester derived from renewable resources like corn starch, provides transparency and durability, making it a viable replacement for petroleum-based plastics [6]. By incorporating bioactive compounds and functional additives, biodegradable packaging can not only reduce plastic waste but also extend the shelf life of food products, fulfilling both consumer demand and industrial requirements by actively preventing microbial development and oxidation. Bioactive substances including essential oils, antioxidants, and antimicrobial agents can prolong the freshness of food. Biodegradable packaging becomes more competitive with traditional plastics when functional additions, such as natural polymers and nanomaterials, improve its mechanical, barrier, and thermal qualities. These advances help maintain food quality, prevent spoilage, and contribute to a more sustainable food packaging system without compromising performance [7, 8]. Among these biopolymers, chitosan, a natural polysaccharide derived from chitin found in crustacean shells (e.g., shrimp and crab) has demonstrated exceptional potential in food packaging applications. In addition to being biodegradable and biocompatible, chitosan exhibits inherent antimicrobial properties, making it highly effective in preventing foodborne contamination and enhancing food preservation. Its capacity to break down bacterial cell membranes and attach to negatively charged microbial surfaces, so preventing their development, is what gives it its antibacterial effect. Additionally, chitosan-based coatings and films can serve as moisture and oxygen barriers, lowering microbial spoiling and oxidative deterioration. Flexible and transparent packaging options are made possible by its film-forming capabilities, and its compatibility with various biopolymers and bioactive chemicals further improves its functional qualities for increased food safety and longer shelf life [9]. Studies have shown that chitosan actively inhibits the growth of pathogens such as Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, significantly improving food safety, because its positively charged amino groups break down bacterial membranes, resulting in leakage and cell death, chitosan has antibacterial properties. Its capacity to chelate metal ions also prevents microbiological metabolism. Its effectiveness can be increased by altering its molecular weight, level of deacetylation, or by adding bioactive substances like essential oils and nanoparticles. Films made of chitosan, a natural preservative, increase the shelf life of perishable foods and lessen the need for artificial preservatives [10]. The development of advanced chitosan-based films has further expanded its applicability in food packaging. For instance, gelatin-based pouches infused with nano-emulsified chili seed oil have been shown to reduce UV light transmittance, control color changes, and delay spoilage indicators such as lipid oxidation and microbial growth in fresh chicken breast cubes, thereby extending shelf life. These films serve as multipurpose barriers, shielding food from elements that are known to cause food degradation, such as light, oxygen, and moisture. By adding nano-emulsified chili seed oil, the film's antimicrobial and antioxidant qualities are strengthened, adding another line of protection against spoiling. Additionally, the bioactive compound's stability and even distribution inside the film matrix are enhanced by its nanoscale dispersion, guaranteeing constant protection. Such advances demonstrate the potential of chitosan-based packaging in replacing traditional plastic while boosting food quality and safety [11]. Similarly, chitosan-based films embedded with Plectranthus amboinicus essential oil have demonstrated enhanced mechanical strength, opacity, water vapor barrier properties, and antimicrobial efficacy against foodborne pathogens. By strengthening structural integrity, decreasing moisture permeability, and avoiding microbiological contamination, the use of Plectranthus amboinicus essential oil improves chitosan-based films. Strong antibacterial and antifungal qualities are provided by bioactive substances like carvacrol and thymol, which prevent spoiling. While improved flexibility and tensile strength increase longevity, increased opacity guards against light deterioration. These multifunctional properties make chitosan-based films a sustainable alternative to synthetic packaging, ensuring both food protection and preservation [12]. Further advancements in chitosan-based packaging have involved the incorporation of nanomaterials to improve physicochemical properties. For example, green-synthesized cerium oxide (CeO₂) nanoparticle-based chitosan/PVA composite films have exhibited superior antimicrobial activity and mechanical strength, effectively preserving the appearance, weight, and firmness of berry tomatoes for up to 25 days at room temperature. These films also inhibit the growth of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, as well as filamentous fungi, offering a promising eco-friendly alternative for extending food shelf life. CeO₂ nanoparticles improve the chitosan/PVA films’ mechanical strength, moisture barrier qualities, and antioxidant activity, halting oxidative deterioration and spoiling. Their antibacterial action, which is fueled by the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), successfully prevents the growth of bacteria and fungi, guaranteeing prolonged food preservation [13]. Chitosan can also undergo chemical or enzymatic modifications to enhance its functional properties, improving its barrier performance, flexibility, and thermal stability. Its mechanical strength and water resistance are improved by chemical changes such cross-linking with natural polymers or grafting with hydrophobic groups, which makes it more appropriate for use in food packaging. Conversely, enzymatic modifications enable precise structural changes without sacrificing biocompatibility, improving the material’s capacity to form films and degrade over time. These changes increase chitosan's potential for creating sophisticated, high-performing biodegradable packaging materials while also optimizing its physicochemical characteristics [14]. While chitosan alone has limitations in hardness and permeability, the integration of nanomaterials into its matrix has led to the development of films with enhanced mechanical and thermal properties, increasing their effectiveness as food packaging materials. By reinforcing the polymer matrix, nanomaterials including metal oxide nanoparticles, nanoclays, and carbon-based nanostructures increase the material's tensile strength, elasticity, and resistance to gasses and moisture. Because of these improvements, chitosan-based films are more resilient and appropriate for preserving perishable foods while still being environmentally benign and biodegradable. Incorporating nanomaterials can also offer antioxidant and antibacterial properties, increasing shelf life and guaranteeing food safety [15]. One notable innovation is a composite film incorporating TEMPO-oxidized nanocellulose, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), and chitosan, which has demonstrated strong antibacterial properties against E. coli and S. aureus, prolonged fruit freshness, and complete biodegradability within days. The film also minimizes silver release while ensuring flexibility and safety, making it a promising alternative to conventional plastic packaging. TEMPO-oxidized nanocellulose enhances the film’s mechanical strength and water resistance, while chitosan provides additional antimicrobial activity and biocompatibility. The controlled release of AgNPs ensures prolonged antibacterial effects without toxicity concerns, maintaining food safety while reducing environmental impact. This multifunctional composite film exemplifies the potential of advanced biopolymer-based packaging in achieving sustainable and high-performance food preservation solutions [16]. The increasing environmental impact of petroleum-based plastics underscores the urgent need for sustainable alternatives in the food industry [17]. While food packaging plays a crucial role in maintaining product safety, extending shelf life, and reducing food waste, traditional plastic materials significantly contribute to pollution and resource depletion. For hundreds of years, these petroleum-based plastics have remained in the environment, causing serious ecological problems like microplastic pollution and disturbance of marine life. Furthermore, non-renewable fossil fuels are used in their manufacture, which exacerbates environmental deterioration and carbon emissions. Therefore, it is imperative to switch to sustainable and biodegradable packaging substitutes that can offer comparable protective qualities with less of an adverse effect on the environment [18]. This review highlights the critical necessity for eco-friendly alternatives, with a focus on Chitosan-based packaging materials. As a biodegradable and renewable biopolymer, chitosan offers unique advantages, including antimicrobial activity, excellent barrier properties, and compatibility with other biodegradable components, making it a strong candidate for sustainable packaging solutions. Food shelf life is increased by its inherent capacity to suppress bacterial and fungal development, which lessens the need for artificial preservatives. Furthermore, by halting oxidation and moisture loss, its potent film-forming ability and oxygen barrier qualities contribute to the preservation of food freshness. Because chitosan may be combined with other biopolymers including starch, alginate, and gelatin, composite films with enhanced mechanical strength, flexibility, and functional qualities can be created. These qualities make materials based on chitosan a viable substitute for traditional polymers in food packaging [19, 20]. By examining recent innovations in chitosan-based packaging systems, including intelligent and active packaging technologies, this review aims to demonstrate their potential to replace conventional plastics and promote greener practices in the food industry. For example, biodegradable composite films incorporating honeysuckle extract, attapulgite, and natural carbon dots have exhibited enhanced strength, UV shielding, fluorescence, and pH sensitivity, further expanding the functional applications of chitosan-based packaging. By altering hue in reaction to pH changes, these clever packaging methods may serve as freshness indicators, enabling customers to evaluate food quality instantly. Furthermore, attapulgite improves film stability and moisture resistance, while honeysuckle extract offers antibacterial and antioxidant qualities. Incorporating natural carbon dots into food packaging enhances mechanical strength and adds fluorescence, which may be used for anti-counterfeiting and authenticity checks [21]. Through continued research and technological advancements, chitosan-based materials have the potential to revolutionize the food packaging industry, offering effective and environmentally responsible alternatives to traditional plastic packaging. We have discussed various biodegradable coatings based on biopolymers from nature (i.e., lipids, proteins, polysaccharides, biomass, and agriculture waste), as well as bacterial polymers (i.e., PHAs) and synthetic/biobased biodegradable polyesters that are used to tackle the shortcomings of biodegradable substrates for food packaging applications. Firstly, in terms of barrier properties, coatings represent a primary strategy for enhancing the barrier characteristics of biodegradable substrates. To protect food against moisture, hydrophobic materials are the most effective barrier coatings, such as lipid, waxes and PHAs. Proteins and polysaccharides have a poor moisture barrier due to their hydrophilic nature. However, proteins and polysaccharides possess better barrier against gases compared with lipids. Secondly, in regards to mechanical properties, protein-based coatings exhibit superior performance in comparison with coatings based on polysaccharides or lipids. In general, for coatings to improve the barrier and mechanical properties, bonding and interlocking with the substrate is necessary and any delamination failure can have a negative effect on the performance of the coated substrate. Lastly, coatings have the capacity to impart antimicrobial or antioxidant attributes to the underlying substrate. In this context, examples include lipids (e.g., essential oils) and polysaccharides (e.g., chitosan and pectin), as well as the modification of coatings through the integration of inorganic materials such as ZnO nanoparticles. Overall, multilayer packaging, compared with single-layer packaging, has more capacity to boost the performance of biodegradable-based materials, particularly regarding barrier properties. ans_raw: The 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films refers to the inherent challenge of balancing high water vapor barrier and high oxygen barrier performance within a single material. Biodegradable polymers typically exhibit either strong resistance to water vapor *or* oxygen, but rarely both simultaneously. For example, polysaccharides (e.g., cellulose, starch) and proteins (e.g., gelatin) provide good oxygen and gas barriers due to their dense, polar structures but suffer from poor water vapor barriers because of their hydrophilic nature [1, 5, 9]. Conversely, hydrophobic materials like lipids, waxes, or polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) excel in blocking moisture but underperform in oxygen barrier properties [1, 15]. This dichotomy arises from the structural and chemical characteristics of the materials: hydrophilic groups in polysaccharides/proteins facilitate water absorption, while hydrophobic materials lack the molecular polarity to effectively block non-polar gases like oxygen [2, 5, 9]. Multilayer coatings or composite systems are often proposed to mitigate this trade-off, though challenges such as delamination and retained biodegradability persist [1, 15].

Multilayer films have gained relevance in many industrial applications, especially in the fresh food packaging industry, for extending shelf-life [1]. Lamination is widely used to improve polymeric films performance by combining the properties of several types of layers into one film or sheet [2], [3], [4], [5]. However, while the combination of various layers is required for good food preservation, the recyclability or biodegradability of the multilayer packaging could become compromised. The impact of packaging waste on the environment can be minimized by prudently selecting materials and reviewing packaging expectations in terms of environmental impact [6], [7], [8]. Polymers derived from natural products, such as carbohydrates and proteins, offer the greatest opportunities as components of multilayer structures since their biodegradability and environmental compatibility are assured. Protein films are excellent oxygen and aroma barriers at low relative humidity with potential to replace synthetic oxygen-barrier components in multilayer formulations. Nevertheless, such property fails in high moisture environments due to the hydrophilic character of most proteins [4], [9]. In an attempt to overcome this issue, numerous studies have focused on the use of bio-polyesters as protective layers of protein films, including three-layer films from a soybean protein isolate (SPI) laminated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) by means of a solvent-casting procedure [3], [10]; bi-layer PLA-SPI films obtained by casting [7], polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs)- ultrathin zein fibers [5] and bi-layer Bioflex™-isolate whey protein films (IWP) [8]. Most of these materials have proven to be biodegraded under the stimulus of an environmental trigger after use [7], [8]. In a previous work [4], the authors described the design and performance of a biodegradable, high barrier, self-adhesive, three-layer sheet based on glycerol plasticized bovine gelatin layer acting as the oxygen barrier component and PLA as the outer layers produced by compression molding, as a potential thermoforming packaging solution. The favorable combination into a multilayer material enhanced the oxygen barrier of the pure PLA component (a limiting factor for PLA packaging applications), improved moisture resistance, and enhanced the mechanical and impact properties of its plasticized gelatin counterpart [4]. To consider such a multilayer sheet as a viable packaging material, it must retain the physical properties during the in-use period and ensure that lamination does not compromise the inherent biodegradability of the individual components under specific conditions, such as in indoor soil burial experiments.

First published on 5th April 2024 This review article provides a thorough overview of barrier coating materials that have been used in food packaging with a focus on biodegradable (bio-based or petroleum-based) materials, such as lipids, proteins, polysaccharides, agriculture waste and polyesters. The goal is to provide an opportunity to acknowledge progress made in this field, focusing on modifications made to coatings. These modifications aim to address the shortcomings of biodegradable substrates (either plastic or paper) and improve their performance, enabling them to compete with traditional petroleum-based food packaging materials. This includes their barrier against water vapor and oxygen, mechanical and surface characteristics (sealability and adhesion), as well as antimicrobial properties. The barrier of most biodegradable polymers underperforms in comparison with petroleum-based non-biodegradable polymers, which possess either high water vapor barrier or high oxygen barrier. Coating technology is a promising solution particularly in barrier improvement of biodegradable polymers. Currently, there are only metallized, or inorganic nanosheet coatings available for biodegradable films that meet food packaging requirements. There are some challenges in this field, for example, being able to retain the coating's biodegradability despite applied modifications to improve it's performance, the large-scale fabrication of biodegradable coatings, the coating's delamination and heat-sealability during service time, and the migration of the coating into the packaged food. Moreover, green chemistry and its sustainability needs in biodegradable polymeric coatings are also discussed regarding new ideas and possible directions for widespread application of coatings in food packaging. This is the first review that specifically summarizes biodegradable coatings on plastic and paper substrates with a focus on coating modifications to improve the performance of the base substrate to meet the required properties for food packaging applications.

Biopolymers including proteins and polysaccharides are the main natural resources utilized in development of biodegradable packaging material [1]. Proteins films are mechanically more strong than polysaccharide one [2] and show appropriate gas barrier properties [3]. Denaturation followed by association through new intermolecular interactions is the main mechanism for proteins to form film [4]. Gelatin, the product of collagen splitting and depolymerization [5], has excellent film forming and barrier (against oxygen and aroma compounds) properties at low and intermediate relative humidity (RH). Gelatin films suffer from high water vapor permeability (WVP) and poor mechanical and thermal properties [6]. Polysaccharides are usually cost-effective and available raw materials for biodegradable films [4] and different types of them (starches, gums and cellulose derivatives) have been used as packaging and coating materials [7]. There are a large number of polar groups such as hydroxyl along the polysaccharide structure, therefore hydrogen bonds play critical role in the film forming ability of polysaccharides [4]. Good barrier property against gases (O2 and CO2) and poor water vapor barrier properties due to their hydrophilic nature are among the polysaccharide films characteristics [7]. Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as an anionic cellulose derivative has several hydrophilic carboxyl groups along a hydrophobic backbone and hence reveals amphiphilic characteristics [8]. It has been used in a number of edible film formulations. CMC films are transparent, flexible, soluble in water, resistant to oil/fat and of moderate strength, moisture and oxygen barrier properties [9]. Interactions of different origins between proteins and polysaccharides result in tailor-made functional properties [10]. Depending on the molecular charge and concentration, different phenomena including co-solubility, thermodynamic incompatibility, depletion flocculation and thermodynamic compatibility take place in a mixture of protein and polysaccharide [2]. When two partners are oppositely charged, soluble complexes are developed at the first stage, followed by formation of inter-polymeric (insoluble) complexes [6]. Different factors including composition, concentration and ratio of reagents, order of mixing, pH, charge distribution, molecular weight, and conformation, ionic strength and ion type affect the complexation phenomenon [10]. Complex coacervation between different protein/polysaccharide binary mixtures have been extensively studied [[10], [11], [12]]. There are also several research works dealing with the application of protein/polysaccharide mixtures in the fabrication of composite films and coatings [1,2,[13], [14], [15], [16]]. Formation of gelatin-CMC composite films has been studied in limited research works [[17], [18], [19]]. Amsa et al. [17] prepared glutaraldehyde-cross-linked gelatin-CMC films. Their results showed that addition of glutaraldehyde and CMC decreased the triple-helix structure of gelatin and changed its glass transition temperature and macroporous structure. Guo et al. [18] utilized freezing-thawing approach to disperse montmorillonite in continues gelatin films cross-linked by dialdehyde carboxymethyl cellulose. Significant improvement in the film properties has been reported by these researchers. The film characteristics of chicken skin gelatin-CMC were compared with those of bovine gelatin-CMC by Nazmi et al. [19]. They reported that the puncher force, tensile strength, glass transition temperature and WVP of chicken skin gelatin-CMC composite film were higher than that of bovine gelatin-CMC composite one. Firstly, in terms of barrier properties, coatings represent a primary strategy for enhancing the barrier characteristics of biodegradable substrates. To protect food against moisture, hydrophobic materials are the most effective barrier coatings, such as lipid, waxes and PHAs. Secondly, in regards to mechanical properties, protein-based coatings exhibit superior performance in comparison with coatings based on polysaccharides or lipids. ans_rerank: The 'barrier property' trade-off in biodegradable packaging films refers to the inherent challenge of balancing high oxygen barrier performance with effective water vapor resistance. Biodegradable polymers, such as proteins (e.g., gelatin) and polysaccharides (e.g., cellulose derivatives), exhibit excellent oxygen and aroma barrier properties at low humidity due to their dense, polar molecular structures [1], [4], [6]. However, their hydrophilic nature compromises water vapor barrier performance in high-moisture environments, leading to swelling, plasticization, or structural degradation [1], [4], [5], [14]. Conversely, hydrophobic biodegradable polyesters (e.g., PLA, PBAT, PCL) provide better moisture resistance but generally underperform as oxygen barriers compared to proteins or polysaccharides [2], [4], [9]. For example, PLA has relatively high oxygen permeability (~461.7 cm³ m⁻² day⁻¹) compared to synthetic polymers like PET [2], [13]. Multilayer structures combining hydrophilic (e.g., gelatin, chitosan) and hydrophobic (e.g., PLA, PCL) layers aim to mitigate this trade-off but often still face limitations in achieving simultaneous high oxygen and water vapor barriers equivalent to non-biodegradable petroleum-based materials [1], [3], [4], [9], [13]. This compromise arises from the fundamental physicochemical properties of biodegradable materials, necessitating strategies like blending, nanocomposites, or coatings to address the imbalance [2], [4], [7], [13].

The most common strategy for the synthesis of PSI as precursor for PASP is through the thermal condensation of l-aspartic acid at high temperature, usually exceeding 160 °C. The l-aspartic acid starting material is industrially produced via enzymatic conversion of fumaric acid in the presence of ammonia with l-aspartate ammonia-lyase (l-aspartase) [37]. Mainly E. Coli and Cornybacterium Glutamacium are used as producers of l-aspartic acid [38,39]. Fumaric acid in turn is produced through fermentation of glucose by Rhizopus arrhizus, a type of saprophytic fungi [40]. When exploiting this method, a polymer with both D- and L-succinimide units is obtained. Water formed as a by-product during the reaction should be removed to drive the equilibrium of the polycondensation reaction towards the condensation products. Examples of this synthetic pathway carried out both in bulk [41,42] and in solution [34,43,44] and in the absence or presence of a catalyst have already been reported. The use of a catalyst is not required for the polycondensation, but it typically results in PSI with higher molecular weight (Mw > 5000 g mol−1) [[45], [46], [47]]. Several acid catalysts have been reported [44,48], but phosphoric acid (H3PO4) is the most commonly used [30]. The presence of a catalyst also has an influence on the biodegradability of the resulting polymer. A structure-biodegradability relationship study of sodium polyaspartate showed that employing a H3PO4 catalyst in the thermal polycondensation reaction resulted in polymers that were linear and completely biodegradable while polycondensation in the absence of a catalyst resulted in more branched structures with limited biodegradability (about 70 %) [49,50]. Although high Mw PSI can be obtained in bulk using an acid catalyst, this method is characterized by an inefficient heat transfer and the formation of semi-solid materials which are difficult to be heated uniformly. Therefore, the synthesis is also frequently carried out in solvent. The use of solvents improves the heat transfer and promotes dispersion and mixing of the reactants maintaining homogeneous conditions during the reaction. Biocompostable and bio-based polymers have received considerable attention in the past two decades because of the environmental concerns and sustainability issues associated with petroleum-based polymers.1 Poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is one of few commercialized biocompostable polymers with balanced thermal and mechanical properties, and thermoplastic processability compared with other plastics such as poly(hydroxybutyrate), poly(lactic acid), poly(propylene), and polyethylene.2 Currently, commercial PBS is mainly obtained from polymerization of petroleum-based succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, however, the two monomers can be derived from renewable resources via fermentation.3, 4 As a result, PBS becomes a very promising material as a substitute for conventional plastics. PBS and its copolymers have been utilized to produce fast food packages, bottles, supermarket bags, flushable hygiene products, mulch film, and compost bags etc. On the other hand, PBS and its copolymers are used to improve the performance of other biopolymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) or poly(hydroxybutyrate) (PHB).5, 6 However, high molecular weight PBS is not feasible via a direct polycondensation of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol monomers, because in this equilibrium reaction water is formed which is difficult to remove when the viscosity rises during the course of the polymerization, resulting in insufficient properties of PBS for wide use as a biocompostable plastic.2 Therefore, it is necessary to further increase their molecular weight to improve its performance, e.g., tear resistance, impact toughness, and melt strength. The molecular weight of PBS can be increased via (i) chain extension using a chain extender such as hexamethylene diisocyanate,7 (ii) copolymerization with a small amount of multi-functional monomer (e.g., triols) to form branching molecular structure,8 and (iii) crosslink of PBS with peroxide or irradiation.9-12 Irradiation is an effective technique to induce crosslinking. Bahari et al.12 investigated the electron-beam radiation crosslinked PBS foam and its biodegradation. They found that the crosslinking induced by irradiation effectively improved the melt strength of the PBS. Suhartini et al.13 studied the irradiation crosslinking of PBS in the presence of inorganic fillers and its biodegradability. The presence of inorganic filler such as silicon dioxide and carbon black enhanced the gel formation. In a recent study, PBS was also crosslinked using ultraviolet in the presence of a photoinitiator (1-hydroxycyclohexylphenyl ketone) and a crosslinking agent (triallyl isocyanurate).14 The effect of photoinitiator concentration, crosslinking agent content, and the irradiation time on the crosslink behavior was investigated. Compared with irradiation using γ-ray or electron beams, the route to crosslink PBS by using peroxide is more economic and environmentally friendly. Kim et al.9 crosslinked PBS with dicumyl peroxide (DCP) and studied its physical and thermal properties and biodegradation behavior. It was found that the mechanical properties of the PBS were improved, meanwhile, the crystallization temperature was increased which was ascribed to an assumption that the crosslink points or by-product of reaction acts as nucleating agents. Li et al.15 increased the melt viscosity of PBS by using >3 phr DCP in combination with trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate (TMPTMA) as a curing co-agent, leading to a preparation of PBS foam. The influences of various factors on the foaming process and the properties of PBS foams were investigated. In our previous work, in situ crosslinked PLA/PBS, PHB/PBS, and poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-valerate) (PHBV)/PBS blends were studied in the presence of DCP.5, 6 The interfacial and mechanical properties of the above blends were significantly improved due to the in situ reaction. Furthermore, it was found that PBS was more reactive than PHB or PHBV with DCP in terms of gel formation. Lim et al.16 added two types of polyisocyanates as branching agents into PBS matrix to increase the viscosity and finally prepared PBS foams. Jin et al.17 reported the crosslinking of unsaturated PBS (copolymerized with maleic acid) by using benzoyl peroxide (BPO) and multi-functional co-agent. Teramoto et al.18 studied the crosslinking and biodegradation of PBS-based prepolymers containing unsaturated itaconic or maleic acid units in the main chain using BPO as an initiator. Although a considerable work has been reported on the properties and application (e.g., foam) of crosslinked PBS, the structure-property relationships of the crosslinked PBS were still not well understood. For example, the crosslinking density (υe) and the average molecular weight between two neighboring crosslink points (), have not been reported yet, which, in the authors' view, is crucial to understand from molecular scales the influence of crosslinking on the thermal and mechanical properties. The primary objective of this work is to provide a deeper fundamental understanding on the structure-property relationships of the partially crosslinked PBS initiated by DCP. The crosslink structure, crystallization, and rheology of the PBS gel are the first time reported in details. A mechanism of the accelerated crystallization process after crosslinking was revealed based on this study. Furthermore, the effect of crosslinking on the spherulitic morphology, impact and flexural properties, and the stress/strain behavior was also firstly reported in the present work.

Biobased and biodegradable polymers have received extensive attention from both academia and industry point of views in the recent decades due to global increasing concern over the lasting behavior of plastics on the environment [1], [2]. Since it can be synthesized from succinic acid (SA) and butanediol (1,4-BDO), which are building blocks currently industrially obtained by biotechnologies from renewable resources, poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) is nowadays considered as one of the most promising sustainable alternative to conventional fossil-based polymers [1]. Indeed, PBS shows high melting temperature, excellent mechanical properties close to some polyolefins, biodegradability and easy processability [3], [4] that make it suitable for short term applications such as disposable packaging, agriculture or biomedical products [4], [5]. The growing interest in PBS is also connected with the strong development of the production of biobased SA from different companies through the world, such as BioAmber, Succinity, Reverdia, Mitsubishi or Myriant. However, to broaden its range of application and properties, modification of PBS architecture can be performed. As a route to develop materials with improved properties, tailor-made aliphatic copolyesters were synthesized by combining different building blocks. To date, PBS derivatives to random copolyesters have been developed with various diacids, such as furan dicarboxylic acid, adipic acid (AA) and terephthalic acid [6], [7], or diols, such as ethylene glycol, propanediol (1,3-PDO) and isosorbide [8], [9], [10]. Electrospinning is a high-performance and simple process for producing continuous fibers in nano and micro sizes for application in various fields, for example, drug delivery, catalyst structure, sensor design and fabrication, textiles, and especially in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine (TERM) [1-6]. TERM introduces functional substitutes to the repair and regeneration of damaged tissues and organs. It employs various sciences, including biology, chemistry, and engineering, to arrive at these goals. TERM needs three integral components: scaffold, cells, and biological signals, to facilitate cell growth, differentiation, and angiogenesis [4, 7]. Nanofibrous structures exhibit multiple advantages, such as a range of fiber diameters similar to the fibrillary ECM, high porosity, and large surface-to-volume area [8]. Fabricated scaffolds should mimic the 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) and provide a biocompatible environment for cell homing, proliferation, and differentiation toward tissue repair and regeneration. Along with biodegradability and sufficient mechanical strength, the porous structure of scaffolds facilitates the transportation of nutrients and oxygen while must be nontoxic, capable of being sterilized, and simple to manufacture and handle [9-12]. The nanofibers fabricated with electrospinning can recapitulate the nanofibrous structure of natural ECM. However, the structures prepared by traditional electrospinning are two-dimensional and cannot simulate a three-dimensional structure of native ECM. The porosity and fibrous structure of the native ECM could be simulated using nanofiber-based scaffolds with networking structures mimicking collagen fibrils [13]. 2D scaffolds have limitations such as insufficient porosity, low cell infiltration, and restriction of cell-cell and cell-ECM interaction. These limitations led to the emergence of 3D scaffolds that overcome 2D-associated limitations. 3D scaffolds create a microenvironment mimicking the in vivo tissue interconnectivity where cells create molecular gradients within the implanted scaffolds [14]. Moreover, 3D scaffolds provide a three-dimensional environment for cell transfer and infiltration, cell-cell interactions, and nutrient and waste exchange, which is essential for cell-cycle regulation and tissue function. Soft-tissue organs have unique ECM compositions that enable tightly regulated biochemical and mechanical properties for specific lineage commitment and differentiation during organ development and maintenance of cellular function in adult organs. Healthy soft-tissue stromal ECM is composed of an insoluble backbone of ECM proteins and soluble hydrogel-forming glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) of varying concentrations, depending on the organ. The mechanical and biochemical cues from the ECM (e.g. composition, topography, pore size, porosity, viscoelasticity) modulate cell viability, growth, homeostasis, migration, and differentiation. For example, the topography, pore size, and porosity modulate the amount of ECM backbone material interacting with the cell and thereby affect cell viability and growth [11, 12]. The matrix viscoelastic properties and the extent of cell attachment to the matrix regulate the cell-generated traction forces and the substrate resistance that the cells experience in response, which impact cell phenotype and differentiation [13-18]. As matrix mechanics drive cell health and disease progression, artificial matrices for in vivo implantation and in vitro culture must closely emulate the native, healthy ECM to maintain cellular function as expected in a healthy organ. Synthetic scaffolds of various types, including nanofiber (NF) mats, sponges, hydrogels, and NF-hydrogel composites, have been engineered to simulate various aspects of ECM. NF mats have fibrous topography, impenetrable pores, and high stiffness, typically in the MPa range or higher [19, 20], which make them good candidates for basement membrane mimetics for monolayer epithelial or endothelial growth [21-24]. However, they fail to mimic both the 3D topography and the stiffness of soft-tissue stromal ECM within the connective tissue compartment. Sponges fabricated by freeze-drying, particulate- or salt-leaching, gas foaming, or phase separation have excessive ECM backbone and excessively large pore sizes (>100 µm) when stiffness is in the sub-kPa range; hence, cells attach flush against the backbone, similar to 2D culture [13]. Hydrogels allow tunable stiffness in the kPa range for soft tissue scaffolds. However, bulk hydrogels, e.g. alginate, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), lack an insoluble fibrous backbone that mechanically supports cells. Their extremely small pore sizes, in the submicron range, support molecular movement but, without cell attachment sites, impede cellular movement crucial for cell migration and organization. While existing hybrid NF-hydrogel scaffolds reinforce hydrogels with a fibrous backbone, they may have a non-homogenous distribution of cell anchorage points [25]. Hence, a new fabrication strategy is necessary to produce scaffolds that concurrently mimic these essential properties of soft-tissue stromal ECM, including porous topography with 10-50 μm pores [26-29], minimal insoluble fibrous backbone, soluble hydrogel cushion, and sub-kPa range stiffness (∼100-600 Pa) [30-34]. Cryoelectrospinning, also known as cryogenic electrospinning, low temperature electrospinning, and cold plate electrospinning, is an emerging technique to fabricate 3D nanofibrous scaffolds with high porosity and low bulk stiffness. The cryoelectrospinning process includes a cold collector plate, maintained at a temperature less than 0 °C [35-37] (figure S1 available online at stacks.iop.org/BF/14/035010/mmedia), to collect deposited electrospun scaffolds, which are then lyophilized, a major difference from traditional electrospinning techniques. The cryogenically cooled collector plate promotes deposition of atmospheric water vapor as ice crystals on the collector plate and between deposited fibers. Upon contacting the collector plate at sub-zero temperature, the aqueous electrospun solution freezes to form ice crystals as well. When homogenous solutions with multiple components freeze, the solutes and solvent undergo phase separation, and the frozen water can subsequently be lyophilized to produce porous scaffolds. The nucleation of ice crystals allows scalable 3D growth, increased porosity, and consequentially, reduced scaffold density and kPa-range bulk stiffness [38]. The remainder of the cryoelectrospinning process is similar to traditional electrospinning, in which a viscous, long-chain polymer solution becomes electrically charged when passed through a needle tip at high voltage (5-20 kV), and the electrostatic repulsion in the charged fluid exceeds the forces of surface tension, thereby pulling the charged droplet at the needle tip to the nearest electrical ground. The chain-chain interactions of the polymer molecules in the charged droplet prevent the droplet from falling to the electrically grounded collector plate as a drop and instead pull the droplet as a fiber with micro/nanometer diameter to the electrical ground. While the fibers deposit to form a 2.5D NF mat in traditional electrospinning, when cryoelectrospun, they form a 3D fibrous scaffold following lyophilization. While synthetic polymers are easier to manipulate, they do not provide biochemical cues that can be recognized by cells and non-biodegradable polymers require further chemical modification to be biodegradable [47, 48]. Additionally, organic solvents, even at low residual amounts, can have toxic effects on cells [49] and when used in combination with natural proteins, may alter the conformation of the proteins. We hypothesized that cryoelectrospinning of natural biomaterials, comprising ECM proteins and hydrogel materials with water as the solvent could yield biocompatible scaffolds that mimic the topography and viscoelasticity of soft-tissue stromal ECM.

With the ability to form nanofibrous structures, a drive to mimic the native ECM has begun. Electrospinning is capable of fabricating nanometer-scale fibers that yield very high specific surface area. Electrospun (e-spun) nanofibers are therefore very useful for developing a variety of structures whose functional efficiency is surface area dependent. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex microenvironment that provides structural, mechanical, and biochemical cues to cells, which ultimately dictate their fate.1, 2 The ECM is composed of a variety of polymeric biomacromolecules, varying between different tissues. In general, ECM components include: proteins, glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and polysaccharides.3, 4 Collagen is one of the main components of the ECM of all connective tissues.5 In tissues, collagen is presented as fibers, but its morphological features such as fiber diameter and organization vary between different types of tissues. For instance, collagen forms highly aligned fibers in cardiac tissues, while in some regions of cartilage collagen forms a random structure with a diameter range between 10 and 100 nm.6 Collagen provides strength and structure to the ECM by directly interacting with cells and other ECM molecules.7 Cell-matrix interactions imply cells interact with collagen, indicating that cells contain receptors for specific collagen peptide sequences.5 Collagen is considered a family of closely related but genetically distinct molecules. There are 28 different types recognized, but 80-90% of collagens in the body belong to types I, II, and III.8 Type I collagen is found abundantly in the skin, bone, tendon, ligaments, and cornea.9 Type II collagen is present in the eye vitreous humor, in the nucleus pulposus of the vertebral discs, and is the main component of cartilage.9 Type III collagen is abundant in the loose connective tissue on the walls of blood vessels, the skin dermis, and the stroma of various glands.9 Due to its abundance in nature, collagen has become an attractive biopolymer for the engineering of ECM mimetic scaffolds to be used in tissue regeneration.
Electrospinning is a primary method for producing low-cost, multifunctional scaffolds for tissue engineering, affording microsized and nanosized scaffolds that imitate the extracellular matrix (ECM).7 The size and structural resemblance of electrospun nanofibers to ECM makes them ideal for tissue regeneration.8,9 Significantly, the nanotopographical characteristics exhibited by electrospun nanofibers influence the morphology, migration, and differentiation. The short diameter, adequate contact surface area, and high porosity of electrospun nanofibers have established electrospinning as a frequently employed fabrication method for tissue engineering scaffolds, particularly in wound healing and cartilage, tendon, and nerve tissue regeneration.10 However, conventional electrospinning does not replicate the organization found in tendon fibers. To address this limitation, gap electrospinning, which can produce uniaxially parallel fibers by manipulating the electric field across the electrode poles, has been developed. Another technique for obtaining aligned nanofibers involves the use of the rapidly rotating-mandrel technique, which is energy- and time-consuming. Moreover, transferring fibers fabricated via this method is difficult because they stick to the collecting surface. In contrast, uniaxially aligned nanofibers prepared by gap electrospinning rest on an air gap between the poles, which facilitates the fiber collection procedure.11 Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a biodegradable, nontoxic polymer with good mechanical properties.12,13 However, its poor hydrophilicity and cytocompatibility are unfavorable for creating a cell-friendly scaffold. Accordingly, the surface modification of the PCL fibers without altering their bulk properties is essential.14 We immobilize collagen on PCL fibers by aminolysis to enhance its cytocompatibility. In contrast to conventional transplantation methods, the technique of tissue engineering (or regenerate medicine) provided new medical therapy, which used biomaterials with or without living precursor.1 The ultimate purpose of tissue engineering is to reestablish the destroyed human tissues or organs by provide scaffolds for functional tissue regeneration. In human tissue, extracellular matrix (ECM) is a chemically and physically cross-linked complex network with structural fibers such as collagen fibers and elastin fibers having diameters ranging from several ten to several hundred nanometers.2 These protein fibers entangle with each other to form a nonwoven mesh which provides tensile strength and elasticity for cells. In addition to providing a physical support, they also create a substrate with for cell adhesion, migration, and regulate cellular proliferation. Electrospinning technology is a simple and versatile method to prepare ultrathin fibers from polymer solutions or melts. The obtained fibers usually have a diameter from several nanometers to a few micrometers, and mostly in hundreds of nanometers. Therefore, the scaffolds generated from electrospun nanofibers could be capable to mimic the natural ECM.3 The ultrathin diameters of electrospun nanofibers make them possess large specific surface areas. Additionally, the nonwoven fabrics (mats) from electrospun polymer nanofibers offer a unique capability to control the pore sizes among nanofibers.4 Unlike nanorods, nanotubes, and nanowires that are produced mostly by synthetic, bottom-up methods, electrospun nanofibers are produced through a top-down nanomanufacturing process, which results in continuous and low-cost nanofibers that are also relatively easy to be aligned, assembled, and processed into applications. Many synthetic and/or natural polymers including, but not limited to, polylactide (PLA),5 poly(ε-caprolactone),6 poly(L-lactide-co-caprolactone),7, 8 proteins (e.g., collagen),9 and polysaccharides (e.g., chitosan)10 have been electrospun into nanofibrous mats as tissue engineering scaffolds.
There are currently a variety of strategies for the treatment of vascular disease (a subset of CVD focusing on the vessels), including extracellular matrix (ECM) mimicking structures, the use of native ECM components, and functionalized protein laden scaffolds.2-5 Combining ECM with polymers to manufacture electrospun bioscaffolds has previously been utilized to harness the repeatable mechanical properties of the polymer with the biochemical and mechanical properties of the ECM.5-8 Electrospinning polymers produces a network of fibers that can be heavily tailored depending on the properties desired.9 They can be designed to have isotropic or anisotropic mechanical properties, along with three-dimensional architectural properties that favor cell survival and growth.10 It is possible through electrospinning to include bioactive cues into a repeatable polymer structure and alter its mechanical and physical properties.5-7, 11 This has huge implications in tissue engineering where mimicking the physical and biological properties of the native ECM are major research focusses, especially when the final aim is generation of new functional tissue. Previous studies have shown that including ECM or ECM proteins into an electrospun polymer scaffold alters its mechanical properties and positively affects seeded cells.5-7, 12 Therefore, in this study, we propose electrospinning a combination of aortic ECM with polycaprolactone (PCL) at two different ECM concentrations and biomechanically evaluating the resulting fibrous scaffolds along with a conventional PCL-only scaffold. Aortic ECM has been chosen as we are looking at a novel solution for the treatment of vascular disease, and therefore have decided to use a type of native ECM directly from a vascular source. Bovine aorta was harvested from a 2 year old female cow. Samples were frozen within 4 h of harvesting at −80 °C and stored until required. A 40 mm diameter sample from the aortic arch was cut out, and all connective tissue was removed after cleaning with ethanol and bathing in water for 30 min to remove blood. A 2 mm punch was used to punch out pieces of aorta for decellularization. The pieces were placed in a decellularizing device and perfusion decellularized with 0.5% w/v sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) in diH2O for 36 h as previously described.13 Aorta samples were then perfused with 20 L of diH2O at 170 mL/min to remove remnant SDS. Samples were frozen and lyophilized in a FreeZone 4.5 freeze-drier (Labconco). Dry ECM was then milled in a plenary ball mill PM 100 (Retsch). ECM powder was then collected and stored at 4 °C for use in electrospinning.

Electrospinning is one of the most common methods to produce fibrous substrates for tissue engineering applications by use of natural and synthetic polymers. Ideally, a substrate should mimic both the form and functionality of the native extracellular matrix (ECM) [1]. It is known that morphology, architecture and surface properties have strong influence on cells growth, spreading, activity and functions [2]. Thereby, scaffolds formed by electrospinning are gaining increasing interest due to their tunable properties to provide ideal microenvironments for various kinds of cell types. Naturally occurring polymers such as collagen (Col) and gelatine (Ge) do not cause foreign body response [3], [4]. PCL does elicit such a response, though minimal. As major drawbacks the poor mechanical properties and their variable physical properties have been identified [5]. In contrast, synthetic biopolymers have predictable and reproducible mechanical and physical properties (e.g. tensile strength, elastic moduli and degradation rate) and they can be synthesised with high reproducibility. Most synthetic polymers incorporate strong hydrophobic surface properties which present poor cell adhesion sites and thus promote a low level of cell attachment. Thereby, different approaches have been realised to adjust surface wettability properties e.g. by chemical and coating routes. A timely fashioned way is the use of hydrophilic and water soluble native extracellular matrix materials such as Col or Ge to form a hybrid of natural and synthetic polymers. In that way, scaffolds are generated which combine the advantages of both types of material and mainly alter materials surface properties. Up to now, various research works describe influencing parameters such as morphology and architecture of electrospun patches with respect to cell growth and proliferation (e.g. [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13]). Focusing on blend nanofibers, Col/elastin [14], [15], polyurethane/polycaprolactone (PCL) [16], and PCL/Ge [17], PCL/Col [18], [19] have been described. However most of them concentrate on morphological topics, chemical structure and biological investigations (cell morphology, cytotoxicity and proliferation). For instance, Chong et al. showed reasonable growth of human dermal fibroblast on polyurethane - PCL/Ge sandwiched structures being promising candidates for wound healing applications [19]. Zhang et al. prepared PCL/Ge 1:1 electrospun nanofibers and found improved bone marrow stromal cell attachment compared to pure synthetic PCL nanofiber scaffolds. Cellular infiltration was demonstrated on the blend fibres of up to 114 μm in-depth [20]. PCL/Col electrospun fibres were investigated by Lee et al. [18]. Compared to pure PCL, the Col-added nanofibers showed better cell responses (adhesion and growth) in vitro and penetration in vivo.

The hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance in amphiphilic block copolymers refers to the relative proportion and arrangement of hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments, which critically determines the self-assembly, drug encapsulation efficiency, stability, and stimuli-responsive release behavior for drug delivery applications. This balance governs the formation of micellar structures where the hydrophobic core encapsulates poorly soluble drugs while the hydrophilic shell provides aqueous stability [3,5,8,11]. 

Optimizing this balance allows for fine control over material properties, including critical micelle concentration (CMC), micelle size, drug loading capacity, and responsiveness to environmental triggers like pH, temperature, or enzymes [3,4,11]. For instance, a higher hydrophobic content typically enhances drug encapsulation but may reduce colloidal stability, whereas increased hydrophilicity improves solubility and prolongs circulation but may compromise drug loading [3,4,11]. The architecture (e.g., linear, star-shaped) and molecular weights of the blocks further modulate this balance, influencing micelle stability upon dilution and drug release kinetics [11,12].

Specifically, the balance enables:
1. **Stimuli-responsive behavior**: Proper tuning allows response to tumor-specific triggers such as low pH or high enzyme levels, facilitating targeted drug release [1,3,4].  
2. **Improved drug solubility**: Hydrophobic segments shield drugs from water, while hydrophilic segments ensure miscibility in aqueous media [4,5].  
3. **Enhanced mucoadhesion and permeability**: Hydrophobic moieties interact with mucosal surfaces, improving adhesion and cellular uptake [6,7].  
4. **Degradation control**: The ratio affects hydrolysis rates of labile bonds (e.g., esters), enabling controlled release profiles [4,9,12].  

Thus, precise manipulation of the hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance is essential for designing efficient amphiphilic copolymer-based drug carriers [1,3,4,6,11].

Based solely on the provided evidence, the "hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance" in amphiphilic block copolymers for drug delivery refers to the critical ratio or proportion between the hydrophilic and hydrophobic segments within the copolymer structure. This balance governs key properties essential for effective drug delivery:

1.  **Micellization and Stability:** The balance determines the ability to form micelles with a hydrophobic core (for drug encapsulation) and a hydrophilic shell (for aqueous stability). It directly influences the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), where a lower CMC indicates greater micelle stability upon dilution in the bloodstream. The architecture (e.g., star-shaped) and composition (molar mass of blocks) impact this balance and thus the CMC [4].

2.  **Drug Loading and Release:** The hydrophobic segment's nature and length relative to the hydrophilic segment control the capacity to solubilize hydrophobic drugs within the core and modulate the release kinetics (e.g., preventing burst release, enabling sustained release). The balance also affects compatibility with the drug molecule [2, 3, 4, 5].

3.  **Stimuli-Responsiveness:** Fine control over the hydrophilic-hydrophobic balance allows the design of copolymers responsive to specific physiological stimuli (e.g., temperature, pH). For example, it dictates the Lower Critical Solution Temperature (LCST) in thermosensitive systems [3, 6] and the pH-dependent swelling or degradation behavior for pH-sensitive release [3, 8].

4.  **Biodegradation Rate:** The ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic components, particularly in specific polymer systems like poly(organophosphazene), plays a crucial role in controlling the rate of hydrolytic degradation of the copolymer [3].

5.  **Physicochemical Properties:** The balance dictates bulk microstructure, surface properties, hydration, swelling behavior, and overall compatibility with biological systems [2, 3, 4, 5]. It is fundamental to achieving desired characteristics like prolonged circulation time and effective drug encapsulation.

PLLA and PHB are known for their biodegradability and high stiffness. However, amorphous PLLA and crystalline PHB are fragile under tension,[14, 25] with low elongation at breaks ε = 3% and ≈6%, respectively. Most reported PLA blends/copolymers with high elongations used very ductile phases (elastomer such as PBS, PBAT, or rubbers), which often reduced their stiffness and strength. PLLA-PHB binary blends exhibit brittle fracture due to their immiscibility at high Mw.[29] PMMA is also a brittle plastic with ε = 7%.[23] Surprisingly, adding 2.5% of PMMA into PLLA/PHB blends leads to significant increase of ε from 3% to 112%, a 38-fold increase compared to matrix PLLA, and the ultimate toughness (UT) from 1 to 30 MJ m−3. More notably, M5 exhibits stable plastic deformation at ≈118%, while M7.5 exhibit a maximum ε ≈ 165%, up to 55-fold compared to neat PLLA, while the strength is maintained at ≈50 MPa (Figure 3a). Further increasing the PMMA content reduces the ultimate elongation and toughness. This may arise from a thicker PMMA interfacial layer that is more susceptible to internal crack formation as PMMA is inherently brittle. Compared with binary blends developed previously,[23] the ternary biocomposites require much less non-biodegradable PMMA to achieve optimum performance, thus maximizing the biodegradability (Figure S4, Supporting Information). The ternary biocomposites exhibit a combination of high strength and tensile toughness that exceeds commercial polymer blends and advanced biocomposites (Figure 3b). The tensile toughening effects can be attributed to strong polymer chain entanglements at the phase interfaces with PMMA layer. Entanglements are closely related to crazing and shear yielding,[30, 31] as evidenced by clear stress-whitening and necking of M7.5, while M0 sample only shows minor whitening near the crack tip (Figure S4, Supporting Information). While PLLA, PHB and PMMA are all susceptible to fracture under bending, the PLLA/PHB/PMMA biocomposites exhibit malleability similar to ductile metals, enduring bending and torsion up to 180° (Figure 3c,d). Such malleable property allows for facile shape transformation at room temperature, which is desirable for wearable devices and implants. Even after 100 cycles of 180° bend (Figure 3e), the M7.5 blend retains a satisfactory strength (≈43.5 MPa) and elongation at break (≈200%), demonstrating its mechanical robustness.

The randomness of the biosynthesized PHA copolymers, as evaluated by 13C NMR analysis, was D = 20.8 (Fig. 2), indicating that they were blocky copolymers. Monomer sequences in the copolymer chain are known to be affected by the polymerization activity of PHA synthase toward comonomers and the timing of the comonomer supply in the cell.45, 70, 71 Generally, introducing 3H4PE units into the P(3HB) sequence causes defects in the crystalline structure, decreasing the crystallinity (enthalpy of fusion) and Tm of the polymer.12, 72 However, because the PHA copolymer synthesized in this study was blocky, its thermal properties differed from those of typical random copolymers. The Tm of the PHA copolymers was similar to that of P(3HB), even when incorporating more than 12 mol% 3H4PE (Table 3, Fig. 4). Grafting thiol-PEG (MW 2000) onto the PHA side chains increases flexibility of the polymer chains, resulting in a decrease in Tg. A similar phenomenon has also been observed for mcl-PHAs with long side chains ranging from C6 to C12;73, 74 however, the crystallization behaviors of PEG-grafted PHAs and mcl-PHAs were different. Crystallization of mcl-PHAs is generally difficult.73, 74 For the PEG-grafted PHAs, the Tcc of PHA19-g-PEG was 36.4 °C, which is lower than the values for neat PHA19 (48.4 °C) and P(3HB) (42 °C), implying easier crystallization. This was presumably because PEG functioned as a nucleating agent for the P(3HB) chain, facilitating the crystallization of PHA19-g-PEG. Some reports have indicated that PEG promotes the crystallization of PHA and PLA.75, 76 Two representative PHA-degrading bacteria R. pikettii9, 18 and P. stutzeri56, 57 secrete extracellular PhaZs to hydrolyze ester bonds in PHA chains. The SBD of PhaZs plays a critical role in their adsorption onto the PHA surface, which is the initial step in the biodegradation process. The antifouling properties of PEG probably inhibit the adsorption of PhaZs, leading to the modulated biodegradability of PEG-grafted PHAs. Nevertheless, PEG is a biodegradable polymer in natural environments.32, 33 Thus, PEG-grafted PHAs eventually biodegrade. In contrast, PHA-degrading bacteria formed clear zones around their colonies on PHA12-g-3M1P (Fig. 6) because 3M1P has no antifouling ability. Previous studies have shown that PEG-terminated PHAs exhibit increased hydrophilicity because of PEG attachment.26-31 However, in PEG-terminated PHAs, only one short PEG molecule (usually MW 1000 or less) can be introduced per PHA chain, raising uncertainties regarding their antifouling functionality. In contrast, PEG grafting onto PHA side chains allows the attachment of multiple PEG molecules to the PHA chain. This structural difference suggests that PHA-g-PEG exhibits higher hydrophilicity and enhanced antifouling properties compared to PEG-terminated PHAs. In this study, PHA copolymers containing 6-19 mol% 3H4PE units with unsaturated side chains were synthesized as novel, chemically modifiable PHAs. The PHAs were grafted with 3M1P and thiol-PEG via a thiol-ene reaction. Regarding thermal properties, both Tg and Tcc decreased with PEG grafting, but Tm did not change because of the blocky nature of the PHA copolymers. Furthermore, PEG grafting conferred an antifouling ability to the PHA surface. In the biodegradability assay, the PHA-degrading bacteria did not form a clear zone around their colonies on PHAs grafted with 12 wt% PEG. This suggests that PEG grafting reduced the adsorption of PhaZs secreted by PHA-degrading bacteria onto the PHA surface. These observations provide valuable insights for the development of technologies aimed at controlling the biodegradation rates and material properties of PHAs, which may be crucial for various applications of biodegradable polymers.

Finally, optimized processing techniques, including controlled temperature, reduced residence time in the melt phase, lowering shear stress, and nitrogen purging, are crucial to mitigating thermal degradation during manufacturing. For industrial processes, combining melt compounding with film or sheet formation in a single setup, such as integrating a sheet die or blow-molding device with the extruder, minimizes thermal degradation while enhancing efficiency. Although this may not always achieve optimal homogenization of the components. Injection blow molding is another widely used technique, particularly for bottle production [41]. By addressing these challenges and optimizing PHA blend formulations, the processing and performance of PHA-based materials can be significantly improved for packaging and other applications. The plasticization of PHAs, particularly PHB, has emerged as a promising strategy to address issues like brittleness, high Tg, and challenging melt-processing characteristics. Introducing plasticizers reduces intermolecular forces, enhances chain mobility, lowers melt viscosity, and improves flowability, significantly boosting PHB’s flexibility and thermal properties. These include low-molecular-weight plasticizers like PEG, which can migrate to the surface over time, causing a deterioration of the polymer’s physical properties. Alternatives include oligomeric plasticizers, such as aliphatic polyester oligomers, and bio-based plasticizers. However, the use of petroleum-based plasticizers, such as phthalates, in biodegradable polymers raises concerns about their impact on biodegradability, biocompatibility, and environmental impact [56]. To address these issues, “green plasticizers” derived from renewable sources like vegetable oils, fatty acids, and lignocellulosic biomasses are gaining attention. Despite their eco-friendly profile, these green plasticizers face challenges like high production costs, low efficiency, high leachability, and limited versatility with different polymers [57]. Furthermore, some commercial green plasticizers, such as 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester (DINCH) and acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC), have raised safety concerns due to their potential toxicity and environmental persistence [58], [59]. These issues, along with high leachability, have raised doubts about the safety of these plasticizers. Recent research has focused on developing bio-based and biodegradable plasticizers, often termed bioplasticizers, which not only mitigate the limitations of PHB but also align with environmental sustainability goals. These bioplasticizers, especially at optimal concentrations, derived from renewable resources such as natural oils, organic acids, and GLY derivatives, have effectively lowered PHB’s Tg and improved its mechanical performance, such as elongation at break, making the brittle polymer more ductile and less prone to cracking. They also provide an eco-friendly alternative to conventional petrochemical-based options [60].

Thermogravimetric analysis has been performed on prepared samples to investigate their thermal stability. Figure 5 showed TGA and differential thermogravimetry (DTG) diagrams of samples while the extracted data are given in Table 2. As it is illustrated in Figure 5A, the weight loss began in the lower temperature for TPS sample rather than others due to moisture loss below 100°C. Also, the water evaporation has occurred in PLA/TPS blends and decomposition onset was gradually delayed to higher temperatures with increasing PLA content because of hydrophobic nature of PLA. Next step of weight loss until 250°C was attributed to plasticizer volatilization in TPS and PLA/TPS blends. These phenomena would result in decreasing of the thermal stability temperature, T10%, of samples with increasing the TPS content as also proved by other researchers.14, 23 The next step in weight loss was observed above 310°C because of the thermal degradation of the starch and the PLA chains. The presence of the only one decomposition peak below 400°C in DTG diagrams, which is reported as Tmax in Table 2, can be attributed to the high interdependency of TPS and PLA phases,24 pointing out the effectiveness of physical compatibilization approach for the preparation of PLA/TPS blends. Generally, the Tmax was increased by increasing PLA content in PLA/TPS samples, and eventually, 100PLA has the highest Tmax rather than others. While, interestingly, the lowest Tmax was observed in 20PLA blend, mainly because of the high amount of TPS plasticizers migrated into PLA phase in this sample. It is reported that the Tmax reduction with increasing TPS content can be explained by increasing the emission of some gases such as CO, CO2, H2O, CH4, C2H4, and CH2O during the starch decomposition, which can promote the PLA chain scission.25 Indeed, in 20PLA sample because of its decreased Tg, as denoted in Table 2, diffusion of mentioned gases into PLA phase can be facilitated, leading to PLA chain scission in lower temperatures. This result also highlights the role of morphology on thermal behavior of PLA/TPS blends. Carbon burning at 400°C to 450°C is the fourth step in TGA investigation of studied samples.26 It is important to note that the final residual mass at 600°C has not reached to 0 in TPS sample because of performing TGA test in an inert environment (N2 gas), which caused the char formation, as also observed by others.14, 18, 23, 24 However, changing the atmosphere to oxygen and increasing the temperature up to 800°C can reach the complete oxidation of starch in the form of CO2 as the final product.18 In the other literature, it has been reported that the thermal degradation of chemical structure of starch prone to form a thermal resistance layer, which gives a high degree of residual ash.27 The residual mass of PLA/TPS blends reached near to zero above 500°C, while PLA reached at 420°C and was appeared in DTG graphs as short peaks around 500°C. It can be explained that the PLA/TPS samples became the porous mass after thermal decomposition at Tmax, because of the complete oxidation and extraction of PLA phase. Therefore, unlike the TPS sample, which faced with the atmosphere only by its outer interfaces, the PLA/TPS samples had the inner interface areas that were contacted to outer medium after PLA extraction. We believed that the continuity of TPS phase can influence the extraction of residual mass in the last peak. In this way, the residual mass in the mentioned peaks, which appeared around 500°C in DTG diagrams versus PLA content, has been plotted in Figure 6. As it is shown in this figure, residual mass significantly dropped after blend having 60 wt% of PLA. This behavior could be related to the morphology inversion and decreasing of TPS continuity. This hypothesis confirmed the continuity of TPS phase, which is shown in Figure 3, and revealed the impact of morphology on thermal properties of blend PLA/TPS blends.

Proximity of thermal degradation temperatures to Tm creates a narrow processing window, as decomposition via chain-scission can occur near these temperatures [1, 2, 4]. For example, PHB (a common PHA) has a Tm around 174–184°C and a thermal degradation onset (Tonset) near this range, limiting melt-processing temperatures [1, 2, 4]. However, blending with additives like PMMA can improve thermal stability: PHB/PMMA blends showed increased Tonset by 21.6°C and maximum degradation temperature (Tmax) by 15.7°C, expanding the processing window [4, 5]. Unmodified PHB degrades with a DTG peak at ~295°C, but composites with cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) reduce thermal resistance by ~20°C [12]. Thus, the thermal stability limit during processing typically aligns with Tm (174–184°C) for unmodified PHAs, but copolymerization or blending can enhance this limit by raising degradation temperatures [1, 3, 4, 5].

Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are biological polyesters synthesized by many microbial species as intracellular carbon and energy reserve.1-3 The biopolyesters can be melted and molded like conventional petroleum-based plastics and, after use, completely degraded into benign products via microbial activities.4-7 The thermal properties of PHAs are of great interest to polymer processors. Many studies have been conducted on thermal degradation of poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (P3HB), the most ubiquitous member of PHAs.8-17 It has been found that P3HB is highly susceptible to thermal degradation. Because of its high melting point (170−180°C), P3HB is processed around 190°C, above which thermal breakdown of the polyester backbone rapidly occurs, resulting in a significant decrease in molecular weight and, consequently, deterioration of the mechanical properties.5 One possible solution is to reduce the melting temperature of bioplastic by introducing a second or even third monomer unit in the PHB backbones such as 3-hydroxyvalerate (3HV) and 4-hydroxyvarelate (4HV). Because of the reduced crystallinity, the melting temperature of copolyesters can be reduced by 40−60°C, depending on the mole percentage of 3HV and 4HV.18 In this low temperature range (120−150°C), it is expected that the thermal degradation of poly(3HB-co-3HV-co-4HV) (P3HB3HV4HV) copolymers is under control with improved thermal stability. The PHA bioplastics can therefore be processed like conventional thermoplastics. There is little evidence, however, that a random P3HB3HV4HV or its blends can be processed at a low temperature with improved thermal stability. The thermal degradation of P3HB proceeds mainly via a random chain scission (cis-elimination) reaction, forming a six-member ring structure of 3HB monomer, and releasing a crotonic acid and/or oligomers of crotonyl end group.19 The primary degradation products may undergo further decomposition above the melting temperature to form pyrolysis products. Similar to P3HB, P3HB3HV4HV copolymers may generate various degradation products including the monomeric crotonic acid, 2-pentanoic acid, as well as the oligomers with crotonyl or 2-pentanoyl end groups as shown in Scheme 1. Thus, it is very interesting to know whether or not the different monomers (3HB, 3HV, and 4HV) in PHA backbones have the same vulnerability in thermal degradation. If not, which monomer is more vulnerable? Many studies on PHA thermal degradation are conducted in a relatively narrow temperature range, either around melting point to study the thermal stability in melting, or at very high temperature to study thermal decomposition or pyrolysis. In the latter case, the products are often analyzed with GC/MS or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) without separation of the degradation products.9, 11 Size exclusion chromatography plus NMR (SEC-NMR) analysis may reveal more information because it can separate the degradation products or oligomers according to their molecular size and then determine their unsaturated end groups. The relative abundance of the end groups derived from different monomers may reveal the vulnerability of the monomers in copolyesters.

Thermal and mechanical properties of polyhydroxyalkanoates Isostatic PHB displays a number of properties comparable to petroleum-based polymers (e.g., poly-propylene), such as high melting temperature (175 °C) and relatively high tensile strength (30-35 MPa). However, pure PHB has had only limited use mainly because of its intrinsic brittleness (presenting low strain at break) and the narrow processing window of this plastic. Indeed, the elongation at break is very different between PHB (5 %) and PP (400 %). PHB/V (polyhydroxybutyrate/valerate) is also brittle, its elongation at break is less than 15 %, its modulus and fracture stress are 1.2 GPa and 25 MPa [17]. There are many reasons for the brittleness of PHB and PHB/V: the secondary crystallization of the amorphous phase takes place during storage at room temperature; the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PHB is close to room temperature; PHB has a low nucleation density, therefore large spherulites exhibit inter-spherulitic cracks. Several authors ( [18, 19]) have examined secondary crystallization, which occurs during storage time at room temperature. Due to its natural origin, PHB is free of heterogeneities, like catalystresidues or other impurities that can act as heterogeneous nuclei, promoting the onset of crystallization [20]. This affects the crystallization kinetics of the polymer, which often starts from homogeneous nuclei, unless specific nucleating agents are added. The slow crystallization kinetics of PHB permits to tune the crystallinity level, which, in turn, is expected to affect also the rigid amorphous chains coupled with the crystals. By the addition of a nucleating agent, the number of small spherulites increases. It is reported that the rigid amorphous fraction of low molar- mass PHB of 5 kDa is only 5-10 %, and at best half of that of high-molar-mass PHB of almost 500 kDa,despite identical crystallinity. The larger rigid amorphous fraction and higher degree of reversible melting and crystallization in PHB of high molar mass, consistently and independently, is attributed to enhanced covalent coupling of crystals and amorphous structure, and/or de-coupling of segments of macromolecules which traverse between phases, respectively [21]. Molecule segments in the amorphous phase exhibit a reduced mobility if they are covalently connected with the crystalline phase.

Copolymers like poly(3HB-*co*-3HV-*co*-4HV) reduce melting temperatures by 40–60°C (to ~120–150°C) through reduced crystallinity, enabling processing in this lower range with improved stability [1,8]. However, excessive additives (e.g., wood flour >20 wt%) or non-optimized blends may reduce stability [11]. Thus, the thermal stability limit during processing is highly dependent on material design: ~190°C for PHB homopolymers and ~120–150°C for copolymers or stabilized blends [1,3,8,14].
