First published on 7th January 2011 Spider silk shows great potential as a biomaterial: in addition to biocompatibility and biodegradability, its strength and toughness are greater than native biological fibres (e.g.collagen), with toughness exceeding that of synthetic fibres (e.g.nylon). Although the ultimate tensile strength and toughness at failure are unlikely to be limiting factors, its yield strain of 2% is insufficient, particularly for biomedical application because of the inability to mimic the complex ultrastructure of natural tissues with current tissue engineering approaches. To harness the full potential of spider silk as a biomaterial, it is therefore necessary to increase its yield strain. In this paper, we discuss the means by which the mechanical properties of spider silk, particularly the yield strain, can be optimized through structural modifications.
Spider silk has garnered attention as a structural material and a medical resource for next generation because it is tough, lightweight, and biodegradable. Nonwoven silk fabrics are emerging in research and industries owing to advanced electrospinning techniques. Several studies have reported nonwoven fabrics made of spider silk-like proteins, which are originated from recombinant expression systems, with lower molecular weights than the natural counterpart. The lower molecular weight causes a lack of mechanical strength and durability, preventing the evaluation of industrial potential of the spider silk-based nonwoven fabric to use as a structural and medical material. In this study, an electrospun nonwoven fabric is produced using native spider silk fibers forcibly reeled from live spiders. The spider silk-based nonwoven fabrics demonstrate cell compatibility, and the mechanical properties are superior to the silkworm silk-based nonwoven fabrics. The availability of spider silk-based nonwoven fabrics introduces an unexplored set of potential uses, along with the context of sustainable development goals. Silk is a natural structural material used in the outer shell of silkworm cocoons and as a lifeline by spiders.1 Biodegradable proteinous fibers can replace petroleum-based manmade fibers and be used as a promising bio-based material to meet sustainable development goals (SDGs).2 Furthermore, silk displays excellent mechanical features with high strength and ductility.3 The silkworm silk fiber is the most abundantly produced and studied silk worldwide.4 It is a traditionally expensive clothing textile owing to its lightness, drapability, softness, and lustrous appearance.5 Silkworm silk is not limited to textile use: they have also been utilized as surgical sutures for decades because of the excellent knot strength and biocompatibility of silk.6

Its exceptional combination of Young′s modulus, tensile strength, and toughness makes it a highly versatile material with extensive potential applications.8 This remarkable performance originates from the unique molecular architecture of spider silk, characterized by stacked β-pleated crystallites surrounded by a disordered (amorphous) matrix rich in glycine.9 The amorphous polypeptide chains in silk are interconnected through β-sheet crystallites, which enhance the structural integrity of the protein strands under high strains as reinforcing elements. The presence of the amorphous region enhances the exceptional stretchiness of silk through the provision of entropic elasticity.10 Regenerated silk fibroin, mimicking this structure with anti-parallel β-sheet nanocrystals and an amorphous matrix composed of α-helices and random coils, offers a promising route for replicating the properties of spider silk in artificial materials.11 In this study, we presented a biomimetic approach through hydrogen bonding-induced self-assembly to enhance both the mechanical characteristics and self-repairing effectiveness of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels, inspired by the heterogeneous structure of spider silk (Figure 1a). Additionally, the incorporation of TA provided the hydrogel with antibacterial and antioxidant properties. Spider silk is a polymer with potential shape and mechanical behavior memory. Spiders, as one of the oldest species on the Earth's mainland, constitute a vast family with a great variety of species and a wide range of distribution. These phylogenetic and ecological varieties has led to the appearance of specific adaptations to the most diverse various environmental conditions over nearly 400 million years [1,2]. Among these adaptations, the complex and diverse family of spiders evolved to span up to different different silk-derived materials with specific compositions, structures, and properties [[3], [4], [5]]. The most extensively studied of all these silk types is the silk spun from the major ampullate gland, commonly referred to as dragline silk or MAS, which exhibits exceptional mechanical properties, boasting a mechanical behavior that greatly exceeds that of Kevlar in terms of work to fracture [6,7]. In addition, MAS possesses not only excellent mechanical properties, but is also biocompatible and biodegradable, making it suitable for a wide range of applications in biomedicine, as well as in the chemical, aerospace and defense industries, among other fields [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12]]. However, due to the limited availability of natural spider silk (from now on, unless otherwise indicated, spider silk will be used as a synonym for MAS), mimicking natural silk to produce bionic materials with specific properties has become the focus of many researchers [13]. In this regard, the composition of spider silk proteins and the spinning process have evolved to form an inseparable and unique natural spinning system, whose complexity has posed a significant challenge in efforts to understand the effects of each component on spider silk [14]. Basic spider silk spinning mechanisms have been established, however, the findings primarily focus on fundamental theoretical principles [[15], [16], [17]]. In particular, the existing knowledge about the natural spinning process of spiders provides limited practical assistance for the artificial bioimitation of spider silk in production applications [18]. However, we can still benefit from the rich interplay between protein composition, unique structure and singular properties function, to continue optimizing the production and properties of biomimetic materials. All types of silk proteins, known as spidroins, exist in an aqueous solution within the abdominal glands of spiders in which the various silk types for different applications are produced [19,20]. MAS is mainly made up of two groups of proteins termed major ampullate spidroin 1 (MaSp 1) and major ampullate spidroin 2 (MaSp 2). Both types comprise large proteins with a molecular weight in the range 250-350 kDa, and show a characteristic structure with a highly repetitive core region, and two non repetitive N- and C-termini [[21], [22], [23]]. Members of the MaSp1 type generally exhibit the motifs GGX, (GA)n, and (A)n, while spidroins of the MaSp2 exhibit the (A)n and, most significantly, the GPGXX motif. A third type, termed major ampullate spidroin 3 (MaSp3), whose role in the formation of the fiber is less clear than that of MaSp1 and MaSp2 has been described and is characterized by the presence of the SSX motif, and the absence of the G(A)n motifs [24,25]. However, the reported spider silk protein sequences (primary structure) are mostly fragmented due to the large size of these proteins, and the extensive repetition of the motifs indicated previously [26,27]. With the development of Next Generation Sequencing technologies, overall diversity and complexity of the repetitive structures in the existing studies were found to be higher than expected when compared to the previously sequenced fragments. Needless to say, the usage of fragmented sequences presented obvious limitations in the study of the secondary structure, tertiary structure and in function of spider silk protein [24,[28], [29], [30], [31]]. Zhao et al. utilized for the first time a variety of strategies to isolate full-length MaSp1 and MaSp2 cDNAs in the wasp spider A. bruennichi, and reported partial amino acid sequence of MaSp1 that lacks the N-termini as well as full-length amino acid sequence of MaSp2 [32]. Subsequently, Sheffer et al. has reported the spider reference genome for A. bruennichi in 2021 [33], however, the reported full-length amino acid sequence of spider silk was so scarce at that time that MaSp was not identified and analyzed. In summary, the current study only reports one full-length amino acid sequence for MaSp2, thus it is crucial to conduct identity and analysis based on complete amino acid sequences to investigate the relationship between sequence-structure-function and the mechanical properties of major ampullate silk of A. bruennichi.
In recent years, natural fiber-reinforced biodegradable thermoplastics are being recognized as an emerging new environmentally friendly material for industrial, commercial, and biomedical applications. Among different types of natural fibers, silk fiber is a common type of animal-based fiber, has been used for biomedical engineering and surgical operation applications for many years because of its biocompatible and bioresorbable properties. On the basis of our previous study, a novel biodegradable biocomposite for biomedical applications was developed by mixing chopped silk fiber and polylactic acid (PLA) through the injection molding process. De Novo Design of Recombinant Spider Silk Proteins for Material Applications Spider dragline silk is nature's high-performance fiber, outperforming even the best man-made materials by displaying extraordinary mechanical properties on a strength-to-weight basis.1, 2 In addition, spider silk is biocompatible and biodegradable, which makes it suitable for biomaterials. The impressive mechanical properties of silk fibers and the efficiency of silk spinning in nature have allowed insight into the nature of silk processing from biosynthesis to silk spinning into fibers. However, many aspects and mechanisms of this process remain to be revealed. Silk fibers are fine, lustrous and consist of β-sheet crystals with a high degree of molecular orientation. These fibers are formed under ambient temperature and pressure,3 spun from an aqueous solution, and the resulting fiber is insoluble in water due to an irreversible phase transition during the spinning process. An oriented liquid crystalline state of silk with highly ordered precrystalline molecules can help explain the natural process, which transforms random coils in aqueous solution to an insoluble oriented fiber.4, 5 Artificial variants of silk would be desirable in order to gain insight into these mechanisms while also tuning physical properties, diameter, cross-section, as well as morphology and structure. Understanding processing conditions that induce hierarchical self-assembly of spider silk leading to the excellent physical properties would also help in materials-related applications for these proteins. Controlling how a protein interacts with itself, other proteins or the environmental milieu, is important in order to understand self-assembly. Methods to reprocess silk proteins into new morphologies including films, foams, meshes,6 nanoscale diameter fibers,7 fiber bundles8 and tissue engineering scaffolds9, 10 have been reported. For instance, 3D porous scaffolds were derived from regenerated Bombyx mori silk fibroin solution using either an all aqueous process or an organic solvent (hexafluoroisopropanol) (HFIP) with salt leaching, gas foaming, and freeze-drying modes to generate inter-connected pore structures in 3D matrices.9, 11 A number of recent studies have explored a tissue-engineering approach using silk fibroin scaffolds in various formats to repair bone with diverse morphologies.11-13 Silk fibroin hydrogels, membranes or nets without preseeded cells have been used for bone regeneration. The highly porous scaffold prepared by salt leaching possesses a useful combination of compressive strength and uniform, interconnected pores with controllable size distribution.9, 11, 12 The morphological structural features of the scaffolds depend on number of variables including silk concentration, salt particle size, and the use of aqueous- or HFIP- driven process. A phase diagram for the formation of the aqueous and HFIP-derived 3D porous scaffolds has been generated based on these approaches.11 Silk fibroin scaffolds, regardless of their processing, undergo a structural transition from random coil to β-sheets.11 The mechanism of silk processing, including formation of globular micelles as a key step in formation of silk fibers has been reported.14 The pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic domains in the silk fibroin includes larger hydrophilic domains at the termini, smaller internal hydrophilic domains, and larger hydrophobic domains.15 Based on thermodynamics, silk fibroin acts as a tri-block copolymer, with the formation of micellar structures in water in which the larger hydrophilic termini define the outer edges, while the hydrophobic blocks are present inside the micelles.14 However, the structural and conformational changes in the assembly process remain challenging to control in order to regulate nanostructure formation. The hydrophobic blocks are assumed to form more regular structures, while the hydrophilic blocks move to the surface of micelles to interact with water by chain folding, reducing the free energy of the silk fibroin-water system. Thus, fundamental questions related to silk protein assembly,16 processing parameters, and the formation of physical cross-links via β-sheet formation to stabilize proteins in solution, should lead to a versatile set of spider silk-based biomaterials with a range of properties. With these goals in mind, we investigated how pH, salt, and water interacted with the spider silk-like block copolymer, HBA6 (H, B, and A are hexahistidine tag, hydrophilic, and hydrophobic blocks, respectively) to produce different morphologies.
Natural polymer materials mainly include hyaluronic acid, collagen, polylactic acid [18, 19], etc., which have good biocompatibility and degradable absorption. However, they exhibit limited mechanical strength, rapid degradation [20], and the potential to produce acidic degradation products that can disrupt the local acid-base environment. Silk, as a natural protein fiber, has excellent mechanical properties comparable to synthetic polymers. Meanwhile, it displays high biocompatibility [21-23], does not elicit significant inflammatory responses [24]. Besides, it can be fully degraded and absorbed, and can regulate the degradation rate [25]. It has been employed as a novel biomaterial for tissue regeneration, including in tendon and rotator cuff repair [26-29]. There are two main categories of silk fibroin materials: natural silk fibroin materials (derived from raw silk degumming) and regenerated silk fibroin materials [30]. In terms of mechanical properties, the β-sheet structure plays an important role in the mechanical properties of silk [31], which is the main factor that endows silk fibroin with high strength and high elastic modulus [32]. However, the protein secondary structure of regenerated silk fibroin has been changed after dissolution, dialysis, and freeze-drying. The mechanical properties of regenerated silk fibroin are weak and brittle [33, 34]. The tensile strength of regenerated silk fibroin films is about 0.02 GPa, and the elongation at break is < 2% [35, 36]. Furthermore, the random coil and α-helix structures can be transformed into β-sheet structures through the application of specific external factors, including temperature, pH value, organic solvent, and shear stretching [37, 38]. This process can enhance the mechanical properties. Compared with the tensile strength of natural fibers about 0.5-0.6 GPa and the elongation at break of 10%-40%, there is still a huge gap. In terms of degradation rate, the degradation rate of regenerated silk fibroin materials is significantly faster than that of natural silk fibroin materials [39], which cannot match the tissue growth rate. Nevertheless, while natural silk protein materials exhibit superior mechanical properties and degradation rates compared to regenerated silk fibroin materials, natural silk fibroin materials have some limitations in processing and molding. The majority of studies currently concentrate on the utilization of electrospinning [40], freeze-drying, 3D printing [41, 42], self-assembly [43] and other technologies for the preparation of regenerated silk fibroin materials, which exhibit inadequate mechanical strength and are unsuitable for the repair of extensive soft tissue defects. Although the mechanical properties can be improved by producing composite materials with a multi-layer structure [44], this also increases the thickness and weight of the material. Concurrently, the cost is greater, and the capacity for large-scale production is limited.
Aromatic polyesters are, however, commonly used in engineering, constructional, and structural applications because of their low cost, high stiffness, strength, dimensional stability, low water absorption, and favorable chemical and electrical resistance. A problem with these aromatic polyesters is that they do not biodegrade under normal environmental conditions [4, 5]. Biocomposites of thermoplastic polymers and natural fibers can completely degrade in soil or compost. The use of fiber reinforcement is an attractive method to improve the mechanical properties of biodegradable plastics [6-9]. Among these thermoplastic polyesters, PBT is a popular because it displays a high mechanical strength and modulus compared with other thermoplastic polyesters, such as PBS, PVA, and PLA. Unfortunately, PBT is expensive; however, its cost can be reduced through the blending of PBT composites with natural biomaterials. Plant fibers that increase the tensile strength of composites have recently been used as a means of reinforcing polymer matrices for replacement with synthetic fibers. Sisal is an abundant natural fiber with excellent tensile strength that can improve the mechanical properties of materials. Moreover, although sisal fibers (SFs) range in length and require a compatibilizing agent to wet the fibers [10, 11], the highly hydrophilic nature of PBT results in the natural wetting of SF. Thus, composites of PBT and SF offer advantages in both biocompatibility and cost [12, 13].
Due to the limitations on the use of petroleum-based plastics as a solution to environmental problems in recent years, the increase in the number of studies on the use of renewable and environmentally friendly natural biopolymers such as chitosan, sericin, keratin, alginate, and cellulose obtained from animals or plants is remarkable. They are preferred because of their advantages, such as being suitable for changing the structure of many naturally occurring biopolymers by chemical modification techniques, structural compatibility with certain target regions of microbial cells, and economical, antibacterial, and not posing an ecological hazard. At the same time, it is clear that composites prepared from natural polymers in the form of fibers can be among the sustainable multifunctional textile materials of the future.[1] Silkworm silk, one of the natural fiber polymers included in the class of polypeptides and proteins (collagen, silk fibroin, and albumin), has superior physical properties such as luster, soft feeling, and mechanical strength,[2] physicochemical properties such as water absorbability, and microbial resistance after the degumming process removes the sericin component. For example, many properties, such as wettability, adhesion, and reactions in biological environments result from the polymer surface's interaction with the environment.[12] One of the techniques frequently applied for the surface modification of silk is the graft copolymerization technique. While this technique is applied to the surfaces physically or chemically with the help of plasma in polymers with completely inert surfaces,[12] it is widely used in chemical bonding in polymer materials with surfaces that can interact chemically. For example, a hydrogel formation was performed on silk by co-grafting acrylamide and acrylic acid on fibroin fabric obtained from Tasar silkworm species and then crosslinking reaction with N,N'-methylene bisacrylamide in the literature. After coating the as-modified silk fabric surface with zinc oxide, it has been reported that the antimicrobial activity and cytocompatibility of the material were significantly improved compared to an untreated silk fibroin, making the silk a promising material for wound dressing.[13]

Spiders, as one of the oldest species on the Earth's mainland, constitute a vast family with a great variety of species and a wide range of distribution. The most extensively studied of all these silk types is the silk spun from the major ampullate gland, commonly referred to as dragline silk or MAS, which exhibits exceptional mechanical properties, boasting a mechanical behavior that greatly exceeds that of Kevlar in terms of work to fracture [6,7]. In addition, MAS possesses not only excellent mechanical properties, but is also biocompatible and biodegradable, making it suitable for a wide range of applications in biomedicine, as well as in the chemical, aerospace and defense industries, among other fields [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12]]. However, due to the limited availability of natural spider silk (from now on, unless otherwise indicated, spider silk will be used as a synonym for MAS), mimicking natural silk to produce bionic materials with specific properties has become the focus of many researchers [13]. In this regard, the composition of spider silk proteins and the spinning process have evolved to form an inseparable and unique natural spinning system, whose complexity has posed a significant challenge in efforts to understand the effects of each component on spider silk [14]. Basic spider silk spinning mechanisms have been established, however, the findings primarily focus on fundamental theoretical principles [[15], [16], [17]]. In particular, the existing knowledge about the natural spinning process of spiders provides limited practical assistance for the artificial bioimitation of spider silk in production applications [18]. All types of silk proteins, known as spidroins, exist in an aqueous solution within the abdominal glands of spiders in which the various silk types for different applications are produced [19,20]. In the past decades, growing emphasis on environmental concerns and exhausting depletion of petroleum sources have triggered the exploration of natural fibers as a “green” alternative for synthetic polymer fibers in composites. Because of their advantages such as low cost, low density, renewability, biodegradability and acceptable specific strength etc., a bulk of natural fibers have been utilized for structural/semi-structural materials in various fields including aerospace, automotive, building, furniture, packaging and sports articles. However, most of them are originated from lignocellulosic fibers [1], [2], [3]. Bombyx mori silkworm silk, a representative animal fiber of luster and fineness, has been used in the textile industry for centuries. It structurally consists of a fibrous core protein named fibroin, and a family of glue-like proteins named sericin that surround the fibroin threads to cement them together. The high crystallinity of β-sheets (ca. 50%) as well as the well orientation of these nanocrystallites in the core filament [4] gives silkworm silk the remarkable mechanical properties, especially strength (0.4 GPa) and extensibility (20%) [5], [6]. In addition, the homogeneous physicochemical properties of silkworm silk as a continuous fiber allow for the fabrication facilities via filament winding and pultrusion processes. Recently, silkworm silk has received great interest as a filling material in composites. For example, chopped silk and commercial silk fabric have been used to reinforce biodegradable or synthetic polymers such as poly(butylene succinate) [7], [8], poly(ɛ-caprolactone) [9], poly(lactic acid) [10], or even polychloroprene rubber [11]. However, chopped silk loses the mechanical merits as a continuous fiber, and commercial silk fabric suffers from the wetting problem of twisted fibroin threads in the matrix, both of which may result in the uncompetitive mechanical performance of the reported silk composites. It is well known that the adhesion between components (e.g. the fiber phase and the matrix phase) is crucial for the mechanical performance of a composite. On one hand, Jin et al. [8] modified silk fabric with carbon nanotubes to improve its compatibility with poly[(butylene succinate)-co-(butylene adipate)], and obtained a composite with fairly increased mechanical properties. On the other hand, Li et al. [12] directly composed silk fabric with regenerated silk fibroin (RSF); however, the overall mechanical properties of the composite were still unsatisfactory. This was likely caused by the immiscibility between the different fine structures of silk fibroin, i.e., the well-ordered β-sheet in silk fiber [13] and either the amorphous state [14] or the randomly-aligned β-sheet [15] in RSF matrix. Furthermore, due to the highly-repeating GAGAGS (G = glycine, A = alanine and S = serine) motifs and the highly-ordered structure, silk fiber presents a water-resistant feature [16] that indicates its inadequate wettability with RSF solution. Since partial fiber dissolution (either by solvent or by thermal melting) seems a straightforward approach to prepare fiber composites with good interface adhesion [3], [17], [18], [19], [20], a moderate concentration of LiBr aqueous solution (i.e. 6 mol L−1) was applied on silk fiber to improve its adhesion with RSF matrix in this work. Therefore, a robust and tough all-silk composite was successfully produced by embedding the LiBr-pretreated silk fibers in alignment to the high concentration of RSF aqueous solution and through an eco-friendly solution casting process.
Recent advancements in biomimetic materials have brought spider silk to the forefront of scientific attention. Its exceptional combination of Young′s modulus, tensile strength, and toughness makes it a highly versatile material with extensive potential applications.8 This remarkable performance originates from the unique molecular architecture of spider silk, characterized by stacked β-pleated crystallites surrounded by a disordered (amorphous) matrix rich in glycine.9 The amorphous polypeptide chains in silk are interconnected through β-sheet crystallites, which enhance the structural integrity of the protein strands under high strains as reinforcing elements. The presence of the amorphous region enhances the exceptional stretchiness of silk through the provision of entropic elasticity.10 Regenerated silk fibroin, mimicking this structure with anti-parallel β-sheet nanocrystals and an amorphous matrix composed of α-helices and random coils, offers a promising route for replicating the properties of spider silk in artificial materials.11 In this study, we presented a biomimetic approach through hydrogen bonding-induced self-assembly to enhance both the mechanical characteristics and self-repairing effectiveness of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels, inspired by the heterogeneous structure of spider silk (Figure 1a). Specifically, the β-sheet crystallite domain of spider silk was simulated by the addition of tannic acid (TA) to induce the formation of a β-folded structure of silk fibroin (SF) through hydrogen bonds. Concurrently, the dynamic hydrogen-bonded amorphous domain of spider silk was emulated through acylhydrazone bond cross-linking between aldehyde hyaluronic acid (AHA) and a synthesized cross-linking agent 3,3′-dithiobis (propionohydrazide) (DTP), which contains hydrazide groups and disulfide bonds (Figure 1b). Additionally, the incorporation of TA provided the hydrogel with antibacterial and antioxidant properties. We comprehensively investigated the rheological properties, swelling kinetics, and morphology of the resulting hydrogel. Mechanical testing was used to quantitatively analyze the hydrogel′s mechanical properties, adhesion, and self-healing ability. This study presented a promising direction for the development of high-performance hydrogels with diverse biomedical applications. First published on 10th February 2021 Oxygen supply is essential for the long-term viability and function of tissue engineered constructs in vitro and in vivo. The integration with the host blood supply as the primary source of oxygen to cells requires 4 to 5 weeks in vivo and involves neovascularization stages to support the delivery of oxygenated blood to cells. Consequently, three-dimensional (3D) encapsulated cells during this process are prone to oxygen deprivation, cellular dysfunction, damage, and hypoxia-induced necrosis. Here we demonstrate the use of calcium peroxide (CaO2) and polycaprolactone (PCL), as part of an emerging paradigm of oxygen-generating scaffolds that substitute the host oxygen supply via hydrolytic degradation. The 35-day in vitro study showed predictable oxygen release kinetics that achieved 5% to 29% dissolved oxygen with increasing CaO2 loading. As a biomaterial, the iterations of 0 mg, 40 mg, and 60 mg of CaO2 loaded scaffolds yielded modular mechanical behaviors, ranging from 5-20 kPa in compressive strength. The other controlled physiochemical features included swelling capacities of 22-33% and enzymatic degradation rates of 0.8% to 60% remaining mass. The 3D-encapsulation experiments of NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, L6 rat myoblasts, and primary cardiac fibroblasts in these scaffolds showed enhanced cell survival, proliferation, and function under hypoxia. During continuous oxygen release, the scaffolds maintained a stable tissue culture system between pH 8 to 9. The broad basis of this work supports prospects in the expansion of robust and clinically translatable tissue constructs. The success of in vivo tissue constructs relies on the proper integration with the host vasculature. The vascular integration of these constructs is responsible for delivering growth factors, cell signals, nutrients, and most critically, oxygen. Oxygen supply is essential for cell viability, proliferation, and function. The first 4 to 6 weeks post-implantation of a tissue construct involves tissue remodelling stages which are necessary for wound healing and neovascularization.16 Regardless, the absence of vasculature during this time can halt cell growth and repair, and lead to further tissue damage by hypoxia-induced necrosis.6,17 Moreover, the cells within tissue constructs often become oxygen deficient, the scaffold dimensions are greater than 100 μm to 200 μm, due to diffusion limitations to oxygen transport.18 Recent strategies to minimize these effects involve treating cell samples and co-encapsulating cells in scaffolds with growth factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), that promote vascularization.19-22 The shortcoming of these methods is that they may lead to an undesired non-homogeneous distribution of vascular networks in three-dimensional (3D) biomaterial scaffolds.5,23-25 Other microfluidic approaches support neovascularization in vitro by generating vasculature-like structures within a tissue scaffold. These techniques while useful are also limited by the level of resolution achieved and are time-consuming due to troubleshooting steps often required to optimize parameters that will result in a homogeneous channel formation throughout the 3D tissue construct.18,26-28 Using these methods in combination to work synergistically is possible; however, the lack of an immediate oxygen source until vascularization occurs might still cause cellular dysfunction or damage within the tissue construct.

Prior to our further mechanistic investigation of the effect of additives on PCL degradation, it would be necessary to understand the process of lipase-enabled PCL degradation first. Different from hydrophilic polyesters, which typically experience bulk erosion via hydrolytic scission of the backbone bonds under physiologic conditions, (7,27,28) lipase-enabled enzymatic PCL degradation would occur most likely through surface erosion (Figure 5A). However, the presence of those small holes between crystalline structures (Figure 5B, arrows) on the surface of the PCL film might allow the enzyme to more easily access the interior of the disc and therefore facilitate degradation. Time-dependent topology changes of PCL discs were monitored by SEM. As shown in Figure 5B-D, PCL discs incubated with lipase for 0, 6, 12, and 18 h displayed a morphological evolution from relatively smooth to rough (6 h) and to highly porous (12 and 18 h). After treatment with lipase for 12 h, large macropores on the scale of 50-100 μm in diameter were found throughout the surface (Figure 5B(a-d)), along with small nanopores at a high magnification (Figure 5B (biii-diii)). Meanwhile, those small pores and dipped regions of the crystalline boundaries enlarged over the period of incubation (Figure 5). In addition, the lipase-induced PCL erosion seems to take place following the “microwrinkles” of the PCL surface (Figure 5B (aiii)), which is probably due to the high surface area allowing for increased lipase adsorption to the disc surfaces. Interestingly, the PCL film became much thinner over the incubation time (Figure 5B (c vs. d)), but the surface features remained comparable. By 24 h, all of the PCL film discs almost completely disappeared. As noted from the mass loss kinetics (Figure 4), either PCL or PCL composites reached the inflection point of the degradation between 5 and 6 h. Thus, a 6 h incubation time was particularly chosen to further study the morphology and changes of various composites containing the hydrophilic additives upon lipase incubation. To affirm that surface erosion is the primary degradation mechanism, micro-CT was employed for nondestructive 3D visualization of internal features and quantitative assessment of porosity in fragile 6 h-degraded specimens. As shown in Figure S3, 3D reconstructions of PCL films before (Figure S3A) and after 6 h lipase incubation (Figure S3B) revealed degradation patterns consistent with SEM observations. The air-side surface view confirmed the topographical features comparable to SEM, while the transverse reconstructions highlighted the presence of small pores (approximately 6.4 ± 6.3 μm) and recessed regions along the crystalline boundaries. Importantly, no reduction in bulk density or appearance of new internal pores was observed after 6 h of incubation, further supporting the conclusion that lipase-mediated degradation primarily proceeds via surface erosion. Water-soluble gelatin is often added to PCL to improve the hydrophilicity and cell attachment of the prepared scaffolds. (8) In this study, two PCL/gelatin ratios (P3G1 and P2G1) were chosen to examine the effect of gelatin on PCL degradation. SEM examination of PCL/gelatin composite discs incubated with PBS (nondegradation control) or lipase (1 U/mL) for 6 h revealed surprising differences (Figure 6). As shown in Figure 6B, both P3G1 and P2G1 incubated in PBS showed no obvious morphological change from the as-prepared ones. However, the zoom-in examination revealed the presence of small micropores (0.3-1 μm) uniformly distributed across the surface, which were not seen with PCL-only discs. Interestingly, the discs with a higher gelatin amount (P2G1) showed noticeably larger micropores than those with a lower gelatin amount (P3G1). To further understand how these micropores were formed, P3G1 discs, as-prepared or upon incubation in PBS for 6 h at room temperature (RT) or 37 °C, were visualized by SEM. Close examination of the surface of as-prepared P3G1 discs showed the presence of microbead-like protrusions (approximately 0.5 μm), but no micropores were identified. In contrast, on the surface of those discs incubated in PBS at RT or 37 °C, microbead-like protrusions and micropores coexisted; however, considerably more micropores were seen with those incubated at 37 °C (Figure S4, Supporting Information). It is known that gelatin is highly soluble in water at higher temperatures, (24) which would lead to the formation of micropores upon dissolution of gelatin-rich regions (microbead-like islands) during incubation at 37 °C and would explain why much larger micropores are seen with P2G1 discs with large gelatin-rich microregions (Figure 6A). Measurement of the protein level in PBS after 24 h of incubation confirmed the dissolution of gelatin from both P3G1 and P2G1 discs, where much more gelatin was detected from P2G1, nearly double (194%) of that from P3G1. This large difference was much higher than the initial gelatin ratio between P2G1 and P3G1 (133%) (Figure S5, Supporting Information), suggesting that more gelatin from P2G1 was dissolved in PBS. Indeed, fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) examination of P2G1 discs after 6 h incubation in PBS showed low gelatin protein absorbance peaks at 1565 cm-1 (amide II) and 1630 cm-1 (amide I), compared to P3G1 (Figure S6, Supporting Information). With the rapid dissolution of gelatin out of P2G1, the remaining mass would be mainly composed of PCL. Thus, degradation of P2G1 would be similar to that of the PCL-only film. Indeed, the KM and mass loss at 24 h were comparable between PCL and P2G1 but slightly higher in P2G1, which might be attributed to the presence of micropores favoring lipase access (see Table 1). SEM examination of the surfaces of 6 h-degraded P2G1 revealed somewhat a similar morphology to that of 6 h-degraded PCL, but with the presence of abundant micropores (Figure 6B(d)). As confirmed by micro-CT examination of P2G1 films before (Figure S3A, Supporting Information) and after 6 h lipase incubation (Figure S3B, Supporting Information), the incorporation of gelatin accelerated surface erosion, with recessed regions rapidly developing into pores while bulk density remaining unchanged, complementing SEM observations. In the case of the P3G1 film, despite some protein release, a fair amount of gelatin was still trapped within the PCL (Figure S6, Supporting Information) to attract the water onto the surface, limiting the access of lipase to PCL and thereby significantly decelerating the degradation (see Figure 6B (b) and Table 1). The possible mechanism of lipase-enabled degradation of PCL/gelatin composite films is summarized in Figure 6A. To recapitulate compositional similarity to native ECM, collagen is typically combined with PCL to yield a cell-friendly surface for cell attachment. (29,30) We therefore created composites of PCL and type I collagen at ratios of 3:1 and 2:1 (i.e., P3C1 and P2C1) to study the effect of collagen on PCL degradation in composite films. Notably, P3C1 and P2C1 displayed marked differences in terms of morphology change upon lipase (1 U/mL) incubation for 6 h (Figure 7B(b) vs B(d)). It seemed that more erosion/degradation occurred to P3C1 discs after lipase incubation, leading to the formation of deep grooves between the island structures, while the secondary structures of microwrinkles became much more pronounced. High-magnification examination of the lipase-incubated specimens further revealed the presence of abundant micropores (1-3 μm) and submicron pores (0.2-1 μm) on the surface of P3C1, in contrast to much less porous P2C1 (Figure 7B(a-iii) vs B(d-iii)). We also performed micro-CT on 6 h-degraded P2C1 films and observed that the films became only thinner and partial delamination without noted internal density changes (Figure S3B, Supporting Information). The delamination most likely comes from sample preparation (air drying and sectioning prior to scanning) instead of degradation. Similarly, there were also noted differences in terms of KM and mass loss at 24 h (Table 1). To our surprise, a faster degradation happened to P3C1 instead of P2C1. To better understand the possible mechanism, we examined the morphology of P3C1 and P2C1 discs incubated in PBS at 37 °C for 6 h. SEM examination of the incubated discs revealed the presence of circular elevated regions at a low magnification for both composite films, while submicrometer beads were observed at a high magnification (Figure 7B(a-iii) and B(c-iii)). Different from PCL/gelatin samples, in which the microbeads were readily dissolved after DI water incubation, the submicron beads present in PCL/collagen films remained on the surface without dissolution. Compared to P3C1, much larger microbeads were seen on the surface of P2C1, and the size of such microbeads also increased upon PBS incubation, indicating the possible swelling of collagen due to its hydrophilic nature (23) (Figure S7, Supporting Information). Although the protein level in PBS after 24 h of incubation was much higher with P2C1 than that with P3C1 (barely measured) (Figure S5, Supporting Information), the swelling/hydrated collagen stuck to the film surface would most likely minimize the access of lipase to PCL, particularly at the early period of degradation, and subsequently decelerate the degradation process. On the other hand, the collagen in P3C1 was relatively less and mainly trapped within PCL, which would attract less water to the film surface, thereby causing less interference to the binding of lipase to PCL for degradation. FTIR examination of P2C1 and P3C1 films after 6 h incubation in PBS and lipase showed comparable absorbance peak intensities at 1565 cm-1 (amide II) and 1630 cm-1 (amide I) (Figure S8, Supporting Information), suggesting that a good amount of collagen remains within the composite film. Based on the above-described observations, the possible mechanism of the lipase-enabled degradation of the PCL/collagen composite film is captured in Figure 6A.

Among the synthetic bioplastics, poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is a widely used polymer for its excellent biocompatibility, bioresorbability, nontoxicity, and processability. PCL also exhibits good thermal stability and mechanical properties and is used in high-pressure water treatment applications such as microfiltration and nanofiltration [26, 27]. However, PCL is hydrophobic (water contact angle [WCA] ~110° [28]) and exhibits slow hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation [29]. However, these limitations of PCL can be circumvented by suitable modifications. For instance, Rouba et al. modified the electrospun PCL membrane surface by plasma treatment which significantly enhanced water wettability due to the attachment of oxygen-containing functional groups on the surface and improved adhesion with adipose-derived stem cells [30]. Arbade et al. found improved hydrophilicity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility of PCL by adding poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and poly(L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone-co-glycolide) (PLCG) [31]. Also, they reported that the addition of chloramphenicol drug [32] and Emblica officinalis [28] improved the hydrophilicity of PCL. PCL-based membranes and nanofiber mats for capturing water contaminants have been studied extensively in the literature. For example, Tu et al. prepared electrospun PCL membranes by incorporating 10% TiO2 and 1% rectorite, achieving over 98% efficiency in breaking down rhodamine B dye through photocatalysis [33]. Nivedita et al. prepared PCL membranes with 10% unmodified (UMMT) and organically modified montmorillonite (OMMT) clay by phase-inversion method. Based on the provided evidence, oxygen plasma treatment enhances PCL surfaces primarily through **surface functionalization with oxygen-rich groups**, which improves hydrophilicity and facilitates subsequent modifications. Specifically:

1.  **Introduces hydrophilic functional groups**: Oxygen plasma treatment generates carboxyl (-COOH) and hydroxyl (-OH) groups on the PCL surface, significantly increasing its hydrophilicity. This reduces the water contact angle and enhances water absorption [2], [3], [9].

2.  **Improves biocompatibility and cell interactions**: The increased hydrophilicity and chemical activation of the plasma-treated PCL surface promote cell adhesion and proliferation (e.g., with human keratinocytes and fibroblasts) compared to untreated PCL [2], [3].

3.  **Enables biomolecule immobilization**: The functionalized surface provides reactive sites for grafting biocompatible molecules like gelatin. This electrostatic interaction enhances cell attachment and spreading [2], [3], [9].

4.  **Minimal impact on mechanical properties**: The treatment primarily affects the surface layer (less than 1% of total fiber mass), preserving the tensile strength and bulk mechanical integrity of PCL scaffolds [9].

5.  **Increases biodegradation rate**: Functionalization with oxygen-rich groups accelerates enzymatic degradation, as observed in cellulose fabrics (mechanism inferred for PCL) [4], [9]. However, this effect is surface-driven and does not imply bulk degradation.

In summary, oxygen plasma enhances PCL surfaces by oxidizing the polymer surface to create hydrophilic functional groups, thereby improving wettability, cell-material interactions, and grafting capabilities while maintaining core mechanical properties [2], [3], [4], [9].

First published on 27th January 2016 Polymeric packaging materials are preferred because they are lightweight and cost-effective as compared to conventional packaging. Plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) of organo-silicon compounds is one of the ways to deposit silicon oxide (SiOx) coating on polymers to improve barrier properties. In this paper, a tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) precursor was used to deposit a SiOx coating on corn starch/poly(ε-caprolactone) (CSPCL) films through PECVD. The effect of the deposition time on various properties was studied. ATR-FTIR, XPS and XRD revealed that the coating has a highly cross-linked SiOx glass like structure. AFM and SEM suggested a smooth and conformal morphology. Adhesive properties were studied from the peel strength and correlated with the work of adhesion. Barrier properties were studied from the water vapor and the oxygen transmission rates and showed significant improvement. The effect of the plasma polymerized TEOS (ppTEOS) coating on the biodegradation of CSPCL films was evaluated using an indoor soil burial method (to simulate natural degradation) with the single micro-organism, Bacillus subtilis MTCC 121 (BS 121) (to understand the interaction between micro-organisms & the modified surface). Biodegradation through the indoor soil burial method was assessed by measuring the change in tensile properties and growth of soil micro flora on the surface using optical light microscopy. Biodegradation by BS 121 was assessed by measuring the increase in its number along with the changes it brought about on the sample surface using optical light microscopy and SEM. It was observed that there was a reduction in the adhesion of soil flora and reduced growth of BS121 on ppTEOS coated CSPCL films. Thus ppTEOS coated CSPCL films seem to be an attractive option for environmentally benign packaging applications. After utilization, the long-term existence of conventional packaging materials in the ecosystem creates environmental concerns due to their non-degradability and synthetic origin. The use of biodegradable polymers as packaging has been initiated.18 However, for their application as packaging materials, it is necessary to improve their barrier properties. Applying silicon oxide coatings on biodegradable polymers using the PECVD technique provides a novel way to utilize biodegradable polymers as packaging materials, having good barrier properties and retaining their biodegradability. The deposition of silicon oxide film on biodegradable polymers like chitosan, starch, and polylactic acid (PLA) for various applications has been studied.19-22 However, the deposition of silicon oxide film using PECVD on a starch-polycaprolactone system has not been explored much. Instead of synthesizing new polymers, researchers are working on blends of existing polymers to obtain the desired properties for specific applications from an economical point of view. Starch-based biodegradable polymers are very useful in this context. Starch is a natural biopolymer and as a synthetic biodegradable polymer, poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) has inherent biodegradability, good mechanical properties, compatible with other polymers, hydrophobic nature, and easily available. Starch and PCL blends, possessing comparable properties, have been synthesized and studied by various researchers to provide an environmental friendly substitute for currently used synthetic and non-degrading polymers.

Surface modification treatments of polymers based on atmospheric plasma technologies are acquiring high relevance at industrial level. In fact, these treatments show an easy implementation in manufacturing processes, easy automation; in addition, atmospheric plasma techniques are environmentally friendly, as it does not generate wastes.8-10 Atmospheric plasma allows selective modification of the topmost layers without affecting the bulk material. Previous studies have been carried out with PLA and atmospheric plasma focusing on improving energy surface for a better adhesion to substrates PLA-PLA.11, 12 By the control of the process parameters, nozzle-polymeric substrate distance and substrate advance rate, different surface properties can be tailored, as for example the wettability of inks and dyes, adhesion,13-15 growth of other layers, etc. In general, an interesting increase of the solid surface energy is produced by the action of two main plasma-acting mechanisms. From the physical point of view, atmospheric plasma produces surface abrasion that brings a change in the surface roughness. From the chemical point of view, the highly energetic species in the air plasma react with the topmost layers of the polymer surface and the overall effects are chain scission, hydrogen removal (and subsequent free radical formation), and surface oxidation.16, 17 These mechanisms have a synergistic effect that produces an important increase in polymer surface energy; therefore, it also improves its hydrophilic behavior.18, 19 In this research work, atmospheric air plasma treatment is used on PLA surface in order to improve mechanical performance of PLA-PLA adhesion joints with the main aim of increasing the relatively low PLA surface energy. The adhesive used are ecologic bio-based. Adhesives used are from its most natural resources (55%), these stickers have the advantage of being biodegradables, as well as the substrate used.20 In order to achieve it, the optimal conditions (plasma processing parameters) are determined. Changes in surface topography were evaluated by using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) techniques; in addition, chemical changes at the topmost layers were followed by using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).21

There is a significant interest in using synthetic polymers, such as polycaprolactone (PCL), in engineering skin to avoid the need for donor sites with autografts, immunological rejection issues with allograft and reproducibility issues with using natural polymers. PCL is promising as it is a US Food and Drug Administration-approved biodegradable polymer with good mechanical properties. However, its hydrophobic nature is not optimal for cellular interaction and biodegradation in skin tissue engineering. In this study, titanium oxide-PCL composite films were prepared using an in situ, one-step synthesis method. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) was introduced to improve the wetting properties of the hydrophobic polymer and so enhance the cell-material interactions and material biodegradation to be more suitable for skin regeneration. Results showed that the simple synthesis method produced nano- and submicron TiO2 particles well dispersed within the PCL matrix. Spin-coated composite films showed increasing hydrophilicity with increasing concentration of TiO2. Degradation of the composite films and pure PCL films were compared using gel permeation chromatography of the films after 14-day-immersion experiments. Molecular weights of PCL after immersion were found to steadily decrease by up to ~65 % with increasing concentration of TiO2. Rates of water penetration into the composite films were found to increase with the concentration of TiO2 and correlate with the molecular weight decreases observed. In vitro experiments with fibroblasts demonstrated enhanced cell adhesion and proliferation on the composite films. This synthesis method therefore provides a simple means of tuning the wetting properties of hydrophobic polymers to enhance their cellular interactions, as well as tuning their biodegradation properties to suit applications such as skin tissue engineering. Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are a group of biodegradable polyesters that were firstly synthesized in the 1970s by the ALZA Corporation in order to develop materials that may potentially undergo surface erosion degradation process, which is not commonly found in biodegradable polyesters [138], [139]. The high hydrophobicity provided by the orthoesther linkages ensures that the degradation proceeds faster than the H2O diffusion into the material. POEs are synthesized by using diols having different chain flexibility. Till the date, four types of these surface eroding materials have been reported [140], [141]. 1st generation POEs (or POE I) are obtained upon transesterification of a diol together with diethoxytetrahydrofuran. POE II (2nd generation) were developed to avoid the release of acidic by-products during its degradation (as occurring in POE I). Such materials are obtained by reacting diols with diketene acetal 3,9-bis(ethylidene 2,4,8,10-tetraoxaspiro[5,5]undecane). POE III (3rd generation) could be obtained upon direct polymerization of a triol together with an orthoester, yielding a highly mechanically flexible gel-like material. Finally, 4th generation POEs (POE IV, Fig. 2) were developed to solve the up-scaling difficulties of POE III and, similarly to POE II, they can be obtained by incorporating soft segments based on LA and GA into the chain backbone. Although generally speaking POE IV show weak mechanical properties, their good biodegradability has boosted their use in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications [142]. This last group of POE presents a scalable synthetic procedure and has the highest versatility as their properties could be tuned by properly selecting the nature of diols and the amount of LA or GA in the main chain [141], [143], [144]. Thus, depending on the flexibility of the diol chain, a wide variety of thermo-mechanical properties can be achieved; from hard, glassy materials showing a high glass transition temperature to semi-solid polymers showing low glass transition temperature. As polyesters usually display rather brittle mechanical behaviour which is not adequate for some biomedical applications, novel elastomeric biodegradable polyesters such as poly(diol citrates) and poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) have been synthesized for soft tissue engineering applications (Fig. 2) [145], [146]. Poly(diol citrates) can be synthesized via polycondensation reactions using non-toxic and inexpensive monomers, such as citric acid. Besides, considering the availability of various diols with different chain flexibility, biodegradable elastomers with tuneable mechanical properties can be obtained through relatively simple synthesis procedures. In this sense, a series of poly(diol citrates) were synthesized by reacting citric acid with various diols: poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC) and poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) [147]. All the synthesized polymers were totally amorphous and displayed low Tg ranging from −5 to 10 °C. Regarding the mechanical properties, which are summarized in Table 5, all the poly(diol citrates) displayed an elastomeric behaviour with no permanent deformation. Moreover, these mechanical properties were finely adjusted, not only by the selected diol, but also through cross-link density, by adjusting the post-polymerization temperature and time [148]. Similar to the poly(alkylene dicarboxylate)s based on dicarboxylic acids and dihydroxy compounds analysed in the previous section, polymers based on glycerol can also be synthesized, being PGS the most studied one within this category. The first polymerization of PGS was reported in 2002 through polycondensation reaction of equimolar ratios of glycerol and sebacic acid reacted at 120 °C in the absence of a catalyst under inert conditions [145]. Owing to its physico-mechanical properties and easy of synthesis, these non-toxic polyesters show a huge potential for developing inexpensive and biodegradable elastomeric materials for tissue engineering applications [146]. The thermo-mechanical properties of PGS, which have been recently reviewed by Rai et al. [149], can be adjusted by varying the glycerol to sebacic acid ratio, curing temperature and time. In general, this thermoset polymer shows a Tg at around −37 °C. Regarding its mechanical properties, it shows elastomeric behaviour with elastic modulus ranging from 0.025 to 1.2 MPa, ultimate tensile strength >0.5 MPa and elongation at break >330%. Poly(propylene fumarate) (PPF), depicted in Fig. 2, is another type of linear polyester. It has an unsaturated linear structure and could be obtained via a transesterification reaction of fumaric diester [150]. Thanks to the presence of fumarate double groups in its main backbone, PPF shows a unique property to form crosslinked structures [151], resulting in higher mechanical strength material that can be employed as an injectable material as bone cement [152]. Overall, the physico-mechanical properties of PPF are mainly dependant on the molecular weight and crosslinking. For example, the compressive strengths and modulus of PPF samples crosslinked with biocompatible poly(ethylene glycol)-dimethacrylate (PEG-DMA) increased from 5.9 to 11.2 MPa and from 30.2 to 58.4 MPa, respectively, when the double-bond ratio of PEG-DMA/PPF increased from 0.38 to 1.88 [153]. In a different study [154], where PPF-diacrylate was employed as a crosslinking agent, compressive modulus up to 1.7 GPa were reported.

Because of its special qualities, elastomers-a type of polymer with a low modulus and high elasticity-can rapidly return to their initial form following the removal of an external force. Because of these qualities, they are indispensable in both daily life and the economy [1,2,3,4]. Elastomers have been the subject of ongoing research and development to improve their strength, stability, aging resistance, and wear resistance in order to fulfill the ever-increasing performance requirements. However, these advantages make it harder to dispose of the waste products made from conventional elastomers, which pollutes the environment over time [5, 6]. However, the majority of elastomers are derived from poorly sustainable non-renewable fossil fuels. The creation of novel elastomers that are not dependent on fossil fuels has become highly demanded in recent times due to the immense strain imposed by carbon emissions. Bio-based elastomers are a great way to reduce carbon emissions and conserve resources in the elastomer sector since they may be made from natural plants directly or by synthesizing them from bio-based monomers produced from biomass resources. Due to excellent biodegradability, aliphatic polyester became a prominent area of research for environmentally-friendly products. Linear polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), polyglycolide acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and their copolymers, have been extensively studied in the field of plastic for many years. And their industrial production is seeing tremendous growth [7,8,9]. Polyesters having a three-dimensional network have gained increasing interest, motivated by these linear polymers [10, 11]. Like vulcanized rubber, the cross-linked network is formed by the incorporation of "star" monomers to create multi-branched chains, enabling the material to rapidly regain its shape when subjected to substantial deformation. Poly (glycerol sebacate) (PGS), polyoctyl citrate (POC), and their copolymers are the primary biodegradable polyester elastomers that have undergone substantial research. The pioneering work is the synthesis of PGS, an in-situ cross-linked polyester elastomer with a three-dimensional network structure and exceptional robustness, conducted by Langer et al. successfully synthesized in 2002 [10, 12]. In 2011, Zhang et al. firstly introduced chemically crosslinked polyester elastomer [13]. Subsequently, many other bio-based elastomers have been created [14, 15]. It is well known that monomers of longer chain are easier to be synthesized to be polyester with higher stability, due to the lower density of ester linkage. For example, PCL and PBS are commercially mature materials, which employ 4- or 6- carbon chain monomer [16], while polyglycolide acid (PGA) with 2-carbon monomer is unstable to hydrolysis and its commercial application is very limited [17]. However, on the other hand, when the goal of our research is to obtain elastomers, the high crystallinity and rigidity due to longer chains becomes a disadvantage. Hereby a technical difficulty arises, how to construct biodegradable polyester with decent stability, cross-linkage network, and sufficient elasticity? That is, we probably need longer chain monomers, multi-functional “star” monomer, and some component to lower the crystallinity.

The rapid development of polymer materials has greatly enhanced our daily lives. However, the widespread use of these products has led to significant environmental pollution due to discarded polymers. Biodegradable polymers are a specific type of polymer that can be broken down and decomposed by microorganisms or their secretions under suitable and demonstrable natural environmental conditions.[1, 2] This degradation process results in a decrease in molecular weight, as well as changes in physical and chemical properties, ultimately leading to the formation of small molecules such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). Biodegradable elastomers, in particular, offer notable advantages in clinical applications and have been extensively used in biomedical fields, including drug delivery systems,[3, 4] repair materials,[5, 6] surgical sutures,[7] tissue scaffolds,[8, 9] and implantable devices.[10, 11] Since many tissues and organs in the human body are elastic, these elastomers must provide excellent flexibility and compatibility with the corresponding tissues.[12, 13] Additionally, biodegradable elastomers need to endure repeated tensile recovery without losing mechanical properties or causing irritation to the surrounding tissues.[2, 14] Poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC) is a notable biodegradable elastomer that has gained significant attention in materials science and biomedical engineering in recent years.[15-18] It offers a combination of excellent properties, including good elasticity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility.[16, 19] These characteristics provide new opportunities to overcome the limitations of traditional materials, especially in sustainable development and biomedical applications.[15, 20] POC elastomer is a copolymer synthesized through the condensation reaction of 1,8-octanediol and citric acid.[19] The 1,8-octanediol is a water-soluble and nontoxic aliphatic diol that contributes a flexible, long-chain structure, giving the material its flexibility and elasticity.[21] Meanwhile, citric acid introduces multiple carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, which not only participate in the polymerization process but also significantly influence the material's hydrophilicity, biodegradability, and interaction with biomolecules.[22] POC elastomers exhibit excellent elastic recovery due to the chemical cross-linking network, allowing them to quickly return to their original shape after being stretched by external forces. Poly(ortho esters) (POEs) are a group of biodegradable polyesters that were firstly synthesized in the 1970s by the ALZA Corporation in order to develop materials that may potentially undergo surface erosion degradation process, which is not commonly found in biodegradable polyesters [138], [139]. The high hydrophobicity provided by the orthoesther linkages ensures that the degradation proceeds faster than the H2O diffusion into the material. POEs are synthesized by using diols having different chain flexibility. Till the date, four types of these surface eroding materials have been reported [140], [141]. 1st generation POEs (or POE I) are obtained upon transesterification of a diol together with diethoxytetrahydrofuran. POE II (2nd generation) were developed to avoid the release of acidic by-products during its degradation (as occurring in POE I). Such materials are obtained by reacting diols with diketene acetal 3,9-bis(ethylidene 2,4,8,10-tetraoxaspiro[5,5]undecane). POE III (3rd generation) could be obtained upon direct polymerization of a triol together with an orthoester, yielding a highly mechanically flexible gel-like material. Finally, 4th generation POEs (POE IV, Fig. 2) were developed to solve the up-scaling difficulties of POE III and, similarly to POE II, they can be obtained by incorporating soft segments based on LA and GA into the chain backbone. Although generally speaking POE IV show weak mechanical properties, their good biodegradability has boosted their use in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications [142]. This last group of POE presents a scalable synthetic procedure and has the highest versatility as their properties could be tuned by properly selecting the nature of diols and the amount of LA or GA in the main chain [141], [143], [144]. Thus, depending on the flexibility of the diol chain, a wide variety of thermo-mechanical properties can be achieved; from hard, glassy materials showing a high glass transition temperature to semi-solid polymers showing low glass transition temperature. Poly(diol citrates) can be synthesized via polycondensation reactions using non-toxic and inexpensive monomers, such as citric acid. Besides, considering the availability of various diols with different chain flexibility, biodegradable elastomers with tuneable mechanical properties can be obtained through relatively simple synthesis procedures. In this sense, a series of poly(diol citrates) were synthesized by reacting citric acid with various diols: poly(1,6-hexanediol-co-citrate) (PHC), poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC), poly(1,10-decanediol-co-citrate) (PDC) and poly(1,12-dodecanediol-co-citrate) (PDDC) [147]. Thanks to the presence of fumarate double groups in its main backbone, PPF shows a unique property to form crosslinked structures [151], resulting in higher mechanical strength material that can be employed as an injectable material as bone cement [152]. For example, the compressive strengths and modulus of PPF samples crosslinked with biocompatible poly(ethylene glycol)-dimethacrylate (PEG-DMA) increased from 5.9 to 11.2 MPa and from 30.2 to 58.4 MPa, respectively, when the double-bond ratio of PEG-DMA/PPF increased from 0.38 to 1.88 [153]. Polydioxanone (PDO, PDS) undergoes hydrolytic degradation through a combination of both surface and bulk erosion mechanisms. When degraded in aqueous buffer solution (pH:7.4) at 37 °C, PDO films show a mass loss of ~50% after 270 days [293], which can be accelerated to yield a mass loss of ~50% after 50 days by increasing the surface area of the material [261]. A pH drop from 7.40 to 5.64 after 10 weeks was observed, suggesting the release of acidic by-products to the degrading medium (the resulting glyoxylic acid (pKa = 3.3) can be excreted in the urine or converted into glycine and then into CO2 and H2O by the human body) [261]. Poly(ortho ester)s are hydrophobic polyesters having hydrolytically labile linkages that undergo through surface erosion degradation. POEs display a degradation profile that could be easily tuned by controlling the pH of the degrading medium by using acidic or basic excipients [141]. The hydrolytic degradation of POE I yields the initial diol and γ-butyrolactone as a by-product, which is further hydrolyzed to 4-hydroxybutanoic acid. To avoid the autocatalytic behaviour during the degradation of POE I, POE II was developed, which yields neutral products as a by-product (which include pentaerythritol dipropionate and the diol) [5]. The degradation rate of this polymer can be modulated by adding acid excipient such as itaconic and adipic acids. POE III yields 5-flurouracil, acetic acid and 1,2,6-hexanetriol. POE IV yields LA or GA which further autocatalize the degradation, which can be tuned by the proportion of glycolic or lactic acid in the sequence to last from days to months [197]. Overall, as a segment having a carboxylic acid end-group initially catalyzed the ortho ester hydrolysis to generate a diol (or a mixture of them), the hydrolytic degradation profile of POEs can be tuned upon controlling the ratio of the diol to the latent acid in the backbone [141]. Segmented poly(ester amide)s (PEAs) consisting on amide blocks linked to amorphous polyester matrix display tuneable mechanical, thermal and degradation properties depending on their hard-to-soft ratio [133]. The scission of ester bonds result in the formation of water-soluble and non-toxic bisamide-diol monomers/oligomers which can be excreted by the kidneys [262]. In this line, Lips et al. thoroughly studied the in vitro and in vivo degradation of aliphatic poly(ester amide)s comprising 1,4‐butanediol/dimethyl adipate and dimethyl adipate/ε‐caprolactone/1,4‐diaminobutane or 1,2‐diaminoethane [133]. Degradation tests carried out in PBS at 37 °C (0.03 wt% sodium azide as antibacterial agent) showed a weight loss of ~ 3% (depending on the composition) after 7 months. Results suggested that the degradation takes place via ester bond cleavage with a bulk degradation process. The degradation of polyesters containing below 50% amide content showed no cytotoxic response, while the sample having 50% of amide content resulted in mild undesired body reactions. Due to these inherent characteristics, PEAs emerge as perfect candidates for long-term biomedical implants as they offer tuneable degradation rate (the degradation is favoured with the ester content) with lower pH drop in comparison with more widely used polyesters [264]. As poly(propylene fumarate) (PPF) is usually crosslinked to obtain polymer networks, it is difficult to find the time required for the hydrolytic degradation of neat PPF. A slow degradation rate with a mass loss of 22% after 70 days in PBS solution at 37 °C was found (bulk degradation process) [265], yielding fumaric acid (pKa = 4.4) and propylene glycol (pKa = 14.9) as a by-product [266]. As a combination of these two by-products, medium pH remains unchanged (±0.1) upon degradation [267], which is in contrast with the pH decrease suffered by the medium degrading other polyesters. Poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) is other interesting biodegradable polyester which shows a surface erosion mechanism [268]. Agitation for 60 days in PBS solution at 37 °C yields a weight loss of 17%, while the in vivo degradation is much faster in comparison with in vitro conditions [145]. The degradation rate of PGS could be varied by modifying processing parameters; i.e., when PGS is synthesized at 110 °C it shows a fast degradation, while a negligible degradation was observed when synthesized at 130 °C [146]. Degradation products are non-toxic as sebacic acid is the natural metabolic intermediate in ω-oxidation of medium- to long-chain fatty acids and glycerol has been approved by the FDA to be used as humectant in foods [149]. This fact emphasizes the need of comprehensive works aimed at determining the end-of-life of furanic aliphatic/aromatic polyesters.

Hereby a technical difficulty arises, how to construct biodegradable polyester with decent stability, cross-linkage network, and sufficient elasticity? That is, we probably need longer chain monomers, multi-functional “star” monomer, and some component to lower the crystallinity.

The rapid development of polymer materials has greatly enhanced our daily lives. However, the widespread use of these products has led to significant environmental pollution due to discarded polymers. Biodegradable polymers are a specific type of polymer that can be broken down and decomposed by microorganisms or their secretions under suitable and demonstrable natural environmental conditions.[1, 2] This degradation process results in a decrease in molecular weight, as well as changes in physical and chemical properties, ultimately leading to the formation of small molecules such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). Biodegradable elastomers, in particular, offer notable advantages in clinical applications and have been extensively used in biomedical fields, including drug delivery systems,[3, 4] repair materials,[5, 6] surgical sutures,[7] tissue scaffolds,[8, 9] and implantable devices.[10, 11] Since many tissues and organs in the human body are elastic, these elastomers must provide excellent flexibility and compatibility with the corresponding tissues.[12, 13] Additionally, biodegradable elastomers need to endure repeated tensile recovery without losing mechanical properties or causing irritation to the surrounding tissues.[2, 14] Poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) (POC) is a notable biodegradable elastomer that has gained significant attention in materials science and biomedical engineering in recent years.[15-18] It offers a combination of excellent properties, including good elasticity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility.[16, 19] These characteristics provide new opportunities to overcome the limitations of traditional materials, especially in sustainable development and biomedical applications.[15, 20] POC elastomer is a copolymer synthesized through the condensation reaction of 1,8-octanediol and citric acid.[19] The 1,8-octanediol is a water-soluble and nontoxic aliphatic diol that contributes a flexible, long-chain structure, giving the material its flexibility and elasticity.[21] Meanwhile, citric acid introduces multiple carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, which not only participate in the polymerization process but also significantly influence the material's hydrophilicity, biodegradability, and interaction with biomolecules.[22] POC elastomers exhibit excellent elastic recovery due to the chemical cross-linking network, allowing them to quickly return to their original shape after being stretched by external forces. By optimizing the synthesis process and adjusting the monomer ratio, their tensile strength can be enhanced to meet the basic strength requirements for various practical applications.[19] Furthermore, POC can be prepared under mild conditions without the addition of toxic catalysts and cross-linkers, which offers significant advantages over other biodegradable bioelastomers.[19] Numerous cell experiments have demonstrated that POC elastomers exhibit good compatibility with various cell lines and show minimal cytotoxicity.[15, 17] When designing scaffolds for cartilage tissue engineering, POC elastomers effectively mimic the mechanical properties of natural cartilage, creating an optimal microenvironment for the growth and proliferation of chondrocytes. As a result, POC elastomers have emerged as one of the ideal materials for tissue engineering scaffolds, thanks for their outstanding elasticity, biodegradability, and biocompatibility.[23] Delara et al. investigated the use of POC as a material for artificial blood vessel for transplanting human arterial endothelial cells.[24] They found that POC exhibits excellent compatibility with blood, indicating its potential to serve as a replacement for blood vessels in the human body. In the treating cardiovascular diseases, POC elastomers can be utilized to create biodegradable materials for cardiovascular interventions, such as vascular stents. These stents provide support to the walls of blood vessels and help restore vascular patency after implantation. Additionally, POC elastomers can serve as versatile substrate materials for flexible sensors and wearable electronic devices.[12, 25] Their high elasticity and remarkable flexibility ensure that these devices perform optimally, even when subjected to bending or stretching. For example, encapsulating devices with POC elastomers can enhance their mechanical and electrochemical stability, making them more resilient to the deformations caused by repeated stretching.[26] Although POC has several advantages, including ease of processing, excellent biocompatibility, and non-toxicity, it is limited by poor mechanical properties, particularly low elongation at break due to dense chemical cross-linking. To address these challenges, numerous studies have focused on improving its mechanical and chemical properties through copolymerization or physical blending.[27-33] Notably, the copolymerization strategy offers the benefits of adjustable molecular chain structures and enhanced compatibility. For instance, silica-based monomers or sols have been incorporated into POC to improve tensile strength, modulus, and elongation at break. One example is the addition of polysilsesquioxane sols to the POC prepolymer, which are cross-linked during a thermal curing process. This addition improves the thermomechanical properties and chemical resistance of the POC elastomer.[34] In another study, Yang et al. developed a biodegradable elastomer known as poly(octamethylene maleate (anhydride) citrate) (POMaC) using citric acid, maleic anhydride, and 1,8-octanediol. POMaC possesses dual networks of carbon-carbon cross-linking and ester bond cross-linking. It demonstrates excellent biocompatibility with cells and tissues, as well as mechanical properties that are comparable to those of soft biological tissues.[35]
