Improving the impact strength of PLA by direct mechanical blending with inexpensive non-degradable polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide), poly(vinyl acetate), polyisoprene, acrylonitrile/butadiene/styrene copolymer, and polyethylene has successfully reduced cost and expanded its commercial applications.7, 10 However, the majority of these blends require compatibilizers to improve the miscibility between the impact modifier and the PLA. Therefore, using a commercially cost-effective impact modifier which is compatible with PLA would produce greater advantages. In response to this challenge, DuPont Packaging and Industrial Polymers has introduced Biomax strong 100®. This is a petroleum-based ethylene/acrylate copolymer (EAC) for commercial applications, noted as compatible with PLA and maintains its biodegradability at low concentrations.14 The feasibility of using this EAC as an impact modifier has been explored in a few studies and reported in literature. One study produced and analyzed not only PLA blend films with either Sukano PLA im S550 or EAC as additives for tensile properties and clarity but also correlated these properties to their micro-structures. EAC at a loading rate of 12% resulted in elongation at break of 255%, a significant improvement over that of neat PLA with about 90%.15 Another study reported the use of EAC as an impact modifier for neat PLA and highly filled PLA/calcium sulfate composites.16 Addition of 5-10% EAC into highly filled composites (30-40% of filler) led to a threefold increase of impact strength as compared to the compositions without the modifier.16 However, these studies failed to extensively account for the more subtle considerations of this impact modifier on different grades of PLA (effectiveness) and concentrations of impact modifier (efficiency)17 as well as providing detailed fracture mechanisms of impact modified PLA samples tested under various environmental conditions.
Although the commercial PLA and PHAs are intensively studied as alternatives for the petroleum-based plastics, they have not gained desirably widespread usage in human life because of their high cost and performance deficiency. For the stiff PLA, poor flexibility and toughness is the key obstacle for its wide application.5 Besides, PLA is also greatly limited in high temperature applications scenarios because of its poor crystallization ability. Its heat deflection temperature is determined by its glass transition temperature (only at 50-60°C). These physical shortcomings combining with its high cost greatly hinder the widespread applications of PLA. As for PHAs, most of them usually show extremely poor thermal processability and brittleness. Especially for the commercially available PHB and PHBV, the narrow processing window and low impact strength greatly limit their widely practical applications. To reduce the cost and improve the performance of PLA and PHAs, researchers have adopted various modification methods, including chemical copolymerization and physical blending strategies, and so forth. Owing to the advantages of simple operation, low cost and easy mass production, melt-blending approach has become the most popular and commonly used method to prepare high-performance PLA or PHAs based materials.9 Especially in recent years, multiphase blending strategy has attracted tremendous attention in development new high-performance biobased polymer materials. Compared with the simple binary blending method, the multiphase-blending approach usually shows better compatibility and more balanced physical properties through elaborately selecting the components with complementary properties.10, 11 Among the toughening blending components, flexible biobased polyesters,12-14 have aroused intensive interests because of their eco-friendly advantages. For instance, Mohanty et al.15 have reported fully renewable ternary blends from PHBV, PLA, and PBS with good performances owing to the complementary properties of the components. Whereafter, they also have extended the multiphase blending strategy to other bioplastics systems.16, 17 Favis et al.18 have systemically studied a series of biobased polyesters multiphase blends and made great contribution for understanding the phase structure. Recently, we also studied renewable copolymerized epichlorohydrin-ethylene oxide rubber as toughening agent for renewable PLA and P34HB blends through the melt processing method.19 However, several main challenges still greatly limited effectiveness of the multiphase blending strategy for the bio-polyesters blends. One problem is the poor miscibility of PLA or PHAs with other biobased polyesters, which was pursued to be resolved by adding copolymer compatibilizer or reactive compatibilization.11, 20-22 However, these compatibilizing methods usually are complicated, resulting in further increasing the cost. Another key challenge for the multiphase biobased polyesters blends is that there are too few flexible biobased polyesters species commercially available in the market. It is extremely difficult to obtain suitable components for the melting processing blend. These challenges greatly limit our deeply understanding on the structure- property relationship of the multiphase biobased plastic blends. Poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), a flexible and completely biodegradable polyester produced by the catalytic polymerization of propylene oxide (PO) and CO2 as monomers, is another important and environmentally friendly polyester in the market. Since using CO2 resources as the monomer, widely applying PPC can greatly contribute to resolving the global warming challenge by alleviating greenhouse effect. Moreover, due to its interesting features of good biodegradability, biocompatibility and excellent barrier effect on oxygen and water, PPC exhibits wide promising application prospects, including biodegradable packaging films, reactive hot-melt adhesives for plastics, thermoplastic polyurethane adhesives, and biomedical materials.23-26 Different with the other polyesters, PPC has ether bonds in its main chain, which makes it be very flexible with poor strength and excellent tensile toughness.27 These properties of PPC felicitously complement with the high strength and brittleness of PLA and PHAs such as PHB and PHBV. Blending PPC with PLA and PHAs will not only improve the ductility of PLA and PHAs, but also modify PPC's own defects such as low stiffness and poor thermal stability.20, 21 From the above description, we can learn that PLA, PPC and PHAs are the most promising candidates to develop multiphase biobased materials with desirable performance for the low-carbon and sustainable development. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, there is seldom report on ternary blends from PPC, PHAs, and PLA.28 Considering the good complementary properties of PLA, PPC, and PHAs components, it is very necessary to systematically study the multiphase blend from PLA, PPC, and the PHAs family to deeply understand the phase behavior and property relationship. In present work, we prepared a ternary blend of PLA, PPC, and PHAs with different chemical chain structures by the cost-effective melt-blending method to obtain a fully sustainable and toughened multiphase biobased polyesters blends with a good balance of properties. The compatibility, phase structure, thermal, and mechanical properties of the ternary blends were thoroughly analyzed by varying the composition and species of the PHAs to figure out the structure-property relationship.
Although PLA possesses good characteristics and can be molded with standard polymer processing equipments,[5] it shows certain drawbacks, primarily related to its thermal and mechanical properties, which limit its production and use in different applications.[1] PLA has a low glass transition temperature (Tg) (55-60 °C) and crystallization rate, limiting the usage of PLA to applications with relatively low service temperatures.[1, 4, 6, 7] On the other hand, PLA also suffers from inherent brittleness and a very low toughness at room temperature. Hence, the use of PLA may be limited in applications where high elongation or plastic deformation at high impact rates are required.[8, 9] A widespread and cost-effective method to overcome the drawback of the mechanical properties is to blend PLA with ductile polymers.[7, 10] Poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is a ductile semicrystalline aliphatic polyester, with Tg and Tm ≈−60 °C and 55-70 °C, respectively.[1, 11] Although it is a nonbiobased polymer, PCL is biodegradable and biocompatible, as well as PLA. These characteristics make PCL a suitable candidate to be blended with PLA since biodegradability and biocompatibility will be maintained.[1, 11] Due to its low Tg, PCL exhibits high elongation at break (≈600%[8]) and toughness. Therefore, adding PCL to PLA as a secondary phase could improve the ductility and toughness of PLA.[1] In general, elongation at break of PLA has been easily enhanced (85-400%) by melt blending it with PCL,[12-18] even if, in some cases, poor or no increment has also been reported.[19-23] However, owing to the immiscibility between both polymers, improving the impact toughness of PLA/PCL blends is more challenging, though some good attempts have been made in this field. In this sense, it has been proved that the PCL concentration, the crystallinity of the PLA matrix, the PLA/PCL viscosity ratio, and the processing conditions are key factors that need to be optimized to improve the impact strength of PLA.[24-29] Nevertheless, achieving the optimal composition, processing conditions, and morphology is not always possible. That is why, high impact strength values or supertoughness are not usually reported in the literature for PLA/PCL blends.[12-14, 19]
Despite these attractive properties, PLA has relatively few commercial applications, concentrating mainly in textile and specialty biomedical niches such as sutures and drug delivery devices.6, 7 Additionally, it is being used as a commodity polymer for packaging food and consumer goods where the physical properties of PLA make it suitable for manufacture of rigid containers and bottles. However, the widespread applicability of PLA in flexible sheets and films is limited because of its brittleness, lower impact resistance at room temperature, and narrow processing window.1, 5-8 These factors severely hinder its use, particularly in packaging applications where production lines for flexible films cannot tolerate film cracking or tearing when folded or subjected to force during manufacturing.1 Therefore, it is of paramount importance to find a tougher and more ductile variant of the polymer in order to overcome these difficulties and broaden the range of its commercial applications.1, 6, 8 In order to improve the properties of PLA, it is often blended or copolymerized with other materials.9-13 Blending of PLA with a biodegradable second polymer such as poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(caprolactone), poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), polyhydroxyalkanoate, and poly(butylene succinate) has predominantly been used in biomedical applications to maintain bio-compatibility and biodegradability while also improving mechanical properties.8 For example, significant improvement in flexibility (up to 180% elongation at break compared to 4% for neat PLA) and impact resistance (over 200% increase) were obtained with the use of up to 10 wt% low molecular weight PEG.9 However, these additives are relatively costly rendering their PLA blends expensive. Alternatively, the use of inexpensive non-biodegradable polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide), poly(vinyl acetate), polyisopropene, acrylonitrile/butadiene/styrene copolymer, and polyethylene has successfully reduced cost.8 The use of plasticizers such as low molecular weight esters, oligomeric lactic acid, etc., has been investigated to obtain PLA with improved mechanical properties.9, 10 In the case of semicrystalline polymers like PLA, an efficient plasticizer reduces the glass transition temperature (Tg), thereby increasing the flexibility to overcome the difficulties of cracking or tearing, especially in packaging film production lines.10
PLA is a biodegradable polymer sold worldwide on a large scale, estimated to have an annual growth rate of 10% to 15%, while the global plastics market is growing at 3.5% to 4% annually.13 It can be used in many applications, including packaging, household goods, and biomedical parts.14 The versatility of PLA applications is attributed to its good mechanical properties, comparable to polystyrene (PS) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET), including high mechanical strength and elastic modulus.15, 16 In addition, PLA can be processed in conventional polymer industry and additive manufacturing equipment.17, 18 However, PLA has drawbacks, including its high brittleness, degradability during processing in the presence of humidity and high temperatures, and low heat deflection temperature.19, 20 Researchers are trying to improve PLA's mechanical and thermomechanical performance in this context, primarily through polymer blends.21-24 There are scientific reports on the development of PLA blends with ethylene-propylene-diene (EPDM),25, 26 polycaprolactone (PCL),27, 28 polyolefin elastomers,29, 30 poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT),7, 31 poly(butylene succinate) (PBS),32, 33 and natural rubber (NR),34, 35 exploring their mechanical, thermal, rheological, and morphological properties. Although the polymer blends of PLA showed improved impact strength and elongation at break, the main setback has been severe losses in elastic modulus, tensile strength, and heat deflection temperature (HDT). Alternative routes have been investigated to produce PLA blends with higher mechanical and thermomechanical properties,36, 37 enabling their use in applications requiring semi-biodegradable materials with more robust properties. Recently,38-40 engineering polymers have been used to produce PLA-based blends, such as polyamide and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS). Fazli and Rodrigue41 developed PLA/PA 11 blends compatibilized with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO), indicating improvements of 292% and 104 in impact strength and elongation at break, respectively. The authors also noted a slight decrease in the tensile strength of the PLA/PA611/PEO blend (40/40/20 wt%), which indicates a reasonable balance of mechanical properties. One of the strategies largely explored to improve the mechanical properties of PLA-based blends is reactive compatibilization, inducing crosslinking between phases.42 In such cases, organic peroxides are broadly used as free radical initiators for the constituents of polymer blends during molten state processing.43, 44 A vulcanized thermoplastic is formed when two crosslinkable phases react in a polymer blend. The vulcanized thermoplastic has the properties of vulcanized rubber, yet it can be processed like a conventional thermoplastic.45 The crosslinking of PLA-based blends has been significantly explored, mainly using poly (ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) (EVA)43, 46-48 and natural rubber (NR)22, 49, 50 as impact modifiers. However, the incorporation and crosslinking of engineering impact modifiers in PLA have yet to be studied in the scientific literature. Therefore, for the first time in the polymer blend literature, the acrylonitrile-EPDM-styrene (AES) terpolymer will be crosslinked with PLA to tailor its mechanical and thermomechanical properties. AES is broadly used to produce parts for the automotive industry due to its high impact strength, thermal stability, chemical resistance, and photo-oxidative stability.1, 51
Several approaches can be made to enhance the performance and physical properties of PLA such as plasticization, copolymerization and blending. During long-term use, the plasticizers are possible to migrate to the surface of the material, causing brittleness. However, plasticizers are necessary to lower glass transition temperature, increase ductility and improve processability of PLA. Copolymerization is another great choice to improve the properties of PLA, but the process to commercialize a new copolymer is often long and the cost is very high. Thus, it is less practicable to be an option [3]. While blending is a cost-effective method which combines the advantages of different polymers to obtain a material with the desirable properties, significant amount of work has been performed to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of PLA via PLA-based polymer blend composites [4]. Polyhydroxybutyrate-valerate (PHBV) is a type of biodegradable polymers synthesized by fermentation of bacteria or other microorganisms. PHBV has gained a lot of attention due to its remarkable features like good biocompatibility and biodegradability [1]. At very low hydroxy-valerate (HV) content, PHBV is alike to conventional thermoplastics such as polypropylene (PP) in term of crystallinity, mechanical properties and melting temperature [5]. Polyethylene glycols (PEG), which have the general formula of H(OCH2CH2)n OH are liquid or solid polymers. Low molecular weight PEG is in the liquid form, while higher molecular weight PEG is in the solid form at room temperature. PEG is an appropriate plasticizer for PLA due to its miscibility, biodegradability and food contactable application [6].

With the growing concern on petroleum depletion and plastic waste accumulation, polymer researchers are dedicated to developing high performance sustainable polymers for the substitution of traditional petroleum-based nonbiodegradable plastics.1-3 Bioplastics such as polylactide (PLA), polyhydroxy acids (PHAs), and poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) play an important role in addressing the concerns.4 Among them, PLA has led the academic and industry research interest for its biorenewable and compostable at the end-of-life. It is expected that the market of PLA would reach an estimated revenue of $12 billion by 2035 at a growing CAGR of approximately 15.20% globally, finding applications from packaging, mulching film to automotive and electronics.5 However, there are certain obstacles to accept the wide application of PLA in market, such as cost, inadequate thermal-mechanical performance, and lack of large compost site.6 The inadequate mechanical performance is mainly resulted from its low toughness of which the elongation at break (EB) and notched impact strength (IS) of pure PLA is only about 3% and 20 J/m. Therefore, improving the toughness of PLA has long been researched. Different stratagems have been used to toughening the PLA matrix, mainly melt blending,7 plasticization,8 copolymerization, condensed matter structure regulation,9 and nano or microcomposites.10 Different modification methods show different effects and have their unique advantages and disadvantages. For example, melt blending exhibits versatile, low-cost, and simple, which can be widely applied and embraced by the relative industries.7 The development of PLA-based blends is expanding annually, driven by advancements in processing characteristics and cost reduction. The primary objective in researching binary compositions of PLA is to enhance the plasticity and impact properties of PLA products with minimal compromise on strength and elastic modulus.11 However, the natural immiscibility between different phases greatly limits the efficiency of this method, thus normally high contents of second toughening phase need to be incorporated. On the other hand, the added toughening materials are required to be biodegradability so that the biodegradability of PLA will not be affected. Therefore, biodegradable plastics with high toughness such as poly (butylene succinate) (PBS), PBAT, and polycaprolactone (PCL) have been incorporated to improve the toughness of PLA. Basil D. Favis' group has conducted numerous researches on the phase morphology and compatibility of different biodegradable blends.12-15
Despite its eco-friendly advantages, PLA exhibits inherent drawbacks including brittleness [9], low impact resistance, and inferior mechanical strength/toughness [10] relative to petroleum-based plastics. Its thermal instability which is evidenced by decomposition at elevated temperatures and low melt viscosity at low temperatures, restricts high-temperature processing and limit barrier performance [11]. High crystallinity also introduces processing defects (e.g., warping, shrinkage) that compromise product aesthetics and functionality [12]. While modifications like gamma-ray-induced grafting (e.g., PLA-g-PVP composites) can enhance degradation rates and expand medical applications, such strategies often add complexity and cost. These limitations necessitate ongoing research to optimize PLA properties for broader industrial adoption. Heat resistance of PLA is improved through heat stabilizers [13] or cross-linking [14,15], while brittleness is mitigated via plasticizers [16], fillers [17,18], or polymer blending [19,20]. Li et al. [21] achieved PLA toughening using an amphiphilic block copolymer, with optimal micelle dispersion enhancing toughness. Sherwani et al. [22] demonstrated PLA/sugar palm fiber bio-composites (30 wt% fiber) with strong interfacial adhesion via SEM [23,24]. These strategies expand PLA's use in automotive parts [25], high-strength packaging [26], and improve processability via molecular and rheological tuning [27]. This study aims to develop an innovative composite film by integrating PLA, PCL, and TiO2 nanoparticles through physical blending. The ternary system synergistically enhances PLA's mechanical properties, UV resistance, and anti-yellowing performance. Specifically, PCL (a biocompatible and biodegradable polymer) improves rigidity and toughness of PLA by forming a homogeneous composite matrix, thereby optimizing both mechanical strength and processability. Concurrently, TiO2 nanoparticles address UV-related degradation through dual mechanisms: UV shielding via light scattering and reflection, and photocatalytic activity under UV irradiation. The latter generates electron-hole pairs that decompose organic pollutants and inhibit bacterial growth, significantly delaying material aging. The design of this PLA/PCL/TiO2 composite not only overcomes inherent limitations of PLA but also expands its potential applications in environmentally sensitive sectors such as sustainable packaging and biomedical devices. Future research will focus on optimizing material ratios and fabrication processes to further enhance performance and scalability, aligning with global goals for eco-friendly material innovation. The effect of plasticizer on PLA blending was also studied by several researchers. The blending of origin PLA or mixing with other nanofillers produced brittle product. The plasticizer acts as a processing aid in flow improvement, mostly for films and cables. Instead of reducing the ductility, the plasticizer also functions in the mechanical and thermal properties enhancement. Plasticizers work by embedding themselves between the chains of polymers, spacing them apart, and thus, significantly lower the T g for the plastic and makes it softer. A list of ester-like plasticizers for PLA has been studied, such as glucose monoesters, partial fatty acids, citrates, glycerol esters, and dicarboxylic esters [174-180]. Unfortunately, the low molecular weight plasticizers have the problem of migrating, owing to their high mobility within the PLA matrix. Therefore, the high molecular weight plasticizers with low mobility are suitable, such as poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG) [174, 181, 182], poly(propylene) glycol (PPG) [183], and atactic poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (a-PHB) [184]. Besides lowering the T g, they do not crystallize and miscible with PLA. Table 6 shows the recent studies using plasticizers, mostly PEG in PLA blends and their thermal analysis. The choice of plasticizer used as a modifier for PLA is limited by legislative or the applications. On the other hand, the plasticizer has to be biodegradable, non-toxic for food contact (for packaging), and biocompatible (for medical applications). Commonly, the amount of plasticizers that range from 10 to 20 % is required to provide both a substantial reduction of T g of the PLA matrix, and adequate mechanical properties. In environmental issues, the biodegradable or bioresorbable; and non-volatile plasticizer is preferred, with a relatively low molecular weight to produce the desired decrease of the Young’s modulus value. Additionally, the ranging amount between 20 and 30 % of plasticizer in PLA matrix leads to phase separation. It must be remembered that the percentage of plasticizer determines the plasticization of PLA blend.
PLA is a bio-based, biodegradable, and biocompatible polyester, which has strength and elastic modulus comparable to those of conventional petroleum-based polymers such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) and polystyrene [1]. PLA has attracted increasing attention in recent years as the environmentally benign and biomedical materials usable for agriculture, automobile, diary commodities, tissue engineering and controlled drug delivery etc. [2]. However, it exhibits brittle fracture behavior. It has also a low heat distortion temperature due to the low glass transition temperature (T g) (ca. 60 °C), and no back-up of the elastic modulus above T g due to a low rate of crystallization. Therefore, a great deal of efforts has been made to modify the properties of PLA in both industry and academia [3, 4]. Melt blending of PLA with some flexible biodegradable polyesters, such as poly(butylene succinate) [5-7], poly(butylene succinate-co-L-lactate) [8, 9], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [10-14] and poly(butylene adipapte-co-terephthalate) [15, 16] is an effective way to improve the ductility of PLA. Unfortunately, all the blending inevitably leads to a dramatic deterioration in originally poor heat resistance of PLA, which is not acceptable for many commercial applications. Interestingly, Oyama found the annealing induced crystallization of PLA matrix for the blends of PLA and poly(ethylene-glycidyl methacrylate) improves both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness [17]. Bai also reported the improvement of both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness for PLA/PCL blend is capable by the control of the PLA matrix crystallization and PCL particle size [18]. On the other hand, PLA-based polymer networks and semi-interpenetrating polymer networks (semi-IPNs) are promising strategies to improve the thermal and mechanical properties of PLA. Koo et al. reported that a crosslinked PLA by UV irradiation exhibits a little higher tan δ peak temperature and a higher toughness by 22.5 % in spite of a little lower elongation at break than PLA [19]. He et al. reported tough semi-IPNs composed of PLA and the crosslinked polyurethane prepared by reacting 4,4’-methylenediphenyl diisocyanate with poly(ethylene glycol) and glycerol [20]. In the past studies, simultaneous improvements of T g, toughness and ductility for the PLA-based polymer network and semi-IPNs compared with those of PLA have not been accomplished.

In this study, a biocomposite was developed as a promising sustainable alternative to traditional fossil-based plastics, designed for both flexible and rigid packaging applications. The composite featured bio-based, renewable, and biodegradable ingredients, which are, PLA, a plasticizer derived from vegetable oils, and tomato by-products from the agri-food industry. The material was successfully produced by extrusion and subsequently processed by 3D printing and hot-pressing to make a prototype. The characterization results confirmed the suitability of POMOPLA2 for applications within the food packaging sector, both rigid (POMOPLA2-20) and flexible (POMOPLA2-5), offering a good compromise between mechanical, thermal, and transparency properties. As expected, adding the plasticizer improved PLA's flexibility and toughness, making it suitable for industrial applications requiring high elongation, such as flexible food packaging. However, LABD shows limited compatibility with PLA, as observed in the SEM images for LABD content > 5% w/w. At the same time, the incorporation of the TPs added lightness and helped to reduce the cost of neat PLA from an estimate of 2.44 €/kg to about 1.85 €/kg, with economic savings of up to 25%. In conclusion, POMOPLA2 could represent a cost-effective alternative for companies, closer to the standard costs of PP, PE, and PET-approximately 1.04, 1.21, and 1.04 €/kg, respectively, as reported by GRANTA EduPack v.2022 software. From the environmental point of view, POMOPLA2 reduces the need for virgin PLA, minimizes agricultural waste, and temporarily stores carbon emissions, thereby delaying CO₂ release. This material accelerates biodegradation, lessens environmental impact during disposal, and supports circular economy principles. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Interesting and cheap ways to improve PLA properties are based on elastomeric polymers addition. The validity of this way is justified also by considering that the addition of appropriate elastomers to non-biodegradable polymers and polymer blends proved to increase properties such as, for instance, impact strength and elongation at break.11-13 Nijenhuis et al.14 investigated the miscibility and the mechanical properties of PLA/poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) blends, finding significant increases of elongation at break upon increasing PEO amount, but also some reduction of the tensile strength. Anderson et al.15 prepared PLA/linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE) blends, finding that LLDPE enhanced impact strength, even though semicrystalline PLA should be used instead of amorphous one. Piorkowska et al.16 studied the influence of poly(propylene glycol) (PPG) on PLA. This polymer had plasticizing effects and significantly reduced Tg and elastic modulus, while elongation at break was greatly increased. On the other hand, it showed a strong tendency to phase separation (higher upon increasing the molecular weight).
Some researchers prepared nanocomposites based on PLA and nanofillers such as montmorillonite or calcium carbonate.1, 4-6 It was found that the nanocomposites had higher thermal stability and the nanofiller acted as nucleating agent; the use of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) significantly facilitated intercalation. Calcium carbonate and organomodified clay nanocomposites showed different impact breaking mechanisms: the former broke by crazing (due to microvoids), while the latter by shear yielding. Some papers are also available on blends based on PLA and other biodegradable polymers. Lopez-Rodriguez et al.7 studied crystallization behavior, morphology and mechanical properties of PLA/polycaprolactone blends. PCL showed poor compatibility with PLA throughout all the composition range investigated and influenced also PLA crystallization. Shibata et al.8 investigated mechanical properties, morphology and crystallization of poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA)/poly(butylene succinate) and PLLA/poly[(butylene succinate)-co-lactide] blends. None of the blends showed miscibility but, on the contrary, clear phase separation as testified by formation of microdomains. Other researchers prepared blends of PLA and other biodegradable polymers such as poly(butylene adipate terephtalate) (PBAT) and polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA).9, 10 In the former, reductions of elastic modulus and of tensile strength were observed, while impact strength significantly increased; in the latter, significant enhancements of the global mechanical properties were found. Toughened PLA blends show lower melt viscosity and easier mold-release than neat PLA. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is a biodegradable and compostable aliphatic polyester produced from renewable resources such as dextrose [1]. Its high modulus and tensile strength, comparable to commodity polystyrene, make PLA a promising alternative to petroleum-based polymers. In the past application of PLA was limited to the biomedical field as a result of its high manufacturing cost. Nowadays the surcharge of PLA verses poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is small enough (15-25%) to allow its use in packaging and other consumer applications. [2,3] However, pristine PLA is inherently brittle under ambient conditions. Various strategies have been developed to toughen PLA, including copolymerization, plasticization, blending with flexible polymers and addition of rigid fillers [3]. Immiscible blends of PLA with other rubbery polymers are extensively studied and used because of their facile fabrication and low cost. However, one common drawback of immiscible blends is the loss of transparency, eliminating them from many applications where optical appearance is essential. This deficiency results from the fact that when dispersed in the PLA matrix, the secondary phase typically forms micron-sized domains. To address this limitation, two approaches are usually adopted: (i) use of a secondary phase with a refractive index close to PLA; (ii) dispersion of the secondary phase into small enough domains to eliminate light scattering. This work aims to prepare tough and optically clear PLA blends, utilizing a series of Pluronic® (BASF) compounds as the dispersed secondary phase. These additives are commercially viable poly(ethylene oxide)-poly(propylene oxide)-poly(ethylene oxide) triblock copolymers (referred to as EPE in the following text) that have a refractive index matched with PLA. We have carried out a systematic investigation to understand the role of the molecular architecture of these triblocks with respect to their morphological and mechanical property consequences in PLA blends. Polyethylene oxide (PEO) is a semi-crystalline polyether and is partially miscible with PLA. Its miscibility decreases with increasing molecular weight [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. In PLA/PEO blends, phase separation occurs when the PEO polymer exceeds a certain concentration threshold depending on its molecular weight and the mixing temperature. PLA blends modified with short PEO chains typically exhibit good ductility owing to their plasticization effect. However, the crystallization of both PEO and PLA tends to drive phase separation, reducing ductility. Moreover, because PEO is water-soluble, leaching of PEO from the blend during contact with water limits the applications [8].
Historically, the high cost of PLA production limited its use to the specialty biomedical niches such as sutures and drug delivery devices due to its biodegradability and biocompatibility.6 Presently technological innovations have slightly decreased PLA production cost while the recent increasing crude oil and natural gas prices has conversely increased the cost of traditional petroleum derived plastics, enhancing PLA economic competitiveness.6 More recently, PLA has been used as packaging materials for food and consumer goods (transparent bottles, meat trays, bags, films, etc.), with the polymer typically discarded after use. These applications benefit from their ability to decompose relatively quickly in landfill or compost environments. Unfortunately, PLA has not been used extensively beyond these areas due to its brittleness and lower impact resistance at room temperature,1, 2 resulting in splitting and other handling problems during sheet manufacture.8, 10-12 The necessity for improvement in its impact strength and toughness, which would eliminate the processing and handling deficiencies, precedes the possibility for widespread utilization and substitution for commodity plastics. The toughening of PLA includes blending with other polymers,5-7, 9-12 an exceptional method that is industrially relevant.13 Blending of PLA with rubbery polymers, as previously mentioned, has predominantly emphasized biomedical applications, resulting in the use of biodegradable and biocompatible polymers such as poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(ε-caprolactone), poly(ethylene glycol), polyhydroxyalkanoate, and poly(butylene succinate) as second-phase polymers.7, 12 These impact modifying additives are relatively exorbitant rendering their PLA blends expensive. Improving the impact strength of PLA by direct mechanical blending with inexpensive non-degradable polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide), poly(vinyl acetate), polyisoprene, acrylonitrile/butadiene/styrene copolymer, and polyethylene has successfully reduced cost and expanded its commercial applications.7, 10 However, the majority of these blends require compatibilizers to improve the miscibility between the impact modifier and the PLA. Therefore, using a commercially cost-effective impact modifier which is compatible with PLA would produce greater advantages. In response to this challenge, DuPont Packaging and Industrial Polymers has introduced Biomax strong 100®. This is a petroleum-based ethylene/acrylate copolymer (EAC) for commercial applications, noted as compatible with PLA and maintains its biodegradability at low concentrations.14 The feasibility of using this EAC as an impact modifier has been explored in a few studies and reported in literature. One study produced and analyzed not only PLA blend films with either Sukano PLA im S550 or EAC as additives for tensile properties and clarity but also correlated these properties to their micro-structures. EAC at a loading rate of 12% resulted in elongation at break of 255%, a significant improvement over that of neat PLA with about 90%.15 Another study reported the use of EAC as an impact modifier for neat PLA and highly filled PLA/calcium sulfate composites.16 Addition of 5-10% EAC into highly filled composites (30-40% of filler) led to a threefold increase of impact strength as compared to the compositions without the modifier.16 However, these studies failed to extensively account for the more subtle considerations of this impact modifier on different grades of PLA (effectiveness) and concentrations of impact modifier (efficiency)17 as well as providing detailed fracture mechanisms of impact modified PLA samples tested under various environmental conditions.

Although the commercial PLA and PHAs are intensively studied as alternatives for the petroleum-based plastics, they have not gained desirably widespread usage in human life because of their high cost and performance deficiency. For the stiff PLA, poor flexibility and toughness is the key obstacle for its wide application.5 Besides, PLA is also greatly limited in high temperature applications scenarios because of its poor crystallization ability. Its heat deflection temperature is determined by its glass transition temperature (only at 50-60°C). These physical shortcomings combining with its high cost greatly hinder the widespread applications of PLA. As for PHAs, most of them usually show extremely poor thermal processability and brittleness. Especially for the commercially available PHB and PHBV, the narrow processing window and low impact strength greatly limit their widely practical applications. To reduce the cost and improve the performance of PLA and PHAs, researchers have adopted various modification methods, including chemical copolymerization and physical blending strategies, and so forth. Owing to the advantages of simple operation, low cost and easy mass production, melt-blending approach has become the most popular and commonly used method to prepare high-performance PLA or PHAs based materials.9 Especially in recent years, multiphase blending strategy has attracted tremendous attention in development new high-performance biobased polymer materials. Compared with the simple binary blending method, the multiphase-blending approach usually shows better compatibility and more balanced physical properties through elaborately selecting the components with complementary properties.10, 11 Among the toughening blending components, flexible biobased polyesters,12-14 have aroused intensive interests because of their eco-friendly advantages. For instance, Mohanty et al.15 have reported fully renewable ternary blends from PHBV, PLA, and PBS with good performances owing to the complementary properties of the components. Whereafter, they also have extended the multiphase blending strategy to other bioplastics systems.16, 17 Favis et al.18 have systemically studied a series of biobased polyesters multiphase blends and made great contribution for understanding the phase structure. Recently, we also studied renewable copolymerized epichlorohydrin-ethylene oxide rubber as toughening agent for renewable PLA and P34HB blends through the melt processing method.19 However, several main challenges still greatly limited effectiveness of the multiphase blending strategy for the bio-polyesters blends. One problem is the poor miscibility of PLA or PHAs with other biobased polyesters, which was pursued to be resolved by adding copolymer compatibilizer or reactive compatibilization.11, 20-22 However, these compatibilizing methods usually are complicated, resulting in further increasing the cost. Another key challenge for the multiphase biobased polyesters blends is that there are too few flexible biobased polyesters species commercially available in the market. It is extremely difficult to obtain suitable components for the melting processing blend. These challenges greatly limit our deeply understanding on the structure- property relationship of the multiphase biobased plastic blends. Poly(propylene carbonate) (PPC), a flexible and completely biodegradable polyester produced by the catalytic polymerization of propylene oxide (PO) and CO2 as monomers, is another important and environmentally friendly polyester in the market. Since using CO2 resources as the monomer, widely applying PPC can greatly contribute to resolving the global warming challenge by alleviating greenhouse effect. Moreover, due to its interesting features of good biodegradability, biocompatibility and excellent barrier effect on oxygen and water, PPC exhibits wide promising application prospects, including biodegradable packaging films, reactive hot-melt adhesives for plastics, thermoplastic polyurethane adhesives, and biomedical materials.23-26 Different with the other polyesters, PPC has ether bonds in its main chain, which makes it be very flexible with poor strength and excellent tensile toughness.27 These properties of PPC felicitously complement with the high strength and brittleness of PLA and PHAs such as PHB and PHBV. Blending PPC with PLA and PHAs will not only improve the ductility of PLA and PHAs, but also modify PPC's own defects such as low stiffness and poor thermal stability.20, 21 From the above description, we can learn that PLA, PPC and PHAs are the most promising candidates to develop multiphase biobased materials with desirable performance for the low-carbon and sustainable development. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, there is seldom report on ternary blends from PPC, PHAs, and PLA.28 Considering the good complementary properties of PLA, PPC, and PHAs components, it is very necessary to systematically study the multiphase blend from PLA, PPC, and the PHAs family to deeply understand the phase behavior and property relationship. In present work, we prepared a ternary blend of PLA, PPC, and PHAs with different chemical chain structures by the cost-effective melt-blending method to obtain a fully sustainable and toughened multiphase biobased polyesters blends with a good balance of properties. The compatibility, phase structure, thermal, and mechanical properties of the ternary blends were thoroughly analyzed by varying the composition and species of the PHAs to figure out the structure-property relationship.

PLA has several Limitations that affect its broader adoption. One significant drawback is its relatively low thermal resistance; PLA products can deform above 60 °C, limiting their use in high-heat applications. The mechanical properties of PLA, such as brittleness and low impact resistance, also limit its use in applications that require more durable materials. Furthermore, while PLA is biodegradable, its degradation requires specific conditions in industrial composting facilities, such as high temperatures and specific humidity levels [118]. As a result, PLA may not readily break down in natural environments, such as landfills or oceans, posing environmental challenges if not correctly disposed of. Lastly, PLA’s production cost remains higher than that of conventional plastics, which can be a barrier to its widespread use despite the growing emphasis on sustainability. Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are biodegradable polymers (Fig. 3) produced through microbial fermentation, where microorganisms synthesize these biopolymers from organic carbon sources as a form of intracellular energy storage. PHAs possess various properties, including biocompatibility and non-toxicity, as well as mechanical characteristics similar to those of conventional plastics, such as polypropylene [62]. They exhibit high melting points, typically ranging from 50 °C to 180 °C depending on the specific type, and offer good resistance to moisture and chemicals. The flexibility, elasticity, and mechanical strength of PHAs can be tailored by adjusting the polymer composition, Making them suitable for a wide range of applications. While PHAs are biodegradable, their degradation rates vary; under industrial composting conditions, they can degrade within a few months, but degradation can take significantly longer in natural environments. Furthermore, PHAs typically have lower thermal stability, with degradation beginning at temperatures as low as 100 °C. Despite these limitations, research continues to improve the production efficiency and properties of PHAs, to expand their commercial and industrial applications. Starch-based plastics are biodegradable materials derived from natural starch, a polysaccharide (Fig. 3) in plants such as corn, potatoes, and wheat. These plastics are created by processing starch into thermoplastic starch (TPS) or by blending it with other biodegradable polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) or polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) [4]. Starch-based plastics possess several key properties that Make them attractive in multiple industries. They are biodegradable, breaking down into non-toxic components such as carbon dioxide, water, and biomass under appropriate conditions. For instance, under composting conditions, starch-based films can degrade by 90% within six months. They also exhibit good mechanical properties, including tensile strength ranging from 10 to 50 MPa and elongation at break varying from 20 to 100%, depending on the specific formulation and the type of starch used. The applications of starch-based plastics are diverse, including packaging materials such as bags, films, and containers, which benefit from their biodegradability [4].
Although PLA possesses good characteristics and can be molded with standard polymer processing equipments,[5] it shows certain drawbacks, primarily related to its thermal and mechanical properties, which limit its production and use in different applications.[1] PLA has a low glass transition temperature (Tg) (55-60 °C) and crystallization rate, limiting the usage of PLA to applications with relatively low service temperatures.[1, 4, 6, 7] On the other hand, PLA also suffers from inherent brittleness and a very low toughness at room temperature. Hence, the use of PLA may be limited in applications where high elongation or plastic deformation at high impact rates are required.[8, 9] A widespread and cost-effective method to overcome the drawback of the mechanical properties is to blend PLA with ductile polymers.[7, 10] Poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) is a ductile semicrystalline aliphatic polyester, with Tg and Tm ≈−60 °C and 55-70 °C, respectively.[1, 11] Although it is a nonbiobased polymer, PCL is biodegradable and biocompatible, as well as PLA. These characteristics make PCL a suitable candidate to be blended with PLA since biodegradability and biocompatibility will be maintained.[1, 11] Due to its low Tg, PCL exhibits high elongation at break (≈600%[8]) and toughness. Therefore, adding PCL to PLA as a secondary phase could improve the ductility and toughness of PLA.[1] In general, elongation at break of PLA has been easily enhanced (85-400%) by melt blending it with PCL,[12-18] even if, in some cases, poor or no increment has also been reported.[19-23] However, owing to the immiscibility between both polymers, improving the impact toughness of PLA/PCL blends is more challenging, though some good attempts have been made in this field. In this sense, it has been proved that the PCL concentration, the crystallinity of the PLA matrix, the PLA/PCL viscosity ratio, and the processing conditions are key factors that need to be optimized to improve the impact strength of PLA.[24-29] Nevertheless, achieving the optimal composition, processing conditions, and morphology is not always possible. That is why, high impact strength values or supertoughness are not usually reported in the literature for PLA/PCL blends.[12-14, 19]
Despite these attractive properties, PLA has relatively few commercial applications, concentrating mainly in textile and specialty biomedical niches such as sutures and drug delivery devices.6, 7 Additionally, it is being used as a commodity polymer for packaging food and consumer goods where the physical properties of PLA make it suitable for manufacture of rigid containers and bottles. However, the widespread applicability of PLA in flexible sheets and films is limited because of its brittleness, lower impact resistance at room temperature, and narrow processing window.1, 5-8 These factors severely hinder its use, particularly in packaging applications where production lines for flexible films cannot tolerate film cracking or tearing when folded or subjected to force during manufacturing.1 Therefore, it is of paramount importance to find a tougher and more ductile variant of the polymer in order to overcome these difficulties and broaden the range of its commercial applications.1, 6, 8 In order to improve the properties of PLA, it is often blended or copolymerized with other materials.9-13 Blending of PLA with a biodegradable second polymer such as poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(caprolactone), poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), polyhydroxyalkanoate, and poly(butylene succinate) has predominantly been used in biomedical applications to maintain bio-compatibility and biodegradability while also improving mechanical properties.8 For example, significant improvement in flexibility (up to 180% elongation at break compared to 4% for neat PLA) and impact resistance (over 200% increase) were obtained with the use of up to 10 wt% low molecular weight PEG.9 However, these additives are relatively costly rendering their PLA blends expensive. Alternatively, the use of inexpensive non-biodegradable polymers such as poly(ethylene oxide), poly(vinyl acetate), polyisopropene, acrylonitrile/butadiene/styrene copolymer, and polyethylene has successfully reduced cost.8 The use of plasticizers such as low molecular weight esters, oligomeric lactic acid, etc., has been investigated to obtain PLA with improved mechanical properties.9, 10 In the case of semicrystalline polymers like PLA, an efficient plasticizer reduces the glass transition temperature (Tg), thereby increasing the flexibility to overcome the difficulties of cracking or tearing, especially in packaging film production lines.10
PLA is a biodegradable polymer sold worldwide on a large scale, estimated to have an annual growth rate of 10% to 15%, while the global plastics market is growing at 3.5% to 4% annually.13 It can be used in many applications, including packaging, household goods, and biomedical parts.14 The versatility of PLA applications is attributed to its good mechanical properties, comparable to polystyrene (PS) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET), including high mechanical strength and elastic modulus.15, 16 In addition, PLA can be processed in conventional polymer industry and additive manufacturing equipment.17, 18 However, PLA has drawbacks, including its high brittleness, degradability during processing in the presence of humidity and high temperatures, and low heat deflection temperature.19, 20 Researchers are trying to improve PLA's mechanical and thermomechanical performance in this context, primarily through polymer blends.21-24 There are scientific reports on the development of PLA blends with ethylene-propylene-diene (EPDM),25, 26 polycaprolactone (PCL),27, 28 polyolefin elastomers,29, 30 poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT),7, 31 poly(butylene succinate) (PBS),32, 33 and natural rubber (NR),34, 35 exploring their mechanical, thermal, rheological, and morphological properties. Although the polymer blends of PLA showed improved impact strength and elongation at break, the main setback has been severe losses in elastic modulus, tensile strength, and heat deflection temperature (HDT). Alternative routes have been investigated to produce PLA blends with higher mechanical and thermomechanical properties,36, 37 enabling their use in applications requiring semi-biodegradable materials with more robust properties. Recently,38-40 engineering polymers have been used to produce PLA-based blends, such as polyamide and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS). Fazli and Rodrigue41 developed PLA/PA 11 blends compatibilized with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO), indicating improvements of 292% and 104 in impact strength and elongation at break, respectively. The authors also noted a slight decrease in the tensile strength of the PLA/PA611/PEO blend (40/40/20 wt%), which indicates a reasonable balance of mechanical properties. One of the strategies largely explored to improve the mechanical properties of PLA-based blends is reactive compatibilization, inducing crosslinking between phases.42 In such cases, organic peroxides are broadly used as free radical initiators for the constituents of polymer blends during molten state processing.43, 44 A vulcanized thermoplastic is formed when two crosslinkable phases react in a polymer blend. The vulcanized thermoplastic has the properties of vulcanized rubber, yet it can be processed like a conventional thermoplastic.45 The crosslinking of PLA-based blends has been significantly explored, mainly using poly (ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) (EVA)43, 46-48 and natural rubber (NR)22, 49, 50 as impact modifiers. However, the incorporation and crosslinking of engineering impact modifiers in PLA have yet to be studied in the scientific literature. Therefore, for the first time in the polymer blend literature, the acrylonitrile-EPDM-styrene (AES) terpolymer will be crosslinked with PLA to tailor its mechanical and thermomechanical properties. AES is broadly used to produce parts for the automotive industry due to its high impact strength, thermal stability, chemical resistance, and photo-oxidative stability.1, 51
Several approaches can be made to enhance the performance and physical properties of PLA such as plasticization, copolymerization and blending. During long-term use, the plasticizers are possible to migrate to the surface of the material, causing brittleness. However, plasticizers are necessary to lower glass transition temperature, increase ductility and improve processability of PLA. Copolymerization is another great choice to improve the properties of PLA, but the process to commercialize a new copolymer is often long and the cost is very high. Thus, it is less practicable to be an option [3]. While blending is a cost-effective method which combines the advantages of different polymers to obtain a material with the desirable properties, significant amount of work has been performed to improve the mechanical and thermal properties of PLA via PLA-based polymer blend composites [4]. Polyhydroxybutyrate-valerate (PHBV) is a type of biodegradable polymers synthesized by fermentation of bacteria or other microorganisms. PHBV has gained a lot of attention due to its remarkable features like good biocompatibility and biodegradability [1]. At very low hydroxy-valerate (HV) content, PHBV is alike to conventional thermoplastics such as polypropylene (PP) in term of crystallinity, mechanical properties and melting temperature [5]. Polyethylene glycols (PEG), which have the general formula of H(OCH2CH2)n OH are liquid or solid polymers. Low molecular weight PEG is in the liquid form, while higher molecular weight PEG is in the solid form at room temperature. To further improve their blood compatibility, lots of modification methods have been developed, such as plasma treatment, wet chemical treatment, ozonation treatment, and photochemical treatment.9-12 Among these methods, graft copolymerization is one of the most effective methods to modify the physical, chemical, and hemocompatibility of PU with synthetic and natural polymers. A large number of materials have been grafted onto the surface of PU, such as poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG),13 heparin,14 phospholipid polymer,16-18 natural materials (gelatin, collagen, chitosan), alginate, or biotin, etc.19-23 Polyethylene glycol is considered to possess excellent blood compatibility of hydrophilic score. In previous studies, it has been proved that a single PEG grafted layer on PU surface could restrain the protein adsorption and then improve the blood-compatibility.24 Moreover, based on the PEG-modified PU biomaterials, some special biomolecules were immobilized to the surface through a PEG layer to further enhance the biocompability.25-27 Chitosan (CS), a chitin's deacylated derivative, has good biological activity, including good biocompatibility, biodegradable no antigen, nontoxic.23 Recent studies have focused on the surface modification of PU with natural CS to prepare new biomaterials with excellent mechanical property, good biocompatibility, increasing anticoagulation effect, and so on.4 Some previous studies, both CS was immobilized onto the PU surface through poly(acrylic acid) spacer31 and CS was grafted onto the surface of waterborne PU through the assembly of polyelectrolyte in aqueous emulsion,32 prove better blood-compatility. Zhu et al.35 discovered that the poly(ethylene terephtha) (PET) surface coupling CMCS shows excellent anti-clotting properties. During the last few decades, there is a growing demand for tissues and organs for transplantation and this considerable needs have facilitated the rapid development of tissue engineering [1]. In tissue engineering strategies biodegradable and biocompatible polymer scaffolds played a crucial role because they served as a physical support and provided a template to enable cell adhesion, migration, proliferation and eventually tissue regeneration [2, 3]. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), a well-known FDA approved non-toxic, non-antigenic, non-immunogenic and hydrophilic polyether, has been widely copolymerized with polyethylenimine (PEI), poly(ester-amide), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) to tailor their hydrophilic and biocompatible properties for biomedical applications [4-7]. Especially, copolyesters composed of poly(ethylene glycol) terephthalate and poly(butylene terephthalate) (PEGT/PBT, Polyactive®) have drawn much attention recently due to their unique physical properties, good biocompatibility and relative low costs [8-10]. The results indicated that incorporation of lactate moieties into the aromatic polyester effectively improved the degradability of copolymers and the degradation rate could be easily tailored by adjusting the ratio of TPA/OLLA.

Hence, PGA is usually processed by thermal compression or injection molding.51 The by-products of PGA degradation are acidic which becomes a limitation to some biomedical and TE applications. In drug delivery domain, poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) has played a major fundamental role as both biocompatible and biodegradable carrier along with its other beneficial aspects. Biofouling is an extremely problematic issue for a wide variety of applications,47-49 and thus has generated rigorous interest in the literature for trying to mitigate its prevalence.50 For example, polyethylene glycols (PEGs) have long been used as an antibiofouling coating because it resists the adsorption of free proteins in serum.51, 52 Similarly, PEG can be used to create so-called “stealth” particles, which evade uptake by cells (especially macrophages) and thus have prolonged circulation.53 However, while there have been some studies that address the effect of PEGylation on the properties of responsive structures,54-56 there has been less focus on how PEG copolymers affect the performance of polyelectrolyte multilayers as responsive devices. In particular, the impact of PEGylation on the organization of the multilayers and the subsequent effect on mechanical strength and toughness is largely unexamined. This approach, however, comes with the downside of increased complexity and often introduces nonbiocompatible elements to achieve these effects. Clearly, changing the properties of a final microcapsule without relying on extensive chemical modification is desirable to tuning a final product. Despite this need, few studies involving microcapsule synthesis (and particularly with those involving complex macromolecules) explore how processing conditions alter transport and mechanical behavior. In this report, we focus on one class of biopolymers derived from silk fibroin as materials for thin shell microcapsules. Silk fibroin has long been recognized as an excellent biomaterial, due to its negligible cytotoxicity, easy processability, high robustness, and low immunogenicity.57, 58 In addition, silk fibroin has been shown to have exceptional mechanical properties as a thin film, though stable, robust films often require treatment with methanol to crystalize the silk proteins.59, 60 This requirement can be avoided by grafting silk fibroin with short oligomeric chains consisting of a repeat unit of an amino acid with either an amine or carboxyl group as its side group (Figure 1A). These silk derivatives are referred to as silk ionomers, as they consist of weak polybases or polyacids (depending on the species), covalently bonded to the silk fibroin backbone as pendant group moieties.61 The addition of charged groups allows for the use of LbL processing techniques, which we use to construct both planar films and hollow, 3D microspheres and microcapsules. These molecules have been previously shown to have a high degree of biocompatibility when used to encapsulate cells.62 Silk fibroins exploited here are silk grafted with poly-l-lysine (SF-Plys) and silk fibroin grafted with poly-l-glutamic acid (SF-Pglu), which form positively and negatively charged molecules, respectively (Figure 1). In addition, we use a variant of the positively charged silk ionomer species that consists of silk fibroin grafted to poly-l-lysine-block-polyethylene glycol (SF-Plys-PEG), which we have previously shown to significantly alter the intermolecular properties of the silk ionomers.63 In this work, all of the grafted poly-l-lysine and poly-l-glutamic acid groups are made from 20 repeat units of their component amino acids, and are all grafted to the serine and glutamic acid residues of the silk fibroin backbone. This report demonstrates the results of PEGylation and contrasts it to variations due to changes in processing parameters using low grafting silk ionomers as a model system. This length and grafting density is significantly shorter than silk ionomer species that have previously been utilized in making microcapsules, and thus have a lower charge density per molecule. These molecules have been shown to be more cytocompatible when used as cellular coatings and have around 1-2 orders of magnitude less substituted amino acids than the highly grafted silk ionomer species.64 The results of these studies indicate that the microcapsules have a relatively open porous structure that becomes denser at acidic pH, where some of the anionic charge can be reduced. In addition, the different processing strategies to produce the microcapsules lead to different pore structures, which play a critical role in determining the ultimate properties of the microcapsules.

Based solely on the provided evidence, the biocompatibility mechanism of Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) coatings primarily involves:

1.  **Repelling Nonspecific Protein Adsorption:** The intrinsic hydrophilicity of PEG creates a surface that repels nonspecific protein adsorption. This is critical as protein adsorption is often the first step in adverse biological responses like biofouling, thrombosis, and immune recognition [1], [3], [6].
2.  **Resisting Bacterial and Animal Cell Adhesion:** The hydrophilic PEG layer prevents the adhesion of bacteria and animal cells, reducing the risk of infection and foreign body reactions [1], [6].
3.  **Evading Cellular Uptake (Stealth Effect):** PEG coatings create "stealth" particles or surfaces that evade uptake by cells, particularly macrophages, leading to prolonged circulation times in biological systems [15].
4.  **Improving Blood Compatibility (Hemocompatibility):** Specifically for blood-contacting applications, a single PEG grafted layer on surfaces (e.g., polyurethane) restrains protein adsorption, which is a key factor in improving blood compatibility and reducing thrombus formation [7], [10].

The use of polymers in biomedical applications is continuously increasing [1], [2], [3]. In spite of the recent development, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is still one of the most preferable candidate [4], [5]. Properties, such as the hydrophyilicity, biocompatibility and its low interaction with the blood components, make PEG one of the best option for bio-applications [6]. In addition, PEG has been already approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) which facilitates the commercialization of PEG based products. PEG is the most employed polymer when we referred to the stealth polymers and it has been widely used to transport drugs, gene or a protein through the blood due to its excellent circulation time and biocompatibility. Moreover, PEG is capable to transport the compound before being recognized by the immunologic system. It has been reported that high molar mass polymers is the best scenario for biomedical applications [6], as in these conditions the renal clearance is diminished and the long term stability is augmented [1], [2], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]. Consequently, high molar mass PEG leads to increase the capability of targeting the desired properties owing to longer residence time in vivo. Moreover, several studies have demonstrated that the toxicity of PEG is inversely proportional to the molar mass, decreasing the in vivo cytotoxicity increasing the molar mass [12], [13]. Although there are many advantages about using PEG, there are also drawbacks. The most apparent disadvantage of PEG is the lack of degradability and can be accumulated in vivo after finishing its function. Therefore, there are different solutions to overcome the problem. Recently, it has been demonstrated the possibility of a slow biodegradation of PEG by oxidative degradation under biologically significant conditions [14]. However, when faster degradability of the polymer is desired the design of new polymers is required. As a partial solution, block copolymers can be synthesized, having PEG as non-degradable block, and polylactic acid [15] or polycaprolactone [16] as degradable block. On the other hand, high molar mass PEG with hydrolysable linkages within the polymer structure will also facilitate its clearance from the body [17]. The generation with degradable linkages has given several alternatives on the design of PEG based degradable polymers. For instance, esters [18], [19], urethanes [20], [21], [22], disulfides [23] and thiols [24], [25] are some of the functional groups that have been incorporated so far to induce degradability to PEG based polymers. Thus, the polymer will possess high molar mass favouring the targeting and at the same time will have the potential to degrade in vivo after completing the function. Depending on the moiety introduced to PEG, the degradation mechanism and time will be different. Moreover, the incorporated degradable linkages can generate some side products upon degradation, conditioning the application and the effectiveness of the polymer.
Of the polymers that can be incorporated into chitosan-crosslinked networks to yield semi-IPNs, poly(ethylene) glycol (PEG) (Figure 1) attracted our attention. PEG is a synthetic and FDA-approved polymer for use inside the human body.28 It is considered to be biologically inert, biocompatible, and safe to use in drug formulations. Its hydrophilic nature with an incredible thirst for water finds use in a broad range of applications such as laxatives for whole bowel irrigation,29 PEGylated interferon for injectable treatment of hepatitis C infections30 and PEG-coated virus vectors for gene therapy.31 Recently, PEG showed promise in treating spinal-cord damage due to its ability to fuse cells, repair cell membranes, and restore the motor function.32 Based on a broad range of diverse studies employing PEG, it is possible to envisage that incorporation of PEG into a genipin-crosslinked chitosan network could yield a semi-IPN hydrogel with an improved reproducibility, enhanced physiological efficiency, good biocompatibility, improved mechanical performance, and tunable porosity (as a function of concentration of constituents and conditions used during synthesis). Tunable porosity is of importance when the ability to alter responsiveness to pH changes is of interest. Furthermore, being able to alter porosity would offer an additional degree of freedom when aiming to use such hydrogels as a delivery vehicle for bioactive molecules. However, a literature search revealed only a handful of studies involving genipin-crosslinked chitosan-PEG hydrogels. Jin and colleagues21 developed a hydrogel film containing chitosan, PEG, and genipin using a solution casting technique. The tensile strength and elongation were confirmed by tensometer and swelling behavior was determined in different pH buffer solutions at 23°C and 38°C. They found that by crosslinking chitosan with genipin, the tensile strength increased to more than twice (compared to uncrosslinked film). For the fixed amount of genipin, the highest tensile strength was found in the film with 20% of PEG while the highest elongation at break was observed in the film with 65% of PEG. For the fixed PEG amount, the film with a genipin content of 0.1% showed the greatest increase in elongation at break compared to film with 0.5% or 0.8% of genipin. The swelling behavior was dependent on genipin and PEG content, as well as pH and temperature of the medium. Liu et al. investigated the swelling behavior and release kinetics of genipin-crosslinked chitosan-PEG hydrogels by varying PEG and genipin content and the molecular weight of PEG.33 The swelling ratio of the crosslinked gel was higher in acidic medium, proportional to PEG content, and inversely proportional to genipin content. The morphological study was carried out with swollen gels in various pH media with smaller pores seen in gels in pH 7 medium and larger pores seen in gels in pH 2 medium. Currently, little is known about the gelation kinetics of this semi-IPN network. Understanding the gelation kinetics would unveil the dynamics at which the network is formed which is important to understand for further development of these hydrogels and translation to medical applications, in particular as injectable forms. Furthermore, the effect of PEG addition on the morphological characteristics and mechanical stability of hydrogel samples is not sufficiently understood. Mechanical properties are important as they indicate the material's feasibility for a specific medical purpose. At the same time, to fully understand role of each constituent, we would benefit from understanding chemical changes induced by the crosslinking reaction between chitosan and genipin, and interactions with PEG. Until these studies are conducted, these promising materials will remain experimental. Therefore, work presented in this article offers important insights into the key physico-chemical properties of smart hydrogels formed from chitosan, PEG, and genipin. Biodegradable and biocompatible polyurethane (PU)-based thermoresponsive hydrogels have recently received increasing attention.6,7 PUs offer attractive mechanical properties and have been studied in regenerative medicine applications.8 They are synthesized from a variety of polyols, diisocyanates, and chain extenders or crosslinkers, offering the flexibility of tailoring their properties to match specific requirements. The thermoresponsive properties of PU-based hydrogels are dependent on the balance of hydrophilic/hydrophobic groups and their interactions with water molecules via hydrogen bonding, in which the polymer chain network collapses or swells in response to the change in temperature of the aqueous medium.1,9 Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is one of the most used polyols for designing PU-based hydrogels and it has been approved for use in medical applications by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).10,11 PEG presents attractive physicochemical and biological properties, including hydrophilicity, solubility in water and polar organic solvents, non-toxicity and non-immunogenicity.2,12 Hence, the modulation of PU-based hydrogels with PEG improves the biocompatibility, and enables the adjustment of degradability and mechanical properties by varying the molecular mass or concentration of the PEG.7,13 The ability to design PU-based hydrogels using a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer building block, either natural2,12,14 or synthetic,2,12,15,16 is an essential feature in tailoring their biodegradability and biocompatibility. Natural polymers are generally biocompatible, however their poor mechanical properties, fast degradation rates, poor reproducibility and potential immunogenicity restrict their use.2 In contrast, synthetic polymers have more predictable and reproducible physical and biological properties.2 Poly(glycerol sebacate) (PGS) is a synthetic biodegradable and biocompatible elastomer, specifically designed for soft tissue applications.17,18 It is synthesized via a polycondensation reaction of glycerol and sebacic acid, forming a meltable and soluble pre-polymer (pre-PGS) which subsequently cures to create a covalently crosslinked PGS network.17,18 PGS can sustain and recover from deformations in mechanically dynamic environments, which is attributed to its 3D molecular structure and elastomeric nature.19 PGS is bioresorbable and both of its monomers haven been approved by the FDA for the utilization in medical applications.17 Previous in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated good cell compatibility with minimal inflammatory response to PGS implants,17,20-22 as well as relatively linear degradation kinetics and good retention of mechanical strength during degradation due to its surface erosion patterns.17,20-22 While PGS itself exhibits tunable properties,18 the functional hydroxyl groups of PGS also allow one to incorporate different functionalities by reacting with the hydroxyls and hence tailoring its physiochemical properties, as shown by recently developed PGS-based copolymers, blends and composites.18,23-26 For instance, hydrophilic segments such as citric acid or PEG were successfully incorporated into the PGS backbone, resulting in PGS-based copolymers with improved and tunable hydrophilic properties,24,26,27 and the use of isocyanate-based crosslinkers allowed researchers to design mechanically highly tunable PU-based elastomers under mild reaction conditions.23 However, most of these studies aimed to either improve the processability of PGS, or modify the mechanical properties, degradation behaviour or hydration properties of PGS.18 While pristine PGS has been recently investigated for basic one-way shape-memory effects,28 the development of reversibly stimuli-responsive PGS-related hydrogels has not been reported. In this work, we report novel thermoresponsive, stretchable and biodegradable polyester-based polyurethane (PEU) hydrogels, synthesized from pre-PGS and PEGs of different molecular masses (MWts), both containing hydroxyl groups, with aliphatic hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI). HDI was selected due to its extensive use in synthesizing biocompatible polyurethanes.23,29 We hypothesized that the synthesis of the PEU using (I) biodegradable pre-PGS as the main macromolecular crosslinker, (II) hydrophilic PEG as the main polyol component, and (III) hydrophobic HDI as the diisocyanate component, could create a chemically crosslinked thermoresponsive hydrogel with the combined advantages of PGS, PEG and PU. The structure of the PEUs was characterized by spectroscopic and calorimetric measurements, the mechanical properties were analyzed via quasi-static and cyclic tensile and compression tests, and the hydration kinetics and swelling behavior were studied under various medium temperatures. Drug encapsulation and release as well as temperature-induced actuation behaviour were studied. The potential of fabricating the PEU material into different forms such as microspheres and large 3D porous scaffolds was also demonstrated.

Mechanical properties are important as they indicate the material's feasibility for a specific medical purpose. At the same time, to fully understand role of each constituent, we would benefit from understanding chemical changes induced by the crosslinking reaction between chitosan and genipin, and interactions with PEG. Until these studies are conducted, these promising materials will remain experimental. Therefore, work presented in this article offers important insights into the key physico-chemical properties of smart hydrogels formed from chitosan, PEG, and genipin. This may be due to the lack of suitable pre-existing materials, as well as the high cost and complexity of developing new materials. Metallic materials often corrode via complex mechanisms that produce a wide range of products, and the rates and products of corrosion can differ fundamentally between in vitro and in vivo conditions.61 This has made it difficult to translate success at the bench top into a successful stent. Consequently, the scientific and industrial community has engaged in more than a decade-long focus on Mg and Fe62 that has failed to realize the promise of acceptable fully bioabsorbable metallic alternative to the emerging fully biodegradable polymeric stents. Mechanical strength similarity to conventional stents allows clinicians to have reasonable deployment expectations when using a biodegradable metallic stent. The potentially beneficial bioactivity of corrosion products63 raises the exciting prospect that pathogenic cell responses to stent implantation may be modulated as the stent corrodes.
