The treatment of coronary artery disease has gone through three revolutions since the first plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA), which was performed in 1977 and published in the first volume of Lancet on Feb. 4, 1978.[1] Bare metal stents overcome the re-narrowing of coronary arteries after POBA,[2] but they show high incidence of in-stent restenosis in longer-term results, which promoted the development of drug-eluting stents (DES) as the second revolution.[3-5] However, the permanent presence of the metal implants may impair the physiological vasomotor and lead to chronic inflammation, thrombosis, late luminal loss, and neoatherosclerosis, as indicated by some experts.[6] As the third revolution, the biodegradable stents have the potential to circumvent these drawbacks owing to the temporary caging.[7-10] The company of Abbott Vascular pioneered the first biodegradable stent approved by U.S. Food and Drug Administration, yet the Absorb Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold was withdrawn from the market mainly due to the increased rate of stent thrombosis and target lesion revascularization.[11-13] This is pertinent to the thick struts, which came from the lower mechanical strength of polylactide (PLA) compared to cobalt-chromium alloy, the currently main-stream raw material of coronary stent.[13, 14] Magmaris (Biotronik AG, Bülach, Switzerland), the latest generation of magnesium-based biodegradable stent, showed the safety and performance up to 12 months in BIOSOLVE-IV.[15] The struts are still thick (150 µm) mainly due to the lower mechanical strength of magnesium alloy,[16, 17] which was associated with high late lumen loss[18] and a long duration of dual antiplatelet therapy.[13, 15] Pure zinc and zinc-based alloys were also tried to make degradable vascular stents with good degradation performance.[19-22] Extensive investigations are still needed to meet the strict clinical criteria. While these previous efforts are great and both PLA, magnesium, and zinc stents have space to be further improved, the fourth alternative choice of raw materials will be helpful for research and development (R & D) of new-generation biodegradable stents appropriate for interventional treatments. Iron is of better mechanical properties than polymer and magnesium alloy as coronary stents, and its feasibility as a biodegradable stent material was preliminarily examined through the first implantation into the native descending aorta of New Zealand rabbits.[23] Compared with PLA and magnesium alloy, iron-based materials have the potential to make the struts as thin as the permanent DES, which may minimize blood flow perturbations, and reduce restenosis and thrombosis.[24] However, the biodegradation of iron is much slower than other candidates,[25] which inspired the development of alloying method[26-28] and nitriding technology.[29, 30] Nevertheless, the degradation period was still overly long, and some alloying elements, especially Mn, may be detrimental to cells.[31] To further shorten the biodegradation period, a metal-polymer composite strategy was proposed in our previous study.[32] The strategy was applied to fabricate a metal-polymer composite stent (MPS), which showed a satisfactory biodegradation rate and a promising efficacy in vivo. The manufacturing process of MPS and the percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) are schematically presented in Figure S1, Supporting Information. The effect of the metal-polymer composite strategy on the degradation of iron and in particular the corresponding biocompatibility evaluation will be investigated in the present article. It is well-known that an ideal biodegradable stent should not only have good mechanical properties and an appropriate degradation rate, but also keep a good biocompatibility. In light of fundamental research closely relevant to the potential clinical translation, iron-base biomaterials are faced with a critical argument about its possible cytotoxicity. Some in vitro studies have reported that the extracts of iron materials were non-cytotoxic to cells.[32-34] Furthermore, no thrombosis or pronounced inflammation and no systemic or local toxicity were observed in vivo studies, indicating the safety of iron-based biodegradable stents preliminarily.[30, 35, 36] However, a new issue has been raised up to focus on the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) during iron corrosion, which was ignored in the traditional cytotoxicity tests via extracts.[37] In 2020, a paper entitled as “Hydroxyl radicals and oxidative stress: the dark side of Fe corrosion” was published; Scarcello et al. kindly warned that the oxidative stress caused by iron corrosion was detrimental to endothelial cells in vitro[38] and rat aortic rings ex vivo.[39] This is a serious problem related to any effort of an iron-based biomaterial eventually implanted into body.
Fe-based and Mg-based alloys are two typical and widely investigated biodegradable metallic materials for fabricating biodegradable stents.1-3 Recently, Zn-based materials also emerged as alternative biodegradable stent materials.4-6 Compared with Mg-based and Zn-based alloys, Fe-based stents are more advantageous in terms of their comparable mechanical properties to 316L stainless steel (316L SS).2 In addition, iron is an essential element for the body, and it could reduce the proliferation rate of vascular smooth muscle cells.7 A period of 6-12 months is required for the vessels to undergo the remodelling process and then the stents are expected to degrade and to be eliminated from the patient after implantation for 12-24 months.2 Early in vivo experimental results demonstrated that the degradable iron stents could be safely implanted into the descending aorta of New Zealand white rabbits without significant inflammation, neointimal proliferation, or thrombotic events,8 and the pure iron stent strut still remained within the blood vessel even after 12 months.9 The slow degradation rate of Fe may result in the long term presence of this metallic stent. Compared with the vascular tissues, the metallic stents are much harder and more rigid, and their long term presence within the blood vessels may possibly cause damage to and irritations of the vascular tissues or induce undesired biological reactions. Therefore, a faster degradation rate of iron stents is desirable for clinical applications to avoid the potential side effects that result from the slow degradation rate. Many methods have been exploited to produce iron-based materials with increased degradation rate, such as developing novel iron alloys10 or producing pure iron by using electroforming technique.11 Surface engineering is an effective technique to mediate the biological and physicochemical properties of biomaterials. Iron can be patterned cost-effectively with vertically oriented α-Fe2O3 nanotubes through a simple and facile electrochemical technique for their potential applications as photocatalysts (similar to TiO2).12 Considering their application as biodegradable stents, pure iron with nanotubular topography has three advantages: (I) better cellular responses, (II) faster degradation rate, and (III) great potential for being exploited as drug-eluting stents. (I) A case in point is that, compared with the flat Ti surface, the adhesion and proliferation as well as motility of the endothelial cells are significantly improved on nanotubes with a diameter of 15 nm,13-15 indicating that nanotubular coatings can display strong stimulation of cellular activities. (II) Another example is that these nanotubes were expected to improve the cyto-compatibility and enhance the anodic dissolution of the iron substrate by the Fe2O3/Fe interfacial micro-galvanic reactions.16 (III) The implantation of bare metal stent is always accompanied by two major complications, the delayed endothelialization of the stents and the proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), resulting in the formation of thrombosis and in-stent restenosis, respectively. To tackle this problem, the nanotubular structures could be exploited as drug-delivery depots17 to inhibit VSMC proliferation and prevent restenosis.18 Fe2O3 has been reported to be applied in the vascular stents.19,20 To the best of our knowledge, there are no studies attempting to evaluate the biocompatibility of Fe2O3 nanotubes on pure iron and to explore the possibility of utilizing Fe2O3 nanotubes as drug depots/carriers for their applications as degradable vascular stents. Therefore, in our study, Fe2O3 nanotube arrays were prepared on iron and drug-loaded (rapamycin) by a simple dipping method. Rapamycin (also known as sirolimus), a carboxyl lactone-lactam macrolide, is a natural fermentation product produced by Streptomyces hygroscopicus21 and has been widely used as a cardiovascular drug due to its potent inhibitory effects on the proliferation and migration of smooth muscle cells, which was reported to remarkably reduce the restenosis rate to almost 0%.20,22,23 Moreover, due to the open-structure, and the high drug loading amount and the concentration gradient of the coating, the release of the drug directly from nanotubes would be very rapid,24 which could not endow these drug-containing stents with desired properties (sustained drug-release time and effective drug-release dosage) for clinical practice. In order to alleviate those undesired effects, in our study, these nanotubes were further coated by PLGA films through a simple spin-coating process.
First published on 16th April 2020 As a new type of intestinal stent, the MAO/PLLA/paclitaxel/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd alloy stent has shown good degradability, although its biocompatibility in vitro and in vivo has not been investigated in detail. In this study, its in vivo biocompatibility was evaluated by animal study. New Zealand white rabbits were implanted with degradable intestinal Mg-Zn-Y-Nd alloy stents that were exposed to different treatments. Stent degradation behavior was observed both macroscopically and using a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Energy dispersion spectrum (EDS) and histological observations were performed to investigate stent biological safety. Macroscopic analysis showed that the MAO/PLLA/paclitaxel/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd stents could not be located 12 days after implantation. SEM observations showed that corrosion degree of the MAO/PLLA/paclitaxel/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd stents implanted in rabbits was significantly lower than that in the PLLA/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd stent group. Both histopathological testing and serological analysis of in vivo biocompatibility demonstrated that the MAO/PLLA/paclitaxel/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd alloy stents could significantly inhibit intestinal tissue proliferation compared to the PLLA/Mg-Zn-Y-Nd alloy stents, thus providing the basis for designing excellent biodegradable drug stents. Biodegradable stents (BDS) made of magnesium alloys demonstrate superior performance to their polymeric counterparts due to excellent mechanical properties similar to SS316L stainless steel, which cannot be achieved by polymers.7 Some studies have shown that magnesium alloys can be used as orthopedic implants or cardiovascular stents.8-15 However, it is well known that magnesium alloys will gradually corrode under natural conditions. And the major limitation of biodegradable magnesium alloy stents is their low corrosion resistance. To lengthen the degradation time, alloying is used as one of the methods to enhance corrosion resistance and mechanical strength. Moreover, scaffold surface polymer coating is also important for mechanical strength.16 Degradable polymers, such as PLLA, PLGA, have good plasticity, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility, which are most commonly used biomaterials for surface modification of alloys to enhance the corrosion resistance of alloys.17-21 Therefore, PLLA is considered as a coating material to improve the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloy surface in this paper. At present, there are many ways to improve the corrosion resistance of the alloy surface, besides polymer coating, micro-arc oxidation (MAO) process is also one of the surface modification technologies of magnesium alloys. At high breakdown voltage, various processes such as electrochemical, thermodynamic and plasma chemical reactions occur, accompanied by spark discharge to produce thicker, harder and wear-resistant ceramic coatings that can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the alloy surface.22,23 However, to reduce neointimal growth, biodegradable magnesium alloy stents can be coated with polymers containing antiproliferative drugs. Even though previous research report refered to that the clinical efficacy of paclitaxel was affected by drug resistance, in view of its excellent antiproliferation property in the treaty of breast cancer paclitaxel was regarded as one of the effective antiproliferative drugs.24 At the same time, it has been reported in literatures that both paclitaxel and sirolimus can effectively inhibit neointimal hyperplasia of coronary artery within a month dose range, and the effect has a certain degree of safety.24-27 It can effectively reduce the degree of vascular restenosis. Therefore, paclitaxel and sirolimus are commonly used in drug-eluting stents for the treatment of coronary stenosis. However, whether paclitaxel that can effectively inhibit the occurrence of vascular endothelialization, as well as the biological safety of the paclitaxel-eluting intestinal stent to important organs and tissues of human body, are unknown. Therefore, paclitaxel is selected as a sustained-release drug of the stent to explore the compatibility of the drug-eluting stent in intestinal environment in this study. However, few studies to date have reported on the biocompatible and biodegradable properties of magnesium alloy in the intestine.
Currently available DES are often a stainless steel or cobalt chromium platform with a permanent polymer overlayer containing a specific drug. For example, CoCr is the platform for the second generation Xience V and Endeavor stents; stainless steel is used for Sirolimus-eluting and Paclitaxel-eluting stents. Early trials by Johnson & Johnson Company et al. have shown that DES are capable of reducing the rate of restenosis to zero within six months.36 Although the DES provide significantly improved outcomes within one year, the long term outcomes are not statistically different relative to bare metal stents.37 The concept of bioabsorbable stents has probably been around since the introduction of metallic stents,38 but this different paradigm has only now gained momentum. Because of this, the idea of degradability is perceived as potentially “revolutionary” in stent research (third generation stents). The current belief is that biodegradable stents will drastically reduce, if not eradicate, all of the long-term health risks associated with bare metal stents and DES.[3, 39] Particularly well designed biodegradable metallic stents could conceivably eliminate all the drawbacks of bare and drug-eluting metallic stents such as stent thrombosis and in-stent restenosis (Figure 1). A series of attempts to bring this concept to reality date back more than a decade, to the beginning of the XXIst century.40 In the last ∼15 years, each major stent manufacturer has shown interest in this new concept, along with dozens of academic laboratories in the Americas, Europe, and Asia. The concept may be achieved by engineering stents that retain mechanical properties for approximately 4-6 months before being broken down, metabolized, and harmlessly excreted by the body.[3, 4, 39] Already, as early as in 2011, the European Medicines Agency approved the use of Absorb BVS (Abbott Vacular) made of a biodegradable poly L-lactic acid (PLLA) polymer (Table 1). Biodegradable polymers have been tested for cardiovascular stent applications since the late 1980s. Biodegradable metals, although considered for implants much earlier (in XVII century for Fe41 and at the turn of the XIX century for Mg),42 practically attracted interest for cardiovascular applications at the beginning of XXI century. Pure Fe was the first metal tested, although the majority of research was done on Mg and its alloys. All of these materials were implanted in animal arteries (Table 3) and were proven safe and reliable. As of today only Mg-based and PLLA-based stents went beyond animal testing and were tested clinically in humans (Tables 3 and 4).

The introduction of permanent metallic stents was a major advance over balloon angioplasty in the treatment of arterial diseases, being highly effective in preventing acute vessel closure due to balloon-induced dissection, and in reducing the rate of restenosis [1]. However, it has been suggested that the role of the stent is temporary and limited to the intervention and shortly thereafter, until healing and re-endothelialization of the vessel wall is achieved [2]. In fact, after six months arterial remodeling typically enters a stable phase where substantial scaffolding is no longer needed to prevent recoil [3]. Afterwards, the presence of a permanent stent, besides requiring a lifelong anticoagulant therapy, can lead to late thrombosis and chronic inflammation, and can hinder the lumen expansion associated with late vessel remodeling. Biodegradable stents have therefore emerged as one of the most promising approaches in obstructive cardiovascular disease treatment due to their potential in providing mechanical support while it is needed and then, once they are bioabsorbed, leaving behind only the healed natural vessel. This would allow the restoration of vasoreactivity and possibly vessel remodeling as well as to avoid the aforementioned concerns related with the presence of a permanent metallic implant [2]. In addition, biodegradable stents are particularly needed in the case of pediatric cardiovascular treatments where a permanent stent usually requires a second surgery since the target vessel grows with the child [3]. A number of biodegradable stents made of metallic or polymeric materials have been investigated over recent years [4, 5]. Mg alloys are by far the most investigated biodegradable metallic materials for intravascular stent development [6, 7]. The first metallic bioabsorbable stent implanted in humans was the Mg alloy stent studied in the ‘Clinical Performance and Angiographic Results of Coronary Stenting with Absorbable Metal Stents’ trial [8]. Aliphatic polyesters, such as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(glycolic acid), poly(D,L-lactic-co-glycolic acid), and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), have been widely investigated for biodegradable stents development due to their relatively long degradation rate and suitable mechanical properties [5, 9]. The Igaki-Tamai stent (Kyoto Medical Planning, Japan), the first biodegradable stent implanted in humans, consists of an extruded high molecular weight PLLA filament with a zig-zag helical coil design [10]. The stent received the CE marking in 2007 for the treatment of peripheral artery diseases, and recent clinical outcomes showed its long term safety as coronary scaffold that could disappear within three years [11]. The ABSORB Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold based on PLLA (Abbott Vascular, CA) was the first bioabsorbable drug-eluting stent to have clinical outcomes similar to those following metallic drug-eluting stent implantation [12]. Other biodegradable stents that are currently under clinical investigation are the REVA Medical stent made of tyrosine polycarbonate (REVA Medical Inc., CA), the IDEAL stent made of a polyanhydride and salicylic acid (Bioabsorbable Therapeutics Inc., CA), and the novolimus-loaded DESOlve stent made of PLLA (Elixir Medical Corporation, CA) [8, 9]. Polymeric stents are generally composed by interconnected tubular elements with a zig-zag or sinusoidal structure. They are fabricated starting from a tubular body, obtained by injection molding or melt extrusion, whose wall is made porous by means of selective material removal through laser ablation, mechanical machining or chemical etching [3]. Alternatively, polymeric stents are made through melt extrusion of a monofilament that is then woven into a braid-like embodiment. Flege et al [13] recently reported on the development of stents made of PLLA or PLLA-co-PCL by means of a Selective Laser Melting technique. As highlighted by the authors, an additive manufacturing (AM) approach to stents fabrication allows achieving superior freedom in structural design and mechanical performance in comparison to conventional fabrication techniques. In fact, AM techniques allow fabrication of 3D objects with a predefined composition, geometry and size as well as a porous architecture characterized by a fully interconnected network of pores with customizable size, shape and distribution [14].
Among cardiovascular diseases, coronary artery disease is responsible for 18 million deaths around the globe [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. During various coronary artery treatments such as angiography, coronary stent implantation renders intra-arterial assistance [[5], [6], [7]]. For a stent to be ideal for clinical use, several fundamental merits are required such as mechanical strength, ductility, and biocompatibility [8]. Unfortunately, after stent implantation, a significant number of patients develop late restenosis [9,10]. Extensive anticoagulant medication is also not useful in the case of such patients. Non-degradable bare metallic stents (BMS) possess excellent mechanical properties with good biocompatibility but still, they cause late thrombosis and restenosis due to chronic inflammation and neointimal hyperplasia [11]. Drug-eluting stents (DES) are also employed which reduce thrombosis and restenosis in the early stages but in the latter stages due to the permanent implantation in the blood vessels, thrombosis and restenosis can occur after a year or two [[12], [13], [14]]. Biodegradable stents are a promising class to mitigate the shortcomings of the BMS and DES stents [15]. Magnesium and its alloys are an alluring class of metals for implants due to their biodegradable and mechanical properties [[16], [17], [18]]. After implantation, the spontaneous degradation and the resorption by the vascular tissue is a promising strategy. Despite the appreciable biocompatibility of the Mg stents, fast degradation hinders its vast clinical application [19,20]. For reducing the degradation rate, surface modification by surface coating is considered an efficient technique. Several surface coating techniques are used to achieve corrosion resistance, such as inorganic coating, chemical conversion, and organic coatings [[21], [22], [23]]. For a coating to be effective, it should be biocompatible and reduce the corrosion rate to an acceptable rate. Among the broad range of coatings, chemical conversion is considered an advantageous method offering simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency. Chemical conversion by treatment with hydrofluoric acid for the formation of magnesium fluoride (MgF2) improves the fast degradation of the Mg by reducing the corrosion rate [20]. Among the polymer coatings, Poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and Polycaprolactone (PCL) are biodegradable polymers with good biocompatibility and excellent mechanical properties [20]. It has been reported previously PLLA has a better adhesion strength to the Mg substrate as compared to PCL [24]. However, the use of only polymer coating can have shortcomings such as acidic degradation products and undesired capillary pores that can limit the control of the degradation of Mg alloy. The acidic degradation products can also cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue environment of the implant [25]. The hydrophobicity of the polymer coating can hinder cell attachment [26]. HAp particles have high biocompatibility and due to the inorganic ions present in HAp, the degradation products are alkaline in nature. The hydrophilic nature of the HAp makes the cell attachment and proliferation favorable. If used alone on Mg substrate HAp coating can suffer fracture due to its brittle nature resulting in the lessen adhesion to the metal surface. Combining the polymer organic coating with inorganic HAp can assist to overcome the respective disadvantages while combining the advantages [18]. The inorganic alkaline degradation products can be neutralized by the polymeric acidic products and the intermolecular interactions between the different polymer layers and HAp can increase the adhesion strength of the coatings [27]. The degradation rate of the coating can be improved with increased bioactivity by combining polymeric organic coating with inorganic HAp.
In 2018, the US FDA reported that the design of the staples is the main crucial factor, and among the approximate 1 lakh cases of staple failure, more than ten thousand serious injuries occurred due to the abnormal deformation of the staple shape. (15) The design of Mg staples often references that of Ti staples. However, Mg staples, being biodegradable, are subjected to physiologically stressful environments, which may lead to stress corrosion cracking (SCC) during normal physical activities. (16) Studies have reported that Mg staples can degrade rapidly and break easily after deformation into a B shape due to their susceptibility to stress corrosion. (17−19) For instance, Gao et al. (20) found that applying tensile stress to a high-purity (HP) Mg bar will accelerate the corrosion process in vitro, resulting in severe pitting corrosion and SCC. After immersing the homogenized WE54 alloy in simulated body fluid (SBF), Asgharinezhad Baloochi et al. (21) found that corrosion pits and cracks are the primary causes of the initial fatigue crack formation. Generally, stress and strain distribution in biodegradable implants with plastic deformation can be finely regulated through structural design. (17,22) Wu et al. (23) designed staples in a U shape with interior angles of 90 and 100°. The finite element analysis (FEA) results indicated that the staple with a 100° interior angle was optimal as it effectively distributed residual stress at the staple’s tip upon closure, thereby reducing the risk of stress corrosion. The maximum incidence of staple failure is caused by deformation in the leg sections due to stress propagation and subsequent stress concentration. (15) The compression force of staples fired from the dispenser is greater than that in other regions. Staples in different open and closed stages may experience varying levels of stress concentration in the leg area. To prevent rapid corrosion or premature fracture at the bending points, the structure of Mg staples needs to be optimally designed to reduce stress and strain concentrations at the joints of the staple legs during the deformation process into a B shape. In this study, HP Mg (99.98 wt %) was adopted to develop biodegradable staples for intestinal anastomosis. Finite element numerical simulations were conducted to optimize the interior angle and height of the staple, aiming to minimize the stress concentration. Subsequently, Mg staples with optimized structures were manufactured, and the mechanical properties were characterized through tensile tests and burst pressure measurements, while the in vitro corrosion behaviors were evaluated using immersion tests and electrochemical measurements in modified simulated body fluid (m-SBF). At last, the effectiveness of biodegradable staples was verified, demonstrating that an optimized design could facilitate the accelerated clinical translation of magnesium-based anastomotic staples. Ten U-shaped Mg staples were designed according to ref (24), and as listed in Table 1, the interior angles and the height of the staple were the two factors to be optimized. After finite element numerical simulation, the staple with the optimized structure was chosen for the experimental studies. At the same time, a reference staple group was set up for comparison to verify the effectiveness of the structure optimization.
Advantages of braided Mg stents for biliary reconstruction Different biliary stents associated with the alteration of materials and structures have been reported in the literature for obtaining optimal stent design [25]. The radial compression force is of importance for maintaining the structure of the biliary tract. Figure 8 shows the radial compression force in unit length of the several braided fibrous stents including nitinol and diverse polymers stents [12, 26, 27]. It is noted that the compression force of commercial MTN-DA biliary stent (produced by Micro-Tech Co., Ltd. China) fully coved with PCL is about 0.14 N mm−1, and that of nitinol stents braided by machine with a diameter of 0.15 is 0.02-0.72 N mm−1. The stents fabricated with polyamide and polyester demonstrate good compression properties, but they are hard to degrade in the body. Additionally, PDO is another biodegradable material with promising applications in recent years. The stents braided with PDO monofilament then fully covered with PCL also have enough radial compression force, but overmuch PCL takes too long to degrade completely. The strength of Mg alloys has long been controversial especially in the process of degradation. However, comparing to these reported studies, it could be noticed that the studied Mg stent has a relatively high compression force though the diameter of wire is smaller than polymers, which is beneficial to the endothelialization of the stent to improve the success rate of implantation [28]. Moreover, the fluorinated Mg stents and them with PCL coating can maintain 0.08-0.26 N mm−1 for 3 days immersion and 0.08-0.23 N mm−1 for 20 days immersion respectively. On the other hand, for the benign CBD construction, an ideal biliary stent should disappear automatically after healing. Previous studies of biodegradable Mg alloys have reported they did not perform well because of their rapid degradation, especially in the position with mechanical action and fluid environment for long time healing [10]. Nevertheless, in the field of bile duct surgery, the support time required after CBD surgery is approximately 7 to 10 days, and the non-degradable stent generally needed removed 1 week later [14]. As a result, biodegradable stents have become a prominent research focus and development direction in the field of cardiovascular stents [6]. However, in physiological environments containing large amount of polar corrosive media, Mg alloys exhibit excessively fast and uncontrollable degradation behaviors, leading to premature mechanical support loss and unpredictable structural damage [8], [9]. To enhance the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys, a series of anticorrosion strategies have been extensively explored, including impurity content reduction, alloy element regulation [10], [11], improvement of the forging process [12], surface deposition [13] and utilization of surface coating technologies [9], [14]. Bioabsorbable stents are designed to provide mechanical support for the arterial wall during the remodeling period and to degrade with the progression of tissue regeneration.65 Ideally, in order to achieve the appropriate scaffolding, the mechanical properties of the candidate materials should be close to those of 316L stainless steel, which has been traditionally considered the gold standard material for stent constructs.66 The stent material itself and its degradation products should also be non-toxic and compatible in the cardiovascular environment.67 As briefly reviewed in Section 2.2, biodegradable polymers and two metals (Fe and Mg) went through a number of animal and clinical studies, proving of being non-toxic and promising materials for cardiovascular applications. Specific design criteria that have been suggested for biodegradable stent materials in the scientific literature are listed in Table 5. It should be recognized that although a material tensile strength of >300 MPa is recommended, stents made of polymers-with much less favorable mechanical properties-were demonstrated in recent years and even reached clinical trials, as discussed in the previous section. The mechanical properties and degradation rates for polymers and metals tested for cardiovascular stent applications are compiled in Tables 6 and 7. The mechanical properties reported in these tables include elastic (Young's) modulus (YM), yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation. These mechanical properties are indicators of stent radial strength, acute and chronic recoil, axial and radial flexibility, deliverability, profile and lifetime integrity.70 The YM provides a measure of how well the stent material resists deformation. Stents are typically delivered through a balloon catheter and then expanded upon proper positioning in the artery. The stent material needs to sustain deformations without cracking or fragmenting during delivery. The critical value for the YM of materials used for stents is not well defined but it is preferable to have a high value to reduce stent recoil. As shown in Table 6, polymers generally exhibit a one order of magnitude lower YM than metals. Additionally, polymers are typically viscoelastic and can deform permanently over their lifetime when in use under stress. Although rarely mentioned in the stent literature, viscoelasticity is a disadvantage of using polymers for stent applications.

Fe-based and Mg-based alloys are two typical and widely investigated biodegradable metallic materials for fabricating biodegradable stents.1-3 Recently, Zn-based materials also emerged as alternative biodegradable stent materials.4-6 Compared with Mg-based and Zn-based alloys, Fe-based stents are more advantageous in terms of their comparable mechanical properties to 316L stainless steel (316L SS).2 In addition, iron is an essential element for the body, and it could reduce the proliferation rate of vascular smooth muscle cells.7 A period of 6-12 months is required for the vessels to undergo the remodelling process and then the stents are expected to degrade and to be eliminated from the patient after implantation for 12-24 months.2 Early in vivo experimental results demonstrated that the degradable iron stents could be safely implanted into the descending aorta of New Zealand white rabbits without significant inflammation, neointimal proliferation, or thrombotic events,8 and the pure iron stent strut still remained within the blood vessel even after 12 months.9 The slow degradation rate of Fe may result in the long term presence of this metallic stent. Compared with the vascular tissues, the metallic stents are much harder and more rigid, and their long term presence within the blood vessels may possibly cause damage to and irritations of the vascular tissues or induce undesired biological reactions. Therefore, a faster degradation rate of iron stents is desirable for clinical applications to avoid the potential side effects that result from the slow degradation rate. Many methods have been exploited to produce iron-based materials with increased degradation rate, such as developing novel iron alloys10 or producing pure iron by using electroforming technique.11 Surface engineering is an effective technique to mediate the biological and physicochemical properties of biomaterials. Iron can be patterned cost-effectively with vertically oriented α-Fe2O3 nanotubes through a simple and facile electrochemical technique for their potential applications as photocatalysts (similar to TiO2).12 Considering their application as biodegradable stents, pure iron with nanotubular topography has three advantages: (I) better cellular responses, (II) faster degradation rate, and (III) great potential for being exploited as drug-eluting stents. (I) A case in point is that, compared with the flat Ti surface, the adhesion and proliferation as well as motility of the endothelial cells are significantly improved on nanotubes with a diameter of 15 nm,13-15 indicating that nanotubular coatings can display strong stimulation of cellular activities. (II) Another example is that these nanotubes were expected to improve the cyto-compatibility and enhance the anodic dissolution of the iron substrate by the Fe2O3/Fe interfacial micro-galvanic reactions.16 (III) The implantation of bare metal stent is always accompanied by two major complications, the delayed endothelialization of the stents and the proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), resulting in the formation of thrombosis and in-stent restenosis, respectively. To tackle this problem, the nanotubular structures could be exploited as drug-delivery depots17 to inhibit VSMC proliferation and prevent restenosis.18 Fe2O3 has been reported to be applied in the vascular stents.19,20 To the best of our knowledge, there are no studies attempting to evaluate the biocompatibility of Fe2O3 nanotubes on pure iron and to explore the possibility of utilizing Fe2O3 nanotubes as drug depots/carriers for their applications as degradable vascular stents. The degradation of polymeric materials is a very important issue, not only from the point of view of polymer science, but it is crucial in the context of the majority of applications, especially in the biomedical field.1, 2 The majority of biodegradable polyesters used for orthopedic implants, including polylactide, polyglicolide, and their copolymers, suffer from in situ hydrolytic degradation in aquatic environments.3, 4 The resulting changes in the biophysical and biochemical properties of the polymers have a significant effect on the behavior of tissue-engineered components. Hydrolysis is the dominant mechanism in the degradation of bioresorbable polyesters. Almost immediately after a polymer is placed into an aquatic environment, water molecules diffuse into the polymeric matrix. After some time, a large concentration of water molecules accumulates in the material. The water molecules reduce the strength of the chemical bonds of the polymeric chains. This causes them to divide into water-soluble shorter chains (oligomers and monomers) characterized by carboxylic ends, which are known to autocatalyze ester hydrolysis. These oligomers and monomers are able to diffuse inside the polymer matrix. The chain scissions inside the polymer matrix cause a reduction in the molecular weight of the polymer. The water-soluble monomers that are located near to the surface of the implant can leach out before total degradation occurs, whereas those that are located deep inside the polymer matrix remain entrapped and contribute to the autocatalytic effect.5, 6 This causes the degradation of large-size devices to proceed heterogeneously and to occur more rapidly internally than at the surface.

Higher porosity generally accelerates degradation due to increased water absorption and surface area exposure, which enhance hydrolytic chain scission and enzymatic activity [1, 10]. The controlled porosity, along with the presence of bredigite, enhances mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and promotes the adhesion and proliferation of osteoblasts, rendering these freeze-dried scaffolds promising for applications in bone tissue engineering and repair [12]. An increase in porosity frequently results in a reduction of mechanical strength, as the area capable of bearing load is diminished; this correlation is generally characterized by a nonlinear nature. Characteristics such as pore size and morphology play a crucial role, with larger pore dimensions leading to a more pronounced loss of strength [22]. Porosity level will also enhance the degree of biocompatibility by providing an ideal environment for cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation in certain applications in bone and tissue engineering [23]. These support the implant's integration with the surrounding tissues because of better vascularization, with interconnected pore architectures allowing cell penetration, thereby improving the long-term biocompatibility of the implant [24]. On the other hand, excess porosity means a greater surface area, which may be more exposed to protein binding and bacterial colonization, promoting inflammation and implant failure. Pores size for biocompatibility differs for any particular application, but in the case of bone tissue engineering, 100-500 μm was found to be most optimal in facilitating sufficient ingrowth of bones [22, 24]. To address the challenges associated with bone tissue engineering, in this study, a multidisciplinary approach was employed to develop a novel scaffold for bone tissue engineering. The properties associated with biocompatibility and biodegradability concerning scaffold materials are of paramount significance, as they play a crucial role in establishing an environment that is conducive for the effective seeding of cells [25]. The scaffold was fabricated by combining three biocompatible and biodegradable materials: gelatin (Gel), polylactic acid (PLA), and bredigite. Gelatin, a denatured variant of collagen, is composed of a unique sequence of amino acids and is characterized by a high concentration of specific amino acids, including glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline, which closely resemble the structure of collagen [26]. Furthermore, gelatin exhibits properties similar to glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), allowing it to effectively mimic the architecture of the natural extracellular matrix (ECM) [26, 27]. In order to improve the mechanical characteristics of gelatin, PLA was chosen as a secondary component, recognized for its significant tensile strength and biodegradability properties [28, 29]. Additionally, bredigite, a mineral component, contributed to the scaffold's ability to form a strong bond with bone tissues. By strategically combining these materials, the researchers were able to create a highly functional scaffold that can potentially aid in the repair or regeneration of bone tissues [17-19]. In a study by Farzam Far et al., PLA/gel nanofiber scaffolds were formed using the phase separation method induced by heat and the electrospinning method. Combining platelet-enriched plasma with PLA scaffolds improved mechanical properties, porosity, cell attachment, and viability under laboratory conditions compared with pure PLA [28]. Nadi et al. developed a novel and functional scaffold by the PLA/ PCL composite polymers and strontium-doped bredigite nanoparticles that Ca was substituted by Sr, and the scaffolds exhibited the best potential to regenerate bone tissue [30]. The development of composite matrix scaffolds comprising a Gel/PLA composite reinforced with bredigite ceramic has been recognized for its advantages in bone tissue engineering. These scaffolds were fabricated and characterized, employing gelatin due to its biocompatibility and degradable nature, PLA for its biocompatible attributes, mechanical strength, and biological degradability, as well as bredigite for its robust formation of chemical bonds with bone tissues. This study ultimately assessed the scaffolds' bioactivity, biocompatibility, bonding capabilities, mechanical properties, and antibacterial effectiveness.

In healing bone defects, it is important to account for the degradation of scaffolds that have been used as implants to support the healing process. In order for bone ingrowth to take place, the degradation rate of the scaffolds should correspond to the rate of bone formation. Therefore, the ability to control the degradation rate of scaffolds is a key aspect and one of the advantages of using polyesters for scaffolding is that they offer more flexibility in controlling the degradation rate when compared to natural polymers. Moreover, it is necessary to take into consideration the change in scaffold structure over time as the porous structure evolves as the material degrades. Also, as mentioned earlier, aliphatic polyesters degrade via bulk erosion, which results in an accumulation of acidic byproducts and a reduction in pH, which can negatively affect nearby tissues. Therefore, it is important to evaluate the degradation rate and pH of the environment during the degradation process as well as to determine the structural changes that occur with scaffolds during this process. Previous studies have characterized the degradation of PLGA (50:50)/PCL scaffolds under physiological conditions.52 Polymeric scaffolds were reported to lose significant weight in dynamic conditions due to the rapid degradation of PLGA (50:50) over time, and once the PLGA(50:50) was fully degraded, degradation rate would slow down to match the rate of PCL.53 Additionally, their quantitative and qualitative SEM analyses showed that the microporosity of the scaffolds has evolved over time. In their proposed results, scaffolds containing two different polymers of PLGA (50:50) and PCL would allow for fine-tuning of the degradation rate of newly developed polyester-based scaffolds. In accordance with these results, the degradation rate of our scaffolds with PCL and PLGA (85:15) as slow-degrading components increased when PGA and PLGA (50:50) were added as fast-degrading components. It appears that adding the fast-degrading polyester to the slow-degrading polyester modulated the degradation rate of the newly formed polyester composite scaffolds. In addition, our SEM analysis indicated a consistent increase in the porosity of the scaffolds over the course of the degradation study as the fast-degrading component degrades. To address the issue of acidic environments after polyester degradation, each composite contained 20% TCP. It was shown in our previous study that the use of bioceramic TCP in composite scaffolds over 20% typically results in the separation of the polymer and ceramic phases and compromises the mechanical stability of the composite scaffold. According to our results, the addition of TCP to the compositions counterbalanced the acidic degradation of polyester composite scaffolds and increased the pH of degradation media. The results of our study are in agreement with those obtained by several other studies in which it was shown that basic degradation of ceramic particles can neutralize the acidic environment in which polyester degradation occurs.54-56 Overall, we were able to develop a polyester composite scaffold that exhibits mechanical properties similar to that of trabecular and cortical bone. The scaffolds were capable of developing a porous structure dynamically without compromising mechanical stability as the fast-degrading polyester components of the composite degraded slowly over time. Additionally, TCP, which mimics the structure of bone and increases the bioactivity of the scaffolds, was able to resolve the acidity issue related to the degradation of the polyester compound. It is essential that the scaffold in the BTE application be nontoxic to the cells and osteoinductive so that the MSCs can differentiate into preosteoblasts and initiate the formation of bone. An in vitro study using hMSCs was conducted to determine whether the scaffolds are non-toxic and osteoinductive. In our cell culture studies, PCL served as a control group. The choice of PCL as the control group was based on its long-standing medical history as well as its low degradation rate that does not cause acidity over the course of the study. It was shown that cell attachment and proliferation were significantly greater on polyester composite scaffolds after adding TCP, as well as an increase in matrix mineralization and ALP production similar to the PCL positive control group. In the presence of TCP, cells were more viable and spread throughout the scaffolds compared to before TCP addition, confirming our original hypothesis that adding TCP neutralizes the acidity and enhances the biocompatibility of polyester composite scaffolds by neutralizing the acidity. It has been demonstrated that the addition of TCP and its controlled release by polyester degradation and formation of porous structures is extremely important, as scaffolds with TCP, particularly for PLGA (50:50)/PCL and PLGA (50:50)/PLGA (85:15), demonstrated a greater level of cell attachment and proliferation, ALP activity, and calcium deposition similar to the PCL control group without significant differences. The results of our study agree with those of other studies that indicated that adding hydroxyapatite (HA) to porous PLGA scaffolds results in a controlled release of HA and promotes superior bone marrow stromal cell adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation compared with control groups.57 The expression levels of Collagen 1 (Coll 1) as an important component of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and bone sialoprotein (BSP) as a marker of mature osteoblasts were measured to further understand the osteochondral progression of hMSCs under osteoinduction. There are two types of proteins that make up the ECM which are collagens and noncollagenous proteins. Approximately 90% of the proteins in the bone matrix are collagens, mostly type I collagens. Noncollagenous proteins such as Osteopontin, Osteocalcin, Matrix gla protein, and BSP make up the bone extracellular matrix in lesser amounts but still contribute significantly to it.58 PLGA (50:50)/PCL and PLGA (50:50)/PLGA (85:15) composite scaffolds expressed high levels of both Coll 1 and BSP proteins after adding TCP, similar to the PCL control scaffold. According to our results, the addition of TCP to polyester composite scaffolds, with its porous structure developed as the fast-degrading component degrades, is effective for osteoblast maturation. Biomaterials used as a drug delivery vehicle or as a scaffold in tissue engineering must be biocompatible and biodegradable. It is also crucial that the degradation byproducts of the material are nontoxic and can be easily removed from the system. The in vivo evaluation of polymeric scaffold biocompatibility using animal models, particularly rats, has become a standard method for determining the tissue response to these scaffolds. As part of this method, histological examinations can be used to examine the inflammation of subcutaneous tissue and the thickness of the fibrous capsule, which are two of the most common host defense responses. In our previous research, we examined the biocompatibility of cellulose acetate (CA) as a natural polymer and compared it to PLGA, a synthetic polymer using a subcutaneous rat animal model. Histological and histomorphometric analysis revealed a higher foreign body response in PLGA after 8 weeks of implantation, while the immune response in CA was significantly lower.59 Our results showed that a change in the pH of the environment associated with the degradation of PLGA as an aliphatic polyester may cause an adverse immune response over time. In the present study, a polyester composite scaffold containing 20 wt.% TCP exhibited minimal tissue response, as indicated by thinner fibrous capsules and fewer macrophages than a composite without TCP. In addition, fibroblasts that produce new collagen and extracellular matrix were seen to increase significantly on polyester composite scaffolds containing TCP, confirming the effectiveness of the wound healing process.60 Based on this approach, we have demonstrated that adding TCP to polyester composite scaffolds significantly neutralized acidity of degradation byproducts and reduced foreign body responses as compared to the cases before adding TCP after 8 weeks of implantation, indicating a higher level of biocompatibility and a more successful healing process.

The pore structure (pore size, strut size, and porosity) of biomedical scaffolds is known to be an important processing parameter because the structure can greatly influence the cellular responses and mechanical properties. Generally, to successfully achieve hard-tissue regeneration, the pore size within the internal microstructure is recommended to be above 300 µm because this size provides functional migration and proliferation of the cultured cells [16]. Therefore, in this work, we fixed the pore size of the fabricated scaffold at 350 µm. Figures 2(a)-(c) show the optical and SEM images of the fabricated scaffolds. As shown in the SEM images, the average pore size was 352, 371, and 386 µm for PA, AP-1, and AP-2, respectively. Additionally, the PCL component in the porous alginate was well coated on the AP-1 and AP-2 scaffolds. Also, it has been known that a higher porosity of scaffold can encourage the cell migration and it is ominously supportive for the fast replacement of the scaffold with bone and cartilage tissues [17]. However, according to Fisher et al, the porosity (57-75%) cannot significantly impact to new bone formation in cranial defect model of rabbits [18]. Additionally, too high porosity can induce low mechanical properties and rapid biodegradation, so careful selection of the porosity of scaffolds should be considered. This paper presents for the first time that poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) nanofibers can show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33) by using an electrospinning method. First, the electrospun fiber bundles are characterized by scanning electron microscope, X-ray, and piezoelectric coefficient measurements. The data show that the supercritical CO2 treatment can greatly enhance the piezoelectricity of electrospun PLLA fibers, which can be resulting from the increased crystallinity of the fibers. Later, it is found that the electrospun PLLA fiber can generate a current of 8 pA and a voltage of 20 mV by a simple push-release process. Further, a single PLLA fiber-based blood pulse sensor is also fabricated and tested and shows around a 2 pA output for blood pulse. Due to easy fabrication and relatively simple structure, this device enables a broad range of promising future applications in the medical sensor area. As a widely used biopolymer, poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) based piezoelectric polymers have attracted a great deal of research attention due to their biocompatibility, flexibility, and relatively large piezoelectric coefficient.1-4 Previously, many researchers have utilized a uniaxial stretching method to process PLLA film and show piezoelectricity along the shear direction of PLLA film.5-7 Recently, we reported that electrospun poly(γ-benzyl-α, L-glutamate fibers can show piezoelectricity along the d33 direction and can be used in microphone sensor applications.8-10 In this paper, we report for the first time that the electrospun PLLA nanofibers can show piezoelectricity along the fiber length direction (d33) after electrospinning. Based on this property, electrospun PLLA fibers show a wide range of promising future applications in the areas of nanogenerators and diagnostic sensors. Since the 1990s, it has been found that, by using a uniaxial stretching method or a magnetic field, the main carbon chain of PLLA material can easily be oriented in a parallel or antiparallel direction to show piezoelectricity along the shear direction.11, 12 Recently, many researchers have used the electrospinning method to fabricate PLLA nanofibers for biomedical applications, such as scaffolding, tissue engineering, and filters.13, 14 In 2012, Sencadas et al. have studied the piezoelectric properties in a PLLA single fiber along the diameter direction of the fiber.15 However, the conformation structure of PLLA material mostly exhibits the α or β form, with a 103 or 31 helical structure, respectively.16-19 Normally, the two adjacent main carbon chain will arrange along the antiparallel direction. Due to the helical structure, the dipole components along the perpendicular direction of the main carbon chain will cancel out each other.19 Therefore, it is hard to exhibit piezoelectricity in PLLA material along the diameter direction and the piezoelectricity will only exhibit along the shear direction. In this paper, we report for the first time that the dipoles inside the PLLA nanofibers can be twisted toward the fiber direction using an electrospinning method. During the process, the shear force generated from a high DC electric field is applied to a PLLA polymer solution and all the dipole component along the main carbon chain can be aligned along the fiber direction during the electrospinning process. Therefore, the electrospun PLLA fibers will show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33).

Generally, these materials can be divided into synthetic polymers and natural piezoelectric ones. PLA is synthesized by polycondensation of lactic acid (LA) monomers, or by ring-opening polymerization of lactides.[45] To obtain the pure L-stereoisomer (PLLA), the synthesis should start from the optically pure L-LA isomer; this is attained only when LA is synthesized by microbial fermentation. The piezoelectric properties observed in PLA and PLLA derive from their semicrystalline structure, characterized by a chiral conformation and the alignment of electric dipoles in the CO groups along the polymer backbone. In the thermodynamically stable α-form of PLA, the CO groups exhibit random orientation, resulting in negligible piezoelectric effects. Conversely, in the β-crystalline form, the CO groups align along the main chain, imparting piezoelectric properties to the material.[46] Achieving this orientation in PLA and PLLA necessitates specific processing techniques, such as thermal stretching or electrospinning, which promote the rearrangement of molecular chains along the stretching direction. Piezoelectricity is often found in natural structures, including human body tissues. Since the discovery of piezoelectric polarization in wool and hair in 1941,[3] piezoelectricity has been observed in various human tissues, including bone, tendon, and skin.[4] At a smaller scale, piezoelectricity has been observed in proteins, amino acids, and polysaccharides, wherein the physical principles of piezoelectricity varied with respect to inorganic materials. The piezoelectric property of poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) arises from its semi-crystalline structure, where aligned electric dipoles of C=O bonds along the polymer backbone generate shear-mode piezoelectricity (d₁₄ coefficient: 7–12 pC N⁻¹) when molecular chains are oriented via stretching, electrospinning, or thermal processing [1–3,6,15]. This alignment transforms the thermodynamically stable α-crystalline phase (random dipole orientation) into the β-crystalline phase, enhancing piezoelectric response [3,6,7]. Key factors influencing piezoelectricity include crystallinity, molecular orientation, and stereoisomer purity (lower D-isomer content improves performance) [6,7].

Biomedical relevance stems from PLLA's biocompatibility, biodegradability, and flexibility. Applications include:  
1. **Biodegradable sensors/actuators**: Force sensors for physiological pressure monitoring, ultrasonic transducers for drug delivery, and blood-brain barrier modulation [1,2].  
2. **Tissue engineering**: Electrospun PLLA nanofibers enable piezoelectric scaffolds for bone healing and cell differentiation [3,5,13].  
3. **Wearable devices**: Self-powered blood pulse sensors and nanogenerators for detecting physiological signals (e.g., carotid pulse) [5,13].  
4. **Air filtration**: Piezoelectric PLLA membranes in face masks use electrostatic adsorption to capture particulate matter (e.g., PM2.5) while being eco-friendly [1–4].  
5. **Surgical tools**: Medical catheters with piezoelectric actuators for thrombosis removal [13,15].  

PLLA avoids the need for electrical poling due to intrinsic shear piezoelectricity, making it advantageous for transient implantable devices [2,3,6]. However, its piezoelectric coefficients remain lower than inorganic materials like PZT [3,6].

This paper presents for the first time that poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) nanofibers can show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33) by using an electrospinning method. First, the electrospun fiber bundles are characterized by scanning electron microscope, X-ray, and piezoelectric coefficient measurements. The data show that the supercritical CO2 treatment can greatly enhance the piezoelectricity of electrospun PLLA fibers, which can be resulting from the increased crystallinity of the fibers. Later, it is found that the electrospun PLLA fiber can generate a current of 8 pA and a voltage of 20 mV by a simple push-release process. Further, a single PLLA fiber-based blood pulse sensor is also fabricated and tested and shows around a 2 pA output for blood pulse. Due to easy fabrication and relatively simple structure, this device enables a broad range of promising future applications in the medical sensor area. As a widely used biopolymer, poly(l-lactic acid) (PLLA) based piezoelectric polymers have attracted a great deal of research attention due to their biocompatibility, flexibility, and relatively large piezoelectric coefficient.1-4 Previously, many researchers have utilized a uniaxial stretching method to process PLLA film and show piezoelectricity along the shear direction of PLLA film.5-7 Recently, we reported that electrospun poly(γ-benzyl-α, L-glutamate fibers can show piezoelectricity along the d33 direction and can be used in microphone sensor applications.8-10 In this paper, we report for the first time that the electrospun PLLA nanofibers can show piezoelectricity along the fiber length direction (d33) after electrospinning. Based on this property, electrospun PLLA fibers show a wide range of promising future applications in the areas of nanogenerators and diagnostic sensors. Since the 1990s, it has been found that, by using a uniaxial stretching method or a magnetic field, the main carbon chain of PLLA material can easily be oriented in a parallel or antiparallel direction to show piezoelectricity along the shear direction.11, 12 Recently, many researchers have used the electrospinning method to fabricate PLLA nanofibers for biomedical applications, such as scaffolding, tissue engineering, and filters.13, 14 In 2012, Sencadas et al. have studied the piezoelectric properties in a PLLA single fiber along the diameter direction of the fiber.15 However, the conformation structure of PLLA material mostly exhibits the α or β form, with a 103 or 31 helical structure, respectively.16-19 Normally, the two adjacent main carbon chain will arrange along the antiparallel direction. Due to the helical structure, the dipole components along the perpendicular direction of the main carbon chain will cancel out each other.19 Therefore, it is hard to exhibit piezoelectricity in PLLA material along the diameter direction and the piezoelectricity will only exhibit along the shear direction. In this paper, we report for the first time that the dipoles inside the PLLA nanofibers can be twisted toward the fiber direction using an electrospinning method. During the process, the shear force generated from a high DC electric field is applied to a PLLA polymer solution and all the dipole component along the main carbon chain can be aligned along the fiber direction during the electrospinning process. Therefore, the electrospun PLLA fibers will show the piezoelectricity along the fiber direction (d33).

Several examples of biodegradable piezoelectric materials derive from various sources, with different structures and degradation pathways. Generally, these materials can be divided into synthetic polymers and natural piezoelectric ones. The former include poly lactic acid (PLA) and poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA, a conformation of PLA containing only the L-stereoisomer), polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly-γ-benzyl-L-glutamate (PBLG), or poly-γ-methyl-L-glutamate (PMLG). PLA is synthesized by polycondensation of lactic acid (LA) monomers, or by ring-opening polymerization of lactides.[45] To obtain the pure L-stereoisomer (PLLA), the synthesis should start from the optically pure L-LA isomer; this is attained only when LA is synthesized by microbial fermentation. The piezoelectric properties observed in PLA and PLLA derive from their semicrystalline structure, characterized by a chiral conformation and the alignment of electric dipoles in the CO groups along the polymer backbone. In the thermodynamically stable α-form of PLA, the CO groups exhibit random orientation, resulting in negligible piezoelectric effects. Conversely, in the β-crystalline form, the CO groups align along the main chain, imparting piezoelectric properties to the material.[46] Achieving this orientation in PLA and PLLA necessitates specific processing techniques, such as thermal stretching or electrospinning, which promote the rearrangement of molecular chains along the stretching direction. PLLA exhibits piezoelectricity predominantly along the Z-axis, characterized by a d14 coefficient typically ranging from 9 to 11 pC N−1,[47] which is notably lower than inorganic piezoelectric materials. Nevertheless, PLLA continues to be extensively utilized in various biomedical applications owing to its biocompatibility and biodegradability. Furthermore, post-treatment procedures aimed at enhancing its molecular orientation and crystallinity can potentially increase its piezoelectric performance (d14 coefficient) up to 20 pC N−1. The piezoelectric properties of PLLA also depend on its optical purity and molecular weight. Tajitsu demonstrated that PLLA with a lower D-isomer content and high molecular weight might result in films with a higher piezoelectric response.[48] Similarly, Schönlein et al. showed that by increasing the D-content from <1% up to 12%, the d14 decreases from 3.7 ± 0.3 pC N−1 to 0.[49] PHB is a biodegradable polyester that belongs to the class of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), naturally occurring biopolymers synthesized by microorganisms under conditions of nutrient limitation.[50] The piezoelectric features of PHA-based materials stem from the presence of an asymmetric carbon atom linked to a polar oxygen group.[51] In the case of pure PHB electrospun nanofibers, the piezoelectric coefficients are ≈3.25 pC N−1 (d31) and 4.13 pC N−1 (d33).[50] The molecular weight of PHB impacts its piezoelectric properties; in fact, it has been observed that a decrease in the molecular weight from 803 to 102 kDa resulted in a lower number of piezoelectric domains in PHB films, leading to a lower piezoresponse.[52]

1.  **Piezoelectric Mechanism**: PLLA exhibits piezoelectricity due to its semi-crystalline structure and chiral conformation. The electric dipoles of aligned C=O bonds perpendicular to the polymer backbone generate piezoelectricity when subjected to mechanical stress. Piezoelectricity primarily manifests in shear mode (d₁₄ coefficient of 7-12 pC N⁻¹) along the z-axis, though longitudinal piezoelectricity (d₃₃) can be achieved in electrospun nanofibers where dipoles align along the fiber direction. [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [8], [10]

2.  **Enhancement via Processing**: The piezoelectric properties depend on crystallinity and molecular orientation. Processing techniques like uniaxial stretching (drawing ratio ~2.5-4.5), electrospinning of aligned nanofibers, and nano-confinement significantly enhance piezoelectricity by promoting the transformation from the α-crystalline phase (random dipoles) to the β-crystalline phase (aligned dipoles) and increasing crystallinity (up to 70% improvement reported). Supercritical CO₂ treatment also enhances piezoelectricity by increasing fiber crystallinity. [1], [2], [3], [8], [10]

3.  **Biomedical Relevance**: PLLA's biocompatibility, biodegradability, and piezoelectricity make it highly suitable for biomedical applications:
    *   **Implantable Sensors**: Biodegradable force/pressure sensors for monitoring physiological pressures (e.g., diaphragmatic contraction, blood pulse) and vascular pressures. They function reliably during degradation (e.g., 4 days in PBS). [1], [2], [6], [15]

As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. Blending PLA with another immiscible or miscible polymer with higher melt viscosity is perhaps a less expensive and practical alternative way to prepare a variety of useful composites and alloys. Blends of PLA with PCL,11, 12 atactic poly[(R, S)-3-hydroxybutyrate],13 poly(ethylene succinate),14 hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol),15 poly(methyl methacrylate),16 poly(ethylene glycol),17 and poly(vinylphenol),18 have been investigated. Most of the above studies revealed that blending PLA with other polymers can substantially modify the mechanical and thermal properties, degradation rate, and permeability, but few distinct evidence of the improvement for melt viscosity can be found in these blends. Recently, Jiang et al.19 showed that the melt elasticity of the biodegradable PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends increased with the concentration of PBAT increasing via blending process, but the viscosity increase is limited. Carboxyl-ended polyester (CP) and solid epoxy (SE) have been widely used in polyester powder coating because they can form a crosslinking structure, and the viscosity of PLA will increase after in situ crosslink if CP and SE are added into the PLA matrix. In this article, CP and SE are used as the modifier of PLA to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA. Compared with the above-mentioned methods (increasing molecular weight, branching/crosslinking and incorporating new functional groups into PLA backbone), this method with CP/SE as the modifier has some outstanding advantages. For instance, the reaction temperature of CP/SE is close to the processing temperature of PLA; CP/SE has a high melt viscosity after reaction, and abundant functional end groups, which are easily accessible. With the unique crosslinking structure after reaction, CP/SE results in the different dispersion phase size and stereo hindrance for the linear polymer. Furthermore, the abundance of hydroxyl end groups attached to CS/SE may have some H-bonding interactions with PLA.20 Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the incorporation of CP/SE into PLA may bring about either the improved melt viscosity or the increased strength.

Many of the methods explored to improve the dispersion and compatibility of CNCs in PLA involve solvent casting or melt-blending processes. In the case of solvent casting, the reported surface modifications include acetylation by reaction with acetic anhydride [13], [14], silanization [15], [16], and grafting (‘to’ or ‘from’) polyesters such as PLA [17], [18]. Grafting of amine terminated PEO on 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) oxidized CNCs was also explored and blends with PLA were prepared by solvent casting using chloroform. An improvement in mechanical properties was achieved, but the matrix glass transition temperature (Tg) decreased [19]. Surfactant pairing has also been used to disperse CNCs in PLA [20], [21], [22], [23]. Surfactants in solution-cast composites generally function as plasticizers that result in reduced composite Tg values [20], [21], [22], [23]. Solvent exchange has been used to develop an understanding of modified-CNC/polymer nanocomposites, but the approach is unpractical due to the large volumes of solvent required. For industrial production of polymer-CNC nanocomposites, melt-processing appears to be the most economical method. Melt processing of CNCs tend to result in CNC-aggregates and phase-separation from the matrix, impeding improvements in materials properties. Several approaches to overcome this problem are to wrap CNCs within another polymer, small-molecule CNC modifications and grafting strategies [6]. In one example, a polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-CNC aqueous dispersion was prepared and then co-extruded with PLA. However, the unmodified CNCs were located predominantly within the co-continuous PVA phase [24]. Good reinforcement by CNCs of the matrix was achieved by silanization of CNCs in citrate buffer which were then dried before being melt blending with PLA [25]. CNCs suspended in toluene after solvent exchange were modified by ‘grafting from’ reactions with l-lactide. The resulting CNC-g-PLA was melt-blended with PLA and good mechanical properties were achieved [17]. Fischer esterification, a one-pot procedure combining both cellulose acid-catalyzed hydrolysis and surface-modification, was recently reported as efficient method to obtained acetylated CNCs [26]. The reaction is performed by dispersing cellulose in an organic acid (e.g. acetic and butyric acid) with addition of a catalytic quantity of hydrochloric acid [26]. By this approach, cellulose hydrolysis and CNC esterification occur concurrently and the resulting modified freeze-dried CNCs are “ready-to-use” [18], [31]. By this method, modifications can be achieved to modulate the surface properties of CNC without the need for tedious and non-practical solvent-exchange protocols.
Processes of PLA melt blending and molding require high operating temperatures above the polymer melting point (up to 200°C) and/or high pressures.16, 19, 22, 24, 39, 56-68 After being melted, PLA is shaped into the desired form by molding (with or without a mechanical press) and cooled down to stabilize its dimensions.23The resulting material can be shaped into a film, fiber, or monolith, but it is non-porous form. Drawbacks of these processes include high-energy consumption and the use of high temperatures that can lead to thermal degradation of PLA leading to the formation of LA monomers.23 On the other hand, PLA degradation is also related to a residence time.23 Schematic presentation of these processes can be seen in Figure 3a,b. Huda et al.59 reported the preparation of PLA films (thickness 0.1-0.2 mm) by compression molding at temperature 180°C. The film showed a clear transition in dynamic mechanical properties. Its recovery of elasticity was faster as process temperature was higher. Alias et al.69 and Klinkajorn & Tanrattanakul62 processed PLA via melt mixing using an internal mixer at 180°C followed by compression molding. Obtained films showed elongation at break of 5%. Rojas-Lema et al.16 exposed PLA beads to thermo-compression at 180°C with a pressure of 40 MPa tons for 3 min by two hot plates and air-cooled at room conditions. Films with a thickness of approximately 250 μm, elongation at break 3.5%, and elastic modulus 2846 MPa were obtained. Melt spinning of PLA was one of the first method used for the preparation of textile fibers.23, 41, 70 After PLA is melted (usually at 185-240°C), it is pumped through a spinneret (die) with numerous holes (one to thousands). PLA is the only biobased and biodegradable polymer which can be processed on a large-scale into textile fibers with sufficient strength.41 A variation of the melt spinning process is electrospinning of PLA melt using a laser.23 This technique relies on using a laser beam (Figure 3d) to melt the PLA locally thus minimizing thermal degradation and electrostatic force to draw fibers.23 This technique allows production of fibers with diameters smaller than 1 μm.23 Hot-melt extrusion (HME) is commercially applied for continuous processing of PLA and is particularly advantageous for an easy material homogenization. A standard unit for HME includes an extruder barrel with rotating screw(s) that mixes polymer melt and pushes it forwards trough the reduced opening (die) where expansion and shaping of the final product occurs.71 HME of PLA takes place at temperatures between 180 and 230°C.72 The extruder can be a stand-alone unit or a part of forming machine for injection molding, melt spinning, and 3D printing. The final material is usually non-porous. PLA can be processed by HME alone or with the addition of other polymers as well as different organic and inorganic substances.72-84 When the molten PLA is extruded through a sheet die and quenched on polished chrome rollers that are cooled with circulating water, PLA films (usual thickness 0.076 mm) and sheets (usual thickness 0.25 mm) are produced.23 To produce a PLA foam, different substances can be added to PLA melt during extrusion including expanded graphite nanoplatelets along with an organic peroxide,85 CO2,86, 87 and water.88 Introduction of CO2 in an extruder barrel lowers polymer viscosity, which allows work at lower temperatures and a decrease in energy consumption compared to standard extrusion processes.
