Molecular weight decrease caused by thermal, hydrolytic, and mechanical degradation of PLA is a major concern during melt processing. Modeling and predicting degradation is essential to minimize material deterioration and material property changes. Current kinetic degradation models show potential to describe degradation, but they are limited to rheometry and focus on thermal and/or hydrolytic degradation only. There is no model yet that describes degradation during melt processing techniques such as injection molding or extrusion. The aim of this work is to establish a degradation model that predicts the molecular weight decrease of PLA throughout single-screw extrusion. A combination of experimental extrusion data and numerical simulations is used to establish the model. Subsequently, the model is experimentally validated to check its predictive quality. The results show good similarity between predictions and measurements for multiple process variables. The maximum deviation between both was found to be 5%. Combining experimental data with numerical simulations allows us to describe the extrusion process in an equipment-independent way, which is essential to use the model for different extruders or dies. Overall, minimizing degradation during processing will avoid the loss of valuable resources, materials, and time, and will result in obtaining high quality products. The sensitivity of the ester bonds in poly(lactic acid) or PLA is a major concern during processing, since polymer chains of molten PLA have the tendency to degrade [1]. The potential presence of moisture in the granules, combined with high shear stresses and temperatures during extrusion or injection molding, may result in hydrolytic, thermal, and mechanical degradation. Chain scission of the polymer chains, caused by the three types of degradation, leads to a decrease in molecular weight, depending on the applied process parameters [2-5]. The selection of process parameters is crucial to minimize polymer degradation, which is nowadays often based on experience by the process operator, recommendations on the technical data sheet of the material supplier or by trial-and-error. Generally, it is not investigated or known whether the selected process parameters result in degradation. Nevertheless, degradation may strongly affect PLA's material properties [2]. In the work of Teixeira et al. [6], the complex viscosity was reported to decrease from 2680 Pa s to around 1300 Pa s at the die end due to degradation during processing. A similar conclusion was reported by Benvenuta-Tapia and Vivaldo-Lima [7], where a decrease from 2300 Pa s for neat PLA to 330 Pa s was observed after processing PLA. Aside from rheological properties, also thermal properties are affected by processing PLA. Due to a decreasing molecular weight caused by degradation, the mobility of the polymer chains increases and allows faster crystallization. A decrease of the cold crystallization temperature from 103.0°C to 97.1°C and an increase of the crystallization temperature from 96.8°C to 100.2°C was reported in the work of Lv et al. [8]. Other researchers [9, 10] confirmed a change in the crystallization behavior. Also the mechanical properties are affected by degradation, such as a reported decrease in the stress at break from 66 to 25 MPa after repeated injection molding cycles [10], explained by a lower number of entanglements due to chain scission. The impact strength was also affected by degradation, as shown in the work of Zenkiewicz et al. [11] where a decrease of 0.19 kJ m−2 (7.4%) occurred in the first reprocessing cycle. Yellowing of PLA can also occur due to degradation, as reported in the work of Agüero et al. [12] by an increase of (blue-yellow value in LAB color space definition) from 10.75 to 20.59. In order to limit the change of PLA's properties and to obtain high quality products after extrusion or injection molding, it is essential to understand the severity of degradation during processing.

Based solely on the provided evidence, the reduction in viscosity of PLA during melt processing is indicative of **molecular weight decrease due to degradation**. This degradation occurs through chain scission reactions caused by:

1.  **Thermal degradation**: Exposure to high processing temperatures breaks polymer chains [1][3][13].
2.  **Hydrolytic degradation**: Residual moisture absorbed by PLA prior to processing leads to hydrolysis of ester bonds in the extruder [2][13].
3.  **Mechanical/Shear degradation**: High shear stresses experienced during processing (e.g., in the extruder screw elements) contribute to chain scission [2][13].

This chain scission reduces the mean molecular weight of the PLA, which directly results in a concurrent decrease in its melt viscosity [1][3][13]. Evidence [2] and [13] explicitly state that thermo-mechanical degradation and hydrolysis during extrusion increase the viscosity ratio of blend components and reduce the matrix shear stress, confirming the link between degradation (chain scission) and viscosity reduction.

In this work, the influence of melt compounding and incorporation of talc on a commercial grade of poly (lactic acid) was studied. The neat material was mixed, for different backflow times, to monitor the effect of processing on this resin. The apparent viscosity of the PLA decreases with compounding time, as the material is subject to thermo mechanical degradation. The elastic modulus of neat PLA, was measured on injection molded dog shape tensile bars. The elastic modulus slightly increases with compounding time, probably because of the molecular weight reduction due to degradation. Concerning the incorporation of talc, it was found that it increases the viscosity measured during the compounding, but it also enhances the stability of the material viscosity during the mixing. Furthermore, the talc, acting as a nucleating agent, has a strong effect on crystallization kinetics, so that by adding 1 % of micrometric talc crystallization the half time reduces one order of magnitude with respect to the pure PLA processed in the same way.
Viscosity is chiefly determined by entanglement in polymer chains. Polymer chains within a polymer melt typically orient in alignment with the applied force, exhibiting shear-thinning behavior, thereby decreasing viscosity with increasing shear rate.5 This phenomenon has been observed in PLA/PVB blends and PLA/PVB/kaolin composites, as shown in Figure 8. An increase in solubility often leads to a rise in viscosity owing to chain entanglement. As detailed in Table 2, Figure 8A,C, PVB, with a larger molecular weight (MW) compared to PLA, demonstrated high complex viscosity and lowest melt flow index (MFI). Moreover, the PLA/PVB blends and composites closely mirrored characteristics of PLA owing to the predominance of PLA (80 wt%). The incorporation of kaolin to PLA/PVB increased the viscosity and reduced the MFI, attributed to the filler effect. Composites featuring modified kaolin exhibited a pronounced viscosity decrease with increasing frequency compared to PLA/PVB and PLA/PVB/K5, indicating the compatibilizing role of modified kaolin. The applied shear force disrupted interfacial interactions among PLA, PVB, and kaolin. In the case of H2SO4, extensive chain scission led to fewer entanglements, resulting in less pronounced viscosity changes. Incorporating both HNO3-K5 and H2SO4-K5 resulted in higher MFI owing to the chain scission effect. Particularly with HNO3-K5, the combination of chain scission and low complex viscosity at moderate shear rates yielded the highest MFI. Incorporating H2SO4-K5 yielded a lower MFI compared to HNO3-K5 because of the introduction of more functional groups, fostering stronger physical interactions in the composites. Acid/calcination-treated K5 exhibited a decrease in viscosity compared to acid-treated K5 due to the removal of residual impurities during calcination and subsequent dehydroxylation. The difference in molecular weight between HCl-K5 and HCl-K5-Cal was insignificant, as indicated in Table 2, resulting in similar MFI values. In contrast, HNO3-K5-Cal and H2SO4-K5-Cal displayed higher molecular weights, leading to lower MFI values compared to HNO3-K5 and H2SO4-K5. This comprehensive investigation into the PLA/PVB/kaolin composites has examined the role of surface-modified kaolin in enhancing the interfacial compatibility and overall performance of polymer blends. The employment of acid and calcination treatments on kaolin improved its compatibility with the PLA/PVB matrix and the mechanical and thermal properties of the composites. Analyses using SEM, GPC, DSC, XRD, FTIR, and rheometer have provided valuable insights into the morphological, molecular, thermal, rheological, and bonding modifications induced by the inclusion of treated kaolin. We also observed various cases of MW reduction and increase using various treatments. The findings reveal that whereas the composite containing H2SO4-K5 represented reduction in mechanical properties owing to the chain scission, that containing HNO3-K5-Cal most effectively enhanced the mechanical properties, indicating the importance of chemical modification in achieving good material characteristics. Despite a reduction in impact strength, the overall enhancements affirmed the potential of utilizing modified inorganic fillers to advance the development of high-performance, sustainable polymer composites. In particular, when HNO3 was used, an improvement in mechanical properties (tensile strength) was observed, while the viscosity decreased and the MFI value increased. This indicates that the incorporation of modified kaolin into the blend can yield a material with good mechanical properties that is easy to process. This study paves the way for future research on the application of diverse inorganic fillers and treatment processes to further refine and expand the utility of biodegradable polymer blends in various industrial applications. Effect of Processing Conditions on Process‐Induced Degradation of Poly(Lactic Acid) During Single‐Screw Extrusion The sensitivity of the ester bonds in poly(lactic acid) or PLA is a major concern during processing, since polymer chains of molten PLA have the tendency to degrade [1]. The potential presence of moisture in the granules, combined with high shear stresses and temperatures during extrusion or injection molding, may result in hydrolytic, thermal, and mechanical degradation. Chain scission of the polymer chains, caused by the three types of degradation, leads to a decrease in molecular weight, depending on the applied process parameters [2-5]. The selection of process parameters is crucial to minimize polymer degradation, which is nowadays often based on experience by the process operator, recommendations on the technical data sheet of the material supplier or by trial-and-error. Generally, it is not investigated or known whether the selected process parameters result in degradation. Nevertheless, degradation may strongly affect PLA's material properties [2]. In the work of Teixeira et al. [6], the complex viscosity was reported to decrease from 2680 Pa s to around 1300 Pa s at the die end due to degradation during processing. A similar conclusion was reported by Benvenuta-Tapia and Vivaldo-Lima [7], where a decrease from 2300 Pa s for neat PLA to 330 Pa s was observed after processing PLA. Aside from rheological properties, also thermal properties are affected by processing PLA. Due to a decreasing molecular weight caused by degradation, the mobility of the polymer chains increases and allows faster crystallization. A decrease of the cold crystallization temperature from 103.0°C to 97.1°C and an increase of the crystallization temperature from 96.8°C to 100.2°C was reported in the work of Lv et al. [8]. Other researchers [9, 10] confirmed a change in the crystallization behavior. Also the mechanical properties are affected by degradation, such as a reported decrease in the stress at break from 66 to 25 MPa after repeated injection molding cycles [10], explained by a lower number of entanglements due to chain scission. The impact strength was also affected by degradation, as shown in the work of Zenkiewicz et al. [11] where a decrease of 0.19 kJ m−2 (7.4%) occurred in the first reprocessing cycle. Yellowing of PLA can also occur due to degradation, as reported in the work of Agüero et al. [12] by an increase of (blue-yellow value in LAB color space definition) from 10.75 to 20.59. In order to limit the change of PLA's properties and to obtain high quality products after extrusion or injection molding, it is essential to understand the severity of degradation during processing.

Without thermo-mechanical degradation of PLA in the extrusion process, the viscosity ratio of the blend components (ηPP1/ηPLA) should be lower than 1 at 200 °C and higher shear rates (kneading elements in the extruder) because of the higher pseudoplastic character of the PP1 dispersed phase than that of PLA. But this viscosity ratio should lower than 1 at high shear rates in the blends with PP2 as dispersed phase. Nonetheless, the reduction of the PLA viscosity by thermo-mechanical degradation and/or hydrolysis reactions in the extruder increases these viscosities ratios along the extruder sections. The influence of processing conditions during melt extrusion on the degradation of poly (lactic acid) has been already investigated [16, 27-31]. This degradation is influenced by the temperature, residence time in the extruder (screw rotation speed and mass flow rate), and the moisture content. Taubner and Shishoo [31] found a reduction in shear viscosity of about 50% at 230 °C and 120 rpm for the samples conditioned at 65% of relative humidity (RH) before measurements. In polymer blends research, the drop breakup phenomenon has been study extensively but the effect of the degradation (chain scission reactions) of the continuous phase (PLA) during the mixing process has not been fully explored [4, 5, 16]. In the extrusion process, the shear viscosity of PLA (matrix) is reduced and a negative effect on the dispersion of the minority phase (PPs) should be expected. Then, there is an enhancement of the viscosities ratios (ηPP1/ηPLA and ηPP2/ηPLA) and a reduction of the matrix shear stress with time. Consequently, an increase of the droplet sizes of the dispersed phase should be obtained. This explains the large sizes of the dispersed phases in the blends without sepiolite clay (Table 6). On the other hand, it has been reported that SEBS-g-MA is an efficient emulsifying agent in PP/PA-6 blends and number-average diameters of the dispersed phases lower that 1 μm have been found in these blends These results have been explained by the emulsifying process where the SEBS-g-MA compatibilizer agent migrates to the melted dispersed phase and a copolymer is formed at the interface that reduces the coalescence of the dispersed phase droplets [4, 5, 32-36]. Nonetheless, in this study, PP1-g-MA seems more efficient than SEBS-g-MA in emulsifying PLAPP1 blends, although one would expect the material with the highest grafting degree to be more reactive toward the PLA (see Table 3). In that sense, the thermal properties of the blend components should have some influence in the morphology of these blends [35].
As a kind of linear aliphatic polyesters synthesized by the ring-opening polymerization of lactides, PLA is typically derived from corn starch fermentation,1 and has good mechanical properties, thermal plasticity, biocompatibility, and ease of fabrication.2 These characteristics enable PLA as a promising polymer for various applications.3 Another feature of PLA is the good safety upon exposure to heat. For example, it does not produce any toxic nitrogen oxide gases and only one third of the combustible heat of polyolefins is generated when it is burned, so it does not damage the incinerator and provides significant energy savings.4 However, the instable processability of PLA needs to be concerned, that is, thermo-oxidative, hydrolytic degradations, and so on. The instability of PLA usually leads to break the polymer chains, as a result to decrease its molecular weight.5 And it would further result in a deterioration of rheological properties, which should be avoided for a processing purpose, especially when high levels of melt viscosity and strength are required. For example, the viscosity and strength of material has significant influence on their final performance when they are in blow molding, blow film, extrusion, and foaming. As is well known, PLA has a very low viscosity and melt strength, so the fabricated films are far away from stability and close to rupturing during blow-film process; and the lower melt tension is not beneficial to obtain satisfying products during blow-molding process. To overcome such shortcomings, attempts to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA have motivated considerable research efforts. One of the most important techniques is increasing the molecular weight of PLA, which can efficiently improve the intrinsic melt intensity of PLA. However, the productivity would decrease for high molecular PLA because of the prolonged reaction time, and the degradation or the color changing is usually inevitable. Furthermore, some investigations on the free radical branching/crosslinking of PLA has been also carried out in the melt mixing process in an extruder or in a kneader with the presence of trace amounts of various peroxides (served as radical initiators).6-8 In these process, branching or crosslinking reaction of PLA molecule chain can happen to some extent because of the reaction of capturing hydrogen by peroxides. However, some of new problems would appear because of the high reactivity of peroxides, such as the excessive crosslinking reaction and the degradation of PLA, which is hard to avoid during such processing. Another method is incorporating some new functional groups onto the PLA backbone to improve its melt viscosity, which paves the way to prepare composites, coated items, and composites/alloys. For example, multi-isocyanate9 and multi-epoxide10 are often used to endow PLA functional groups through copolymerizing reactions during reactive extrusion process, but a good knowledge on the reaction and control of polymerization during manufacturing are necessary. However, the copolymerization reaction is often difficult to realize anticipative results because of the difference of reactive activity between lactide and copolymerizing ester, and the melt intensity of PLA can be seldom improved. Therefore, extensive investigations on polymer blend technology have been also carried out. Blending PLA with another immiscible or miscible polymer with higher melt viscosity is perhaps a less expensive and practical alternative way to prepare a variety of useful composites and alloys. Blends of PLA with PCL,11, 12 atactic poly[(R, S)-3-hydroxybutyrate],13 poly(ethylene succinate),14 hydrophilic poly(vinyl alcohol),15 poly(methyl methacrylate),16 poly(ethylene glycol),17 and poly(vinylphenol),18 have been investigated. Most of the above studies revealed that blending PLA with other polymers can substantially modify the mechanical and thermal properties, degradation rate, and permeability, but few distinct evidence of the improvement for melt viscosity can be found in these blends. Recently, Jiang et al.19 showed that the melt elasticity of the biodegradable PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) blends increased with the concentration of PBAT increasing via blending process, but the viscosity increase is limited. Carboxyl-ended polyester (CP) and solid epoxy (SE) have been widely used in polyester powder coating because they can form a crosslinking structure, and the viscosity of PLA will increase after in situ crosslink if CP and SE are added into the PLA matrix. In this article, CP and SE are used as the modifier of PLA to improve the melt rheological properties of PLA. Compared with the above-mentioned methods (increasing molecular weight, branching/crosslinking and incorporating new functional groups into PLA backbone), this method with CP/SE as the modifier has some outstanding advantages. For instance, the reaction temperature of CP/SE is close to the processing temperature of PLA; CP/SE has a high melt viscosity after reaction, and abundant functional end groups, which are easily accessible. With the unique crosslinking structure after reaction, CP/SE results in the different dispersion phase size and stereo hindrance for the linear polymer. Furthermore, the abundance of hydroxyl end groups attached to CS/SE may have some H-bonding interactions with PLA.20 Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the incorporation of CP/SE into PLA may bring about either the improved melt viscosity or the increased strength.
Figure 3 shows the viscosity index (VI) obtained to assess the stability and flow of the polymeric fluids. This dimensionless parameter indicates how the viscosity of PLA and PLA/AES blends varied with temperature (190°C). Therefore, a higher viscosity index is required to form a consistent fluid and to minimize melt fracture. PLA has a viscosity index of around 0.96, slightly lower than the PLA/AES blend (0.98). The morphological changes of PLA and PLA/AES blends before and after annealing were analyzed using SEM analysis and correlated with the mechanical properties. Figure 4a,b shows SEM images (magnifications of 1000×) of fracture surfaces of PLA and PLA/AES blends. A distinct fracture morphology was observed between PLA and PLAT, indicating that the heat treatment affected the deformation mechanism. PLA fracture surface shows a smooth texture characteristic of a fragile material. In addition, well-defined and delineated striations are observed, with alternating smooth regions. Although PLA exhibits brittle behavior, the fracture aspect indicates some resistance to crack propagation. Contrastingly, the morphology of PLAT indicated a more homogeneous fracture, with no separation of smooth regions by striations. The PLAT deformation mechanism favored rapid crack propagation under mechanical impact stress, confirming the trend shown later in Figure 9. The annealing heat treatment of PLAT formed a structure with a high level of crystallinity and large spherulites, resulting in a smoother fracture surface. The higher crystallinity is particularly detrimental to the mechanical behavior on impact since the number of inter-spherulite binding molecules decreases as the size of the spherulites increases.59 As a result, crack propagation occurs more rapidly, confirming the lower impact performance of PLAT. Figure 4(c,e,g,i,k,m) shows the fracture surface of PLA/AES blends (70:30%) without annealing treatment as a function of DCP. The PLA/AES blends show phase separation, with AES particles dispersed in the PLA matrix. This morphology is typical of immiscible blends, even showing voids between phases that indicate pulled-out AES particles (see red circles). However, the existence of refined AES particles adhered to the PLA matrix indicates a partial affinity between these phases (see white circles). The affinity is probably due to the polar interactions of the AES acrylonitrile fraction with the PLA carbonyl. The acrylonitrile/carbonyl interaction provides some level of compatibilization through secondary interactions, which is crucial to strengthen the PLA/AES interface and contribute to toughening. The average AES particle size reduced as DCP concentration increased in the PLA/AES blend, probably due to crosslinking. The crosslinking of the PLA/AES blend promoted higher adhesion of the dispersed phase, which suggests a more prominent molecular entanglement between PLA and AES, as discussed in torque rheometry and MFI. However, the morphology of the PLA/AES/DCP blends revealed a critical DCP content to optimize wettability between PLA and AES, as seen in Figure 4k. Incorporating 0.8 phr DCP into the PLA/AES blend promoted the formation of a more stable morphology with refined, adhered, well-distributed, and dispersed AES particles. Meanwhile, the PLA/AES/DCP (0.8 phr) blend had a higher uniformity in the particle size of the dispersed phase and a marked void reduction. These observations evidence that the PLA/AES interface withstood and distributed stresses more effectively, indicating an optimized crosslinking process with 0.8 phr DCP. The compatibility within the PLA/AES/DCP (0.8 phr) blend revealed by the morphology of the fracture surface confirms the high impact strength and elongation at break results of this system, which were superior to the other materials (see Figure 8 and S2). Therefore, even though there is an increasing crosslinking reaction in PLA and AES with DCP presence, as evidenced by torque rheometry, there is a critical DCP content to form free radicals and optimize the degree of crosslinking.

Molecular weight decrease caused by thermal, hydrolytic, and mechanical degradation of PLA is a major concern during melt processing. Modeling and predicting degradation is essential to minimize material deterioration and material property changes. Current kinetic degradation models show potential to describe degradation, but they are limited to rheometry and focus on thermal and/or hydrolytic degradation only. There is no model yet that describes degradation during melt processing techniques such as injection molding or extrusion. The aim of this work is to establish a degradation model that predicts the molecular weight decrease of PLA throughout single-screw extrusion. A combination of experimental extrusion data and numerical simulations is used to establish the model. Subsequently, the model is experimentally validated to check its predictive quality. The results show good similarity between predictions and measurements for multiple process variables. The maximum deviation between both was found to be 5%. Combining experimental data with numerical simulations allows us to describe the extrusion process in an equipment-independent way, which is essential to use the model for different extruders or dies. Overall, minimizing degradation during processing will avoid the loss of valuable resources, materials, and time, and will result in obtaining high quality products. curved composite parts The processing of polymers usually leads to degradation, which affects the nucleation rate, viscosity and mechanical properties, especially for PLA.[43] The effect of different processing conditions on the mechanical properties of PLA copolymers is presented in Table 3. Both process conditions and molecular weight of PLA influence the mechanical properties of PLA after molding. The mechanical properties of PLA were all reduced by extrusion followed by the thermoforming process, but Young's modulus of the material was higher after thermoforming compared to extrusion followed by a blow molding process. However, for the same process conditions, as the molecular weight of PLA increased, the tensile strength and elongation at break first increased and then decreased, and the best mechanical properties were obtained at a molecular weight of 160 kDa. Temperature is one of the key influencing factors in the injection molding of PLA. Powder solids were unable to form tensile samples at 180 °C when extruded from the nozzle of the injection molding machine, whereas they could be formed at higher temperatures (i.e., 200-230 °C). This may be due to the similarity in polarity of PLLA and PDLA when blended they form stereo-complex poly(lactic acid) with paired helix formation acting as nucleation sites and the polarity of both results in high crystallinity of the material, which cures immediately at 180 °C.[44-46] In addition, the properties of lactic acid-based polymers depend greatly on the ratio and distribution between the two stereoisomers, and better mechanical properties are more likely to be obtained for semi-crystalline PLA compared to amorphous PLA.[47] The crystallization rate of PLLA and PDLA blends on cooling after injection is much more rapid than that of pure PLLA due to the formation of stereoconjugates between the two during high-temperature blending.[46] It has been indicated that when L-lactic acid and D-lactic acid form block copolymers, there is a possibility that they can become nucleating agents for the crystals of stereoconjugates or bulking agents for PLLA and PDLA.[45] The stereocomplex formed by PLLA50/PDLA50 was added to the PLLA matrix to realize the self-nucleation of PLLA, and the results showed that the stereocomplex greatly improved the elongation at break of PLLA.[46] Moreover, the steric complexes were much more effective than the commonly used nucleating agent talc in increasing the crystallization rate of PLLA.[48] It is worth noting that the incorporation of nucleating agents is one of the most widely used methods for accelerating the crystallization process and increasing the crystallinity content of PLA.[49, 50] A study has been conducted to analyze the relationship between the level of crystallinity and mechanical properties of PLA injection molded specimens. To blow PLA resins at extremely high rates, the melt index (MI) values of PLA needed to be increased to proper values. Addition of plasticizer (e.g. citrate ester25 and triacetine (TAc)26, 27) in PLA resins was proven as an effective way to increase the MI and processability of PLA resins. In comparison with citrate ester, the thermal stability of TAc is relatively poor and liable to degrade during the melt-blown processes of PLA. Moreover, PLA resins are prone to hydrolysis or degrade at relatively high temperatures during their melt-blown processes. They are also well known for their low tearing resistance and brittle characteristics, especially for melt-blown nonwovens encountered with hydrolysis or thermal degradation. Addition of toughening agents in PLA resins was proven as an efficient way to improve their toughness.28, 29 Among these toughening agents, poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) has attracted many attentions because of their highly compatibility with PLA and good processability even after melt-blending with PLA resins.28 In fact, many commercial biodegradable films were prepared by melt-blending of proper amounts of PBAT in PLA before film-blowing of the PLA/PBAT resins. Our early investigation28 found that the values of elongation at break of PLA/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) blends did improve significantly after addition proper amounts of the PBAT in PLA resins. However, the melting temperature of PBAT is significantly lower than that of PLA that can lead to poor compatibility or even phase separation between PLA and PBAT phases during the melt crystallization processes of PLA/PBAT blends. In fact, demarcated PBAT droplets were found dispersed in PLA matrices that often lead to poor tearing resistance and toughness of the PLA/PBAT blends.28 In comparison with PBAT, our latest research29 used biodegradable poly(ethylene glutaric-co-terephthalate) copolyester “FePol” (FP) with relatively higher melting temperature as the toughening agent for PLA. Somewhat interestingly, the tear resistance values of PLA/FP blown films improved significantly after addition of proper amounts of FP resins, in which the tear resistance values of PLA/FP blown films are significantly better than those of the PLA/PBAT blown films with the same amounts of toughening agent. As far as we know, no investigation has ever been reported on the preparation of PLA melt-blown nonwoven using FP as toughening agent. In this study, FP together with a kind of citrate ester plasticizer named acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC) was chosen to prepare PLA/FP/ATBC blends for melt blowing. The influences of the compositions of ATBC and FP on the morphology, rheological and tensile properties of PLA/FP/ATBC nonwovens are reported.

Based on the provided evidence, the viscosity reduction of PLA during melt processing is indicative of **molecular weight decrease caused by chain scission due to degradation**. This degradation arises from thermo-mechanical, hydrolytic, or thermal mechanisms under high-temperature and high-shear processing conditions like extrusion or injection molding [1][2][3][5][6][10]. 

Key supporting observations include:
1. Degradation breaks ester bonds in PLA chains, reducing molecular weight and entanglement density, which directly lowers viscosity [5][10].
2. The viscosity decrease correlates with reduced molecular weight, as seen in reduced complex viscosity values (e.g., from 2300 Pa·s to 330 Pa·s) after processing [5][10].
3. Chain extenders (e.g., PLA-MA) can counteract viscosity loss by restoring molecular weight via branching or chain extension, confirming the inverse relationship between molecular weight and viscosity [1][2].
4. Fillers like talc may initially increase viscosity but do not prevent degradation-induced viscosity reduction over processing time [3].
5. Acid treatments (e.g., H₂SO₄) exacerbate viscosity reduction by promoting chain scission [4].

question: What is the 'burst release' phenomenon in drug delivery microspheres?
ground_truth: Burst release is the uncontrolled, rapid release of a significant portion of the loaded drug (often 20-50%) immediately upon administration. It occurs due to drug trapped on the surface or in pores connected to the surface dissolving before the polymer matrix degrades. This is often undesirable as it can lead to toxicity.

Many methods, such as spray drying, ionotropic gelation, coacervation, emulsification/solvent evaporation and crosslinking, have been developed for preparation of chitosan microspheres [32, 33]. In ionotropic gelation and coacervation processes, the pH of the solution must be strictly controlled, and morphology and size of the prepared microspheres are generally nonuniform and uncontrollable [32, 34]. Compared to the methods mentioned above, the crosslinked method has a strong potential in development of polymer microspheres to overcome the above defects, while meanwhile providing narrow particle size distributions and good morphology of the microspheres, which prolongs the retention time frame and controls the release behavior of the active agent [14]. The CS-microspheres crosslinked with chemical crosslinkers, including formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, ethylene glycol, diglycidyl ether, tripolyphosphate and disulfide, have been reported for favorable stability and for providing a controlled release ability of many drugs [28, 35, 36], but has disadvantages of cytotoxicity and physiological incompatibility [37]. 1.  **Burst release** refers to the phenomenon where "more than 50% of the drug is released at the initial stage or in a very short time" from a delivery system. This is a common problem in drug delivery systems, including microspheres. [1]
2.  In microspheres specifically, it manifests as a "significant sudden release phenomenon at an early stage". [8] Evidence describes observations like a "massive burst release" with "approximately 80 to 100% of the payload being released within the first 6 h" in physiological ionic strength environments. [3] Conversely, formulations can also exhibit "very low burst release". [6]
3.  **Causes** associated with burst release in microspheres include:
    *   Surface characteristics and properties of the sample. [1]
    *   Drug location: Significant burst release can occur when a substantial amount of drug is located at or near the surface of the microspheres, making it susceptible to rapid diffusion or dissolution upon contact with the release medium. [7]
    *   Processing conditions: Methods like spray drying can make encapsulation difficult and lead to an "obvious" burst release effect. [7] Similarly, fast solvent evaporation during microsphere formation can create large surface pores, allowing drug near the surface to be washed off easily, reducing encapsulation efficiency and contributing to low burst release if surface drug is minimized. [6]
    *   Drug-carrier interactions: Electrostatic interactions between the drug and carrier polymer are weakened by high ionic strength in physiological environments (e.g., PBS or saline), leading to rapid burst release due to charge screening. [3] Weaker binding of hydrophobic drugs can also contribute to undesired spontaneous release. [3]
    *   Polymer hydrophilicity: Highly hydrophilic polymer matrices can lead to rapid water uptake and drug diffusion, causing initial burst release. [5]

question: What is the 'hydrolysis half-life' of anhydride bonds compared to ester bonds?
ground_truth: Anhydride bonds are much more hydrolytically unstable than ester bonds. The half-life of an anhydride bond can be minutes to hours, leading to rapid surface erosion of polyanhydrides (days to weeks). In contrast, ester bonds (in PLA, PCL) have half-lives of months to years, leading to slower bulk erosion.

The long-term goal of Langmuir monolayer degradation experiments is to predict the degradation kinetics of the corresponding bulk material. A recent study found a lifetime of about 55 days for PCL films at very high pH.35 The comparable values hint that the degradation rate constants determined in monolayers are applicable to bulk materials, but to truly understand how the kinetic data from Langmuir monolayers can be applied to bulk materials, experiments comparing bulk degradation and Langmuir monolayer degradation kinetics over a range of different materials and conditions have to be carried out. Currently, the most widely used method for synthesizing polymer hydrogels revolves around utilizing a diverse range of dynamic interactions. These interactions contain reversible covalent bonds such as Diels-Alder, disulfide, borate ester, and imine reactions, as well as supramolecular interactions including host-guest interactions, metal coordination, ionic interactions, and hydrogen bonding. The borate ester (B-O) bond is a hexagonal or pentagonal ring [16], [17] when boric acid reacts with cis-1,3- or 1,2-diol. This structure is reversible and dependent on the pH and temperature of the environment [18], [19]. The B-O bond easily forms in water-based solutions that contain water-soluble polyols or other substrates with electron-donating groups [20]. Therefore, B-O bond cooperation is widely employed as a network strategy in the synthesis of hydrogel materials [21], [22], [23]. He et al. reported an extremely flexible hydrogel with self-healing properties and a double cross-linked network. This network is achieved through the formation of boric acid ester bonds via polyvinyl alcohol and borax, as well as acylhydrazone bonds formed by aldehyde-based nanocellulose and adipic acid dihydrazide-modified alginate [24]. The incorporation of dynamic acylhydrazone bonds notably enhanced the hydrogel's flexibility, leading to a substantial increase in elongation from 480 % to around 1440 %. Li et al. developed a polyethylene-based flexible hydrogel crosslinked with borax, utilizing sodium alginate (SA), tannic acid (TA), and alcohol (PVA) [25]. The toughness of the hydrogel prepared via a simple one-pot method reached 587.1 KJ m−1. Du et al. developed a double-network supramolecular hydrogel by combining phenylboronic acid, galactomannan (GG), tannic acid (TA), metal ion Al3+ and polyacrylamide (PAM) chains. This unique combination results in the formation of borate ester bond dynamic crosslinks and MBA (N, N′-methylene bisacrylamide) covalent crosslinks [26]. The dynamic nature of the borate ester bond facilitates controlled modulation of the catechol group, achieving a reversible transition between viscosity and debonding. This dual-network architecture establishes a robust electron transport pathway for aluminum ions, resulting in a conductivity of 4.9 mS·cm−1. Most borate-based hydrogels exhibit rapid self-healing characteristics, allowing the healing hydrogel to effectively recover its mechanical strength [27], [28], [29]. However, these borate-based hydrogels often exhibit poor mechanical strength, facing a challenge to balance the performance between strength and toughness [30], [31], [32]. The toughness of these hydrogels is usually weak, with toughness values at the kilojoule level [33], [34], which limits their application as strain sensors. Additionally, conductive hydrogels using pure water as the dispersing medium will freeze and lose their original conductivity below zero degrees Celsius [35], [36], [37]. Therefore, improving mechanical properties such as stress, strain, flexibility, and conductivity under different conditions (room temperature and low temperature) while maintaining strong self-healing abilities remains a critical issue for borate ester bond hydrogels used as strain sensors. The decrease in conductivity of hydrogels at lower temperatures is primarily attributed to an increase of hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Two main strategies exist to reduce the hydrogen bonding between water molecules. The first method is to introduce polyelectrolyte or zwitterionic polymer to construct intrinsic antifreeze hydrogels. The second method is to introduce polyols (ethylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, etc.) or to add ions [38], [39]. Considering the conductivity of the hydrogel, the incorporation of ions is currently the most feasible and low-cost method for obtaining antifreeze hydrogels. Lithium chloride is an excellent water retention agent and antifreeze. It can not only be used as an antifreeze to reduce the freezing point of water, but also as an electrolyte to provide conductive ions and improve the conductivity of the gel.
Thanks to the low activation energy of the formation and cleavage, the imine bond has been widely investigated and used in dynamic polymers (e.g., self-healing and recyclable thermosets).[6, 13, 14, 16-18] Meanwhile, due to the low activation energy induced fast reaction kinetics, the imine bond is an ideal linkage in stimuli-responsive components.[19] However, the imine bond is unstable in water. Even though biodegradable polymers can gain significant benefits from the imine bond considering the water content in living organisms,[20] the imine bonds as DCBs suffer from the water-stability issue. Substitutions, including aryl, hydrazone, acyl hydrazone, or oxime, can improve their water stability. These imine derivatives can simply be prepared via click reactions (Scheme 2).[21, 22] Another strategy is to replace the carbonyl with 1,3-dicarbonyls to form vinylogous urethane (Scheme 3) with high thermodynamically chemical stability below 100 °C.[23, 24] With the promising characteristics of imine chemistry, it has been extensively involved in stimuli-dynamic polymers and responsive polymers including hydrogels and vitrimers.[19, 25] For instance, one group has prepared hydrogels with imine bonds by the Schiff base reaction between dialdehyde-modified hyaluronic acid (AHA) and cystamine dihydrochloride (Cys) under mild reaction.[26] With the increase of Cys content, the storage moduli (G′) of the produced hydrogels increased from ≈100 to ≈1000 Pa, possibly due to the formation of high cross-linking density networks contributed by both imine bonds and electrostatic interactions between amino and carboxylic groups. In addition, the hydrogels exhibited good self-healing behaviors at the pH range of ≈3-4. Although the hydrogel was injectable due to its short gelation time, cytotoxic problems arose from the generation of hydrolysis products and the presence of HCl (required for the Schiff reaction), thus limiting their application in biomedical fields. To reduce the hydrolysis potential of the formed imine bonds, the group has replaced the Cys with 3, 3′-dithiobis (propionyl hydrazide) (DTP) in their follow-up investigation as illustrated in Figure 2.[27] This allows the generation of more stable hydrazone bonds without the use of HCl during the gelation, which significantly improved the biocompatibility of the corresponding hydrogels. Compared to the AHA/Cys hydrogel, AHA/DTP exhibited a shorter gelation time (≈50 s for AHA/DTP hydrogel and ≈100 s for AHA/Cys hydrogel) and stiffness in the range of 2-20 kPa. The similar stiffness achieved by AHA/DTP hydrogel compared to native tissue (0.1-16 kPa) made it suitable to be used in spinal cord injury (SCI) repair. Moreover, with a specific molar proportion (aldehyde/amine = 1/8), the hydrogels exhibited an outstanding self-healing efficiency in terms of strain and stress. Due to the abundance of hydrophilic sites in polysaccharides, hydrogen bonds play a large role in their cohesion. In cellulose, besides the β-glucose’s OH (HB donor and acceptor, OOH), ether groups (HB acceptor, OCOC) are also able to participate in HBs (see Figure 7). We observed a number of 0.78 hydrogen bonds per donor group in cellulose (Figure 8b). These hydrogen bonds occur predominantly (79%) among the hydroxyl groups and showed a relatively high average lifetime (ca. 4 ns). Moreover, as seen in Figure 8b, while the presence of PLA induces a marginal decrease in the number of HBs per donor in cellulose, it triggers an increase in the HB lifetime (reaching ca. 5 ns). In chitin, besides hydroxyl and ether groups, amide (NCO) groups also participate in hydrogen bonds both as HB donors (NH) and acceptors (CO). We observed that in chitin, OH groups interact relatively evenly with themselves (0.32 HB/OOH), NCO (0.29 HB/OOH), and ether groups (0.24 HB/OOH), resulting in a slightly higher number of HBs (0.85) per group than in cellulose. On the other hand, NCO interacts much better with OH groups (0.29 HB/NCO) and themselves (0.25 HB/NCO) than with ether groups (0.04 HB/NCO), resulting in a much lower HB count for the group (0.58). Furthermore, as seen in Figure 8b, differently than in cellulose, τLT values in chitin are considerably lower with HBs involving at a time hydroxyl groups or amide groups lasting for, respectively, only 2.7 and 3.5 ns. Both the smaller number of hydrogen bonds per acetyl group and the ephemerality of its hydrogen bonds could explain the less effective chitin’s self-reorganization (cf. Figures 3 and 5) in the presence of PLA. We studied PLA associations with cellulose and chitin in terms of their mutual morphology, mechanical properties, and underlying mutual interactions. Our modeling and simulation strategy demonstrated a full-scale reordering of polysaccharide macromolecules upon large PLA concentrations and a reversed subtle reorienting of PLA molecules upon polysaccharides. Finally, we carried out an extensive nanoscopic analysis of the main interactions taking place in these components, shedding light on the single- and dual-phase interactions between PLA and cellulose or chitin. We expect that these results will offer meaningful insights into the development of higher performing PLA-based biopolymer materials.

Hydrogels are highly hydrated polymeric networks that have been extensively researched for various biomedical applications. In particular, synthetic hydrogels can be designed to be nondegradable or degradable depending on the targeted application. The majority of hydrolytically degradable hydrogels are engineered to contain ester linkages located either in the cross-link or the backbone of the hydrogel. The hydrolysis of these ester bonds has been widely studied in the literature where the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions (i.e., neutral, acid and base). The rate of ester hydrolysis is both pH and temperature dependent. The hydrolysis rate has been shown to generally increase with the acidity or alkalinity of the environment.1 Also, it has been reported that heat can accelerate the hydrolysis rate by providing more energy to the reactants to overcome the activation energy required to initiate the hydrolysis reaction.2-4 Interestingly, although the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions, similar end products, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, are obtained.4 The hydrolysis kinetics of ester bonds also vary depending on the chemical structure of the ester,5, 6 as well as other factors such as polymer crystallinity and wettability.7 It was reported that ester bonds associated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) degrade much more rapidly than ester linkages of polycaprolactone (PCL).8, 9 Moreover, changes made to the polymer structure and size may also affect the degradation mechanisms. For example, bulk PLA has been shown to degrade in both acidic and basic environments, whereas PLA brushes only degrade in basic conditions.10, 11 Conversely, other studies of cross-linked polymers containing esters in the cross-link have demonstrated that their gels were nondegradable on the timeframes studied. Hennink et al. have reported that dextran hydrogels with high cross-linking density were resistive to hydrolysis despite having an ester group in the cross-links.12 Hydrogels formed from poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) conjugated with an ester containing methacrylate moiety were also shown to be hydrolytically stable over a period of several months.13, 14 One major advantage of hydrolytically degradable synthetic hydrogels is that the degradation rate of these gels can be tailored according to the targeted biomedical application. Previous studies have shown that hydrogels of tuned degradation profile can be engineered by varying the number of degradable linkages, macromer concentration and degree of cross-linking.15 Martens et al. successfully tailored the degradation of PVA gels grafted with ester acrylate groups from 1 to 12 to 35 days by varying the macromer concentration from 10 to 15 to 20 wt % respectively.15 Moreover, increasing the cross-linking density of the PVA ester acrylate gels from 0.3 to 0.64 mol/L by fabricating the gels using macromers of different molecular weights also increased the degradation time from 12 to 45 days.15 The ability to tune the degradation rate of these hydrogels is a major advantage in terms of designing tissue engineering matrices for various biomedical applications, such as drug delivery.16 For example, tailoring the hydrogel degradation also controls the drug release rate, which then permits stable clearance of the drug from the body without exerting too much stress on the kidney.17
In fact, to ensure the durability and reliability of hydrogels, substantial effort and progress have been devoted to the intrinsic self-healable hydrogels. One of the most widely used approaches for endowing hydrogels with intrinsic self-healability is the exploitation of supramolecular chemistries on the basis of the reversible non-covalent interactions,[8, 14-19] such as hydrogen-bonding, electrostatic or ionic interactions, metal coordination, hydrophobic associations, host-guest interactions, and π-π stacking. In addition to the noncovalent self-healing mechanisms, the recent advances in dynamic covalent chemistry have also offered an alternative strategy to the construction of self-healable hydrogels.[18, 20-22] Several dynamic covalent bonds with the reversibility and dynamic nature, such as disulfide bonds (thiol-disulfide interchange reaction), cyclohexenes (Diels-Alder thermoreversible cycloaddition reaction), carbon-nitrogen bonds (imine or acylhydrazone exchange reactions), and especially the boronate ester linkages (boronic acid-diol reversible reaction) have been successfully applied to generate self-healing hydrogels. Despite the great progress achieved previously, one of the long-standing challenges in the field of intrinsic self-healing hydrogels is to resolve the tradeoff between the mechanical property and self-healing capacity.[7, 10, 13, 16] Apparently, the unstable and highly reversible noncovalent or dynamic covalent bonds behind self-healable systems conflict with the high mechanical performances that typically company with stable and strong intermolecular bonds. In addition, the mobility and dynamics of polymer chains within the hydrogel matrix play a key role in ensuring self-healing. Therefore, there is also a conflict between robust structure for mechanical strength and high chain mobility for self-healing, when it comes to robust self-healing hydrogels. As a result, even though there are numerous reported instances of self-healable hydrogels, the hydrogels with both high strength and high self-healability are rather unusual, which severely limit the applications of these hydrogels. Recently, a series of strategies, such as nanocomposite[4, 22-27] and double-network (DN)[8, 28, 29] approaches, have been developed to cope with the above-mentioned dilemma. Especially, the DN hydrogels consisted of two asymmetric polymer networks, have demonstrated to be able to effectively reinforce the hydrogels and dissipate the energy during deformation.[8, 30-33] However, the self-healing capacity of conventional DN hydrogels was usually sacrificed.[8, 10, 31, 34] In sum, to expand application scopes of hydrogels, it is imperative to explore a simple and efficient strategy to develop intrinsic self-healing hydrogels while simultaneously achieving good mechanical properties. In this study, we designed a facile but effective approach to balance the tradeoff between strength and healability of self-healing hydrogels via synergistic integration of dynamic covalent bonds and hydrogen bonds within DN hydrogel matrix. As shown in Scheme 1, the photo-initiator IRGACURE 1173 and a special monomer (N-acryloyl glycinamide (NAGA)) with demonstrated capability of forming the strong intra/intermolecular multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions[30, 35, 36] were dissolved and dispersed in polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-borax slime. As a widely used polyhydroxy hydrogel material, PVA can be crosslinked by borax to obtain PVA-borax slime with high self-healing capacity, due to the formation of interchain dynamic diol-borax complexations[22, 26, 37, 38] The PVA-borax slime, as one of the most widely studied self-healing hydrogel systems, has extremely weak mechanical properties and very low stability. However, after initiating in situ polymerization of NAGA by UV exposure, the poly(N-acryloyl glycinamide) (PNAGA) chains and the resultant PNAGA/PVA noncovalent DN were constructed by the intra/intermolecular hydrogen-bonding interactions. Compared with the neat PVA-borax hydrogels,[38-40] the prepared PNAGA/PVA-borax DN hydrogels (denoted as PN-x/PB hydrogels) displayed significant improvement in mechanical strength while without significant compromise in self-healing ability. The effects of different concentrations of PNAGA on the mechanical and rheological properties as well as the self-healing process of these hydrogels were investigated. The results indicated our success in developing a simple but promising one-pot method to prepare robust self-healing hydrogels, especially considering the readily prepared starting materials and easy preparation process. Hydrogels based on cross-linking of PVA with borax have received much attention and widespread industrial interest due to their desirable features, such as non-toxicity, cheap cost, and ready availability.[21, 22, 26, 38, 41-44] In addition, the water-soluble and biocompatible PNAGA as ideal hydrogel materials can undergo crosslinker-free gelation through hydrogen-bonding interactions.[35, 36, 45] However, their mechanical properties were still poor. The PVA-borax hydrogels, more like slime, exhibited non-Newtonian behavior, which can flow under low stress and have limited dimensional stability[43, 44] The PNAGA hydrogels were also of high viscosity and low strength. The DN hydrogels have been demonstrated to be able to effectively improve the mechanical properties, but often at the expense of the self-healing capacity.[8, 30-33] However, the physically or dynamically crosslinked DN hydrogels are expected to simultaneously improve the mechanical properties and self-healability.[10] Inspired by such, the PNAGA/PVA-borax (named as PN-x/PB) DN hydrogels were designed and constructed via synergistic integration of dynamic boronate bonds and multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions (Scheme 1). The PN-x/PB hydrogels were obtained by using a UV-initiated in situ polymerization of NAGA in PVA-borax slime (Figure 1). It also can be seen from Figure 1 that, after integrating PNAGA into PVA-borax slime, the transparent and flowable hydrogel finally turned into white, opaque, and robust hydrogel with improved mechanical strength and self-healing capability.

Our work demonstrates how the small molecule tannic acid behaves as a binder for silicon anodes. Despite having a much lower molecular weight compared with popular polymeric binder materials, tannic acid is effective due to the large number of hydrogen-bonding groups (14.8 mmol of OH/g of TA), which is even greater than poly(acrylic acid) (13.8 mmol of −COOH/g of repeat unit of PAA) and polydopamine (13.3 mmol of −OH/g of repeat unit of polydopamine) (see Table S3). As shown in Table S1, the cycling performance of our silicon electrode with TA binder was comparable to other water-based binders reported in the literature. This comparison shows that the TA electrodes reported here compare favorably. One other recent study reported excellent performance in silicon anodes with citric acid as a binder. (70) Our work along with this recent study indicates that branched, functional small molecules may be superior (or comparable) to many polymers as binders for silicon anodes. Because it is difficult to compare performance of binders across different reports due to differences in electrode composition, loading, battery assembly, and cycling conditions, we performed an in-house comparison with a few common binders. Figure S14 shows the cycling performance of silicon electrodes with poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF), poly(acrylic acid) (PAA), and sodium alginate (Alg). We purposefully used similar active material loading, battery assembly, and cycling conditions. The 70/10/20 Si/TA/CB anode possessed the best performance in this in-house comparison. Si/PVDF/CB demonstrated the lowest capacity due to the absence of hydrogen-bonding groups. Si/PAA/CB showed lower capacity than Si/TA/CB, possibly due to lower density of −COOH groups. Si/Alg/CB also showed lower capacity than Si/TA/CB despite having higher density of −OH groups (18.3 mmol of −OH/g of repeat unit of Alg), which can be attributed to the lack of a branched structure. Therefore, this in-house comparison demonstrates the importance of hydrogen-bonding groups and branched structures for effective silicon anode binders. This report isolated the effects hydrogen bonding of the small molecule binder tannic acid for silicon anodes. With few exceptions, silicon anodes primarily incorporate high molecular weight polymeric binders. However, tannic acid, which is a small, branched, water-soluble polyphenol with a large number of −OH functional groups, performs comparably to many polymeric binders and excelled in an in-house comparison to PVDF and PAA. An optimal electrode composition of 70 wt % Si, 10 wt % TA, and 20 wt % CB was identified, which balanced both electronic conductivity and active material accessibility. This electrode demonstrated a discharge capacity of 850 mAh/g at the 650th cycle at 0.5 C. Cycling did bring about some volume expansion and surface cracking, but no delamination or widespread cracking was apparent. Elemental mapping demonstrated evidence of the hydrogen-bonding mechanisms between SiO2 at the silicon nanoparticle surface and TA. A well-formed SEI layer was observed, which likely contributed to the stable cycling performance. The in-house comparison with other polymeric binders demonstrated the importance of not only hydrogen bonding but also branching in the molecular structure. Looking to the future, other small molecules may prove to be effective binders, so long as they are branched and have numerous noncovalent interactions with the silicon nanoparticle surface.

The long-term goal of Langmuir monolayer degradation experiments is to predict the degradation kinetics of the corresponding bulk material. Ester bonds play a fundamental role during the degradation process because they can undergo hydrolytic scission more easily than other chemical bonds. The urethane and urea linkages are less sensitive to hydrolysis than the ester bonds.29 An initially homogeneous sample undergoes hydrolysis, with consequent cleavage of the ester bonds confirmed by a decrease in the mass. On the FTIR spectra shown in Figures 12 and 13, a very broad absorbance band develops in the 3300-3000 cm−1 area during the first half of the composting experiment. This can probably be associated to the presence of carboxylic acid groups resulting from hydrolytic chain scissions. The velocity of the hydrolysis is determined by the “concentration” of reaction partners, water, and labile bonds.30 From water uptake tests NE elastomers resulted to be more hydrophilic (7.1%) than the E elastomers (2.3%), and, after 10 days, the absorption peaks of ester bonds substantially decreased. This is in accordance with the larger weight loss occurred to nonenergetic binders. The inherent more hydrolytic resistance of the energetic polyurethane must be attributed to the presence of the azide group in the backbone chains. The final hydrolysis products of the polyesters will be degraded by microorganisms to smaller end products after they are released in a natural environment. But, at this stage of the work, no ecotoxicity tests were conducted. This work aimed to produce an energetic biodegradable polyurethane elastomer. The first step was devoted to the production of a low-molecular-weight prepolymer. The synthesized azide polyol was suitable for being modified by an azidation reaction and being included in polyurethane elastomer formulation. Copoly(ester/ethers) of PECH and SA were prepared by two standard polycondensation methods to evaluate the appropriate operation conditions. First, direct polycondensation of PECH with SA was conducted in toluene using a Dean Stark apparatus. Even if different reaction conditions and catalysts were tried, a copolymer of satisfactory molecular weight was not produced. On the other hand, pyridine-promoted polycondensation of PECH with SC resulted in producing copolymers of higher molecular weight (6000-25,000 g/mol, relative to polystyrene standard). Biodegradable cross-linked energetic and nonenergetic polyurethanes (binders) were prepared from PCL and copolymers of PECH and SC as soft segments and LDI as hard segments. The cross-linked elastomers showed good biodegradability in the compost. The rate of weight loss was significantly higher for the nonenergetic binders with respect to energetic ones. This was due to the presence of the chlorine group in the molecular chains on nonenergetic binder. The ether/ester bonds of the energetic polyurethane were found to be less susceptible to hydrolysis, probably because the azide group affecting the steric hindrance reduced the possibility of cleavage of the molecular chains. These biodegradable binders with elastomeric properties may be used in military applications where more environmentally acceptable products are sought. Future work includes the optimization of the mechanical properties of these novel materials.

Hydrogels are highly hydrated polymeric networks that have been extensively researched for various biomedical applications. In particular, synthetic hydrogels can be designed to be nondegradable or degradable depending on the targeted application. The majority of hydrolytically degradable hydrogels are engineered to contain ester linkages located either in the cross-link or the backbone of the hydrogel. The hydrolysis of these ester bonds has been widely studied in the literature where the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions (i.e., neutral, acid and base). The rate of ester hydrolysis is both pH and temperature dependent. The hydrolysis rate has been shown to generally increase with the acidity or alkalinity of the environment.1 Also, it has been reported that heat can accelerate the hydrolysis rate by providing more energy to the reactants to overcome the activation energy required to initiate the hydrolysis reaction.2-4 Interestingly, although the esters undergo different hydrolysis mechanisms at different conditions, similar end products, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, are obtained.4 The hydrolysis kinetics of ester bonds also vary depending on the chemical structure of the ester,5, 6 as well as other factors such as polymer crystallinity and wettability.7 It was reported that ester bonds associated with poly(lactic acid) (PLA) degrade much more rapidly than ester linkages of polycaprolactone (PCL).8, 9 Moreover, changes made to the polymer structure and size may also affect the degradation mechanisms. For example, bulk PLA has been shown to degrade in both acidic and basic environments, whereas PLA brushes only degrade in basic conditions.10, 11 Conversely, other studies of cross-linked polymers containing esters in the cross-link have demonstrated that their gels were nondegradable on the timeframes studied. Hennink et al. have reported that dextran hydrogels with high cross-linking density were resistive to hydrolysis despite having an ester group in the cross-links.12 Hydrogels formed from poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) conjugated with an ester containing methacrylate moiety were also shown to be hydrolytically stable over a period of several months.13, 14 One major advantage of hydrolytically degradable synthetic hydrogels is that the degradation rate of these gels can be tailored according to the targeted biomedical application. Previous studies have shown that hydrogels of tuned degradation profile can be engineered by varying the number of degradable linkages, macromer concentration and degree of cross-linking.15 Martens et al. successfully tailored the degradation of PVA gels grafted with ester acrylate groups from 1 to 12 to 35 days by varying the macromer concentration from 10 to 15 to 20 wt % respectively.15 Moreover, increasing the cross-linking density of the PVA ester acrylate gels from 0.3 to 0.64 mol/L by fabricating the gels using macromers of different molecular weights also increased the degradation time from 12 to 45 days.15 The ability to tune the degradation rate of these hydrogels is a major advantage in terms of designing tissue engineering matrices for various biomedical applications, such as drug delivery.16 For example, tailoring the hydrogel degradation also controls the drug release rate, which then permits stable clearance of the drug from the body without exerting too much stress on the kidney.17
Change of tensile modulus (A,A′), strength (B,B′) and elongation at break (C,C′) of PBAF and PBSF copolyesters during hydrolytic degradation in a pH 7.0 PBS buffer solution at 25 °C for 22 weeks. [Color figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com] Hydrolytic degradation is usually the basis of biodegradation of polyesters. However, hydrolysis during storage and use often leads to property deterioration and therefore is not desired. Therefore, degradability and durability is a pair of contradiction, and too quick hydrolysis is not desired for biodegradable polyesters. However, when the hydrolysis is slow enough, the polyester can retain certain durability for storage and use. From Figure 9, it can be seen that the copolyesters hydrolyzed slowly so that they retained enough high tensile properties after 22-week (or 5-month) hydrolysis: E 40-210 MPa, σb 4-18 MPa and εb 150-680% for PBAFs, and E 80-280 MPa, σb 13-26 MPa, and εb 420-820% for PBAFs. Such results suggest good balance between hydrolytic degradability and durability. Further studies on accelerated hydrolytic degradation under acid or basic conditions, compost degradation, and storage stability for these copolyesters are under way. The results will be reported later. In this study, hydrolytic degradability of PBAF and PBSF copolyesters with copolymer composition (BF unit molar fraction, ϕBF) of 40-60% was assessed at 25 °C in PBS buffer solution with pH 7.0. Although the mass loss was slight (only 1-2%), the intrinsic viscosity decreased exponentially by 35-44% after hydrolysis for 22 weeks, validating hydrolytic degradability of the copolyesters. PBAFs degraded slightly faster than PBSFs with the same composition. The apparent hydrolytic degradation rate decreased with increasing ϕBF and initial crystallinity of the copolyesters. Accompanied by decrease in intrinsic viscosity, the ϕBF and crystallinity increased slowly with degradation time, suggesting that the aliphatic moiety is more susceptible to hydrolysis than the aromatic one and the amorphous region is more vulnerable to hydrolysis than the crystalline region. The variation or deterioration of tensile properties exhibited complicated dependence on the type and composition of the copolyesters as they are affected by many factors including molecular weight, composition, crystallinity as well as water absorption. In brief, the decline degree of tensile properties exhibited such an order: strength > elongation > modulus. After a 22-week hydrolysis time, the copolyesters retained relatively high tensile properties: E 40-210 MPa, σb 4-18 MPa, and εb 150-680% for PBAFs, and E 80-280 MPa, σb 13-26 MPa, and εb 420-820% for PBAFs. In summary, the PBAF and PBSF copolyesters are hydrolytic degradable under mild conditions, the hydrolysis rate can be tuned by copolymer composition and crystallinity, and they retain sufficient mechanical properties, suggesting good balance between hydrolytic degradability and durability.

Fig. 8 presents degradability behavior of the hydrogel samples based on the hydrolysis in PBS solution at 37 °C. By penetration of water into the material, the cleavage of sensitive bonds to hydrolysis (amide and ester bonds) and the fragmentation of the long polymeric chains to short ones will occur. With the time more chains would be converted to smaller fragments which eventually produce low molecular weight oligomers that are able to leave the polymer network [48]. The BIS0.5 hydrogel showed the highest degradation rate (up to 40% at day 14). This is clearly related to the lack of crosslinking for the gelatin chains by EDC-NHS solution which caused the dissolution of gelatin at 37 °C [49]. The BIS0.5-EDC-GO showed a slightly higher degradation in all time points as compared to BIS0.5-EDC. Although GONS could provide additional crosslinking sites in the hydrogel structure, the positive effect of GO on hydrophilicity of polymer network and the porous structure of this sample could accelerate the degradation process [32]. Nanocomposite hydrogels with the BIS concentration of 0.25, 0.5, and 1.5%, presented a remaining mass percentage of 71, 74, and 82% after 14 days of incubation in PBS. A higher crosslink density usually would require the cleavage of greater number of crosslinks in order to be able to release PAA/gelatin chains. This would slow down the degradation process. On the contrary, a decrease in the equilibrium swelling rate would limit the penetration of water into the polymer network while the increased porosity would expose a larger area for degradation. Since a reduction in degradation rate of the samples was detected it can be concluded that application of BIS as crosslinking agent in hydrogel structure could be beneficial to resist hydrolysis degradation [50], [51]. However, by addition of further amount of BIS (2.5%), the degradation rate was significantly increased particularly at the day 3 and 7. The inhomogeneous structure as well as less crosslinking density was led to a fast degradation behavior in BIS2.5-EDC-GO. Fig. 9 presents the microstructure of BIS0.5, BIS0.5-EDC, and BIS0.5-EDC-GO samples after hydrolytic degradation process. The samples showed a clear shrinkage in thickness which indicated that the degradation of hydrogels was dominated by surface erosion mechanism [52]. The BIS0.5 sample was generally retained the pore size and shape while its structure was collapsed (Fig. 9a). For BIS0.5-EDC, the morphology of pores was converted from polygon to round shape with wrinkled and crumpling edges. No sign of brittleness was observed for this sample probably because of a great number of crosslinking loss (Fig. 9b). The addition of GONS was inducted a distinct degradation behavior (Fig. 9c). The BIS0.5-EDC-GO was maintained its orderly structure after degradation with an increase in the pore size. The pore walls became thin so as a consequence the adjacent pores were merged to form cavities in the structure. Based on these observations it seems that the incorporation of GONS could facilitate the bulk degradation of nanocomposite hydrogels [32], [53].

Table 1 summarizes the relationship between the number of H-bonds in the entire composite hydrogel and the water content. H-bonds between water molecules (H2O-H2O) and between water molecules and polymers (H2O-Poly) increased with hydration, as expected. Except for PVDF/CEL, the increase in H2O-Poly is most pronounced between 30 and 40%, exceeding the counts observed at 60% and above. This observation explains the superior mechanical properties at 40%, which represents the maximum efficiency of H2O-Poly, reflected in higher H2O-Poly efficiency, preventing excessive water-phase dominance and ensuring appropriate mechanical strength. Similarly, in PVDF/CEL, a significant increase in H2O-Poly is observed from 70 to 80%. As water molecules are continuously introduced, the system becomes increasingly crowded, and water molecules must form more H-bonds to compensate, thereby stabilizing the system's energy. Since H-bonds formed between H2O-H2O tend toward saturation, they must overcome hydrophobic interactions to form more H-bonds with PVDF, thereby stabilizing the system's energy. In all systems, H2O-Poly bonds rapidly decreased from 40 to 50% and cannot fully recovery by 60%, remaining below 40%. This trend is consistent with the changes observed in CED, binding energy, and RDF, collectively indicating that after the hydration degree exceeds 50%, the binding state transitions from polymer-dominated to water-dominated. To elucidate the hydration-dependent H-bonding behavior in composite hydrogels, we analyzed the maximum probability density functions (PDFs) of H-bond angle \({(\theta }_{OHO})\) and bond length (O-O distance) for both H2O-H2O and H2O-Poly interactions at different water contents (Fig. 4). For the H2O-H2O interaction (Fig. 4a,b), the shortest bond lengths were observed in the PVA/CEL, PAN/CEL, and PVDF/CEL systems at 40% water content, while the corresponding bond angles remained similar to those observed at higher water contents. These results indicate that although 40% hydration belongs to a polymer-dominated regime, the spatial arrangement of water molecules is very similar to that in a water-dominated regime (50-80%), suggesting structural convergence between different hydration states. The resulting water network spatial configuration facilitates optimal H-bonding with polymer chains, as evidenced by the favorable H-bond geometries observed in systems like PVA/CEL and PAN/CEL. Currently, the most widely used method for synthesizing polymer hydrogels revolves around utilizing a diverse range of dynamic interactions. These interactions contain reversible covalent bonds such as Diels-Alder, disulfide, borate ester, and imine reactions, as well as supramolecular interactions including host-guest interactions, metal coordination, ionic interactions, and hydrogen bonding. The borate ester (B-O) bond is a hexagonal or pentagonal ring [16], [17] when boric acid reacts with cis-1,3- or 1,2-diol. This structure is reversible and dependent on the pH and temperature of the environment [18], [19]. The B-O bond easily forms in water-based solutions that contain water-soluble polyols or other substrates with electron-donating groups [20]. Therefore, B-O bond cooperation is widely employed as a network strategy in the synthesis of hydrogel materials [21], [22], [23]. He et al. reported an extremely flexible hydrogel with self-healing properties and a double cross-linked network. This network is achieved through the formation of boric acid ester bonds via polyvinyl alcohol and borax, as well as acylhydrazone bonds formed by aldehyde-based nanocellulose and adipic acid dihydrazide-modified alginate [24]. The incorporation of dynamic acylhydrazone bonds notably enhanced the hydrogel's flexibility, leading to a substantial increase in elongation from 480 % to around 1440 %. Li et al. developed a polyethylene-based flexible hydrogel crosslinked with borax, utilizing sodium alginate (SA), tannic acid (TA), and alcohol (PVA) [25]. The toughness of the hydrogel prepared via a simple one-pot method reached 587.1 KJ m−1. Du et al. developed a double-network supramolecular hydrogel by combining phenylboronic acid, galactomannan (GG), tannic acid (TA), metal ion Al3+ and polyacrylamide (PAM) chains.
