Due to the biodegradability, high thermal stability, and ease of processing, poly(lactic acid)-based (PLA) films are widely used in applications of tissue engineering, actuators, and sensors. In this investigation, PLA films are prepared using a solution casting method for high energy density capacitor applications. It is found that the stretched poly(d-lactic acid) (PDLA) film exhibits an energy density and charge discharge efficiency of 18.5 J cm−3 and 95%, respectively, at room temperature. Furthermore, after a heating time of 30 min at 100 °C, it is found that the energy density and chargedischarge efficiency of the stretched PDLA films are maintained at 11.2 J cm−3 and 76%, respectively. In comparison, the energy density and efficiency of the stretched PDLA film are 1.03-fold and 53% higher, respectively, than those of the stretched poly(vinylidene fluoride-hexafluoropropylene) film at 100 °C with the same heat treatment. Compared with a high temperature polyimide material, the energy density of the stretched PDLA film is 1.98-fold higher at 100 °C. The PLA-based material shows great promise for application in high energy density capacitors operating at a high temperature (100 °C). Dielectric capacitors play a key role in high power electronics, electric vehicles, and medical devices due to their high energy density and relatively high charge-discharge efficiency.[1-3] However, the capacitance of a dielectric material is determined by the dielectric constant and electric breakdown field. Generally, the energy storage density (Ue) of dielectric materials can be described as , where is the vacuum permittivity (8.85 × 10−12 F m−1), is the relative dielectric constant of the dielectric material and E is the applied electric field.[4] Therefore, the energy storage density of the dielectric material can be enhanced by increasing the dielectric constant () and/or the electric breakdown strength (Eb).[5] Moreover, the high charge-discharge efficiency is critical for energy storage applications. A low discharge efficiency means that more electrical energy is consumed by the orientation of molecular chains inside the material, which can generate considerable heat and damage the capacitor in the during operation.[6] In addition, thermal stability is critical for application of dielectric capacitors, especially in electrical vehicles and power electronics. In some cases, the environmental temperature can be close to 100 °C.
Conventional electrostatic capacitors are mainly classified as polymer capacitors and ceramic capacitors.7 As comparison of ceramic counterparts, polymer dielectrics are increasingly concerned in recent years, owing to their intrinsic advantages of great flexibility, high voltage ratings, and ease of production process.8-10 However, the most fatal problem is the low energy density of conventional polymer dielectrics (<4 J/cm3), which hinders devices of miniaturization and lightweight.11 One of the most effective strategies is polymer-inorganic composites, where the incorporation of high dielectric constant inorganic fillers (e.g., TiO2,12,13 BNNS,14,15 BaTiO3,16,17 and Al2O318) into the polymer matrix can significantly increase the dielectric constant, thereby improving the ability to store energy. The agglomeration and interphase delamination of inorganic particles compromise mechanical properties and breakdown strength of polymer-inorganic composites, resulting in reducing energy storage density and reliablity.19,20 These problems prevent the use of polymer-inorganic composites for commercial production on a large scale in the short term. To address these issues, all-organic polymer dielectrics are currently the most appropriate energy storage materials for large-scale production. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) as biodegradable polymers has asymmetric carbon atoms in its backbone chain and exists in two types of optically active enantiomers: poly-D-lactic acid (PDLA) and poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA). The low crystallization rate and low crystallinity of the PLLA limit its range of applications. There are many methods for improving the thermal stability of PLA-based materials, of which stereocomplexation between PLLA and PDLA is the most promising and effective. For example, a stereocomplexation crystal structure, different from PLLA or PDLA, can be produced from a 1:1 mixture of PLLA and PDLA.21-24 The complementary helical structures of the two isomers and their unique hydrogen bonding (C=O···H3C) and dipole-dipole interactions lead to the formation of the stereocomplexation crystal structure (SC-PLA).25 The mechanical properties and melting temperature (Tm) of stereocomplexation PLA (SC-PLA) with 230 °C are superior to those of pristine PLLA or PDLA (Tm ∼ 180 °C).21 Moreover, there have been relatively few investigations into the influence of the crystal structure on energy storage performance of SC-PLA. Along this way, the stereocomplex crystals of poly(lactic acid) (SC-PLA) are prepared by the method of solution blending in the ratio of 1:1 co-blended PLLA and PDLA. The mechanical properties and breakdown strength of SC-PLA films are remarkably improved as comparison of PLLA and PDLA films, thus achieving an excellent energy density (Ud) of 13.7 J/cm3 accompanied with a high efficiency (η) of 92.8%. In addition, the SC-PLA films also exhibit a good high-temperature energy storage performance and an excellent reliability.
The continuous innovations in the field of new energy and the mushroom growth of the electronics and electrical industry promote the demands for dielectric capacitors to miniaturization, portability, flexibility, and high performance. (1−3) They basically rely on the polarization of dielectric materials under an electric field for charge storage and control. Dielectric capacitors possess the outstanding characteristics of high power density, good cycle stability, and high charge-discharge efficiency, leading to their wide use in high power weapons, hybrid electric vehicles, pulse electronic devices, and so on. (4,5) Theoretically, the discharged energy density (Ue) is involved in the polarization and insulation of the dielectrics, (6,7) which can be expressed as Ue = ∫EdD, where E is the applied electrical field and D is the electrical displacement. Hence, it is a basic requirement for dielectric capacitors to seek excellent dielectric materials with both high Ue and efficiency (η). Polymer-based dielectric composites feature flexible preparation process, good breakdown strength, and low energy loss, such as poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF), (8−13) poly(vinylidene fluoride-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP), (14−16) poly(vinylidene fluoride-trifluoroethylene) (P(VDF-TrFE)), (17) and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). (18) However, apparently, these synthetic polymers derived from petroleum are nonbiodegradable and nonrenewable. In recent years, the consumption of energy and the consequent burden on the environment have been skyrocketing day by day. Developing green energy storage materials and devices with excellent comprehensive performance is of great significance for environmental conservation and sustainable development. (19) Cellulose, the most abundant natural polysaccharide, is one of the most promising substitutes of petroleum-derived synthetic polymers. (20−23) Besides the natural advantages of abundant reserves and recycling, cellulose also features excellent stability, high mechanical strength, and flexibility. (24,25) This green material with outstanding properties has triggered extensive concerns in various energy fields. (26,27) A series of flexible dielectric composite films based on cellulose have been reported in our group, which shows that cellulose is a superior dielectric material with great potential for dielectric capacitors. (28−31) The stubborn cellulose can be rapidly dissolved in a green and high-efficiency solvent composed of alkali, urea, and water at low temperatures with no pollution to the environment. (32,33) However, compared with ceramics with a high dielectric constant, cellulose has a low intrinsic dielectric constant, which greatly hinders the development of this new dielectric material. The strategy of combining inorganic materials with polymers is a good approach. The common ceramics with high dielectric constant, such as BaTiO3, (34,35) BaxSr1-xTiO3, (36) and CaCu3Ti4O12, (37) render the electric field between interfaces distorted in terms of the difference of permittivity, leading to a reduced breakdown strength. Also, the relatively high remnant polarization ends in an undesirable energy density and low efficiency. Different from these ferroelectric ceramics, NaNbO3 is generally treated as an exceptional lead-free antiferroelectric piezoelectric material with roughly a moderately high εr of 300 at 1 kHz and low remnant polarization. (38−40) It also has a wide energy band gap (∼3.29 eV), which is beneficial to reducing the loss and improving the efficiency and breakdown strength and is expected to broaden its application in energy storage. Recently, some NaNbO3/polymer composite dielectric materials have been reported. Chen (41) found that the PVDF-based nanocomposite film with 3 vol % NaNbO3@SiO2 nanowires at 430 MV/m had a Ue of 12.1 J/cm3, but η was just 59.2%. Pan (42) prepared the NaNbO3@PDA NWs/PVDF composites with a high Ue of 12.26 J/cm3 at 410 MV/m and bearing a relatively low η of 63%. Low energy storage efficiency does not contribute to cost control and sustainable economic development. The charge-discharge efficiency is crucial to obtain high Ue and stability for dielectric capacitors. (43) Moreover, the morphology of fillers exerts a direct impact on Ue and η of dielectric composites. (44) The one-dimensional (1D) fillers, such as nanowires and nanofibers, possess larger dipole moment compared with nanoparticles, thus the dielectric constant can be improved at a lower number of fillers. (45,46) With the breakdown path of the composites more tortuous by 1D filler, the breakdown strength also can be raised considerably. One-dimensional NaNbO3 nanowires display appealing and excellent distinctions and are expected to comprehensively promote the properties of cellulose-based dielectric energy storage materials.
In general, polymers are amorphous or semi crystalline. In amorphous polymers, there are many localized charge carrier levels called trapping sites and the carrier mobility is very low [3]. The dielectric properties of polymers doped with micro or nano fillers have attracted considerable attention, due to their technological importance for devices such as heating elements, electrical igniters and antistatic shielding of electronic components, electrodes for fuel cells, and crucible for vacuum induction furnace and electric feed [4]. Extensive investigations have been made by several researchers on the molecular motion and the charge carrier migration in a variety of polar/nonpolar polymers containing one or more fillers [5-7]. Although the dielectric properties of a number of polymers have been investigated, the molecular orientation behavior and the associated relaxation mechanisms of the polymers are not fully understood [8]. The study of dielectric behavior as a function of temperature and frequency is one of the most convenient and sensitive methods of investigating the polymer structure. The polarization of a dielectric is contributed by the electronic, ionic, and dipolar polarization [8]. Electronic polarization occurs during very short intervals of time and the process of ionic polarization occurs in the range of seconds, while the dipole polarization requires relatively longer time. In the case of polar polymers, the dielectric constant begins to drop after a certain critical frequency. The dipole molecules cannot orient themselves in the lower temperature region. However, as the temperature increases, the orientation of dipoles is facilitated and this increases the dielectric constant [9, 10]. Intensive work has been carried out on various organic polymers in different forms [11-13]. The electrical transport behavior of thin polyvinylchloride (PVC) films deposited by the solution growth technique has been investigated [11]. The conductivity of PVC films is increased on doping with iodine. This is interpreted on the basis of the formation of charge-transfer complexes in the film. The barrier height decreases with increasing iodine concentration in the PVC films. Similarly, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is one of the promising representatives of polymeric materials and there are numerous proposals for its application in electronics, as well as packaging textile and food products due to its high clarity, lack of charge density properties, and excellent durability. Recently, a considerable amount of work has been reported on conduction properties of PVA [14]. More recently, PVA-based nanocomposites have been developed to improve its properties and to widen its application window [15-20]. In PVA/silica composites, the crystal growth of the PVA was remarkably inhibited by silica network. In PVA/saponite composites, the thermal stability of the hybrids increased linearly with increase in nano clay loading. The introduction of montmorillonite (MMT) clay into PVA matrix, results in improvement of tensile strength, elongation at break, and thermal stability of the nanocomposites. Overall, the clay particles in the polymer matrix affect both the thermal stability and the tensile properties of the polymer/clay nanocomposites. PVA is a synthetic polyhydroxy polymer that has been studied intensively because of its good film-forming character and physical properties, high hydrophilicity, processability, non-toxic, bio-compatibility, and bio-degradability [21]. PVA has been applied in wide range of fields because of particular properties such as water soluble and adhesive properties. Moreover, PVA is known as ecological polymer due to its biodegradability. In this paper, the effect of zinc oxide-cerium oxide (ZnO-Ce2O3) nanoparticles loading on PVA performance has been reported. The dielectric permittivity, dielectric loss, and conductivity of PVA/ZnO-Ce2O3 nanocomposites at different frequencies have been studied to probe the role of filler in PVA matrix. The primary focus of the present investigation is to explore the potential of ZnO-Ce2O3 nano filler in hydrophilic PVA without modification.

With the rapid advancement of electronic equipment and the increasing emphasis on sustainable development, there is a growing need for high dielectric environmental-friendly materials.1 Polymer materials are widely recognized as suitable candidates for developing dielectric materials due to their desirable properties, such as low dielectric loss, processability, and flexibility.2 Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is suitable as a substrate for polymeric dielectric materials due to its biodegradability and biocompatibility.3 However, low dielectric constant (ε’) and poor toughness limit its application in the electronics industry. The brittleness of PLA limits its application in polymeric dielectrics. Blending is a cost-effective method for tailoring the properties of polymeric materials,4 including mechanical properties and processing characteristics.5 By blending PLA with other compatible polymers, it becomes possible to achieve a broader range of customized properties, thus expanding the potential applications of PLA in polymeric dielectric materials. Polycaprolactone (PCL), being a biodegradable material with excellent elongation at break, holds the potential to improve the toughness of PLA.6 However, the incompatibility of the two polymers can lead to significant phase separation, making the toughening effect unsatisfactory.7 During processing, poor interfacial bonding may lead to phase separation and mechanical loss.8 Overcoming these challenges requires finding solutions to enhance the compatibility between PLA and PCL. By developing methods to improve interfacial bonding and mitigate phase separation, the full potential of PLA/PCL blends can be harnessed, ultimately enhancing their toughness and overall mechanical properties. The main methods used in current research to improve incompatibility are the addition of compatibilizers for reactive compatibilization9-11 and the addition of nanoparticles for compatibilization.12 However, the addition of nanoparticles to increase compatibility is often less satisfactory and requires consideration not only of their degree of dispersion in the matrix but also the selective localization of nanoparticles in both phases, which is often difficult to control. In contrast, the incorporation of compatibilizers enables the achievement of physical interlocking between the PLA and PCL phases, facilitating reactive compatibilization. This process can be easily controlled.13 To enhance the interfacial bonding between the two phases, researchers have introduced reactive compatibilizers, such as L-lysine triisocyanate (LTI), in PLA/PCL blends. This allowed NCO to react with the OH of PLA and PCL, respectively, thereby improving compatibility and interfacial adhesion between the two polymers. Rastegar et al.14 conducted molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the impact of pristine and surface-treated boron nitride nanosheets on the mechanical properties of PLA. The results indicate that the introduction of OH or PLA chains on BNNS enhances the toughness of PLA. In another study, Guan et al.15 synthesized functionalized Janus nanosheets (JNSs) by grafting PU chains and epoxide groups onto opposite sides of silica nanosheets. This modification significantly increased the elongation at the break of PLA/TPU blends from 31.4% to 362.6%. Furthermore, Yang et al.16 capacitated PLA/PBAT blends by synthesizing a highly reactive silica nanosheet (HRN) with an average of 10 reactive epoxy groups per chain and increased the elongation at break from 12% to 132%. To overcome the inherent drawback of poor dielectric properties in PLA, the addition of high-conductive fillers or ceramic fillers with high dielectric constants can be employed. Ceramic fillers, despite their high dielectric constants, are often limited by their low dielectric strength and fragility.17 The conductive fillers can form microcapacitors with a polymer matrix, which can be used to improve the ε’ effectively.18 Among them, carbon nanotube (CNT) and graphene (GRA), due to their high aspect ratio, high elasticity, and excellent electrical conductivity, can be used to improve the dielectric properties of PLA.19, 20 Kashi et al.21 dispersed graphene nanosheets (GNPs) in PLA/PBAT by melt mixing and found that the addition of GNPs greatly increased the dielectric constants of both polymers. Wang et al.2 introduced CNTs into PLA/EVA-g-GMA copolymer and the dielectric constants of the copolymer increased from 5.81 to 11.08 with the addition of only 1% CNTs, indicating that the introduction of CNTs can significantly improve the dielectric properties of the copolymer. In addition, designing multilayer structured polymers with an insulating modification layer on the surface of the conductive fillers is a common approach to increase the storage capacity of the material by reducing the dielectric loss (tanδ) while maintaining the high ε′. By combining poly (dopamine) encapsulated graphene oxide with XNBR, Ning et al. successfully obtained dielectric composites with low tanδ, high breakdown strength, and high ε′.22 Xia et al.23 developed a hierarchical model to quantitatively evaluate the tunable AC response of modified coated carbon nanotubes in PDA@PVDF composites. The results show that by suppressing the interfacial leakage current, the modified interface can significantly reduce the dielectric loss of the modified composites while ensuring high dielectric constants.
Dielectric capacitors with a high energy-storage density and efficiency are urgently required for miniaturization and integration of power electronics and pulsed power system. Herein, single-layered stretched P(VDF-HFP) with a certain content of poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) and two kinds of sandwich-structured films are prepared to optimize and compare energy-storage performance. The results revealed that the crystallization transition behavior of stretched P(VDF-HFP) films contributed to enhance its electric polarization, while the introduction of linear type PMMA resulted in an enhancement of voltage tolerance of stretched films by improving the mechanical properties and suppressing leakage current. What’s more, the effects of crystalline orientations and structure design on the breakdown mechanism of stretched films were revealed by finite element theoretical simulation. As a consequence, the stretched sandwich-structured 0-25-0-S (pure P(VDF-HFP) serves as the outer layer, and blends represent the middle layer; the digit representing PMMA content in the P(VDF-HFP)) displayed a high Ue of 28.71 J/cm3 and η of 74% under 680 MV/m. This work provides a workable and effective method for developing capacitive films with great energy-storage performance. Dielectric materials display a promising prospect in the applications of electronic equipment because of their high-power density, ultrahigh charge-discharge speed as well as low dielectric loss. (1−4) The application and removal of an external electric field would induce the phenomenon of polarization and depolarization, which leads to capacitive behavior. The dielectric polarization and the electric field applied on the dielectric materials determine the energy storage of dielectric materials, which can be defined as Ue = ∫E dD, where E is the applied electric field, D refers to the displacement of dielectrics. (5,6) Most polymers are good candidates for dielectric capacitors because of excellent voltage resistance, elegant breakdown failures, and prominent flexibility, yet the relatively lower polarization limits their energy-storage performance. Taking biaxially oriented polypropylene (BOPP) as an example, the kind of commercialized electrostatic capacitor shows a low discharged density of 2 J/cm3 under 700 MV/m because of low dielectric constant (2.2 @ 1 kHz). (7,8) Over the past decade, polar organic materials, such as poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) and their copolymers, have attracted much interest, because molecular chains containing strong dipole moments can display a higher dielectric constant than other nonpolar polymers. (9−12) Although the dielectric response of PVDF is higher than that of other organic dielectric materials, the acceptable discharge energy density cannot be obtained in pure PVDF-based polymers. To optimize the energy-storage performance of a polymer, inorganic nanofillers, such as TiO2, (13,14) BaTiO3, (15−18) Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3, (19,20) and NaNbO3, (21,22) have recently been added into the polymer matrix to further improve the electric displacement and capacitive performances. Liang has introduced BT@HPCs as nanofillers into the PVDF matrix to obtain nanocomposites with a dielectric constant of 38 and a Ue of 10.2 J/cm3 under 360 MV/m. (23) Although the introduction of nanofillers enhances the polarization of the inorganic/organic nanocomposite, inevitable side effects occur with an increasing load of fillers. It is accepted that the improved dielectric constant is often obtained at the cost of the breakdown strength, which is caused by mismatched dielectric constant between fillers and matrix. (24,25) Consequently, it remains a huge challenge to explore suitable approaches to achieve advanced dielectrics with enhanced electric response, high breakdown strength, and excellent discharged energy density.
The pore-forming methods, on the other hand, have been reported as an effective method to decrease the dielectric constant when considering that the incorporated pores occupied by air have ultralow dielectric constant (k ≈ 1). These methods include chemical or physical foaming [23], phase inversion [24], and template-etching [25], organic-inorganic or inorganic materials with nano-pores [26] etc. However, For PLA materials, the above processing methods faces two problems: (1) the introduction of pores inevitably results in a deterioration of mechanical properties such as stiffness, and the inherent brittleness of PLA is also hard to conquer; (2) the above methods and post-treatment process is not green enough for large-scale production of porous PLA dielectrics [19]. As a result, it is increasingly necessary to develop a green and large-scale pore-forming method for porous PLA-based low-k materials with excellent comprehensive properties. It is commonly known that a serious of porous polymeric materials fabricated by the dry stretching technique have been commercialized, such as the microporous polypropylene (PP) membranes Celgard® as separators for lithium-ion batteries [25] and the expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) materials Gore-Tex® with breathability and waterproof used in clothing [27]. Being facile and energy saving, the dry stretching method for porous polymeric materials can be divided into two paths: (1) stretching of the polymer composites containing incompatible materials (i.e. inorganic fillers or the dispersive second polymer phase) via interfacial debonding and (2) direct stretching via stress-induced cavitation. For PLA, the stretching path (1) have been applied by adding starch [27] or silica [28] fillers and further uniaxial stretching to prepare microporous PLA films. Despite their successes, the introduction of polar additives seriously deteriorates the low-k performance of porous PLA. For PLA as a low-k materials, it is promising to achieve porous structure through the direct stretching. However, it is believed that the crystallization kinetics of PLA is hindered and the cavitation phenomenon is hardly generated due to the presence of optical isomers in the L-rich backbone and molecular chain rigidity. In our previous works, a direct stretching technique named “casting-thermal stretching” has been achieved to rapidly formulate a tough and robust PLA film with aligned amorphous chains and robust oriented crystallites [29]. We believe that the formation of porous structure can be promoted by the existence of as-formed oriented crystallites [30] as the rigid porogen in PLA, similar to the addition of fillers. Herein, this scalable strategy is further applied to fabricate porous PLA films. Moreover, PLA with different optical purities (content of l-isomer: >99%, 98% and 96%) are also adopted to systematically investigate the influence of optical purity on the crystallization and formation of porous structure in detail. Finally, the dielectric performance, mechanical robustness, thermal stability and hydrophobicity of PLA films are evaluated.

In recent years, there has been a great deal of research into the synthesis, miniaturization, and fast operation of novel dielectric materials as a result of advances in electronic information technology. Dielectric materials are suitable for storing large amounts of electrical energy, which is desirable for many electronic and power devices. The dielectric constant (ɛr) is the polarization property of materials and the stored charge is supplied in parallel to the plates that function as a capacitor [1,2,3]. The ratio of condenser capacitance in reality to condenser capacitance in vacuum has been studied [4]. A higher degree of polarization was suggested a greater dielectric constant and the interfacial polarization developed in heterogeneous materials due to conductivity differences between the filer and matrix. Moreover, the interfacial polarization effect can be observed due to a high dielectric constant at low frequency. It is also suggested that the entire orientation of polar molecules is higher in low frequency regions due to polarization orientation. Because of the shorter time interval, electrical dipole orientation is restricted at higher frequencies. Thus, the dielectric constant was impacted by the presence of fillers and polar groups, as well as the frequency of the external electric field [5, 6]. The dielectric loss is the amount of energy lost after applying voltage to the circuit because the materials are insulated. The dissipation factor (tan δ) or energy dissipation is represented by the loss tangent, and it is computed by dividing the electric power dissipation of materials by the net power of the circuit. The tan δ of insulating materials is crucial for determining the amount of electrical energy transferred into heat. The majority of the heat promoted its breakdown and raised the temperature of the insulator. The loss factor is the average power factor during a certain time period, which also reveals transmission and distribution losses. The viscoelastic nature of the polymer resulted in responses to both electrical and mechanical stimuli. Moreover, there are two primary loss factors attributing to dipole polarization and ionic conductance. This property results from the deformation-induced reorientation of polarization inside the material, leading to the development of an electric field where the current can be obtained. A voltage delivered through the material, on the other hand, will cause the intramolecular dipoles to align [7]. Conventional dielectric materials are ceramic, which has excellent dielectric properties and the thermal stability of ceramic, but the limitation of ceramic is that it is difficult to process because it requires a relatively high processing temperature. Polymer-based materials can provide a better possibility for processing. Hence, polymer nanocomposite is the best solution to combine the properties of these two materials. They combine the outstanding dielectric properties of ceramics with good processability, chemical stability, and mechanical properties to produce better electrical characteristics at low processing temperatures and low operating costs. However, in the last decade, environmental pollution has become a problem because of plastic waste. One of the effective ways to solve the issue is to use biodegradable polymers. Thus, nano-biocomposites were achieved by adding nanofillers to biopolymers, resulting in improved properties with preservation of the material's biodegradability and without ecotoxicity. Poly(lactic acid), or PLA, is a biodegradable, renewable, and biobased aliphatic thermoplastic polyester that has been studied for over two decades for use in a variety of applications [8,9,10,11]. Recently, there are many research that have been focused and studied the dielectric behavior of biodegradable polymers [12, 13]. PLA has unique dielectric properties due to the chiral compound of lactic acid, which distinguishes it from traditional ceramics and other piezoelectric polymers such as poly(vinylidene difluoride) (PVDF) [14,15,16,17]. The dielectric constant of PLA is related to the product of the C = O dipole orientations in all directions along the main chain [18, 19]. Hence, increasing the dielectric constant of PLA could be performed by orienting molecular chains with the C = O aligned along the major chain segments, along with increasing other polarizations. The dielectric properties of PLA and their nanocomposites with montmorillonite have been reported by Jeszka et al. They found that nanoclay had a weak influence on segmental (αs) and local (β) relaxation in PLA. Because of the ionic species found in nanoclay, a significant increase in dielectric constant can be observed above Tg and it also causes the Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars (MWS) interfacial polarization and an increase in the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity at high temperatures and low frequencies [20]. Elsawy et al. later studied on manocomposite of PLA and chitosan nanoparticles (CsNP) as a new type of dielectric material. However, all the blends presented all the stages of thermal degradation of the UTPS and PCL, but shifted to higher temperatures, due to the increase of PCL content in the blend, because PCL presents higher thermal stability than UTPS. In all the blends, the mass loss up to 120 °C can be attributed to the evaporation of water, and other volatile compounds present in UTPS, followed by the thermodegradation of urea, and thermal degradation of the corn starch occurred between 250 and 330 °C. The PLA/PCL blend studied by Carmona et al.[151] showed a slight reduction of about 1.5 °C in Tm of both neat PLA and PCL. Sharma et al.[152] studied the thermal transitions of the electrospun PLA/PCL blend and observed two distinct peaks that correspond to the of the separate phases of PLA and PCL at ≈160 and 60 °C, respectively, which is indicative of immiscibility between the two phases.[152, 153] Kiani et al.[154] reported an increase in PLA Xc from 8.9% (neat PLA) to 10.5 and 8.9% in the PLA/PCL blend containing 10 and 20 wt% PCL, respectively. Based on this, PLA Xc can increase by adding as low an amount as 10 wt% PCL. In general, PLA Xc can be increased by adding nucleating agents, including applying a post-annealing process.[88] Dadras Chomachayi et al.[47] studied the effect of silk fibrion nanoparticles (SFNP) on the PLA/PCL (70/30 w/w) blend. They reported an increase in PLA Tcc from 111.9 to 117.0 °C, while the PCL crystallization enthalpies (ΔHc) of PCL decreased from 15.0 to 10.4 °C. They based their conclusions on the interfacial bonding in PLA/PCL, which improved because of the SFNP compatibilization effect. The improved intermolecular interaction between PLA and PCL reduced the chain mobility of the polymers and, as a result, influenced the crystallization process. Researchers have also reported the thermal stability of biodegradable polymer blends, which have been labeled as one of the important properties of polymeric materials. It is important that researchers fully understand the thermal stability and kinetic parameters in the design of materials for specific use.[155] Generally, in many industrial processes, it is important to characterize the thermal degradation behavior to know the temperature limits of the material.[156] However, PLA and PCL are characterized by different thermal stability profiles because of their structural differences and different degradation mechanisms. The degradation mechanism of PLA is the reaction of exchange of backbite esters, caused by a non-radical mechanism that involves the ends of the ─OH chain, and that of PCL is the random chain scission, by which the pyrolysis of the ester group releases CO2, H2O, and hexane acid.[157] However, PLA is sensitive to thermal degradation, while PCL has higher thermal stability and longer degradation times than PLA.[25] Literature studies have shown the PLA/PCL immiscibility through morphological characteristics, implying that its thermal stability depends on compatibilization.[158, 159] In this sense, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) of PLA/PCL blends has two degradation steps, and the weight loss level corresponds to the content of each polymer.[75, 83] Recently, Sharma et al.[152] observed the presence of two distinct degradation steps, indicating the immiscibility between PLA and PCL. Davis et al.[160] studied the thermal stability of the PLA/PCL blend and reported a rapid degradation state of PLA with a 2% onset of decomposition at 326 °C. In contrast, PCL degradation followed at 366 °C. In a study by Zhou et al.,[52] the initial decomposition temperature values were above 200 °C in PLA/PCL blends with a PLA content that varied between 10 and 50%. The authors emphasized that the observed decomposition temperature range indicates that the blends have good thermal stability. For example, Przybysz-Romatowska et al.[95] compared two peroxide initiators, dicumyl peroxide (DCP) and BIB, in a PCL/PLA 75/25 wt% blend. They reported a decrease in thermal stability corresponding to a 50% mass loss of the PLA/PCL blend from 394 to 384 and 365 °C with the addition of DCP and BIB, respectively. The decrease in thermal stability with the addition of peroxides may be due to the high amount of BIB added to the blends. In another study, Przybysz-Romatowska et al.[94] organic peroxide had an insignificant effect on the thermal stability of the PLA/PCL blend. The results show that MPSs containing unsaturated keto-groups have no remarkable differences on their Vicat softening temperatures. Properties such as the chain elasticity, side group, branching, cross-bond, and mole weight in polymers affect the temperature of softening. Glassy transition temperature of polymers having elastic chains is lower than polymers having hard chains.50 According to Table II, bonding of unsaturated keto-group to the structure of PS provided elasticity for PS and elongation value at the time of rupture increased from 0.42% to 2.9%. On the other hand, since branching in chains limits approaching of chains and increases the volume, softening temperatures of branched polymers are lower than those of linear structures.50 When MPSs having aliphatic and aromatic keto-groups are compared, they have lower softening temperatures due to the steric volume of the aromatic group. Because of these results, as compared with all MPSs with keto-groups having unmodified PS, they have lower Vicat softening points. The mechanical properties of polymers are influenced by molecular weight, crosslinking, branching, segmental motion, morphology, and external conditions such as temperature, pressure, loading rate, environmental condition, extent of compound, etc.50-54 The structure of the side-chain substituents on the polymer backbone is a major compositional factor impacting polymer functionality. Important aspects of substitution are the chemical structure of the substituents, the extent of backbone substitution, and the uniformity of substitution. The nature of the side chain substituent type also significantly impacts mechanical properties. Increasing the amount of highly polar, ionic side-chains tends to result in an increased tensile strength.55 The effect of side group structure on the compressive strength of novel biodegradable polyphosphazene based polymers was investigated by Sethuraman et al. Results of mechanical testing studies demonstrated that the nature and the ratio of the pendent groups attached to the polymer backbone play a significant role in determining the mechanical properties of the resulting polymer. The compressive strength of polymer with aliphatic alanine side group was significantly higher than polymers with aromatic alanine groups.56 To investigate physicomechanical properties, such as tensile strength, elongation at break and hardness of the MPSs, mechanical testing was performed. The Mg-Y-Zn-Mn alloys are promising as biodegradable alloys because Mg, Zn and Mn are human tissue nutrients and essential in the human body for healthy bone structure [34]. In the literature the both information about the cytotoxic response of Y or its metabolic inactivity can be found [17]. The hot extrusion of various Mg-Y-Zn based alloys typically results in a bimodal and inhomogeneous microstructure. This structure consists of large grains elongated along the extrusion direction, small recrystallized grains, and fibers of LPSO phase, which are also elongated along the extrusion direction [29], [38]. As the content of Zn and Y increases, the volume fraction of the LPSO phase increases at the expense of the coarse non-recrystallized grains [38]. Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys are representative materials in the fields of engineering and biomedical applications owing to their low density and superior biocompatibility [1-4]. For a few years, Mg-based products have been offered in the market owing to the tireless work of researchers [5-7]. Specially, many implants, such as vascular stents and screws, have been successfully fabricated from Mg alloys [8-11]. Numerous in vitro and in vivo trials promote Mg implants conduct or is going to conduct clinical studies. At present, Mg alloys are mainly produced by casting and plastic deformation process. The forming processes play a key role in mechanical properties of Mg alloys [12]. As for biodegradable metals, mechanical requirements should be met: tensile strength >300 MPa, and elongation >15% [13]. According to previous researches, the tensile strength of cast and deformed Mg alloys is lower than 300 MPa [14]. This low strength indicates that it is difficult to apply biodegradable Mg alloys to load-bearing parts. Moreover, strength of biodegradable Mg alloys is related to the final size of biomedical products [15]. High-strength Mg alloys are more conducive for the preparation of stents and screws with smaller diameters [16]. This is beneficial for healing damaged tissues and organic matter. In addition to their mechanical properties, the rapid degradation of Mg alloys is a big concern because of their low standard electron potential. Mg is susceptible to form Mg(OH)2 via combining with hydroxide ion in an aqueous solution. The formation of corrosion products is unable to prevent Mg substrate because their structure is not dense. The mechanical integrity of biodegradable Mg alloys is lost when they undergo rapid biodegradation. High-purity pure Mg has very good corrosion resistance, but its mechanical properties are poor [17, 18]. Therefore, it is vital to design and construct Mg-based implants with a good balance between mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.
Magnesium (Mg) alloys have significant application prospect in aerospace, automobile and electronic industries because the advantages of high specific strength, high specific stiffness, high damping resistance and low density exhibit great potentials for manufacturing lightweight products [1,2,3]. Recently, the studies on Mg-Mn alloys, which is regarded as a typical type of Mg alloys, are attracting increasing attention because of the excellent corrosion resistance, good strength and low cost [4,5,6]. Gu et al. [5] reported that addition of Mn could purify the melt by hindering the coarsen process of Fe-rich particles during near-solid-melt treatment process, and eventually optimized the corrosion resistance of pure Mg. Zhao et al. [6] compared the microstructures and mechanical properties of hot-extruded pure Mg and Mg-Mn alloys. They found that addition of Mn significantly decreased the grain size and texture intensity, resulting in the good mechanical properties with a tensile yield strength of 201.4 MPa and a fracture elongation of 20.7%. However, the insufficient creep resistance of Mg-Mn alloys at medium-to-high temperatures is still a challenge which needs to be preferentially considered and resolved, and increasing works are dedicated to the increment in creep life and the enhancement of creep resistance [7, 8]. Addition of rare earth (RE) elements is a common method to increase the mechanical properties of Mg alloys because of the significant solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, grain boundary strengthening and texture weakening effects [3, 9,10,11]. Among various RE elements, Ce element is identified as one of the effective elements which can obviously enhance both strength and ductility of Mg alloys, and numerous studies have reported the influence of Ce addition on the microstructures and mechanical properties of Mg-Mn alloys [7, 12,13,14,15]. question: How does 'layer-by-layer' (LbL) assembly create functional coatings on biodegradable films?

The LbL self-assembly method can be used to construct nanoscale ultra-thin films on solid substrates. This strategy is based on electrostatic interactions between polyelectrolytes or other ionic species with opposite charges, which promotes the deposition of materials via alternating adsorption. Specifically, the substrate is alternately exposed to solutions containing positively and negatively charged substances, leading to the spontaneous and orderly adsorption of these substances on the substrate surface to form a highly organized multilayer membrane structure [7] The LbL self-assembly technology applied in this study is characterized by precise microstructural control, high reproducibility, wide material adaptability, broad application prospects, and environmental friendliness [8]. Controllability is a particularly valuable advantage because it enables command over the structural and physicochemical properties of the obtained multilayer films according to the properties of the raw materials and the assembly conditions (e.g., pH, ionic strength, temperature) [9]. To date, the LbL self-assembly strategy has been applied in various fields, including the preparation of anti-corrosion films on the surface of magnesium alloys. For example, Xiao et al. [10] prepared polyelectrolyte-coated magnesium alloys using the LbL self-assembly method with polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) and sodium alginate (ALG), which increased the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Chen et al. [11] used phytic acid (PA), branched polyethylenimine (BPEI), and graphene oxide (GO) to prepare films on Mg-1Zn alloys via LbL self-assembly, thereby forming a physical barrier against corrosion. These studies demonstrated that an LbL self-assembled multilayer film can increase the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Despite these promising applications, existing LbL multilayer coatings for magnesium alloy protection still face several critical challenges that limit their practical implementation: (1) the hydrophilic nature of polyelectrolytes makes the coatings susceptible to delamination during prolonged immersion, (2) inadequate interfacial adhesion between the coating and magnesium substrate compromises long-term durability, and (3) the continued use of non-environmental solvent systems in some fabrication processes contradicts the sustainable advantages inherent to LbL technology. Urushiol, a naturally occurring phenolic compound extracted from lacquer trees (Toxicodendron spp.), has gained increasing attention as a sustainable and eco-friendly material for advanced coatings and functional applications [12, 13]. Its unique molecular structure, comprising catechol groups and long alkyl chains (C15-C17 with 0-3 olefins), endows it with intrinsic hydrophobicity and the ability to form dense crosslinked networks upon polymerization, significantly enhancing corrosion resistance and waterproofing properties [14]. Notably, the catechol moieties mimic mussel-adhesive proteins, enabling urushiol to form robust chemical bonds with diverse substrates, including metals, polymers, and inorganic surfaces, thereby improving interfacial adhesion and long-term durability [15]. Beyond its protective capabilities, urushiol exhibits remarkable biological activity, such as antioxidant, antibacterial, and antitumor effects, making it a promising candidate for biomedical and environmental applications [16]. For instance, Fang et al. [17] demonstrated that urushiol-modified melamine sponges (UMS) exhibit excellent hydrophobicity and selective oil-adsorption capacity, while Jie et al. [15] developed chitosan-urushiol nanofiber membranes with enhanced acid resistance and broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. Given its renewable sourcing, biodegradability, and multifunctionality, urushiol presents a viable green alternative to synthetic coatings, combining environmental sustainability with high-performance material characteristics. To address these persistent challenges in LbL coatings for magnesium alloys, this study proposes an innovative approach by introducing urushiol, a molecule containing catechol groups, as a self-assembly building block. The catechol moieties in urushiol can not only form strong bonds with the magnesium alloy substrate through chelation but also undergo crosslinking reactions during film formation, significantly enhancing coating stability. Based on this design, we report for the first time the LbL assembly of branched polyethyleneimine (BPEI) and urushiol on magnesium alloy surfaces to construct a novel eco-friendly protective coating. This strategy is expected to simultaneously overcome the challenges of weak interfacial adhesion and solvent sustainability, providing new insights for developing high-performance surface coatings for magnesium alloys.
Slot die coating is a relatively unexplored lab-scale film preparation method that can easily be translated into a large-scale and low-cost roll-to-roll process. The instrument uses a die head having a thin slot from which metered solution exits onto a moving substrate. The encountered shear thinning on the applied solution is particularly useful to improve barrier properties due to the alignment of polymer chains and suspended barrier filler in the resulting film.20, 21 In this work, we report a slot die coating method that can be translated into large-scale roll-to-roll manufacturing of high-barrier, self-standing biodegradable films for water-soluble packaging applications. Waterborne layered films made of Hec with either PVOH, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC), or sodium alginate (alginate) were evaluated as a packaging material in terms of water solubility, gas barrier properties, mechanical performance, and optical properties. CO2 evolution of the layered films in wastewater is compared to the same polymer film without Hec to ensure improvements in physical properties do not come at a sacrifice to biodegradability. A roll-to-roll process easily enables the incorporation of multiple functional layers, unlike traditional solvent casting which is practically limited to a single monolayer. The layered structure of these films prevents complications that come with compounding a nematic Hec suspension with biopolymers like high viscosities, aggregation of filler, or embrittlement that limits high clay loadings.19 At the same time, the exceptional barrier enhancement expected from the use of high aspect ratio nanosheets is ensured, producing biodegradable, high-performance, and scalable packaging films. With water being the only solvent employed, the production of the films aims to fulfill the 12 Principals of Green Chemistry.22
Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a versatile technique based initially on the adsorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (PELs) on a substrate.1 LbL assembly was designed in the first place for macroscopic surfaces.2 Recently, coating of nanoparticles (NPs) with PELs using the LbL technique has received great interest due to the advantage of obtaining NPs with controlled surface properties. Indeed, the shell can be tuned in thickness, composition, and functionality by choosing various constituents and adjusting the layer number, offering several applications in the biomedical and pharmaceutical field such as drug3 and siRNA delivery.4 Generally, core-shell NPs obtained via the LbL self-assembly technique are formed by the consecutive deposition of polymers interacting through intermolecular forces such as electrostatic interactions5 or hydrogen bonding.6 So far, a wide range of synthetic PELs such as poly(diallyl-dimethyl-ammonium chloride),7 poly(ethyleneimine),3 poly(allylamine) hydrochloride,8 poly(styrenesulfonate),8 and poly(acrylic acid)3 or natural PELs like alginate or chitosan5 have been studied to build several layers onto NPs. The buildup of multilayers could be monitored using several characterization techniques such as fluorescence,8 dynamic light scattering (DLS),9 ζ-potential,10 UV and IR spectroscopy11 or gravimetric analysis using a quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) dissipation.9 Inorganic cores such as gold12 or magnetic NPs13 are usually reported as they display several advantages like superior mechanical and thermal stabilities14 compared with the cores based on a polymeric system as micelles,6 liposomes,5 microcapsules,15 nanocapsules,16 microparticles,17 or NPs.11, 18 However, the major interest of using polymer cores lies in their ability to load lipophilic drugs. For biomedical applications, polymers should display biocompatibility and biodegradability properties. Hence, ideal candidates could be biodegradable polyesters polymer such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA),3, 9 poly(lactic acid) (PLA),18 or poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV).15, 19 In drug delivery, particularly, LbL self-assembly is an appealing technique to extend drug action. Indeed, by controlling the layer number, it becomes possible to reduce the initial burst release.3 In our previous work,20 core-shell NPs have been designed and fully characterized. They are based on a hydrophobic and biodegradable PLA core and an adsorbed neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer (poly-β-CD) shell. β-Cyclodextrins (β-CDs) are torus-shaped cyclic oligosaccharides composed of seven d-glucopyranose residues, which have a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic internal cavity.21 We have demonstrated that benzophenone (BP), a lipophilic molecule, can be incorporated into these NPs and we have investigated the release mechanisms.22 It has been shown that the release was mainly controlled by the diffusion of BP through the NPs and by its host-guest interaction with the β-CD cavities present at the surface of the NPs. Quantitative analysis in terms of diffusion coefficient and equilibrium constant determinations have indicated that the poly-β-CD layer played a major role in the control of the release. Core-shell NPs bearing β-cyclodextrin polymers have also been reported in Ma's group.23, 24 These NPs, though assembled via host-guest associations, have shown sustained release as well. Further studies have also reported the incorporation of β-cyclodextrin polymers into LbL films using either electrostatic interactions, for instance, between a cationic polymer and a neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer complexing low-molecular-weight polyanions25 or host-guest interactions between a β-cyclodextrin polymer and an amphiphilic polymer-bearing guest groups.26 In the latter case, the growing of the multilayer films was limited to 3-4 layers because of the competition between host-guest associations in solution and at interfaces. In the present work, an electrostatic association process was chosen to grow LbL onto the NPs. The performance of this kind of core-shell NPs is essentially related to the concentration of β-CD on the shell surface. Thus, the main objective of this work was to design NPs with larger amount of β-CD on the surface of the PLA NPs by using the LbL technique allowing a better control of the release of the encapsulated molecule. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of NPs coated with PELs using charged β-CD polymers. This paper starts with the description of the synthesis of the anionic and cationic β-CD polymers and the buildup of the LbL shell. Then, the physicochemical properties of the NPs are presented and finally, the results of the release behavior of an entrapped lipophilic molecule, BP, are discussed.

Based on the provided evidence, layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly creates functional coatings on biodegradable films through the following mechanisms:

1.  **Alternating Deposition of Charged Materials:** LbL assembly builds coatings by sequentially depositing oppositely charged substances (e.g., polyelectrolytes, nanoparticles, functional molecules like urushiol or modified graphene oxide) onto the film surface via electrostatic interactions. This creates a highly organized multilayer structure [1], [3], [9], [14].
2.  **Precise Control and Tailoring:** The technique allows precise control over coating thickness, composition, and functionality by adjusting the number of layers and selecting specific materials. This enables the customization of surface properties such as wettability, viscoelasticity, barrier performance, and bioactivity [1], [8], [9], [14].
3.  **Incorporation of Functional Components:** LbL enables the incorporation of functional materials into the coating layers. Examples include:
    *   Urushiol for enhancing corrosion resistance, hydrophobicity, and interfacial adhesion via catechol groups [1].
    *   Hectorite clay platelets for improving barrier properties, where shear during processing aligns the platelets to create an impermeable wall [6], [15].
    *   Carboxylated graphene oxide (GO-COOH) and anthocyanin-decorated chitosan for UV-blocking, antioxidant activity, water resistance, and mechanical strength enhancement [14].
    *   β-Cyclodextrin polymers for controlled release of encapsulated molecules (e.g., drugs) via host-guest interactions [3], [9].
4.  **Improved Interfacial Adhesion:** Components within the LbL coating, such as catechol groups in urushiol or hydrogen bonding between layers (e.g., carbonyl groups of PLA and peptide bonds in gelatin), can form strong bonds with the underlying biodegradable film substrate. This enhances coating adhesion, durability, and overall performance [1], [10], [14].
5.  **Enhanced Film Performance:** The resulting LbL coatings significantly improve the functional properties of biodegradable films, including:
    *   Increased corrosion resistance (e.g., on magnesium alloys) [1].
    *   Enhanced gas and water vapor barrier properties [6], [10], [15].
    *   Improved mechanical strength and toughness [10], [14].
    *   Added functionalities like UV protection, antioxidant activity, and controlled release [3], [9], [14].
    *   Better moisture resistance and surface hydrophobicity [10], [14].
6.  **Maintaining Biodegradability:** The materials used in LbL assembly (such as chitosan, alginate, gelatin, β-cyclodextrin, urushiol, hectorite) are often biodegradable or derived from natural sources. The layered structure itself does not inherently prevent biodegradation, as evidenced by studies showing significant biodegradation rates for layered films [6], [15].

First published on 5th October 2017 The adhesion of bacteria is one of the most important stages in biofilm formation and bacterial infection. Once bacteria have adhered to a biomaterial surface, it is hard to eliminate them, and bacterial growth and infection are inevitable. In the current study, we have designed and constructed enzymatically degradable (hyaluronic acid/chitosan)n-(hyaluronic acid/polylysine)n ((HA/CHI)n-(HA/PLL)n) composite multilayer films via a layer-by-layer self-assembly method. Spectroscopic ellipsometry and scanning electron microscopy cross section measurements showed the exponential growth behavior of (HA/CHI)10-(HA/PLL)10 multilayer films (∼2 μm). The increased secretion of hyaluronidase and chymotrypsin in the bacterial infection microenvironment led to the fast degradation of the outer (PLL/HA)n multilayer films in the first 24 h. Enzymatic degradation of the multilayer films efficiently reduced the adhesion of both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli (>99%). Bacterial live/dead staining demonstrated the bactericidal action of the remaining bottom (CHI/HA)n multilayer films against the two kinds of bacteria. In vivo subcutaneous tests on New Zealand white rabbits, wound appearance and histopathology analysis showed that the implantation of composite multilayer film-modified PDMS promoted wound healing and the materials demonstrated a self-defense antibacterial effect. The material demonstrated both anti-adhesive and bactericidal properties and could be used to modify biomedical implants. The development of bacterial infections can be divided into three stages: bacterial adhesion, bacterial growth and biofilm formation, among which bacterial adhesion is the first and most crucial stage.5-7 Once bacterial adhesion becomes irreversible, biofilm formation and bacterial infections are inevitable.8-10 To date, many kinds of antibacterial surfaces, including those incorporating conventional anti-adhesive/anti-fouling properties,11,12 bactericidal properties13,14 and the release of antibacterial agents,15,16 have been developed to reduce the incidence of infection. However, it is difficult for antibacterial surfaces with just one type of antibacterial property to produce ideal and long-term efficacy.17-19 For example, hydrophilic coatings (such as polyethylene glycol, polyvinyl alcohol, and polyvinylpyrrolidone) can be contaminated by adhesive proteins, blood platelets and inflammatory cells in body fluids after being implanted in the body and their anti-adhesive properties can be compromised.20-22 In addition, pure bactericidal surfaces without an antifouling function will be covered by the remains of dead bacteria, which can facilitate bacterial adhesion, making the situation worse.23-25 Consequently, bio-inspired antibacterial surfaces, multi-functional composite antimicrobial surfaces and smart antibacterial surfaces that are responsive to the bacterial infection microenvironment have attracted increasing attention.

The highly cytocompatible nature of the film-forming and -degrading conditions is assessed in the c-ST/ALG-shell formation and degradation of S. cerevisiae. Nature-derived biopolymers are strong candidates for the cytocompatible LbL assembly.16,17 Among them, marine polysaccharides, such as alginic acid, chitosan, chondroitin sulfate, heparin, and hyaluronic acid, have widely been employed in the formation of LbL films because of their diversity in chemical composition, properties, and functions.18 In particular, the varied charge identities in marine polysaccharides make them highly suitable for electrostatically driven LbL process.19,20 For instance, alginic acid is negatively charged at the neutral pH,21,22 and chitosan is positively charged under mild acidic conditions.23,24 In comparison, starch (ST), the most abundant polysaccharide in the plant, has scarcely been used for the formation of LbL films due to its low charge density.25-27
Biomimetic systems play an important role in biomedical sciences. Native tissues follow a hierarchical conformation and organization, from the nano to macroscales, which are difficult to mimic using conventional methodologies, such as solvent casting, freeze-drying or melt-based technologies. The use of non-physiological processing conditions and also the inability to control spatial distribution over the material triggered urgent investigation for multiscale-based devices for biomedical applications [1], based on both bottom-up and top-down methodologies. The layer-by-layer (LbL) method has been exploited to produce such controllably sized-architectures and has been growing fast [2, 3]. This technique was first suggested by Decher et al [4], and follows a very simple foundation of consecutive and alternative deposition of oppositely charged polyelectrolyte solutions, being usually described as a user-friendly way to prepare thin coatings. LbL technology promises control over the architecture at both nano and microscales, mainly due to the possibility of using different adsorption conditions such as pH, ionic strength, charge density, polymer nature, functionality and concentration [5-9]. Other advantages include the abilities to incorporate different biomolecules, from synthetic [6] to natural polymers [10, 11] and different bioactive agents like growth factors [12], polypeptides [13] and nuclei acids [14], to repeat the process of assembly hundreds of times and to extend from planar substrates [15] to three dimensional (3D) ones [16, 17]. LbL approaches have mostly been applied for surface modification of different substrates; for example, Cai et al [18] improved the biocompatibility of titanium films by modifying their surface with the alternate deposition of chitosan (CHT) and gelatin. The possibility of producing structural 3D systems using such technology has permitted the extension of its applicability in the biomedical field [2]. In particular, efforts have been made to develop freestanding films from polyelectrolyte multilayers (PEMs) [18, 19]. These are obtained by removing the multilayer assembly from a solid substrate, where they were absorbed, using different strategies like neutralization of charged layers, sacrificial layers, dissolution of initial layers or even by applying mechanical forces [15]. Jiang et al [20] took advantage of a sacrificial layer of cellulose acetate to fabricate freely suspended nanocomposite polyelectrolyte membranes. Even so, the use of solvents or even mechanical forces can compromise the morphology and respective integrity of the membrane [15, 21]. To overcome this drawback, the production of easily detachable freestanding membranes was obtained via spontaneous detachment from an underlying low surface energy substrate [22]. The studied membranes were based on the combination of CHT and alginate. Upon crosslinking, the biological properties of the membranes were improved, but their maximum tensile strain decreased significantly [23]. Many biomedical applications require the use of more stretchable membranes, with elastic stretchablility being an important characteristic of the living tissues; thus other polyelectrolyte combinations should be explored. CHT has been broadly studied with LbL approaches, with many prospective works revealing its high potential for biomedical and tissue engineering applications [24, 25]. Furthermore, CHT is a positively charged biopolymer, widely available from natural resources, biodegradable and is also a nontoxic compound [26]. Besides alginate, other natural polymers have been combined with CHT; Schneider and her group [27] combined CHT with hyaluronic acid to observe the improvements on cell viability, elasticity and biodegradability and Neto et al [28] functionalized hyaluronic acid with dopamine to obtain a bioactive LbL coating, with more adhesive properties. Chondroitin sulfate (CS) is a naturally-derived polyanion and constituent of an extracellular matrix, with an important role in the elasticity and function of cartilage and connective tissues [29, 30]: we combined CHT and CS to produce reservoirs for calcium phosphate biomineralization [31] and to fabricate 3D, highly porous scaffolds [32].
The LbL self-assembly method can be used to construct nanoscale ultra-thin films on solid substrates. This strategy is based on electrostatic interactions between polyelectrolytes or other ionic species with opposite charges, which promotes the deposition of materials via alternating adsorption. Specifically, the substrate is alternately exposed to solutions containing positively and negatively charged substances, leading to the spontaneous and orderly adsorption of these substances on the substrate surface to form a highly organized multilayer membrane structure [7] The LbL self-assembly technology applied in this study is characterized by precise microstructural control, high reproducibility, wide material adaptability, broad application prospects, and environmental friendliness [8]. Controllability is a particularly valuable advantage because it enables command over the structural and physicochemical properties of the obtained multilayer films according to the properties of the raw materials and the assembly conditions (e.g., pH, ionic strength, temperature) [9]. To date, the LbL self-assembly strategy has been applied in various fields, including the preparation of anti-corrosion films on the surface of magnesium alloys. For example, Xiao et al. [10] prepared polyelectrolyte-coated magnesium alloys using the LbL self-assembly method with polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) and sodium alginate (ALG), which increased the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Chen et al. [11] used phytic acid (PA), branched polyethylenimine (BPEI), and graphene oxide (GO) to prepare films on Mg-1Zn alloys via LbL self-assembly, thereby forming a physical barrier against corrosion. These studies demonstrated that an LbL self-assembled multilayer film can increase the corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys. Despite these promising applications, existing LbL multilayer coatings for magnesium alloy protection still face several critical challenges that limit their practical implementation: (1) the hydrophilic nature of polyelectrolytes makes the coatings susceptible to delamination during prolonged immersion, (2) inadequate interfacial adhesion between the coating and magnesium substrate compromises long-term durability, and (3) the continued use of non-environmental solvent systems in some fabrication processes contradicts the sustainable advantages inherent to LbL technology. Urushiol, a naturally occurring phenolic compound extracted from lacquer trees (Toxicodendron spp.), has gained increasing attention as a sustainable and eco-friendly material for advanced coatings and functional applications [12, 13]. Its unique molecular structure, comprising catechol groups and long alkyl chains (C15-C17 with 0-3 olefins), endows it with intrinsic hydrophobicity and the ability to form dense crosslinked networks upon polymerization, significantly enhancing corrosion resistance and waterproofing properties [14]. Notably, the catechol moieties mimic mussel-adhesive proteins, enabling urushiol to form robust chemical bonds with diverse substrates, including metals, polymers, and inorganic surfaces, thereby improving interfacial adhesion and long-term durability [15]. Beyond its protective capabilities, urushiol exhibits remarkable biological activity, such as antioxidant, antibacterial, and antitumor effects, making it a promising candidate for biomedical and environmental applications [16]. For instance, Fang et al. [17] demonstrated that urushiol-modified melamine sponges (UMS) exhibit excellent hydrophobicity and selective oil-adsorption capacity, while Jie et al. [15] developed chitosan-urushiol nanofiber membranes with enhanced acid resistance and broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. Given its renewable sourcing, biodegradability, and multifunctionality, urushiol presents a viable green alternative to synthetic coatings, combining environmental sustainability with high-performance material characteristics. To address these persistent challenges in LbL coatings for magnesium alloys, this study proposes an innovative approach by introducing urushiol, a molecule containing catechol groups, as a self-assembly building block. The catechol moieties in urushiol can not only form strong bonds with the magnesium alloy substrate through chelation but also undergo crosslinking reactions during film formation, significantly enhancing coating stability. Based on this design, we report for the first time the LbL assembly of branched polyethyleneimine (BPEI) and urushiol on magnesium alloy surfaces to construct a novel eco-friendly protective coating. This strategy is expected to simultaneously overcome the challenges of weak interfacial adhesion and solvent sustainability, providing new insights for developing high-performance surface coatings for magnesium alloys.

Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a versatile technique based initially on the adsorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (PELs) on a substrate.1 LbL assembly was designed in the first place for macroscopic surfaces.2 Recently, coating of nanoparticles (NPs) with PELs using the LbL technique has received great interest due to the advantage of obtaining NPs with controlled surface properties. Indeed, the shell can be tuned in thickness, composition, and functionality by choosing various constituents and adjusting the layer number, offering several applications in the biomedical and pharmaceutical field such as drug3 and siRNA delivery.4 Generally, core-shell NPs obtained via the LbL self-assembly technique are formed by the consecutive deposition of polymers interacting through intermolecular forces such as electrostatic interactions5 or hydrogen bonding.6 So far, a wide range of synthetic PELs such as poly(diallyl-dimethyl-ammonium chloride),7 poly(ethyleneimine),3 poly(allylamine) hydrochloride,8 poly(styrenesulfonate),8 and poly(acrylic acid)3 or natural PELs like alginate or chitosan5 have been studied to build several layers onto NPs. The buildup of multilayers could be monitored using several characterization techniques such as fluorescence,8 dynamic light scattering (DLS),9 ζ-potential,10 UV and IR spectroscopy11 or gravimetric analysis using a quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) dissipation.9 Inorganic cores such as gold12 or magnetic NPs13 are usually reported as they display several advantages like superior mechanical and thermal stabilities14 compared with the cores based on a polymeric system as micelles,6 liposomes,5 microcapsules,15 nanocapsules,16 microparticles,17 or NPs.11, 18 However, the major interest of using polymer cores lies in their ability to load lipophilic drugs. For biomedical applications, polymers should display biocompatibility and biodegradability properties. Hence, ideal candidates could be biodegradable polyesters polymer such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA),3, 9 poly(lactic acid) (PLA),18 or poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV).15, 19 In drug delivery, particularly, LbL self-assembly is an appealing technique to extend drug action. Indeed, by controlling the layer number, it becomes possible to reduce the initial burst release.3 In our previous work,20 core-shell NPs have been designed and fully characterized. They are based on a hydrophobic and biodegradable PLA core and an adsorbed neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer (poly-β-CD) shell. β-Cyclodextrins (β-CDs) are torus-shaped cyclic oligosaccharides composed of seven d-glucopyranose residues, which have a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic internal cavity.21 We have demonstrated that benzophenone (BP), a lipophilic molecule, can be incorporated into these NPs and we have investigated the release mechanisms.22 It has been shown that the release was mainly controlled by the diffusion of BP through the NPs and by its host-guest interaction with the β-CD cavities present at the surface of the NPs. Quantitative analysis in terms of diffusion coefficient and equilibrium constant determinations have indicated that the poly-β-CD layer played a major role in the control of the release. Core-shell NPs bearing β-cyclodextrin polymers have also been reported in Ma's group.23, 24 These NPs, though assembled via host-guest associations, have shown sustained release as well. Further studies have also reported the incorporation of β-cyclodextrin polymers into LbL films using either electrostatic interactions, for instance, between a cationic polymer and a neutral β-cyclodextrin polymer complexing low-molecular-weight polyanions25 or host-guest interactions between a β-cyclodextrin polymer and an amphiphilic polymer-bearing guest groups.26 In the latter case, the growing of the multilayer films was limited to 3-4 layers because of the competition between host-guest associations in solution and at interfaces. In the present work, an electrostatic association process was chosen to grow LbL onto the NPs. The performance of this kind of core-shell NPs is essentially related to the concentration of β-CD on the shell surface. Thus, the main objective of this work was to design NPs with larger amount of β-CD on the surface of the PLA NPs by using the LbL technique allowing a better control of the release of the encapsulated molecule. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of NPs coated with PELs using charged β-CD polymers. ans_rerank: Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly creates functional coatings on biodegradable films by alternately depositing oppositely charged or interacting polyelectrolytes, nanoparticles, or bioactive molecules through electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, or other intermolecular forces [1, 5, 7]. This sequential adsorption enables precise control over film thickness, composition, and architecture at the nanoscale, allowing the integration of multifunctional properties such as enhanced mechanical strength [1], UV-blocking [1], hydrophobicity [1], antimicrobial activity [2], and controlled biodegradability [3]. For example, chitosan (CS)-based films functionalized with anthocyanins and carboxylated graphene oxide (GO-COOH) via LbL assembly exhibit improved tensile strength (53.52 MPa) and UV resistance due to hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions between layers [1]. Similarly, enzymatic degradation of cationic starch/alginate multilayers enables controlled release of encapsulated agents in biomedical applications [3]. The technique also facilitates the incorporation of bioactive agents (e.g., hyaluronic acid, polylysine) to mimic extracellular matrix components or respond to infection microenvironments, as seen in composite films that degrade upon exposure to bacterial enzymes to prevent biofilm formation [2, 4]. Additionally, LbL coatings enhance barrier properties (e.g., oxygen/water vapor resistance) by aligning polymer chains or fillers like cellulose derivatives, as demonstrated in polycaprolactone/chitosan multilayers [10]. The modularity of LbL allows tailored combinations of biodegradable polymers (e.g., CS, alginate) and functional additives (e.g., graphene oxide, urushiol) to address specific challenges such as corrosion resistance [5] or flame retardancy [9].

Besides studies at the laboratory scale, field tests are also conducted to certify that these structures can fully disintegrate at the commercial composting facility scale.[8-10] Laboratory tests are conducted under specific national and international standards. The main standards available regarding the criteria for certifying composting conditions are ASTM D6400-21,[11] ASTM D6868-21,[12] and EN13432.[13] The main standards describing the disintegration and biodegradation tests needed to meet the requirements of ASTM D6400, ASTM D6868 and EN13432 are described in ASTM D5338-15,[14] ISO 14855 part 1 and ISO 14855 part 2,[15, 16] respectively. These tests can take between 90 and 180 days, depending on the simulated compost environment (i.e., yard, food, or manure compost) and the rate of biodegradation of the positive control, in general, cellulose powder.[11] Methods to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers have surged because of two main reasons: a) the temporal gap between time frames observed for biodegradation of polymers in thermophilic composting conditions and other common organic wastes, such as food and garden waste, creating a low-quality and non-stabilized final product; and b) to accelerate the testing of an array of compostable polymer. In general, even certified compostable products may take more time to meet the requirements of ultimate degradation, reflected by the standards, than do food and garden waste, creating operative challenges for composting facilities when managing waste containing both biodegradable plastics and common organic waste. Moreover, lengthy biodegradation tests are needed to determine the right compostable polymer, delaying the adoption, and commercialization of these compostable plastics. This review concentrates on approaches to accelerate the biodegradation of biodegradable polymers, considering thermophilic aerobic composting conditions as a common baseline.
