For the aliphatic/aromatic polyester PBAT, mineralization in compost has been reported at around 60% at day 45.[28] PBAT is frequently used for mulch films in agricultural environments where a crosslinking effect can be observed due to photodegradation, affecting its ultimate biodegradation in this environment.[28, 29] As observed, in composting conditions these polymers passed the criteria established by international standards, such as ISO and ASTM, when evaluated in simulated environments. A more complex situation is presented when evaluating post-consumer biodegradable products under these environments. Some organizations, such as Biodegradable Products Institute (BPI),[30] TÜV Austria,[31] DIN CERTCO,[32] Australasian bioplastics,[33] and Japan bioplastics association[34] are the main ones providing certification of products for compostability following international standards in simulated laboratory conditions (ASTM D6400, D6868, and EN13432). However, simulated laboratory tests are conducted under ideal controlled conditions, which are not always reflected in industrial composting facilities. For example, in real conditions, compostable polymers could be mixed with the compost during the degradation time and, due to their low density and pile turning, may be exposed to the surface of the compost pile. This creates a non-ideal biodegradation condition, with samples in industrial composts not being exposed to the same conditions as samples in laboratory settings. Furthermore, a longer period is generally needed for biodegradable polymers, also reflected in the standards, in comparison to the short terms of around one to two months employed by some industrial composters for organic waste.[35] In the UnitedStates (U.S.), the BPI certifies samples and products for bio-based content and compostability in industrial composting facilities,[30] and in Europe the certification is mostly run by the TÜV AUSTRIA Group.[31] Most certifications in other regions are based on the requirements provided by the ASTM and ISO framework.

The OECD Guidelines have been developed for chemicals, i.e. small molecules that are either water-soluble or water-dispersible. Biodegradation of solid substances is a heterogeneous reaction because it happens at the solid/liquid interface, where the microbial enzymes present in the liquid phase interact with the macromolecules available at the surface of the solid plastic sample subjected to biodegradation [5]. The term bio-based refers to materials derived from renewable biological sources, such as plants, rather than fossil fuels [48]. Biodegradable refers to materials that microorganisms can break down into essential compounds such as water, carbon dioxide, and organic matter in the natural environment. These definitions align with internationally recognized standards, ensuring consistency in the classification and understanding of bioplastics globally [104],. The certification of biodegradable plastics is governed by stringent composting conditions standards, which outline the specific criteria these materials must meet to be considered compostable. The standards provide detailed guidelines on the requirements for biodegradation, disintegration, and the absence of adverse effects on the resulting compost. ASTM D6400-19, for example, outlines three essential requirements for a product to be considered compostable in industrial or municipal aerobic composting systems. After being sieved through a 2-mm mesh, the product must disintegrate within 84 days, leaving no more than 10% of its initial Mass. Second, to indicate effective biodegradation, at least 90% of the product’s organic carbon must be transformed into carbon dioxide in 180 days. Lastly, compared to composts made from bio-waste that do not contain the product, the final compost must not impede plant growth [119].

According to this study: “The resulting fragments will remain in the environment.”18 The so called “oxo-biodegradable” plastic bags have been introduced in the market during the last decades. Polyethylene has been widely applied in our daily life such as agricultural mulch film, disposal shopping bag, packaging film owing to its versatile, lightweight, durable, flexible and inexpensive qualities. However, the enormous increase in usage has also created many challenges associated with disposal and their impact on the environment because of their exceptional properties against degradation, resistance to peroxidation and biologically inert properties [1,2,3,4]. In order to reduce the accumulation of polyethylene in the environment, the new forms of plastic are required to be developed as quickly as possible. They must both retain all of the physical properties needed by the consumer and be easy degradable in the natural environment after disuse. Degradable plastic has been the research issue in order to solve the problem. Generally, degradable plastic are classified as photodegradable, thermo-degradable and biodegradable plastics. Photodegradable plastics have been studied extensively in recent years [5,6,7,8,9]. Photo-catalysts have been utilized to create photodegradable plastics. One of the most representatives is nano-TiO2 owing to its excellent properties such as inexpensiveness, photo-stability, non-toxicity and high photo-catalytic activity [10, 11]. This also causes an increase in cost and a decrease in photodegradable efficiency of the photodegradable film [17, 18]. In recent years, the study of thermo-degradable plastics has become a hot topic of research [19,20,21]. The mechanism of thermo-degradable plastics is adding thermo-degradable catalyst such as Co, Ni, Mn and Fe, transition metals, carboxylates and oxides into polymer. Roy et al. [22, 23] have reported ferric stearate, cobalt stearate and manganese stearate as effective pro-oxidants for polyethylene. Abdullah et al. have reported that the accelerating weathering degradation properties of polypropylene were improved by integration with cobalt stearate and ferric stearate as pro-oxidants [24]. But the degradable efficiency was low and the biodegradation behaviors of the residue of films were not involved.

According to this study: “The resulting fragments will remain in the environment.”18 The so called “oxo-biodegradable” plastic bags have been introduced in the market during the last decades. The present work is part of an experimental study aimed at investigating the long-term degradation behavior of the remains and fragments of mulching films made out of LLDPE with pro-oxidants (oxo-degradable or photodegradable or fragmentable films), under real soil burial conditions. Their degradation behavior during the cultivation season is described in Ref. 27. The remains of these naturally aged materials remained intact after 8.5 years in the soil, even though they were further degraded.28

Flow behavior of LDPE and its blends with LLDPE I and II: A comparative study Packaging polymers, particularly polyethylene films, have been considered to be the major culprit for causing the rising environmental pollution problem. These polymers, after completing their useful short lifecycle as packaging films, find their way to constitute the major fraction of solid municipal waste, where they refuse to degrade because of their hydrophobic nature. The problem aggravates due to the high molecular weight associated with these polymers. An acceptable solution to this problem is the use of oxo-degradable polyethylene, which first disintegrates to small pieces, thereby reducing their ubiquitous visual presence. In the process, their molecular weight is reduced and these become potentially biodegradable organics, which can be subsequently consumed by the microorganism to form biomass.1-3 Major strategies to facilitate the disintegration and subsequent biodegradation of polyethylene are mainly focused on the direct incorporation of carbonyl groups within the backbone of the polymer (ethylene CO copolymer)4 or by addition of certain pro-oxidants (Scott-Gilead Process) during the processing stage.5, 6 These pro-oxidants, in the presence of either light or heat lead to the generation of free radicals on the polymer chain, which further react with oxygen to form carbonyl groups through a series of reactions. These carbonyl groups, then undergo photochemical reactions (Norrish Type I, II, and III) to finally lead to chain scission and physical embrittlement.4 In the recent years, linear low density polyethylene (LLDPE) is fast replacing low density polyethylene (LDPE) as packaging films, because of its better mechanical properties and comparable cost. Keeping in mind the increased use of LLDPE, we felt the need of performing accelerated degradation studies on LDPE, LLDPE, and LLDPE -LDPE blends. As a part of our ongoing efforts towards development of oxo-degradable polyethylene, we have reported the pro-oxidative action of cobalt stearate on LDPE,7, 8 which first leads to the abiotic disintegration of the matrix. The degradation of these disintegrated films by bacterial consortium has also been reported.9 The effect of such pro-oxidants is expected to be less pronounced for LLDPE because of the lesser degree of branching in the polymer chain, therefore requiring higher concentrations of the pro-oxidant to reach the same level of degradation, which has been confirmed by our investigations.10 To avoid the slight bluish tinge in the films containing higher concentrations of cobalt stearate, the present investigation was performed on films containing manganese stearate which also belong to the broad category of pro-oxidants.11
Biodegradable bioplastics are predominantly employed in the manufacture of disposable products designed for short-term use, whereas non-biodegradable bioplastics are prized for their superior durability and long service life [91]. Based on their degradation pathways, bioplastics can be broadly classified into two categories: oxo-biodegradable and hydro-biodegradable [21]. Oxo-biodegradable plastics are typically petroleum-derived polymers augmented with metal salt additives that catalyze oxidative chain scission, thereby facilitating fragmentation and subsequent microbial assimilation [166]. In contrast, hydro-biodegradable plastics are synthesized from plant-based feedstocks such as corn, wheat, or sugarcane. These materials generally degrade more rapidly than oxo-biodegradable counterparts and release methane as a byproduct of anaerobic decomposition, rendering them suitable for composting applications and use as soil amendments [186]. Bioplastics derived from renewable biomass are classified as bio-based, and these can be further divided into two principal types: (i) drop-in bioplastics and (ii) dedicated bioplastics. Drop-in bioplastics are molecularly identical to their fossil-derived analogues but are synthesized from bio-based precursors through established industrial processes. Examples include bio-based ethylene, polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Although these materials are generally non-biodegradable, they offer a reduced carbon footprint compared to their petroleum-based equivalents [187].
This study is an attempt to investigate the effect of a representative pro-oxidant (manganese stearate) on the degradation behavior of 70 ± 5 μ thickness films of LDPE, LLDPE and their blends. Films were prepared by film blowing technique in the presence of varying quantities of manganese stearate (0.5-1% w/w) and subsequently subjected to accelerated degradative tests: xenon arc exposure and air-oven exposure (at 70°C). The physico-chemical changes induced as a result of aging were followed by monitoring the mechanical properties (Tensile strength and Elongation at break), carbonyl index (CI), morphology (SEM), melt flow index (MFI), oxygen content (Elemental analysis), and DSC crystallinity. The results indicate that the degradative effect of pro-oxidant is more pronounced in LDPE than LLDPE and blends, due to the presence of larger number of weak branches in the former. The degradation was also found to be proportional to the concentration of the pro-oxidant. Abiotic degradation occurs when the inclusion of pro-oxidant additives in LDPE films accelerate the degradation process under photo and thermal conditions.7, 8 This degradation is observed by the Mw reduction. Contextual caveats: biodegradability and land-use change While biodegradability is often promoted as a key sustainability advantage of bio-based polymers particularly for single-use disposable products, its environmental benefits are heavily conditional on proper disposal environments, such as industrial composting or anaerobic digestion facilities. In the absence of such controlled conditions, biodegradable plastics may persist, fragment into microplastics, and act as vectors for persistent organic pollutants and heavy metals through trophic transfer, thus posing substantive risks to both ecological systems and human health [120]. Additionally, many earlier assessments have overstated the carbon benefits of bio-based plastics by primarily accounting for carbon sequestration gains linked to land use, while neglecting the foregone carbon sequestration potential of pre-existing ecosystems. Notably, land-use change (LUC) emissions are frequently excluded from conventional LCA inventories, despite their critical influence. For example, reverting land to secondary forest can substantially decrease atmospheric CO₂ fluxes and deliver co-benefits for biodiversity and hydrological cycles. Conversely, diverting land for dedicated bioplastic feedstock cultivation can intensify ecosystem stress, reduce habitat complexity, and undermine soil carbon stocks. Under certain scenarios such as planting feedstocks on long-cultivated croplands increases in both soil and aboveground carbon stocks have been observed. However, these outcomes are highly system-specific and necessitate rigorous environmental and socio-economic analyses to validate their sustainability credentials [129]. Persisting industry gaps

First published on 5th March 2024 To reduce global CO2 emissions in line with EU targets, it is essential that we replace fossil-derived plastics with renewable alternatives. This provides an opportunity to develop novel plastics with improved design features, such as better reusability, recyclability, and environmental biodegradability. Although recycling and reuse of plastics is favoured, this relies heavily on the infrastructure of waste management, which is not consistently advanced on a worldwide scale. Furthermore, today's bulk polyolefin plastics are inherently unsuitable for closed-loop recycling, but the introduction of plastics with enhanced biodegradability could help to combat issues with plastic accumulation, especially for packaging applications. It is also important to recognise that plastics enter the environment through littering, even where the best waste-collection infrastructure is in place. This causes endless environmental accumulation when the plastics are non-(bio)degradable. Biodegradability depends heavily on circumstances; some biodegradable polymers degrade rapidly under tropical conditions in soil, but they may not also degrade at the bottom of the sea. Biodegradable polyesters are theoretically recyclable, and even if mechanical recycling is difficult, they can be broken down to their monomers by hydrolysis for subsequent purification and re-polymerisation. Additionally, both the physical properties and the biodegradability of polyesters are tuneable by varying their building blocks. question: What is the 'drug release mechanism' from a surface-eroding polyanhydride wafer?
ground_truth: In surface-eroding polymers (like Polyanhydrides), the drug is released proportionally to the mass loss of the polymer. As the polymer erodes layer by layer from the outside in, the drug entrapped in those layers is released. This allows for near zero-order (constant rate) release kinetics, which is difficult to achieve with bulk-eroding polyesters.

Polyanhydrides (PAs) are a class of biodegradable polymers characterized by the presence of anhydride linkages (COOCO) within their backbones. They degrade in vivo primarily through hydrolytic degradation, facilitated by their anhydride repeat units. PAs are known to degrade faster than polyesters, polyamides and polyethers,5 where their diacid degradation products can be metabolized and eliminated from the body. Due to their rapid degradation, PAs have been used in short-term controlled delivery of drugs or bioactive agents.6-9 It has been reported that the rate of water penetration into the PA matrix is slower than the cleavage of anhydride bonds, consequently classifying PAs as surface-eroding drug delivery carriers.10 In addition, the rate of drug delivery is significantly influenced by the polymer erosion rate, which is governed by factors such as polymer structure, crystallinity, pH of the release medium and the size and design of the device. PAs have been synthesized with a variety of backbones, including aliphatic, aromatic, unsaturated, aliphatic-aromatic, ester-anhydride, ether-anhydride, and amino-, glycol- or fatty acid-modified anhydrides, owing to the broad functionality of available monomer precursors.11 Various synthesis methods have been employed, such as melt condensation, ring-opening polymerization, interfacial condensation, dehydrochlorination and dehydrative coupling.12 For example, poly(sebacic anhydride) and glycol-modified poly(sebacic anhydride) have been synthesized from sebacic acid and excess acetic anhydride under melt condensation conditions for use as drug carriers.13 It was reported that the degradation rate and in vitro drug release profile of glycol-modified poly(sebacic anhydride) were slower than that of poly(sebacic anhydride) without glycol modification, due to the introduction of glycolate esters. The work started with the synthesis of two different PA structures through melt-condensation polymerization of dicarboxylic acids and excess anhydride monomers: poly[(propionic anhydride)-co-(succinic anhydride)] (PASA) synthesized from succinic acid and propionic anhydride and poly[(propionic anhydride)-co-(sebacic anhydride)] (PASEA) synthesized from sebacic acid and propionic anhydride. Biodegradable polymers offer a unique combination of properties that can be tailored to suit nearly any controlled drug delivery application. The most common biodegradable polymers used for biomedical applications are semicrystalline polyesters and polyethers which possess good mechanical properties and have been used in many controlled release applications. Drug release from these polymers may be controlled by several mechanisms and these include diffusion of drug through a matrix, dissolution of polymer matrix and degradation of the polymer. Several factors can affect drug release from polylactide coglycolide (PLGA)-based formulations, including polymer and drug properties, formulation components, manufacturing processes, and environmental in vitro or in vivo conditions. To achieve optimal release profiles for specific drug delivery applications, it is crucial to understand the mechanistic processes that determine drug release from PLGA-based formulations. In the current study, we developed a mechanistic model for the in vitro drug release of PLGA-based solid implants. The model accounts for all known critical quality attributes (CQAs) and considers the most important release rate processes, including water or dissolution medium influx into the porous structure of the implant, initial noncatalytic hydrolysis of PLGA, autocatalytic hydrolysis, dissolution of oligomers and monomers into the aqueous medium, the liberation of the trapped solid drug from the polymer matrix, dissolution of the solid drug into the wetted pore network, diffusion of the dissolved drug out of the implant, and distribution of the dissolved drug into the dissolution medium. The model has been validated using in vitro release data obtained from implants of four drugs (buserelin, afamelanotide, brimonidine, and nafarelin). The model presented in this manuscript provides valuable insights into the kinetics and mechanism of drug release from PLGA-based solid implants and has demonstrated the potential for optimizing formulation design. The in vitro release model, coupled with physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, can predict the in vivo performance of implants and can be used to support bioequivalence studies in a drug development program. Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA)-based formulations were first approved for clinical use by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1989 in the case of Lupron Depot. (1) Since then, the FDA has approved 24 other innovator drug products using PLGA as the main excipient to achieve sustained release. (2) PLGA-based formulations offer a therapeutic advantage in the treatment of diseases requiring long durations of drug exposure with sustained levels of therapeutic concentrations. (3−8) PLGA is biodegradable and biocompatible, so PLGA-based drug products were approved for parenteral use by regulatory authorities. Biodegradation of PLGA is driven by an initial water influx followed by pH-driven rate-controlled degradation (ester hydrolysis) into short-chain oligomers. Further degradation of oligomers results in the formation of free acid molecules, resulting in a further drop in the pH, which further increases the hydrolysis rate. This phenomenon is termed autocatalytic degradation. The time-dependent degradation of polymers results in an increase in the porosity of the polymeric matrix, leading to drug release. Consequently, PLGA formulations offer rate-controlled drug release predominantly by diffusion through the water-filled porous structure of the polymeric matrix, osmotic pumping, and erosion. (10) discussed that drug release from PLGA-based formulations is influenced by several physicochemical properties of the polymer (molecular weight, lactic acid (LA) to glycolic acid (GA) ratio, acid or ester end-capping, crystallinity), drug (chemical properties, drug loading, content uniformity), drug delivery system (size, porosity, density, and shape), in vitro (release medium composition, pH, temperature, stirring rate, osmolality), and in vivo conditions (immune response, sink conditions, enzymes, lipids). Drug release is influenced not only by the physicochemical properties of the polymer and drug but also by the processes employed in manufacturing. (9,10) For example, the hot melt extrusion method leads to less porous implants compared to implants produced by direct compression. Recent developments in the treatment of atherosclerosis have focused on the use of metallic stents to reduce restenosis after angioplasty. Antiproliferative agents, e.g., paclitaxel or sirolimus, and anti-inflammatory drugs, e.g., dexamethasone, have been used to generate drug eluting stents (DES) [1], [2], [3], [4]. Presently, drug release from stent coatings represents an area of great activity. Eventually the permanent presence of polymer may lead to complications such as inflammatory response and neointimal hyperplasia at the implant site of DES [5], [6]. It is therefore desirable to develop degradable coating to avoid these unfavorable effects. There are many degradable polymers but the most widely used come from the polyester family and include polylactic acid (PLA), polyglycolic acid (PGA) and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) copolymers [7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Drug release from PLGA-based drug delivery system is however complex [13]. PLGA matrices present a triphasic release profile: initial burst release from the surface, followed by a phase where the drug diffuses more slowly out of the bulk and then finally a final drug release due to bulk degradation. Poly(3-hydroxyalkanoate)s constitute another class of biodegradable and biocompatible polyesters, making them attractive for biomedical devices. PHAs are classified into several types according to their chain length: short chain length, scl-PHAs ([R]-hydroxyalkanoates of C3-C5) and medium chain length mcl-PHAs ([R]-hydroxyalkanoates of C6-C14). Many PHAs monomer structures have been reported [14], [15], [16]. To enhance hydrophilicity and degradability, tailor-made products have been prepared by chemical modification of functional substituents [17]. Thus, unsaturated groups of poly(3-hydroxyoctanoate-co-3-hydroxyundecenoate) PHO75U25 have been turned into carboxyl groups leading to a functionalized polyester noted PHO75COOH25 [18], [19], [20]. In fact, PHAs have a wide range of potential applications such as scaffolds in tissue engineering, matrix for long-term release of bioactive molecules, or implant materials [21], [22], [23]. A layer of these different PHAs containing drug (20% sirolimus) was deposited onto the metallic stent by a spray process. Mechanical performances of the coated stents were evaluated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) examinations. The rate of sirolimus release was studied to compare the influence of the nature of the polyesters on their ability to control drug release. To modulate the rate of drug release, bilayer coatings were proposed. Degradability of the coatings was also studied by gravimetry, SEM and size exclusion chromatography (SEC). Based solely on the provided context evidence, the drug release mechanism from a surface-eroding polyanhydride wafer is **controlled surface erosion**. Here's the mechanistic explanation:

1.  **Surface Erosion Dominates:** Unlike bulk-eroding polymers (e.g., polyesters like PLA, PLGA, PCL), polyanhydrides degrade primarily via surface erosion. This means hydrolytic degradation (cleavage of anhydride bonds) occurs predominantly at the polymer-water interface, with the rate of water penetration into the polymer matrix being slower than the rate of bond cleavage at the surface [1], [4].
2.  **Layer-by-Layer Degradation:** As a result, the polymer erodes layer-by-layer from the surface inwards [4], [5], [6].
3.  **Drug Release Mechanism:** The drug embedded within the polymer matrix is released as the surface layer containing it erodes away. The rate of drug release is therefore directly governed by, and proportional to, the rate of polymer surface erosion [1], [2], [4], [5], [6]. This contrasts with diffusion-controlled release from stable polymers or the complex triphasic release (initial burst, diffusion, bulk erosion) typical of polyesters like PLGA [4], [11], [12].
4.  **Factors Influencing Erosion/Release:** The polymer erosion rate (and thus drug release rate) is controlled by factors such as polymer structure (e.g., aliphatic vs aromatic monomers), crystallinity, and the presence of modifiers (e.g., glycolate esters, PEG chains which increase hydrophilicity) [1], [5], [6]. The size and design of the device also influence the release [1].
